nodes.name: The five great court epics (pañca-mahākāvya)
nodes.summary: The conventional canon of five Sanskrit mahākāvyas — Kālidāsa’s Raghuvaṃśa and Kumārasambhava, Bhāravi’s Kirātārjunīya, Māgha’s Śiśupālavadha and Śrīharṣa’s Naiṣadhīyacarita. Four of the five rework episodes of the epics.
nodes.details: The grouping is a later pedagogical canon: these five poems, with Mallinātha’s commentaries, became the standard school texts of kāvya. The list is not fixed in any early source, and some lists substitute other poems (e.g. the Bhaṭṭikāvya).

nodes.name: Raghuvaṃśa
nodes.summary: Kālidāsa’s mahākāvya in nineteen cantos on the kings of the solar line, from Dilīpa and Raghu through Aja and Daśaratha to Rāma (cantos 10–15), his descendants and the dissolute Agnivarṇa.
nodes.details:
Cantos 1–2: Dilīpa serves Vasiṣṭha’s cow Nandinī to obtain a son. 3–4: Raghu’s birth and conquest of the quarters. 5–8: Aja wins Indumatī at her svayaṃvara; her sudden death and his lament. 9: Daśaratha, his hunting and the killing of the ascetic’s son. 10–15: the Rāma story, ending with Sītā’s entry into the earth (15.81–84) and Rāma’s departure. 16–19: Kuśa and his successors down to Agnivarṇa.

At 15.63–64 Kuśa and Lava sing “the Rāmāyaṇa first composed by Prācetasa” — “Rāma’s story, Vālmīki’s work” — so the poem names its Rāma source.

dates.label: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)
dates.basis: date of Kālidāsa; named in the Aihole inscription of 634/635 CE

nodes.name: Indumatī
nodes.summary: Princess of Vidarbha, sister of king Bhoja, who chooses Aja at her svayaṃvara (Raghuvaṃśa 6) and dies when a celestial garland falls on her breast (canto 8).

earliestText.label: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

nodes.name: Sudakṣiṇā
nodes.summary: Queen of Dilīpa and mother of Raghu in the Raghuvaṃśa; with Dilīpa she serves the cow Nandinī to obtain a son.

sources.quote: nidānam ikṣvākukulasya saṃtateḥ sudakṣiṇā daurhṛdalakṣaṇaṃ dadhau

earliestText.label: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

nodes.name: Nandinī / Śabalā (Vasiṣṭha’s cow)
nodes.summary: The wish-granting cow of Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage, daughter of Surabhi. Her seizure by King Viśvāmitra starts the sages’ feud — Vālmīki calls her Śabalā, the Mahābhārata Nandinī — and she produces the armies that defeat the king; in Raghuvaṃśa 1–2 King Dilīpa tends her and offers his life to save her from a lion.
nodes.details: Distinct from deity:nandin (Śiva’s bull). Merged in verification round 2 with the Purāṇa agent’s record char:vasishtha-cow (the Viśvāmitra feud); Vālmīki’s Śabalā and the Mahābhārata/Raghuvaṃśa Nandinī are one tradition figure under text-specific names.

sources.quote: anindyā nandinī nāma dhenur āvavṛte vanāt

nodes.name: Agnivarṇa
nodes.summary: The last king of the Raghuvaṃśa, a pleasure-loving ruler who dies of consumption; his pregnant queen rules as regent at the poem’s end (canto 19).

sources.quote: rājñī rājyaṃ vidhivad aśiṣad bhartur avyāhatājñā

earliestText.label: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

nodes.name: Dilīpa and the cow Nandinī
nodes.summary: The childless king Dilīpa and queen Sudakṣiṇā tend Vasiṣṭha’s cow Nandinī; when a lion (Śiva’s servant) seizes her, Dilīpa offers his own body, and the cow grants him a son, Raghu (Raghuvaṃśa 1–2).

earliestText.label: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

nodes.name: Aja and Indumatī
nodes.summary: Aja wins Indumatī at her svayaṃvara among many kings (Raghuvaṃśa 6–7); years later she dies when a celestial garland falls on her, and Aja’s grief (8) leads to his death.

earliestText.label: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

nodes.name: Daśaratha kills the ascetic’s son
nodes.summary: Hunting by night, the young Daśaratha shoots at the sound of a pitcher being filled, thinking it an elephant, and kills the only son of a blind ascetic couple; the dying father curses him to die of grief for a son (later tradition names the boy Śravaṇa).
nodes.details: In the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (CE 2.57–58) the dying Daśaratha recalls the deed to Kausalyā; the boy is unnamed. Kālidāsa (Raghuvaṃśa 9.72–81) moves it to the hunting canto and places it on the river Tamasā; the name Śravaṇa (Śravaṇa Kumāra) belongs to later retellings.

sources.quote: athāndhakāre tv aśrauṣaṃ jale kumbhasya paryataḥ

nodes.name: Kumārasambhava
nodes.summary: Kālidāsa’s mahākāvya on the courtship and marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī — Pārvatī’s birth to Himālaya, the gods’ plight under the demon Tāraka, Kāma’s incineration by Śiva’s third eye, Pārvatī’s penance and the wedding; cantos 9–17 (Kumāra’s birth and Tāraka’s death) are usually held to be a later continuation.
nodes.details: The GRETIL text has cantos 1–8 (the portion commented on by Mallinātha). Canto 2 (Tāraka’s oppression, Ks 2.1, 2.32); 3 (Kāma reduced to ashes, 3.72); 4 (Rati’s lament); 5 (Pārvatī’s austerities); 6–7 (betrothal and wedding); 8 (the couple’s love). Ānandavardhana and later critics criticised canto 8’s depiction of the divine parents’ love-making.

dates.label: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)
by c. 800 CE (Vāmana quotes Kumārasaṃbhava 1.1)
dates.basis: quotation in Vāmana’s Kāvyālaṃkārasūtravṛtti; Vāmana is placed at Jayāpīḍa’s court in Kashmir (late 8th c.)

sources.quote: asty uttarasyāṃ diśi devatātmā himālayo nāma nagādhirājaḥ

nodes.name: Abhijñānaśākuntalam
nodes.summary: Kālidāsa’s seven-act nāṭaka on king Duḥṣanta (Duṣyanta) and Śakuntalā. It reworks the Mahābhārata’s Śakuntalopākhyāna (MBh 1.62–69) by adding the sage Durvāsas’s curse, which makes the king forget her, and the recognition-ring (abhijñāna) whose loss and recovery drive the plot.
nodes.details:
Acts 1–3: the meeting in Kaṇva’s hermitage and the gāndharva union. Act 4: Durvāsas, slighted by the distracted Śakuntalā, curses her to be forgotten until the king sees a token (4.1a); she leaves for the court. Act 5: the king does not recognise her; the ring is missing (5.21a). Act 6: a fisherman finds the ring in a fish, memory returns. Act 7: reunion at Mārīca’s (Kaśyapa’s) hermitage; their son Sarvadamana will be called Bharata (7.33).

The text circulates in several recensions (Bengali, Devanāgarī, Kashmiri, South Indian); the GRETIL text follows M. R. Kale’s edition.

dates.label: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

nodes.name: Durvāsas
nodes.summary: An irascible sage, son of Atri, whose curses and boons drive several stories: in the Mahābhārata he gives Kuntī the mantra by which she summons gods; in Kālidāsa’s Śākuntala his curse makes Duḥṣanta forget Śakuntalā; in Purāṇic tellings his curse on Indra leads to the churning of the ocean.
nodes.details: Bāṇa’s Harṣacarita (opening prose) calls him “son of Atri, brother of the Moon”. The Purāṇic curse on Indra is recorded by the purana agent at psg:vip-1-9.

sources.quote: munir atres tanayas tārā-pater bhratā nāmnā durvāsā

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Durvāsas’s curse and Śakuntalā’s ring
nodes.summary: Kālidāsa’s addition to the Śakuntalā story: lost in thought of the king, Śakuntalā fails to greet Durvāsas, who curses her to be forgotten until her lover sees a token; the king’s signet ring, lost while bathing, is found by a fisherman and restores his memory.
nodes.details: Neither the curse nor the ring occurs in the Mahābhārata’s Śakuntalopākhyāna, where Duḥṣanta knowingly denies Śakuntalā and accepts her only after a voice from the sky (MBh (CE) 1.68.19; 1.69.28–29, 40–41). See cmp:shakuntala-ring-curse.

earliestText.label: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

nodes.name: Meghadūta
nodes.summary: Kālidāsa’s lyric “messenger poem”: an exiled yakṣa at Rāmagiri sends a monsoon cloud with a message to his wife in Alakā. The opening places him among hermitages “whose waters are hallowed by the bathing of Janaka’s daughter”, and the wife is to greet the cloud as Maithilī greeted the son of the Wind.
nodes.details: The poem is the model for the whole later genre of saṃdeśa/dūta-kāvya. Its Rāmāyaṇa allusions — Sītā’s bathing places at Rāmagiri (v. 1), the hill marked by Raghupati’s footprints (v. 12), and the cloud likened to Hanumān bringing Rāma’s message to Sītā (v. 97) — frame the yakṣa’s separation as a reprise of Rāma’s. Rāmagiri is often identified with Ramtek near Nagpur, an identification argued, not stated, by the text.

dates.label: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

sources.quote: yakṣaś cakre janakatanayāsnānapuṇyodakeṣu snigdhacchāyātaruṣu vasatiṃ rāmagiryāśrameṣu

nodes.name: The yakṣa of the Meghadūta
nodes.summary: The unnamed yakṣa, a servant of Kubera exiled for a year for neglecting his duty, who speaks the Meghadūta’s message to the cloud.

earliestText.label: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

nodes.name: Āyus (son of Purūravas)
nodes.summary: Son of Purūravas and Urvaśī; in Kālidāsa’s Vikramorvaśīya the boy, brought up secretly in a hermitage, is revealed to his father in the last act. In the Purāṇic genealogies he continues the Lunar line through his son Nahuṣa.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Bhāsa
nodes.summary: A Sanskrit dramatist praised by Bāṇa (Harṣacarita, introductory verse 15) for plays “begun by the sūtradhāra”. Thirteen anonymous plays found in Kerala and published by T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī from 1912 are attributed to him — an attribution that remains disputed.
nodes.details: Bhāsa is named as a celebrated predecessor by Kālidāsa (prologue of the Mālavikāgnimitra), by Bāṇa and by later critics, who quote a Svapnavāsavadatta under his name. Nothing reliable is known of his life. Estimates of his floruit range from the 4th c. BCE to the 4th c. CE; if the Trivandrum plays are his, a date in the early centuries CE is commonly proposed.

dates.label: before Kālidāsa; proposals range from c. 4th c. BCE to c. 4th c. CE
dates.basis: literary references (Kālidāsa, Bāṇa); language and dramaturgy of the attributed plays

dates.label: named by Bāṇa, Harṣacarita intro v. 15 (c. 640 CE)
dates.basis: Bāṇa wrote at the court of Harṣa (r. 606–647)

sources.quote: sūtra-dhāra-kṛtârambhair nāṭakair bahu-bhūmikaiḥ / sa-patākair yaśo lebhe bhāso deva-kulair iva

nodes.name: The Trivandrum plays (“Bhāsa-nāṭaka-cakra”)
nodes.summary: Thirteen anonymous Sanskrit plays preserved in Kerala manuscripts and the Kūṭiyāṭṭam performance tradition, published by T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī in the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series (1912–15) as the works of Bhāsa. Seven retell the Mahābhārata or the Kṛṣṇa story, two the Rāmāyaṇa.
nodes.details: Mahābhārata plays: Dūtavākya, Dūtaghaṭotkaca, Karṇabhāra, Ūrubhaṅga, Madhyamavyāyoga, Pañcarātra; Kṛṣṇa play: Bālacarita; Rāmāyaṇa plays: Pratimānāṭaka, Abhiṣekanāṭaka; Udayana plays: Svapnavāsavadatta, Pratijñāyaugandharāyaṇa; others: Avimāraka, Cārudatta. Shared features — the opening “nāndyante tataḥ praviśati sūtradhāraḥ”, the absence of the author’s name in the prologue, a closing benediction (bharatavākya) for a king called rājasiṃha — underlie the claim of common authorship.

dates.label: 1912–1915 (Trivandrum Sanskrit Series)
dates.basis: publication dates of the editio princeps

nodes.name: The Trivandrum plays are the works of Bhāsa
nodes.summary: T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī’s thesis (1912) that the thirteen Kerala plays are the lost dramas of Bhāsa praised by Kālidāsa and Bāṇa. Many scholars accept a common origin for the corpus but doubt or deny that it is Bhāsa’s; a widely held alternative treats the plays as Kerala acting versions (perhaps abridged) prepared for Cākyār performance.
nodes.details: For: the plays open with the sūtradhāra entering after the nāndī, as Bāṇa says of Bhāsa’s plays; a Svapnavāsavadatta is ascribed to Bhāsa by later critics and the Trivandrum play of that name fits several citations; the corpus shares style and conventions. Against: several verses quoted from Bhāsa by later authorities are absent from the Trivandrum texts; the same stage conventions occur in other Kerala manuscripts of plays by known later authors; Tieken (1993) argues the corpus is a Kerala product shaped by Kūṭiyāṭṭam. The dataset therefore links the plays to Bhāsa with ATTRIBUTED_TO, never COMPOSED_BY.
openQuestions: Does the Kerala transmission preserve abridged stage versions of older plays, or new compositions?
Which citations of “Bhāsa” in later critics match the Trivandrum texts, and which do not?

nodes.name: Pratimānāṭaka
nodes.summary: A seven-act Rāma play attributed to Bhāsa, from Rāma’s exile to his coronation after Rāvaṇa’s death. Its eponymous invention is the statue-house (pratimā-gṛha) of the Ikṣvāku kings, where the returning Bharata learns of his father’s death by seeing Daśaratha’s statue.

dates.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

sources.quote: svargaṃ gatasya bhartur daśarathasya pratimā-gehaṃ draṣṭum

nodes.name: Abhiṣekanāṭaka
nodes.summary: A six-act Rāma play attributed to Bhāsa, from the killing of Vālin to Rāma’s consecration (abhiṣeka) after the war.

dates.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

sources.quote: sarva-vānarā^dhipatiṃ hema-mālinaṃ vālinaṃ hantuṃ samudyogaḥ pravartate

nodes.name: Dūtavākya
nodes.summary: A one-act play attributed to Bhāsa on Kṛṣṇa’s embassy to Duryodhana: Duryodhana insults him and tries to bind him; Kṛṣṇa reveals his cosmic form and summons his personified weapons, led by the discus Sudarśana.

dates.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Dūtaghaṭotkaca
nodes.summary: A one-act play attributed to Bhāsa set after Abhimanyu’s death: Ghaṭotkaca comes to the Kauravas as Kṛṣṇa’s envoy with a warning of Arjuna’s vengeance.

dates.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Karṇabhāra
nodes.summary: A one-act play attributed to Bhāsa: on the battlefield, with Śalya as his charioteer, Karṇa gives his natural armour and earrings to Indra disguised as a brahmin, and is sent the spear Vimalā in return.

dates.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Ūrubhaṅga
nodes.summary: A one-act play attributed to Bhāsa on Duryodhana’s death after Bhīma breaks his thighs. Unusually for Sanskrit drama, the hero dies on stage — repentant, reconciled, forbidding vengeance — while Balarāma rages and Aśvatthāman vows the night massacre.

dates.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Madhyamavyāyoga
nodes.summary: A one-act play attributed to Bhāsa: Ghaṭotkaca, sent by Hiḍimbā to find her a human meal, seizes the “middle” son of a brahmin family; Bhīma, the middle Pāṇḍava, offers himself instead, and father and son recognise each other.

dates.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Pañcarātra (Bhāsa)
nodes.summary: A three-act play attributed to Bhāsa: as his sacrificial fee Droṇa asks Duryodhana to give the Pāṇḍavas half the kingdom; Duryodhana agrees if they are found within five nights (pañcarātra), and the Virāṭa cattle-raid reveals them — an invented happy ending to the quarrel.

dates.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Bālacarita
nodes.summary: A five-act play attributed to Bhāsa on Kṛṣṇa’s childhood, from his birth in Kaṃsa’s prison through the exploits in the cowherd settlement to the killing of Kaṃsa.

dates.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Svapnavāsavadatta
nodes.summary: The best-known of the Trivandrum plays, on king Udayana of Vatsa and his queen Vāsavadattā, who is thought dead; a play of this name is ascribed to Bhāsa by later critics, which anchors the attribution of the whole corpus.

dates.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Durjaya (son of Duryodhana, in the Ūrubhaṅga)
nodes.summary: Duryodhana’s young son in Bhāsa’s Ūrubhaṅga, who wants to sit on his dying father’s lap; Duryodhana tells him to serve the Pāṇḍavas, obey Kuntī and honour Draupadī and Subhadrā as mothers.
nodes.details: The Mahābhārata critical text names Duryodhana’s son Lakṣmaṇa; the name Durjaya and the scene are the play’s. Whether the play means the same son is not stated.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Bharata in the statue-house (Pratimānāṭaka)
nodes.summary: Bhāsa’s invention in the Pratimānāṭaka: returning from his uncle’s house, Bharata enters the shrine where statues of the dead Ikṣvāku kings stand, sees a new statue of Daśaratha, and so learns of his father’s death.
nodes.details: In the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa Bharata learns of Daśaratha’s death from Kaikeyī on arriving in Ayodhyā (VR (CE) 2.66). The statue-house has been discussed as evidence for royal portrait statues (cf. the Kuṣāṇa devakula at Māṭ); the play does not establish such a practice.

sources.quote: svargaṃ gatasya bhartur daśarathasya pratimā-gehaṃ draṣṭum

nodes.limits: A literary invention; it does not document an actual Ikṣvāku or Kosalan statue shrine.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Bhīma meets Ghaṭotkaca (Madhyamavyāyoga)
nodes.summary: The plot of the Madhyamavyāyoga: Ghaṭotkaca, hunting a human for his mother Hiḍimbā, demands the “middle” son of a brahmin; Bhīma, the middle Pāṇḍava, goes in his place, fights him, and the two recognise each other as father and son.
nodes.limits: Not in the Mahābhārata; a dramatist’s invention built on MBh 1.143.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Karṇa gives away his armour and earrings
nodes.summary: Indra, disguised as a brahmin, begs Karṇa for the armour and earrings he was born with; Karṇa, warned beforehand by the Sun, cuts them from his body and in the Mahābhārata obtains in exchange Indra’s unfailing spear, good for one kill.
nodes.details: MBh (CE) 3.284–294 (the Kuṇḍalāharaṇa): Sūrya warns Karṇa in a dream (3.284), Indra comes as a brahmin (3.294), Karṇa bargains for the spear (3.294.20–23) and flays off the armour (3.294.38). The spear is later spent on Ghaṭotkaca (7.154). In Bhāsa’s Karṇabhāra the gift takes place on the battlefield, Karṇa asks nothing, and Indra sends the spear “Vimalā” afterwards through a messenger (see cmp:karna-armour-gift).

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Bhavabhūti
nodes.summary: Sanskrit dramatist of the early 8th century, author of the Mahāvīracarita and Uttararāmacarita (Rāma plays) and the Mālatīmādhava. Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī (4.144) places him with Vākpatirāja at the court of Yaśovarman of Kānyakubja.
nodes.details: His prologues call him Śrīkaṇṭha, of the Udumbara brahmins of Padmapura in Vidarbha, a pupil of Jñānanidhi. Vāmana’s Kāvyālaṃkārasūtravṛtti (late 8th c.) quotes Uttararāmacarita 1.39 (“iyaṃ gehe lakṣmīḥ …”), giving a terminus ante quem; Yaśovarman’s defeat by Lalitāditya of Kashmir is usually placed in the 730s–740s.

dates.label: early 8th c. CE
dates.basis: Kalhaṇa’s synchronism with Yaśovarman of Kānyakubja; quoted by Vāmana

nodes.name: Mahāvīracarita
nodes.summary: Bhavabhūti’s seven-act play on Rāma’s early career, from Viśvāmitra’s hermitage and the breaking of Śiva’s bow to the war and coronation. Its chief innovation is to make Rāvaṇa’s minister Mālyavat the schemer behind events Vālmīki leaves to chance or to Kaikeyī, such as Śūrpaṇakhā’s disguise as Mantharā.
nodes.details: The play as transmitted may not be wholly Bhavabhūti’s: the last part (from act 5.46 or so) exists in different completions in the manuscripts, one ascribed to Subrahmaṇya and one to Vināyaka.

nodes.name: Uttararāmacarita
nodes.summary: Bhavabhūti’s seven-act play on “Rāma’s later life”: the banishment of the pregnant Sītā, Rāma’s grief on revisiting Pañcavaṭī where the invisible Sītā watches him (act 3), the meeting with his sons, and a final play-within-a-play staged by Vālmīki after which Sītā is restored and reunited with Rāma — reversing Vālmīki’s ending.
nodes.details: Bhavabhūti makes karuṇa (pathos) the play’s dominant sentiment. In act 7 the gods, Gaṅgā and the Earth bring Sītā back before the assembled citizens, who accept her; Rāma and Sītā are reunited with Lava and Kuśa. The Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (CE 7.88) instead has Sītā swear by her purity and enter the earth. See cmp:sita-fate-uttararamacarita.

nodes.name: Candraketu (son of Lakṣmaṇa)
nodes.summary: Son of Lakṣmaṇa and Ūrmilā; in the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (CE 7.92) Rāma installs him and his brother Aṅgada as kings in the west and north. In Bhavabhūti’s Uttararāmacarita he guards the sacrificial horse and fights his cousin Lava.

nodes.name: Mālyavat (rākṣasa)
nodes.summary: Eldest son of the rākṣasa Sukeśa and brother of Sumālin, Rāvaṇa’s maternal grandfather (VR (CE) 7.5–6). Bhavabhūti’s Mahāvīracarita makes him Rāvaṇa’s scheming minister who engineers the plot against Rāma.

sources.quote: mālyavantaṃ sumāliṃ ca māliṃ ca balināṃ varam

nodes.name: Kirātārjunīya
nodes.summary: Bhāravi’s mahākāvya in eighteen cantos expanding a short episode of the Āraṇyakaparvan: urged by Draupadī and Bhīma and advised by Vyāsa, Arjuna performs austerities on Mount Indrakīla, resists the apsarases sent to test him, fights Śiva disguised as a mountain hunter over a boar, and receives the Pāśupata weapon.
nodes.details: Cantos 1–3: the forest-dweller’s report, Draupadī’s (1.27ff) and Bhīma’s (2) speeches, Vyāsa’s counsel (3.10). 4–6: autumn and the journey to the Himālaya and Indrakīla (7.17). 7–10: the apsarases’ seduction attempt. 11: Indra visits as an old ascetic (11.1, 11.46). 12–13: Śiva as leader of a kirāta army; the boar (12.37–42, 13.23). 14–17: the battle. 18: Arjuna’s hymn to Śiva and the gift of the weapon (18.44); the guardians of the quarters add theirs (18.46). Canto 15 is a showpiece of citra (verbal-pattern) verses.

dates.label: 6th c. CE
dates.basis: Bhāravi named in the Aihole inscription (634/635 CE)

sources.quote: sa varṇiliṅgī viditaḥ samāyayau yudhiṣṭhiraṃ dvaitavane vanecaraḥ

nodes.name: Mūka (the boar-demon)
nodes.summary: A son of Diti who takes the form of a boar to kill Arjuna at his austerities and is shot simultaneously by Arjuna and Śiva-as-kirāta, setting off their quarrel (MBh (CE) 3.40.7–16).
nodes.details: Bhāravi leaves the demon unnamed: an asura in boar-guise (varāhamāyā, Kirātārjunīya 12.37).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Māgha
nodes.summary: Sanskrit poet of western India, author of the Śiśupālavadha. In the poem’s closing verses on his family (not in the GRETIL text) he names his grandfather Suprabhadeva as minister of a king Varmalāta, who is usually identified with the Varmalāta of a Vasantgaḍh inscription of 625 CE, placing Māgha in the later 7th or 8th century.

dates.label: late 7th–8th c. CE
dates.basis: grandfather the minister of Varmalāta (inscription of 625 CE)

nodes.name: Śiśupālavadha
nodes.summary: Māgha’s mahākāvya in twenty cantos: Nārada asks Kṛṣṇa to kill Śiśupāla; Kṛṣṇa, torn between that duty and Yudhiṣṭhira’s invitation to the rājasūya, takes counsel with Balarāma and Uddhava, journeys to Indraprastha, and at the sacrifice beheads the insulting king of Cedi, whose radiance enters Kṛṣṇa’s body.
nodes.details: The poem was composed in emulation of Bhāravi’s Kirātārjunīya (both begin with the word śrī). Cantos 4–13 are descriptive set pieces (Mount Raivataka, seasons, water-sports, the march); 14 the rājasūya; 15 Śiśupāla’s protest at the honour given to Kṛṣṇa; 16–20 the embassy, battle and killing. 20.79: the light from Caidya’s body enters Upendra’s.

nodes.name: Bhaṭṭi
nodes.summary: Author of the Rāvaṇavadha (Bhaṭṭikāvya), a Rāma poem that doubles as a textbook of Pāṇini’s grammar. Its last verse says it was composed at Valabhī in the realm of king Śrīdharasena, one of the Maitraka kings of that name (6th–7th c.).

dates.label: c. 6th–7th c. CE (reign of a Maitraka Śrīdharasena at Valabhī)
dates.basis: author’s own statement of place and patron (Bhk 22.35); four Maitraka kings bore the name

nodes.name: Śrīharṣa
nodes.summary: Twelfth-century poet and philosopher, author of the Naiṣadhīyacarita and of the Advaita dialectical treatise Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya. The colophon verses of his poem name his parents Śrīhīra and Māmalladevī; tradition places him at the Gāhaḍavāla court of Kānyakubja.
nodes.details: Distinct from King Harṣa (Harṣavardhana), author of the Ratnāvalī and Nāgānanda.

nodes.name: Naiṣadhīyacarita
nodes.summary: Śrīharṣa’s mahākāvya in twenty-two cantos on Nala and Damayantī, the last and most elaborate of the five classical mahākāvyas. It expands the first part of the Mahābhārata’s Nala story — the golden goose as go-between, the gods’ courtship, the svayaṃvara at which four gods take Nala’s form, and the marriage — and ends before Nala’s fall.

nodes.name: Murāri
nodes.summary: Sanskrit dramatist, author of the Anargharāghava; he names his parents as Vardhamānaka and Tantumatī and is placed in the 9th–10th centuries (before the 12th-century Maṅkha, who praises him).

nodes.name: Anargharāghava
nodes.summary: Murāri’s seven-act Rāma play, from Viśvāmitra’s request for Rāma to the return to Ayodhyā; celebrated by later critics for its learned, ornate style rather than its stagecraft.

nodes.name: Rājaśekhara
nodes.summary: Sanskrit and Prakrit poet-critic (c. 880–920), teacher of the Gurjara-Pratihāra king Mahendrapāla I and poet at the court of Mahīpāla; author of the Bālarāmāyaṇa, Bālabhārata, the Prakrit Karpūramañjarī, the Viddhaśālabhañjikā and the Kāvyamīmāṃsā.

dates.label: c. 880–920 CE
dates.basis: synchronism with Pratihāra kings Mahendrapāla I and Mahīpāla named in his prologues

nodes.name: Bālarāmāyaṇa (Rājaśekhara)
nodes.summary: Rājaśekhara’s ten-act Rāma play — among the longest Sanskrit dramas — in which Rāvaṇa appears as a rejected suitor at Sītā’s svayaṃvara, giving the war a romantic motive.

nodes.name: Bālabhārata (Pracaṇḍapāṇḍava)
nodes.summary: Rājaśekhara’s unfinished Mahābhārata play, of which two acts survive (Draupadī’s svayaṃvara and the dice game).

nodes.name: Kṣemendra
nodes.summary: Kashmiri polymath of the 11th century, son of Prakāśendra and pupil of Abhinavagupta, who abridged the great narrative works into “mañjarīs” (Rāmāyaṇamañjarī, Bhāratamañjarī, Bṛhatkathāmañjarī) and wrote the Daśāvatāracarita, satires and works on poetics. His Bhāratamañjarī colophon calls him “Vyāsadāsa”.

dates.label: c. 1040–1070 CE (11th c.)
dates.basis: dated colophons (Daśāvatāracarita, Samayamātṛkā) in the reigns of Ananta and Kalaśa of Kashmir

nodes.name: Bhāratamañjarī
nodes.summary: Kṣemendra’s verse abridgement of the whole Mahābhārata, parvan by parvan, ending with the Harivaṃśa section and a hymn to Vyāsa; about 10,000 verses.
nodes.details: Because Kṣemendra follows his Kashmiri Mahābhārata closely, the Bhāratamañjarī is a witness to the 11th-century Kashmiri (Śāradā) version of the epic; the BORI editors used it in establishing the critical text.

dates.label: c. 1037 CE (often cited); 11th c.
dates.basis: colophon and the author’s other dated works

nodes.name: Rāmāyaṇamañjarī
nodes.summary: Kṣemendra’s verse abridgement of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, including the Uttarakāṇḍa; like the Bhāratamañjarī it reflects the Kashmiri (north-western) version of its source.

nodes.name: Daśāvatāracarita
nodes.summary: Kṣemendra’s poem on the ten avatāras of Viṣṇu, one of the earliest datable literary lists to include the Buddha among them; its colophon dates it to 1066 CE.

dates.label: 1066 CE
dates.basis: colophon date as reported by Warder; not checked against an edition here

nodes.name: Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa (author of the Veṇīsaṃhāra)
nodes.summary: Dramatist named in the prologue of the Veṇīsaṃhāra (“the work of the poet Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa, whose emblem is the lion”). Bengali genealogical tradition makes him one of five brahmins brought from Kānyakubja by king Ādiśūra; he is generally placed before c. 800 CE.
nodes.details: Not the Kashmiri Śaiva hymnist Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa, author of the Stavacintāmaṇi.

nodes.name: Veṇīsaṃhāra
nodes.summary: Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa’s six-act play on the Mahābhārata war, built on Bhīma’s vow to bind Draupadī’s braid — loosened when Duḥśāsana dragged her by the hair — with hands wet with Duryodhana’s blood; the play ends with Bhīma binding the braid.
nodes.details: Act 1: Bhīma’s vow (1.21). Act 2: Duryodhana and queen Bhānumatī. Act 3: Droṇa’s death and Karṇa’s quarrel with Aśvatthāman. Acts 4–5: Duḥśāsana and Karṇa killed; Duryodhana before the duel. Act 6: false news of Bhīma’s death, the rākṣasa Cārvāka’s ruse, Bhīma’s return, and the binding of the braid. The play was a favourite source of examples for the dramaturgical theorists (e.g. the Daśarūpaka).

sources.quote: styānāvanaddhaghanaśoṇitaśoṇapāṇi- ē̃ ruttaṃsayiṣyati kacāṃstava devi bhīmaḥ
kṛṣṇāyāḥ keśapāśaḥ kupitayamasakho dhūmaketuḥ kurūṇāṃ ē̃ so 'yaṃ baddhaḥ

nodes.name: Bhānumatī (wife of Duryodhana)
nodes.summary: Duryodhana’s queen as named in Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa’s Veṇīsaṃhāra, where in act 2 she has an ill-omened dream and performs rites for her husband’s safety. The Mahābhārata critical text does not name Duryodhana’s wife.
nodes.limits: Her name is attested here from the drama; the dataset does not claim that the CE names her.

nodes.name: The binding of Draupadī’s braid
nodes.summary: Draupadī leaves her hair unbound after Duḥśāsana drags her by it in the assembly; Bhīma vows to bind it again with hands red with Duryodhana’s blood, and does so after the war — the plot-frame of the Veṇīsaṃhāra.
nodes.details: The Mahābhārata critical text has Bhīma’s vows to drink Duḥśāsana’s blood and break Duryodhana’s thigh (2.61.45; 2.63.14) and Draupadī showing Kṛṣṇa her hair seized by Duḥśāsana (5.80.36); the braid-binding vow and its fulfilment are the drama’s.
nodes.limits: A dramatic elaboration, not a CE episode.

nodes.name: Kumāradāsa
nodes.summary: Author of the Sanskrit mahākāvya Jānakīharaṇa. Sri Lankan tradition identifies him with King Kumāradhātusena of Anurādhapura (6th c.), an identification many scholars treat with caution; he is usually placed in the 6th–8th centuries.

dates.label: c. 6th–8th c. CE
dates.basis: Sinhalese royal identification vs literary-historical arguments

nodes.name: Jānakīharaṇa
nodes.summary: Kumāradāsa’s mahākāvya on the Rāma story in the manner of Kālidāsa’s Raghuvaṃśa. For long known chiefly through a Sinhalese word-by-word gloss (sannaya) and anthology citations, its Sanskrit text was later recovered from South Indian manuscripts.

nodes.name: Hāla
nodes.summary: A Sātavāhana king to whom the Prakrit anthology Gāhā Sattasaī is traditionally attributed as compiler; the Purāṇic king-lists of the Āndhras include a Hāla.

dates.label: 1st c. CE (as placed in Purāṇic Sātavāhana lists)
dates.basis: Purāṇic king-lists; no dated inscription of Hāla

nodes.limits: No inscription of Hāla is known; the attribution of the anthology to him is traditional, and the collection grew over centuries.

nodes.name: Yogavāsiṣṭha
nodes.summary: A vast philosophical dialogue (about 29,000 verses in the vulgate) in which the sage Vasiṣṭha instructs the despondent young Rāma in a non-dualist teaching through many illustrative tales; framed as part of the Rāmāyaṇa and traditionally attributed to Vālmīki.
nodes.details: The frame opens where Viśvāmitra asks Daśaratha for Rāma (cf. VR (CE) 1.18–20): Rāma’s dispassion is answered by Vasiṣṭha’s six books (Vairāgya, Mumukṣu, Utpatti, Sthiti, Upaśama, Nirvāṇa). Slaje has shown that the Yogavāsiṣṭha is a Vedāntic reworking of the Kashmiri Mokṣopāya (c. 10th c.).

dates.label: Mokṣopāya c. 10th c. (Kashmir); Yogavāsiṣṭha redaction c. 11th–14th c.

nodes.name: Hanumannāṭaka (Mahānāṭaka)
nodes.summary: A loosely dramatic Rāma play in verse, transmitted in two recensions — a western one of 14 acts arranged by Dāmodaramiśra and an eastern one of 9–10 acts by Madhusūdana. Legend says Hanumān himself composed it on rocks and threw it into the sea so as not to eclipse Vālmīki.

nodes.name: Jayadeva (author of the Prasannarāghava)
nodes.summary: Dramatist and rhetorician, author of the Prasannarāghava and the Candrāloka (poetics), usually placed in the 12th–13th centuries; distinct from Jayadeva of the Gītagovinda.

nodes.name: Prasannarāghava
nodes.summary: Jayadeva’s seven-act Rāma play, known for its lyrical verses (including river-personifications); later borrowed into vernacular Rāma literature, notably by Tulsīdās.

nodes.name: Dhīranāga (Diṅnāga)
nodes.summary: Author of the Kundamālā, a play on Sītā’s banishment; manuscripts name him Dhīranāga or Diṅnāga (not the Buddhist logician). His date is uncertain (proposals from the 5th to the 10th c.).

nodes.name: Kundamālā
nodes.summary: A six-act play on Rāma’s later life: the abandoned Sītā gives birth in Vālmīki’s hermitage; Rāma recognises her garland of kunda flowers floating on the river; the twins recite the Rāmāyaṇa; and, as in Bhavabhūti, the play ends with Sītā’s vindication and reunion.

nodes.name: Śaktibhadra
nodes.summary: Kerala dramatist, author of the Āścaryacūḍāmaṇi; tradition makes him a pupil of Śaṅkara, and he is usually placed in the 9th century.

nodes.name: Āścaryacūḍāmaṇi
nodes.summary: Śaktibhadra’s seven-act Rāma play from Kerala, from Śūrpaṇakhā’s mutilation to Sītā’s vindication; named after the “wonderful crest-jewel” and ring that protect the couple. Its acts are staple pieces of Kūṭiyāṭṭam (Śūrpaṇakhāṅkam, Aṅgulīyāṅkam).

nodes.name: Campū Rāmāyaṇa (Rāmāyaṇa Campū)
nodes.summary: A Rāma story in mixed prose and verse (campū), the first five kāṇḍas attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja and the Yuddhakāṇḍa supplied later by Lakṣmaṇasūri.

nodes.name: Trivikramabhaṭṭa
nodes.summary: Poet of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa court, author of the Nalacampū (Damayantīkathā), the earliest surviving Sanskrit campū; he composed the eulogy of the Bagumra (Nausari) copper plates of Indra III dated 915 CE.

dates.label: 915 CE (Bagumra plates of Indra III)
dates.basis: authorship of a dated copper-plate eulogy, as reported in literary histories

nodes.name: Nalacampū (Damayantīkathā)
nodes.summary: Trivikramabhaṭṭa’s campū on Nala and Damayantī, in seven ucchvāsas, unfinished — it breaks off before Nala’s misfortunes.

dates.label: early 10th c. CE
dates.basis: date of the author (915 CE plates)

nodes.name: Villiputtūrār
nodes.summary: Tamil poet, author of the Villi Pāratam, a Tamil Mahābhārata in about 4,350 viruttam verses; usually dated to the 14th century, under the patronage of a chief Varapati Āṭkoṇṭāṉ.

nodes.name: Villi Pāratam
nodes.summary: Villiputtūrār’s Tamil Mahābhārata, which ends with the eighteenth day of the war; it became the standard Tamil Bhāratam and a source for Terukkūttu and the Draupadī cult of Tamil Nadu.

nodes.name: Kāśīrāma Dāsa
nodes.summary: Bengali poet of the 16th–17th century whose Bengali Mahābhārata (the “Kāśīdāsī Mahābhārata”) became the standard Bengali version; by tradition he completed only the first parvans and relatives or successors completed the rest.

nodes.name: Kāśīdāsī Mahābhārata
nodes.summary: The Bengali verse Mahābhārata associated with Kāśīrāma Dāsa (16th–17th c.), widely read and recited in Bengal; often printed together with Kṛttibās’s Rāmāyaṇa as the two Bengali epics.

dates.label: late 16th–17th c. CE
dates.basis: date of the author and continuators

nodes.name: Anukramaṇīparvan (MBh 1.1)
nodes.summary: The table of contents: Ugraśravas arrives at Naimiṣa and outlines the epic, including Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s lament “yadāśrauṣam …”.
nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.34). The adhyāya range 1.1 was established by reading the opening and closing chapters in the GRETIL e-text of the critical edition, which does not carry the CE’s upaparvan headings; boundaries therefore rest on content.

nodes.name: Parvasaṃgrahaparvan (MBh 1.2)
nodes.summary: The summary of the parvans, which names the hundred upaparvans (1.2.34–70) and outlines the eighteen books.
nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.34). nodes.summary: Janamejaya and the dog’s curse; the stories of Āruṇi, Upamanyu, Veda and Uttaṅka, whose quest for the queen’s earrings motivates the snake sacrifice.

nodes.summary: Ugraśravas at Śaunaka’s sacrifice; the Bhārgava stories of Pulomā, Cyavana and Ruru.

nodes.name: Ādivaṃśāvataraṇaparvan (MBh 1.54–58)
nodes.summary: Vyāsa comes to Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice and Vaiśaṃpāyana begins the Bhārata with its summary and the origins of the dynasties.

nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.35). nodes.summary: The tournament of the princes, Karṇa’s challenge and the plot to burn the Pāṇḍavas in the house of lac at Vāraṇāvata, and their escape.

nodes.summary: At Ekacakrā Bhīma takes the brahmin family’s turn to feed the man-eater Baka and kills him.

nodes.summary: On the way to Pañcāla Arjuna defeats the gandharva Citraratha, who tells the stories of Tapatī, Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra and urges them to take a priest.

nodes.summary: Draupadī’s svayaṃvara: Arjuna, disguised as a brahmin, strings the bow and hits the target, and the Pāṇḍavas fight off the angry kings.

nodes.summary: The debate over Draupadī’s marriage to five husbands, Vyāsa’s justifications (including the Five Indras, 1.189) and the wedding.

nodes.summary: The Kauravas learn the Pāṇḍavas survived; Vidura is sent to bring them back to Hāstinapura.

nodes.summary: The Pāṇḍavas receive half the kingdom at Khāṇḍavaprastha; Nārada tells the story of Sunda and Upasunda to warn them about sharing Draupadī.

nodes.summary: At the Raivataka festival Arjuna falls in love with Kṛṣṇa’s sister Subhadrā and carries her off with Kṛṣṇa’s consent.

nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.59). The adhyāya range 9.1–28 was established by reading the opening and closing chapters in the GRETIL e-text of the critical edition, which does not carry the CE’s upaparvan headings; boundaries therefore rest on content.

nodes.name: Hradapraveśanaparvan (MBh 9.29–30)
nodes.summary: Duryodhana hides in a lake; the Pāṇḍavas find him and goad him out.
nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.59). nodes.name: Gadāyuddhaparvan (MBh 9.31–64)
nodes.summary: The mace duel of Bhīma and Duryodhana (enclosing the Sārasvata section, 9.34–53), Balarāma’s anger and Duryodhana’s lament.
nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.59). nodes.name: Sārasvataparvan (MBh 9.34–53)
nodes.summary: Balarāma’s pilgrimage along the Sarasvatī, told as he arrives for the duel.
nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.60). nodes.name: Sauptikaparvan (the night raid) (MBh 10.1–9)
nodes.summary: Aśvatthāman, inspired by an owl killing crows, attacks the sleeping camp; Duryodhana dies on hearing the news (10.9).
nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.60). nodes.name: Aiṣīkaparvan (MBh 10.10–18)
nodes.summary: The pursuit of Aśvatthāman; his brahmaśiras weapon is diverted into Uttarā’s womb; Kṛṣṇa curses him and he gives up his crest-jewel.
nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.61). The adhyāya range 10.10–18 was established by reading the opening and closing chapters in the GRETIL e-text of the critical edition, which does not carry the CE’s upaparvan headings; boundaries therefore rest on content.

nodes.name: Jalapradānikaparvan (MBh 11.1–8)
nodes.summary: Vidura and Vyāsa console Dhṛtarāṣṭra in his grief.
nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.61). nodes.name: Strīparvan (the laments) (MBh 11.9–25)
nodes.summary: The women go to the battlefield; Dhṛtarāṣṭra crushes the iron Bhīma; Gāndhārī’s lament over the dead (11.16–25) ends in her curse on Kṛṣṇa.
nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.61). The adhyāya range 11.9–25 was established by reading the opening and closing chapters in the GRETIL e-text of the critical edition, which does not carry the CE’s upaparvan headings; boundaries therefore rest on content.

nodes.name: Śrāddhaparvan (MBh 11.26–27)
nodes.summary: The funeral rites; Kuntī reveals that Karṇa was her son.
nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.62). nodes.name: Āśramavāsaparvan (MBh 15.1–35)
nodes.summary: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī, Kuntī, Vidura and Saṃjaya retire to the forest; Vidura’s death.
nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.67). nodes.name: Putradarśanaparvan (MBh 15.36–44)
nodes.summary: Vyāsa makes the dead warriors rise from the Gaṅgā for one night (15.40).
nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.67). nodes.name: Nāradāgamanaparvan (MBh 15.45–47)
nodes.summary: Nārada reports that Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī and Kuntī died in a forest fire.
nodes.details: One of the hundred upaparvans named in the Parvasaṃgraha (MBh (CE) 1.2.34–70; this one at 1.2.67). nodes.name: Baka (rākṣasa of Ekacakrā)
nodes.summary: A man-eating rākṣasa who exacts a daily tribute of food and a human from the town of Ekacakrā until Bhīma, taking the brahmin family’s turn, kills him (MBh (CE) 1.145–152).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kirmīra
nodes.summary: A rākṣasa, brother of Baka, who bars the exiled Pāṇḍavas’ way into the Kāmyaka forest and is killed by Bhīma (MBh (CE) 3.12).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Jaṭāsura
nodes.summary: A rākṣasa who, disguised as a brahmin, carries off Yudhiṣṭhira, the twins and Draupadī, and is killed by Bhīma (MBh (CE) 3.154).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Citrasena (gandharva king)
nodes.summary: King of the gandharvas, friend of Arjuna (who learnt music and dance from him in Indra’s heaven); in the Ghoṣayātrā he captures Duryodhana and releases him at the Pāṇḍavas’ request.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Uttara (son of Virāṭa)
nodes.summary: Prince of the Matsyas, son of Virāṭa and brother of Uttarā. In the cattle raid he boasts, panics at the sight of the Kuru army and is made charioteer by Bṛhannaḍā (Arjuna), who routs the Kurus; he dies in the war.
nodes.details: Distinct from his sister Uttarā (char:uttara), wife of Abhimanyu. In the CE he is also called Bhūmiṃjaya/pṛthivīṃjaya (4.64.1).

sources.quote: tato rājñaḥ suto jyeṣṭhaḥ prāviśat pṛthivīṃjayaḥ

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Mudgala (the gleaner)
nodes.summary: A sage who lives by gleaning a measure of rice (vrīhidroṇa) every fortnight, feeds even Durvāsas without anger, and declines heaven when he learns its limits (MBh (CE) 3.245–247).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The killing of Baka
nodes.summary: At Ekacakrā, where the Pāṇḍavas live disguised as brahmins, Bhīma takes the place of their host’s family as the rākṣasa Baka’s victim and kills him.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Arjuna carries off Subhadrā
nodes.summary: During his exile Arjuna sees Kṛṣṇa’s sister Subhadrā at the Raivataka festival and, with Kṛṣṇa’s connivance, carries her off in his chariot; Kṛṣṇa then reconciles the angry Vṛṣṇis.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The killing of Kirmīra
nodes.summary: As the exiles enter the Kāmyaka forest the rākṣasa Kirmīra, Baka’s brother, blocks their way; Bhīma kills him.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Arjuna in Indra’s heaven
nodes.summary: After the Kirāta encounter the world-guardians give Arjuna their weapons and Indra’s charioteer Mātali takes him to Indra’s heaven, where he lives for five years learning weapons and, from Citrasena, music and dance.
nodes.details: Urvaśī’s advances and her curse that Arjuna live as a eunuch — which later explains his disguise as Bṛhannaḍā — are in the CE apparatus (Appendix 1, no. 6 after 3.45.8), not the constituted text.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The killing of Jaṭāsura
nodes.summary: A rākṣasa disguised as a brahmin carries off Yudhiṣṭhira, Nakula, Sahadeva and Draupadī while Bhīma is away hunting; Bhīma overtakes and kills him.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Nahuṣa the python
nodes.summary: A huge python seizes Bhīma in the Himālaya; it is king Nahuṣa, cursed by Agastya for his arrogance as Indra. Yudhiṣṭhira frees Bhīma, and Nahuṣa from the curse, by answering his questions about brahminhood and conduct.

sources.quote: nahuṣo nāma rājāham āsaṃ pūrvas tavānagha

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Duryodhana’s cattle expedition (Ghoṣayātrā)
nodes.summary: Duryodhana goes to Dvaitavana on the pretext of inspecting his cattle in order to flaunt his wealth before the exiles; the gandharva king Citrasena captures him, the Pāṇḍavas free him at Yudhiṣṭhira’s order, and the humiliated Duryodhana resolves to fast to death until the dānavas dissuade him.

sources.quote: duryodhanaṃ citraseno virathaṃ patitaṃ bhuvi abhidrutya mahābāhur jīvagrāham athāgrahīt

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Jayadratha abducts Draupadī
nodes.summary: While the Pāṇḍavas are out hunting, Jayadratha king of Sindhu carries Draupadī off from the Kāmyaka hermitage; the brothers overtake him, Bhīma spares his life at Yudhiṣṭhira’s word, and Jayadratha is shaved and released in humiliation.

sources.quote: sindhurājo jayadrathaḥ vimucya kṛṣṇāṃ saṃtrastaḥ palāyanaparo 'bhavat

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Mudgala and the measure of rice
nodes.summary: Vyāsa consoles Yudhiṣṭhira with the story of Mudgala, who lives on gleanings, feeds the testing Durvāsas, and refuses the heaven offered him because merit there is exhausted.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The cattle raid on Virāṭa (Gograhaṇa)
nodes.summary: At the end of the year of concealment the Trigartas and then the Kurus raid Virāṭa’s cattle; Arjuna, disguised as the eunuch dance-teacher Bṛhannaḍā, takes his weapons from the śamī tree, makes prince Uttara his charioteer and routs Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa and Duryodhana.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The marriage of Abhimanyu and Uttarā
nodes.summary: When the Pāṇḍavas reveal themselves, Virāṭa offers his daughter Uttarā to Arjuna, who accepts her as daughter-in-law for his son Abhimanyu, since he had been her teacher.

sources.quote: snuṣārtham uttarāṃ rājan pratigṛhṇāmi te sutām

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The vision of the cosmic form (Viśvarūpa-darśana)
nodes.summary: At Arjuna’s request Kṛṣṇa reveals his “sovereign form” (aiśvaraṃ rūpam), many-armed and many-faced, containing all beings and devouring the warriors of both armies; Arjuna, terrified, begs him to resume his familiar form (Bhagavad Gītā 11).
nodes.details: MBh (CE) 6.33 = Bhagavad Gītā chapter 11 (the CE’s 6.23–40 = Gītā 1–18). Kṛṣṇa also shows a cosmic form in the Kuru assembly during his embassy (5.129); Bhāsa’s Dūtavākya stages that scene.

sources.quote: darśayām āsa pārthāya paramaṃ rūpam aiśvaram

nodes.name: Arjuna’s vow and the killing of Jayadratha
nodes.summary: Blaming Jayadratha for blocking the Pāṇḍavas at the array where Abhimanyu died, Arjuna vows to kill him before the next sunset or enter the fire; after a day of fighting through the Kaurava host he beheads Jayadratha as the sun sets.

sources.quote: satyaṃ vaḥ pratijānāmi śvo 'smi hantā jayadratham

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Aśvatthāman’s Nārāyaṇa weapon
nodes.summary: Enraged at his father’s killing, Aśvatthāman looses the Nārāyaṇa weapon on the Pāṇḍava army; on Kṛṣṇa’s advice the warriors lay down their arms and dismount, and the weapon subsides — Bhīma, who resists, is dragged from his chariot by Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna.

sources.quote: prāduścakre tato drauṇir astraṃ nārāyaṇaṃ tadā

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Bhīma drinks Duḥśāsana’s blood
nodes.summary: On the seventeenth day Bhīma kills Duḥśāsana and drinks his blood, fulfilling the vow he made when Duḥśāsana dragged Draupadī into the assembly; onlookers flee crying that he is not human.

sources.quote: eṣa te rudhiraṃ kaṇṭhāt pibāmi puruṣādhama

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The death of Śalya
nodes.summary: On the eighteenth day the Kaurava commander Śalya, king of the Madras, is killed by Yudhiṣṭhira with a spear.

sources.quote: tāṃ sarvaśaktyā prahitāṃ sa śaktiṃ; yudhiṣṭhireṇāprativāryavīryām

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Balarāma’s pilgrimage on the Sarasvatī
nodes.summary: Unwilling to fight his kin, Balarāma spends the war on a pilgrimage up the Sarasvatī from the sea; the tīrthas he visits are described as he arrives at Kurukṣetra for the mace duel.

sources.quote: tīrthayātrāṃ yayau rājan kurūṇāṃ vaiśase tadā sarasvatīṃ pratisrotaḥ samudrād abhijagmivān

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Aśvatthāman’s brahmaśiras and Kṛṣṇa’s curse (Aiṣīka)
nodes.summary: Pursued after the night massacre, Aśvatthāman looses the brahmaśiras weapon from a blade of grass; Arjuna counters, and when Aśvatthāman cannot recall his weapon he turns it into the wombs of the Pāṇḍava women. Kṛṣṇa curses him to wander for three thousand years and promises to revive Uttarā’s child.

sources.quote: brahmaśiro nāma dahed yat pṛthivīm api

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The lament of the women (Strīvilāpa)
nodes.summary: After the war Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī and the Kuru women go to the battlefield; given divine sight, Gāndhārī describes to Kṛṣṇa the dead sons, husbands and brothers and the grieving widows, and ends by cursing him.

sources.quote: evam uktvā tu gāndhārī kurūṇām āvikartanam apaśyat
paśya mādhava putrān me śatasaṃkhyāñ jitaklamān

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The revival of Parikṣit
nodes.summary: Uttarā’s son is born dead, killed in the womb by Aśvatthāman’s weapon; Kṛṣṇa, keeping his promise, restores him to life, and the child is named Parikṣit.
nodes.details: Vaiśaṃpāyana addresses Janamejaya: “then your father regained life” (14.69.3).

sources.quote: tataḥ prāṇān punar lebhe pitā tava janeśvara

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Yudhiṣṭhira’s horse sacrifice
nodes.summary: To expiate the war Yudhiṣṭhira performs the aśvamedha: the horse wanders for a year guarded by Arjuna, who fights the Trigartas, Babhruvāhana and others; the sacrifice is completed at Hāstinapura, after which a half-golden mongoose belittles it.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s retirement and death in the forest fire
nodes.summary: Fifteen years after the war Dhṛtarāṣṭra retires to the forest with Gāndhārī, Kuntī, Vidura and Saṃjaya; two years later Nārada reports that the three elders died in a forest fire, which their own sacred fires had kindled.

sources.quote: dāvāgninā samāyukte sa ca rājā pitā tava

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The night of the risen dead (Putradarśana)
nodes.summary: At the elders’ forest hermitage Vyāsa, at Gāndhārī’s and Kuntī’s plea, makes the dead warriors of both sides rise from the Gaṅgā for one night, free of enmity, before returning to their worlds.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Arjuna fails against the Ābhīras
nodes.summary: After the destruction of the Yādavas Arjuna escorts the Vṛṣṇi women from Dvārakā, which the sea engulfs; on the way Ābhīra herdsmen attack, his weapons and strength fail him, and many women are carried off.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Yudhiṣṭhira in heaven and hell (Svargārohaṇa)
nodes.summary: Arriving in heaven Yudhiṣṭhira finds Duryodhana enthroned and his brothers absent; led to a hell where he hears their cries, he chooses to stay with them — and the hell vanishes, an illusion devised by Indra. Bathing in the heavenly Gaṅgā he takes a divine body, and the heroes return to their divine origins.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Hanumān meets Sītā in the Aśoka grove
nodes.summary: Searching Laṅkā, Hanumān finds Sītā guarded by rākṣasīs in Rāvaṇa’s aśoka grove, witnesses Rāvaṇa’s threats, then reveals himself, gives her Rāma’s signet ring and receives her crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi) as a token for Rāma.

nodes.name: Hanumān burns Laṅkā
nodes.summary: Captured and brought before Rāvaṇa, Hanumān has his tail set on fire as punishment; he escapes his bonds and leaps from roof to roof setting the city ablaze, then checks that Sītā is unharmed.

nodes.name: Hanumān brings the mountain of herbs
nodes.summary: When Indrajit’s weapon fells Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and the vānara host, Jāmbavat sends Hanumān to the Himālaya for four healing herbs; unable to identify them, Hanumān uproots the whole peak and carries it to Laṅkā.
nodes.details: In the CE this happens once, after Indrajit’s brahmāstra (6.61); later versions add a second occasion after Lakṣmaṇa is struck by Rāvaṇa’s spear.

sources.quote: hanūmān dṛśyate vīro dvitīya iva parvataḥ

nodes.name: Rāma kills Rāvaṇa
nodes.summary: In the final duel Rāma, on Mātali’s advice, looses the Brahmā weapon given by Agastya, which pierces Rāvaṇa’s heart; the rākṣasa women come out lamenting.

nodes.name: Rāma’s horse sacrifice at Naimiṣa
nodes.summary: Rāma performs the aśvamedha in the Naimiṣa forest with a golden image of Sītā as his ritual wife; it is there that Vālmīki’s pupils Kuśa and Lava sing the Rāmāyaṇa before him.

sources.quote: yajñe yajñe ca patnyarthaṃ jānakī kāñcanī bhavat

nodes.name: Itihāsa (the epics)
nodes.summary: The Sanskrit category itihāsa (“thus indeed it was”) designates the two great epics, the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, which present themselves as accounts of the past and as authoritative teaching on dharma.
nodes.details:
The Mahābhārata calls itself an itihāsa (e.g. MBh (CE) 1.1.17, “bhāratasyetihāsasya”, and 1.56.19, “jayo nāmetihāso ’yam”), while the Rāmāyaṇa is traditionally styled the ādikāvya, the first poem. Later tradition groups the two (sometimes with the Purāṇas) as a “fifth Veda” accessible to all. Scholarship treats both as products of centuries of oral and written growth (Brockington 1998).

This collection node gathers the two epics, the Mahābhārata’s embedded texts (Bhagavad Gītā, Rāmopākhyāna) and its supplement (khila) the Harivaṃśa.
nodes.limits: A genre label used within the tradition; it does not establish that the narrated events are historical.

nodes.name: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: The Sanskrit epic of Rāma attributed to the sage Vālmīki, in seven books (kāṇḍas); in the Baroda Critical Edition 606 sargas and c. 18,760 verses. Most scholars regard Books 2–6 as the older core and the Bālakāṇḍa and Uttarakāṇḍa as later.
nodes.details:
Structure (Baroda Critical Edition, counted from the GRETIL e-text): Bālakāṇḍa 76 sargas, Ayodhyākāṇḍa 111, Araṇyakāṇḍa 71, Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa 66, Sundarakāṇḍa 66, Yuddhakāṇḍa 116, Uttarakāṇḍa 100 — 606 sargas and 18,761 numbered verses. The traditional count of the vulgate is “24,000 ślokas”.

Transmission: the manuscripts fall into a northern (N) and a southern (S) recension, each with sub-versions (north-eastern/Bengal, north-western, western; southern editions printed at Bombay, Madras and Kumbhakonam with commentaries such as those of Govindarāja and Nāgeśa/Rāma). Gorresio printed the Bengal recension (Paris 1843–67). The Baroda Critical Edition (Oriental Institute, gen. eds. G. H. Bhatt and U. P. Shah; Bālakāṇḍa fascicles from 1958, Uttarakāṇḍa 1975) reconstructs the text shared by both recensions and relegates the rest to star passages and appendices; Goldman et al. translate it (Princeton 1984–2017).

Dating and growth: Jacobi (1893) and many later scholars, including Goldman and Brockington, treat Books 2–6 as the core and Books 1 and 7 as additions, partly because only these books consistently present Rāma as Viṣṇu incarnate and because the frame (Vālmīki, Lava and Kuśa) is set out there. Pollock (1984) argued instead that a divine kingship is integral to the poem throughout. Goldman places the core’s oral composition c. 750–500 BCE; Brockington places the primary stage in the 5th–4th c. BCE with later stages to c. the 3rd c. CE.

The Mahābhārata contains its own shorter Rāma story, the Rāmopākhyāna (MBh (CE) 3.257–275), whose relation to Vālmīki’s poem is debated.

dates.label: c. 750–500 BCE
dates.basis: linguistic, cultural and geographical internal evidence

dates.event: expansion (later stages incl. much of Bāla- and Uttarakāṇḍa)
dates.label: c. 3rd century BCE – 3rd century CE
dates.basis: stylistic stratification; divinisation of Rāma; frame material
publication record of the Oriental Institute, Baroda

sources.locator: vol. I, Bālakāṇḍa fasc. 1 (1958) – vol. VII, Uttarakāṇḍa (1973–75)

attributes.critical edition: Baroda, Oriental Institute (G. H. Bhatt, U. P. Shah, gen. eds.)

nodes.limits: Scholarly dates are for the composition of the poem, not for any events it narrates. Sarga and verse counts refer to the Baroda Critical Edition; vulgate and regional editions number differently.
openQuestions: How far the Bālakāṇḍa and Uttarakāṇḍa are later, and whether Rāma’s divinity is integral (Pollock) or accretive (Jacobi, Brockington)?
The date of the earliest surviving manuscripts (Nepalese palm-leaf manuscripts) was not checked in this pass.

nodes.name: Mahābhārata
nodes.summary: The Sanskrit epic of the Bhārata war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas, attributed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa; in the Pune Critical Edition 18 parvans, 1,995 adhyāyas and c. 74,000 verses, with the Harivaṃśa as its supplement (khila).
nodes.details:
Frame: the bard Ugraśravas, son of Lomaharṣaṇa, comes to Śaunaka’s twelve-year sacrifice in the Naimiṣa forest and repeats the stories that Vaiśampāyana, Vyāsa’s disciple, told King Janamejaya at his snake sacrifice (MBh (CE) 1.1.1–19). The text speaks of itself as Jaya (1.56.19) and says Vyāsa made a Bhārata-saṃhitā of 24,000 verses “without the upākhyānas” (1.1.61).

Critical Edition: prepared at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune, from 1 April 1919 and completed in 1966 (completion announced 22 September 1966); general editors V. S. Sukthankar (1925–43, whose Prolegomena appeared with the Ādiparvan in 1933), S. K. Belvalkar (from 1943) and P. L. Vaidya (from 1961). It collated some 1,259 manuscripts and prints the reconstructed text with a full apparatus; passages found in only part of the tradition appear as star (*) passages or appendices. Counting the GRETIL e-text, the constituted text has 1,995 adhyāyas and c. 73,900 numbered verses (BORI’s own description speaks of “more than 89,000 verses”, apparently counting differently). The vulgate (Calcutta 1834–39; Bombay with Nīlakaṇṭha’s commentary) is commonly said to have over 100,000 ślokas including the Harivaṃśa.

Dating: most scholars see a long growth from c. 400 BCE to c. 400 CE (Brockington; the older Winternitz–Hopkins span), with final form in the early Gupta period. Hiltebeitel (2001) argued instead for composition as a written work between the mid-2nd century BCE and the turn of the era. The earliest external list of its parvans is in the Spitzer manuscript from Kizil (radiocarbon c. 130 CE), whose list lacks the Virāṭa- and Anuśāsanaparvans; the Aihole inscription of 634–35 CE dates itself 3,735 years after the Bhārata war.

dates.label: c. 400 BCE – 400 CE
dates.basis: stratification of language, metre, content; external references

dates.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era
dates.basis: literary-historical argument (post-Aśokan, pre-Gupta milieu; written “committee” composition)

dates.event: earliest external attestation (parvan list in the Spitzer manuscript)
dates.label: c. 130 CE (radiocarbon 80–230 CE); palaeography c. 200–230 CE (Franco)
dates.basis: radiocarbon and palaeography of the Kizil manuscript

dates.event: external reference to the Bhārata war era (Aihole inscription of Pulakeśin II)
dates.label: 634–635 CE (Śaka 556)
3102 BCE (Kali-yuga epoch; implied by the Aihole reckoning)
dates.basis: traditional era: 3,735 years before Śaka 556 / 634–35 CE

attributes.metre: chiefly anuṣṭubh, with triṣṭubh and prose
attributes.critical edition: BORI, Pune, 1919–1966; general editors Sukthankar, Belvalkar, Vaidya

nodes.limits: Composition dates concern the text, not the historicity of the war. The Aihole figure is a traditional era-reckoning recorded in 634–35 CE, not evidence for a war in 3102 BCE.
openQuestions: Reconcile BORI’s “more than 89,000 verses” with the c. 73,900 numbered verses of the GRETIL e-text (different counting of half-verses/prose?).
Whether the Spitzer list’s different parvan titles represent an earlier arrangement or simply different names.

nodes.name: Bhagavad Gītā
nodes.subtype: philosophical dialogue embedded in the epic
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa’s 700-verse teaching to Arjuna on the eve of battle, embedded in the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata: MBh (CE) 6.23–40 (= chapters 25–42 of the Bhīṣmaparvan in the vulgate numbering).
nodes.details:
In the Critical Edition the Gītā runs from 6.23.1 (“dhṛtarāṣṭra uvāca: dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre …”) to 6.40.78 (verified in the GRETIL e-text); Sañjaya reports the dialogue to Dhṛtarāṣṭra. The vulgate numbers the same chapters 6.25–42. The standard count of 700 verses in 18 chapters goes back at least to Śaṅkara’s commentary (8th c.).

Dating is debated: many scholars place it c. 2nd–1st century BCE, others earlier (Upadhyaya: 5th–4th c. BCE) or later (written form in the first centuries CE). Some (e.g. Garbe, Otto) proposed an older theistic core with later additions; others (e.g. van Buitenen) stress its literary unity with the Bhīṣmaparvan.

dates.label: c. 2nd–1st century BCE
dates.basis: doctrinal and linguistic comparison with Upaniṣads, Sāṃkhya and epic layers

dates.event: fixing of the 700-verse text in commentary
dates.label: 8th century CE (Śaṅkara’s Gītābhāṣya)

nodes.limits: The CE/vulgate chapter equivalence is for the Bhīṣmaparvan as a whole; verse numbering inside the Gītā is the same in both.
openQuestions: The Kashmir recension’s additional verses and their relation to the CE text.

nodes.name: Harivaṃśa
nodes.summary: The “Genealogy of Hari”, transmitted as the khila (supplement) of the Mahābhārata, narrating the Yādava genealogy and Kṛṣṇa’s life from birth among the cowherds to his rule in Dvārakā. Critical Edition by P. L. Vaidya (BORI 1969–71): 118 adhyāyas, c. 6,000 verses — about a third of the vulgate.
nodes.details:
Vaidya’s constituted text is divided into Harivaṃśaparvan (adhyāyas 1–45: creation, genealogies of kings and the Yādavas), Viṣṇuparvan (46–113: Kṛṣṇa’s birth, childhood in Vraja, the killing of Kaṃsa, the founding of Dvārakā, marriages and wars) and Bhaviṣyaparvan (114–118). The vulgate is roughly three times longer.

The Harivaṃśa is one of the earliest connected accounts of Kṛṣṇa’s childhood: the birth (HV 48), the subduing of Kāliya (55–56), the lifting of Govardhana (61–62), the night sports with the cowherd women (63.24–35) and the killing of Kaṃsa (76), all verified in the GRETIL e-text.

Dates proposed range from the 1st to the 4th century CE: Masson and Ingalls (language no later than the 2nd–3rd c.), Couture (Kuṣāṇa-period Mathurā), Vaidya (CE text c. 300 CE), Hazra (4th c.).

dates.label: c. 1st–3rd century CE
dates.basis: language and cultural references (e.g. Kuṣāṇa-period Mathurā)

dates.event: redaction of the critically reconstructed text
dates.label: c. 300 CE
4th century CE
dates.basis: comparison of the rāsa/hallīsaka description with Purāṇic parallels

sources.locator: MBh (CE) 1.2 (Parvasaṃgraha lists the Harivaṃśa and Bhaviṣya among the parvans)

nodes.limits: Its status as an appendix (khila) is how the tradition and the CE classify it; whether it was composed as part of the Mahābhārata project is debated.

nodes.name: Rāmopākhyāna (Mahābhārata)
nodes.summary: The Mahābhārata’s own telling of the Rāma story, narrated by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya to Yudhiṣṭhira after Jayadratha’s attempt to abduct Draupadī: MBh (CE) 3.257–275, Āraṇyakaparvan.
nodes.details:
Frame: Janamejaya asks what the Pāṇḍavas did after Draupadī’s rescue (3.257.1); Yudhiṣṭhira asks Mārkaṇḍeya whether anyone was ever more unfortunate (3.257.10), and Mārkaṇḍeya tells of Rāma (3.258–275), ending with consolation (3.276).

Content (verified in the CE): it opens with Rāvaṇa’s origins from Pulastya and Viśravas and the rivalry with Kubera (3.259); Brahmā announces that four-armed Viṣṇu has descended to kill Rāvaṇa and orders the gods to beget monkey and bear allies, while the gandharvī Dundubhī is born as Mantharā (3.260); Sītā is Janaka’s daughter fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ (3.258.9) — there is no furrow-birth and no bow contest. The war is shorter; after Rāvaṇa’s death Rāma rejects Sītā, who swears an oath and is vindicated by Vāyu, Agni, Varuṇa and Brahmā; Brahmā reveals that Nalakūbara’s curse had protected her; Daśaratha appears (3.275.10–36). There is no fire-entry and no later banishment.

Scholars disagree whether it abridges a form of Vālmīki’s poem (the majority view, with debate over which stage) or preserves an independent or older version.

dates.label: within the epic’s growth, c. 3rd century BCE – 3rd century CE

nodes.limits: The CE’s Rāmopākhyāna excludes many star passages present in vulgate manuscripts (e.g. the 11,000-year reign line at *1307 after 3.275.69).
openQuestions: Whether the Rāmopākhyāna depends on a written Vālmīki text, an oral Rāma tradition, or both.

nodes.name: Bālakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 1)
nodes.summary: The “Book of Youth”: the frame (Nārada’s summary to Vālmīki, the krauñca curse and the invention of the śloka, the teaching of Lava and Kuśa), the sacrifice for sons, Viṣṇu’s decision to be born, the births of the four princes, Viśvāmitra’s expedition, Ahalyā, the breaking of Śiva’s bow and the marriages, and the encounter with Paraśurāma.
nodes.details: Widely regarded as one of the later books (Jacobi, Goldman, Brockington). Sarga and verse totals are counted from the GRETIL e-text of the Baroda Critical Edition.

nodes.name: Ayodhyākāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 2)
nodes.summary: The “Book of Ayodhyā”: the planned consecration, Kaikeyī’s two boons, Rāma’s exile with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, Daśaratha’s death, Bharata’s refusal and the sandals.
nodes.details: Part of the core (Books 2–6). Sarga and verse totals are counted from the GRETIL e-text of the Baroda Critical Edition.

nodes.name: Araṇyakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 3)
nodes.summary: The “Book of the Forest”: life among the sages of the Daṇḍaka, Śūrpaṇakhā’s mutilation, the war with Khara, the golden deer, Sītā’s abduction, Jaṭāyu’s death, Kabandha and Śabarī.
nodes.details: Part of the core; translated by Pollock in the Princeton series (1991). Sarga and verse totals are counted from the GRETIL e-text of the Baroda Critical Edition.

nodes.name: Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 4)
nodes.summary: The “Book of Kiṣkindhā”: Hanumān’s meeting with Rāma, the alliance with Sugrīva, the killing of Vālin and the search for Sītā.
nodes.details: Part of the core. Sarga and verse totals are counted from the GRETIL e-text of the Baroda Critical Edition.

nodes.name: Sundarakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 5)
nodes.summary: The “Beautiful Book”: Hanumān’s leap to Laṅkā, his search, his meeting with Sītā in the aśoka grove, the token ring, and the burning of the city.
nodes.details: Part of the core; widely recited separately in devotional practice. Sarga and verse totals are counted from the GRETIL e-text of the Baroda Critical Edition.

nodes.name: Yuddhakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 6)
nodes.summary: The “Book of the War”: Vibhīṣaṇa’s defection, the causeway built by Nala, the war, the deaths of Kumbhakarṇa, Indrajit and Rāvaṇa, Sītā’s fire ordeal and Brahmā’s hymn, and the return and consecration in Ayodhyā.
nodes.details: Part of the core, though passages such as Brahmā’s hymn identifying Rāma with Nārāyaṇa (6.105) are often considered late. Sarga and verse totals are counted from the GRETIL e-text of the Baroda Critical Edition.

nodes.name: Uttarakāṇḍa (Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Book 7)
nodes.summary: The “Last Book”: Rāvaṇa’s origins and earlier conquests, Hanumān’s childhood, the banishment of Sītā, the birth of Lava and Kuśa in Vālmīki’s hermitage, the Śambūka episode, the recitation of the poem by the twins, Sītā’s return into the earth and Rāma’s return to Viṣṇu’s form.
nodes.details: Widely regarded as the latest book. Sarga and verse totals are counted from the GRETIL e-text of the Baroda Critical Edition.

nodes.name: Ādiparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 1)
nodes.summary: The “First Book”: the frame narratives, the snake sacrifice, the origins of the Bhārata line (Śakuntalā, Śantanu, Bhīṣma’s vow), the births and youth of the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas, the house of lac, Draupadī’s svayaṃvara and marriage, Indraprastha and the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest.
nodes.details: Adhyāya and verse totals counted from the GRETIL e-text of the Pune Critical Edition (numbered verses; star passages excluded). The vulgate (Calcutta/Bombay; Ganguli’s translation) divides the parvan into different numbers of chapters (“sections”).

nodes.name: Sabhāparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 2)
nodes.summary: The “Book of the Assembly Hall”: the hall built by Maya, the killing of Jarāsandha, the rājasūya and the killing of Śiśupāla, the dice game, Draupadī’s humiliation and the second game that sends the Pāṇḍavas into exile.
nodes.details: Adhyāya and verse totals counted from the GRETIL e-text of the Pune Critical Edition (numbered verses; star passages excluded). The vulgate (Calcutta/Bombay; Ganguli’s translation) divides the parvan into different numbers of chapters (“sections”).

nodes.name: Āraṇyakaparvan (Vanaparvan) (Mahābhārata, Book 3)
nodes.summary: The “Book of the Forest”: twelve years of exile, Arjuna’s acquisition of weapons (Kirāta), pilgrimages, and many embedded tales — Nala and Damayantī, the Rāmopākhyāna, Sāvitrī — ending with the theft of Karṇa’s earrings and the Yakṣa’s questions.

nodes.name: Virāṭaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 4)
nodes.summary: The “Book of Virāṭa”: the thirteenth year in disguise at the Matsya court, the killing of Kīcaka, the cattle raid and Uttarā’s marriage to Abhimanyu.
nodes.details: Adhyāya and verse totals counted from the GRETIL e-text of the Pune Critical Edition (numbered verses; star passages excluded). The vulgate (Calcutta/Bombay; Ganguli’s translation) divides the parvan into different numbers of chapters (“sections”).

nodes.name: Udyogaparvan (Mahābhārata, Book 5)
nodes.summary: The “Book of the Effort”: embassies and preparations for war, Vidura’s and Sanatsujāta’s counsels, Kṛṣṇa’s embassy and theophany at the Kaurava court, Kṛṣṇa’s and Kuntī’s approaches to Karṇa, and the story of Ambā/Śikhaṇḍin.

nodes.summary: The “Book of Bhīṣma”: the first ten days of battle under Bhīṣma’s command, containing the Bhagavad Gītā (6.23–40), ending with Bhīṣma’s fall onto a bed of arrows (6.114).

nodes.summary: The “Book of the Horse Sacrifice”: the Anugītā (14.16–50), the revival of the still-born Parīkṣit by Kṛṣṇa, and Yudhiṣṭhira’s horse sacrifice.

nodes.summary: The “Book of the Hermitage”: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī, Kuntī and Vidura retire to the forest; Vyāsa shows the dead warriors to the living; the elders die in a forest fire.

nodes.name: Harivaṃśaparvan (Harivaṃśa)
nodes.summary: Book 1 of the Harivaṃśa (CE): cosmogony, the solar and lunar dynasties and the genealogy of the Yādavas down to Kṛṣṇa.

nodes.name: Viṣṇuparvan (Harivaṃśa)
nodes.summary: Book 2 of the Harivaṃśa (CE): the life of Kṛṣṇa from the gods’ plan and his birth to Devakī (HV 48) through his childhood in Vraja, the killing of Kaṃsa (76), the move to Dvārakā (85–86) and later wars and marriages.

nodes.name: Bhaviṣyaparvan (Harivaṃśa)
nodes.summary: Book 3 of the Harivaṃśa (CE): a short concluding section on the future and the close of Janamejaya’s line.

nodes.name: Nalopākhyāna (MBh 3.50–78)
nodes.summary: The story of Nala and Damayantī, told by the sage Bṛhadaśva to Yudhiṣṭhira during the forest exile (MBh (CE) 3.49 frame; 3.50–78 story).

nodes.name: Pativratāmāhātmya / Sāvitrī-upākhyāna (MBh 3.277–283)
nodes.summary: The story of Sāvitrī, who wins back her husband Satyavān from Yama, told by Mārkaṇḍeya to Yudhiṣṭhira (MBh (CE) 3.277–283).

nodes.name: Śakuntalopākhyāna (MBh 1.62–69)
nodes.summary: The story of King Duḥṣanta and Śakuntalā and the birth of Bharata, eponym of the Bhāratas (MBh (CE) 1.62–69).

nodes.name: The churning of the ocean (MBh 1.15–17)
nodes.summary: The Mahābhārata’s account of the churning of the ocean for amṛta, told by Ugraśravas to explain the horse Uccaiḥśravas (MBh (CE) 1.15–17; 1.18.1 closes “thus I have told you how the amṛta was churned”).

nodes.name: Aṃśāvataraṇa: the partial incarnations (MBh 1.61)
nodes.summary: The catalogue of which gods, demons and others were born as the epic’s characters — e.g. Kṛṣṇa as a portion of Nārāyaṇa, Balarāma of Śeṣa, Karṇa of the Sun, Draupadī of Śrī, Duryodhana of Kali (MBh (CE) 1.61.63–99).

nodes.name: Pañcendropākhyāna: the five Indras (MBh 1.189)
nodes.summary: Vyāsa’s account to Drupada of five former Indras born as the Pāṇḍavas with Śrī as their common wife, followed by the tale of the sage’s daughter who asked Śiva five times for a husband (MBh (CE) 1.189.1–49).

nodes.name: Dyūtaparvan: the dice game (MBh 2.43–65)
nodes.summary: The sub-book of the first dice game, from Duryodhana’s envy at Indraprastha to Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s boons to Draupadī and the Pāṇḍavas’ release (MBh (CE) 2.43–65); the return match follows in 2.66–72.

nodes.name: Ambopākhyāna (MBh 5.170–193)
nodes.summary: Bhīṣma’s narration of Ambā’s abduction, her rejection, his duel with Paraśurāma, her rebirth as Śikhaṇḍinī and the sex-exchange with the yakṣa Sthūṇa (MBh (CE) 5.170–193).

nodes.name: Kuṇḍalāharaṇa: the theft of Karṇa’s earrings (MBh 3.284–294)
nodes.summary: Sūrya warns Karṇa that Indra will beg his armour and earrings; the narrative of Kuntī’s boon, Karṇa’s birth and abandonment in a basket on the Aśvanadī, and his rescue by Adhiratha and Rādhā; Indra receives the armour and gives the spear (MBh (CE) 3.284–294).

nodes.name: The Yakṣa’s questions (MBh 3.297–298)
nodes.summary: At the poisoned lake the yakṣa — the god Dharma — questions Yudhiṣṭhira and restores his brothers (MBh (CE) 3.297–298).

nodes.name: Viduranīti / Prajāgara (MBh 5.33–40)
nodes.summary: Vidura’s night-long counsel on policy and conduct to the sleepless Dhṛtarāṣṭra (MBh (CE) 5.33–40).

nodes.name: Sanatsujātīya (MBh 5.42–45)
nodes.summary: The sage Sanatsujāta’s teaching to Dhṛtarāṣṭra on death and liberation (MBh (CE) 5.42–45).

nodes.name: Bhagavadyāna: Kṛṣṇa’s embassy (MBh 5.70–137)
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa’s peace mission to Hāstinapura, including his theophany when the Kauravas plan to seize him (5.129) (MBh (CE) 5.70–137).

nodes.name: Rājadharma (MBh 12.1–128)
nodes.summary: Bhīṣma’s instruction on the duties of kings (MBh (CE) 12.1–128).

nodes.name: Āpaddharma (MBh 12.129–167)
nodes.summary: Bhīṣma’s instruction on conduct in emergencies (MBh (CE) 12.129–167).

nodes.name: Mokṣadharma (MBh 12.168–353)
nodes.summary: Bhīṣma’s instruction on liberation, incorporating Sāṃkhya, Yoga and Nārāyaṇa theology (MBh (CE) 12.168–353).

nodes.name: Nārāyaṇīya (MBh 12.321–339)
nodes.summary: The Nārāyaṇīya section of the Mokṣadharma, an early Pāñcarātra-related account of Nārāyaṇa worship, Nārada’s visit to Śvetadvīpa and the vyūha doctrine (MBh (CE) 12.321–339).

nodes.name: Viṣṇusahasranāma (MBh 13.135)
nodes.summary: The thousand names of Viṣṇu, taught by Bhīṣma to Yudhiṣṭhira (MBh (CE) 13.135).

nodes.name: Anugītā (MBh 14.16–50)
nodes.summary: After the war Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa to repeat the Gītā; Kṛṣṇa says he cannot and teaches anew (MBh (CE) 14.16–50).

nodes.name: Āstīkaparvan (MBh 1.13–53)
nodes.summary: The story of Jaratkāru, Āstīka and Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice, which forms the outer frame of Vaiśampāyana’s recitation (MBh (CE) 1.13–53).

nodes.name: Saṃkṣepa Rāmāyaṇa: Nārada’s summary (VR 1.1)
nodes.summary: The opening sarga in which Vālmīki asks Nārada who is the most virtuous man living and Nārada summarises Rāma’s story (VR (CE) 1.1).

nodes.name: The krauñca episode and the first śloka (VR 1.2)
nodes.summary: Vālmīki’s grief at a hunter killing one of a pair of krauñca birds turns into the first śloka, “mā niṣāda …” (VR (CE) 1.2.14).

nodes.name: Brahmā’s hymn to Rāma (VR 6.105)
nodes.summary: After Sītā’s fire ordeal Brahmā tells Rāma that he is Nārāyaṇa and that Sītā is Lakṣmī (VR (CE) 6.105.12, 25).

nodes.name: Rāma
nodes.summary: Prince of Ayodhyā, eldest son of Daśaratha and Kausalyā and hero of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; exiled for fourteen years, he recovers his wife Sītā from Rāvaṇa and rules as the model righteous king. Vaiṣṇava tradition regards him as an avatāra of Viṣṇu.
nodes.details:
Portrayal: Nārada’s summary that opens the poem (VR (CE) 1.1.8–19) describes Rāma as an Ikṣvāku prince endowed with every virtue, “equal to Viṣṇu in valour” (1.1.17); in the Bālakāṇḍa he is born as “half of Viṣṇu” (viṣṇor ardham, 1.17.6), and in the Yuddhakāṇḍa Brahmā’s hymn declares him Nārāyaṇa (6.105.12).
