Elsewhere in Books 2–6 he acts and grieves as a human king, which underlies the long debate on whether his divinity is original (Pollock 1984) or a later accretion concentrated in Books 1 and 7 (Jacobi, Brockington).

Key acts: kills Tāṭakā under Viśvāmitra’s guidance (1.25); breaks Śiva’s bow and marries Sītā (1.65–72); accepts exile to keep his father’s word (Book 2); kills Vālin from concealment to aid Sugrīva (4.16–18), an act the text itself has Vālin protest; kills Rāvaṇa with the Brahmā weapon given by Agastya (6.97); subjects Sītā to public repudiation (6.103) and later banishes her because of popular rumour (7.42–44); kills the śūdra ascetic Śambūka (7.67); at the end enters the Vaiṣṇava radiance with his brothers (7.100.10).

The Mahābhārata retells his story in the Rāmopākhyāna (MBh (CE) 3.258–275) and lists him among exemplary kings.
nodes.limits: A literary and religious figure; the dataset records what texts and traditions say and does not assert historicity.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

earliestMaterial.label: second half of the 5th century CE

nodes.name: Sītā
nodes.summary: Daughter of King Janaka of Videha — found in a ploughed furrow — and wife of Rāma; abducted by Rāvaṇa, she is vindicated by an ordeal of fire but later banished, and finally returns into the earth. Brahmā’s hymn in the Yuddhakāṇḍa identifies her with Lakṣmī.
nodes.details:
Birth: Janaka tells Viśvāmitra that while he was ploughing a field she rose from the plough’s furrow and was named Sītā (“furrow”) (VR (CE) 1.65.14); she is “not born of a womb” (ayonijā, 1.65.27). The Mahābhārata’s Rāmopākhyāna by contrast simply calls her Janaka’s daughter, fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ for Rāma (MBh (CE) 3.258.9). The Uttarakāṇḍa adds that she was earlier Vedavatī, who cursed Rāvaṇa (7.17.31).

Key acts: insists on accompanying Rāma into exile (Book 2); is carried off by Rāvaṇa (3.47–49); resists Rāvaṇa in the aśoka grove and recognises Hanumān by Rāma’s ring (5.34); after the war is publicly repudiated, asks Lakṣmaṇa for a pyre and enters the fire, invoking Agni as witness (6.104.18–26), and is returned by Agni (6.106); in the Uttarakāṇḍa she is abandoned near Vālmīki’s hermitage, bears Lava and Kuśa (7.58), and at the horse sacrifice calls on the earth goddess Mādhavī, who receives her on a throne (7.88.10–14).

She is the subject of comparisons across the epic’s versions (see cmp:sita-ordeal-banishment).
nodes.limits: Birth and divine identification differ between texts and are recorded as text-qualified assertions.

earliestMaterial.label: second half of the 5th century CE

nodes.name: Lakṣmaṇa
nodes.summary: Son of Daśaratha and Sumitrā, twin of Śatrughna, who accompanies Rāma and Sītā into exile and fights beside Rāma; he mutilates Śūrpaṇakhā, kills Indrajit, and in the Uttarakāṇḍa leaves Sītā in the forest at Rāma’s command.
nodes.details: Born with Śatrughna to Sumitrā, both “endowed with half of Viṣṇu” in the Bālakāṇḍa’s apportionment (VR (CE) 1.17.9); marries Ūrmilā (1.72.18). He builds the pyre for Sītā’s ordeal (6.104.21), kills Indrajit (6.78), and later carries Sītā to the forest (7.46). Later tradition regards him as a form of Śeṣa.

earliestMaterial.label: second half of the 5th century CE

nodes.name: Bharata (brother of Rāma)
nodes.summary: Son of Daśaratha and Kaikeyī, for whom Kaikeyī demands the throne; he refuses it, seeks Rāma in the forest, and rules from Nandigrāma as regent with Rāma’s sandals on the throne.
nodes.details: Called “a quarter of Viṣṇu” in the Bālakāṇḍa (VR (CE) 1.17.8). Marries Māṇḍavī (1.72.19). Receives the gold-adorned sandals from Rāma (2.104.21–23). Distinct from Bharata son of Duḥṣanta and Śakuntalā (char:bharata-dauhshanti).

nodes.name: Śatrughna
nodes.summary: Youngest son of Daśaratha, Lakṣmaṇa’s twin by Sumitrā and companion of Bharata; in the Uttarakāṇḍa he kills the demon Lavaṇa and founds Madhurā (Mathurā).
nodes.details: Marries Śrutakīrti (VR (CE) 1.72.20). On his way to fight Lavaṇa he spends the night at Vālmīki’s hermitage on the night Sītā gives birth (7.58.1). The founding of Mathurā by Śatrughna is an Uttarakāṇḍa tradition (recall; locator not checked).

nodes.name: Hanumān
nodes.summary: Vānara minister of Sugrīva, son of the wind god Vāyu and Añjanā (wife of the vānara Kesarin), who leaps the ocean to find Sītā in Laṅkā and becomes Rāma’s loyal servant and messenger; later devotional traditions make him the model devotee (bhakta).
nodes.details:
Parentage: Jāmbavān tells Hanumān that the apsaras Puñjikasthalā, known as Añjanā, wife of the vānara Kesarin, was embraced by Māruta (Vāyu); “you are Kesarin’s son by his field (kṣetraja) and Māruta’s own (aurasa) son” (VR (CE) 4.65.8–28). The Uttarakāṇḍa retells his childhood: he leaps for the sun thinking it a fruit, is struck by Indra’s thunderbolt, and Vāyu’s withdrawal forces the gods to grant him boons (7.35–36).

Key acts: approaches Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa for Sugrīva (4.2–3); leaps the ocean (5.1); finds Sītā and gives her Rāma’s ring (5.34.2); his tail is set alight and he burns Laṅkā (5.51–52); in the war he fetches healing herbs (Yuddhakāṇḍa; locator not checked here).

In the Mahābhārata he meets his half-brother Bhīma (both sons of Vāyu) in the Āraṇyakaparvan (MBh (CE) 3.146–150; “hanūmān vāyutanayo vāyuputram abhāṣata”, 3.147.4). His later cult as a deity in his own right — devotional texts such as the Hanumān Cālīsā and countless shrines — is documented by Lutgendorf (2007).
nodes.limits: The cult of Hanumān as an independent deity is a later development than the epic narrative; see the regional and temple domains.

nodes.name: Rāvaṇa
nodes.summary: Ten-headed rākṣasa king of Laṅkā, son of the sage Viśravas and the rākṣasī Kaikasī, made invulnerable to gods and demons by Brahmā’s boon; he abducts Sītā and is killed by Rāma.
nodes.details:
Origins (Uttarakāṇḍa): Kaikasī is sent by her father to choose the sage Viśravas, grandson of Pulastya (VR (CE) 7.9.3–15); she bears Daśagrīva, then Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā and Vibhīṣaṇa (7.9.26–27). Through austerities he asks Brahmā to be unslayable by suparṇas, nāgas, yakṣas, daityas, dānavas, rākṣasas and gods — not naming humans (7.10.17). He drives his half-brother Kubera (Vaiśravaṇa) from Laṅkā, marries Mandodarī, daughter of the dānava Maya (7.12.16), and fathers Meghanāda/Indrajit (7.12.26).

Key acts: abducts Sītā using Mārīca as a golden deer (3.40–49); kills Jaṭāyu; is killed by Rāma with the Brahmā weapon (6.97). The Rāmopākhyāna gives a parallel genealogy through Pulastya and Viśravas (MBh (CE) 3.259) and explains that Nalakūbara’s curse — that his head would split if he forced an unwilling woman — protected Sītā (3.275.32–33); in the Vālmīki Uttarakāṇḍa the curse follows his assault on Rambhā, Nalakūbara’s wife (VR (CE) 7.26).

earliestMaterial.label: second half of the 5th century CE

nodes.name: Vibhīṣaṇa
nodes.summary: Righteous younger brother of Rāvaṇa who urges him to return Sītā, defects to Rāma, and is installed as king of Laṅkā after the war.
nodes.details: Youngest son of Kaikasī, devoted to dharma (VR (CE) 7.9.27–30); Brahmā praises his righteousness when granting boons (7.10.24–26). He crosses to Rāma’s camp, standing in the sky above the northern shore (6.11.8–9). In the Rāmopākhyāna he fights Prahasta (MBh (CE) 3.270).

nodes.name: Sugrīva
nodes.summary: Vānara prince of Kiṣkindhā, son of the Sun, exiled by his brother Vālin; he allies with Rāma, who kills Vālin and restores him, and in return sends the vānara armies in search of Sītā.
nodes.details: Called “son of Bhāskara (the Sun)” (VR (CE) 4.4.20; “sūryātmaja” 4.14.21). The alliance (sakhya) with Rāma is sealed before fire (4.5).

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Vālin
nodes.summary: Vānara king of Kiṣkindhā, son of Indra and elder brother of Sugrīva, whom he had driven out; he is killed by Rāma’s arrow during his duel with Sugrīva and is succeeded by his son Aṅgada as heir.
nodes.details: Called “Mahendra’s son” as he lies dying (VR (CE) 4.17.11). His rebuke of Rāma for striking from concealment and Rāma’s justification (4.17–18) are a classic crux of epic ethics. His wife Tārā laments him (4.19–20).

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

earliestMaterial.label: second half of the 5th century CE

nodes.name: Jaṭāyu
nodes.summary: King of the vultures and friend of Daśaratha, who tries to stop Rāvaṇa carrying off Sītā, is mortally wounded, and tells Rāma what happened before dying.
nodes.details: Introduces himself as Jaṭāyu, king of the vultures (VR (CE) 3.48.3); found dying by Rāma (3.63–64). The Rāmopākhyāna calls him Daśaratha’s friend, son of Aruṇa and brother of Saṃpāti (MBh (CE) 3.263.1).

nodes.name: Daśaratha
nodes.summary: Ikṣvāku king of Ayodhyā, father of Rāma, Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna; bound by two boons promised to Kaikeyī, he exiles Rāma and dies of grief.
nodes.details: Kaikeyī reminds him of the two boons granted when she saved him in the war of gods and demons (VR (CE) 2.9.13–21). Before dying he recalls killing an ascetic’s son by mistake and the curse that he would die grieving for a son (2.57–58). In the Rāmopākhyāna he is son of Aja (MBh (CE) 3.258.6) and appears from heaven after the war (3.275.35).

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Kaikeyī
nodes.summary: Princess of Kekaya, wife of Daśaratha and mother of Bharata, who, prompted by the servant Mantharā, claims her two boons: Bharata’s consecration and Rāma’s fourteen-year exile.
nodes.details: The boons are recalled in VR (CE) 2.9.13–21. In the Rāmopākhyāna, Mantharā is the gandharvī Dundubhī born on earth at Brahmā’s order to stir enmity (MBh (CE) 3.260.9–15).

nodes.name: Kausalyā
nodes.summary: Chief queen of Daśaratha and mother of Rāma.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Janaka (father of Sītā)
nodes.summary: King of Videha at Mithilā (Sīradhvaja Janaka in the Rāmāyaṇa) who found Sītā in a furrow while ploughing and set the stringing of Śiva’s bow as the condition for her marriage.
nodes.details: Kept distinct from the Upaniṣadic Janaka of Videha (char:janaka-videha); “Janaka” is a dynastic name. He gives Sītā to Rāma and Ūrmilā to Lakṣmaṇa (VR (CE) 1.70.21–22), and his brother Kuśadhvaja’s daughters Māṇḍavī and Śrutakīrti to Bharata and Śatrughna (1.72.19–20).
nodes.limits: The identification of this Janaka with the philosopher-king of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka is not assumed.

nodes.name: Vālmīki
nodes.summary: Sage to whom the Rāmāyaṇa is attributed: he hears the story from Nārada, invents the śloka metre in grief at a krauñca bird’s death, composes the poem and teaches it to Rāma’s sons Lava and Kuśa, at whose hermitage Sītā lives after her banishment.
nodes.details: In the frame Vālmīki questions Nārada (VR (CE) 1.1.1), utters the first śloka “mā niṣāda …” (1.2.14), and teaches the poem to the two singers Kuśa and Lava (kuśīlavau) (1.4.3–4). In the Uttarakāṇḍa he is a friend of Daśaratha (7.46.16), shelters Sītā and names her twins (7.58), and sends them to sing the poem at Rāma’s sacrifice (7.84.3). Later traditions (not in the CE) make him a reformed highway robber; Leslie (2003) traces how such traditions shaped modern Vālmīki communities.
nodes.limits: Authorship is traditional attribution recorded as ATTRIBUTED_TO; scholars treat the poem as the work of many hands.

nodes.name: Kumbhakarṇa
nodes.summary: Gigantic brother of Rāvaṇa who sleeps for long periods; roused for the war, he devastates the vānara army before Rāma kills him.
nodes.details: Born after Rāvaṇa (VR (CE) 7.9.26). Killed by Rāma in VR (CE) 6.55 (6.55.129: “having killed Kumbhakarṇa … Bharata’s elder brother rejoiced”). In the Rāmopākhyāna, by contrast, Lakṣmaṇa burns him with the Brahmā weapon (MBh (CE) 3.271.16).

nodes.name: Indrajit
nodes.summary: Son of Rāvaṇa and Mandodarī, born as Meghanāda and called Indrajit (“conqueror of Indra”) after capturing Indra; a master of illusion who twice binds Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with serpent-arrows and is finally killed by Lakṣmaṇa.

nodes.name: Śūrpaṇakhā
nodes.summary: Sister of Rāvaṇa who propositions Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa in the Pañcavaṭī forest; Lakṣmaṇa cuts off her nose and ears, provoking the war with Khara and then Rāvaṇa’s abduction of Sītā.

nodes.name: Ahalyā
nodes.summary: Wife of the sage Gautama, seduced by Indra and cursed by her husband to do penance unseen in the hermitage until Rāma’s arrival restores her.
nodes.details: In the Vālmīki Bālakāṇḍa Ahalyā knowingly consents to Indra (VR (CE) 1.47.17–21) and is restored when Rāma enters the hermitage (1.48.11–20); the motif of her turning to stone and being freed by Rāma’s foot belongs to later retellings (e.g. the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa and Rāmcaritmānas).

nodes.name: Śabarī
nodes.summary: Female ascetic of the Śabara community living at the Pampā lake, who receives Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa and then ascends to heaven.
nodes.details: In VR (CE) 3.70 she honours the brothers at her hermitage on the western shore of the Pampā. The well-known motif of her tasting the berries before offering them is a later devotional elaboration.

nodes.name: Lava
nodes.summary: One of the twin sons of Rāma and Sītā (the younger), born in Vālmīki’s hermitage, named by Vālmīki and taught by him to sing the Rāmāyaṇa, which they perform before Rāma.
nodes.details: Vālmīki protects the newborns with a handful of kuśa grass and its lower part (lava); the first-born is to be called Kuśa and the other Lava (VR (CE) 7.58.4–6). The Bālakāṇḍa frame calls the pair “kuśīlavau” (1.4.3).

nodes.name: Kuśa
nodes.summary: One of the twin sons of Rāma and Sītā (the elder), born in Vālmīki’s hermitage, named by Vālmīki and taught by him to sing the Rāmāyaṇa, which they perform before Rāma.
nodes.details: Vālmīki protects the newborns with a handful of kuśa grass and its lower part (lava); the first-born is to be called Kuśa and the other Lava (VR (CE) 7.58.4–6). The Bālakāṇḍa frame calls the pair “kuśīlavau” (1.4.3).

nodes.name: Sumitrā
nodes.summary: Wife of Daśaratha and mother of the twins Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna.

nodes.name: Ūrmilā
nodes.summary: Daughter of Janaka and younger sister of Sītā, married to Lakṣmaṇa.
nodes.details: Vālmīki gives her little more than her marriage (VR (CE) 1.72.18); later poets (e.g. Maithilīśaraṇ Gupta’s Hindi Sāket) made her separation from Lakṣmaṇa a theme.

nodes.name: Māṇḍavī
nodes.summary: Daughter of Kuśadhvaja (Janaka’s brother) married to Bharata.

nodes.name: Śrutakīrti
nodes.summary: Daughter of Kuśadhvaja married to Śatrughna.

nodes.name: Mandodarī
nodes.summary: Chief queen of Rāvaṇa, daughter of the dānava architect Maya and the apsaras Hemā, and mother of Indrajit.
nodes.details: Hanumān sees her asleep and first mistakes her for Sītā (VR (CE) 5.8.48). Maya offers her to Rāvaṇa (7.12.16).

nodes.name: Aṅgada
nodes.summary: Son of Vālin and Tārā, made heir-apparent of Kiṣkindhā under Sugrīva; leads the southern search party and serves as Rāma’s envoy to Rāvaṇa.

nodes.name: Tārā
nodes.summary: Wife of Vālin and mother of Aṅgada, whose lament over Vālin and counsel to Sugrīva are prominent in the Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa.

nodes.name: Mantharā
nodes.summary: Hunchbacked servant of Kaikeyī who persuades her to claim her boons; in the Mahābhārata’s Rāmopākhyāna she is the gandharvī Dundubhī born on earth at Brahmā’s command.

nodes.name: Mārīca
nodes.summary: Rākṣasa, son of Tāṭakā, who at Rāvaṇa’s command takes the form of a golden deer to lure Rāma away from Sītā and is killed by him.

nodes.name: Tāṭakā
nodes.summary: Yakṣī turned demoness who ravages the forest near the Gaṅgā; Rāma kills her at Viśvāmitra’s instruction.

nodes.name: Kabandha
nodes.summary: Headless monster of the forest, freed from a curse when Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa cut off his arms and cremate him; he directs them to Sugrīva.

nodes.name: Saṃpāti
nodes.summary: Elder brother of Jaṭāyu, a vulture with burnt wings who tells the searching vānaras that Sītā is in Laṅkā.

nodes.name: Trijaṭā
nodes.summary: Rākṣasī guard of Sītā in the aśoka grove who dreams of Rāvaṇa’s ruin and befriends Sītā.

nodes.name: Kesarin
nodes.summary: Vānara chief, husband of Añjanā, in whose “field” Hanumān is born; Hanumān is thus his kṣetraja son while being Vāyu’s own son.

nodes.name: Añjanā
nodes.summary: Apsaras Puñjikasthalā living as a vānarī, wife of Kesarin and mother of Hanumān by the wind god.

nodes.name: Viśravas
nodes.summary: Sage, son of Pulastya, father of Kubera (Vaiśravaṇa) and, by Kaikasī, of Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā and Vibhīṣaṇa.
nodes.details: The Rāmopākhyāna makes Viśravas “half of Pulastya’s body born from anger” (MBh (CE) 3.259.1), a different account from the Uttarakāṇḍa’s.

nodes.name: Kaikasī
nodes.summary: Daughter of the rākṣasa Sumālin, who at her father’s bidding chooses the sage Viśravas and becomes the mother of Rāvaṇa and his siblings.

nodes.name: Kubera (Vaiśravaṇa)
nodes.summary: Son of Viśravas, lord of wealth and guardian of a direction, first ruler of Laṅkā, who is driven out by his half-brother Rāvaṇa.
nodes.details: Modelled here as a character node for the epic genealogy; a fuller deity record (worship, iconography) belongs to other domains.

nodes.name: Vedavatī
nodes.summary: Daughter of the sage Kuśadhvaja (son of Bṛhaspati) who, molested by Rāvaṇa, enters the fire vowing to be reborn for his destruction; the Uttarakāṇḍa identifies her with Sītā.

nodes.name: Śambūka
nodes.summary: Śūdra ascetic performing austerities, whom Rāma beheads in the Uttarakāṇḍa after a brahmin’s son dies prematurely; the episode is a focus of modern criticism.

nodes.name: Gautama (husband of Ahalyā)
nodes.summary: Sage of Mithilā’s forest whose wife Ahalyā is seduced by Indra; he curses both and later receives her back purified.

nodes.name: Guha
nodes.summary: Niṣāda chief of Śṛṅgaverapura on the Gaṅgā, Rāma’s friend, who hosts the exiles and ferries them across the river.

nodes.name: Jāmbavān
nodes.summary: King of the bears (ṛkṣas) in Rāma’s army, eldest counsellor of the search party, who reminds Hanumān of his parentage and powers before the leap.
nodes.details: In the Harivaṃśa and Purāṇas a Jāmbavān gives his daughter Jāmbavatī to Kṛṣṇa after the Syamantaka jewel affair; later tradition treats them as the same long-lived figure (not asserted here).

nodes.name: Nala (vānara engineer)
nodes.summary: Vānara son of Viśvakarman who builds the causeway (setu) across the ocean to Laṅkā — distinct from King Nala of Niṣadha (char:nala).
nodes.details: The Ocean tells Rāma that Nala, “son of Viśvakarman”, can build the bridge; Nala confirms he is Viśvakarman’s own son by a boon to his mother on Mount Mandara (VR (CE) 6.15.8–12).

nodes.name: Ṛśyaśṛṅga
nodes.summary: Sage, son of Vibhāṇḍaka, brought to Daśaratha’s court on Sumantra’s advice to perform the sacrifice that produces the four princes; married to Śāntā.

nodes.name: Bharadvāja
nodes.summary: Sage whose hermitage at Prayāga hosts Rāma and later Bharata in the Rāmāyaṇa; in the Mahābhārata he is the father of Droṇa.
nodes.details: Bharadvāja directs the exiles to Citrakūṭa (VR (CE) 2.48.26–34). The epic’s Bharadvāja is the eponym of a Vedic seer-lineage; this record covers the epic figure only.
nodes.limits: The Vedic ṛṣi Bharadvāja (Rigveda maṇḍala 6) and the epic figure share a name and lineage claim; their identity is a matter of tradition.

earliestMaterial.label: 8th century CE (reign of Nandivarman II, c. 731–796)

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa
nodes.summary: Vṛṣṇi prince, son of Vasudeva and Devakī, cousin and ally of the Pāṇḍavas, Arjuna’s charioteer and the teacher of the Bhagavad Gītā; the Mahābhārata calls him a portion of Nārāyaṇa, the Harivaṃśa and Purāṇas narrate his cowherd childhood, and Vaiṣṇava traditions worship him as Viṣṇu’s avatāra or, for some schools, the supreme Lord himself.
nodes.details:
In the Mahābhārata: the aṃśāvataraṇa says “that eternal god of gods called Nārāyaṇa — his portion among men was mighty Vāsudeva” (MBh (CE) 1.61.90); Vyāsa adds that Nārāyaṇa plucked a white and a black hair that entered Rohiṇī and Devakī, becoming Baladeva and Keśava (1.189.31). He wins Draupadī’s regard at the svayaṃvara, burns the Khāṇḍava forest with Arjuna (1.214–225), has Jarāsandha killed (2.22), beheads Śiśupāla with his discus (2.42.21), goes as envoy to the Kauravas and reveals a cosmic form (5.129), tests Karṇa with the secret of his birth (5.138), teaches the Gītā (6.23–40), devises stratagems that kill Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa and Duryodhana, curses Aśvatthāman (10.16), is cursed by Gāndhārī (11.25), revives Parīkṣit (14.68–69), and dies from the hunter Jarā’s arrow in the sole of his foot after the Yādava self-slaughter (16.4–5).

In the Harivaṃśa: birth to Devakī in Kaṃsa’s prison and exchange with Yaśodā’s daughter (HV 47–48), childhood feats in Vraja including Kāliya (55–56) and Govardhana (61–62), the night sports with the gopīs (63), the killing of Kaṃsa (76) and the founding of Dvārakā (85–86).

Theology: the Viṣṇu Purāṇa keeps the hair motif (ViP 5.1.60–64), whereas the Bhāgavata Purāṇa states that the other descents are portions but “Kṛṣṇa is the Lord himself” (BhP 1.3.28), the basis of the Gauḍīya view of Kṛṣṇa as source of the avatāras. Historians (Bhandarkar 1913; Raychaudhuri 1920; Jaiswal 1981) see the epic Kṛṣṇa as a fusion of Vāsudeva of the Sātvatas/Vṛṣṇis, a cowherd god (Gopāla) and Nārāyaṇa–Viṣṇu.
nodes.limits: The dataset records the literary portrayals and traditional theologies separately; the identity of the epic figure with Vāsudeva of early inscriptions or the Chāndogya’s Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra is a scholarly argument (see claim:krishna-devakiputra-identity).

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Vyāsa
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, the island-born son of the sage Parāśara and Satyavatī, credited with arranging the Vedas and composing the Mahābhārata; he fathers Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu and Vidura by niyoga and repeatedly intervenes in the story he authors.
nodes.details:
Birth: Parāśara meets Satyavatī (the fisher-girl Matsyagandhā) on a pilgrimage; she immediately bears Dvaipāyana on an island in the Yamunā, “thus Dvaipāyana was born to Satyavatī from Parāśara” (MBh (CE) 1.57.56–71).

Niyoga: when Vicitravīrya dies childless, Satyavatī calls on her son; Ambikā closes her eyes and bears the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Ambālikā turns pale and bears Pāṇḍu, and a servant woman bears Vidura, “Dharma in Vidura’s form” (1.100.15–28).

Authorship and transmission: he makes a Bhārata-saṃhitā of 24,000 verses without the upākhyānas (1.1.61) and has his disciple Vaiśampāyana recite it at Janamejaya’s sacrifice (1.54.21). The episode of Gaṇeśa writing to Vyāsa’s dictation is not in the CE constituted text (absent from the GRETIL e-text of 1.1 with its star passages; relegated to the apparatus). Sullivan (1990) and Hiltebeitel (2001) read Vyāsa’s double role as author and grandfather as central to the epic’s design.
nodes.limits: Authorship is a traditional attribution; the critical scholarship treats the epic as the product of many generations.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Bhīṣma
nodes.summary: Devavrata, son of King Śantanu and the river goddess Gaṅgā, who renounces the throne and marriage so that his father may marry Satyavatī; grand-uncle of both Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas, he commands the Kaurava army for ten days, falls to Arjuna and Śikhaṇḍin, and instructs Yudhiṣṭhira from his bed of arrows.
nodes.details: Birth: incarnation of one of the eight Vasus born of Gaṅgā to Śantanu because of Vasiṣṭha’s curse (MBh (CE) 1.61.68–69). Vow: “from this day, fisherman, I shall be celibate” (1.94.88), earning the name Bhīṣma (“the terrible”). Training: learned arms from Jāmadagnya Rāma (Paraśurāma) (1.94.35), whom he later fights over Ambā (5.178–186), each calling the other guru (5.178.17–26). Fall: struck by Arjuna with Śikhaṇḍin in front, he lies on a bed of arrows (6.114.84–92). Teaching: Rājadharma, Āpaddharma and Mokṣadharma (Book 12) and the Anuśāsanaparvan (Book 13, incl. the Viṣṇusahasranāma 13.135), dying at the winter solstice (13.154).

attributes.vow: lifelong celibacy and renunciation of the throne

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Yudhiṣṭhira
nodes.summary: Eldest Pāṇḍava, son of Kuntī by the god Dharma and legal son of Pāṇḍu; the “Dharma king” who loses his kingdom, brothers and wife at dice, endures exile, wins the war and rules, and is tested to the end by Dharma himself.
nodes.details: Born when Kuntī invokes Dharma (MBh (CE) 1.114.1); “a portion of Dharma” (1.61.84). Stakes and loses Draupadī (2.58.31). Answers the Yakṣa, who is Dharma in disguise (3.297). Refuses to enter heaven without the dog that followed him (17.3.7–10). Hiltebeitel (2001) reads the epic as the “education of the Dharma king”.

earliestText.label: within the epic’s growth, c. 3rd century BCE – 3rd century CE

nodes.name: Bhīma
nodes.summary: Second Pāṇḍava, son of Kuntī by the wind god Vāyu, of enormous strength and appetite; he kills Hiḍimba, Baka, Jarāsandha, Kīcaka, Duḥśāsana and the Kaurava brothers, and breaks Duryodhana’s thighs.
nodes.details: Kuntī calls Vāyu (MBh (CE) 1.114.9). Marries the rākṣasī Hiḍimbā, father of Ghaṭotkaca (1.143). Meets his elder half-brother Hanumān (3.146–150). Strikes Duryodhana’s thighs in the mace duel, against the rules (9.57.43–44).

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Arjuna
nodes.summary: Third Pāṇḍava, son of Kuntī by Indra, the supreme archer who wins Draupadī, marries Ulūpī, Citrāṅgadā and Subhadrā, obtains divine weapons from Śiva and Indra, and receives the Bhagavad Gītā from Kṛṣṇa, his charioteer and friend.
nodes.details: Born when Kuntī calls Śakra (MBh (CE) 1.114.27); Vyāsa names him Indra’s portion among the five former Indras (1.189.32). Droṇa’s favourite pupil, for whose pre-eminence Ekalavya’s thumb is demanded (1.123.26–39). Wins Draupadī at the svayaṃvara; during exile marries the nāga Ulūpī (1.206) and Citrāṅgadā of Maṇipūra (1.207), and carries off Subhadrā (1.211–212). Fights Śiva disguised as a kirāta and receives the Pāśupata weapon (3.40). Despairs before battle and is taught by Kṛṣṇa (6.23–40). Kills Bhīṣma (with Śikhaṇḍin), Jayadratha and Karṇa (8.67). In the Āśvamedhika he is killed and revived in a fight with his son Babhruvāhana (14.78–80).

earliestText.label: c. mid-4th c. BCE or later (terminus post quem c. 350 BCE)

nodes.name: Nakula
nodes.summary: One of the twin Pāṇḍavas (with Sahadeva), sons of Mādrī by the Aśvins and legal sons of Pāṇḍu.
nodes.details: Portions of the Aśvins (MBh (CE) 1.61.85); Mādrī uses Kuntī’s mantra to invoke the twin gods (1.115). In the final journey Sahadeva falls for pride in his wisdom and Nakula for pride in his beauty (17.2).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Sahadeva
nodes.summary: One of the twin Pāṇḍavas (with Nakula), sons of Mādrī by the Aśvins and legal sons of Pāṇḍu.
nodes.details: Portions of the Aśvins (MBh (CE) 1.61.85); Mādrī uses Kuntī’s mantra to invoke the twin gods (1.115). In the final journey Sahadeva falls for pride in his wisdom and Nakula for pride in his beauty (17.2).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Draupadī
nodes.summary: Daughter of King Drupada, born from the sacrificial altar, won by Arjuna at her svayaṃvara and married to all five Pāṇḍavas; staked and dragged into the assembly hall at the dice game, her question whether Yudhiṣṭhira could stake her after losing himself and her humiliation drive the epic’s conflict.
nodes.details:
Birth: a portion of Śrī born “from the middle of the altar” in Drupada’s line (MBh (CE) 1.61.95); she and her brother Dhṛṣṭadyumna arise from Drupada’s sacrifice (1.155).

Marriage: when the brothers return with her, Kuntī — not looking — tells them to “enjoy it together” (1.182.2). Drupada calls a woman with many husbands adharma (1.188.7); Yudhiṣṭhira cites the precedent of Jaṭilā Gautamī, wife of seven sages, and the authority of a mother’s word (1.188.14–16); Vyāsa privately tells Drupada of the five former Indras and Śrī (1.189.1–40) and of a sage’s daughter who asked Śiva five times for a husband (1.189.41ff; also told at 1.157.6–16).

Dice game: Yudhiṣṭhira stakes her (2.58.31); she asks whether he lost himself first (2.60.7–8); when Duḥśāsana pulls at her garment “another garment of the same kind appeared, many times over” (2.61.41). In the CE constituted text no prayer to Kṛṣṇa precedes this; the invocations “govinda dvārakāvāsin …” are star passages (*542–*547 after 2.61.40).

Later acts: rescued from Jayadratha (3.248–256) and Kīcaka (4.13–23); loses her five sons in Aśvatthāman’s night attack (10.8); falls first on the final journey, “because she was partial to Arjuna” (17.2.3–6). Her cult as a goddess in South India is studied by Hiltebeitel (1988).

attributes.sons: the five Draupadeyas (Prativindhya, Sutasoma, Śrutakīrti, Śatānīka, Śrutasena)

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Karṇa
nodes.summary: Son of Kuntī by the Sun god, born before her marriage with innate armour and earrings, set adrift and raised by the charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Rādhā; made king of Aṅga by Duryodhana, he remains loyal to the Kauravas even after learning he is the eldest Pāṇḍava, and is killed by Arjuna.
nodes.details:
Birth: the maiden Kuntī calls the Sun (arka) with Durvāsas’s mantra (MBh (CE) 1.104.8–10) and abandons the child; “the husband of Rādhā” takes him up (1.104.14). The Āraṇyakaparvan retells it at length — a basket on the Aśvanadī that drifts into the Carmaṇvatī, Yamunā and Gaṅgā (3.292.6–26) to Adhiratha and Rādhā (3.293). He is “a portion of the Sun” (1.61.89).

Status: at the tournament Bhīma scorns him as a sūta’s son unfit for Aṅga (1.127.5–7). Karṇa learns weapons from Paraśurāma by passing as a Bhārgava brahmin and is cursed when discovered; a brahmin also curses him that his chariot wheel will sink (12.2–3). He gives Indra his armour and earrings (3.284–294).

Revelations: Kṛṣṇa tells him he is Kuntī’s son born before Yudhiṣṭhira and offers him the throne (5.138.11–27); Kuntī asks him to join his brothers and he promises to spare all but Arjuna (5.142–144). After his death Kuntī reveals the truth to the Pāṇḍavas (11.27), Yudhiṣṭhira grieves (12.1), and Kuntī tells Vyāsa she abandoned the secretly born child in water (15.38.14). Killed by Arjuna while his wheel is stuck (8.67).
nodes.limits: How the different parvans present his birth and status is tabulated in cmp:karna-parentage.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Duryodhana
nodes.summary: Eldest of the hundred sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, rival of the Pāṇḍavas, who contrives the house of lac and the dice game, refuses any settlement and dies after Bhīma breaks his thighs.
nodes.details: Born of a portion of Kali (MBh (CE) 1.61.80). His envy at the Indraprastha hall begins the Dyūtaparvan (2.43). Some regional traditions honour him (e.g. a temple at Poruvazhy, Kerala) — see the regional domain.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Duḥśāsana
nodes.summary: Second Kaurava, who drags Draupadī into the assembly hall and pulls at her garment; Bhīma kills him in battle and drinks his blood, fulfilling a vow.
nodes.details: Bhīma seizes and kills him in the Karṇaparvan (MBh (CE) 8.61.1–3).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Droṇa
nodes.summary: Brahmin teacher of arms to the Kuru princes, son of the sage Bharadvāja born from a vessel (droṇa), who demands Ekalavya’s thumb, takes half of Drupada’s kingdom, commands the Kaurava army after Bhīṣma, and is killed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna after being told that “Aśvatthāman” is dead.
nodes.details: A portion of Bṛhaspati, “not born of a womb” (MBh (CE) 1.61.63). Marries Kṛpī, sister of Kṛpa, who bears Aśvatthāman (1.121.11–12). Learns weapons from Jāmadagnya Rāma (1.121.16–17). Defeats Drupada through his pupils, leaving him Kāmpilya (1.128.15). Killed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna (7.165).

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

earliestMaterial.label: 8th century CE (reign of Nandivarman II, c. 731–796)

nodes.name: Aśvatthāman
nodes.summary: Son of Droṇa and Kṛpī, born of the combined portions of Mahādeva, Antaka, Kāma and Krodha; after the war he massacres the sleeping Pāñcālas and Draupadī’s sons and is cursed by Kṛṣṇa to wander for three thousand years.
nodes.details: Kṛṣṇa’s curse — “for three thousand years you will wander this earth” (MBh (CE) 10.16.10) — follows Aśvatthāman’s directing a weapon at the wombs of the Pāṇḍava women.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

earliestMaterial.label: 8th century CE (reign of Nandivarman II, c. 731–796)

nodes.name: Vidura
nodes.summary: Son of Vyāsa by a servant woman of Ambikā, wise counsellor of the Kurus and uncle of the Pāṇḍavas, an incarnation of Dharma owing to the sage Māṇḍavya’s curse.
nodes.details: “Dharma in the form of Vidura, because of the curse of that great-souled one” (MBh (CE) 1.100.28), the curse being Aṇī-Māṇḍavya’s (1.101). The aṃśāvataraṇa list instead says “know Vidura … the son of Atri” (1.61.79), an internal variation noted here, not harmonised. His night counsel to Dhṛtarāṣṭra is the Viduranīti (5.33–40).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kuntī
nodes.summary: Pṛthā, daughter of the Yādava Śūra and sister of Vasudeva, given in adoption to King Kuntibhoja; with Durvāsas’s mantra she bears Karṇa by the Sun before marriage and, as Pāṇḍu’s wife, Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma and Arjuna by Dharma, Vāyu and Indra.
nodes.details: “Śūra, best of the Yadus, was Vasudeva’s father”; he gave his first-born daughter Pṛthā to his childless friend Kuntibhoja (MBh (CE) 1.104.1–3), making Kuntī the paternal aunt of Kṛṣṇa. She and Mādrī are incarnations of Siddhi and Dhṛti (1.61.98). Dies in the forest fire with Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī (Book 15).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Gāndhārī
nodes.summary: Princess of Gandhāra, daughter of Subala and sister of Śakuni, who blindfolds herself on marrying the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra, bears the hundred Kauravas and a daughter, and after the war curses Kṛṣṇa with the destruction of his clan.
nodes.details: An incarnation of Mati (MBh (CE) 1.61.98). Her curse on Kṛṣṇa (11.25) is fulfilled in the Mausalaparvan.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Dhṛtarāṣṭra
nodes.summary: Blind king of the Kurus, son of Vyāsa and Ambikā by niyoga, husband of Gāndhārī and father of the hundred Kauravas; his indulgence of Duryodhana allows the dice game and the war, which Sañjaya narrates to him.
nodes.details: Blind “through his mother’s fault and the sage’s anger” (MBh (CE) 1.61.78). His question “dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre …” opens the Gītā (6.23.1).

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Pāṇḍu
nodes.summary: King of the Kurus, son of Vyāsa and Ambālikā by niyoga, cursed to die if he approaches a woman; he authorises Kuntī and Mādrī to bear sons by gods and is the legal father of the five Pāṇḍavas.
nodes.details: Named for the pallor (pāṇḍu) of his mother (MBh (CE) 1.100.17). He urges Kuntī to invoke Dharma (1.113.39–42).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Mādrī
nodes.summary: Princess of Madra, second wife of Pāṇḍu, who bears the twins Nakula and Sahadeva by the Aśvins and joins Pāṇḍu on his funeral pyre.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Śakuni
nodes.summary: Prince of Gandhāra, son of Subala and brother of Gāndhārī, the expert dicer who wins for Duryodhana against Yudhiṣṭhira; an incarnation of the Dvāpara age.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Balarāma
nodes.summary: Elder brother of Kṛṣṇa, son of Vasudeva and Rohiṇī, wielder of the plough and club, teacher of Duryodhana and Bhīma in mace fighting, who stays neutral in the war; the Mahābhārata calls him a portion of the serpent Śeṣa.
nodes.details: “The portion of the serpent Śeṣa was mighty Baladeva” (MBh (CE) 1.61.91); from Nārāyaṇa’s white hair entering Rohiṇī (1.189.31). Goes on pilgrimage along the Sarasvatī during the war (Śalyaparvan) and dies in yoga as a great serpent leaves his mouth and enters the ocean (MBh (CE) 16.5.12–13). His identity with the deity Saṅkarṣaṇa of early inscriptions and coins is a scholarly identification.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Abhimanyu
nodes.summary: Son of Arjuna and Subhadrā, married to Uttarā, who breaks into Droṇa’s circular array on the thirteenth day and is killed after being surrounded; father of the posthumously born Parīkṣit.
nodes.details: An incarnation of Suvarcas, son of Soma (MBh (CE) 1.61.86). Killed by Duḥśāsana’s son with a mace (7.48.4–12).

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Subhadrā
nodes.summary: Sister of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, abducted with Kṛṣṇa’s approval by Arjuna and married to him; mother of Abhimanyu.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

earliestMaterial.label: begun under Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga, early–mid 12th c.; completion given as 1161 in Wikipedia’s infobox

nodes.name: Śantanu
nodes.summary: Kuru king, husband of Gaṅgā (mother of Bhīṣma) and then of Satyavatī (mother of Citrāṅgada and Vicitravīrya).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Satyavatī
nodes.summary: Fisherman’s daughter (born from a fish, raised by the chief of fishermen) who bears Vyāsa to Parāśara and then marries Śantanu on condition that her son inherit, prompting Bhīṣma’s vow; matriarch of the Kuru line.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Drupada
nodes.summary: King of Pañcāla, Droṇa’s estranged boyhood friend, who sacrifices for a son to kill Droṇa and receives Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Draupadī from the fire; father also of Śikhaṇḍin.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Śikhaṇḍin
nodes.summary: Child of Drupada born female (Śikhaṇḍinī), the reborn Ambā, who becomes male through an exchange with the yakṣa Sthūṇa; Bhīṣma refuses to fight him, and Arjuna shoots Bhīṣma from behind him.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Ekalavya
nodes.summary: Niṣāda prince, son of Hiraṇyadhanus, who learns archery before a clay image of Droṇa after being refused as a pupil; when his skill surpasses Arjuna’s, Droṇa demands his right thumb as teacher’s fee, and Ekalavya gives it.
nodes.details: “Let your right thumb be given to me” (tvayāṅguṣṭho dakṣiṇo dīyatāṃ mama, MBh (CE) 1.123.35); afterwards he draws with his fingers and is no longer as fast (1.123.38). In later Harivaṃśa/Purāṇic tradition he is said to be killed by Kṛṣṇa (not checked).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Jarāsandha
nodes.summary: King of Magadha, born in two halves joined by the demoness Jarā, enemy of Kṛṣṇa and the Yādavas, killed by Bhīma in a wrestling match before the rājasūya.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Śiśupāla
nodes.summary: King of Cedi and cousin of Kṛṣṇa who objects to Kṛṣṇa’s receiving the first honour at Yudhiṣṭhira’s rājasūya and is beheaded by Kṛṣṇa’s discus.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Sañjaya
nodes.summary: Charioteer and minister of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, given divine sight by Vyāsa to narrate the battle — including the Bhagavad Gītā — to the blind king.

nodes.name: Ghaṭotkaca
nodes.summary: Son of Bhīma and the rākṣasī Hiḍimbā, who fights for the Pāṇḍavas and is killed at night by Karṇa with the spear Indra had given him — the weapon Karṇa had reserved for Arjuna.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Parīkṣit
nodes.summary: Son of Abhimanyu and Uttarā, born still-born after Aśvatthāman’s weapon and revived by Kṛṣṇa; he succeeds Yudhiṣṭhira and dies of the bite of the serpent Takṣaka, which prompts his son Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice.
nodes.details: Uttarā’s lament and the revival are narrated in MBh (CE) 14.68–69. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa is addressed to him by Śuka.

nodes.name: Janamejaya
nodes.summary: Kuru king, son of Parīkṣit, at whose snake sacrifice Vaiśampāyana recites the Mahābhārata; his questions punctuate the narrative.
nodes.details: After the sacrifice he returns from Takṣaśilā to Gajāhvaya (Hāstinapura) (MBh (CE) 18.5.29).

earliestText.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

nodes.name: Vaiśampāyana
nodes.summary: Disciple of Vyāsa who, at his teacher’s instruction, recites the Mahābhārata to King Janamejaya during the snake sacrifice.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Devakī
nodes.summary: Wife of Vasudeva and mother of Kṛṣṇa, whose earlier children are killed by her cousin Kaṃsa; Kṛṣṇa is born to her in captivity and exchanged with Yaśodā’s daughter.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Vasudeva (father of Kṛṣṇa)
nodes.summary: Yādava (Vṛṣṇi) noble, son of Śūra, brother of Kuntī and husband of Devakī and Rohiṇī; father of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma. Kept distinct from the deity Vāsudeva.
nodes.limits: Not to be confused with Vāsudeva (patronymic, “son of Vasudeva”) used for Kṛṣṇa and for the deity of early inscriptions (deity:vasudeva).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Nanda
nodes.summary: Chief of the cowherds of Vraja who, with his wife Yaśodā, fosters Kṛṣṇa (and Balarāma) after Vasudeva brings the infant from Mathurā.

nodes.name: Yaśodā
nodes.summary: Wife of Nanda and foster mother of Kṛṣṇa; she gives birth to a daughter at the same time as Devakī bears Kṛṣṇa, and the children are exchanged.
nodes.details: “Devakī and Yaśodā gave birth at the same time” (HV (CE) 48.11).

nodes.name: Kaṃsa
nodes.summary: King of Mathurā, son of Ugrasena and cousin of Devakī, who kills her children fearing a prophecy and is killed by Kṛṣṇa in the wrestling arena.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Rukmiṇī
nodes.summary: Princess of Vidarbha, daughter of Bhīṣmaka, abducted by Kṛṣṇa before her intended marriage to Śiśupāla; Kṛṣṇa’s chief queen and mother of Pradyumna. Later tradition identifies her with Lakṣmī.

nodes.name: Pradyumna
nodes.summary: Son of Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī, carried off as an infant by the demon Śambara and later kills him; the Mahābhārata calls him an incarnation of Sanatkumāra.

nodes.name: Nala
nodes.summary: King of Niṣadha, son of Vīrasena, whose love for Damayantī, loss of his kingdom at dice under the influence of Kali, and eventual restoration form the Nalopākhyāna (MBh 3.50–78) — distinct from the vānara engineer Nala (char:nala-vanara).
nodes.details: “There was a king named Nala, son of Vīrasena” (MBh (CE) 3.50.1). The story is told to console Yudhiṣṭhira, another king who lost his kingdom at dice; at its end Bṛhadaśva teaches him the secret of the dice (3.78).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Damayantī
nodes.summary: Princess of Vidarbha who chooses Nala over the gods at her svayaṃvara, is abandoned by him in the forest, and through her resourcefulness recovers him.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Sāvitrī
nodes.summary: Daughter of King Aśvapati of Madra who chooses the exiled prince Satyavān knowing he will die within a year, follows Yama when he takes Satyavān’s life, and wins back her husband by her eloquence and boons.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Śakuntalā
nodes.summary: Daughter of the sage Viśvāmitra and the apsaras Menakā, raised by the sage Kaṇva, who marries King Duḥṣanta by gāndharva rite and, when he later disowns her, compels his recognition of their son Bharata.
nodes.details: In the epic she argues her own case before the king (MBh (CE) 1.69: “rājan sarṣapamātrāṇi paracchidrāṇi paśyasi …”); Kālidāsa’s drama Abhijñānaśākuntala introduces the curse and the ring.

earliestText.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

nodes.name: Rohiṇī (wife of Vasudeva)
nodes.summary: Wife of Vasudeva and mother of Balarāma; in Vyāsa’s account Nārāyaṇa’s white hair enters her womb, while in the Harivaṃśa Devakī’s seventh embryo is transferred to her.
nodes.details: Distinct from the lunar asterism and from the cow-mother Rohiṇī of MBh 1.60.65.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Ambā
nodes.summary: Eldest princess of Kāśī, abducted by Bhīṣma for Vicitravīrya, rejected by her chosen suitor Śālva and by Bhīṣma; she does austerities for Bhīṣma’s death and is reborn as Śikhaṇḍinī, daughter of Drupada.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Ambikā
nodes.summary: Second princess of Kāśī, wife of Vicitravīrya, who by niyoga with Vyāsa bears the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Ambālikā
nodes.summary: Youngest princess of Kāśī, wife of Vicitravīrya, who by niyoga with Vyāsa bears Pāṇḍu.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Parāśara
nodes.summary: Sage, grandson of Vasiṣṭha, who fathers Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa on Satyavatī during a pilgrimage and restores her virginity.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Vicitravīrya
nodes.summary: Younger son of Śantanu and Satyavatī, married to Ambikā and Ambālikā, who dies childless, occasioning the niyoga with Vyāsa.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Citrāṅgada (son of Śantanu)
nodes.summary: Elder son of Śantanu and Satyavatī, installed by Bhīṣma and killed young by a gandharva of the same name — distinct from Citrāṅgadā of Maṇipūra.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Uttarā
nodes.summary: Daughter of King Virāṭa of Matsya, taught dance by the disguised Arjuna, whom Arjuna accepts as daughter-in-law for Abhimanyu; mother of Parīkṣit.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Ulūpī
nodes.summary: Nāga princess who takes Arjuna beneath the Gaṅgā during his exile and becomes his wife; mother of Irāvat.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Citrāṅgadā (of Maṇipūra)
nodes.summary: Daughter of King Citravāhana of Maṇipūra, married to Arjuna on condition that their son continue her father’s line; mother of Babhruvāhana.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Babhruvāhana
nodes.summary: Son of Arjuna and Citrāṅgadā, king of Maṇipūra, who fights and kills his father during the horse-sacrifice campaign; Arjuna is revived by Ulūpī’s jewel.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Irāvat
nodes.summary: Son of Arjuna and the nāga Ulūpī, killed in the war; in South Indian traditions worshipped as Aravāṉ.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Adhiratha
nodes.summary: Charioteer (sūta) of the Kurus, husband of Rādhā, who finds the infant Karṇa in a basket on the river and raises him as his son.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Rādhā (foster mother of Karṇa)
nodes.summary: Wife of the charioteer Adhiratha, childless until she takes in the infant Karṇa found floating in a basket; Karṇa is called Rādheya after her. Distinct from Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa’s beloved (char:radha).
nodes.limits: Kept separate from char:radha (the gopī beloved of Kṛṣṇa in later literature); the two share only a name.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Hiḍimbā
nodes.summary: Rākṣasī of the forest who falls in love with Bhīma after he kills her brother Hiḍimba; with Kuntī’s leave she lives with him and bears Ghaṭotkaca.

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Kṛpa
nodes.summary: Brahmin teacher of arms to the Kuru princes before Droṇa, son of the sage Śaradvat, adopted with his twin sister Kṛpī by Śantanu; one of the three Kaurava survivors.
nodes.details: Born with his sister from Śaradvat’s seed falling on a clump of reeds, found and raised by Śantanu “out of compassion (kṛpā)” (MBh (CE) 1.120.16); counted among the Rudras (1.61.71).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kṛpī
nodes.summary: Twin sister of Kṛpa, wife of Droṇa and mother of Aśvatthāman.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Śalya
nodes.summary: King of Madra and brother of Mādrī, maternal uncle of Nakula and Sahadeva, tricked by Duryodhana into fighting for the Kauravas; Karṇa’s charioteer and the last Kaurava commander, killed by Yudhiṣṭhira.
nodes.details: Mādrī is “daughter of the lord of Madra” (MBh (CE) 1.105.4); Nakula wins over “his maternal uncle Śalya” (mātulaṃ … śalyaṃ, 2.29.13) and Yudhiṣṭhira later honours “his maternal uncle, the lord of Madra” (6.41.83). Duryodhana wins him over on his way to the Pāṇḍavas (5.8); Yudhiṣṭhira kills him (9.16).

earliestText.label: disputed: from the last centuries BCE or early centuries CE (if by Bhāsa) to the late first millennium CE (Kerala stage versions)

nodes.name: Virāṭa
nodes.summary: King of the Matsyas at whose court the Pāṇḍavas spend the thirteenth year of exile in disguise; father of Uttarā and Uttara, ally of the Pāṇḍavas in the war.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kīcaka
nodes.summary: Commander of Virāṭa’s army and brother of Queen Sudeṣṇā, who harasses the disguised Draupadī and is killed at night by Bhīma.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Bhīṣmaka
nodes.summary: King of Vidarbha (Kuṇḍina), father of Rukmiṇī and Rukmin, a vassal-ally of Jarāsandha.

nodes.name: Satyabhāmā
nodes.summary: Beloved wife of Kṛṣṇa, daughter of Satrājit, who in the Āraṇyakaparvan asks Draupadī how she keeps five husbands devoted.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Ugrasena
nodes.summary: King of the Vṛṣṇis/Andhakas at Mathurā, father of Kaṃsa, deposed by his son and restored by Kṛṣṇa.

nodes.name: Sāmba
nodes.summary: Son of Kṛṣṇa and Jāmbavatī whom the Yādava youths dress as a pregnant woman to mock visiting sages; the sages’ curse that he will bear an iron club brings about the Yādavas’ destruction.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Jarā (the hunter)
nodes.summary: Hunter whose arrow, mistaking Kṛṣṇa’s foot for a deer, strikes the sole of Kṛṣṇa’s foot as he lies in yoga, causing his death.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Dhṛṣṭadyumna
nodes.summary: Son of Drupada born from the sacrificial fire with Draupadī, destined to kill Droṇa; commander of the Pāṇḍava army, he beheads Droṇa and is killed in his sleep by Aśvatthāman.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Sātyaki
nodes.summary: Vṛṣṇi warrior, pupil of Arjuna and loyal ally of the Pāṇḍavas; an incarnation of the Maruts.
nodes.details: Also called Yuyudhāna.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kṛtavarman
nodes.summary: Vṛṣṇi/Bhoja warrior who fights for the Kauravas, one of the three survivors who join Aśvatthāman’s night raid.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Jayadratha
nodes.summary: King of the Sindhus, husband of Duḥśalā, who tries to abduct Draupadī during the exile and is killed by Arjuna on the fourteenth day.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Duḥśalā
nodes.summary: The only daughter of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, married to Jayadratha.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Yuyutsu
nodes.summary: Son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra by a vaiśya woman, who crosses over to the Pāṇḍavas before the battle and survives it.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kuntibhoja
nodes.summary: Childless king, friend of Śūra, who receives Śūra’s first daughter Pṛthā in adoption; she is therefore called Kuntī.

nodes.name: Śūra (Yādava)
nodes.summary: Yādava chief, father of Vasudeva and of Pṛthā (Kuntī), whom he gives in adoption to Kuntibhoja.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Subala
nodes.summary: King of Gandhāra, father of Gāndhārī and Śakuni.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Duḥṣanta
nodes.summary: Paurava king who meets Śakuntalā while hunting, marries her by gāndharva rite and later acknowledges their son Bharata.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Bharata (son of Śakuntalā)
nodes.summary: Son of Duḥṣanta and Śakuntalā, universal sovereign from whom the Bhārata lineage and the epic take their name — distinct from Rāma’s brother Bharata.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kaṇva
nodes.summary: Sage of the Kāśyapa line who raises Śakuntalā in his hermitage.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Menakā
nodes.summary: Apsaras sent by Indra to distract Viśvāmitra; mother of Śakuntalā.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Satyavān
nodes.summary: Son of the blind, exiled king Dyumatsena, chosen by Sāvitrī as husband though fated to die within a year.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Aśvapati
nodes.summary: King of Madra, father of Sāvitrī, who obtains her by worshipping the goddess Sāvitrī.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Dyumatsena
nodes.summary: Exiled, later blind king of the Śālvas, father of Satyavān, whose sight and kingdom are restored by Sāvitrī’s boons.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Bṛhadaśva
nodes.summary: Sage who visits the exiled Pāṇḍavas and tells Yudhiṣṭhira the story of Nala and Damayantī.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Māṇḍavya
nodes.summary: Sage (Aṇī-Māṇḍavya) wrongly impaled as a thief, who curses Dharma for punishing a childhood fault too severely; Dharma is therefore born as Vidura.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Ugraśravas
nodes.summary: Bard (sūta, paurāṇika), son of Lomaharṣaṇa, who comes to Śaunaka’s twelve-year sacrifice in the Naimiṣa forest and recites the Mahābhārata as he heard it from Vaiśampāyana.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Lomaharṣaṇa
nodes.summary: Bard (sūta), father of Ugraśravas, regarded in Purāṇic tradition as a disciple of Vyāsa who received the Purāṇas.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Śaunaka
nodes.summary: Kulapati (head of a family of sages) of the Naimiṣa forest, at whose twelve-year sacrifice Ugraśravas recites the Mahābhārata.
nodes.limits: The epic’s Śaunaka is a frame figure; identification with the Vedic Śaunaka (Atharvaveda school, Ṛgveda anukramaṇīs) is traditional, not assumed.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Takṣaka
nodes.summary: Serpent king whose bite kills Parīkṣit, provoking Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Āstīka
nodes.summary: Son of the sage Jaratkāru and the nāga woman Jaratkāru who halts Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice and saves Takṣaka.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Maya (dānava architect)
nodes.summary: Asura (dānava) master-builder and magician: he builds the three cities of Tripura, which Śiva burns (the Matsya and Śiva Purāṇas let him survive); in the Mahābhārata he builds the Pāṇḍavas’ assembly hall in gratitude for being spared in the Khāṇḍava fire; in the Rāmāyaṇa’s Uttarakāṇḍa he is the father of Mandodarī.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176
Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

nodes.limits: Treated as one figure because both epics call him a daitya/dānava architect named Maya; that the texts intend the same being is a reasonable but traditional identification.
nodes.details: Merged in verification round 2 with the Purāṇa agent’s record char:maya-asura, which described the same figure.

nodes.name: Kāliya
nodes.summary: Many-headed serpent poisoning a pool of the Yamunā in Vraja, subdued by the boy Kṛṣṇa, who dances on his heads and banishes him to the ocean.

nodes.name: Dharma (the god)
nodes.summary: Dharma personified as a god in the Mahābhārata: the divine father of Yudhiṣṭhira, born as Vidura through Māṇḍavya’s curse, the yakṣa who questions Yudhiṣṭhira at the lake and the dog who follows him to heaven. The epic at times identifies him with Yama.
nodes.details: Kuntī invokes “Dharma the imperishable” to conceive Yudhiṣṭhira (MBh (CE) 1.114.1). Vidura is “Dharma in Vidura’s form” (1.100.28). At the lake Dharma takes the form of a crane and then a yakṣa (3.297.11–18); in the Mahāprasthānika the dog is Dharma (17.3). Hopkins (1915) documents the epic’s fluctuating identification of Dharma with Yama (Dharmarāja).
nodes.limits: Distinct from concept:dharma (the norm itself); the identification with Yama is text- and passage-dependent and is recorded as an IDENTIFIED_WITH assertion.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Dharma
nodes.summary: The central normative concept of the epics — right order, duty, law and virtue — whose subtlety (sūkṣmatā) the Mahābhārata repeatedly stresses, notably in Draupadī’s question, Yudhiṣṭhira’s dilemmas and Bhīṣma’s teachings.
nodes.details: Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s “because of the subtlety of dharma we do not know its course” (na tu dharmasya sūkṣmatvād gatiṃ vidmaḥ, MBh (CE) 1.188.11) during the debate on Draupadī’s marriage is one of many such statements. The Rāmāyaṇa presents Rāma as dharma embodied; the Gītā links dharma to one’s own duty (svadharma). The concept long predates the epics (Vedic dhárman) and is elaborated in Dharmaśāstra (Kane).
nodes.limits: This node represents the epic usage; Vedic and śāstric developments belong to other domains.

nodes.name: Rāma’s exile
nodes.summary: Rāma’s fourteen-year banishment to the forest with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, imposed through Kaikeyī’s boons and accepted by Rāma to keep his father’s word.
nodes.details: Kaikeyī asks for Bharata’s consecration and Rāma’s exile “for fourteen years” (VR (CE) 2.9.15). The exile spans Books 2–6 and passes Śṛṅgaverapura, Prayāga, Citrakūṭa, the Daṇḍaka forest and Pañcavaṭī.

nodes.name: The breaking of Śiva’s bow and Sītā’s marriage
nodes.summary: At Mithilā Rāma lifts and breaks the great bow of Śiva that Janaka had set as the test for Sītā’s hand; the four brothers are then married to Sītā, Ūrmilā, Māṇḍavī and Śrutakīrti.
nodes.details: Janaka promises Sītā, “not born of a womb”, to whoever strings the bow (VR (CE) 1.65.27). In Vālmīki it is not a svayaṃvara in the sense of Sītā choosing; the Rāmopākhyāna has no bow episode at all.
nodes.limits: The registry label “svayaṃvara” reflects later usage; the Vālmīki text presents a vīryaśulka (bride-price of valour) contest (1.70.21).

nodes.name: The abduction of Sītā
nodes.summary: Rāvaṇa, having sent Mārīca as a golden deer to draw Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa away, carries Sītā off from the Pañcavaṭī hermitage through the sky to Laṅkā, mortally wounding Jaṭāyu who tries to stop him.

nodes.name: Hanumān’s leap and search in Laṅkā
nodes.summary: Hanumān leaps the ocean from the southern shore, searches Laṅkā by night, finds Sītā in the aśoka grove, gives her Rāma’s ring, is captured and has his tail set on fire, and burns the city before returning.

nodes.name: The building of the bridge to Laṅkā
nodes.summary: At the Ocean’s suggestion the vānara Nala, son of Viśvakarman, directs the vānaras in building a causeway across the sea to Laṅkā.
nodes.limits: A narrative episode. The claim that the natural shoal chain called Adam’s Bridge is this structure is a separate claim (claim:rama-setu-built, owned by the material domain).

nodes.name: The war in Laṅkā and the death of Rāvaṇa
nodes.summary: The war between Rāma’s vānara army and Rāvaṇa’s rākṣasas, culminating in the deaths of Kumbhakarṇa, Indrajit and Rāvaṇa, whom Rāma kills with the Brahmā weapon given by Agastya.

nodes.name: Sītā’s ordeal by fire
nodes.summary: After Rāvaṇa’s death Rāma publicly refuses Sītā; she has Lakṣmaṇa build a pyre and enters the fire calling Agni to witness her fidelity; Agni returns her unharmed and the gods proclaim Rāma’s divinity.
nodes.details: The Rāmopākhyāna has the repudiation and divine testimony but no fire-entry (MBh (CE) 3.275.10–36). See cmp:sita-ordeal-banishment.

nodes.name: The banishment of Sītā and her return to the earth
nodes.summary: Hearing that his subjects gossip about Sītā’s stay in Rāvaṇa’s house, Rāma has Lakṣmaṇa abandon the pregnant Sītā near Vālmīki’s hermitage; years later, asked to prove her purity again at the horse sacrifice, she calls upon the Earth, who receives her.
nodes.details: Found only in the Uttarakāṇḍa among the Sanskrit epic versions; absent from the Rāmopākhyāna.

nodes.name: The krauñca bird and the first śloka
nodes.summary: Vālmīki sees a hunter kill one of a pair of mating krauñca birds; his grief (śoka) issues spontaneously as the first verse (śloka), and Brahmā bids him compose Rāma’s story in that metre.

sources.quote: mā niṣāda pratiṣṭhāṃ tvam agamaḥ śāśvatīḥ samāḥ / yat krauñcamithunād ekam avadhīḥ kāmamohitam

nodes.name: The sacrifice for sons and the birth of the four princes
nodes.summary: Daśaratha’s sacrifice performed by Ṛśyaśṛṅga, the gods’ request that Viṣṇu be born as a man to kill Rāvaṇa, and the births of Rāma, Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna as portions of Viṣṇu.

nodes.name: Rāma kills Tāṭakā
nodes.summary: On Viśvāmitra’s instruction the young Rāma kills the demoness Tāṭakā, his first deed against the rākṣasas.

nodes.name: The release of Ahalyā
nodes.summary: Passing Gautama’s hermitage, Rāma ends the curse on Ahalyā, who had been seduced by Indra.

nodes.name: Rāma and Paraśurāma
nodes.summary: On the way back from Mithilā, Jāmadagnya Rāma (Paraśurāma) challenges Dāśarathi Rāma to string Viṣṇu’s bow; Rāma does so and Paraśurāma yields.

nodes.name: Kaikeyī’s two boons
nodes.summary: Incited by Mantharā, Kaikeyī reminds Daśaratha of the two boons he granted when she saved him in battle and demands Bharata’s consecration and Rāma’s exile.

nodes.name: The death of Daśaratha
nodes.summary: Grieving for Rāma, Daśaratha recalls how he once killed an ascetic’s son and was cursed to die lamenting a son, and dies in the night.

nodes.name: Bharata and the sandals
nodes.summary: Bharata seeks Rāma at Citrakūṭa and begs him to return; Rāma refuses, and Bharata takes his gold-adorned sandals to rule in his name.

nodes.name: The mutilation of Śūrpaṇakhā
nodes.summary: Rāvaṇa’s sister Śūrpaṇakhā propositions Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa at Pañcavaṭī and attacks Sītā; Lakṣmaṇa cuts off her nose and ears, setting the war with the rākṣasas in motion.

nodes.name: The golden deer
nodes.summary: At Rāvaṇa’s command Mārīca takes the form of a jewelled golden deer near the hermitage; Sītā asks Rāma to catch it, and Mārīca, dying, cries out in Rāma’s voice to draw Lakṣmaṇa away.

nodes.name: Jaṭāyu’s fight with Rāvaṇa
nodes.summary: The vulture king Jaṭāyu attacks Rāvaṇa to free Sītā, is mortally wounded, and lives long enough to tell Rāma what happened.

nodes.name: The alliance of Rāma and Sugrīva
nodes.summary: Hanumān brings Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to Sugrīva on Ṛśyamūka; they swear friendship before fire, Rāma promising to kill Vālin and Sugrīva to search for Sītā.

nodes.name: The killing of Vālin
nodes.summary: During Sugrīva’s second duel with Vālin, Rāma shoots Vālin from concealment; the dying Vālin reproaches him and Rāma defends the act.

nodes.name: Vibhīṣaṇa joins Rāma
nodes.summary: Rebuked by Rāvaṇa for urging Sītā’s return, Vibhīṣaṇa flies to Rāma’s camp; despite Sugrīva’s suspicion Rāma accepts him and promises him Laṅkā.

nodes.name: The death of Kumbhakarṇa
nodes.summary: Roused from sleep for the war, Kumbhakarṇa devastates the vānaras until he is killed — by Rāma in Vālmīki’s Yuddhakāṇḍa, by Lakṣmaṇa with the Brahmā weapon in the Mahābhārata’s Rāmopākhyāna.

nodes.name: The death of Indrajit
nodes.summary: Lakṣmaṇa kills Rāvaṇa’s son Indrajit after a long duel.

nodes.name: The return to Ayodhyā and Rāma’s consecration
nodes.summary: Rāma returns to Ayodhyā with Sītā and is consecrated king, as the gods consecrated Indra.

nodes.name: Rāvaṇa’s boon from Brahmā
nodes.summary: Through austerities Rāvaṇa obtains from Brahmā invulnerability to gods, demons, nāgas, yakṣas and other beings — but not to humans; Vibhīṣaṇa asks only for steadfastness in dharma.

nodes.name: Vedavatī’s curse
nodes.summary: The ascetic Vedavatī, molested by Rāvaṇa, enters the fire vowing to be reborn for his destruction; the Uttarakāṇḍa says she is reborn as Sītā.

nodes.name: Hanumān’s childhood leap at the sun
nodes.summary: The infant Hanumān leaps at the rising sun thinking it a fruit, is struck down by Indra’s thunderbolt; the wind god withdraws in grief until the gods restore the child and grant him boons.

nodes.name: The killing of Śambūka
nodes.summary: When a brahmin’s son dies prematurely, Rāma finds the śūdra Śambūka performing austerities and beheads him, after which the boy revives.

nodes.name: Lava and Kuśa sing the Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: At Vālmīki’s instruction the twins sing the whole poem in Rāma’s presence during his horse sacrifice, leading to their recognition as his sons.

nodes.name: Rāma’s return to Viṣṇu’s form
nodes.summary: At the end of his reign Rāma, with his brothers, enters the Sarayū and, at Brahmā’s invitation, the radiance of Viṣṇu.

nodes.name: The dice game
nodes.summary: Duryodhana, envious of the Pāṇḍavas’ wealth, has Śakuni challenge Yudhiṣṭhira to dice in the new hall at Hāstinapura; Yudhiṣṭhira loses his wealth, kingdom, brothers, himself and Draupadī, and in the return match the Pāṇḍavas are condemned to twelve years’ exile and a thirteenth incognito.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The humiliation of Draupadī in the assembly hall
nodes.summary: Draupadī, staked and lost, is dragged by her hair into the hall in a single garment; she asks whether Yudhiṣṭhira lost himself before staking her; Duḥśāsana tries to strip her and her garment is miraculously renewed; Dhṛtarāṣṭra finally grants her boons.
nodes.details: In the CE constituted text the miracle is stated without an agent (“another garment of the same kind appeared, many times over”, 2.61.41); Draupadī’s prayers to Kṛṣṇa are found only in star passages *542–*547 inserted after 2.61.40.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Draupadī’s svayaṃvara
nodes.summary: At Drupada’s city the disguised Arjuna strings the great bow and hits the target to win Draupadī; Kuntī’s unwitting instruction to share leads to her marriage to all five Pāṇḍavas, justified in several ways in the text.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The house of lac
nodes.summary: Duryodhana has a house of lac built at Vāraṇāvata to burn the Pāṇḍavas and Kuntī; warned by Vidura, they escape through a tunnel and are thought dead.
nodes.details: Duryodhana broods (MBh (CE) 1.129), the Pāṇḍavas are sent to Vāraṇāvata (1.130–131), Purocana’s house is fired and the townspeople find the remains (1.136–137), and the family escapes (1.138).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The Kurukṣetra war
nodes.summary: The eighteen-day war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas at Kurukṣetra, narrated in the Bhīṣma-, Droṇa-, Karṇa- and Śalyaparvans, which ends in the death of almost all the warriors on both sides.
nodes.limits: The war is a narrative event; dates proposed for a “historical” war (e.g. 3102 BCE by traditional reckoning) are recorded as traditional, not as facts.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa’s discourse to Arjuna (the Gītā)
nodes.summary: On the battlefield, Arjuna, seeing his kinsmen and teachers arrayed against him, lays down his bow; Kṛṣṇa teaches him on duty, action without attachment, knowledge and devotion, and reveals his universal form.

nodes.name: The destruction of the Yādavas and Kṛṣṇa’s death
nodes.summary: Thirty-six years after the war, the Yādavas, cursed through Sāmba and fulfilling Gāndhārī’s curse, kill one another at Prabhāsa with clubs grown from erakā grass; Balarāma departs in yoga and Kṛṣṇa is shot in the foot by the hunter Jarā.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The birth of Kṛṣṇa
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa is born to Devakī and Vasudeva in Kaṃsa’s prison at Mathurā, after Kaṃsa has killed her earlier children; he is carried to Vraja and exchanged with the daughter born to Yaśodā at the same time.

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa lifts Mount Govardhana
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa persuades the cowherds to honour the mountain instead of Indra; when Indra sends a deluge he uproots Govardhana and holds it up for seven days to shelter Vraja, and Indra comes to honour him.

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa subdues the serpent Kāliya
nodes.summary: The boy Kṛṣṇa plunges into the pool of the Yamunā poisoned by Kāliya, subdues the serpent by dancing on its heads and sends it away to the ocean.

nodes.name: The killing of Kaṃsa
nodes.summary: Summoned to Mathurā for a wrestling festival, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma kill the wrestlers, and Kṛṣṇa drags Kaṃsa down by the hair and kills him, restoring Ugrasena.

nodes.name: Nala and Damayantī
nodes.summary: Damayantī chooses Nala over the gods; possessed by Kali, Nala loses his kingdom at dice to his brother Puṣkara and abandons her in the forest; after many trials, disguised as a charioteer, he is recognised and regains his kingdom.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Sāvitrī and Satyavān
nodes.summary: Sāvitrī marries Satyavān knowing he will die in a year; when Yama takes his life she follows and, winning boon after boon by her words, obtains his life back.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Ugraśravas’ recitation at Naimiṣa
nodes.summary: The outer frame of the Mahābhārata: the bard Ugraśravas arrives at Śaunaka’s twelve-year sacrifice in the Naimiṣa forest and recites the epic he heard at Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice
nodes.summary: To avenge his father Parīkṣit, killed by Takṣaka, Janamejaya performs a sacrifice that draws the serpents into the fire; Āstīka stops it. During its intervals Vaiśampāyana recites the Mahābhārata.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Bhīṣma’s vow
nodes.summary: To let his father Śantanu marry Satyavatī, whose father demands that her son inherit, Devavrata renounces the throne and vows lifelong celibacy, and is thenceforth called Bhīṣma.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Vyāsa’s niyoga: the births of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu and Vidura
nodes.summary: After Vicitravīrya dies childless, Satyavatī asks her son Vyāsa to raise offspring on his widows; Ambikā bears the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Ambālikā the pale Pāṇḍu, and a servant woman Vidura.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The birth and abandonment of Karṇa
nodes.summary: The unmarried Kuntī tests Durvāsas’s mantra on the Sun and bears Karṇa with armour and earrings; fearing disgrace she sets him adrift, and the charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Rādhā raise him.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The births of the Pāṇḍavas
nodes.summary: Cursed never to approach his wives, Pāṇḍu asks Kuntī to use her mantra: she bears Yudhiṣṭhira by Dharma, Bhīma by Vāyu and Arjuna by Indra; Mādrī bears the twins by the Aśvins.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Ekalavya’s thumb
nodes.summary: The niṣāda Ekalavya, refused by Droṇa, teaches himself archery before a clay image of him; when Arjuna sees his skill, Droṇa demands Ekalavya’s right thumb as fee, and Ekalavya cuts it off.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The tournament of the Kuru princes
nodes.summary: At the public display of the princes’ skill Karṇa enters and matches Arjuna; challenged on his birth, he is made king of Aṅga by Duryodhana, and Adhiratha’s arrival exposes him to Bhīma’s scorn as a sūta’s son.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Bhīma and Hiḍimbā
nodes.summary: After escaping the house of lac Bhīma kills the man-eater Hiḍimba and, with Kuntī’s consent, lives with his sister Hiḍimbā, who bears Ghaṭotkaca.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The burning of the Khāṇḍava forest
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna help the fire god Agni consume the Khāṇḍava forest against Indra’s rains; Agni gives Arjuna the bow Gāṇḍīva and Kṛṣṇa the discus, and the spared Maya later builds the Pāṇḍavas’ hall.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The killing of Jarāsandha
nodes.summary: Before the rājasūya, Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma and Arjuna enter Magadha disguised as brahmins and Bhīma kills Jarāsandha in a wrestling match.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The rājasūya and the killing of Śiśupāla
nodes.summary: At Yudhiṣṭhira’s royal consecration Bhīṣma proposes Kṛṣṇa for the first honour; Śiśupāla protests and insults Kṛṣṇa, who beheads him with his discus.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Arjuna and the Kirāta
nodes.summary: Seeking divine weapons in the Himālaya, Arjuna fights a hunter (kirāta) over a boar; the hunter is Śiva, who, pleased, gives him the Pāśupata weapon.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The Yakṣa’s questions
nodes.summary: At a lake whose water kills his brothers, Yudhiṣṭhira answers the questions of a yakṣa — the god Dharma — and wins back their lives.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The killing of Kīcaka
nodes.summary: At Virāṭa’s court the general Kīcaka harasses Draupadī (disguised as Sairandhrī); Bhīma meets him at night in the dancing hall and kills him.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa’s embassy to the Kauravas
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa goes to Hāstinapura to seek peace; when Duryodhana plots to seize him he reveals his cosmic form, then leaves, taking Karṇa aside to reveal his birth.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Ambā’s revenge and Śikhaṇḍin
nodes.summary: Ambā, rejected after Bhīṣma’s abduction, seeks his death, is reborn as Drupada’s daughter Śikhaṇḍinī and becomes the man Śikhaṇḍin through an exchange of sex with the yakṣa Sthūṇa.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kuntī meets Karṇa
nodes.summary: Before the war Kuntī goes to Karṇa on the bank of the Gaṅgā and asks him to join his brothers; he refuses but promises to spare all but Arjuna, so that she will still have five sons.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The fall of Bhīṣma
nodes.summary: On the tenth day, with Śikhaṇḍin before him, Arjuna pierces Bhīṣma with arrows; Bhīṣma falls and lies on a bed of arrows awaiting the winter solstice.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The death of Abhimanyu
nodes.summary: On the thirteenth day Abhimanyu breaks into Droṇa’s circular array, is surrounded by several warriors and killed by Duḥśāsana’s son with a mace.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The death of Ghaṭotkaca
nodes.summary: In the night battle Karṇa uses Indra’s infallible spear, reserved for Arjuna, to kill Ghaṭotkaca.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The death of Droṇa
nodes.summary: Told that “Aśvatthāman” is dead — an elephant of that name killed by Bhīma, confirmed by Yudhiṣṭhira — Droṇa lays down his weapons and is beheaded by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The death of Karṇa
nodes.summary: On the seventeenth day Karṇa’s chariot wheel sinks into the earth; while he struggles to free it, Arjuna, urged by Kṛṣṇa, kills him.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The mace duel and the breaking of Duryodhana’s thighs
nodes.summary: In the final mace duel, prompted by Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, Bhīma strikes Duryodhana below the navel, breaking his thighs as he had vowed, to Balarāma’s anger.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The night massacre
nodes.summary: Aśvatthāman, with Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman, enters the Pāṇḍava camp by night and kills Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the Draupadeyas and the sleeping warriors.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Gāndhārī curses Kṛṣṇa
nodes.summary: Lamenting on the battlefield, Gāndhārī blames Kṛṣṇa for not preventing the slaughter and curses him and his clan to perish in thirty-six years.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Bhīṣma’s instruction from the bed of arrows
nodes.summary: At Kṛṣṇa’s urging, the dying Bhīṣma instructs Yudhiṣṭhira at length on kingship, emergencies, liberation and many other topics before dying at the winter solstice.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era
