nodes.name: The great departure of the Pāṇḍavas
nodes.summary: Renouncing the kingdom, the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī walk towards Mount Meru; one by one they fall, and only Yudhiṣṭhira, followed by a dog that proves to be Dharma, reaches Indra’s chariot.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Śakuntalā and Duḥṣanta
nodes.summary: King Duḥṣanta meets Śakuntalā in Kaṇva’s hermitage and marries her by gāndharva rite; when she later brings their son to court he denies her until a heavenly voice confirms her, and the boy Bharata becomes heir.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa carries off Rukmiṇī
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa takes Rukmiṇī, daughter of Bhīṣmaka of Vidarbha, away from her intended marriage to Śiśupāla and defeats her brother Rukmin.

nodes.name: Ayodhyā
nodes.summary: Capital of Kosala and of the Ikṣvāku kings in the Rāmāyaṇa, Rāma’s birthplace and royal seat; traditionally identified with Ayodhya on the Sarayū (Ghaghara) in Uttar Pradesh, and with ancient Sāketa.
nodes.limits: The present-day town’s identification with the epic city is traditional and widely accepted in devotion; the epic’s description is literary. Archaeological occupation of the modern site does not establish the narrative.

nodes.name: Mithilā
nodes.summary: Capital of Videha ruled by Janaka, where Rāma breaks Śiva’s bow and marries Sītā; traditionally identified with Janakpur in the Nepal Terai, within the wider Mithilā region of north Bihar and Nepal.
nodes.limits: Janakpur’s identification is traditional; Sītāmaṛhī (Bihar) is separately revered as Sītā’s birthplace. The epic city is not archaeologically located.

nodes.name: Laṅkā (in the Rāmāyaṇa)
nodes.summary: Rāvaṇa’s island fortress-city beyond the southern ocean, earlier the seat of Kubera; widely identified in tradition with the island of Sri Lanka, though some scholars have proposed locations in central India.

location.label: Traditional identification with Sri Lanka (disputed) — the literary Laṅkā is not a surveyed place

nodes.limits: Kept separate from the modern island: the narrative Laṅkā is a literary place. Its identification with Sri Lanka is traditional and widely held; alternative central-Indian locations have been argued (e.g. discussed by Sankalia 1973). Coordinates are the island’s centroid, for mapping only.
openQuestions: Which central-Indian locations were proposed, by whom (M. V. Kibe, Sankalia and others), and on what textual evidence — to be checked.

nodes.name: Kiṣkindhā
nodes.summary: Cave-city of the vānara kings Vālin and Sugrīva near the Pampā lake and Ṛśyamūka hill; traditionally identified with the Hampi–Anegundi area on the Tuṅgabhadrā in Karnataka.

location.label: Anegundi, near Hampi, Vijayanagara district, Karnataka, India

nodes.limits: The Hampi identification is traditional (local sites named Ṛṣyamūka, Añjanādri, Pampā sarovara); the epic’s geography is not mapped by the text with that precision.

nodes.name: Citrakūṭa
nodes.summary: Hill in the forest south of the Yamunā where Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa first settle in exile on Bharadvāja’s advice, and where Bharata finds them; identified with Chitrakoot on the Uttar Pradesh–Madhya Pradesh border.

location.label: Chitrakoot Dham (Karwi), Uttar Pradesh / Chitrakoot, Madhya Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification; pilgrimage sites at Chitrakoot commemorate the episode.

nodes.name: Pañcavaṭī
nodes.summary: Forest spot on the Godāvarī recommended by Agastya, where Rāma builds his hermitage and from which Sītā is abducted; traditionally identified with Panchavati in Nashik, Maharashtra.

location.label: Panchavati, Nashik, Maharashtra, India (Kalaram temple area)

nodes.limits: Traditional identification; coordinates are those of the Kalaram temple in the Panchavati quarter of Nashik.

nodes.name: Daṇḍaka forest
nodes.summary: The vast forest of the exile, peopled by sages and harassed by rākṣasas, stretching (in later understanding) between the Narmadā and the Godāvarī/Kṛṣṇā; the modern Dandakaranya region of central-eastern India takes its name from it.

location.label: Dandakaranya region (Bastar, Chhattisgarh, with parts of Odisha, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra), India

nodes.limits: A literary forest; the modern regional name is a later application. Coordinates (Jagdalpur) mark the modern region for mapping only.

nodes.name: Hastināpura
nodes.summary: Capital of the Kuru kings and seat of the Kauravas; identified with Hastinapur in Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, where B. B. Lal excavated Painted Grey Ware levels (1950–52).

location.label: Hastinapur, Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: The identification is traditional and was adopted by Lal; the excavated settlement establishes ancient occupation, not the epic narrative.

nodes.name: Indraprastha
nodes.summary: City founded by the Pāṇḍavas on the Yamunā after clearing the Khāṇḍava forest, seat of Yudhiṣṭhira’s rājasūya; traditionally identified with the area of the Purana Qila in Delhi.
nodes.limits: The Purana Qila identification is traditional; excavations there found early historic occupation (incl. Painted Grey Ware sherds), which does not establish the epic city.

nodes.name: Kurukṣetra
nodes.summary: The “field of the Kurus” where the eighteen-day war is fought, also called Samantapañcaka and dharmakṣetra; identified with the Kurukshetra region in Haryana, an important pilgrimage area.
nodes.limits: The region is named Kurukṣetra already in Vedic literature; specific battle sites shown to pilgrims are traditional.

earliestText.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

nodes.name: Dvārakā
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa’s city by the western sea, to which the Yādavas move from Mathurā, and which the sea submerges after Kṛṣṇa’s death; identified with Dwarka in Gujarat (with Bet Dwarka island also associated).

location.label: Dwarka, Devbhumi Dwarka district, Gujarat, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification; claims that offshore remains are Kṛṣṇa’s city are a separate, disputed claim (claim:dwarka-submerged).

nodes.name: Mathurā
nodes.summary: City of the Śūrasenas on the Yamunā, ruled by Kaṃsa, where Kṛṣṇa is born and kills Kaṃsa; the modern city in Uttar Pradesh, an important early centre of Vāsudeva–Kṛṣṇa worship.
nodes.limits: The modern city’s identification is secure as a continuously named place; that it is the setting of the narrated events is a matter of tradition.

nodes.name: Vṛndāvana
nodes.summary: Forest near the Yamunā to which the cowherds move from their first settlement and where Kṛṣṇa’s childhood feats and sports with the gopīs take place; identified with Vrindavan near Mathura.

location.label: Vrindavan, Mathura district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: The modern town was developed as a pilgrimage centre especially from the 16th century (Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava activity); identification with the Harivaṃśa’s forest is traditional.

nodes.name: Naimiṣa forest
nodes.summary: Forest where Śaunaka holds his twelve-year sacrifice and Ugraśravas recites the Mahābhārata (and, in Purāṇic frames, the Purāṇas); identified with Nimsar (Neemsar) on the Gomatī in Sitapur district, Uttar Pradesh.

location.label: Nimsar (Naimisharanya), Sitapur district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification; coordinates from the location link on the Wikipedia article (approximate).

nodes.name: Kāmpilya
nodes.summary: Capital of southern Pañcāla left to Drupada after Droṇa’s victory, the setting of Draupadī’s svayaṃvara in tradition; identified with Kampil in Farrukhabad district, Uttar Pradesh.

location.label: Kampil, Farrukhabad district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification of the modern village with the epic city.

nodes.name: Takṣaśilā
nodes.summary: City in Gandhāra from which Janamejaya returns to Hāstinapura after his snake sacrifice (MBh 18.5.29); identified with Taxila in Punjab, Pakistan.
nodes.limits: The identification of Takṣaśilā with Taxila is secure for the historical city; that Janamejaya’s sacrifice took place there is the epic’s own statement.

nodes.name: Virāṭanagara
nodes.summary: Capital of King Virāṭa of the Matsyas, where the Pāṇḍavas spend the thirteenth year in disguise; traditionally identified with Viratnagar (Bairat) in Jaipur district, Rajasthan.
nodes.limits: Traditional identification; Bairat is better known archaeologically for Aśokan-period remains, which do not bear on the epic.

nodes.name: Prabhāsa
nodes.summary: Coastal tīrtha where the Yādavas gather and destroy one another in drunken strife; identified with Prabhas Patan (Somnath) in Gujarat.

location.label: Prabhas Patan, Gir Somnath district, Gujarat, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification; local sites associated with Kṛṣṇa’s death (e.g. Bhalka) are pilgrimage traditions.

nodes.name: Pampā lake
nodes.summary: Lake near Ṛśyamūka on whose western shore Śabarī lives and near which Rāma meets Hanumān and Sugrīva; identified with Pampa Sarovar near Hampi, Karnataka.

location.label: Pampa Sarovar, near Hampi, Koppal district, Karnataka, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification.

nodes.name: Śṛṅgaverapura
nodes.summary: Town of the niṣāda chief Guha on the Gaṅgā, where Rāma crosses the river at the start of the exile; identified with Shringverpur near Prayagraj.

location.label: Shringverpur, Prayagraj district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification; excavations at Shringverpur (B. B. Lal, 1977–86) concern the ancient settlement, not the narrative.

nodes.name: The Kuru lineage
nodes.summary: The royal line descended from Kuru in the lunar dynasty, ruling from Hāstinapura, to which Śantanu, Bhīṣma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu and both the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas belong.
nodes.details: The epic genealogies (MBh (CE) 1.70–90) run from Dakṣa, Manu and Purūravas through Bharata and Kuru to Śantanu. Historians identify a Kuru polity of the late Vedic period in the upper Gaṅgā–Yamunā doab; the epic line is a literary genealogy.
nodes.limits: The genealogy is narrative; the historical late-Vedic Kuru state is a separate (Vedic-domain) topic.

nodes.name: The Pāṇḍavas
nodes.summary: The five legal sons of Pāṇḍu — Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma and Arjuna (by Kuntī) and Nakula and Sahadeva (by Mādrī), each fathered by a god — with their shared wife Draupadī and their descendants down to Parīkṣit and Janamejaya.

nodes.name: The Kauravas
nodes.summary: The hundred sons (and one daughter) of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, led by Duryodhana; also, more broadly, the Kuru side in the war.
nodes.details: The aṃśāvataraṇa makes the hundred brothers incarnations of Paulastya rākṣasas (MBh (CE) 1.61.82–83). Yuyutsu, son by a vaiśya woman, joins the Pāṇḍavas.

nodes.name: The Yādavas / Vṛṣṇis
nodes.summary: The descendants of Yadu, including the Vṛṣṇi, Andhaka and Bhoja clans of Mathurā and Dvārakā, to which Śūra, Vasudeva, Kuntī, Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and Subhadrā belong; their genealogy fills the Harivaṃśa.
nodes.details: The Mausalaparvan narrates their mutual destruction at Prabhāsa (MBh (CE) 16.4). The Vṛṣṇis appear in early inscriptions (the material domain’s ins:mora-well) in connection with the worship of Vṛṣṇi heroes.

nodes.name: The Paulastyas (line of Pulastya)
nodes.summary: The descendants of the sage Pulastya through Viśravas: Kubera (Vaiśravaṇa) and the rākṣasa siblings Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā and Vibhīṣaṇa.

nodes.name: The vānaras of Kiṣkindhā
nodes.summary: The monkey people of Kiṣkindhā ruled by Vālin and Sugrīva, among them Hanumān, Aṅgada, Nala and Nīla, born — in the Rāmāyaṇa and Rāmopākhyāna — of gods to aid Viṣṇu’s descent.
nodes.limits: The vānaras are narrative beings; anthropological readings (e.g. as forest peoples) are scholarly interpretations not encoded here.

nodes.name: The Pāñcālas (line of Drupada)
nodes.summary: The ruling house of Pañcāla: Drupada and his children Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin and Draupadī, allies of the Pāṇḍavas.

nodes.name: The Bhāratas (line of Bharata Dauḥṣanti)
nodes.summary: The lineage named after Bharata, son of Duḥṣanta and Śakuntalā, from which the Kurus descend and after which the epic (Bhārata, Mahābhārata) is named.

nodes.name: The identification of the Rāmāyaṇa’s Laṅkā with Sri Lanka
nodes.summary: The traditional and widely held view that Rāvaṇa’s island-city Laṅkā is the island of Sri Lanka, set against scholarly proposals that the epic’s Laṅkā lay elsewhere (notably in central India) or is a purely literary geography.
nodes.details:
For: the Rāmāyaṇa places Laṅkā across the southern ocean, reached by Hanumān’s leap and by the causeway built from the southern shore (VR (CE) 5.1; 6.15); later South Indian and Sri Lankan traditions, place-names (Rāma Setu/Adam’s Bridge, Rameswaram) and pilgrimage sites embody the identification.

Against / alternatives: several twentieth-century scholars argued that the epic’s geography south of the Vindhyas is vague and that Laṅkā may have been a hill-fort in central India (proposals discussed by H. D. Sankalia, 1973); others treat Laṅkā as a literary island not mappable onto any real place.
nodes.limits: Recorded as a debatable claim. The dataset keeps the narrative place (place:lanka-narrative) separate from any modern territory.
openQuestions: Name and check the specific central-Indian proposals (M. V. Kibe’s Amarkantak hypothesis is often cited) and their arguments.

nodes.name: Bṛhat Saṃhitā of Varāhamihira
nodes.summary: Varāhamihira’s sixth-century Sanskrit compendium of natural astrology and omens, which also contains the earliest surviving systematic chapters on temple types, image proportions and the iconography of the gods.
nodes.details:
About a hundred chapters cover omens, weather, gems, animals, architecture and images. Four chapters matter for art history (numbers as in Tripathi’s edition on GRETIL; Kern and Bhat number them one higher). Ch. 52 (vāstuvidyā) lays out the 81-square site diagram with Brahmā in the centre and 45 deities (52.42–49). Ch. 55 (prāsādalakṣaṇa) prescribes a 64-square temple plan (55.10), height twice the width (55.11) and a sanctum half the width (55.12), door jambs with guardians (pratīhāra) and auspicious couples (55.14–15), and names twenty temple types from Meru to the sixteen- and eight-sided (55.17–28). It cites Maya, Viśvakarman and Garga (55.29–31).

Ch. 57 (pratimālakṣaṇa) defines a measuring scale of aṅgulas (57.1–2) and the proportions of a standard image (57.4–28), quoting Nagnajit and Vasiṣṭha. It then gives the marks of Viṣṇu with eight, four or two arms (57.31–35), Baladeva, Ekānaṃśā, Sāmba and Pradyumna (57.36–40), Brahmā, Skanda and Indra (57.41–42), Śiva, optionally with the Mountain’s daughter as his left half (57.43), the Buddha and the Jina (57.44–45), Sūrya in northern dress (57.46–48), the liṅga (57.53–55), the Mothers and Revanta (57.56), and Yama, Varuṇa and Kubera (57.57). A verse on Gaṇeśa appears only in Kern’s text (his 58.58). Ch. 59 (pratiṣṭhā) says each god’s image should be installed by his own specialists: Bhāgavatas for Viṣṇu, Magas for the Sun, ash-smeared brahmins for Śiva, and so on (59.19).

dates.label: mid-6th century CE (Varāhamihira fl. c. 505–587)
dates.basis: author’s Pañcasiddhāntikā uses the epoch Śaka 427 = 505 CE; a late commentator gives his death as Śaka 509 = 587 CE

dates.label: 1279 CE palm-leaf manuscript (Cambridge University Library Add. 1706)
dates.basis: manuscript date as reported in the Wikipedia article (not checked against the Cambridge catalogue)

nodes.limits: A prescriptive text: it records what an author of c. 550 CE thought an image or temple should look like, not what every workshop actually made.

nodes.name: Varāhamihira
nodes.summary: Astronomer and astrologer of Avanti (Ujjain), author of the Pañcasiddhāntikā, Bṛhajjātaka and Bṛhat Saṃhitā, active in the sixth century CE.

dates.label: c. 505–587 CE
dates.basis: Pañcasiddhāntikā epoch (505 CE); death date given by the commentator Amarāja (587 CE), doubted by some

nodes.name: Bṛhat Saṃhitā 52: Vāstuvidyā (the science of sites)
nodes.summary: Chapter on house and site planning, with the myth of the Vāstupuruṣa pressed down by the gods (52.2–3) and the 81-square diagram of 45 deities with Brahmā at the centre (52.42–49).

attributes.numberingNote: Tripathi/GRETIL numbering; add one for Kern and Bhat

nodes.name: Bṛhat Saṃhitā 55: Prāsādalakṣaṇa (characteristics of temples)
nodes.summary: Chapter on temples: siting near water and gardens, a 64-square plan, proportions of sanctum and door, door guardians and auspicious couples, and a list of twenty named temple types.

attributes.numberingNote: Tripathi/GRETIL numbering; add one for Kern and Bhat

nodes.name: Bṛhat Saṃhitā 57: Pratimālakṣaṇa (characteristics of images)
nodes.summary: Chapter on images: the aṅgula scale, the proportions of a standard figure, and the distinguishing marks of Viṣṇu, Baladeva, Ekānaṃśā, Brahmā, Skanda, Indra, Śiva, the Buddha, the Jina, Sūrya, the liṅga, the Mothers, Revanta, Yama, Varuṇa and Kubera.

attributes.numberingNote: Tripathi/GRETIL numbering; add one for Kern and Bhat

nodes.name: Bṛhat Saṃhitā 59: Pratimāpratiṣṭhāpana (installation of images)
nodes.summary: Chapter on consecrating an image, ending with the rule that each god is installed by priests of his own cult (59.19).

attributes.numberingNote: Tripathi/GRETIL numbering; add one for Kern and Bhat

nodes.name: Agni Purāṇa 42–43: temple construction and the deities of the temple
nodes.summary: Hayagrīva’s instruction on the general temple (a 16-part square plan, wall and spire proportions; 42) and on placing deities on the building (43).

attributes.speakerFrame: Hayagrīva / Bhagavān instructing Brahmā (Agni Purāṇa frame)

nodes.name: Agni Purāṇa 44–47: images of Vāsudeva, pedestals and śālagrāma stones
nodes.summary: Proportions of the Vāsudeva image (44), the pedestal (piṇḍikā, 45) and the marks and worship of śālagrāma stones (46–47).

attributes.speakerFrame: Hayagrīva / Bhagavān instructing Brahmā (Agni Purāṇa frame)

nodes.name: Agni Purāṇa 48: Caturviṃśatimūrti-stotra (the twenty-four forms of Viṣṇu)
nodes.summary: A hymn naming twenty-four forms of Viṣṇu (Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava … Hari), each distinguished by how the conch, discus, mace and lotus are distributed among the four hands.

attributes.speakerFrame: Hayagrīva / Bhagavān instructing Brahmā (Agni Purāṇa frame)

nodes.name: Agni Purāṇa 49: images of the ten avatāras and other Vaiṣṇava forms
nodes.summary: Prescriptions for Matsya, Kūrma, Bhū-Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma, Balarāma, Buddha and Kalki, the Vāsudeva group of nine, Brahmā, eight-armed Viṣṇu on Garuḍa, Trailokyamohana, a twenty-armed four-faced Viśvarūpa, Hayagrīva and Dattātreya.

attributes.speakerFrame: Hayagrīva / Bhagavān instructing Brahmā (Agni Purāṇa frame)

nodes.name: Agni Purāṇa 50: images of the Goddess and her circle
nodes.summary: Prescriptions for Caṇḍī slaying the buffalo demon, the nine Durgās, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā on the makara and Yamunā on the tortoise, the Mothers, Cāmuṇḍā, Vināyaka, Skanda, and attendants such as Nandīśa.

attributes.speakerFrame: Hayagrīva / Bhagavān instructing Brahmā (Agni Purāṇa frame)

nodes.name: Agni Purāṇa 51: images of Sūrya, the planets, nāgas and lokapālas
nodes.summary: Sūrya on a one-wheeled chariot of seven horses holding two lotuses, with Daṇḍa and Piṅgala (51.1–3); the twelve Ādityas; the planets with their attributes (51.10–12); eight nāgas (51.13); and the two-armed guardians of the directions with their mounts (51.14–16).

attributes.speakerFrame: Hayagrīva / Bhagavān instructing Brahmā (Agni Purāṇa frame)

nodes.name: Agni Purāṇa 52: the sixty-four yoginīs and the retinue of the Mothers
nodes.summary: A list of sixty-four yoginīs (52.1–8), described as eight- or four-armed (52.9), followed by Vīrabhadra on a bull before the Mothers and Caṇḍikā.

attributes.speakerFrame: Hayagrīva / Bhagavān instructing Brahmā (Agni Purāṇa frame)

nodes.name: Agni Purāṇa 53–55: proportions, materials and pedestals of the liṅga
nodes.summary: The liṅga divided into Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva portions (square, octagonal and round, 53), the ranking of liṅgas by material (54) and the pedestal (55).

attributes.speakerFrame: Hayagrīva / Bhagavān instructing Brahmā (Agni Purāṇa frame)

nodes.name: Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa III.35–43: the Citrasūtra (treatise on painting)
nodes.summary: The section of the third book of the Viṣṇudharmottara that teaches painting: proportions, the five male types, postures, colours, and the expression of sentiments (rasa).
nodes.details: The Citrasūtra opens with Mārkaṇḍeya’s statement that the rules of image-making cannot be understood without painting, nor painting without dance and music. Chapter numbers follow the convention in Kramrisch and Shah; vulgate numbering may differ.

nodes.name: Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa III.44–85: image-making (pratimālakṣaṇa)
nodes.summary: The chapters of the third book of the Viṣṇudharmottara that describe how to make images of the gods, including Vaiṣṇava forms, Śiva as Gaurīśvara (Ardhanārīśvara), the planets and the guardians of the directions.
nodes.details: Chapters 44–85 of the third khaṇḍa (118 chapters) treat iconography; 86–93 deal with temple construction. The range follows Shah’s edition as summarised in reference works; it has not been checked against an e-text, because the GRETIL file of book III covers only chapters 343–353 of another numbering.

nodes.name: Citralakṣaṇa of Nagnajit
nodes.summary: An early treatise on painting and the proportions of figures attributed to Nagnajit, lost in Sanskrit but preserved in a Tibetan translation in the Tanjur and reconstructed in Sanskrit.
nodes.details: Varāhamihira twice quotes Nagnajit on facial proportions: a face 14 aṅgulas long, called drāviḍa (57.4), and 16 aṅgulas with the hair (57.15). If that Nagnajit is the author of this Citralakṣaṇa, as its editors assume, the work predates the mid-6th century.

attributes.author: Nagnajit (attributed)
attributes.survival: Tibetan translation (Tanjur); Sanskrit reconstruction ed. Asoke Chatterjee Sastri 1987
attributes.terminusAnteQuem: c. 550 CE, if identical with the Nagnajit cited in BS 57.4 and 57.15 (disputed)

nodes.name: Mayamata
nodes.summary: A South Indian Sanskrit treatise on architecture, settlements, houses, temples and iconography attributed to Maya, one of the two most complete surviving Drāviḍa-tradition vāstu texts (with the Mānasāra).
nodes.details: Its 36 chapters move from choosing and preparing the site through village and town plans, houses, temples of one to twelve storeys, gateways (gopura) and pavilions, to liṅgas, pedestals and images of the gods. It classifies temples as nāgara, drāviḍa or vesara by the shape of the crowning member (square, octagonal or circular). It shares much with the Śaiva Āgamas. The Tamil tradition attributes it to the sage Maya.

dates.label: c. 9th–12th century
dates.basis: relation to Śaiva Āgamas and to dated Cōḻa architecture

dates.label: c. 5th–7th century
dates.basis: popular estimate repeated in reference works

nodes.name: Mānasāra
nodes.summary: A large Sanskrit treatise on architecture and sculpture in 70 chapters from South India, edited and translated by P. K. Acharya, whose name he rendered as “essence of measurement”.
nodes.details: Acharya found eleven manuscripts in five scripts; his edition and translation appeared in the Mānasāra Series (Oxford, 1927–1946). The text sets out measures (tāla), villages and towns, buildings of one to twelve storeys, gopuras, and the proportions of images, and like the Mayamata it names nāgara, drāviḍa and vesara types. Bhattacharyya calls it a “recension of recensions” built up over centuries.

nodes.name: Samarāṅgaṇa Sūtradhāra
nodes.summary: An eleventh-century Sanskrit treatise on architecture attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja of Dhārā, the fullest surviving description of North Indian temple types, including the Bhūmija.
nodes.details: The most complete manuscript has 83 chapters and about 7,430 verses; chapters 52–67 treat temples and list some 64 temple designs, and others cover town planning, houses, painting, sculpture and mechanical devices (yantra, ch. 31). Hardy uses its descriptions to reconstruct the design method of the Bhūmija and Latina temples.

nodes.name: Aparājitapṛcchā
nodes.summary: A Sanskrit treatise of western India attributed to Bhuvanadeva, framed as answers to Aparājita’s questions, important for Nāgara and Māru-Gurjara temple architecture and iconography.
nodes.details: It has some 239 sūtras with over 7,500 verses and includes Jain as well as Hindu material. Dhaky regards it as one of the few and most valuable texts of the Nāgara school.

dates.label: c. 1000–1200 CE (often given as 12th century)
dates.basis: language, cited authorities and correspondence with dated temples

nodes.name: Śilpa Prakāśa
nodes.summary: A medieval Odishan Sanskrit text on temple architecture by Rāmacandra Kaulācāra, which describes Kaliṅga temple forms, their sculpture and tantric yantras placed in the foundations.
nodes.details: Edited and translated by Alice Boner and Sadāśiva Rath Śarmā (1966) from palm-leaf manuscripts held by Odishan craftsmen. It describes the rekhā temple, its divisions and sculptural programme, and female figures (alasakanyā) on the walls.

dates.label: c. 9th–12th century
dates.basis: editors’ estimate from correspondence with Bhubaneswar temples (recall)

nodes.name: Rūpamaṇḍana
nodes.summary: A fifteenth-century Sanskrit manual of iconography by Maṇḍana, sūtradhāra at the Mewar court of Rāṇā Kumbhā, a companion to his Prāsādamaṇḍana on temples.

nodes.name: Prāsādamaṇḍana
nodes.summary: Maṇḍana’s fifteenth-century Sanskrit manual on temple building in the western Indian (Māru-Gurjara) tradition, still used by hereditary Sompura architects.

nodes.name: Maṇḍana (sūtradhāra)
nodes.summary: Master builder (sūtradhāra) at the court of Rāṇā Kumbhā of Mewar in the fifteenth century, author of the Prāsādamaṇḍana, Rūpamaṇḍana and other manuals.

nodes.name: Śilparatna
nodes.summary: A sixteenth-century Sanskrit compendium of architecture and iconography by Śrīkumāra of Kerala, cited by Gopinatha Rao for many iconographic forms.

dates.label: 16th century
dates.basis: patronage of a Kerala ruler named in the text (recall)

nodes.name: Tantrasamuccaya
nodes.summary: A fifteenth-century Kerala manual of temple ritual by Cēnnās Nārāyaṇan Nampūtiri that also governs temple planning and image installation in Kerala.

nodes.name: Toḍala Tantra
nodes.summary: A Śākta tantra in ten chapters, a dialogue of Śiva and the Goddess, whose tenth chapter equates the ten Mahāvidyās with Viṣṇu’s ten avatāras.

dates.label: late medieval (date uncertain)
dates.basis: no firm external date; late medieval Bengal-style Śākta corpus

nodes.name: Vāstuśāstra (science of building)
nodes.summary: The Sanskrit tradition of texts and practice on siting, planning and proportioning settlements, houses and temples; its earliest surviving systematic statement is in the Bṛhat Saṃhitā.
nodes.details: Major texts include the Bṛhat Saṃhitā’s chapters, the Mayamata and Mānasāra (south), and the Samarāṅgaṇa Sūtradhāra, Aparājitapṛcchā and Maṇḍana’s works (north and west). Purāṇas (Matsya, Agni, Viṣṇudharmottara) and Āgamas also contain vāstu chapters.

nodes.name: Śilpaśāstra (science of the arts)
nodes.summary: The texts on making images, painting and other crafts, often overlapping with vāstuśāstra; they prescribe proportions (tālamāna), attributes and gestures for each deity.

nodes.name: Vāstupuruṣa-maṇḍala
nodes.summary: The square grid on which a site or temple is laid out, imagined as the body of the Vāstupuruṣa pressed face down by the gods, with Brahmā in the centre and other deities in the surrounding squares.
nodes.details: Bṛhat Saṃhitā 52.2–3 tells how a being who blocked heaven and earth was seized and laid face down by the gods, who settled where they held him; Brahmā made him the Vāstunara. BS 52.42–49 lays out the 81-square (9 × 9) diagram: 32 deities in the outer squares, 13 within, Brahmā on the central nine. BS 55.10 prescribes 64 squares (8 × 8) for temples. Kramrisch (1946) made the maṇḍala central to her reading of the temple as a cosmic diagram; Meister has questioned how directly built plans follow it.

nodes.name: Tālamāna (iconometry)
nodes.summary: The system of proportional measurement for images, expressing a figure’s height in tālas (face-lengths) and aṅgulas (digits) of its own body; different classes of beings are given different tāla canons.
nodes.details: The Bṛhat Saṃhitā builds its scale from the atom (paramāṇu) through hair-tip, nit, louse and barley-corn to the aṅgula, each eight times the last (57.1–2), measures the face at 12 of the image’s own aṅgulas (Nagnajit: 14) and gives Rāma and Bali 120 aṅgulas, with lesser figures 12 aṅgulas shorter at each step (57.30). Southern texts such as the Mānasāra grade images from 10 tālas (uttama daśatāla) for the highest gods downwards.

nodes.name: Ardhanārīśvara
nodes.summary: Śiva as “the lord who is half woman”: a single figure whose right half is Śiva and left half Pārvatī, expressing the inseparability of god and his śakti.
nodes.details:
The male right half wears matted locks with the crescent and may hold a trident, axe or rosary and lean on Nandin; the female left half has a breast, rounded hip, ornaments and holds a mirror or lotus. The Bṛhat Saṃhitā already allows Śiva to be shown with “the half of the Mountain’s daughter” on his left (57.43). The Viṣṇudharmottara calls the form Gaurīśvara, and South Indian Āgamas and the Śilparatna give detailed rules.

Earliest representations: Kuṣāṇa-period Mathurā images of the 1st–2nd century CE (Government Museum, Mathurā), including a stele with an ithyphallic half-male figure holding a mirror on the female side; Gupta and early Cālukya examples follow (Bādāmi Cave 1, Elephanta).

attributes.posture: standing in ābhaṅga/tribhaṅga with hip thrust on the female side
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Kuṣāṇa Mathurā, 1st–2nd c. CE (Government Museum, Mathurā) — no record in the dataset yet

nodes.limits: The forms and texts show how the deity was imagined and codified; they are not evidence for the dating of any myth.

nodes.name: Harihara
nodes.summary: A composite image whose right half is Śiva (Hara) and left half Viṣṇu (Hari), expressing the identity of the two gods; it is common in sixth- to eighth-century India and in pre-Angkorian Cambodia.
nodes.details:
The Śiva half wears matted locks and holds the trident or axe; the Viṣṇu half wears a cylindrical crown (kirīṭa) and holds the conch or discus. Nandin and Garuḍa may flank the figure. The Harivaṃśa already declares the two gods one, and Purāṇic and Āgamic texts prescribe the image.

Earliest dated representations are the panels of Bādāmi Caves 1 and 3 (Cave 3 dated 578 CE). In Cambodia free-standing Harihara statues of the 6th–7th century (for example from Asram Maha Rosei at Phnom Da, now in the Musée Guimet) are among the masterpieces of pre-Angkorian art.

attributes.posture: samabhaṅga standing
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Bādāmi Caves 1 and 3 (Cave 3 inscription 578 CE)

nodes.limits: Shows a theology of the unity of Śiva and Viṣṇu in practice; does not show that the cults were not also rivals.

nodes.name: Dakṣiṇāmūrti
nodes.summary: Śiva as the south-facing teacher: a youthful ascetic seated under a banyan tree, teaching sages by gesture and silence, his right foot on the dwarf of ignorance.
nodes.details: Gopinatha Rao distinguishes four varieties by what Śiva teaches: yoga, music (vīṇādhara), knowledge (jñāna) and exposition (vyākhyāna). In the common vyākhyāna type the lower right hand shows the cin- or vyākhyāna-mudrā, the upper hands hold a rosary and fire or a serpent, and the lower left holds a book or rests on the knee; sages sit at his feet. In Tamil temples from the Pallava–Cōḻa period on, Dakṣiṇāmūrti occupies the south niche of the main shrine.

attributes.posture: seated, right leg pendant on Apasmāra, left folded
attributes.placement: south niche (koṣṭha) of the vimāna in Tamil temples
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Pallava and early Cālukya temples, 7th–8th c. (no dated example recorded here)

earliestMaterial.label: c. 700 CE (reign of Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha, c. 690–728)

nodes.name: Somāskanda
nodes.summary: A Pallava-born family group in which Śiva sits with Umā and the child Skanda between them (sa-umā-skanda); it became the central processional icon of Tamil Śaiva temples.
nodes.details: In Pallava rock-cut and structural shrines of the 7th–8th century a relief of Somāskanda fills the back wall of the sanctum behind the liṅga, often with Brahmā and Viṣṇu standing behind. Śiva has four arms (axe and deer above), Umā sits at ease, and Skanda appears as a child, sometimes dancing. Under the Cōḻas the group became the chief bronze processional image (utsava-mūrti) of Śiva temples.

attributes.posture: Śiva and Umā seated in sukhāsana on a common seat
attributes.placement: back wall of Pallava sanctums; utsava bronze in Cōḻa temples
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Pallava monuments of Mamallapuram and Kanchipuram, late 7th–early 8th c.

nodes.name: Liṅgodbhavamūrti
nodes.summary: Śiva emerging from a fiery pillar of light, with Brahmā flying upward as a goose and Viṣṇu digging downward as a boar, the iconic form of the Liṅgodbhava myth of Śiva’s supremacy.
nodes.details: The image shows a four-armed Śiva within an opening in the shaft of a liṅga whose ends are lost from view; the goose and the boar are carved above and below, or the two gods stand beside the pillar in worship. In Tamil temples from the Cōḻa period it occupies the west niche, directly behind the main liṅga. Seventh-century Tamil hymns of Appar and Campantar already refer to the episode.

attributes.placement: west niche of the vimāna (Tamil temples)
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Pallava (Kailāsanātha, Kanchipuram) and Rāṣṭrakūṭa (Ellora) examples of the 8th c.

earliestMaterial.label: c. 700 CE (reign of Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha, c. 690–728)

nodes.name: Bhikṣāṭana
nodes.summary: Śiva as a naked, beautiful mendicant wandering with a skull-bowl, followed by a deer and a dwarf attendant, who enchants the wives of the sages of the Pine Forest.
nodes.details: The form belongs to the cycle in which Śiva expiates the cutting of Brahmā’s fifth head by wandering as a beggar (compare Kaṅkāla and Bhairava) and to the Dārukāvana story. He is nude, wears sandals and a serpent, holds a skull-bowl and feeds a deer with grass; a gaṇa carries a bowl on his head. Cōḻa-period bronzes and niche images of the 10th–12th century are its classic expression.

attributes.earliestRepresentation: Cōḻa bronzes and reliefs, 10th–11th c. (no dated example recorded here)

earliestMaterial.label: c. 700 CE (reign of Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha, c. 690–728)

nodes.name: Kalyāṇasundara
nodes.summary: The marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī (pāṇigrahaṇa), with Śiva taking the bride’s hand, Brahmā as officiating priest and, in southern versions, Viṣṇu giving the bride away.
nodes.details: Large panels of the marriage appear at Elephanta (mid-6th c.) and Ellora, and it became a favoured Cōḻa bronze group. In the Tamil tradition the Madurai legend of Mīnākṣī’s marriage to Sundareśvara, with Viṣṇu giving away his sister, is the local version.

figures: Viṣṇu as giver of the bride (southern)
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Elephanta Cave 1, mid-6th c.

nodes.name: Gajāsurasaṃhāra
nodes.summary: Śiva destroying the elephant demon and dancing within its flayed hide, which he holds stretched above him like an arch; a fierce form favoured by Cōḻa and Hoysaḷa sculptors.
nodes.details: Texts place the episode at Vārāṇasī or in the south (Vaḻuvūr). Śiva has eight or more arms, one leg raised in dance, and the elephant’s head lies at his feet; Pārvatī and the infant Skanda sometimes shrink away in fear.

attributes.posture: dancing with one leg raised
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Ellora and Cōḻa examples, 8th–12th c.

nodes.name: Tripurāntaka
nodes.summary: Śiva as the archer who destroys with a single arrow the three flying cities of the asuras, riding a chariot made of the gods with Brahmā as charioteer.
nodes.details: The myth is told in the Mahābhārata (Karṇaparvan) and the Purāṇas. Images show Śiva with bow and arrow (Mount Meru as bow, Vāsuki as string and Viṣṇu as arrow in many versions); in bronze the bow is usually lost and only the drawing gesture remains. The Tripurāntaka paintings in the circumambulatory of the Bṛhadīśvara temple at Thanjavur (c. 1010) are the most famous Cōḻa treatment.

attributes.posture: standing in archer’s stance or in a chariot
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Rāṣṭrakūṭa and Pallava reliefs of the 8th c.; Thanjavur murals c. 1010

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

earliestMaterial.label: c. 756–773 CE (main excavation, reign of Kṛṣṇa I), with later elements

nodes.name: Gaṅgādhara
nodes.summary: Śiva receiving the descending river Gaṅgā in a lock of his hair to break her fall, often with Pārvatī turning away and Bhagīratha in worship.
nodes.details: Gaṅgā is shown as a small woman or a woman with a serpent’s tail descending into Śiva’s raised lock. The Elephanta panel (mid-6th c.) shows a triple-headed Gaṅgā (for Gaṅgā, Yamunā and Sarasvatī). The Pallava relief in the upper cave at Tiruchirappalli, with an inscription of Mahendravarman I (early 7th c.), is among the earliest southern examples.

attributes.posture: standing, one hand raising a lock of hair
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Udayagiri Cave 6, beside the doorway (c. 401–415); Elephanta Cave 1 (mid-6th c.); Tiruchirappalli upper cave of Mahendravarman I (early 7th c.; not yet a dataset record)

earliestMaterial.label: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

nodes.name: Bhairava
nodes.summary: The terrifying form of Śiva: naked, fanged, garlanded with skulls and accompanied by a dog, who in Purāṇic myth cuts off Brahmā’s fifth head and wanders until freed of the skull at Vārāṇasī.
nodes.details: Bhairava is the focus of tantric Kāpālika and Bhairava-tantra cults and the guardian of temples and of the city of Vārāṇasī (Kāla Bhairava as its kotwal). Iconography: nude or in tiger skin, flaming hair, kapāla, trident, ḍamaru, noose and the khaṭvāṅga (skull-topped staff), with a dog; groups of eight Bhairavas (aṣṭa-bhairava) guard the directions.

attributes.dress: nude or tiger skin, serpent ornaments, skull garland

nodes.name: Andhakāsuravadhamūrti
nodes.summary: Śiva as a fierce form impaling the blind demon Andhaka on his trident while catching the demon’s multiplying blood in a skull-bowl, sometimes helped by the Mothers.
nodes.details: The Elephanta panel (mid-6th c.) is the classic early example; Ellora repeats the theme. The Purāṇic story links the Mothers to Andhaka’s blood, connecting this form with Mātṛkā imagery.

attributes.earliestRepresentation: Elephanta Cave 1, mid-6th c.

nodes.name: Caṇḍeśānugrahamūrti
nodes.summary: Śiva, with Umā, blessing his devotee Caṇḍeśa by binding a flower garland on his head, rewarding the boy who struck his own father for disrupting his worship of the liṅga.
nodes.details: Caṇḍeśa (Caṇḍikeśvara), one of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs, receives the office of steward of Śiva’s offerings; every Tamil Śiva temple has his shrine on the north side. The panel at Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram (c. 1035), often read as Rājendra I placing himself in the role of the blessed devotee, is the classic example.

attributes.earliestRepresentation: Cōḻa, 10th–11th c.; Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram panel c. 1035

nodes.name: Rāvaṇānugrahamūrti
nodes.summary: Śiva and Pārvatī seated on Mount Kailāsa while Rāvaṇa, trapped beneath, tries to shake the mountain; Śiva presses it down with his toe and later grants Rāvaṇa grace and a sword.
nodes.details: The image pairs a calm upper register (Śiva, a frightened Pārvatī clinging to him, attendants) with a many-armed Rāvaṇa straining below. The Uttarakāṇḍa of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa tells the episode and explains the name Rāvaṇa (“he who roars”) by the cry he gave when crushed. Classic examples are at Elephanta, Ellora (Kailāsa temple) and, in Cambodia, the pediment of Banteay Srei (967).

attributes.earliestRepresentation: Elephanta Cave 1, mid-6th c.

nodes.name: Kirātamūrti (Kirātārjunamūrti)
nodes.summary: Śiva disguised as a Kirāta hunter, with Pārvatī as a huntress, who fights Arjuna over a boar and then grants him the Pāśupata weapon.
nodes.details: The episode is told in the Mahābhārata’s Āraṇyakaparvan and became the subject of Bhāravi’s Kirātārjunīya (6th c.). Early Cālukya reliefs at Pattadakal and later Cōḻa bronzes of Śiva as hunter (with bow, Pārvatī beside him) represent it.

attributes.earliestRepresentation: early Cālukya reliefs at Pattadakal, 8th c.

nodes.name: Sadāśiva
nodes.summary: Śiva as the five-faced, ten-armed supreme form of Śaiva Siddhānta, whose faces Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna embody five aspects and five mantras.
nodes.details: In Siddhānta theology Sadāśiva is the form in which Śiva is worshipped in the liṅga; the five faces correspond to the five brahmamantras. Images show four faces in the cardinal directions and the fifth (Īśāna) on top, often invisible. Whether the colossal three-headed bust at Elephanta is Sadāśiva, Maheśamūrti or a Trimūrti has long been debated.

attributes.posture: seated or bust

nodes.name: Liṅga (aniconic form of Śiva)
nodes.summary: The cylindrical, usually aniconic emblem in which Śiva is principally worshipped; textual canons divide it into a square Brahmā part, an octagonal Viṣṇu part and a round Rudra part that alone is visible.
nodes.details: The Bṛhat Saṃhitā divides the liṅga’s length into three: square at the base, octagonal in the middle, round above; the square part goes into the ground and the middle into the pedestal (57.53–54). It warns that a thin, long liṅga ruins the country (57.55). The Agni Purāṇa names the three parts after Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva (53.3–4) and ranks liṅgas by material, from salt and ghee to stone, gems and gold (54.1–5). Liṅgas with human faces are called mukhaliṅgas.

attributes.earliestRepresentation: Gudimallam liṅga (2nd–1st c. BCE on the early view; disputed)

nodes.limits: The form and its textual canons do not settle the debated question of the liṅga’s origin or early meaning.

nodes.name: Mukhaliṅga
nodes.summary: A liṅga carved with one or more faces of Śiva projecting from the shaft; one-faced (ekamukha), four-faced (caturmukha) and five-faced (pañcamukha) types are distinguished.
nodes.details: Mukhaliṅgas appear in Mathurā sculpture of the Kuṣāṇa period and are characteristic of Gupta and post-Gupta north India and of Nepal and Cambodia. The faces are usually read with the Sadāśiva doctrine of five faces, the fifth (Īśāna) being the invisible top.

attributes.earliestRepresentation: Kuṣāṇa Mathurā (1st–3rd c.); Bhita liṅga (Lucknow) — no dataset records yet

nodes.name: Ekamukhaliṅga
nodes.summary: A liṅga with a single face of Śiva on its front, the commonest mukhaliṅga of Gupta-period north India.
nodes.details: Gupta examples include the liṅga in Udayagiri Cave 4 (early 5th c.) and those from Khoh and Bhumara (5th–6th c.).

attributes.earliestRepresentation: Udayagiri Cave 4, c. 401–415 CE (reign of Candragupta II)

earliestMaterial.label: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

nodes.name: Caturmukhaliṅga
nodes.summary: A liṅga with four faces of Śiva looking in the four directions, sometimes with a fifth implied on top (pañcamukha).
nodes.details: Well-known examples are the caturmukha liṅga of the Caturmukha Mahādeva temple near Nachna, the four-faced liṅga worshipped at Muṇḍeśvarī, and the Paśupatinātha liṅga in Kathmandu.

nodes.name: Pañcamukhaliṅga
nodes.summary: A liṅga with five faces, four around the shaft and one on top, corresponding to Sadāśiva’s five faces.

earliestMaterial.label: 10th c. (early 10th c. for the main temple)

nodes.name: Umā-Maheśvara
nodes.summary: Śiva seated with Umā (Pārvatī) on his left knee in an embrace (āliṅgana), a conjugal image very popular in Pāla Bengal, Kashmir and Nepal.
nodes.details: Śiva’s left arm embraces Umā while his right hand may hold a lotus or touch her chin; Nandin and a lion lie below. Examples go back to the Kuṣāṇa period at Mathurā.

attributes.posture: seated, Umā on Śiva’s left knee
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Kuṣāṇa Mathurā (no dataset record)

nodes.name: Kālāntaka (Kālāri)
nodes.summary: Śiva bursting out of the liṅga to kick Yama, the god of death, who has come to take the boy-devotee Mārkaṇḍeya clinging to the liṅga.
nodes.details: One of the Tamil “eight heroic deeds” (aṭṭavīraṭṭam) of Śiva, localised at Tirukkaṭavūr. Ellora and Cōḻa reliefs show Śiva with a raised leg kicking Yama, the boy embracing the liṅga.

attributes.posture: one leg raised kicking Yama

nodes.name: Lakulīśa
nodes.summary: The founder-teacher of the Pāśupata Śaivas, venerated as an avatāra of Śiva and shown as a seated ascetic with an erect phallus (ūrdhvaliṅga) holding a club (lakuṭa) and a citron.
nodes.details: Purāṇic lists of Śiva’s yoga-teacher avatāras end with Lakulin, said to have entered a corpse at Kāyārohaṇa (Karvan, Gujarat). The Mathurā pillar inscription of Candragupta II (Gupta year 61, 380 CE) names a teacher in the lineage of Kuśika, often linked with Lakulīśa’s disciples. Images, often on the lintels and gable-fronts of 7th–10th-century temples in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Odisha, show him seated in yoga, sometimes with four disciples.

attributes.posture: seated cross-legged, often in teaching mudrā

nodes.limits: Whether Lakulīśa was a historical person is uncertain; the images attest the cult, not the biography.

nodes.name: Anantaśayana (Śeṣaśāyī Viṣṇu)
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu reclining in cosmic sleep on the serpent Ananta (Śeṣa) on the ocean between creations, with Lakṣmī at his feet and Brahmā born on a lotus from his navel.
nodes.details: The serpent’s hoods canopy Viṣṇu’s head; Lakṣmī (sometimes with Bhū) massages his feet; the demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha, born from his ear-wax, threaten Brahmā; the personified weapons stand in attendance. Udayagiri Cave 13 (early 5th c.) and the south panel of the Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh (c. 500–525) are the classic Gupta examples. In the south the form became the great temple icons of Śrīraṅgam (Raṅganātha), Thiruvananthapuram (Padmanābha) and the reclining-Viṣṇu shrine of the Shore Temple.

attributes.posture: reclining (śayana) on the coiled serpent
definingTexts: Purāṇic creation narratives (e.g. Devī Māhātmya 1, Madhu–Kaiṭabha)
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Udayagiri Cave 13, c. 401–415 CE

earliestMaterial.label: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

nodes.name: Trivikrama
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu in the act of taking his three strides across the worlds after the dwarf Vāmana has won from Bali the land he can cover in three steps; one leg is raised high toward the sky.
nodes.details: The form joins the Ṛgvedic three strides of Viṣṇu to the Purāṇic Vāmana story. Images show eight arms with weapons, Bali and Śukra below, Brahmā washing the raised foot (from which the Gaṅgā flows) and sometimes Rāhu or Jāmbavān in the sky. The Agni Purāṇa lists Trivikrama among the twenty-four forms, holding lotus, mace, discus and conch (48.4). The earliest securely dated large Trivikrama is in Bādāmi Cave 3 (578 CE); Gupta and Licchavi reliefs are close in date.

attributes.posture: āliḍha / leg raised to the sky
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Bādāmi Cave 3, 578 CE (secure); Gupta and Licchavi reliefs of the 5th c.

nodes.name: Vaikuṇṭha Caturmūrti
nodes.summary: A four-faced Viṣṇu with a human face in front, a lion face and a boar face at the sides and a fierce face (Kapila) at the back, developed above all in Kashmir between the 8th and 10th centuries.
nodes.details: Pāñcarātra theology reads the four faces as the four vyūhas (Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha); another reading sees Narasiṃha and Varāha. The Jayākhya Saṃhitā is usually cited as the first text to describe the image (its date is itself debated, 5th or 7th–9th c.). Gupta Mathurā images with three heads (human, lion, boar) are the precursors. The image installed by Yaśovarman in the Lakṣmaṇa temple at Khajuraho, dated 954 CE, is said by its inscription to have come from Kailāsa via the Śāhi king of Kabul.

ayudha: hands on personified mace and discus
attributes.earliestRepresentation: three-headed Mathurā images of the 5th c. (precursors); Kashmir bronzes and stones 8th–10th c.; Khajuraho image dated 954 CE

nodes.name: Viśvarūpa
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu (or Kṛṣṇa) in his universal form, with many heads and arms and the whole cosmos, gods and beings emerging from or contained in his body, as revealed to Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gītā.
nodes.details: The textual locus is the theophany of Bhagavad Gītā 11. The Agni Purāṇa prescribes a twenty-armed, four-faced Viśvarūpa (49.23). Gupta-period Mathurā steles with radiating figures (5th c.) and the Licchavi Viśvarūpa relief at Changu Narayan are among early images.

attributes.earliestRepresentation: Gupta Mathurā stele, 5th c. (no dataset record)

nodes.name: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu seated with Lakṣmī on his left thigh, embracing her, a conjugal image popular in medieval north and central India and in Hoysaḷa Karnataka.

attributes.posture: seated, Lakṣmī on Viṣṇu’s left knee

earliestMaterial.label: 10th c. (main temple, attributed to Sāhila Varman)

nodes.name: Yoga-Narasiṃha
nodes.summary: Narasiṃha seated in yogic posture with his knees bound by a band (yogapaṭṭa), calm rather than in the act of killing Hiraṇyakaśipu; worshipped at many South Indian hill shrines.
nodes.details: Gopinatha Rao groups Narasiṃha images into the seated (āsīna/yoga), the emergent from a pillar (sthauṇa) and the killing (vidāraṇa, Ugra) types. The colossal seated Lakṣmī-Narasiṃha monolith at Hampi (1528) under Kṛṣṇadevarāya shows the seated type with yogapaṭṭa; its Lakṣmī figure is lost.

attributes.posture: utkuṭikāsana with yogapaṭṭa

nodes.name: Bhū-Varāha (Nṛvarāha)
nodes.summary: Varāha as a boar-headed man lifting the Earth goddess (Bhū) out of the ocean on his tusk or arm, one foot on the serpent king; the dominant anthropomorphic form of the boar avatāra.
nodes.details: The Agni Purāṇa prescribes a human-bodied Bhū-Varāha with mace and other weapons, holding conch or lotus in the left hand, with Śrī on his left elbow and the Earth and Ananta at his feet (49.2–3). The colossal relief in Udayagiri Cave 5 (early 5th c.) is the earliest dated monumental example; Bādāmi Caves 2 and 3, the Varāha maṇḍapa at Mamallapuram and Ellora follow.

attributes.posture: ālīḍha, one foot on the nāga king
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Udayagiri Cave 5, c. 401–415 CE

nodes.name: Yajña-Varāha (zoomorphic boar)
nodes.summary: Varāha as a colossal boar whose body is covered with rows of small figures of gods and sages, representing the boar as the embodiment of the sacrifice and of the cosmos.
nodes.details: The colossal boar of Eran, inscribed in the first year of the Hūṇa king Toramāṇa (c. 510), is the earliest dated example; Khajuraho has a later shrine of the zoomorphic boar.

attributes.form: entirely animal; small figures carved over the body
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Eran boar, c. 510 CE

nodes.name: Veṇugopāla
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa as the cowherd playing the flute, standing cross-legged with cows and cowherds around him; a favourite image of Hoysaḷa, Vijayanagara and later Vaiṣṇava art.

attributes.posture: standing with legs crossed (svastika)

nodes.name: Kāliyamardana Kṛṣṇa
nodes.summary: The child Kṛṣṇa dancing on the hoods of the serpent Kāliya in the Yamunā, holding its tail; one of the most popular Cōḻa bronze subjects.
nodes.details: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.16 narrates the episode; Kāliya’s wives (nāginīs) plead for his life. Images show the child with one foot on the central hood, the other raised, left hand holding the tail and right in abhaya.

attributes.posture: dancing on one foot on the serpent’s hood

nodes.name: Govardhanadhara Kṛṣṇa
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa lifting Mount Govardhana on one hand as an umbrella to shelter the cowherds from Indra’s storm; one of the earliest Kṛṣṇa scenes to be made as a cult image.
nodes.details: Gupta-period reliefs from Mathurā and Varanasi (5th c.) and the monumental Phnom Da Kṛṣṇa of Cambodia (6th c.) show the form early; the Kṛṣṇa maṇḍapa at Mamallapuram gives the full pastoral scene.

attributes.posture: standing, left arm raised holding the mountain
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Gupta stele from Varanasi (Bharat Kala Bhavan), 5th c.

nodes.name: Caturviṃśatimūrti (the twenty-four forms of Viṣṇu)
nodes.summary: Twenty-four named standing forms of four-armed Viṣṇu (Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda … Hari, Kṛṣṇa) that look identical except for the order in which the conch, discus, mace and lotus are held in the four hands.
nodes.details: Four objects in four hands can be arranged in exactly 24 ways, and the texts give one name to each arrangement. The Agni Purāṇa’s caturviṃśatimūrti-stotra lists them (48.1–12) and derives them from the vyūhas, each of the original forms dividing threefold (48.13–14). The Padma Purāṇa and the Rūpamaṇḍana give the same scheme with variant orders; medieval images in western and central India often label the form.

attributes.count: 24 = 4! arrangements of śaṅkha, cakra, gadā, padma
attributes.example: Keśava holds lotus, conch, discus and mace (AP 48.1)

nodes.name: Sudarśana (personified discus)
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu’s discus as a deity in its own right: the Cakrapuruṣa of Gupta art, the many-armed Sudarśana (Cakrattāḻvār) of South Indian temples, and the wooden post worshipped beside Jagannātha at Puri.
nodes.details: The Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā of the Pāñcarātra is devoted to the theology of Sudarśana as Viṣṇu’s will-power (saṅkalpa). South Indian images show Sudarśana with eight or sixteen arms against a hexagonal discus, often backed by Yoga-Narasiṃha.

attributes.form: figure in front of a six-pointed discus; back-to-back with Narasiṃha in South India

earliestMaterial.label: begun under Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga, early–mid 12th c.; completion given as 1161 in Wikipedia’s infobox

nodes.name: Āyudhapuruṣa (personified weapons)
nodes.summary: The convention of showing a deity’s weapons as small human attendants, such as the male Cakrapuruṣa (discus) and the female Gadādevī (mace) beside Gupta images of Viṣṇu.
nodes.details: The gender follows the grammatical gender of the weapon’s name (cakra masculine, gadā feminine). Viṣṇu rests his hands on their heads in Gupta images of the 5th century, for example at Udayagiri.

earliestMaterial.label: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

nodes.name: Mahiṣāsuramardinī
nodes.summary: The Goddess (Durgā, Caṇḍikā) slaying the buffalo demon Mahiṣa, the most widespread warrior image of the Goddess, attested from Kuṣāṇa Mathurā to Pāla Bengal, Java and Cambodia.
nodes.details: The earliest images, from Kuṣāṇa Mathurā (1st–2nd c. CE), show a small four- or six-armed goddess pressing down an entirely animal buffalo with her hands. Gupta images (Udayagiri, early 5th c.) add more arms and weapons. At Mamallapuram (7th c.) she rides her lion into battle against a buffalo-headed warrior in a narrative relief. Pāla and later images show the demon in human form emerging from the decapitated buffalo’s neck, as the Agni Purāṇa prescribes: a man with weapon raised springs from the buffalo’s neck, bound by the Goddess’s noose and attacked by the lion (AP 50.4–5); the goddess has twenty or ten arms (50.1–3).

attributes.demon: animal buffalo (early) → buffalo-headed warrior (Mamallapuram) → man emerging from buffalo’s neck (AP, Pāla)
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Kuṣāṇa Mathurā, 1st–2nd c. CE (Government Museum, Mathurā) — no dataset record yet; earliest in the dataset: Udayagiri (c. 401–415)

nodes.limits: The iconographic sequence is reconstructed from surviving images; it does not date the Devī Māhātmya, which is attested by 608 CE.

earliestMaterial.label: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

nodes.name: Gaja-Lakṣmī
nodes.summary: Lakṣmī (Śrī) standing or seated on a lotus while two elephants pour water over her from pots held in their trunks; one of the oldest goddess images in Indian art.
nodes.details: The earliest examples are on the railings of the Buddhist stūpas of Bharhut (c. 125–100 BCE, now in the Indian Museum, Kolkata) and Sanchi (Stūpa 2 railing and Stūpa 1 gateways), on coins of the Indo-Scythian king Azilises (1st c. BCE) and on Kauśāmbī coins. That the oldest images are on Buddhist monuments shows Śrī as a pan-Indian auspicious goddess, not a specifically Brahmanical deity. In medieval temples Gaja-Lakṣmī is the commonest figure on the centre of the door lintel (lalāṭabimba).

attributes.posture: standing or seated on a lotus
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Bharhut railing medallion, c. 125–100 BCE (Indian Museum, Kolkata) and Sanchi — Buddhist monuments; no dataset record yet

nodes.limits: The early images establish the motif, not a separate cult: on Buddhist railings Śrī is an auspicious emblem among yakṣīs and other figures.

nodes.name: Lajjā Gaurī
nodes.summary: A fertility goddess shown squatting with legs drawn up and open, often with a lotus in place of a head, worshipped across the Deccan from about the 1st to the 8th century; her identity and name are reconstructions.
nodes.details: Bolon traces a development from purely symbolic forms (a pot or lotus with limbs) through lotus-headed figures to fully anthropomorphic ones, with examples from Nāgārjunakoṇḍa, Ter, Bhita, Aihole and Bādāmi. The name “Lajjā Gaurī” (“modest Gaurī”) is a modern label; others identify her with Aditi Uttānapad of the Ṛgveda or with Renukā/Yellammā of living Deccan cults.

attributes.posture: uttānapad (squatting, legs open, knees raised)
attributes.head: lotus in place of a head
attributes.earliestRepresentation: terracottas and stone plaques of the early centuries CE (Deccan); no dataset record yet

nodes.limits: Who the worshippers took her to be is not recorded in any contemporary inscription.

nodes.name: Catuḥṣaṣṭi Yoginī (the sixty-four yoginīs)
nodes.summary: A circle of sixty-four powerful female deities of tantric cults, worshipped from about the 9th to the 12th century in circular, roofless temples in Odisha and central India.
nodes.details: Yoginī lists differ widely between texts. The Agni Purāṇa gives sixty-four names, beginning in the east (Aindrī quarter) and ending in the north-east, from Akṣobhyā and Rūkṣakarṇī to Jayantī, Durjayā and Jayāntikā, and describes them as eight- or four-armed, holding whatever weapons they wish (52.1–9). Dehejia’s survey of yoginī temples (Hirapur, Ranipur-Jharial, Bheraghat, Khajuraho, Mitaoli and others) shows each yoginī with her own mount and attributes.

earliestMaterial.label: 9th–10th c. CE (traditionally c. 864 under Queen Hīrādevī)

nodes.name: Daśa Mahāvidyās (the ten Great Wisdoms)
nodes.summary: A group of ten tantric goddesses — Kālī, Tārā, Tripurasundarī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Dhūmāvatī, Bagalāmukhī, Mātaṅgī and Kamalā — understood as forms of the one Goddess.
nodes.details: Kinsley treats the group as a relatively late, medieval development; the classic lists come from late medieval Śākta tantras and the Mahābhāgavata and Bṛhaddharma Purāṇas, where the Mahāvidyās appear to stop Śiva leaving Satī’s father’s sacrifice. The Toḍala Tantra (10.9–11) pairs each with an avatāra of Viṣṇu: Tārā with Matsya, Bagalā with Kūrma, Dhūmāvatī with Varāha, Chinnamastā with Narasiṃha, Bhuvaneśvarī with Vāmana, Mātaṅgī with Rāma, Tripurā with Paraśurāma, Bhairavī with Balabhadra, Mahālakṣmī with the Buddha, Durgā with Kalki, and Kālī herself with Kṛṣṇa.

nodes.name: Tārā (Mahāvidyā)
nodes.summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: dark blue goddess standing on a corpse, with sword, severed head, lotus and skull-cup; the Hindu Tārā shares her name with the Buddhist saviour goddess.

nodes.name: Tripurasundarī (Ṣoḍaśī, Lalitā)
nodes.summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: beautiful sixteen-year-old seated on a couch whose legs are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and Īśvara, holding noose, goad, sugarcane bow and flower arrows; the goddess of the Śrīvidyā tradition.

nodes.name: Bhuvaneśvarī
nodes.summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: mistress of the worlds, golden or red, holding noose and goad and showing varada and abhaya.

nodes.name: Bhairavī (Mahāvidyā)
nodes.summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: fierce red goddess with rosary, book, abhaya and varada, garlanded with skulls.

nodes.name: Chinnamastā
nodes.summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: self-decapitated goddess holding her own head, three streams of blood feeding the head and two attendants, standing on a copulating couple (Kāma and Rati).

nodes.name: Dhūmāvatī
nodes.summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: old widow in a crow-bannered chariot or on a crow, holding a winnowing basket, the inauspicious smoke goddess.

nodes.name: Bagalāmukhī
nodes.summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: yellow goddess pulling the tongue of a demon and raising a club, the power to paralyse an enemy.

nodes.name: Mātaṅgī
nodes.summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: dark-green goddess of speech and music, often playing a vīṇā, associated with pollution and leftovers (ucchiṣṭa).

nodes.name: Kamalā (Kamalātmikā)
nodes.summary: One of the ten Mahāvidyās: Lakṣmī seated on a lotus and bathed by elephants, the gaja-lakṣmī image incorporated into the Mahāvidyā group.

nodes.name: Annapūrṇā
nodes.summary: The Goddess as giver of food, holding a ladle and a bowl of rice, from whom Śiva as a mendicant receives alms; her principal temple is at Vārāṇasī.
nodes.details: Her cult is late medieval; Bhāratcandra’s Bengali Annadāmaṅgal (1752) celebrates her as Annadā. In 2021 an eighteenth-century Annapūrṇā image that had left Vārāṇasī about 1913 was returned from the University of Regina, Canada, and reinstalled at the Kāśī Viśvanātha temple complex.

attributes.posture: seated or standing

nodes.name: Sarasvatī (Jain Śrutadevatā)
nodes.summary: Sarasvatī as worshipped by Jains, the goddess of the scriptures (Śrutadevatā); the earliest dated image of Sarasvatī in any tradition is a Jain one from Kaṅkālī Ṭīlā, Mathurā, of the Kuṣāṇa period.
nodes.details: The Mathurā image, seated and holding a manuscript, carries a donative inscription dated in year 54 of the Kuṣāṇa era (2nd c. CE; the absolute date depends on the Kaniṣka epoch) and is kept in the State Museum, Lucknow. It is recorded here separately from the Vedic and Brahmanical goddess, as the contract requires where traditions differ; the two are linked by an IDENTIFIED_WITH assertion.

attributes.posture: seated, holding a manuscript
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Kaṅkālī Ṭīlā Sarasvatī, year 54 (Kuṣāṇa era), State Museum Lucknow — no dataset record; accession not verified

nodes.limits: The Jain image is the earliest dated Sarasvatī image; it shows a shared goddess, not that Hindu image worship of Sarasvatī derives from Jain practice.
openQuestions: Verify the museum accession number (often cited as J.24) and the reading of the date against the published inscription.

earliestMaterial.label: year 54 = c. 181 CE (if the era began in 127 CE)

nodes.name: Gaṅgā and Yamunā as door guardians
nodes.summary: The placing of the river goddesses Gaṅgā (on a makara) and Yamunā (on a tortoise) on either side of a temple doorway, a Gupta-period innovation that became standard in North Indian temples.
nodes.details: The Agni Purāṇa describes Gaṅgā (Jāhnavī) as white, holding a pot and a lotus, standing on a makara, and Yamunā as dark, holding a pot, standing on a tortoise (50.16–17). In early Gupta doorways the goddesses stand at the top of the jambs (Tigawa, Deogarh, Udayagiri); from about the 6th century they move to the bottom of the jambs. The rivers are read as purifying the devotee who passes between them.

attributes.Gaṅgā: on makara, pot and lotus, white (AP 50.16cd)
attributes.placement: top of the jambs (early Gupta) → base of the jambs (later)

earliestMaterial.label: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

nodes.name: Tortoise (Yamunā’s vāhana)
nodes.summary: The tortoise on which the river goddess Yamunā stands in temple-door iconography, as the makara carries Gaṅgā.

nodes.name: The Gaṇeśa verse of the Bṛhat Saṃhitā is a later addition
nodes.summary: Kern’s edition of the Bṛhat Saṃhitā includes a verse describing Vināyaka (his 58.58) that is absent from Tripathi’s text and Utpala’s commentary; if it is an interpolation, the sixth-century text did not describe Gaṇeśa.
nodes.details: The GRETIL e-text, based on Tripathi with Kern’s variants, prints the verse in brackets marked k.58.58 after the Kubera verse. Its absence from the commented text means it cannot be used to date Gaṇeśa’s iconography to the time of Varāhamihira.

nodes.name: Heramba Gaṇapati
nodes.summary: A five-headed, ten-armed Gaṇeśa riding a lion, popular in Nepal and Bengal, often shown with his consort.

nodes.name: Ucchiṣṭa Gaṇapati
nodes.summary: A tantric form of Gaṇeśa worshipped by the Ucchiṣṭa sect of Gāṇapatyas, shown with a female consort on his lap in an erotic embrace; worship in a state of ritual impurity (ucchiṣṭa) is part of the rite.

attributes.consort: nude śakti on the left knee

nodes.name: Nṛtta Gaṇapati (dancing Gaṇeśa)
nodes.summary: Gaṇeśa dancing, usually with eight arms, one leg raised; a favourite of Pāla Bengal, Hoysaḷa Karnataka and Nepal.

attributes.posture: dancing

nodes.name: Ṣaṇmukha (six-faced Skanda)
nodes.summary: Skanda with six heads and usually twelve arms, the form explained by his being nursed by the six Kṛttikās; in Tamil, Āṟumukam.
nodes.details: The Agni Purāṇa allows Skanda to be one-faced or six-faced (50.28). Six-headed figures appear on copper coins of the Yaudheya republic (2nd–3rd c. CE) labelled for Brahmaṇyadeva/Kārttikeya — the earliest six-headed images, not yet recorded in the dataset.

attributes.earliestRepresentation: Yaudheya coins, 2nd–3rd c. CE (no dataset record)

nodes.name: Devasenāpati (Subrahmaṇya with Vaḷḷi and Devasenā)
nodes.summary: Murukaṉ–Subrahmaṇya standing or seated on his peacock between his two consorts, the celestial Devasenā (Teyvāṉai) and the hunter-girl Vaḷḷi; the standard form in Tamil temples.
nodes.details: Devasenā (“army of the gods”) is Indra’s daughter in Sanskrit myth; Vaḷḷi is a Tamil hill girl. The pairing joins the Sanskrit commander of the divine army with the Tamil hill god.

nodes.name: Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi
nodes.summary: Murukaṉ as a shaven-headed renunciant boy holding a staff, wearing only a loincloth, the form worshipped on the hill at Palani.

earliestMaterial.label: medieval to modern fabric (dating not established in this pass)

nodes.name: Svāminātha
nodes.summary: Murukaṉ as the child teacher who explained the meaning of the syllable Om to his father Śiva, worshipped at Swamimalai.

nodes.name: Udīcyaveṣa Sūrya (Sūrya in northern dress)
nodes.summary: The standard North Indian image of the Sun god, dressed in the “northern” fashion of Central Asia — a long coat (kañcuka), belt and boots that cover him from feet to chest — and holding a lotus in each hand.
nodes.details: The Bṛhat Saṃhitā prescribes northern dress, hidden from the feet to the chest, a crown, earrings, a long necklace, a waist-girdle (viyadga/avyaṅga), a coat (kañcuka) and a jewelled halo, with a lotus in each hand (57.46–48). The Agni Purāṇa places him on a one-wheeled chariot of seven horses, holding two lotuses, with Daṇḍa and Piṅgala at the door (51.1–3). The dress is usually explained by the Iranian (Maga) priests associated with Sūrya worship, whom the same text names as the proper installers of Sun images (BS 59.19). Kuṣāṇa Mathurā Sūryas (2nd c. CE) already show the boots and tunic. South Indian Sūryas, by contrast, are bare-legged.

attributes.vahana: chariot of seven horses driven by Aruṇa (one wheel in AP 51.1)
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Kuṣāṇa Mathurā, 2nd c. CE (no dataset record)

nodes.name: Revanta
nodes.summary: A son of Sūrya, lord of horses and of the hunt, shown riding a horse with attendants, dogs and hunting gear; his images are mostly of the 6th–12th centuries in north and east India.
nodes.details: The Bṛhat Saṃhitā prescribes Revanta mounted on a horse with a retinue for hunting and sport (57.56). The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa tells his birth from Sūrya and Saṃjñā in the form of horses.

nodes.name: Navagraha (the nine planets)
nodes.summary: The nine “seizers” of Indian astral religion — Sūrya, Candra (Soma), Maṅgala, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śani, Rāhu and Ketu — carved as a row on temple door lintels from the post-Gupta period and worshipped in their own shrines in South India.
nodes.details: Early lintels (c. 6th–8th c.) show eight grahas; Ketu was added later to make nine. The Agni Purāṇa gives the attributes: the Moon with water-pot and rosary, Mars with spear and rosary, Mercury with bow and rosary, Jupiter and Venus with water-pot and rosary, Saturn with a girdle of bells, Rāhu with a half-moon, and Ketu with sword and lamp (51.10–12). At Konark a large navagraha slab from the main doorway is still worshipped near the temple.

attributes.placement: door lintels (north India); separate navagraha shrines (south India)
attributes.earliestRepresentation: lintels of the 6th–8th c. with eight grahas

nodes.name: Maṅgala (Mars)
nodes.summary: The planet Mars as a deity, red-complexioned, holding a spear and rosary in the Agni Purāṇa; also called Aṅgāraka and Bhauma (son of the Earth).

nodes.name: Bṛhaspati (Jupiter)
nodes.summary: Bṛhaspati, preceptor of the gods, as the planet Jupiter, holding a water-pot and rosary in the Agni Purāṇa.

nodes.name: Śani (Saturn)
nodes.summary: The planet Saturn as a slow, dark and feared deity, son of Sūrya and Chāyā, shown with a girdle of bells in the Agni Purāṇa and later with a crow or vulture as mount.

nodes.name: Ketu (the descending node)
nodes.summary: The ninth graha, the headless body (or tail) of the eclipse demon, shown with a sword and a lamp in the Agni Purāṇa; often half-serpent in sculpture.

nodes.name: Aṣṭa-dikpāla (guardians of the eight directions)
nodes.summary: The eight guardians of the directions — Indra (east), Agni (south-east), Yama (south), Nirṛti (south-west), Varuṇa (west), Vāyu (north-west), Kubera (north) and Īśāna (north-east) — carved on the corners of temple walls and ceilings.
nodes.details: The Agni Purāṇa makes the lokapālas two-armed: Indra with the thunderbolt on an elephant, Agni with a spear on a goat or ram, Varuṇa with a noose on a makara, Vāyu with a banner on a deer (51.14–16). The Bṛhat Saṃhitā gives Indra a white four-tusked elephant and a horizontal third eye (57.42), Yama a staff and buffalo, Varuṇa a noose but a goose (haṃsa) as mount, and Kubera a man as mount, a crown on the left and a big belly (57.57). In Khajuraho temples each dikpāla stands on the appropriate corner of the wall.

attributes.placement: corner offsets of the wall (jaṅghā); ceiling panels

nodes.name: Nirṛti (guardian of the south-west)
nodes.summary: Nirṛti, a Vedic power of decay and misfortune (female in the Veda), who in temple iconography becomes the male guardian of the south-west, holding a sword and riding a man or a corpse.

nodes.name: Īśāna (guardian of the north-east)
nodes.summary: Īśāna, a name of Śiva/Rudra, as guardian of the north-east, shown like Śiva with trident and bull.

nodes.name: Airāvata
nodes.summary: Indra’s white elephant, said to have emerged at the churning of the ocean; the Bṛhat Saṃhitā gives him four tusks.

nodes.name: Buffalo (Yama’s vāhana)
nodes.summary: The male water buffalo on which Yama, god of death and guardian of the south, rides.

nodes.name: Ram / goat (Agni’s vāhana)
nodes.summary: The ram or he-goat (chāga) on which Agni, guardian of the south-east, rides in temple iconography.

nodes.name: Deer (Vāyu’s vāhana)
nodes.summary: The deer or antelope on which Vāyu, the wind god and guardian of the north-west, rides.

nodes.name: Parrot (Kāmadeva’s vāhana)
nodes.summary: The parrot (śuka) on which Kāmadeva, god of love, rides in later iconography.

nodes.name: Pañcamukha Hanumān
nodes.summary: Hanumān with five faces — his own (east), Narasiṃha, Garuḍa, Varāha and Hayagrīva — and ten arms, a protective tantric form popular in South India from the late medieval period.

nodes.name: Vīra Hanumān
nodes.summary: The heroic, striding or flying Hanumān, often carrying the mountain of healing herbs and raising a mace or his hand in protection; the form at many village shrines and on banners.

attributes.posture: striding or flying

nodes.name: Dāsa Hanumān
nodes.summary: Hanumān as the humble servant of Rāma, standing or kneeling with joined palms (añjali) before Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa; the usual form in Rāma temples.

attributes.posture: standing or kneeling

nodes.name: Nāga (serpent deities)
nodes.summary: Serpent deities shown as hooded cobras or as humans with a canopy of serpent hoods, worshipped since at least the Śuṅga–Kuṣāṇa period as guardians of water, fertility and treasure.
nodes.details: Kuṣāṇa Mathurā produced large standing nāga images, some dated by inscription. The Agni Purāṇa names eight nāgas — Ananta, Takṣaka, Karka(ṭa), Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha and Kulika among them — all with thread, hooded heads and great radiance (51.13). Balarāma (as Śeṣa’s incarnation) and Pārśvanātha share the hood canopy.

attributes.form: human torso with 3, 5 or 7 hoods, or cobra
attributes.earliestRepresentation: Śuṅga–Kuṣāṇa Mathurā nāga images (no dataset record)

nodes.name: Yakṣa
nodes.summary: Nature and wealth spirits worshipped in monumental, pot-bellied standing images from the Maurya–Śuṅga period; Kubera is their king, and yakṣa imagery shaped later Hindu, Buddhist and Jain icons.
nodes.details: The colossal Parkham yakṣa (Government Museum, Mathurā; 2nd–1st c. BCE) and the labelled yakṣas of the Bharhut railing — including one inscribed “Kupiro yakho” (Kubera the yakṣa) — are early examples. Coomaraswamy argued that the yakṣa type is the source of the standing cult image in India.

attributes.earliestRepresentation: Parkham yakṣa (Mathurā Museum) and Bharhut railing yakṣas, 2nd c. BCE — no dataset records yet

nodes.limits: The early images document yakṣa worship; Coomaraswamy’s derivation of later icons from them is an argument, not a documented lineage.

earliestMaterial.label: second half of the 1st century BCE (palaeography of the inscription)

nodes.name: Yakṣī
nodes.summary: Female nature spirits shown as voluptuous women grasping a tree branch (śālabhañjikā) or holding a fly-whisk, among the earliest monumental female figures of Indian art.

attributes.earliestRepresentation: Didarganj yakṣī (Patna; date debated) and Bharhut/Sanchi yakṣīs, 2nd–1st c. BCE — no dataset records yet

nodes.name: Hindu temple architecture (prāsāda)
nodes.summary: The architecture of the Hindu temple as a house and body of the god: a sanctum (garbhagṛha) beneath a tower, reached through halls and enclosed by walls, designed on a square grid and grown from aedicular parts.
nodes.details: Stone and brick temples survive from the Gupta period (5th c.); earlier shrines were of perishable materials. Indian texts and modern scholars distinguish two great families, Nāgara (northern) and Drāviḍa (southern), with hybrid and regional traditions (Vesara/Karṇāṭa-Drāviḍa, Kaliṅga, Kerala, Kashmiri, Bengali, Himalayan and Newar) and the related architectures of Southeast Asia. Hardy analyses both families as compositions of miniature shrine-forms (aedicules) arranged around the central axis.

nodes.name: Nāgara (northern temple style)
nodes.summary: The North Indian temple tradition, whose sanctum is crowned by a curvilinear tower (śikhara) topped by a ribbed āmalaka and a pot finial; its plan is a square made complex by projecting offsets (rathas).
nodes.details: Its sub-types are the Latina (single spire with a mesh of interlaced arches), the Śekharī (clustered spires), the Bhūmija (rows of miniature spires), and the stepped-roof Phāṃsanā and barrel-roofed Valabhī for subsidiary buildings. Regional schools include those of Central India (Candela, Paramāra), Odisha (Kaliṅga), western India (Māru-Gurjara) and the Deccan. Texts: Aparājitapṛcchā, Samarāṅgaṇa Sūtradhāra, Śilpa Prakāśa (for Odisha), Prāsādamaṇḍana.

nodes.name: Latina (single-spired Nāgara)
nodes.summary: The earliest and basic Nāgara tower, a single curvilinear spire whose faces carry vertical bands of interlaced arch motifs (latā, “creeper”), crowned by an āmalaka.
nodes.details: Developed from the 5th–6th century (brick at Bhitargaon and Sirpur, stone at Alampur and Aihole) and dominant until the 10th century. The Odishan rekhā deuḷa is its eastern variant.

nodes.name: Śekharī (clustered-spire Nāgara)
nodes.summary: The composite Nāgara tower in which half-spires (urūśṛṅgas) and miniature spires (śṛṅgas) are clustered against the central Latina spire, building up a mountain-like silhouette from the 10th century.
nodes.details: The Kandarīya Mahādeva at Khajuraho (c. 1025–1050), with 84 miniature spires, is its classic expression; Māru-Gurjara temples use it too.

nodes.name: Bhūmija (storeyed-spire Nāgara)
nodes.summary: A Nāgara tower whose four faces carry central bands of interlaced arches separated by quarters filled with horizontal rows of miniature spires (kūṭastambhas) stacked in storeys (bhūmi), developed in Mālava under the Paramāras in the 11th century.
nodes.details: The Samarāṅgaṇa Sūtradhāra attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja is the main text describing Bhūmija temples; examples spread to Maharashtra (Ambarnath, 1060), Rajasthan and the Deccan.

nodes.name: Drāviḍa (southern temple style)
nodes.summary: The South Indian temple tradition, whose sanctum tower (vimāna) rises in storeys (tala) of miniature pavilions — square kūṭas, oblong śālās and horseshoe-arched pañjaras — to a domed crowning member called the śikhara.
nodes.details: It emerges in Pallava rock-cut monoliths (7th c.) and structural temples (Shore Temple, Kailāsanātha, c. 700), reaches monumental scale under the Cōḻas (Thanjavur, c. 1010) and, from the 12th century on, shifts emphasis to towering gateways (gopuras) and concentric walled enclosures (Śrīraṅgam, Madurai). The Mayamata and Mānasāra are its principal texts and name drāviḍa as the type with an octagonal crowning member.

nodes.name: Vesara
nodes.summary: A term of the southern texts for a temple whose crowning member is circular (or apsidal), now used loosely for the hybrid temple architecture of Karnataka that combines Nāgara and Drāviḍa features.
nodes.details: The Mayamata and Mānasāra classify temples as nāgara (square top), drāviḍa (octagonal) and vesara (circular), a usage that does not map onto the regional styles. Modern authors applied “vesara” to the Later Cālukya and Hoysaḷa temples of Karnataka; Hardy prefers “Karṇāṭa Drāviḍa” for that tradition. See claim:vesara-meaning.

nodes.name: Karṇāṭa Drāviḍa
nodes.summary: Adam Hardy’s term for the Drāviḍa tradition of the Karnataka region from the early Cālukyas (7th c.) through the Rāṣṭrakūṭas, Later Cālukyas and Hoysaḷas (13th c.), marked by increasingly projected, staggered and finally stellate plans.
