nodes.details: Hardy traces how the aedicular components of the Drāviḍa vimāna multiply and project, culminating in the star-shaped plans of the Hoysaḷa temples (Belur, Halebidu, Somanathapura). Dhaky’s study of temple-type names in Karṇāṭa inscriptions underpins the classification.

nodes.name: Kaliṅga (Odishan) temple style
nodes.summary: The temple architecture of Odisha, a regional Nāgara tradition with its own terms: the curvilinear rekhā deuḷa over the sanctum, the pyramidal pīḍhā deuḷa over the hall (jagamohana) and the barrel-roofed khākharā deuḷa.
nodes.details: Bhubaneswar preserves a sequence from the 7th century (Paraśurāmeśvara) through the Mukteśvara (10th c.) and Liṅgarāja (11th c.) to the Jagannātha at Puri (12th c.) and Konark (13th c.). The Śilpa Prakāśa and other Odishan manuals use the local vocabulary (bāḍa, gaṇḍi, mastaka).

nodes.name: Rekhā deuḷa
nodes.summary: The Odishan curvilinear tower over the sanctum, a regional form of the Latina śikhara.

nodes.name: Pīḍhā deuḷa
nodes.summary: The Odishan stepped pyramidal roof of horizontal tiers (pīḍhā), used over the jagamohana and other halls.

nodes.name: Khākharā deuḷa
nodes.summary: The Odishan rectangular shrine with a barrel-vaulted roof (named after a gourd), used chiefly for goddess shrines such as the Vaitāl Deuḷ in Bhubaneswar.

nodes.name: Kerala temple style
nodes.summary: The temple architecture of Kerala: square, circular or apsidal sanctums (śrīkōvil) of laterite and timber under steep conical or pyramidal roofs of tiles or copper, set within a cloistered rectangular court (nālambalam) with a lamp-gallery (vilakkumāṭam).
nodes.details: Ritual and planning are governed by the Tantrasamuccaya (15th c.). The style responds to heavy monsoon rain; many temples combine it with Drāviḍa elements in stone.

nodes.name: Kashmiri temple style
nodes.summary: The stone temple architecture of Kashmir (8th–11th c.), with steep double-pitched pyramidal roofs, trefoil arches set in triangular pediments, fluted columns and colonnaded courtyards.
nodes.details: Mārtaṇḍa (Lalitāditya, 8th c.) and Avantisvāmin (Avantivarman, 9th c.) are the major monuments; Gandhāran and Gupta elements are combined.

nodes.name: Khmer temple architecture
nodes.summary: The temple architecture of Cambodia and its empire (6th–13th c.), culminating in the “temple-mountain”: towers (prasat) on stepped terraces, often in a quincunx, surrounded by concentric galleries and moats, built in brick, laterite and sandstone with corbelled vaults.
nodes.details: Art historians name its phases after key monuments (Phnom Kulen, Preah Ko, Bakheng, Banteay Srei, Angkor Wat, Bayon). The temple-mountain embodies Mount Meru.

nodes.name: Central Javanese temple architecture
nodes.summary: The stone candi architecture of Central Java (c. 7th–10th c.): a square cella on a high base, a doorway framed by kāla-makara ornament, and a stepped roof crowned with miniature shrines or ratnas.
nodes.details: The Dieng temples are among the earliest; Prambanan (inaugurated 856) is the largest Hindu example.

nodes.name: Cham temple architecture
nodes.summary: The brick tower-sanctuaries (kalan) of Champa in central Vietnam (7th–13th c.), with finely carved brick and sandstone decoration, mostly dedicated to Śiva as Bhadreśvara.
nodes.details: Mỹ Sơn preserves the longest sequence; scholars name styles after sites (Mỹ Sơn E1, Hòa Lai, Đồng Dương, Tháp Mẫm).

nodes.name: Bengal temple style (cālā and ratna)
nodes.summary: The brick and terracotta temples of Bengal (16th–19th c.), whose curved roofs imitate thatched huts (cālā types) or carry pinnacles (ratna types), their façades covered in terracotta plaques of epic and Kṛṣṇa scenes.
nodes.details: McCutchion classified the temples into cālā (do-cālā, cār-cālā, āṭ-cālā), ratna (pañcaratna, navaratna), and other types; Bishnupur under the Malla kings is the best-known centre.

nodes.name: Cālā temple (Bengal)
nodes.summary: Bengali temple type whose curved roof imitates the thatched village hut: do-cālā (two slopes), cār-cālā (four) and āṭ-cālā (four with a smaller four-sloped storey above).

nodes.name: Ratna temple (Bengal)
nodes.summary: Bengali temple type with a flat or curved roof carrying one, five (pañcaratna) or nine (navaratna) towers.

nodes.name: Māru-Gurjara (Solaṅkī) style
nodes.summary: The western Indian Nāgara tradition of Gujarat and Rajasthan (c. 10th–13th c. and revived since), with richly carved Śekharī towers, ornate pillared halls and stepped tanks; the term was coined by M. A. Dhaky.
nodes.details: Modhera (1026–27) is a classic monument. The Aparājitapṛcchā and Maṇḍana’s Prāsādamaṇḍana are its texts; hereditary Sompura architects continue it in modern temples, including the rebuilt Somanātha and the Rām Mandir at Ayodhyā.

nodes.name: Hemāḍpanthī style
nodes.summary: A name used in Maharashtra for medieval temples of dry-laid, mortarless stone masonry, traditionally credited to Hemādri (Hemāḍpant), minister of the Yādava kings in the 13th century.
nodes.details: The attribution of the whole style to Hemādri is traditional; architecturally the temples belong to the Bhūmija and Nāgara traditions of the Deccan.

nodes.name: Newar pagoda style
nodes.summary: The multi-roofed temple architecture of the Kathmandu Valley, with tiered roofs of tile or gilt copper on brick cores, supported by carved wooden struts (tunāla) depicting deities.
nodes.details: Paśupatinātha and Changu Narayan are major examples; the Newar architect Araniko is credited with introducing the form to Yuan China.

nodes.name: Rock-cut temple
nodes.summary: A temple excavated into living rock, either as a cave (guhā) behind a pillared façade or as a monolith carved free from the hillside; the dominant form for Brahmanical temples in the Deccan and Tamil country from the 5th to the 8th century.
nodes.details: Caves: Udayagiri (early 5th c.), Bādāmi (6th c.), Elephanta, Ellora, Pallava maṇḍapas. Monoliths: the Pañca Rathas at Mamallapuram (7th c.) and the Kailāsa at Ellora (8th c.).

nodes.name: Gupta flat-roofed shrine
nodes.summary: The earliest type of free-standing stone temple in north India (early 5th c.): a small square sanctum with a flat slab roof and a pillared porch.
nodes.details: Sanchi Temple 17 and the Kaṅkālī Devī temple at Tigawa are standard examples; Nachna adds a covered ambulatory and an upper chamber.

nodes.name: Pañcāyatana plan
nodes.summary: A temple layout with the main shrine at the centre of a platform and four subsidiary shrines at its corners.
nodes.details: Deogarh’s Daśāvatāra temple (early 6th c.) is an early example; the Lakṣmaṇa temple at Khajuraho (954) is a complete one. The Smārta “pañcāyatana pūjā” of five deities is a related ritual idea.

nodes.name: Sāndhāra (temple with ambulatory)
nodes.summary: A temple whose sanctum is enclosed by an inner ambulatory passage within the outer walls, as opposed to a nirandhāra temple without one.

nodes.name: Gajapṛṣṭha (apsidal) plan
nodes.summary: A temple plan with a rounded (apsidal) back, “like an elephant’s back”, derived from early Buddhist caitya halls and used for some Hindu shrines in the Deccan and Tamil country.

nodes.name: Balinese temple (pura)
nodes.summary: The open-air walled temple compound of Bali, with courtyards and multi-roofed meru towers whose number of roofs marks the rank of the deity.

nodes.name: “Vesara” names the hybrid temple style of Karnataka
nodes.summary: A modern art-historical use of the textual term vesara for the Later Cālukya and Hoysaḷa temples of Karnataka; in the Mayamata and Mānasāra the word only denotes a temple with a circular crowning member.
nodes.details: Supporters treat vesara as the “third style” between Nāgara and Drāviḍa; critics, including Hardy, argue that the Karnataka temples are a Drāviḍa tradition with Nāgara borrowings and that the textual tripartition is about crowning shapes, not regions.

nodes.name: Garbhagṛha (sanctum)
nodes.summary: The dark, usually square inner sanctum (“womb-chamber”) housing the principal image or liṅga, at the centre of the temple’s axis.

nodes.name: Vimāna
nodes.summary: In South Indian usage the whole sanctum building with its storeyed tower; in some northern texts a name for particular temple types.

nodes.name: Śikhara (tower / crowning member)
nodes.summary: In the north, the curvilinear tower rising above the sanctum; in Drāviḍa usage, the domed or polygonal crowning member at the top of the vimāna.

nodes.name: Gopura (gateway tower)
nodes.summary: The monumental gateway tower in the enclosure walls of South Indian temples, growing from the 12th century to dwarf the sanctum tower (Chidambaram, Śrīraṅgam, Madurai).

nodes.name: Maṇḍapa (pillared hall)
nodes.summary: A pillared hall in front of or around the sanctum, used for gathering, dance, music or ritual; temples may have several in sequence.

nodes.name: Āmalaka
nodes.summary: The ribbed, cushion-shaped stone disc (named after the āmalaka fruit) that crowns a Nāgara tower beneath the finial; smaller āmalakas mark the storeys of the tower’s corners.

nodes.name: Kalaśa (pot finial)
nodes.summary: The pot-shaped finial at the summit of a temple tower or gateway, the point where the vertical axis meets the sky.

nodes.name: Prākāra (enclosure wall)
nodes.summary: An enclosure wall around a temple; large South Indian temples have up to seven concentric prākāras with gopuras on their axes.

nodes.name: Antarāla (vestibule)
nodes.summary: The vestibule linking the sanctum to the hall in front of it.

nodes.name: Jagamohana
nodes.summary: The Odishan assembly hall in front of the sanctum, roofed with a pīḍhā pyramid; at Konark it is the main surviving structure.

nodes.name: Gavākṣa (candraśālā / kuḍu)
nodes.summary: The horseshoe-shaped arch motif, derived from the window of wooden buildings, that is multiplied into the mesh of Nāgara towers and the kuḍu arches of Drāviḍa cornices.

nodes.name: Pradakṣiṇāpatha (ambulatory)
nodes.summary: The path for clockwise circumambulation of the sanctum, either inside the walls (sāndhāra temples) or around the building.

nodes.name: Dvārapāla (door guardian)
nodes.summary: Guardian figures flanking the sanctum doorway, often fierce, armed with clubs, and in Śaiva temples sometimes identified with Nandin and Mahākāla.

nodes.name: Mithuna (auspicious couple)
nodes.summary: Amorous couples carved on doorways and walls as auspicious, protective images; the Bṛhat Saṃhitā already lists them among the door decorations.

nodes.name: Mathurā school of sculpture (Śaka–Kuṣāṇa period)
nodes.summary: The red-sandstone sculpture of Mathurā from the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE, which produced the earliest anthropomorphic images of many Hindu deities — Vṛṣṇi heroes, Ardhanārīśvara, Mahiṣāsuramardinī, the Mothers, Sūrya, Kārttikeya and nāgas — alongside Buddhist and Jain images.

nodes.name: Gupta-period sculpture
nodes.summary: Sculpture of north and central India in the Gupta and immediately post-Gupta period (c. 320–550), in which most of the standard Hindu iconographic forms first appear in mature, often dated, examples.

nodes.name: Pāla–Sena sculpture
nodes.summary: The sculpture of Bihar and Bengal under the Pāla and Sena dynasties (8th–12th c.), mostly finely carved black stone steles with elaborate back-slabs, crowded attendants and fully codified multi-armed iconography, Buddhist and Hindu alike.

nodes.name: Cōḻa bronzes
nodes.summary: The lost-wax copper-alloy processional images (utsava-mūrti) of the Tamil country made under the Cōḻas (c. 850–1280), designed to be dressed and carried in festivals; they include the classic Naṭarāja, Somāskanda, Bhikṣāṭana and Kāliyamardana types.

nodes.name: The 108 karaṇas
nodes.summary: The 108 units of dance movement defined in the fourth chapter of Bharata’s Nāṭyaśāstra, carved as series of dance panels on Cōḻa and later Tamil temples, where Śiva is understood as their originator.
nodes.details: At the Bṛhadīśvara temple, Thanjavur (c. 1010), a series of karaṇa reliefs of Śiva dancing was begun in the upper passage of the vimāna and left incomplete (81 of 108 are usually reported). At Chidambaram the gateway towers carry all 108 karaṇas danced by a female dancer, with the Nāṭyaśāstra verses inscribed above the panels in the east gopura; Kumbakonam (Sāraṅgapāṇi) and Tiruvannamalai have later series.
openQuestions: The count at Thanjavur (81) and the labelling at Chidambaram are taken from reference works and should be checked against Sivaramamurti 1974 or Vatsyayan.

nodes.name: Abhaya-mudrā (gesture of fearlessness)
nodes.summary: The right hand raised, palm outward, granting protection; the Bṛhat Saṃhitā calls Viṣṇu’s empty hand “peace-giving” (śāntida).

nodes.name: Varada-mudrā (boon-giving gesture)
nodes.summary: The hand lowered, palm outward, bestowing boons.

nodes.name: Vyākhyāna- / cin-mudrā (teaching gesture)
nodes.summary: Thumb and index finger joined in a circle, the other fingers extended, signifying exposition or knowledge; characteristic of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.

nodes.name: Tribhaṅga (thrice-bent posture)
nodes.summary: A standing pose in which the body bends at neck, waist and knee in alternating directions, used for graceful deities, consorts and Kṛṣṇa as flute-player.

nodes.name: Utkuṭikāsana with yogapaṭṭa
nodes.summary: A squatting yogic posture with the knees raised and bound by a cloth band (yogapaṭṭa).

nodes.name: Triśūla (trident)
nodes.summary: Śiva’s three-pronged spear, also carried by Durgā, Māheśvarī and Īśāna.

nodes.name: Śaṅkha (conch)
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu’s conch (Pāñcajanya in the epic), held in a left hand; with discus, mace and lotus it defines his twenty-four forms.

nodes.name: Gadā (mace)
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu’s mace (Kaumodakī), often personified as the female Gadādevī; also carried by Balarāma, Hanumān and Bhīma.

nodes.name: Paraśu (axe)
nodes.summary: The battle-axe held by Śiva in several forms, by Gaṇeśa and by Paraśurāma.

nodes.name: Pāśa (noose)
nodes.summary: The noose, weapon of Varuṇa, Yama and of the Goddess, binding enemies and the bound soul.

nodes.name: Aṅkuśa (elephant goad)
nodes.summary: The elephant goad, held by Gaṇeśa, Indra and the Goddess as Tripurasundarī.

nodes.name: Vajra (thunderbolt)
nodes.summary: Indra’s thunderbolt, carried also by Aindrī and many tantric deities.

nodes.name: Ḍamaru (hourglass drum)
nodes.summary: The small two-headed drum held by Śiva (above all as Naṭarāja), Bhairava and fierce goddesses.

nodes.name: Akṣamālā (rosary)
nodes.summary: The rosary of beads held by ascetic and teaching deities such as Brahmā, Sarasvatī, Dakṣiṇāmūrti and the planets.

nodes.name: Kamaṇḍalu (water-pot)
nodes.summary: The ascetic’s water-pot, the mark of Brahmā and of sages.

nodes.name: Śrīvatsa
nodes.summary: An auspicious mark on the chest of Viṣṇu (and in Jain images of the Jina), the seat of Śrī; the Bṛhat Saṃhitā prescribes it for both.

nodes.name: Śakti / vel (spear)
nodes.summary: The lance of Skanda (the Tamil vel) and of Kaumārī.

nodes.name: Western Himalayan timber temple
nodes.summary: The wooden and timber-laced stone temples of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, built in the kāṭh-kuṇi technique of alternating timber and stone courses, with tiered pent or pagoda roofs and carved wooden façades.
nodes.details: Examples include the Hiḍimbā Devī temple at Manali (1553) and the Bhīmakālī complex at Sarahan; Goetz studied the early wooden temples of Chamba.

nodes.name: Matsya Purāṇa 258–263: images, pedestals and the liṅga
nodes.summary: The block of Matsya Purāṇa chapters on making images of Viṣṇu and Śiva and their forms (Bhairava, Ardhanārīśvara, Umā-Maheśvara and others), on pedestals and on the liṅga, among the oldest Purāṇic iconographic chapters.
nodes.details: Secondary outlines assign Vaiṣṇava images to chapters 258–260, Śiva’s forms including Bhairava to 259 and Ardhanārīśvara, Umā-Maheśvara, Kārttikeya and Gaṇeśa to 260, Śiva on the bull to 261, ten kinds of pedestal to 262 and the liṅga, sized in proportion to the temple, to 263. Elsewhere the Purāṇa lists twenty temple types (Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa …) as the Bṛhat Saṃhitā does. Numbering follows the vulgate (Ānandāśrama) edition of 291 chapters; the GRETIL e-text covers only chapters 1–176.
openQuestions: Check the exact verse ranges against the Ānandāśrama edition; GRETIL does not include these chapters.

nodes.name: Western Kṣatrapas (Kārdamaka line of Caṣṭana)
nodes.summary: Śaka rulers of western and central India (Gujarat, Malwa) from the 1st to the 4th century CE, whose dated records use the Śaka era. Rudradāman I of this line issued the Junagadh rock inscription of year 72.

dates.label: c. 35–415 CE
dates.basis: dated inscriptions and dated coinage in the Śaka era

sources.locator: bk. II, nos. 61–67 (records of Caṣṭana and Rudradāman)
bk. II, ch. II, records of the Śaka satraps

nodes.name: Rudradāman I
nodes.summary: Mahākṣatrapa of the Western Kṣatrapa (Kārdamaka) line, grandson of Caṣṭana. His Junagadh rock inscription of (Śaka) year 72 = c. 150 CE is the earliest long royal praśasti in Sanskrit.

dates.label: c. 130–150 CE
dates.basis: dated inscriptions (Andhau year 52, Junagadh year 72) in the Śaka era

nodes.name: Aśoka (Maurya)
nodes.summary: Mauryan emperor (r. c. 268–232 BCE) whose rock edicts at Girnar share a boulder with the inscriptions of Rudradāman and Skandagupta; the Junagadh inscription names him as the king for whom the Yavana Tuṣāspha built conduits on the Sudarśana lake.

dates.label: c. 268–232 BCE
dates.basis: regnal synchronisms in the edicts (Hellenistic kings named in Rock Edict XIII)

sources.locator: bk. II, no. 67, line 8 (Aśoka the Maurya)

nodes.name: Samudragupta
nodes.summary: Gupta emperor (r. c. 335/350–375 CE), son of Candragupta I and the Licchavi princess Kumāradevī. His conquests are recorded in Hariṣeṇa's praśasti on the Allahabad pillar; his coins include the Garuḍa-standard and aśvamedha types.

dates.label: c. 335/350–375 CE
dates.basis: regnal sequence of the Gupta records; no dated record of his own

nodes.name: Hariṣeṇa
nodes.summary: Gupta minister (sāndhivigrahika, kumārāmātya, mahādaṇḍanāyaka), son of Dhruvabhūti, who composed the praśasti of Samudragupta inscribed on the Allahabad pillar.

nodes.name: Skandagupta
nodes.summary: Gupta emperor (r. c. 455–467 CE), son of Kumāragupta I. His Bhitari pillar records the installation of an image of Viṣṇu (Śārṅgin) and battles with the Hūṇas; his Junagadh rock inscription records the repair of the Sudarśana lake (Gupta years 136–138).

nodes.name: Parṇadatta
nodes.summary: Governor of Surāṣṭra appointed by Skandagupta, named in the Junagadh rock inscription; father of Cakrapālita.

dates.label: c. 455–458 CE
dates.basis: Gupta years 136–138 in the Junagadh inscription

nodes.name: Cakrapālita
nodes.summary: Son of Parṇadatta and officer at Girinagara (Junagadh) who repaired the Sudarśana lake embankment after it burst in Gupta year 136 and, according to Fleet's reading, built a temple of Viṣṇu (Cakrabhṛt) in year 138.

nodes.name: Uditācārya
nodes.summary: Māheśvara (Pāśupata) teacher who in Gupta year 61 (380 CE) installed two liṅgas named after his teachers, Upamiteśvara and Kapileśvara, at Mathurā. The record counts him tenth in descent from Kuśika.

nodes.name: Kadamba dynasty (Banavāsi)
nodes.summary: Dynasty of the western Deccan (4th–6th century CE) with its capital at Vaijayantī (Banavāsi); its founding legend, the brahmin Mayūraśarman turning warrior after a quarrel at the Pallava capital, is told in the Tāḷagunda inscription.

nodes.name: Mayūraśarman
nodes.summary: Founder of the Kadamba dynasty as the Tāḷagunda inscription tells it: a brahmin of the Kadamba family who went to the Pallava capital to study, was humiliated in a quarrel with a Pallava horseman and took up arms.

dates.label: mid-4th century CE
dates.basis: genealogy of the Tāḷagunda inscription counted back from Śāntivarman

nodes.limits: Known almost entirely from a dynastic praśasti written about a century later; the story is foundation narrative, not contemporary report.

nodes.name: Śāntivarman (Kadamba)
nodes.summary: Kadamba king in whose reign the poet Kubja engraved the Tāḷagunda pillar praśasti; grandson of Kākusthavarman.

nodes.name: Kubja (poet of Tāḷagunda)
nodes.summary: Poet who composed and engraved ("lilekha") the Tāḷagunda praśasti of the Kadambas under Śāntivarman.

nodes.name: Parameśvaravarman I (Pallava)
nodes.summary: Pallava king (r. c. 670–695 CE) in whose time the Kūram copper plates were issued for a Śiva temple at Kūram; the grant provides for recitation of the Bhārata.

nodes.name: Sundara Cōḻa (Parāntaka II)
nodes.summary: Cōḻa king (r. c. 957–970 CE), father of Rājarāja I; the Anbil copper plates were issued in his fourth regnal year.

nodes.name: Girnar rock (Junagadh) — Aśokan rock with Rudradāman and Skandagupta inscriptions
nodes.summary: Granite boulder at the foot of Girnar near Junagadh, Gujarat, carrying Aśoka's fourteen rock edicts, the Sanskrit praśasti of Rudradāman (c. 150 CE) and the record of Skandagupta (455–458 CE), all three linked to the Sudarśana reservoir.
nodes.limits: A rock used for successive royal records; it documents how three dynasties used one public surface over seven centuries, not the history of the lake beyond what the texts claim.

nodes.name: Bhitari (Ghazipur district)
nodes.summary: Village in Ghazipur district, Uttar Pradesh, with Skandagupta's inscribed pillar and Gupta-period brick remains; a seal of Kumāragupta II was also found here.

location.label: Bhitari, Ghazipur district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: The pillar dates the installation it records; the surrounding brick structures are not securely dated by the inscription.

nodes.name: Bilsad (Etah district)
nodes.summary: Village in Etah district, Uttar Pradesh, where two inscribed pillars of Gupta year 96 record works at a temple of Svāmi-Mahāsena (Kārttikeya).

location.label: Bilsar, Etah district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: Coordinates are approximate (village level). The pillars attest the temple; its structure is not preserved.

nodes.name: Tāḷagunda (Sthānakuṇḍūra)
nodes.summary: Village in Shikaripura taluk, Shivamogga district, Karnataka, ancient Sthānakuṇḍūra, with the Praṇaveśvara temple and the 5th-century Kadamba pillar inscription.
nodes.limits: Site of a dated-by-reign record; the present temple fabric is later.

nodes.name: Uttaramērūr
nodes.summary: Brahmin village (caturvedimaṅgalam) in Kanchipuram district, Tamil Nadu, whose temple walls carry Pallava and Cōḻa inscriptions, including the assembly (sabhā) regulations of Parāntaka I's 12th and 14th years.

location.label: Uttiramerur, Kanchipuram district, Tamil Nadu, India

nodes.limits: Documents village self-government in a brahmadeya; it does not show that such rules applied outside Brahmin villages.

nodes.name: Junagadh rock inscription of Rudradāman I (year 72)
nodes.summary: Sanskrit prose praśasti cut on the Girnar rock in (Śaka) year 72, c. 150 CE, recording the repair of the Sudarśana lake after a storm. It recalls that the lake was made by Puṣyagupta, provincial governor of Candragupta Maurya, and given conduits by the Yavana Tuṣāspha for Aśoka. It is the earliest long royal record composed in Sanskrit.
nodes.details:
The repair was carried out by the Pahlava minister Suviśākha, son of Kulaipa, without forced labour or extra taxes, the text says. The record praises Rudradāman's learning in grammar, music and logic, and his skill in prose and verse.

Kielhorn edited it in Epigraphia Indica VIII; Sircar reprints it with notes.

dates.label: (Śaka) year 72, Mārgaśīrṣa = c. 150 CE
dates.basis: dated inscription; era identified as the Śaka era of 78 CE

sources.locator: bk. II, no. 67, pp. 175–180 (Junagarh rock inscription of Rudradāman I, year 72; Lüders List no. 965)
bk. II, no. 67, pp. 175–180 (Junagarh rock inscription of Rudradāman I, year 72; Lüders List no. 965)

nodes.limits: Establishes royal use of Sanskrit prose by c. 150 CE and a Gujarati tradition about Mauryan waterworks four centuries earlier; the Mauryan statements are the inscription's own historical memory, not contemporary Mauryan evidence.

nodes.name: Allahabad pillar praśasti of Samudragupta
nodes.summary: Sanskrit praśasti in verse and prose by Hariṣeṇa, cut on an Aśokan pillar now in the Allahabad Fort, listing Samudragupta's conquests in Āryāvarta, the Deccan and the frontiers. It compares the king to Dhanada (Kubera), Varuṇa, Indra and Antaka (Yama) and likens his fame to the Gaṅgā released from Paśupati's matted locks.

location.label: Allahabad Fort, Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: A court eulogy: it shows how Samudragupta wished his rule to be seen and which kings he claimed to have subdued; the extent of real control is debated. The divine comparisons are poetic conventions, not cult evidence.

nodes.name: Bhitari pillar inscription of Skandagupta
nodes.summary: Sanskrit inscription on a sandstone pillar at Bhitari recording that Skandagupta installed an image of Śārṅgin (Viṣṇu bearing the bow Śārṅga) and granted the village to it. It also alludes to his fight with the Hūṇas and gives the Gupta genealogy, calling Kumāragupta I a parama-bhāgavata.

location.label: Bhitari, Ghazipur district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: Records the installation of a Viṣṇu image and a royal claim of victory over the Hūṇas; the image itself is not identified among surviving sculptures.

nodes.name: Junagadh rock inscription of Skandagupta (Gupta years 136–138)
nodes.summary: Sanskrit verse inscription on the Girnar rock recording that the Sudarśana lake burst in Gupta year 136 (455/456 CE) and was repaired by Cakrapālita, son of the governor Parṇadatta, under Skandagupta. It opens by praising Viṣṇu, who took back Śrī from Bali for the sake of Indra — the Vāmana story.
nodes.limits: Shows the Vāmana–Bali story in a dated public text by 455 CE; it does not show which Purāṇic version the poet knew.

nodes.name: Mathurā pilaster inscription of Candragupta II (Gupta year 61)
aliases: Mathura pillar inscription of Chandragupta II
nodes.summary: Inscription dated Gupta year 61 (380 CE), in the fifth regnal year of Candragupta II, son of Samudragupta. It records that the Māheśvara teacher Uditācārya, tenth in descent from Kuśika, installed liṅgas named Upamiteśvara and Kapileśvara in a shrine of his teachers. The earliest dated epigraphic evidence of the Pāśupata teacher lineage.

attributes.repository: Government Museum, Mathurā (as generally reported; not checked)

dates.label: Gupta year 61 = 380 CE
dates.basis: dated inscription (also regnal year 5 of Candragupta II)

nodes.limits: Dates a Pāśupata teaching line and liṅga installation to 380 CE; the identification of Kuśika with a disciple of Lakulīśa comes from later Pāśupata texts, not from this record.

nodes.name: Bilsad pillar inscription of Kumāragupta I (Gupta year 96)
nodes.summary: Inscription of Gupta year 96 (415/416 CE), in the reign of Kumāragupta I, recording works by Dhruvaśarman at the temple (āyatana) of Svāmi-Mahāsena, called brahmaṇya-deva — the god Kārttikeya/Skanda. One of the earliest dated records of a Skanda temple.

location.label: Bilsar, Etah district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: Attests a Mahāsena temple and a donor's works there in 415/416; the temple itself does not survive.

nodes.name: Tāḷagunda pillar inscription of the time of Śāntivarman (Kadamba)
nodes.summary: Sanskrit verse praśasti composed and engraved by Kubja under the Kadamba king Śāntivarman, at the Śiva shrine of Sthānakuṇḍūra. It tells how the brahmin Mayūraśarman went with his teacher Vīraśarman to the Pallava capital to study, was angered by a quarrel with a Pallava horseman, and took up the warrior's life in this Kali age.
nodes.limits: A dynastic foundation story told by the dynasty's own poet about a century after the events; it is evidence of how the Kadambas wished to be remembered (brahmin origin, kṣatriya calling).

nodes.name: Kūram copper plates of Parameśvaravarman I
nodes.summary: Pallava copper-plate grant of Parameśvaravarman I for a Śiva temple (Vidyāvinīta-Pallava-Parameśvara-gṛha) at Kūram near Kanchipuram. It is often cited because the grant also provides for the recitation (vācana) of the Bhārata at the temple.

editions: Hultzsch, EI XVII pp. 340–344 (revised text of two plates)
attributes.repository: Government Museum, Chennai (photographed there by E. Francis, 2008, per DHARMA)

dates.label: c. 670–695 CE
dates.basis: reign of Parameśvaravarman I; undated grant

nodes.limits: Shows institutional recitation of the Mahābhārata in a South Indian temple in the late 7th century; the text recited is not specified beyond "Bhārata".

nodes.name: Kasakudi copper plates of Nandivarman II Pallavamalla
nodes.summary: Pallava copper-plate grant of Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, edited by Hultzsch as SII II no. 73. Its Sanskrit portion traces the Pallava line back through Aśvatthāman, Droṇa and Bharadvāja to Bṛhaspati, Aṅgiras and Brahmā — an epic genealogy claimed by a historical dynasty.

dates.label: 8th century CE (reign of Nandivarman II, c. 731–796)

nodes.limits: The genealogy shows how the Pallavas legitimised themselves through the Mahābhārata's Droṇa line; it is a claim, not evidence of descent.

nodes.name: Velurpalaiyam copper plates of Nandivarman III
nodes.summary: Pallava grant of Nandivarman III (9th century), SII II no. 98. Its genealogy attributes to the ancestor Vīrakūrca a marriage with a Nāga princess; the editor notes that the Rāyakōṭa plates tell the same of Aśvatthāman himself and compares Arjuna's Nāga marriage in the Mahābhārata.

dates.label: mid-9th century CE (reign of Nandivarman III)

nodes.limits: A dynastic origin story; the editor's 1916 inference that Nāgas were "indigenous rulers subdued by northern invaders" is a period interpretation, not established fact.

nodes.name: Tiruvālaṅkāṭu copper plates of Rājendra I (regnal year 6)
nodes.summary: Cōḻa copper-plate charter of Rājendra I, issued in his sixth regnal year (c. 1018 CE). Its long Sanskrit praśasti traces the Cōḻa line back through solar kings — Manu, Ikṣvāku, Śibi and others — to the Sun: a mythic genealogy placed in a royal title deed.

attributes.repository: Government Museum, Chennai (as generally reported; not checked)

dates.label: regnal year 6 of Rājendra I = c. 1018 CE

location.label: Tiruvalangadu, Tiruvallur district, Tamil Nadu, India

nodes.limits: Evidence of how the Cōḻas placed themselves in the Solar dynasty of the epics and Purāṇas around 1018 CE; not evidence for the earlier names in the list.

nodes.name: Anbil copper plates of Sundara Cōḻa (regnal year 4)
nodes.summary: Copper-plate grant of the Cōḻa king Sundara Cōḻa (Parāntaka II) of his fourth regnal year (c. 961 CE), edited by T. A. Gopinatha Rao in EI XV. Like the later Tiruvālaṅkāṭu plates, its Sanskrit praśasti gives the Cōḻas a Purāṇic solar ancestry.

dates.label: regnal year 4 of Sundara Cōḻa (c. 961 CE)

location.label: Anbil, Tiruchirappalli district, Tamil Nadu, India

nodes.limits: Royal genealogical claim; the earliest names are mythic.

nodes.name: Uttaramērūr assembly (sabhā) inscriptions of Parāntaka I (regnal years 12 and 14)
nodes.summary: Tamil inscriptions on the Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ temple at Uttaramērūr recording the rules by which the brahmin assembly chose its committees by lot (kuḍavōlai, the "pot-ticket" system), with qualifications and disqualifications of members, in the 12th and 14th years of Parāntaka I (c. 919 and 921 CE).

dates.label: regnal years 12 and 14 of Parāntaka I (c. 919 and 921 CE)

sources.locator: Uttaramērūr records (assembly of Uttaramērūr-caturvedimaṅgalam), e.g. no. 160

location.label: Uttiramerur, Kanchipuram district, Tamil Nadu, India

sources.locator: Uttaramērūr records (assembly of Uttaramērūr-caturvedimaṅgalam), e.g. no. 160

nodes.limits: Rules of one brahmadeya assembly; they describe intended procedure, not how elections actually ran, and do not describe non-Brahmin villages.

nodes.name: Lakṣmaṇa temple inscription of Yaśovarman, Khajuraho (Vikrama 1011)
nodes.summary: Sanskrit inscription on a slab in the porch of the Lakṣmaṇa temple, Khajuraho, dated Vikrama 1011 (953/954 CE). It records that the Candela Yaśovarman built a temple of Vaikuṇṭha (Viṣṇu) whose image had come from the Bhoṭa (Tibetan) region via the Śāhi king of Kīra and the Pratīhāra Herambapāla.
nodes.limits: Dates the dedication of a Vaikuṇṭha image and gives its claimed provenance; the slab may have been set in the temple when the porch was built, and the story of the image's travels is the record's own.
openQuestions: Kielhorn's exact item number and page in EI I were not checked against the archive.org scan.

nodes.name: Belur consecration inscription of Viṣṇuvardhana (Śaka 1039 = 1117 CE)
nodes.summary: Hoysaḷa record at the Cennakeśava temple, Belur, which dates the consecration of the god Vijayanārāyaṇa (Cennakeśava) by Viṣṇuvardhana to 1117 CE. It is the anchor for dating the temple.

dates.label: 1117 CE (Śaka 1039)
dates.basis: dated inscription as reported in the secondary literature

nodes.limits: Dates the consecration; the temple's sculpture continued to be added for decades afterwards.
openQuestions: Exact Epigraphia Carnatica number (vol. V, Belur taluk) not checked.

nodes.name: Mahākūṭa pillar inscription of Maṅgaleśa
nodes.summary: Sanskrit inscription on a pillar from the Mahākūṭa temple complex near Bādāmi, recording Maṅgaleśa's grant to the god Makuṭeśvaranātha (Śiva) and the conquests of the early Cālukyas. Usually dated c. 595–602 CE. The pillar was removed to the Bijapur museum.

attributes.repository: Archaeological Museum, Bijapur (Vijayapura) — as reported, not checked

nodes.limits: Records a royal grant and dynastic claims; it does not date the surviving Mahākūṭa temples, which are mostly 7th–8th century.
openQuestions: Fleet's Indian Antiquary edition not checked; the year of the grant is quoted differently in the literature.

nodes.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
nodes.summary: Encyclopaedic art museum in New York whose Department of Asian Art holds South and Southeast Asian sculpture, bronzes and paintings; its Open Access programme releases public-domain object images under CC0.

nodes.name: Art Institute of Chicago
nodes.summary: Art museum in Chicago with a major collection of Indian, Himalayan and Southeast Asian sculpture and painting; collection data and public-domain images are released under CC0 through its public API.

nodes.name: Victoria and Albert Museum, London
nodes.summary: Museum of art and design in London whose South Asian collection includes folios from Akbar's Persian Mahābhārata (Razmnāma) and Harivaṃśa, Pahari paintings and Hoysaḷa sculpture.

nodes.name: Government Museum, Chennai
nodes.summary: State museum of Tamil Nadu (founded 1851), holding Pallava and Cōḻa copper-plate charters and one of the largest collections of Cōḻa bronzes.

nodes.name: National Museum of Cambodia, Phnom Penh
nodes.summary: Cambodia's national museum of Khmer art (opened 1920), holding the Phnom Da sculptures (Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa Govardhana, Balarāma, Rāma) and the Harihara of Prasat Andet.

nodes.name: Bangkok National Museum
nodes.summary: Thailand's principal museum of art and archaeology, holding the Sdok Kak Thom stele (K. 235), moved to Bangkok in the 1920s and damaged in a 1960 fire.

nodes.name: National Museum of Vietnamese History, Hanoi
nodes.summary: Vietnam's national history museum, holding the Võ Cạnh stele (a national treasure since 2013) and Cham sculpture.

nodes.name: Museum of Islamic Art, Doha
nodes.summary: Qatar's museum of Islamic art, which holds the illustrated Persian Rāmāyaṇa made for Akbar's mother Ḥamīda Bānū Begum.

nodes.name: Maharaja Sawai Man Singh II Museum, City Palace, Jaipur
nodes.summary: Museum of the former Jaipur royal collection, holding Akbar's imperial copies of the Razmnāma (c. 1584–86) and the Persian Rāmāyaṇa (1588–91).

nodes.name: Freer Gallery of Art (National Museum of Asian Art), Washington
nodes.summary: Smithsonian museum of Asian art holding the "Freer Rāmāyaṇa", the Persian Rāmāyaṇa illustrated for ʿAbd al-Raḥīm Khān-i Khānān (c. 1597–1605).

nodes.name: Allahabad Museum (Prayagraj)
nodes.summary: Museum in Prayagraj holding terracottas and sculpture from Kauśāmbī and the surrounding region, and a Gupta and Kuṣāṇa collection.

nodes.name: University of Allahabad, Department of Ancient History, Culture and Archaeology
nodes.summary: University department that excavated Kauśāmbī (1949–1960s) under G. R. Sharma.

nodes.name: Museum für Asiatische Kunst, Berlin (formerly Museum für Indische Kunst)
nodes.summary: Berlin state museum of Asian art whose predecessor, the Museum für Indische Kunst, excavated Sonkh near Mathurā (1966–74) under Herbert Härtel.

nodes.name: École française d'Extrême-Orient (EFEO)
nodes.summary: French research institute (founded 1900) responsible for most early epigraphic and archaeological work in Cambodia, Vietnam and Laos, including the K- and C-number inventories of Khmer and Cham inscriptions and the excavation of Oc Eo.

nodes.name: DHARMA project (ERC) / Dharmalekha
nodes.summary: European Research Council project "The Domestication of Hindu Asceticism and the Religious Making of South and Southeast Asia" (2019–2025), which publishes digital critical editions of South and Southeast Asian inscriptions as Dharmalekha, incorporating the SIDDHAM Gupta-period corpus.

nodes.name: Kutai (Mūlavarman's kingdom), East Borneo
nodes.summary: Early kingdom on the Mahakam river in East Kalimantan known only from the yūpa inscriptions of Mūlavarman (c. 400 CE), the earliest Sanskrit inscriptions of the Indonesian archipelago. The name "Kutai Martadipura" is a later convention.

nodes.name: Mūlavarman
nodes.summary: King in East Borneo, son of Aśvavarman and grandson of Kuṇḍuṅga, whose sacrifices and gifts to brahmins are commemorated on stone sacrificial posts (yūpa) found at Muara Kaman.

nodes.name: Kuṇḍuṅga
nodes.summary: Grandfather of Mūlavarman named in the Kutai yūpa inscriptions; his non-Sanskrit name, beside the Sanskrit names of his son Aśvavarman and grandson, is often read as a sign of local adoption of Indic court culture.
nodes.limits: The interpretation of the name change is scholarly inference.

nodes.name: Tārumānagara (West Java)
nodes.summary: Kingdom of West Java known from the Sanskrit rock and boulder inscriptions of Pūrṇavarman (Ciaruteun, Tugu, Kebon Kopi, Jambu and others), dated by palaeography to the 5th century CE.

nodes.name: Pūrṇavarman
nodes.summary: King of Tārumānagara in West Java (5th century CE) whose inscriptions compare his footprints to Viṣṇu's and record the digging of the Candrabhāgā and Gomatī channels in his 22nd regnal year.

nodes.name: Sañjaya (king of Mataram, Java)
nodes.summary: King of Central Java who in Śaka 654 (732 CE) established a liṅga on the hill Sthirāṃśa, according to the Canggal (Gunung Wukir) inscription; later Javanese charters count an era from him.
nodes.limits: Distinct from Sañjaya, the charioteer-narrator of the Mahābhārata (char:sanjaya).

nodes.name: Gajayāna (Limva) of Kāñjuruhan
nodes.summary: King of Kāñjuruhan in East Java, son of Devasiṃha, who in Śaka 682 (760 CE) had a black-stone image of the sage Agastya made to replace an ancestral image of cedar wood, according to the Dinoyo (Kanjuruhan) charter.

nodes.name: Udayādityavarman II
nodes.summary: Khmer king (r. 1050–1066) in whose reign the Sdok Kak Thom stele (Śaka 974) was set up; builder of the Baphuon.

nodes.name: Jayavarman II (Khmer)
nodes.summary: Khmer king (c. 770/790–835) presented by the Sdok Kak Thom stele as the founder of royal sovereignty independent of "Java", consecrated on Mahendraparvata (Phnom Kulen) with the devarāja ritual of the brahmin Hiraṇyadāma.

dates.label: c. 770/790–835 CE
dates.basis: retrospective inscriptions (Sdok Kak Thom 1052); his dates are debated

nodes.limits: Almost all that is known of him comes from inscriptions written two centuries later.

nodes.name: Śivakaivalya
nodes.summary: Chaplain (purohita) of Jayavarman II and first member of the priestly family whose nine generations of service to the devarāja the Sdok Kak Thom stele records.

nodes.name: Devānīka
nodes.summary: King ("supreme king of kings") of the Vat Phu region named in the 5th-century stele of Vat Luang Kau (K. 365), who founded a tīrtha called the "new Kurukṣetra" with sacrifices and gifts of cows.

nodes.name: Bhadravarman I (Champa)
nodes.summary: Early king of Champa who founded the god Bhadreśvara (a Śiva named after himself) at Mỹ Sơn and endowed it with land, according to his Sanskrit stele.

nodes.name: Satyavarman (Champa)
nodes.summary: King of Champa (Kauṭhāra region) who, according to his stele at Po Nagar, restored the temple and its mukhaliṅga after seaborne raiders damaged it in the 770s.

nodes.name: Funan
nodes.summary: Chinese name for an early polity of the lower Mekong (c. 1st–6th century CE), associated archaeologically with the port of Oc Eo and the sculpture of Phnom Da. Its own name and extent are uncertain.

dates.label: c. 3rd–6th century CE (Chinese sources)
dates.basis: Chinese dynastic histories; archaeology of Oc Eo

nodes.limits: "Funan" is an exonym from Chinese texts; equating it with a single state or with particular archaeological sites is an interpretation.

nodes.name: Muara Kaman (Kutai), East Kalimantan
nodes.summary: Riverside site on the Mahakam in Kutai Kartanegara regency, East Kalimantan, where the yūpa inscriptions of Mūlavarman were found.

location.label: Muara Kaman, Kutai Kartanegara, East Kalimantan, Indonesia

nodes.limits: Findspot of the yūpas; no settlement of the period has been excavated to modern standards.

nodes.name: Ciaruteun (Bogor), West Java
nodes.summary: Inscribed boulder site at the confluence of the Cisadane, Cianten and Ciaruteun rivers near Bogor, where Pūrṇavarman's footprint inscription stands in situ.

location.label: Ciaruteun Ilir, Cibungbulang, Bogor, West Java, Indonesia

nodes.limits: The boulder was displaced by a flood in 1893 and moved slightly uphill in 1981.

nodes.name: Tugu (Koja, North Jakarta)
nodes.summary: Findspot of Pūrṇavarman's Tugu boulder inscription in the Batutumbuh hamlet of Tugu, North Jakarta.
nodes.limits: Findspot only; the stone was moved to Jakarta in 1911.

nodes.name: Gunung Wukir (Canggal), Central Java
nodes.summary: Hill in Magelang regency, Central Java, with the ruins of a Śaiva temple (Candi Gunung Wukir) where the Canggal inscription of Sañjaya (732 CE) was found.

location.label: Canggal, Salam, Magelang, Central Java, Indonesia

nodes.limits: Identification of the hill with the inscription's "Sthirāṃśa" is by findspot; the surviving temple remains are not dated by the inscription itself.

nodes.name: Dinoyo (Malang), East Java
nodes.summary: Findspot near Malang of the Kanjuruhan charter (760 CE), associated with the nearby Candi Badut.
nodes.limits: The link between the charter's Agastya temple and Candi Badut is a scholarly proposal.

nodes.name: Prasat Sdok Kak Thom (Sa Kaeo, Thailand)
nodes.summary: Khmer temple ruin in Khok Sung district, Sa Kaeo province, Thailand, findspot of the Sdok Kak Thom stele (K. 235).

location.label: Khok Sung, Sa Kaeo province, Thailand

dates.label: mid-11th century CE (stele dated Śaka 974)
dates.basis: dated stele found at the site

nodes.limits: The stele dates the foundation it records; the ruined temple has not been independently dated here.

nodes.name: Vat Luang Kau (Champasak), near Vat Phu
nodes.summary: Village site on the Mekong near Vat Phu in southern Laos, findspot of the 5th-century stele of Devānīka (K. 365) and an early walled settlement.
nodes.limits: Findspot; the "new Kurukṣetra" tīrtha the stele founds has not been located precisely.

nodes.name: Võ Cạnh (Nha Trang)
nodes.summary: Village about 4 km from Nha Trang, Khánh Hòa province, Vietnam, where the Võ Cạnh stele was discovered in 1885.

location.label: Võ Cạnh, Nha Trang, Khánh Hòa, Vietnam

nodes.limits: Findspot only.

nodes.name: Yūpa inscriptions of Mūlavarman (Kutai, East Borneo)
nodes.summary: Seven stone posts in the form of Vedic sacrificial stakes (yūpa), inscribed in Sanskrit verse, commemorating King Mūlavarman's sacrifices and gifts to brahmins (including a gift of many thousands of cows) and naming his father Aśvavarman and grandfather Kuṇḍuṅga. They are the oldest Sanskrit inscriptions of the Indonesian archipelago.

attributes.number: 7 posts (number reported in the secondary literature)
attributes.repository: National Museum of Indonesia, Jakarta (as reported)

nodes.limits: Evidence of a Borneo court adopting Sanskrit, brahmins and the idiom of Vedic sacrifice by c. 400 CE; it does not show how far Vedic ritual was actually performed or how widely Indic religion was practised.
openQuestions: Readings not checked against Vogel 1918; museum inventory numbers not verified.

nodes.name: Ciaruteun inscription of Pūrṇavarman
nodes.summary: Four-line Sanskrit verse (anuṣṭubh) on a boulder near Bogor beside a carved pair of footprints, declaring them the footprints of Pūrṇavarman, lord of Tārumā, like those of Viṣṇu — an image of the god's three strides applied to a king's claim to the land.

location.label: Ciaruteun Ilir, Bogor, West Java, Indonesia

nodes.limits: Shows that a West Javanese king used a Vaiṣṇava image of sovereignty in the 5th century; it does not show a Vaiṣṇava cult organisation.

nodes.name: Tugu inscription of Pūrṇavarman
nodes.summary: Five-line Sanskrit verse inscription on an egg-shaped boulder from North Jakarta recording that in Pūrṇavarman's 22nd regnal year the Candrabhāgā and Gomatī channels were dug, and that brahmins received a gift of 1,000 cows. The river names echo rivers of the Indian Purāṇic geography.

attributes.repository: National Museum of Indonesia, Jakarta, D.124 (Wikipedia)

nodes.limits: Evidence of royal waterworks and brahmanical patronage; the Indian river names show borrowed sacred geography, not migration.

nodes.name: Canggal (Gunung Wukir) inscription of Sañjaya (Śaka 654 = 732 CE)
nodes.summary: Sanskrit stele dated Monday, Kārttika śukla 13, Śaka 654 (732 CE), recording that King Sañjaya established a liṅga on the hill called Sthirāṃśa, with verses to Śiva (Bhava), whose crest bears the moon and the Gaṅgā. It is the earliest dated inscription of the Mataram kingdom of Central Java.

dates.label: Śaka 654 = 732 CE
dates.basis: dated inscription with weekday, tithi and nakṣatra

location.label: Gunung Wukir, Magelang, Central Java, Indonesia

nodes.limits: Dates a royal liṅga foundation; later traditions about Sañjaya as dynastic founder are separate claims.

nodes.name: Dinoyo (Kanjuruhan) charter of Gajayāna (Śaka 682 = 760 CE)
nodes.summary: Sanskrit charter dated Śaka 682 (760 CE), the oldest dated inscription of East Java. King Gajayāna of Kāñjuruhan, devoted to the "pot-born" sage Agastya, replaced an ancestral cedar-wood image of Agastya with one of black stone and had a temple for it built.

attributes.repository: National Museum of Indonesia, Jakarta, stone D.113 (DHARMA editor verified readings there, 2011)

nodes.limits: Attests an Agastya cult and image-making in East Java in 760; the wooden "ancestral" image is known only from this text.

nodes.name: Sdok Kak Thom stele (K. 235), Śaka 974
nodes.summary: Bilingual stele of Śaka 974 (1052/1053 CE) under Udayādityavarman II, tracing nine generations of the Śivakaivalya priestly family who served the devarāja (Old Khmer kamraten jagat ta rāja) from the time of Jayavarman II. It says the brahmin Hiraṇyadāma performed rites so that Kambuja would no longer depend on "Java", and that Jayavarman II was established on Mahendraparvata. It is the principal source for the devarāja cult and for Jayavarman II.

attributes.repository: Bangkok National Museum (damaged in the 1960 fire)

nodes.limits: A priestly family's retrospective account written about 250 years after Jayavarman II; its version of 9th-century events and of the devarāja is interested testimony.

nodes.name: The devarāja was a cult of the deified Khmer king
nodes.summary: The older reading of the Sdok Kak Thom stele, associated with Cœdès, took the devarāja ("god-king") as a cult identifying the king with Śiva through a royal liṅga. Later scholars (e.g. Hermann Kulke; Kamaleswar Bhattacharya) read kamraten jagat ta rāja as a movable protective image — "the god who is king" — tended by one priestly family, not a deification of the ruler.
nodes.limits: The stele names the cult and its priests but does not explain its theology; both readings are interpretations of the same few lines.

nodes.name: Vat Luang Kau stele of Devānīka (K. 365): the "new Kurukṣetra"
nodes.summary: Fifth-century Sanskrit stele from near Vat Phu, Laos, in which King Devānīka founds a great tīrtha named Kurukṣetra — "the new Kurukṣetra" — so that the merit of bathing at the Indian Kurukṣetra, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa and Puṣkara may be gained there. It compares the king to Yudhiṣṭhira in dharma, Dhanañjaya (Arjuna) in victory and Śibi in generosity, and quotes verses in praise of Kurukṣetra of the kind found in the Mahābhārata's tīrtha chapters.
nodes.limits: Shows Mahābhārata figures and Indian tīrtha ideology transplanted to the Mekong by the 5th century; the verse parallels with the Mahābhārata need passage-level comparison before a textual dependence is asserted.

nodes.name: Mỹ Sơn stele of Bhadravarman I (C. 72)
nodes.summary: Sanskrit stele from group A at Mỹ Sơn recording that King Bhadravarman, blessed by the feet of the Lord Bhadreśvara, gave a permanent endowment of land with its cultivators to the god Bhadreśvara, with boundaries given by mountains and the great river. It opens with homage to Maheśvara, Umā, Agni, Brahmā and Viṣṇu and the five elements. It is the founding record of the Mỹ Sơn sanctuary.
nodes.limits: Documents the foundation and endowment of a royal Śiva (Bhadreśvara) at Mỹ Sơn; none of the surviving Mỹ Sơn brick towers is this early.

nodes.name: Po Nagar stele of Satyavarman (781/784 CE)
nodes.summary: Sanskrit record of King Satyavarman at Po Nagar, Nha Trang, reporting that seaborne raiders had damaged the temple and carried off and broken its mukhaliṅga, and that the king restored the temple and re-established the liṅga (781; restoration completed 784).

dates.label: 781–784 CE
dates.basis: dated stele as reported in the secondary literature

location.label: Po Nagar, Nha Trang, Khánh Hòa, Vietnam

nodes.limits: Evidence for raids on the Cham coast and the cult of a mukhaliṅga at Po Nagar in the 770s–780s; the identity of the raiders ("Java") is debated. The surviving towers are mostly 10th–13th century.
openQuestions: The C-number and DHARMA edition were not located; readings not checked.

nodes.name: Võ Cạnh stele
nodes.summary: Sanskrit stele found in 1885 near Nha Trang, naming a royal line descended from Śrī Māra. Often called the earliest Sanskrit inscription of Southeast Asia, it is dated by some to the 2nd–3rd century CE and by others (e.g. Sircar, Zakharov) to the 4th century or later.

attributes.repository: National Museum of Vietnamese History, Hanoi (national treasure, 2013)

dates.label: c. 2nd–3rd century CE
dates.view: early dating (palaeographic; Cœdès linked Śrī Māra to Funan's Fan Shiman)

dates.label: 4th century CE or later
dates.basis: metre (vasantatilakā) and vocabulary (bhṛtya) compared with Gupta-period records

nodes.limits: The "earliest" label depends on the early dating; whatever its date it attests Sanskrit royal epigraphy on the Vietnamese coast before the Cham records of Bhadravarman.

nodes.name: The Võ Cạnh stele is the earliest Sanskrit inscription in Southeast Asia (2nd–3rd century CE)
nodes.summary: Claim resting on an early palaeographic dating; disputed by scholars who date the text to the 4th century or later on grounds of metre and vocabulary.
nodes.limits: Even on the late dating the stele remains among the earliest Sanskrit inscriptions of mainland Southeast Asia.

nodes.name: Candragupta I
nodes.summary: Gupta king (r. c. 319–335/350 CE), father of Samudragupta by the Licchavi princess Kumāradevī; the Gupta era of 319/320 CE is often associated with his accession.

dates.label: c. 319–335/350 CE
dates.basis: Gupta era epoch and regnal sequence

nodes.name: Kumāradevī
nodes.summary: Licchavi princess, queen of Candragupta I and mother of Samudragupta, who is called "Licchavi-dauhitra" (daughter's son of the Licchavis) in the Allahabad praśasti and on Gupta coins and seals.

nodes.name: Standard-type gold coins of Samudragupta (Garuḍa standard)
nodes.summary: The commonest gold type of Samudragupta: the king, haloed, sacrifices at an altar holding a standard, with a Garuḍa standard (garuḍadhvaja) beside him; the reverse goddess on a throne with cornucopia is copied from the late Kuṣāṇa Ardochsho type. Allan reads the Garuḍa standard as the emblem of Viṣṇu and the Gupta seal.
nodes.limits: Shows Garuḍa as a royal emblem and Kuṣāṇa coin models adapted by the Guptas; the reverse goddess's name is not on the coin, so calling her Lakṣmī is an interpretation.

nodes.name: Aśvamedha-type gold coins of Samudragupta
nodes.summary: Rare gold coins commemorating Samudragupta's horse sacrifice: the obverse shows the sacrificial horse before a decorated sacrificial post (yūpa); the reverse a queen holding a fly-whisk, whom Allan identifies as the chief queen who took part in the rite.
nodes.limits: Shows that the Gupta court publicised a Vedic aśvamedha; it does not show how the rite was performed.

nodes.name: Candragupta I–Kumāradevī type gold coins
nodes.summary: Gold coins showing Candragupta I offering a ring or bracelet to Queen Kumāradevī, with the legend "Licchavayaḥ" on the reverse and a goddess seated on a lion. Allan thought they were struck by Samudragupta to commemorate his parents; he identified the goddess as probably Lakṣmī, or Mahādevī (Durgā), whose vehicle is the lion.

dates.label: c. 320–375 CE
dates.basis: attributed either to Candragupta I or, as a commemorative issue, to Samudragupta

nodes.limits: Evidence of the importance the Guptas gave to the Licchavi marriage; the identity of the lion-seated goddess is argued, and the issuer is debated.

nodes.name: King-and-Lakṣmī type gold coins of Skandagupta
nodes.summary: Gold type of Skandagupta, formerly called the "King and Queen" type: the king stands holding a bow, facing a female figure Allan identifies as Lakṣmī, with a Garuḍa standard between them.
nodes.limits: The female figure's identity as Lakṣmī is Allan's reading against the older "queen" interpretation.

nodes.name: Aśvamedha-type gold coins of Kumāragupta I
nodes.summary: Gold coins of Kumāragupta I modelled on Samudragupta's aśvamedha type, with a saddled horse and, on the reverse, a queen holding a fly-whisk and a ceremonial spear.
nodes.limits: Commemorative royal imagery; it does not prove the rite was performed in full.

nodes.name: Huviṣka's gold coins with Skanda, Kumāra, Viśākha and Mahāsena
nodes.summary: Gold coins of the Kuṣāṇa king Huviṣka (c. 150–180/190 CE) naming in Bactrian Greek script the war gods Skando, Komaro, Bizago (Viśākha) and Maaseno (Mahāsena), sometimes together — the earliest coin images of the Skanda–Kārttikeya group, which replaced the Iranian war god Orlagno on his coinage.
nodes.limits: Shows that several names later merged in the single god Skanda-Kārttikeya were still distinguished as separate figures on a 2nd-century royal coinage; it does not show cult practice.
openQuestions: Greek-script legends given from standard numismatic usage; a museum specimen with accession number was not verified.

nodes.name: Huviṣka
nodes.summary: Kuṣāṇa emperor (c. 150–180/190 CE), successor of Kaniṣka I, whose gold coinage displays the widest range of deities of any Kuṣāṇa ruler, including Indian (Skanda, Viśākha, Mahāsena, Oesho, Ommo), Iranian and Greek gods.

nodes.name: Gold coin of the Kuṣāṇa king Vāsudeva I (Cleveland 1999.226)
nodes.summary: Gold coin of Vāsudeva I, the last great Kuṣāṇa emperor, with the king's portrait on the obverse and a deity on the reverse; on Vāsudeva's coinage this is predominantly Oesho with the bull.

attributes.museum dating: c. 142/145+ (Cleveland Museum of Art, on an older Kuṣāṇa chronology)

dates.label: reign of Vāsudeva I (c. 190–230)
dates.basis: dated to the issuing king’s reign as the graph dates it; the museum’s c. 142/145+ follows an older chronology

image.license: CC0 1.0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)

nodes.limits: The reverse deity of this specimen was not described in the museum record; the Oesho identification follows Vāsudeva I's usual coin type and is not verified for this piece.

nodes.name: Vāsudeva I (Kuṣāṇa)
nodes.summary: Kuṣāṇa emperor (c. 190–230 CE), successor of Huviṣka; the first Kuṣāṇa ruler with an Indian name, whose coins almost always show Oesho with the bull Nandi. Not to be confused with the deity Vāsudeva.
nodes.limits: Distinct from deity:vasudeva and char:vasudeva-father.

nodes.name: Yaudheyas
nodes.summary: Republican (gaṇa) people of the eastern Punjab and Haryana, known from Pāṇini, from coins proclaiming "victory to the Yaudheya gaṇa", from Rudradāman's Junagadh inscription (which boasts of defeating them) and from Samudragupta's Allahabad list. Their coins make Kārttikeya their tutelary god.

nodes.name: Yaudheya coins with Kārttikeya (Brahmaṇyadeva)
nodes.summary: Copper coins of the Yaudheya republic showing Kārttikeya standing with a spear, often with a peacock, including a six-headed (ṣaṇmukha) form of the 1st–2nd century CE; other issues carry the legend "yaudheya-gaṇasya jaya". Allan's British Museum catalogue (1936) records issues naming the god as Brahmaṇyadeva Kumāra.
nodes.limits: Attests the god as a collective emblem of a republic; the "Brahmaṇyadeva" legend is given from Allan's catalogue by recall and was not checked.

nodes.name: Audumbaras
nodes.summary: People of the Pathankot–Kangra region of the Punjab hills who issued coins from about the 1st century BCE, including issues of the king Dharaghoṣa and issues in the name of Mahādeva (Śiva).

nodes.name: Audumbara coin of Dharaghoṣa with Viśvāmitra
nodes.summary: Silver coin of the Audumbara king Dharaghoṣa (c. 100 BCE) in Indo-Greek style: a standing ascetic figure labelled with the name of the sage Viśvāmitra, with a bilingual Kharoṣṭhī and Brāhmī legend; the reverse shows a trident-battle-axe and a tree in a railing.
nodes.limits: One of the earliest labelled images of a figure of epic and Vedic narrative; the label names the sage but the coin implies no particular story.

nodes.name: Audumbara coins in the name of Mahādeva (Śiva)
nodes.summary: Audumbara coins of about the 1st century BCE issued in the name of Mahādeva (Śiva), with a bull on one side and an elephant with a trident on the other; a related Audumbara type shows a pillared shrine with a trident standard, often read as an early depiction of a Śiva temple.
nodes.limits: The shrine type and its reading as a Śiva temple were not verified on a specimen; it would be among the earliest images of a free-standing shrine if confirmed.

nodes.name: Durgā slaying the buffalo demon, Kuṣāṇa terracotta from Mathurā (AIC 1985.1108)
nodes.summary: Small molded terracotta of the goddess killing the buffalo demon, attributed to Kuṣāṇa Mathurā in the 2nd century CE. It belongs to the earliest group of Mahiṣāsuramardinī images, in which the goddess presses or lifts the buffalo itself — centuries before the Devī Māhātmya gave the myth its classic form.

dates.label: Kuṣāṇa period, 2nd century CE
dates.basis: museum attribution (style and comparison; no inscription)

nodes.name: G. R. Sharma
nodes.summary: Indian archaeologist (1919–1986) of the University of Allahabad who excavated Kauśāmbī from 1949 and published the 1957–59 seasons; his reading of a brick structure there as a Vedic "śyenaciti" fire altar is contested.

nodes.name: J. P. Joshi
nodes.summary: Indian archaeologist (ASI; Director General 1987–1990) who excavated Bhagwanpura in Haryana in 1975–76, documenting an overlap of Late Harappan and Painted Grey Ware occupation.

nodes.name: Herbert Härtel
nodes.summary: German Indologist and museum director (1921–2017) of the Museum für Indische Kunst, Berlin, who directed the excavation of Sonkh near Mathurā (1966–1974).

nodes.name: Louis Malleret
nodes.summary: French archaeologist (1901–1970) of the EFEO who excavated Oc Eo in the Mekong delta in 1944 and published L'Archéologie du delta du Mékong.

nodes.name: H. G. Quaritch Wales
nodes.summary: British scholar (1900–1981) who surveyed and excavated candi sites in the Bujang Valley, Kedah, in 1936–1940.

nodes.name: K. N. Dikshit
nodes.summary: Indian archaeologist who co-directed the excavation of Śṛṅgaverapura with B. B. Lal (1977–86).
openQuestions: Not the same person as K. N. Dikshit (1889–1946), Director General of the ASI; disambiguation from recall.

nodes.name: B. R. Mani
nodes.summary: Indian archaeologist of the ASI who led the court-ordered excavation at the disputed site in Ayodhya in 2003; he was succeeded during the work by Hari Manjhi.

nodes.name: Sonkh (Mathurā district)
nodes.summary: Mound c. 24 km south-west of Mathurā excavated by the Museum für Indische Kunst, Berlin, under Herbert Härtel (1966–74). Its occupation runs from Painted Grey Ware levels to the Kuṣāṇa period and includes two apsidal shrines associated with Nāga worship of the Kuṣāṇa period, one of the best-stratified sequences for the region that produced the first Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva images.

location.label: Sonkh, Mathura district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: Coordinates are approximate. The Nāga-shrine identification rests on sculptures and plans; the sequence dates are the excavator's.

nodes.name: Śṛṅgaverapura excavations (1977–86)
nodes.summary: Excavation by B. B. Lal and K. N. Dikshit at Singraur on the Gaṅgā above Prayagraj, the place traditionally identified with the Rāmāyaṇa's Śṛṅgaverapura where Rāma crossed the river with the help of Guha. The project, part of Lal's survey of "Rāmāyaṇa sites", found occupation from the late 2nd millennium BCE and a large brick tank of the early centuries CE.

location.label: Singraur, Prayagraj district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: The excavation documents a long-lived Gaṅgā settlement and a monumental tank; it does not establish that the events of the Rāmāyaṇa happened here. The site's identification with the epic's Śṛṅgaverapura rests on the place-name and tradition.

nodes.name: Excavations at "Rāmāyaṇa sites" (Ayodhyā, Śṛṅgaverapura, Bharadvāja Āśrama, Nandigrāma, Citrakūṭa) date the epic's setting
nodes.summary: B. B. Lal's project "Archaeology of the Rāmāyaṇa Sites" (1975–86) excavated places named in the Rāmāyaṇa and found that their earliest occupation began around the early 1st millennium BCE (or slightly earlier); Lal argued this gives an upper limit for the epic's geography. Critics note that a place-name's age says nothing about the historicity of the narrative.
nodes.limits: At most the findings give a terminus post quem for settlement at the sites; they neither confirm nor refute the narrative.

nodes.name: Bhagwanpura (Kurukshetra district)
nodes.summary: Small site in Haryana excavated by J. P. Joshi in 1975–76, where Late Harappan and Painted Grey Ware levels overlap — one of the key sites for the transition from the Harappan to the Iron Age Gaṅgā–Yamunā cultures in the region later called Kurukṣetra.
nodes.limits: Coordinates are regional. The overlap is a cultural-sequence finding; it is sometimes enlisted in arguments about the Mahābhārata's date, which it cannot settle.

nodes.name: Ahichchhatra (Bareilly district)
nodes.summary: Large fortified city mound in Bareilly district, Uttar Pradesh, identified with Ahicchatrā, capital of northern Pañcāla in the Mahābhārata. Excavated by the ASI in 1940–44; it yielded Painted Grey Ware and a long early historic sequence, Pañcāla coins and the Gupta-period terracottas of Gaṅgā and Yamunā from a Śiva temple.

location.label: Ramnagar, Bareilly district, Uttar Pradesh, India

dates.label: c. early 1st millennium BCE – c. 1100 CE

nodes.limits: The identification with the epic Ahicchatrā rests on the name's continuity; it does not make the Pañcāla narratives historical.

nodes.name: Kauśāmbī (Kosam)
nodes.summary: Great walled city on the Yamunā south-west of Prayagraj, capital of the Vatsas in Buddhist and epic tradition, excavated by G. R. Sharma for the University of Allahabad from 1949. The finds include massive ramparts, the Ghositārāma monastery and a brick structure that Sharma interpreted as a Vedic "falcon" fire altar (śyenaciti) used for a puruṣamedha.

location.label: Kosam, Kaushambi district, Uttar Pradesh, India

dates.label: c. early 1st millennium BCE – 6th century CE
early 1st millennium BCE (excavator) or later
dates.basis: stratigraphy; dating of the rampart is debated

nodes.limits: The rampart chronology and the śyenaciti interpretation are both disputed.

nodes.name: A brick structure at Kauśāmbī is a Vedic falcon altar (śyenaciti) used for a puruṣamedha
nodes.summary: G. R. Sharma interpreted a falcon-shaped brick structure by the Kauśāmbī rampart, with skulls and bones, as a śyenaciti altar of the Vedic agnicayana and as evidence of a human sacrifice (puruṣamedha). Most later archaeologists regard the identification and the sacrifice interpretation as unproven.
nodes.limits: Rests on the excavator's interpretation of shape and associated bones.

nodes.name: Bujang Valley (Lembah Bujang), Kedah
nodes.summary: Archaeological landscape in Kedah, Malaysia, with dozens of brick and laterite shrine (candi) foundations, Hindu and Buddhist sculpture and inscriptions from about the 5th to 14th century, including Candi Bukit Batu Pahat with Śaiva finds. Surveyed by H. G. Quaritch Wales (1936–40) and later Malaysian projects; the Sungai Batu complex has much earlier iron-smelting and jetty remains.

dates.label: Sungai Batu: early 1st millennium BCE onward (claimed radiocarbon dates)
dates.basis: radiocarbon (Universiti Sains Malaysia team); disputed early dates

nodes.limits: A heterogeneous landscape; the early Sungai Batu dates are contested, and the religious affiliation of many candis is uncertain.

nodes.name: Oc Eo (An Giang)
nodes.summary: Large early historic port and canal network in the Mekong delta, excavated by Louis Malleret in 1944, associated with the polity the Chinese called Funan (c. 1st–7th century CE). Finds include Indian-style seals, Viṣṇu and Buddha images, gold foils and a Roman gold medallion of Antoninus Pius (dated 152 CE).

location.label: Oc Eo, Thoại Sơn, An Giang, Vietnam

nodes.limits: The link between Oc Eo and the Chinese "Funan" is an interpretation; the Antoninus Pius medallion dates its own minting, not the layer.

nodes.name: Ayodhyā: ASI excavation at the disputed site (2003)
nodes.summary: Excavation carried out by the Archaeological Survey of India between March and August 2003 on the orders of the Allahabad High Court, beneath and around the site of the Babri Masjid (demolished in 1992). The report described a long occupation sequence and, below the mosque, a large structure with some 50 pillar bases, which it said had features of north Indian temples. The report was contested by other archaeologists and was among the evidence considered by the Supreme Court in its 2019 judgment.
nodes.limits: The report's statements concern structural remains and their dating; the interpretation of those remains is disputed, and archaeology cannot address the religious belief that this is Rāma's birthplace.

nodes.name: The structure beneath the Babri Masjid excavated in 2003 was a Hindu temple
nodes.summary: The ASI's 2003 report concluded that a massive structure with pillar bases, beneath the mosque, had features of north Indian temples of the early medieval period. Critics — including archaeologists who observed the excavation for the Sunni Central Waqf Board and the Aligarh Historians Society — disputed the identification of the "pillar bases", the stratigraphic reading and the omission of animal bones and glazed ware. In 2019 the Supreme Court treated the excavation as showing an underlying structure that was not Islamic, while stating that the report did not establish that a temple had been demolished to build the mosque; it decided the title dispute on other evidence.
nodes.limits: Recorded as a contested archaeological interpretation. The graph does not adjudicate the dispute, the 2019 title decision or matters of faith.

nodes.name: Akbar (Mughal emperor)
nodes.summary: Mughal emperor (r. 1556–1605) who set up a translation bureau (maktab-khāna) and commissioned Persian translations of the Mahābhārata (the Razmnāma, 1584–86) and the Rāmāyaṇa, with imperial illustrated copies.

nodes.name: Ḥamīda Bānū Begum
nodes.summary: Mother of Akbar (d. 1604) for whom an illustrated copy of the Persian Rāmāyaṇa was made, now in the Museum of Islamic Art, Doha.

nodes.name: Jagat Singh I of Mewar
nodes.summary: Rāṇā of Mewar (r. 1628–1652) who commissioned the great illustrated Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa of Udaipur (1649–53), painted by Sahib Din, Manohar and an anonymous master.

sources.locator: Curator's perspective: accessing the Mewar Ramayana (2014)

nodes.name: Sahib Din
nodes.summary: Mewar court painter (active c. 1628–1655) who led the illustration of several books of Jagat Singh's Rāmāyaṇa (e.g. the Ayodhyākāṇḍa and Yuddhakāṇḍa volumes in the British Library).

sources.locator: Curator's perspective: accessing the Mewar Ramayana (2014)

nodes.name: Manaku
nodes.summary: Pahari painter of the Guler family of Pandit Seu (c. 1700–1760), elder brother of Nainsukh, who painted the Gīta Govinda series dated 1730 for a woman patron (Mālinī) in the Basohli style.

nodes.name: Banwari the Younger (Banwari Khurd)
nodes.summary: Mughal painter credited with the Razmnāma folio of 1598 showing Vyāsa watching his son Śuka approach (V&A IS.121-1955).

nodes.name: Kamal, son of Khem (Mughal painter)
nodes.summary: Mughal painter whose name is written on the border of the Razmnāma folio "Duryodhana visits Śalya" (V&A CIRC.243-1922) from the copy of c. 1598.

nodes.name: Razmnāma (Persian Mahābhārata)
nodes.summary: Persian prose translation of the Mahābhārata made at Akbar's order in 1584–86: brahmin scholars explained the Sanskrit, Naqīb Khān drafted the Persian and Faiẓī and others revised it; Abū'l-Faẓl wrote the preface (dated 1588 in the imperial copy). Its illustrated copies are among the masterpieces of Mughal painting.

nodes.name: Persian Harivaṃśa (appendix to the Razmnāma)

nodes.name: Persian Rāmāyaṇa of Akbar's court
nodes.summary: Persian translation of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa made at Akbar's court in the 1580s (the historian Badāʾūnī was its principal translator). Illustrated copies were made for Akbar (Jaipur), for his mother Ḥamīda Bānū Begum (Doha) and for the courtier ʿAbd al-Raḥīm (the "Freer Rāmāyaṇa").

nodes.limits: Production history as summarised in secondary literature; the manuscript is not openly published, and its folio count is reported inconsistently.
nodes.name: Imperial Razmnāma of Akbar (City Palace Museum, Jaipur)

It has some 169–176 paintings (counts differ); 147 were reproduced by Hendley in 1883–84.

nodes.name: Eugen Hultzsch
nodes.summary: German Indologist (1857–1927), Government Epigraphist of Madras, who founded the South Indian Inscriptions series and edited the Kūram and Kasakudi plates (SII I–II).

nodes.name: H. Krishna Sastri
nodes.summary: Indian epigraphist (1870–1945) who edited SII II part V (Velurpalaiyam plates) and SII III part III (Tiruvālaṅkāṭu plates) and later served as Government Epigraphist.

nodes.name: T. A. Gopinatha Rao
nodes.summary: Indian archaeologist and epigraphist (1872–1919) of Travancore, author of Elements of Hindu Iconography, who edited the Anbil plates of Sundara Cōḻa in EI XV.

nodes.name: J. Ph. Vogel
nodes.summary: Dutch Indologist (1871–1958) who catalogued the Mathurā museum (1910) and edited the earliest Sanskrit inscriptions of Borneo (Kutai yūpas, 1918) and Java (1925).

nodes.name: George Cœdès
nodes.summary: French epigraphist and historian (1886–1969) of the EFEO, editor of the Inscriptions du Cambodge, who with Pierre Dupont published the Sdok Kak Thom stele (1943) and edited the Vat Luang Kau stele (1956).

nodes.name: Louis Finot
nodes.summary: French Indologist (1864–1935), first director of the EFEO, who published the Mỹ Sơn stele of Bhadravarman I in 1902.

nodes.name: D. C. Sircar
nodes.summary: Indian epigraphist and historian (1907–1985), Government Epigraphist for India, whose Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilization (vol. I, 2nd edn 1965) is the standard reader of early Indian inscriptions.

nodes.name: Naravarman (Aulikara)

nodes.name: Mandsaur inscription of the time of Naravarman (Kṛta year 461)

nodes.limits: Dates the invocation of a cosmic sleeping Puruṣa-Viṣṇu to 404/405 CE; it does not describe a specific image.

nodes.summary: Buddhist stūpa in Satna district, Madhya Pradesh, visited by Alexander Cunningham in 1873 and excavated the following year. Its carved railings (c. 125–100 BCE) and gateway (c. 100–75 BCE, "during the rule of the Sugas") are among the earliest narrative sculpture in India; they were reassembled in the Indian Museum, Kolkata.

Often cited as the earliest dated image of Sarasvatī in any tradition.

nodes.summary: Colossal standing yakṣa from Parkham near Mathurā, now in the Government Museum, Mathurā. Its Prakrit inscription in Brāhmī, which Sircar dates palaeographically to the second half of the 1st century BCE, names the figure as (the yakṣa) Maṇibhadra and says it was made by Gomitaka, pupil of Kunika. The older theory that it portrays the king Ajātaśatru (Kuṇika) is rejected.
