nodes.limits: Shows that the Kṛṣṇa-Gopāla narrative had reached the Mekong delta polity by the 6th–7th century. It does not show how the story was told locally or in which text.

nodes.name: Spitzer manuscript
nodes.summary: A palm-leaf Sanskrit manuscript of more than 1,000 fragments, found in 1906 by the Third German Turfan Expedition (led by Albert Grünwedel) at Ming-öi near the Kizil caves, Xinjiang. It is radiocarbon-dated to c. 130 CE (80–230 CE) and written in Kuṣāṇa-period Brāhmī. Probably the oldest surviving philosophical manuscript in Sanskrit, it contains, among Buddhist and Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika material, a list of the parvans of the Mahābhārata. Dieter Schlingloff (1969) showed that the list lacks the Anuśāsana and Virāṭa parvans.
nodes.details:
The manuscript is named after Moritz Spitzer, whose team first studied it in 1927–28. Eli Franco's two-volume edition appeared in 2004. Contents: Buddhist verses and debate (including on duḥkha and the Four Noble Truths), Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika and tarka-śāstra material, sections referring to the Arthaśāstra and Manusmṛti, and the parvan list of the Mahābhārata.

Repository: mostly the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin, catalogued as SHT 810, with some fragments in the British Library (Or 15005/6–8, /17–21, /30–32). Dating: calibrated radiocarbon gives 130 CE (80–230 CE); Franco's palaeographic estimate is c. 200–230 CE. Schlingloff (1969) argued that the list shows a Mahābhārata still in a different (expanding) arrangement in the Kuṣāṇa period. Brockington (2010) reassessed this.

location.label: Findspot: Kizil caves (Ming-öi), Baicheng county, Xinjiang, China

attributes.findspot: Ming-öi near the Kizil caves, Xinjiang (Third German Turfan Expedition, 1906)
attributes.repository: Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin (bulk); British Library (some fragments)
attributes.script: Brāhmī (Kuṣāṇa, with some early Gupta forms)
attributes.discovered: 1906 (Third German Turfan Expedition under A. Grünwedel)

nodes.limits: Proves that a named, multi-parvan Mahābhārata was known in a Buddhist scholastic milieu in Central Asia by the 2nd–3rd century CE. It is not a manuscript of the Mahābhārata text itself, and the missing parvans may reflect the list's purpose or damage rather than the epic's contents.
openQuestions: Does the Spitzer manuscript also refer to the Rāmāyaṇa? (Not confirmed in the sources checked.)

nodes.name: Skandapurāṇa manuscript dated 810 CE (Kathmandu)
nodes.summary: A palm-leaf manuscript of the early Skandapurāṇa in a transitional Gupta script, in the National Archives, Kathmandu (NAK 2-229; NGMCP microfilm B 11/4). The editors Adriaensen, Bakker and Isaacson date it 810 CE, possibly copied on 10 March 811. It is one of the oldest dated Purāṇa manuscripts and the basis of the Groningen critical edition, which showed that the original Skandapurāṇa differs greatly from the later printed Skanda Purāṇa.
nodes.details: Haraprasad Shastri and Cecil Bendall reported the manuscript around 1898 in a Kathmandu library. It was bound with other, mostly Buddhist, manuscripts. Volume I of the Groningen edition (adhyāyas 1–25) appeared in 1998, followed by vols. IIa (2005), IIb (2014) and III (2013). Michael Witzel dates the manuscript to about 810 CE. Wikipedia reports that the era of the colophon is unclear, so the exact day is uncertain.

dates.label: 810/811 CE (dated colophon)
dates.basis: dated colophon (era conversion by the editors)

attributes.discovered: reported c. 1898 by Haraprasad Shastri and Cecil Bendall

nodes.limits: Securely dates one copy of the early Skandapurāṇa to 810/811 CE, giving a terminus ante quem for that text. It is not a witness of the much later Kāśī-khaṇḍa and other sections of the printed Skanda Purāṇa.
openQuestions: Which era does the colophon use, and does the 811 CE day-date hold?

nodes.name: Rigveda manuscripts at BORI (Memory of the World)
nodes.summary: A collection of 30 manuscripts of the Rigveda at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune, inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2007. It contains Saṃhitā, Padapāṭha and Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya manuscripts: one on birch bark in Śāradā script and 29 on paper in Devanāgarī. The oldest dated is No. 5/1882-83 of 1464 CE. The manuscripts were collected for the Bombay government from 1868 by Georg Bühler, F. Kielhorn and others.
nodes.details:
From the nomination file: titles Ṛgvedasaṃhitā, Ṛgvedasaṃhitā-Padapāṭha and Ṛgvedasaṃhitā-bhāṣya. 16 manuscripts contain Sāyaṇa's commentary and 5 the Padapāṭha. All are in Sanskrit. They were collected from Kashmir, Gujarat, the then Rajputana, the Central Provinces and elsewhere, under the Bombay Presidency's search for manuscripts begun in 1868 by Bühler and Kielhorn. They were later deposited at the Deccan College and then at BORI, whose manuscript library P. K. Gode first supervised.

The nomination says Max Müller used manuscript no. 5/1875-76 (birch bark, Śāradā) for his edition of the Rigveda with Sāyaṇa's commentary. India's National Mission for Manuscripts submitted the nomination on BORI's behalf, and UNESCO's register page gives 2007 as the registration year. Press reports that the manuscripts date from '1800–1500 BCE' confuse the date of composition with the date of copying; the manuscripts are medieval or later.

dates.label: 1464 CE (oldest dated manuscript, No. 5/1882-83)
dates.basis: dated colophon as reported in the nomination file

attributes.accession: 30 MSS incl. No. 5/1882-83 (oldest dated, 1464 CE) and No. 5/1875-76 (birch bark, Śāradā)
attributes.inscribed: UNESCO Memory of the World Register, 2007

nodes.limits: Shows careful transmission of the Rigveda text, accents and Sāyaṇa's commentary in late-medieval manuscripts, alongside the oral tradition. The manuscripts do not date the Rigveda's composition, which is far older and was transmitted orally.
openQuestions: What is the copying date of the birch-bark Śāradā manuscript No. 5/1875-76?

nodes.name: Rigveda manuscript BORI No. 5/1882-83 (1464 CE)
nodes.summary: The oldest dated manuscript in BORI's UNESCO-inscribed Rigveda collection, dated 1464 CE according to the nomination file. It is on paper in Devanāgarī script.
nodes.details: The nomination identifies it only by number and date. Its contents (Saṃhitā, Padapāṭha or Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya) are not specified in the passages checked.

dates.label: 1464 CE
dates.basis: dated colophon (as reported in the nomination file)

nodes.limits: Dates this copy only. It is not evidence for the text's composition date.

nodes.name: Birch-bark Śāradā Rigveda manuscript, BORI No. 5/1875-76
nodes.summary: The only birch-bark manuscript in BORI's Rigveda collection, written in Kashmiri Śāradā script. The nomination file says Max Müller used it for his edition of the Rigveda with Sāyaṇa's commentary, and stresses its importance given the losses of Kashmiri manuscripts.
nodes.details: The accession number shows it entered the government collection in 1875–76. Its copying date is not stated in the passages checked.

dates.label: acquired 1875–76 (accession year; copying date not stated)
dates.basis: accession number in the government manuscript collection

nodes.limits: A key witness of the Kashmiri transmission of the Rigveda. Its date of copying is unknown here, so it cannot be ranked chronologically against the 1464 manuscript.
openQuestions: When was the Śāradā birch-bark Rigveda (5/1875-76) copied?

nodes.name: Mohenjo-daro
nodes.summary: A major city of the Indus (Harappan) civilisation in Sindh, Pakistan, built c. 2500 BCE and abandoned c. 1700 BCE. It was visited by R. D. Banerji in 1919–20 and excavated from 1924 by K. N. Dikshit, John Marshall, Ernest Mackay and later Mortimer Wheeler and George Dales. It was the first UNESCO World Heritage Site in South Asia (1980). The 'Paśupati' seal was found here.

attributes.excavated: 1924–25 K. N. Dikshit; 1925–26 J. Marshall; 1927–31 E. J. H. Mackay; 1945/1950 M. Wheeler; 1964–65 G. Dales
attributes.repository: finds divided between Pakistan and India at Partition

nodes.limits: The site documents a Bronze Age urban civilisation whose script is undeciphered. Any link between its religion and later Hindu traditions is interpretive (see claim:proto-shiva).

nodes.name: Besnagar (Vidiśā)
nodes.summary: The archaeological site of ancient Vidiśā, about 3 km from modern Vidisha on the west bank of the Betwa, Madhya Pradesh. It was an important trade centre from the 6th–5th century BCE under the Śuṅgas, Nāgas, Sātavāhanas and Guptas. It is the site of the Heliodorus pillar and of an excavated elliptical Vāsudeva temple of the 2nd century BCE.
nodes.details: Cunningham inspected the ruins in 1874–75. D. R. Bhandarkar excavated in 1913–15, but work was stopped by the pillar's priest. M. D. Khare excavated in 1963–65 and found the elliptical temple layout beside the pillar. Besnagar lies near Sanchi and the Udayagiri caves.

dates.label: 2nd century BCE (Vāsudeva temple phase beside the pillar)
dates.basis: excavation (Khare 1963–65); association with the Heliodorus pillar

location.label: Besnagar, near Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh, India

attributes.excavated: A. Cunningham (survey 1874–75); D. R. Bhandarkar 1913–15; M. D. Khare 1963–65

nodes.limits: Documents an early historic city with one of the earliest excavated Vaiṣṇava temple sites. It is not evidence for any epic event.

nodes.name: Hastinapur excavations (1950–52)
nodes.summary: Excavations by B. B. Lal (ASI) in 1950–52 at Hastinapur, Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, a site traditionally identified with the Kuru capital Hastināpura of the Mahābhārata. Lal's main aim was to fix the stratigraphic position of Painted Grey Ware (PGW). He found Period I (Ochre Coloured Pottery), Period II (PGW, c. 1100–800 BCE in his dating), a flood-erosion break, Period III (NBPW, early 6th – early 3rd century BCE), Period IV (2nd century BCE – 3rd century CE) and Period V (from c. 11th century CE).
nodes.details:
Period II (PGW) had mud and reed walls, early rice cultivation and copper. Iron ore and slag appear only near the top. Lal proposed a major Gaṅgā flood around 800 BCE, marked by an “erosional scar”, after which the site was deserted for a couple of centuries. He suggested this might give a historical basis to the Purāṇic statement that Hastināpura was washed away by the Gaṅgā in Nicakṣu's reign and the capital moved to Kauśāmbī (claim:hastinapura-flood-nichakshu).

Later work: a 2021 excavation at Ulta-Kheda, published by Garnayak (2022, Puratattva), reports continuous occupation with no flood or fire break. It puts the PGW-dominated bottom layer at c. 1500–1000 BCE and an NBPW phase at c. 1000–500 BCE. That revision has not been checked against the primary report here.

location.label: Hastinapur, Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, India

attributes.periods: I OCP; II PGW; III NBPW; IV early historic; V medieval

nodes.limits: Establishes a PGW settlement at a place bearing the epic name. It does not establish that the Mahābhārata's Hastināpura or its events existed. The name–site link is traditional and the PGW–epic correlation is interpretive.

nodes.name: Aï Khanoum
nodes.summary: A Hellenistic city at the confluence of the Oxus (Amu Darya) and Kokcha rivers in northern Afghanistan. It was probably founded c. 300–285 BCE under Seleucus I or Antiochus I, and captured by nomads c. 145 BCE. The French archaeological mission (DAFA) under Daniel Schlumberger and then Paul Bernard excavated it from 1964 to 1978. In 1970 the palace yielded the Agathocles drachms with Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva.
nodes.details: After 1978 the site was comprehensively looted and its palace walls quarried. A later hoard (1973/74) was dispersed on the Kabul market. Excavated finds went to the National Museum of Afghanistan.

attributes.excavated: 1964–1978, Délégation Archéologique Française en Afghanistan (D. Schlumberger, P. Bernard)

nodes.limits: Shows Indian deities on coins circulating in a Greek city of Bactria. It does not show a Vāsudeva cult practised there.

nodes.name: Dwarka offshore explorations
nodes.summary: Underwater and intertidal explorations off Dwarka and Bet Dwarka (Gujarat) by the Marine Archaeology Centre of the National Institute of Oceanography, Goa, led by S. R. Rao from the 1980s, and later by the ASI. They recorded stone blocks, walls and many stone anchors. Rao identified the remains with Kṛṣṇa's Dvārakā. Later NIO researchers (Gaur, Sundaresh, Tripati 2004) argue from anchor typology that the harbour belongs to the historical period.
nodes.details:
Onshore, H. D. Sankalia's 1963 excavation near the Dvārakādhīśa temple (reported by Z. D. Ansari and M. S. Mate) produced material only about 2,000 years old, according to Tripathi (2005) as cited on Wikipedia. Other digs reported a 9th-century Viṣṇu shrine and a 1st-century BCE settlement. Wikipedia also mentions a settlement possibly of the 2nd millennium BCE. On Bet Dwarka, a Late Harappan site gave a thermoluminescence date of c. 1570 BCE; Rao's team reported a 560 m wall and a TL date of 1528 BCE for pottery.

Offshore, triangular and other stone anchors, dressed blocks and wall alignments were recorded. Gaur et al. (2004) interpret the structures as a jetty and date the harbour's importance to the historical period from anchor typology. A later study of the Okhamandal anchors concluded they may be no earlier than the historical period, by comparison with similar anchors on the Konkan coast.

dates.label: c. 15th century BCE (Rao's interpretation; TL date 1528 BCE from Bet Dwarka pottery)

location.label: Off Dwarka and Bet Dwarka, Devbhumi Dwarka district, Gujarat, India

attributes.excavated: onshore 1963 (H. D. Sankalia et al.); offshore from the 1980s by NIO Marine Archaeology Centre (S. R. Rao); later NIO and ASI work (A. S. Gaur et al.)

nodes.limits: Documents submerged and coastal structures and anchors showing that Dwarka was a port in the historical period. It does not establish that they are the Dvārakā of the Mahābhārata or Harivaṃśa.

nodes.name: Mora (near Mathurā)
nodes.summary: A village about 11 km from Mathurā, Uttar Pradesh, whose well and mound yielded the Mora well inscription of the Vṛṣṇi heroes (c. 15 CE), a carved doorjamb and torsos probably of the heroes. The mound was excavated in 1911–12.

dates.label: early 1st century CE (shrine of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes)

location.label: Mora, Mathura district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: Documents a 1st-century shrine of the Vṛṣṇi heroes; not evidence for the historicity of the Yādava narratives.

nodes.name: Nagari (ancient Madhyamikā)
nodes.subtype: early historic site with cult enclosure
nodes.summary: An early historic site about 13 km north of Chittorgarh, Rajasthan, identified with ancient Madhyamikā. The Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions recording a stone enclosure for Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva come from here and from nearby Ghosuṇḍī. The Hāthībāḍā enclosure is one of the earliest known structures linked to Vāsudeva worship.
nodes.limits: The enclosure is identified as the one the inscriptions describe; its precise relation to the fragments' original positions is uncertain.

nodes.name: Nāṇeghāṭ pass
nodes.subtype: rock-cut cave on a trade route
nodes.summary: A mountain pass in the Western Ghats (Pune district, Maharashtra) on an ancient trade route between the Konkan coast and the Deccan plateau. A rock-cut cave at its head carries the 1st-century BCE Sātavāhana inscriptions of queen Nāganikā and once held relief portraits of the royal family, now lost apart from their labels.

location.label: Naneghat, Junnar taluka, Pune district, Maharashtra, India

nodes.limits: A royal commemorative and ritual-record site; not a temple.

nodes.name: Eran (ancient Airikiṇa)
nodes.summary: An archaeological site on the Bina river, Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh. Its group of Gupta-period temples and monuments includes the colossal Varāha, the Garuḍa pillar of Budhagupta (484/85 CE), an inscription of Samudragupta (now in the Indian Museum, Kolkata), and the Goparāja memorial inscription of Gupta year 191 (510 CE), often cited as an early record of sati.
nodes.details: Cunningham's Report of Tours in Bundelkhand and Malwa (ASI vol. X, 1880) is the first systematic report. The Goparāja inscription does not use the word sati, and Fleet's 1888 edition contains an interpolation.

dates.label: c. 4th – early 6th century CE (Samudragupta to Toramāṇa and Bhānugupta)

location.label: Eran, Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh, India

attributes.excavated: A. Cunningham (survey, published 1880); later ASI and university excavations

nodes.limits: Documents Vaiṣṇava monuments and political transitions (Gupta to Hūṇa) in central India; not evidence for the cosmogonic narratives depicted.

nodes.name: Purana Qila (Old Fort), Delhi
nodes.subtype: multi-period settlement mound under a fort
nodes.summary: A 16th-century fort in Delhi whose mound has been excavated by B. B. Lal (1954–55 and 1969–72/73) and by Vasant Kumar Swarnkar (2013–14, 2017–18), with a further ASI season in 2023. The excavations found Painted Grey Ware sherds (c. 1000 BCE) and a sequence of Mauryan, Śuṅga, Kuṣāṇa, Gupta, Rajput, Sultanate and Mughal levels. Local tradition, Cunningham and India's Ministry of Culture identify the site with the Pāṇḍavas' Indraprastha.
nodes.details: Until the early 20th century the fort was called Pāṇḍavoṃ kā Qilā and the area Indraprastha village. The 2023 season reported early Kuṣāṇa structures at 5.5 m depth, a Vaikuṇṭha Viṣṇu image and a Gaja-Lakṣmī terracotta plaque. Wikipedia notes that linking archaeological cultures with literary and bardic sources is “methodologically almost always impossible”.

dates.label: c. 1000 BCE (PGW sherds) to the Mughal period
16th century CE (surviving fort)
dates.basis: historical record of the fort's construction

nodes.limits: Establishes long occupation from about the PGW period. It does not establish that this was the Indraprastha of the Mahābhārata (see claim:purana-qila-indraprastha).

nodes.name: Kizil caves (Ming-öi)
nodes.summary: A Buddhist cave complex on the north bank of the Muzat river, about 65 km west of Kucha in Baicheng county, Xinjiang, China. The Third German Turfan Expedition (December 1905 – July 1907) worked here under Albert Grünwedel and found the Spitzer manuscript in the Ming-öi area.

dates.label: find context of the Spitzer manuscript (radiocarbon 80–230 CE)
dates.basis: radiocarbon date of the manuscript found here

location.label: Kizil Township, Baicheng county, Aksu prefecture, Xinjiang, China

attributes.excavated: Third German Turfan Expedition 1905–07 (A. Grünwedel; A. von Le Coq until June 1906); Fourth Expedition 1913–14 (Le Coq)

nodes.limits: A Buddhist site; the Sanskrit manuscripts found there attest learned culture along the Silk Road, not Hindu worship at the site.

nodes.name: Gangdhar
nodes.summary: A town on the Kali Sindh river in Jhalawar district, Rajasthan, findspot of the 423/424 CE inscription of the Aulikara king Viśvavarman's minister Mayūrākṣaka, who built temples of Viṣṇu and of the Mothers there.
nodes.limits: The temples named in the inscription are not identified with surviving structures here.

nodes.name: Mandasor (ancient Daśapura)
nodes.summary: The town of Mandsaur, Madhya Pradesh, identified with ancient Daśapura, seat of the Aulikara rulers. It is the findspot of the silk-weavers' Sun-temple inscription (436/437 and 472/473 CE). The Sondani victory pillars of Yaśodharman, who claims a victory over the Hūṇa Mihirakula, stand about 4 km away.
nodes.limits: The Sun temple of the inscription has not been identified with a surviving structure in the sources checked.

nodes.name: Phnom Da
nodes.summary: A hill sanctuary about 3 km south-east of Angkor Borei, Takeo province, Cambodia. It is the findspot of colossal pre-Angkorian sandstone images, among them an eight-armed Viṣṇu and figures of Kṛṣṇa lifting Govardhana, attributed to the reign of Rudravarman (514–539). Its oldest standing temple dates to the 6th century.

location.label: Phnom Da, Angkor Borei district, Takeo, Cambodia

nodes.limits: Documents early Southeast Asian Vaiṣṇava cult images; their local narrative context is unknown.

nodes.name: Goth–Mānglod (Dadhimatī Mātā temple site)
nodes.subtype: temple site (findspot of a dated inscription)
nodes.summary: The site of the Dadhimatī Mātā temple between the villages of Goth and Mānglod, Nagaur district, Rajasthan. A slab dated 608 CE found there quotes the Devī Māhātmya.

location.label: Goth–Mānglod, Jayal tehsil, Nagaur district, Rajasthan, India

nodes.limits: The inscription proves the shrine existed by 608 CE; the date of the surviving temple fabric is not established here.

nodes.name: The claim that offshore remains at Dwarka are Kṛṣṇa’s city
nodes.subtype: identification of archaeological remains with a narrative place
nodes.summary: S. R. Rao and others hold that the submerged walls, blocks and anchors off Dwarka and Bet Dwarka are remains of Kṛṣṇa's Dvārakā, which the Mahābhārata says the sea swallowed after the Yādavas destroyed one another. Most archaeologists, including later NIO researchers, date the recorded structures and anchors to the historical period. They see no archaeological basis for identifying them with an epic city.
nodes.details: For: walls and blocks recorded underwater; a 560 m shoreline wall and TL date of 1528 BCE at Bet Dwarka (Rao); a Late Harappan presence on Bet Dwarka (TL c. 1570 BCE). Against: anchor typology indicates the historical period (Gaur et al. 2004); the 1963 onshore excavation found nothing older than c. 2,000 years; no inscription or object connects the remains to the epic city; coastal erosion explains submergence without a catastrophe.
nodes.limits: Even a 2nd-millennium BCE date for a submerged settlement would show only that a coastal settlement existed; it would not establish the epic narrative.

nodes.name: The claim that Adam’s Bridge is a man-made structure
nodes.subtype: claim about the origin of a natural feature
nodes.summary: Some people hold that Adam's Bridge (Rāma Setu), the 48 km chain of shoals between Pamban island (India) and Mannar island (Sri Lanka), is the remnant of the causeway built by Rāma's vānara army in the Rāmāyaṇa's Yuddhakāṇḍa. Geological and remote-sensing studies describe it as a natural formation of limestone shoals, sandbars and patch reefs. The question became politically salient in the controversy over the Sethusamudram Shipping Canal Project, approved in 2005.
nodes.details:
Geology: the feature consists of parallel ledges of sandstone and conglomerate, hard at the surface. An ISRO Space Applications Centre study describes 103 small patch reefs. During the last glacial period sea level was up to 120 m lower, and the Palk Strait was dry land until it was submerged around 7,000 years ago. Temple records suggest a storm in 1480 broke a surviving land link.

Public record: in a 2007 affidavit to the Supreme Court the ASI and the government said there was no historical proof that Rāma built the bridge, and that affidavit was later withdrawn. NASA said its satellite images had been misinterpreted. A Science Channel programme claimed the structure was man-made, and geologist C. P. Rajendran criticised the controversy. In December 2022 the Minister of State Jitendra Singh told the Rajya Sabha that satellite imagery showed limestone shoals that could not be accurately said to be remnants of a bridge, and could not give direct information on their origin or age. The ICHR announced a pilot study in 2017 and shelved it in 2018.

This graph records the religious significance of the site as tradition (class 6) and keeps it apart from the geological question. Whether the Rāmāyaṇa's Laṅkā is Sri Lanka is itself debated; Sankalia (1973) and others located it in central India.
nodes.limits: The religious significance of Rāma Setu for many Hindus does not depend on its geology, and the geology cannot test the narrative. This claim concerns only whether the physical feature is artificial.

nodes.name: Painted Grey Ware sites as the archaeological horizon of the Mahābhārata
nodes.subtype: correlation of an archaeological culture with an epic
nodes.summary: B. B. Lal argued from his Hastinapur excavation (1950–52) and later surveys that the Painted Grey Ware culture (c. 1200–600 BCE) is found at many sites bearing Mahābhārata place names, such as Hastināpura, Indraprastha (Purana Qila), Kurukṣetra and Mathurā. He proposed it as the material horizon of the epic's core events. Critics stress that pottery cannot be tied to a text without inscriptions, that PGW material culture differs from the epic's descriptions, and that PGW dates are being revised.
nodes.details: PGW is widely associated with the late Vedic Kuru-Pañcāla period, and 1,576 PGW sites were known by 2018 (Uesugi). Its dates range from c. 1300 to 500–300 BCE in recent syntheses, and some radiocarbon dates are earlier. The Wikipedia article on Purana Qila quotes the methodological objection that linking archaeological cultures with literary and bardic sources is “methodologically almost always impossible”.
nodes.limits: A correlation between a pottery horizon and epic place names, even if real, would not establish that the epic narrative is historical.

nodes.name: The Hastinapur flood as the Purāṇic flood of Nicakṣu's reign
nodes.subtype: correlation of a stratigraphic event with a textual tradition
nodes.summary: B. B. Lal suggested that a flood-erosion break at the end of Period II (PGW, c. 800 BCE in his dating) at Hastinapur corresponds to the Purāṇic account. In that account the Gaṅgā carried away Hastināpura in the reign of Nicakṣu, a descendant of Parīkṣit, and the Kuru capital moved to Kauśāmbī.
nodes.details: The Purāṇic statement occurs in the dynastic lists. Wilson's Viṣṇu Purāṇa, book 4, is given here as a coarse locator, and the exact chapter and verse are not verified. A 2021 excavation at Ulta-Kheda (Garnayak 2022, as summarised on Wikipedia) reports continuous occupation without a flood horizon, which weighs against the correlation.
nodes.limits: Even a confirmed flood would show only that the site flooded, not that the Purāṇic genealogy is historical.

nodes.name: Purana Qila is the site of the Pāṇḍavas' Indraprastha
nodes.subtype: identification of a site with a narrative place
nodes.summary: Local tradition, Alexander Cunningham and India's Ministry of Culture identify the Purana Qila mound in Delhi with Indraprastha, the Pāṇḍava capital of the Mahābhārata. Excavations have found PGW sherds of c. 1000 BCE and continuous later habitation, but nothing that names the site or ties it specifically to the epic.
nodes.limits: The identification rests on tradition and place-name continuity (class 6). Archaeology can show early occupation but cannot by itself establish the epic city.

nodes.name: Heliodorus (Heliodoros), son of Dion
nodes.summary: A Greek (Yavana) envoy from Taxila, sent by the Indo-Greek king Antialkidas to king Kāsīputra Bhāgabhadra at Vidiśā. On the Besnagar pillar he calls himself a bhāgavata and records setting up a Garuḍa-standard for Vāsudeva, “god of gods”. He is one of the earliest named foreign devotees in Indian epigraphy.
nodes.limits: Known only from the Besnagar inscription.

nodes.name: Antialkidas (Antialcidas)
nodes.summary: An Indo-Greek king who ruled from Taxila and sent Heliodorus as envoy to Vidiśā. His reign is dated c. 115–95 BCE (Bopearachchi) or c. 130–120 BCE (Senior), and that choice affects the date of the Heliodorus pillar.

nodes.name: Kāsīputra Bhāgabhadra
nodes.summary: A king at Vidiśā in whose 14th regnal year Heliodorus set up the Besnagar pillar. Early scholars identified him with a Śuṅga king of the Purāṇic lists. Later scholars, partly because of excavations at Sonkh near Mathurā, consider him more probably a local ruler.
openQuestions: Is Bhāgabhadra the Purāṇic Śuṅga Bhāgavata or a local king?

nodes.name: Agathocles of Bactria
nodes.summary: A Greco-Bactrian king (c. 190–180 BCE) who issued Indian-standard square and round drachms with Indian imagery. They include the Aï Khanoum drachms showing two deities identified as Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, and a type with Lakṣmī.

nodes.name: Nāganikā (Nāyanikā)
nodes.summary: A Sātavāhana queen, probably the widow of Sātakarṇi, who commissioned the Nāṇeghāṭ cave inscription recording Vedic sacrifices and invoking Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva.

nodes.name: Sarvatāta (Gājāyana)
nodes.summary: A king of the Gājāyana lineage, son of a Pārāśarī mother, performer of an aśvamedha and devotee of Bhagavat. The Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions record that he built a stone enclosure for Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva near Nagari (Madhyamikā).

nodes.name: Śoḍāsa
nodes.summary: An Indo-Scythian (Śaka) Great Satrap (Mahākṣatrapa) of Mathurā, son of Rājuvula, in the early 1st century CE. Dedicatory inscriptions of his time include the Mora well inscription of the Vṛṣṇi heroes and the Vasu doorjamb inscription recording a gateway at the shrine of Bhagavat Vāsudeva.

nodes.name: Wima (Vima) Kadphises
nodes.summary: A Kuṣāṇa emperor, father of Kaniṣka I according to the Rabatak inscription, and the first Kuṣāṇa to issue gold coins. His coins show a deity with trident and bull, generally identified as Śiva, and call him mahiśvara.

nodes.name: Kaniṣka I
nodes.summary: A Kuṣāṇa emperor (c. 127–150 CE in Harry Falk's chronology) whose coins show a mixed Iranian, Greek, Indian and Buddhist pantheon, including Oesho (ΟΗϷΟ). His Rabatak inscription gives his genealogy and records the use of Bactrian.

nodes.name: Candragupta II
nodes.summary: A Gupta emperor (c. 380–415 CE), also called Vikramāditya. His reign is attested by the Udayagiri inscriptions of Gupta year 82 (401/402 CE) and by Vīrasena's cave. He is generally identified with the king Candra of the Delhi iron pillar, and he issued the archer-type gold coins with Śrī-Lakṣmī. Gupta coins and inscriptions call him paramabhāgavata.

nodes.name: Kumāragupta I
nodes.summary: A Gupta emperor (c. 415–455 CE), son of Candragupta II, known for his Kārttikeya-type gold coins. The Mandasor silk-weavers' inscription (436/437 CE) is dated in his reign.

nodes.name: Budhagupta
nodes.summary: A later Gupta emperor whose reign is attested by the Eran Garuḍa pillar inscription of Gupta year 165 (484/485 CE).

nodes.name: Vīrasena Śāba
nodes.summary: A minister of Candragupta II of the Kautsa gotra. His inscription in Udayagiri Cave 8 records that he made the cave as a temple of Śambhu (Śiva) when he came there with the king.

nodes.name: Toramāṇa
nodes.summary: A king of the Alchon Huns (c. 493–515 CE) who conquered the Punjab and parts of central India. The Eran boar inscription is dated in the first year of his reign. He was succeeded by his son Mihirakula.

nodes.name: Dhanyaviṣṇu
nodes.summary: A local Vaiṣṇava ruler at Eran, younger brother of the late mahārāja Mātṛviṣṇu. In the first year of Toramāṇa he built the stone temple of Nārāyaṇa in boar form, to which the colossal Eran Varāha belongs.

nodes.name: Viśvavarman (Aulikara)
nodes.summary: An Aulikara king of western Mālwa, son of Naravarman. His minister Mayūrākṣaka's Gangdhar inscription of 423/424 CE records temples of Viṣṇu and the Mothers.

nodes.name: Bandhuvarman
nodes.summary: An Aulikara ruler of Daśapura (Mandasor), son of Viśvavarman. The silk-weavers' inscription says the Sun temple was built in 436/437 CE while Kumāragupta ruled the earth and Bandhuvarman was lord of Daśapura.

nodes.name: Vatsabhaṭṭi
nodes.summary: A Sanskrit poet who composed the Mandasor praśasti of the silk-weavers' guild (436/437 CE). He names himself in its closing verse.

nodes.name: Kīrtivarman I (Cālukya)
nodes.summary: A Cālukya king of Bādāmi, father of Pulakeśin II and elder (probably half-) brother of Maṅgaleśa. The Bādāmi Cave 3 inscription of Śaka 500 (578 CE) is dated in his reign.

nodes.name: Maṅgaleśa
nodes.summary: A Cālukya king of Bādāmi (c. 592–610 CE) who, as prince under his brother Kīrtivarman I, dedicated the Viṣṇu cave (Cave 3) at Bādāmi in 578 CE. His Mahākūṭa pillar inscription dates to his 5th regnal year (601 CE). His nephew Pulakeśin II overthrew him in a succession war, as the Aihole inscription relates.

nodes.name: Pulakeśin II
nodes.summary: A Cālukya king of Bādāmi (c. 610–642 CE), son of Kīrtivarman I. His court poet Ravikīrti's Aihole inscription (634/635 CE) praises his victories, including one over Harṣa, which Xuanzang's account calls into question.

nodes.name: Ravikīrti
nodes.summary: A Jain poet at the court of Pulakeśin II who composed the Aihole praśasti of 634/635 CE on the Meguti Jain temple. In it he claims fame equal to Kālidāsa's and Bhāravi's.

nodes.name: Narasiṃhavarman I (Māmalla)
nodes.summary: A Pallava king (630–668 CE), son of Mahendravarman I, after whose title Māmalla Mamallapuram is named. Several of its monolithic monuments and reliefs are attributed to his reign.

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa I (Rāṣṭrakūṭa)
nodes.summary: A Rāṣṭrakūṭa king (c. 756–773 CE) to whom later copper plates (Vadodara plates of Karkarāja II, c. 812–813; Kadaba grant) attribute the Kailāsa temple at Ellora.

nodes.name: Mānadeva
nodes.summary: A Licchavi king of Nepal (464–505 CE) whose pillar inscription at Changu Narayan (Saṃvat 386, conventionally 464 CE) is among the oldest dated records of the Kathmandu Valley. He issued coins called mānāṅka.

nodes.name: Dyah Lokapāla (Rakai Kayuwangi)
nodes.summary: A ruler of the Medang (Mataram) kingdom of Central Java who issued the Śivagṛha inscription of 856 CE immediately after the abdication of Rakai Pikatan (Jatiningrat).

nodes.name: Candragupta Maurya
nodes.summary: The founder of the Maurya empire (c. 321–297 BCE), at whose court in Pāṭaliputra Megasthenes served as Seleucid ambassador.

nodes.name: Megasthenes
nodes.summary: A Greek historian and Seleucid ambassador to Candragupta Maurya at Pāṭaliputra (c. 300 BCE; died c. 290 BCE). His lost Indica survives in excerpts by Arrian, Diodorus and Strabo, including the report of the Sourasenoi who honoured 'Herakles'. Strabo already distrusted him.

nodes.name: Kālidāsa
nodes.summary: The classical Sanskrit poet and dramatist, author of Abhijñānaśākuntalam, Raghuvaṃśa and Meghadūta. His dates are debated and he is often placed in the Gupta period (c. 4th–5th century CE). The Aihole inscription of 634/635 CE, which names him, is the firm terminus ante quem.
nodes.details: Created by the material agent because the Aihole inscription is the external anchor for his date; other agents may hold a fuller literary record. See report, cross-agent links.

dates.label: before 634/635 CE (named in the Aihole inscription)
c. 4th–5th century CE (common scholarly view)
dates.basis: literary and historical arguments (link with Candragupta II often proposed)

nodes.name: Bhāravi
nodes.summary: A Sanskrit poet, author of the Kirātārjunīya, which retells Arjuna's penance and his fight with Śiva disguised as a hunter. The Aihole inscription of 634/635 CE names him beside Kālidāsa, giving a terminus ante quem; he is usually placed in the 6th century CE.

dates.label: before 634/635 CE (named in the Aihole inscription)

nodes.name: Alexander Cunningham
nodes.summary: A British army engineer and archaeologist (1814–1893), founder and first head of the Archaeological Survey of India (1861). His tour reports recorded, among many sites, Besnagar and the Heliodorus pillar, Udayagiri, Eran, Deogarh and Nachna.

nodes.name: John Marshall
nodes.summary: A British archaeologist (1876–1958), Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (1902–1928). He directed the excavations at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa and proposed the 'proto-Śiva' reading of the Paśupati seal (Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Civilization, 1931). He also reported the 1909 discovery of the Heliodorus inscriptions.

nodes.name: Ernest J. H. Mackay
nodes.summary: A British archaeologist (1880–1943) who directed excavations at Mohenjo-daro in 1927–31. In Further Excavations at Mohenjo-daro (1938) he numbered the 'Paśupati' seal 420 and assigned it to his Intermediate I period.

nodes.name: Doris Meth Srinivasan
nodes.summary: An American art historian of early Indian art whose studies (1975–76; 1979; 1997) criticised the proto-Śiva reading of the Paśupati seal and analysed early Vaiṣṇava (caturvyūha) and multi-headed imagery.

nodes.name: B. B. Lal
nodes.summary: An Indian archaeologist (1921–2022), Director-General of the ASI (1968–1972). He excavated Hastinapur (1950–52) and Purana Qila, and argued for a link between Painted Grey Ware sites and Mahābhārata places.

nodes.name: S. R. Rao
nodes.summary: Shikaripura Ranganatha Rao (1922–2013), Indian archaeologist who excavated Lothal and led marine archaeology at Dwarka and Bet Dwarka for the National Institute of Oceanography. He argued that the remains were Kṛṣṇa's Dvārakā (The Lost City of Dvārakā, 1999). His claimed decipherment of the Indus script is not accepted by mainstream scholarship.

nodes.name: V. S. Sukthankar
nodes.summary: Vishnu Sitaram Sukthankar (1887–1943), Indologist and first general editor of the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute's Critical Edition of the Mahābhārata (from 1925 until his death). He also worked on the Besnagar inscriptions; his transliteration is among those adapted for the Heliodorus reading on Wikipedia.

nodes.name: D. R. Bhandarkar
nodes.summary: Devadatta Ramkrishna Bhandarkar (1875–1950), Indian epigraphist and archaeologist. He excavated at Besnagar (1913–15) and edited the Hāthībāḍā Brāhmī inscription in Epigraphia Indica vol. 22.

nodes.name: Georg Bühler
nodes.summary: A German Indologist (1837–1898) who, with F. Kielhorn, collected thousands of manuscripts for the Bombay government from 1868, now at BORI, including Rigveda manuscripts. He published the first complete edition of the Nāṇeghāṭ inscription (1883) and, with Bhagvanlal Indraji, early Nepalese inscriptions including the Changu Narayan pillar.

nodes.name: Franz Kielhorn
nodes.summary: A German Indologist (1840–1908) who collected manuscripts for the Bombay Presidency (1868–1882), now part of BORI's holdings, and published the standard revised edition of the Aihole inscription in Epigraphia Indica vol. VI.

nodes.name: J. F. Fleet
nodes.summary: John Faithfull Fleet (1847–1917), British epigraphist whose Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum vol. III (1888) remains the standard edition of Gupta-period inscriptions. He correctly read the Bhārata-war date of the Aihole inscription in 1879.

nodes.name: Dieter Schlingloff
nodes.summary: A German Indologist who studied Sanskrit manuscripts from the Turfan finds. His 1969 article identified the parvan list of the Mahābhārata in the Spitzer manuscript as the oldest extant list.

nodes.name: Eli Franco
nodes.summary: An Indologist who published the two-volume edition of the Spitzer manuscript (2004) and proposed a palaeographic date of c. 200–230 CE.

nodes.name: Paul Bernard
nodes.summary: A French archaeologist who directed the DAFA excavations at Aï Khanoum after Daniel Schlumberger, until work stopped in 1978. The 1970 hoard with the Agathocles drachms of Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva came from his excavations.

nodes.name: I. K. Sarma
nodes.summary: Inguva Karthikeya Sarma, Indian archaeologist who led the ASI excavations around the Gudimallam liṅga in 1973–74.

nodes.name: H. D. Sankalia
nodes.summary: Hasmukh Dhirajlal Sankalia (1908–1989), Indian archaeologist of Deccan College. He led the 1963 onshore excavation at Dwarka and, in Ramayana: Myth or Reality? (1973), questioned the historicity and geography of the Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: J. G. de Casparis
nodes.summary: Johannes Gijsbertus de Casparis (1916–2002), Dutch epigraphist of Indonesia. He edited the Śivagṛha inscription (Prasasti Indonesia II, 1956) and identified its Śiva temple compound with Prambanan.

nodes.name: Maurya empire
nodes.summary: The first empire of most of the Indian subcontinent (c. 322–185 BCE), founded by Candragupta Maurya. Megasthenes was sent to its court at Pāṭaliputra.

nodes.name: Indo-Greek kingdoms
nodes.summary: Greek-ruled kingdoms of the north-west of the subcontinent (c. 180 BCE – c. 10 CE), offshoots of Greco-Bactria. Their kings issued bilingual coins, and their envoy Heliodorus set up the Besnagar pillar for Vāsudeva.
nodes.details: This record also covers, loosely, the Greco-Bactrian king Agathocles, whose Indian-standard coins circulated south of the Hindu Kush. Bactria proper is treated as part of the same Hellenistic horizon.

nodes.name: Śuṅga dynasty
nodes.summary: A north and central Indian dynasty (c. 185–73 BCE) founded by Puṣyamitra after the last Maurya. Some scholars once identified Bhāgabhadra of the Heliodorus pillar with a Śuṅga king; the identification is now doubted.

nodes.name: Sātavāhana dynasty
nodes.summary: A Deccan dynasty whose early queen Nāganikā commissioned the Nāṇeghāṭ inscription. Its chronology is debated between a short chronology (from the 1st century BCE) and a long one (from the late 3rd century BCE), ending in the early 3rd century CE.

dates.label: c. 1st century BCE – early 3rd century CE
c. late 3rd century BCE – early 3rd century CE

nodes.name: Northern Satraps of Mathurā
nodes.summary: Indo-Scythian (Śaka) satraps who governed Mathurā around the turn of the Common Era, including Rājuvula and his son Śoḍāsa. Dedicatory inscriptions of their time record shrines of Vāsudeva and the Vṛṣṇi heroes.

dates.label: c. mid-1st century BCE – early 1st century CE

nodes.name: Kuṣāṇa empire
nodes.summary: A Central Asian dynasty that ruled Bactria and northern India (c. 1st–3rd century CE). Its coinage carried a mixed pantheon including Oesho, Skanda-Kumāra and the Buddha, and its Mathurā workshops produced early Hindu, Buddhist and Jain images.

nodes.name: Gupta empire
nodes.summary: A north Indian empire (c. 320–550 CE) whose kings styled themselves paramabhāgavata. Their period produced the Udayagiri Varāha, Deogarh, Eran and much of the classical iconography of Viṣṇu, Śiva and the Goddess. The Gupta era begins in 319/320 CE.

dates.label: c. 320–550 CE
dates.basis: dated inscriptions in the Gupta era

nodes.name: Aulikara dynasties
nodes.summary: Two lines of rulers in western Mālwa with seats at Daśapura (Mandasor), known almost entirely from inscriptions such as Gangdhar (423/424 CE), Mandasor (436/437 CE) and the Sondani pillars of Yaśodharman (6th century).

nodes.name: Hūṇa (Alchon) kingdom
nodes.summary: The Alchon Huns, a Central Asian power that under Toramāṇa (c. 493–515) and Mihirakula ruled the Punjab and parts of central India. The Eran boar inscription records a Vaiṣṇava local ruler under Toramāṇa.

dates.label: c. 490s–540s CE (in India)
dates.basis: inscriptions of Toramāṇa and Mihirakula; Chinese sources

nodes.name: Licchavi kingdom of Nepal
nodes.summary: The early historic kingdom of the Kathmandu Valley (c. 400–750 CE). Its Sanskrit inscriptions, beginning with Mānadeva's Changu Narayan pillar, record Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva foundations.

nodes.name: Kalacuris of Māhiṣmatī (early Kalacuris)
nodes.summary: A western Indian dynasty of the 6th century under whose king Kṛṣṇarāja the Elephanta Great Cave is now generally thought to have been completed.

nodes.name: Cālukyas of Bādāmi
nodes.summary: A Deccan dynasty (543–753 CE) based at Vātāpi (Bādāmi). Its rulers Kīrtivarman I, Maṅgaleśa and Pulakeśin II patronised the Bādāmi caves (Cave 3 dated 578 CE) and the Aihole praśasti (634/635 CE).

dates.label: 543–753 CE
dates.basis: dated inscriptions (Bādāmi rock inscription of 543; overthrow by Dantidurga)

nodes.name: Pallava dynasty
nodes.summary: A Tamil–Andhra dynasty (c. 3rd century – 897 CE) based at Kāñcīpuram. The rock-cut monuments and reliefs of Mamallapuram were created under its 7th–8th-century kings.

nodes.name: Rāṣṭrakūṭa dynasty
nodes.summary: A Deccan dynasty (c. 753–982 CE) to whose king Kṛṣṇa I the Kailāsa temple at Ellora is attributed by later copper plates.

nodes.name: Medang (Mataram) kingdom, Java
nodes.summary: A Javanese kingdom (c. 732–1016 CE) of Central and later East Java, patron of Borobudur and of the Śaiva temple compound of Prambanan, consecrated according to the Śivagṛha inscription of 856 CE.

dates.label: c. 732–1016 CE
dates.basis: dated inscriptions (Canggal 732 to the fall of the East Javan court)

nodes.name: Cōḻa dynasty
nodes.summary: A Tamil dynasty whose imperial line (c. 848–1279 CE, from Vijayālaya) patronised great temples and the bronze-casting tradition that produced the classic Naṭarāja.

nodes.name: Khmer empire
nodes.summary: The empire centred on Angkor (802–1431 CE). Pre-Angkorian Cambodian kingdoms, such as the one that produced the Phnom Da sculptures (6th century), preceded it.

nodes.name: Candela dynasty
nodes.summary: A central Indian dynasty (c. 831–1315 CE) best known for the temples of Khajuraho.

nodes.name: Eastern Gaṅga dynasty
nodes.summary: An Odishan dynasty whose imperial phase (c. 1078–1434 CE, from Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga) built the Jagannātha temple at Puri and the Sun temple at Konark. Earlier Gaṅga rulers of Kaliṅga are known from the 5th–6th century.

nodes.name: Vijayanagara empire
nodes.summary: A south Indian empire (1336–1646 CE) with its capital at Hampi.

nodes.name: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune
nodes.summary: A research institute founded in Pune in 1917. It produced the Critical Edition of the Mahābhārata (1933–1966) and holds the former Government Manuscripts Library of the Bombay Presidency, including the 30 Rigveda manuscripts inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register (2007).

nodes.name: Archaeological Survey of India
nodes.summary: India's national archaeological agency, founded in 1861 under Alexander Cunningham. It excavated Mohenjo-daro (before 1947), Hastinapur and Purana Qila, protects monuments such as Udayagiri, Eran, Deogarh and Gudimallam, and runs an underwater archaeology wing.

nodes.name: UNESCO
nodes.summary: UNESCO, whose World Heritage Centre maintains the World Heritage List (Mohenjo-daro 1980; Elephanta 1987; Mamallapuram, Ellora, Prambanan and others), whose Living Heritage Entity maintains the Intangible Cultural Heritage lists (Vedic chanting, Rāmlīlā, Kūṭiyāṭṭam, Royal Ballet of Cambodia), and whose Memory of the World Register includes the BORI Rigveda manuscripts (2007).

nodes.name: National Museum, New Delhi
nodes.summary: India's national museum. Among its holdings are the 'Paśupati' seal from Mohenjo-daro, allocated to India at Partition, and the main collection of loose sculpture from the Deogarh Daśāvatāra temple.

nodes.name: National Archives, Kathmandu
nodes.summary: Nepal's national archive, holding a major collection of early palm-leaf manuscripts, including the Skandapurāṇa manuscript dated 810/811 CE (NAK 2-229). Its holdings were microfilmed by the Nepal-German projects.

nodes.name: Cleveland Museum of Art
nodes.summary: An art museum in Cleveland, Ohio, whose Open Access programme releases collection images under CC0. Relevant holdings include the Naṭarāja 1930.331, the gold archer coin of Candragupta II 1977.62 and the Phnom Da Kṛṣṇa Govardhana 1973.106.

nodes.name: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam
nodes.summary: The national museum of the Netherlands. It displays the Cōḻa Naṭarāja AK-MAK-187 on loan from the Royal Asian Art Society in the Netherlands.

nodes.name: Bharat Kala Bhavan, Banaras Hindu University
nodes.summary: The art and archaeology museum of Banaras Hindu University, Varanasi. It holds the Gupta-period Kṛṣṇa Govardhanadhara from Varanasi.

nodes.name: Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin
nodes.summary: The Berlin State Library, which holds most of the Spitzer manuscript (SHT 810) among the Sanskrit manuscripts of the German Turfan expeditions.

nodes.name: British Library
nodes.summary: The national library of the United Kingdom, which holds some fragments of the Spitzer manuscript (Or 15005/…).

nodes.name: Government Museum, Mathurā
nodes.summary: The archaeological museum of Mathurā, holding the Mora well inscription (GMM Q.1), a Vṛṣṇi-hero torso from Mora and the Vasu doorjamb (GMM 13.367), together with major Kuṣāṇa sculpture.

nodes.name: Government Museum, Udaipur
nodes.summary: A state museum in Udaipur, Rajasthan, reported to hold fragments of the Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions.

nodes.name: National Museum of Indonesia, Jakarta
nodes.summary: Indonesia's national museum, holding the Śivagṛha inscription (D.28).

nodes.name: CSIR-National Institute of Oceanography, Goa
nodes.summary: India's national oceanographic institute. Its Marine Archaeology Centre, led first by S. R. Rao, conducted the underwater explorations off Dwarka and Bet Dwarka.

nodes.name: Norton Simon Foundation / Museum, Pasadena
nodes.summary: The California collection that bought the Sivapuram Naṭarāja in 1973 and, under a 1976 settlement with the Government of India, held it for ten years before returning it.

nodes.name: Délégation archéologique française en Afghanistan (DAFA)
nodes.summary: The French archaeological mission in Afghanistan, which excavated Aï Khanoum (1964–1978) under Daniel Schlumberger and Paul Bernard.

nodes.name: Nepal-German Manuscript Preservation / Cataloguing Projects
nodes.summary: German–Nepalese projects (NGMPP, then NGMCP) that microfilmed and catalogued manuscripts in Nepal, including the 810/811 CE Skandapurāṇa manuscript (microfilm B 11/4).

nodes.name: National Mission for Manuscripts
nodes.summary: A Government of India mission (Ministry of Culture) for documenting and conserving manuscripts. It submitted the Rigveda nomination to UNESCO's Memory of the World on behalf of BORI.

nodes.name: The Mothers (Mātṛkās)
nodes.summary: A group of goddesses, the 'Mothers', whose shrine is first dated epigraphically in the Gangdhar inscription of 423/424 CE, which calls it a terrifying abode of the divine Mothers. Groups of Mātṛkās (later usually seven, the Saptamātṛkās) are common in Kuṣāṇa and Gupta sculpture.
nodes.limits: Created by the material agent for the Gangdhar record; the purana agent may hold a fuller theological record (see report).

earliestMaterial.label: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

nodes.name: Indica of Megasthenes (fragments)
nodes.summary: A lost Greek ethnography of India by Megasthenes (c. 300 BCE). It survives only in excerpts and paraphrases by Diodorus (1st century BCE), Strabo (1st century CE) and Arrian (Indica, 2nd century CE), and is the earliest foreign description of Indian religious life. It includes the report of 'Herakles' honoured by the Sourasenoi.
nodes.limits: Survives only through later authors who selected and sometimes doubted it; its Greek interpretive categories (Herakles, Dionysos) distort Indian referents.

nodes.name: Tamil inscriptions of the Rājarājeśvaram, Thanjavur
nodes.summary: The long Tamil inscriptions on the walls and base of the Bṛhadīśvara (Rājarājeśvaram) temple, recording Rājarāja I’s and his successors’ gifts, the temple’s endowments, staff and bronzes; edited by E. Hultzsch in South Indian Inscriptions vol. II.

dates.label: early 11th century CE (reigns of Rājarāja I and Rājendra I)
dates.basis: regnal years stated in the inscriptions

location.label: Bṛhadīśvara temple, Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, India

nodes.limits: The inscriptions document royal gifts, endowments and the temple’s establishment in the early 11th century; they do not date earlier worship at Thanjavur.

nodes.name: Pūtanā
nodes.summary: Child-killing female being sent by Kaṃsa to poison the infant Kṛṣṇa with her breast-milk; he sucks out her life. The Harivaṃśa calls her a bird (śakunī) and Kaṃsa's nurse, the Bhāgavata a rākṣasī.
nodes.details: HV (CE) 50.20–24 describes Pūtanā as a terrifying bird (śakunī) who suckles the child at midnight and is struck down by him; HV 45.6 names her a daughter of Bali. ViP 5.5.7–11 has her offer the poisoned breast at night and fall dead. BhP 10.6 expands the scene (beautiful disguise, her huge corpse, its fragrant smoke on cremation) and makes her death a liberation (pūtanā-mokṣa, 10.6.44). Pūtanā is also the name of a child-afflicting female 'seizer' (graha) in medical and Purāṇic lists (e.g. BhP 10.6.27–28; Agni 298–299).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Tṛṇāvarta
nodes.summary: Whirlwind demon sent by Kaṃsa who carries the infant Kṛṣṇa into the sky and is strangled by him; the episode is found in the Bhāgavata, not in the Harivaṃśa or Viṣṇu Purāṇa.

nodes.name: Aghāsura
nodes.summary: Serpent demon, younger brother of Pūtanā and Baka in the Bhāgavata, who swallows the cowherd boys and calves; Kṛṣṇa enters his mouth and kills him by expanding.

nodes.name: Dhenuka
nodes.summary: Donkey-shaped demon guarding the palm grove (Tālavana), killed by Balarāma, who hurls him into the palm trees.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Cāṇūra
nodes.summary: Kaṃsa's champion wrestler, killed by Kṛṣṇa in the arena at Mathurā.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Muṣṭika
nodes.summary: Kaṃsa's wrestler, set against Balarāma and killed by him in the Mathurā arena.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Kuvalayāpīḍa
nodes.summary: Kaṃsa's war-elephant posted at the gate of the arena to crush Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma; Kṛṣṇa kills it and takes its tusk.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Akrūra
nodes.summary: Yādava elder, son of Śvaphalka, sent by Kaṃsa to bring Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma to Mathurā; on the way he sees them, and Viṣṇu/Śeṣa, in the waters of the Yamunā. In the Syamantaka story he keeps the jewel.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Kālayavana
nodes.summary: 'Black Yavana' king who besieges Mathurā; Kṛṣṇa lures him into the cave of the sleeping Mucukunda, whose glance burns him to ashes.
nodes.details: HV (CE) 85 and ViP 5.23 make him the son of the sage Gārgya by a Yavana queen, born to defeat the Yādavas. The ethnonym yavana (originally 'Ionian', Greek) later covers foreigners generally; no historical individual is implied.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Mucukunda
nodes.summary: Ikṣvāku king, son of Māndhātṛ, who after helping the gods sleeps in a cave with the boon that whoever wakes him will be burnt by his glance; he burns Kālayavana and then praises Kṛṣṇa.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Satrājit
nodes.summary: Yādava owner of the Syamantaka jewel (given him by the Sun in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas), father of Satyabhāmā; later killed by Śatadhanvan for the jewel.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Prasena
nodes.summary: Brother of Satrājit who wears the Syamantaka jewel while hunting and is killed by a lion.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Śatadhanvan
nodes.summary: Yādava who kills Satrājit to take the Syamantaka jewel, leaves it with Akrūra and is killed by Kṛṣṇa.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Jāmbavatī
nodes.summary: Daughter of the bear-king Jāmbavān, given to Kṛṣṇa after their fight over the Syamantaka jewel; mother of Sāmba.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Naraka (Narakāsura, Bhauma)
nodes.summary: Asura king of Prāgjyotiṣa, son of the Earth (Bhūmi), who carries off Aditi's earrings and thousands of maidens; Kṛṣṇa kills him and frees the women.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Bāṇa (Bāṇāsura)
nodes.summary: Thousand-armed asura, eldest son of Bali and devotee of Śiva, whose daughter Uṣā loves Aniruddha; in the ensuing war Kṛṣṇa cuts off all but two of his arms and Śiva intercedes for his life.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Uṣā (daughter of Bāṇa)
nodes.summary: Daughter of the asura Bāṇa who sees Aniruddha in a dream; her friend Citralekhā brings him to her by magic, which leads to the war between Kṛṣṇa and Bāṇa.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Aniruddha
nodes.summary: Son of Pradyumna and grandson of Kṛṣṇa, carried to Bāṇa's city by Citralekhā to be with Uṣā; in Pāñcarātra theology also the name of the fourth vyūha.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Citralekhā
nodes.summary: Uṣā's companion, daughter of Bāṇa's minister Kumbhāṇḍa, who paints the portraits by which Uṣā recognises Aniruddha and brings him to her.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Sudāmā (Kucela), Kṛṣṇa's brāhmaṇa friend
nodes.summary: Poor brāhmaṇa schoolfellow of Kṛṣṇa who brings him a handful of flattened rice and returns home to find himself made rich. The Bhāgavata leaves him unnamed ('a certain brāhmaṇa', 10.80.6); the names Sudāmā/Kucela belong to later tradition.
nodes.limits: The name 'Sudāmā' (and Kucela, from kucaila 'poorly clad') is not in the Bhāgavata's own narrative; it comes from later retellings and performance traditions.

nodes.name: Uddhava
nodes.summary: Yādava counsellor and friend of Kṛṣṇa who carries his message to the gopīs and, before the destruction of the Yādavas, receives his final teaching (the Uddhava Gītā, BhP 11).

nodes.name: Nalakūbara and Maṇigrīva
nodes.summary: Sons of Kubera cursed by Nārada to stand as twin arjuna trees (yamalārjuna) until the child Kṛṣṇa, dragging the mortar to which he is tied, uproots them (Bhāgavata).
nodes.details: In HV (CE) 51 and ViP 5.6.16–20 the twin trees are simply trees; the Bhāgavata adds their identity as Kubera's sons and Nārada's curse.

nodes.name: The gopīs (cowherd women of Vraja)
nodes.summary: The cowherd women of Vraja who love Kṛṣṇa; their nocturnal dance with him (the rāsa) and their longing in separation are central to Bhāgavata devotion.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Tālavana (the palm grove)
nodes.summary: Palm grove near Vṛndāvana guarded by the donkey-demon Dhenuka (narrative place).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Prāgjyotiṣa (Naraka's city)
nodes.summary: City of the asura Naraka in the epic and Purāṇic stories; identified by tradition and by early medieval inscriptions with Kāmarūpa in Assam.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.limits: The narrative city is not thereby located; its identification with Kāmarūpa/Guwahati is traditional and dynastic (the Varman kings of Kāmarūpa claimed descent from Naraka).

nodes.name: Śoṇitapura (Bāṇa's city)
nodes.summary: City of the asura Bāṇa where Aniruddha is held captive; later local tradition identifies it with Tezpur in Assam.
nodes.limits: Identification with Tezpur is local tradition; the text's city is not located by it.

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa and Pūtanā
nodes.summary: The infant Kṛṣṇa sucks the life out of Pūtanā, who has come to poison him with her breast. The Harivaṃśa makes her a bird and places the episode after the overturning of the cart; the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas tell it first.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: The overturning of the cart (Śakaṭa)
nodes.summary: The infant Kṛṣṇa, lying under a cart, kicks it over with his foot. In the Harivaṃśa and Viṣṇu Purāṇa it is simply a cart; the Bhāgavata summary lists it with the demons and later tradition names a cart-demon, Śakaṭāsura.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Tṛṇāvarta, the whirlwind demon
nodes.summary: Sent by Kaṃsa, the whirlwind demon Tṛṇāvarta carries the infant Kṛṣṇa into the sky; Kṛṣṇa grows heavy, seizes his throat and kills him. A Bhāgavata addition, absent from the Harivaṃśa and Viṣṇu Purāṇa.

nodes.name: The butter thief bound to the mortar (Dāmodara) and the twin arjuna trees
nodes.summary: Yaśodā ties the mischievous child Kṛṣṇa to a mortar by a rope round his belly (hence Dāmodara, 'rope-belly'); dragging it, he uproots two arjuna trees. The Bhāgavata frames this with his butter-stealing and makes the trees Kubera's cursed sons.
nodes.details: HV (CE) 51.14–36 explains the name: 'with the rope by which he was bound at the belly in the cattle-station, he is sung by the gopīs as Dāmodara' (51.36). ViP 5.6.14–20 gives the same etymology (5.6.20). BhP 10.8.29 describes him stealing curds and milk 'by thieving devices' (steya-yogaiḥ); 10.9 tells the binding, in which the rope is always two fingers too short until he consents to be bound; 10.10 the liberation of Nalakūbara and Maṇigrīva. The butter-thief (navanīta-cora/mākhan-cor) motif becomes central in later vernacular poetry (Hawley 1983).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa kills Aghāsura
nodes.summary: The serpent-demon Agha opens his mouth like a cave; the cowherd boys and calves walk in, and Kṛṣṇa enters, swells within his throat and kills him, restoring the boys. Bhāgavata only.

nodes.name: Brahmā steals the calves and cowherd boys
nodes.summary: To test Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā hides the calves and cowherd boys for a year; Kṛṣṇa becomes all of them, and Brahmā, seeing every one as four-armed Viṣṇu, praises him (BhP 10.14). Bhāgavata only.

nodes.name: Balarāma kills Dhenuka in the palm grove
nodes.summary: When the boys want the palm fruit of the Tālavana, the donkey-demon Dhenuka attacks Balarāma, who seizes him by the hind legs and dashes him against the palm trees; his kin are also killed.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa takes the gopīs' garments
nodes.summary: Unmarried gopīs keep a month-long vow to Kātyāyanī to win Kṛṣṇa as husband; when they bathe naked in the Yamunā he takes their clothes up a tree and returns them when they come out with joined hands, promising to fulfil their wish. Bhāgavata only.

nodes.name: The rāsa dance (rāsa-līlā)
nodes.summary: On autumn nights Kṛṣṇa sports and dances with the cowherd women of Vraja. The Harivaṃśa gives a short erotic description; the Viṣṇu Purāṇa adds his disappearance, the gopīs' search by his footprints and the circular rāsa dance; the Bhāgavata expands it into five chapters (the rāsa-pañcādhyāyī) with the flute, the 'Gopī-gīta' and Kṛṣṇa multiplied between each pair of women.
nodes.details: Constituted text of HV (CE) 63.15–35 has no disappearance and no explicit rāsa: the girls, 'in rows' and 'in pairs', sing his deeds and imitate him; he is 'adorned with circles (cakravāla) of gopīs' on autumn nights (63.25, 63.35). ViP 5.13.14–62: Kṛṣṇa's song draws the gopīs; he vanishes; they imitate his deeds and trace his footprints and those of a favoured companion (5.13.31–40); he returns and forms the rāsa-maṇḍala holding each gopī by the hand (5.13.47–55). BhP 10.29–33: the flute (10.29), the disappearance (10.29.48), searching and the footprints of a favoured gopī (10.30.24–31), the Gopī-gīta (10.31), the reunion (10.32), and the dance in which Kṛṣṇa stands between every two gopīs (10.33.3), followed by Parīkṣit's question on its propriety (10.33.26–37).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.limits: The narrative is literary-theological; its later identification with particular sites in Vrindavan is traditional.

nodes.name: Akrūra's journey to Vraja and the vision in the Yamunā
nodes.summary: Kaṃsa sends Akrūra to fetch Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma to Mathurā. Akrūra goes rejoicing, takes them amid the gopīs' grief, and while bathing in the Yamunā sees the two of them — and Viṣṇu on Śeṣa — within the water.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Kālayavana and Mucukunda
nodes.summary: Besieged by Jarāsandha and by the invincible Kālayavana, Kṛṣṇa moves the Yādavas to Dvārakā and lures Kālayavana into a cave where King Mucukunda sleeps; woken by a kick, Mucukunda burns Kālayavana with his glance and recognises Kṛṣṇa.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: The Syamantaka jewel
nodes.summary: A wonder-working jewel passes from Satrājit (or Prasena) to Prasena, who is killed by a lion; the bear-king Jāmbavān kills the lion. Suspected of theft, Kṛṣṇa tracks it to Jāmbavān's cave, fights him, receives the jewel and Jāmbavatī, and returns it; later Śatadhanvan kills Satrājit and the jewel ends with Akrūra.
nodes.details: The Harivaṃśa and Viṣṇu Purāṇa tell it within the genealogy of the Vṛṣṇis (HV Harivaṃśaparvan 28–29; ViP book 4, in prose); the Bhāgavata moves it into the Kṛṣṇa book. On where the jewel came from and how long Kṛṣṇa fought Jāmbavān, the versions differ (see the comparison table). ViP 4.13.57 and BhP 10.57.42 promise that whoever remembers the story is freed from false accusation.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa kills Naraka (Narakāsura)
nodes.summary: Indra complains that Naraka, son of the Earth and lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, has taken Aditi's earrings and thousands of maidens. Kṛṣṇa, riding Garuḍa with Satyabhāmā, kills Muru and Naraka, returns the earrings and marries the freed women.
nodes.details: ViP 5.29.31 and BhP 10.59.33 number the captive women at 16,100 (ViP) / 16,000 (BhP); Bhūmi (the Earth) intercedes for Naraka's son. Tradition in western and southern India connects the slaying with Naraka Caturdaśī, the day before (or the first day of) Dīpāvalī; that link is festival tradition, not part of these Purāṇic narratives (see claim:naraka-dipavali-link).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa's killing of Naraka is commemorated on Naraka Caturdaśī / Dīpāvalī
nodes.summary: In much of western and southern India the day before (or the first day of) Dīpāvalī is Naraka Caturdaśī, observed as the day Kṛṣṇa (or Satyabhāmā) killed Naraka. The Purāṇic narratives of the slaying do not themselves found the festival; the association is festival tradition with late textual support.
nodes.details: The Viṣṇu Purāṇa (5.29) and Bhāgavata (10.59) give no festival rubric. Other regional explanations of Dīpāvalī (Rāma's return, Bali's annual visit, Lakṣmī worship) coexist; Kane surveys the medieval nibandha sources for the rites of the day.

sources.locator: vol. V, part 1: Dīpāvalī and Narakacaturdaśī

nodes.limits: Establishes a living traditional association, not a Purāṇic origin for the festival.

nodes.name: Uṣā, Aniruddha and the war with Bāṇa
nodes.summary: Bāṇa's daughter Uṣā dreams of a lover; her friend Citralekhā identifies him as Aniruddha and carries him off from Dvārakā. Bāṇa imprisons him; Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and Pradyumna attack Śoṇitapura, defeat Śiva's fever and Śiva himself, and cut off Bāṇa's arms until Śiva intercedes.
nodes.details: A rare narrative in which Kṛṣṇa (Viṣṇu) fights Śiva; ViP 5.33 and BhP 10.63 end with Śiva's praise of Kṛṣṇa and the sparing of Bāṇa with four (BhP 10.63.49) or two arms. The Harivaṃśa's account (106–113) is the longest; temple tradition at Angkor depicts Kṛṣṇa's victory over Bāṇa.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa's poor brāhmaṇa friend (Sudāmā/Kucela) and the flattened rice
nodes.summary: A destitute brāhmaṇa, Kṛṣṇa's schoolfellow, visits him in Dvārakā with a handful of flattened rice; Kṛṣṇa eats it with delight and the friend returns to find his hut a palace. Bhāgavata only.

nodes.name: Uddhava Gītā (Haṃsa Gītā), Bhāgavata Purāṇa book 11
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa's last and longest teaching, given to Uddhava before the destruction of the Yādavas (BhP 11.6–29): renunciation, the avadhūta's twenty-four teachers, bhakti-yoga, the guṇas and the Haṃsa teaching.
nodes.details: Uddhava asks to be taken along when Kṛṣṇa leaves the world (11.6.43–49); the teaching runs from 11.7 to 11.29, after which Kṛṣṇa sends him to Badarikāśrama (11.29.41). It includes the story of the avadhūta and his twenty-four gurus (11.7–9) and the Bhikṣu Gītā (11.23). Scholars treat it, with book 10, as part of the Bhāgavata's Advaitic-devotional synthesis (Bryant 2003; Rocher 1986).

dates.label: c. 9th–10th c. CE (with the Bhāgavata)
dates.basis: dated with the whole Bhāgavata; no separate date

nodes.name: Tārakākṣa

nodes.name: Śiva burns the three cities (Tripura)
nodes.summary: Three asura brothers obtain three flying cities of gold, silver and iron, built by Maya, that can be destroyed only when they align, by a single arrow. The gods build Śiva a chariot of the cosmos; with Viṣṇu as (part of) the arrow he burns the cities in one shot. Later versions add Viṣṇu's subversion of the asuras' piety and his drinking of their reviving nectar.
nodes.details: The oldest full narrative is in the Karṇaparvan, where Duryodhana tells it to persuade Śalya to be Karṇa's charioteer, as Brahmā was Śiva's (MBh CE 8.24). The Purāṇic versions elaborate in different directions: the Matsya (129–140) makes Maya the hero of a long war; the Liṅga (1.71–72) and Śiva (2.5.1–12) say Viṣṇu first destroyed the asuras' dharma — in the Śiva Purāṇa by creating a shaven-headed teacher of a 'Jina' doctrine (2.5.4–5); the Bhāgavata (7.10.53–70) and Matsya (136.63–65) make Viṣṇu drink the nectar pond that revived the dead asuras (as a cow in BhP, as a bull in Matsya).

nodes.name: Bhṛṅgin (Bhṛṅgi)
nodes.summary: Emaciated, three-legged gaṇa and devotee of Śiva; in the Vāmana and other Purāṇas the asura Andhaka, impaled on Śiva's trident and purified, becomes Bhṛṅgin.

nodes.name: Śiva subdues Andhaka
nodes.summary: Andhaka, a blind son born to Śiva and Pārvatī (from her sweat when she covers Śiva's eyes, in the Śiva Purāṇa) and adopted by the asura Hiraṇyākṣa, grows into a tyrant who desires Pārvatī. Śiva impales him on his trident; purified, he praises Śiva and becomes a gaṇa (Bhṛṅgin).

nodes.name: Jalandhara
nodes.summary: Asura born from the ocean (from the fire of Śiva's third eye, in the Śiva Purāṇa) who conquers the gods and covets Pārvatī; Śiva kills him with a discus drawn with his toe in the water.

nodes.name: Vṛndā (wife of Jalandhara)
nodes.summary: Chaste wife of Jalandhara, daughter of Kālanemi, whose fidelity protects her husband; Viṣṇu deceives her by taking Jalandhara's form, she curses him and enters the fire. Later tradition links her with the tulasī plant.

nodes.limits: The Śiva Purāṇa tells a separate Tulasī story (wife of Śaṅkhacūḍa, 2.5.28–41); the identification of Vṛndā with Tulasī belongs to other texts and to practice (Tulasī-vivāha).

nodes.name: Śiva kills Jalandhara
nodes.summary: The ocean-born asura Jalandhara defeats the gods and even Viṣṇu, then demands Pārvatī. While Viṣṇu breaks the chastity of his wife Vṛndā by impersonating Jalandhara, Śiva kills him with the discus Sudarśana, which he draws in the water with his toe; in the Liṅga Purāṇa Viṣṇu later obtains that discus from Śiva by worshipping him with a thousand names.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay 1906), rev. O. Hellwig after Calcutta 1960; GRETIL e-text

nodes.name: Śaṅkhacūḍa
nodes.summary: Dānava son of Dambha, protected by an amulet of Viṣṇu and by his wife Tulasī's chastity; Śiva kills him after Viṣṇu, disguised, obtains the amulet and violates Tulasī's vow.

sources.edition: Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

nodes.name: Tulasī (wife of Śaṅkhacūḍa)
nodes.summary: Wife of the dānava Śaṅkhacūḍa who, deceived by Viṣṇu in her husband's form, curses him to become a stone (the śālagrāma) and herself becomes the Gaṇḍakī river and the tulasī plant (Śiva Purāṇa).
nodes.details: The Śiva Purāṇa (Rudrasaṃhitā 2.5.27–41) and the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa (Prakṛtikhaṇḍa) tell the story; it underlies the ritual marriage of the tulasī plant with Viṣṇu as śālagrāma (Tulasī-vivāha) on Prabodhinī Ekādaśī.

sources.edition: Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

nodes.limits: The Brahmavaivarta locus was not checked; the festival link is tradition.

nodes.name: Śaṅkhacūḍa, Tulasī and the origin of the śālagrāma
nodes.summary: The dānava Śaṅkhacūḍa, invincible while he wears Viṣṇu's amulet and his wife Tulasī remains chaste, is killed by Śiva after Viṣṇu, disguised, takes the amulet and Tulasī's chastity. Tulasī curses Viṣṇu to become stone; she becomes the Gaṇḍakī river, whose stones are the śālagrāmas.

sources.edition: Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

nodes.name: Gajāsura (son of Mahiṣa)
nodes.summary: Elephant-asura, son of Mahiṣāsura, whom Śiva kills at Kāśī and whose hide he wears (hence Kṛttivāsas); the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga marks the spot.

sources.edition: Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

nodes.name: Śiva kills Gajāsura and wears his hide (Kṛttivāsas)
nodes.summary: Śiva kills the elephant-asura Gajāsura, son of Mahiṣa, at Kāśī, wears his hide and establishes the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga there.

nodes.summary: Sent by Indra to make the ascetic Śiva fall in love with Pārvatī (so that a son can be born to kill Tāraka), Kāma shoots his flower-arrow; Śiva's third eye blazes and reduces him to ashes. Rati laments; Kāma lives on bodiless (Anaṅga) and is later restored.

nodes.name: Menā (wife of Himavat)
nodes.summary: Wife of the mountain-king Himavat and mother of Pārvatī; the Śiva Purāṇa makes her a mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs and dwells on her horror at Śiva's appearance as bridegroom.

sources.edition: Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

nodes.limits: Distinct from the apsaras Menakā (char:menaka), Śakuntalā's mother, though some texts use the same name.

nodes.name: Pārvatī's austerities and her marriage to Śiva
nodes.summary: After Kāma is burnt, Pārvatī wins Śiva by fierce austerities; Śiva, disguised as a brahmacārin, tests her resolve by reviling himself, then reveals himself. The Seven Sages negotiate with Himavat and the wedding is celebrated in the mountain's palace.
nodes.details: The Matsya (154) and the Śiva Purāṇa (Pārvatīkhaṇḍa 2.3.22–54) give full versions; Kālidāsa's Kumārasambhava (cantos 5–7) is the classic kāvya. The sequel — the birth of Skanda to kill Tāraka — is narr:birth-of-skanda.

nodes.name: The origin of Ardhanārīśvara (Śiva as half-woman)
nodes.summary: Two Purāṇic patterns: Rudra is born from Brahmā's anger with a body half male and half female and is told to divide himself (Viṣṇu, Mārkaṇḍeya, Kūrma); or Śiva appears to Brahmā, who cannot make creation multiply, as the androgynous Ardhanārīśvara and separates the Goddess from his body so that sexual creation can begin (Śiva Purāṇa, Liṅga).

nodes.name: Śiva drinks the poison of the churning (Nīlakaṇṭha)
nodes.summary: The deadly poison (hālāhala/kālakūṭa) that rises first from the churned ocean threatens the worlds; at the gods' plea Śiva drinks it and holds it in his throat, which turns blue. The episode is absent from the constituted texts of both epic critical editions.
nodes.details: In the Mahābhārata critical edition the poison and Śiva's blue throat appear only in passages relegated to the apparatus (App. I after 1.16.15 and 1.16.27; star passages *268 and *274), i.e. in some manuscripts but not the constituted text; Vālmīki's critical text (1.44) also lacks it. In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (1.9.95) the nāgas take the poison. The Bhāgavata (8.7.19–46) and Brahmāṇḍa (1.25) tell the full story.

nodes.summary: Every drop of the asura Raktabīja's blood produces a new Raktabīja; the Mothers (Mātṛkās) — the śaktis of Brahmā, Śiva, Skanda, Viṣṇu, Varāha, Narasiṃha and Indra — join the fight, and Kālī/Cāmuṇḍā drinks his blood so that Caṇḍikā can kill him (Devī Māhātmya 8).

nodes.name: Śivadūtī
nodes.summary: Fierce form of the Goddess in Devī Māhātmya 8 who sends Śiva as her messenger to the asuras and is therefore called Śivadūtī.
