nodes.name: Gaṇeśa's birth from Pārvatī and his beheading by Śiva (Śiva Purāṇa)
nodes.summary: Wanting a door-keeper loyal only to her, Pārvatī fashions a son from the dirt of her body; he bars Śiva from her bath, defeats Śiva's gaṇas and the gods, and Śiva cuts off his head with his trident. To appease the furious Goddess and her Mothers, the gods fit him with an elephant's head, revive him and make him lord of the gaṇas, to be worshipped first.
nodes.details: The Śiva Purāṇa itself notes that 'because of differences between kalpas' Gaṇeśa's birth is told otherwise — 'his head, cut off by Śani's glance, was joined to an elephant's' — and announces the Śvetakalpa version (2.4.13.5–6). Gaṇeśa is born on the fourth of the dark half of Bhādrapada (2.4.18.35–37), the basis given for his vrata.

sources.edition: Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

nodes.name: Śani's glance beheads the infant Gaṇeśa (Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa)
nodes.summary: Śani (Saturn), whose glance destroys, reluctantly looks at Pārvatī's newborn son at her insistence; the child's head falls off. Viṣṇu flies on Garuḍa, cuts the head from a sleeping elephant with his discus and joins it to the child.
nodes.details: Gaṇapatikhaṇḍa 11 explains Śani's downcast gaze; ch. 12 tells the beheading (12.5–6) and the elephant head brought by Viṣṇu (12.11–18); Pārvatī curses Śani to limp (12.57). The Śiva Purāṇa knows this version and attributes the difference to another kalpa (ŚivP 2.4.13.5).

sources.edition: Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa (vulgate), Gaṇapatikhaṇḍa; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

nodes.name: Pārvatī's elephant-headed child from bath-unguent (Matsya Purāṇa)
nodes.summary: Pārvatī shapes a figure with an elephant's head from the unguent rubbed off her body and throws it into the Gaṅgā; it grows huge, the Gaṅgā calls him her son, and the gods worship him as Gāṅgeya, while Brahmā gives him lordship over the Vināyakas.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

nodes.name: Śiva becomes the elephant-faced obstacle-maker at the gods' request (Liṅga Purāṇa)
nodes.summary: Because the asuras prosper through their rites, the gods ask Śiva for a maker of obstacles; Śiva himself takes the form of the elephant-faced Gaṇeśvara, born from Ambikā, and is charged to obstruct the dharma of the daityas and protect the devout.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay 1906), rev. O. Hellwig after Calcutta 1960; GRETIL e-text

nodes.name: Gaṇeśa born from Śiva's laughter and cursed with an elephant head (Varāha Purāṇa)
nodes.summary: When the gods ask Śiva for a remover of obstacles to the wicked, a radiant youth springs from Śiva's laughter; when Umā gazes at his beauty, the angry Śiva curses him to have an elephant's face and a pot belly — and from Śiva's sweat many elephant-headed Vināyakas arise.

nodes.name: Siddhi (consort of Gaṇeśa)
nodes.summary: With Buddhi, one of the two daughters of Prajāpati Viśvarūpa married to Gaṇeśa in the Śiva Purāṇa; personifies accomplishment.

sources.edition: Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

nodes.name: Buddhi (consort of Gaṇeśa)
nodes.summary: With Siddhi, Gaṇeśa's wife in the Śiva Purāṇa; personifies intelligence. Their sons are Kṣema and Lābha.

sources.edition: Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

nodes.name: Gaṇeśa and Skanda race around the world
nodes.summary: Śiva and Pārvatī promise to marry first whichever son circles the earth first. Skanda sets off; Gaṇeśa bathes, seats his parents, worships and circumambulates them seven times, declaring that this equals circling the earth. He is married to Siddhi and Buddhi; Skanda returns, feels cheated and withdraws to Mount Krauñca.
nodes.details: Popular versions make the prize a fruit (mango) — notably in the Tamil Palani tradition of Murukaṉ — rather than precedence in marriage; the Śiva Purāṇa version is about marriage.

sources.edition: Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

nodes.limits: The fruit version is regional tradition and is not attested here.

nodes.name: Gaṇeśa writes down the Mahābhārata at Vyāsa's dictation
nodes.summary: In the frame found in many manuscripts and the vulgate (Bombay ed. 1.1.75–79), Brahmā advises Vyāsa to take Gaṇeśa as scribe; Gaṇeśa agrees on condition that the dictation never pauses, and Vyāsa composes knotty verses to gain time. The critical edition excludes the passage from the constituted text.
nodes.details: The CE (Sukthankar, Ādiparvan 1933) prints the Gaṇeśa passage only in its critical notes/appendix (vol. 1 part 2, p. 884); Krishan reports it in 37 of the 59 Ādiparvan manuscripts collated. Winternitz (1898) had already argued it was an interpolation. A check of the constituted text of MBh (CE) book 1 on GRETIL finds no Gaṇeśa/Vināyaka at all.
nodes.limits: The interpolation verdict concerns the passage's manuscript support; the frame is popular and widely illustrated, and some manuscripts carry it.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The Gaṇeśa-as-scribe frame is a late interpolation in the Mahābhārata
nodes.summary: The story of Gaṇeśa writing the Mahābhārata at Vyāsa's dictation is absent from the constituted text of the Critical Edition and is regarded as a late insertion, though it occurs in a majority of the Ādiparvan manuscripts collated.
nodes.details: Verified online: the GRETIL text of MBh (CE) book 1, including its star passages, contains no gaṇeśa/vināyaka in this role; the CE's own placement of the passage (critical notes, vol. 1 pt 2 p. 884) is known from Rocher and Krishan via a reference pointer.

nodes.name: Mohinī distributes the nectar
nodes.summary: When the asuras seize the nectar produced by the churning, Viṣṇu takes the form of an enchanting woman; the infatuated asuras let her divide it, and she gives it all to the gods. Rāhu, disguised among the gods, is beheaded by the discus.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Śiva and Mohinī
nodes.summary: Śiva asks Viṣṇu to show him the enchantress form; seeing Mohinī playing with a ball he loses his composure and pursues her, his seed falling to earth where it becomes gold and silver; Viṣṇu then praises Śiva's mastery of māyā (Bhāgavata).
nodes.details: Śaiva and South Indian traditions develop the union further into the birth of Śāstā/Ayyappan (Hariharaputra), a motif not in the Bhāgavata chapter.

nodes.name: How Viṣṇu came to have a horse's head (Hayagrīva)
nodes.summary: Versions differ: the Nārāyaṇīya has Viṣṇu assume the horse-headed form to recover the Vedas stolen by Madhu and Kaiṭabha; the Devī Bhāgavata says that a termite, sent by the gods, gnawed the bowstring on which the sleeping Viṣṇu rested his head, the string snapped and beheaded him, and a horse's head was fitted so he could kill the horse-headed demon Hayagrīva.

sources.edition: Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa (vulgate); Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Anasūyā
nodes.summary: Wife of the sage Atri, proverbial for chastity, mother of Dattātreya, Durvāsas and Soma, born of portions of Viṣṇu, Śiva and Brahmā (Bhāgavata).

sources.quote: atreḥ patny anasūyā trīñ jajñe suyaśasaḥ sutān

nodes.name: The birth of Dattātreya, Durvāsas and Soma to Atri and Anasūyā
nodes.summary: Atri performs austerities for a son like the Lord of the world; Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva appear together and are born as his sons by Anasūyā — Soma from Brahmā's portion, Datta from Viṣṇu's, Durvāsas from Śiva's (Bhāgavata).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition

nodes.name: Kardama
nodes.summary: Prajāpati who marries Devahūti, daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu; their son is Kapila (Bhāgavata).

nodes.name: Devahūti
nodes.summary: Daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu, wife of Kardama and mother of Kapila, to whom Kapila teaches devotional Sāṃkhya (Bhāgavata 3.25–33).

nodes.name: Kapila teaches his mother Devahūti
nodes.summary: Born to Kardama and Devahūti, Kapila — counted an avatāra — teaches his mother a devotional (bhakti-oriented) Sāṃkhya and yoga, and she attains liberation (Bhāgavata 3.24–33).

nodes.name: Nābhi
nodes.summary: King of Ajanābha/Himavarṣa, grandson of Priyavrata, husband of Merudevī and father of Ṛṣabha in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas (and in Jain tradition, the last kulakara and father of Ṛṣabha).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Bharata (son of Ṛṣabha; Jaḍa Bharata)
nodes.summary: Eldest son of Ṛṣabha after whom, in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas, Bhāratavarṣa is named; he renounces the throne, is reborn as a deer through attachment to a fawn, and then as the outwardly dull (jaḍa) brāhmaṇa who teaches King Rahūgaṇa.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.limits: Distinct from Bharata son of Śakuntalā (char:bharata-dauhshanti), whom the Mahābhārata makes the eponym of the Bhāratas; the texts give competing eponyms.

nodes.name: Ṛṣabhanātha (first Jain tīrthaṅkara)
nodes.summary: In Jain tradition, Ṛṣabha (Ādinātha), the first of the twenty-four tīrthaṅkaras of the present age, son of the kulakara Nābhi and Marudevī, who teaches humanity the arts and renounces kingship.
nodes.limits: Kept separate from the Bhāgavata's Ṛṣabha: the shared names (Nābhi, Marudevī/Merudevī, Bharata) are textual parallels, not an identity the Jain sources accept.

nodes.name: Ṛṣabha's rule and renunciation (Bhāgavata Purāṇa)
nodes.summary: Ṛṣabha, son of Nābhi and Merudevī and a descent of Viṣṇu, rules Ajanābha, gives the kingdom to Bharata, and wanders as a naked avadhūta until his body burns in a forest fire; the Bhāgavata adds that a king of Koṅka-Veṅka-Kuṭaka, Arhat, hearing of him, will spread a heterodox path in the Kali age.
nodes.details: BhP 5.6.9 is commonly read as an allusion to Jainism (the Arhat of Koṅka-Veṅka-Kuṭaka in southern Karnataka); Jaini and Dundas discuss the Hindu appropriation of Ṛṣabha. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa gives only the genealogy and Bharata's accession.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Bharata reborn as a deer and as Jaḍa Bharata
nodes.summary: King Bharata retires to the forest, becomes attached to an orphaned fawn and is reborn a deer; reborn again as a brāhmaṇa he feigns dullness, is pressed into carrying King Rahūgaṇa's palanquin, and teaches the king non-dual knowledge.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Vena
nodes.summary: Wicked king, son of Aṅga, who forbids sacrifice and is killed by the sages; from his churned body come the Niṣāda and then Pṛthu (Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Bhūmi (the Earth, Pṛthivī)
nodes.summary: The Earth personified as a goddess, who flees from Pṛthu as a cow and yields her milk when he makes Manu the calf; also the mother of Naraka and, in Vaiṣṇava theology, a consort of Viṣṇu (Bhūdevī).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Pṛthu milks the Earth
nodes.summary: Born from the churned arm of the dead king Vena, Pṛthu finds the earth withholding her produce; she flees as a cow, he pursues her with his bow, and she agrees to give milk if a calf is provided. With Svāyambhuva Manu as calf he milks out the crops; other beings milk her with their own calves and vessels. The earth is named Pṛthivī after him.
nodes.details: The milking motif goes back to the Atharvaveda (Virāj milked by various beings, AV 8.10) and is told in the Mahābhārata's Ṣoḍaśarājika; the Purāṇic accounts attach it to the first consecrated king.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Ajāmila
nodes.summary: Fallen brāhmaṇa of Kānyakubja who, dying, calls out to his son named Nārāyaṇa; Viṣṇu's messengers rescue him from Yama's, demonstrating the power of the divine name (Bhāgavata 6.1–2).

nodes.name: Ajāmila saved by the name 'Nārāyaṇa'
nodes.summary: Ajāmila, a brāhmaṇa who has abandoned his duties for a slave-woman, calls out his youngest son's name 'Nārāyaṇa' at death; Viṣṇu's attendants stop Yama's messengers, arguing that even an inadvertent utterance of the name removes sin. Ajāmila repents and attains Vaikuṇṭha.

nodes.name: Ambarīṣa (son of Nābhāga)
nodes.summary: Ikṣvāku king and devotee of Viṣṇu; when Durvāsas, offended that Ambarīṣa broke his Dvādaśī fast before the sage's return, sends a demon against him, Viṣṇu's discus Sudarśana pursues Durvāsas through the worlds until he begs the king's pardon (Bhāgavata 9.4–5).

nodes.name: Ambarīṣa, Durvāsas and the discus
nodes.summary: At the end of his Dvādaśī vow King Ambarīṣa sips water before the delayed sage Durvāsas returns; the angry sage creates a fiery being to kill him; Viṣṇu's discus destroys it and chases Durvāsas through the three worlds, until Viṣṇu tells him to seek the forgiveness of his devotee.

nodes.name: Jaya and Vijaya (Viṣṇu's door-keepers)
nodes.summary: Twin door-keepers of Vaikuṇṭha who bar the child-sages Sanaka and his brothers and are cursed to three demonic births — as Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa, Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa, and Śiśupāla and Dantavakra — each time slain by Viṣṇu (Bhāgavata).

nodes.name: The four Kumāras (Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra)
nodes.summary: Mind-born sons of Brahmā who remain eternal children and celibate sages; in the Bhāgavata they curse Jaya and Vijaya and are counted the first descent of Viṣṇu (BhP 1.3.6).

nodes.name: Dantavakra
nodes.summary: King of Karūṣa, ally of Śiśupāla and enemy of Kṛṣṇa, who kills him; the Bhāgavata makes him and Śiśupāla the third birth of Jaya and Vijaya.

nodes.name: The curse of Jaya and Vijaya
nodes.summary: Sanaka and his brothers, appearing as naked boys, are stopped at the gate of Vaikuṇṭha by Jaya and Vijaya; they curse the door-keepers to be born as asuras. Viṣṇu accepts the curse but promises their return: after three births as his enemies, each ended by him, they rejoin him.

nodes.name: Triśaṅku's heaven
nodes.summary: King Satyavrata (Triśaṅku), wanting to ascend to heaven in his body, is refused by Vasiṣṭha and cursed into a caṇḍāla by Vasiṣṭha's sons; Viśvāmitra, whose family Triśaṅku had fed in a famine (Harivaṃśa), sends him up by his own power; thrown down by Indra, he is held head-down in a new heaven Viśvāmitra creates.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Viśvāmitra tries to seize Vasiṣṭha's cow
nodes.summary: King Viśvāmitra, hosted by Vasiṣṭha from his wish-granting cow, tries to take her; she produces armies that crush his forces, and Vasiṣṭha's brahmanic power defeats his weapons. Humiliated, Viśvāmitra undertakes austerities to become a brahmarṣi — the origin of a lasting feud.
nodes.details: Vālmīki (1.51–64) uses the feud as Viśvāmitra's biography; the Mahābhārata (1.164–165) frames it within the Kalmāṣapāda and Vasiṣṭha stories. Their rivalry continues in the Hariścandra story and the āḍi–baka battle of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (7–9). In the Ṛgveda both are poets of Sudās (RV 3.53; 7.33).

nodes.name: The battle of Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra as two birds (āḍi and baka)
nodes.summary: Enraged that Viśvāmitra has ruined Hariścandra and killed his sons, Vasiṣṭha curses him to become a baka (heron); Viśvāmitra curses Vasiṣṭha to become an āḍi bird; their fight shakes the worlds until Brahmā restores and reconciles them (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 9).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition

nodes.name: Śaibyā (wife of Hariścandra)
nodes.summary: Queen of Hariścandra, sold into servitude with her son Rohitāśva when the king keeps his word to Viśvāmitra (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition

nodes.name: Hariścandra's ordeal of truth
nodes.summary: To keep a promise to Viśvāmitra, King Hariścandra gives up his kingdom, sells his wife Śaibyā and son Rohitāśva and himself becomes the servant of a caṇḍāla at the cremation ground; when his wife brings their dead son there, the gods (Dharma, Indra) reveal the test and restore them.
nodes.details: The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (7–8) is the classic Sanskrit telling; the Devī Bhāgavata (7.18–27) retells it. The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa's older Hariścandra is the king who vows his son to Varuṇa (narr:shunahshepa); the Bhāgavata (9.7.7–23) tells that version.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition

nodes.name: Holikā and Prahlāda
nodes.summary: In the legend told for Holī, Holikā, sister of Hiraṇyakaśipu and immune to fire, sits in a pyre with the child Prahlāda to burn him; she burns and he survives. The Nārada Purāṇa's festival rubric names Holikā 'a rākṣasī who frightened Prahlāda', burned in the Phālguna full-moon bonfire — or, 'in another opinion', the burning of Kāma.
nodes.limits: The pyre-and-immunity plot is popular tradition; the checked Sanskrit Purāṇic passage gives only the identification of Holikā as a rākṣasī hostile to Prahlāda, inside a festival rite. The Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas' Prahlāda narratives do not contain Holikā.

nodes.name: Bhūmaṇḍala (the earth-disc of seven continents)
nodes.summary: In Purāṇic cosmography the flat, circular earth: seven ring-shaped continents (dvīpas), each twice the size of the last, separated by seven oceans, with Mount Meru at the centre of Jambudvīpa and the Lokāloka mountain at the rim.
nodes.details: The Viṣṇu (2.2–4), Bhāgavata (5.16–20) and Matsya (113–123) give the system with different orders of continents and oceans (see cmp:dvipa-lists). Gombrich (1975) and Kirfel (1920) treat the Purāṇic and parallel Jain and Buddhist cosmographies comparatively.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.limits: A place in Purāṇic cosmography, not a geographical location; it has no coordinates, and its dimensions are those the texts state within their own system.

nodes.name: Jambudvīpa
nodes.summary: One of the seven continents (dvīpas) of Purāṇic cosmography: the central, innermost continent, named after its giant jambū (rose-apple) tree, with Meru at its centre; Bhāratavarṣa is its southern division.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Plakṣadvīpa
nodes.summary: One of the seven continents (dvīpas) of Purāṇic cosmography: the second continent in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata lists, named after its plakṣa (fig) tree; absent from the Matsya list.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Śākadvīpa
nodes.summary: One of the seven continents (dvīpas) of Purāṇic cosmography: continent named after its śāka (teak) tree, whose inhabitants worship Viṣṇu in the form of the Sun (ViP 2.4.70); later tradition derives the Śākadvīpīya (Maga) brāhmaṇa sun-priests from it; second in the Matsya list.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Puṣkaradvīpa
nodes.summary: One of the seven continents (dvīpas) of Purāṇic cosmography: the outermost continent, divided by the ring-mountain Mānasottara and named after its great lotus (puṣkara), Brahmā's seat.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.summary: In the Matsya Purāṇa's cosmography, the sixth continent (named after Mount Gomeda), which takes the place of Plakṣadvīpa in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata lists.

nodes.name: Mount Meru (Sumeru)
nodes.summary: The golden cosmic mountain at the centre of Jambudvīpa and of the earth-disc, around which the sun and stars revolve; the Viṣṇu Purāṇa gives it a height of 84,000 yojanas above ground and 16,000 below, 32,000 wide at the top and 16,000 at the base, like the pericarp of the earth-lotus.
nodes.details: Four buttress mountains stand around it — Mandara (east), Gandhamādana (south), Vipula (west) and Supārśva (north) — each bearing a giant tree (ViP 2.2.17–18). The Ilāvṛta varṣa surrounds it. Meru is shared with Buddhist and Jain cosmologies, and temple architecture (the śikhara; Angkor's central towers) is often read as its image.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Bhāratavarṣa
nodes.summary: One of the nine varṣas (regions) of Jambudvīpa: the southern varṣa of Jambudvīpa, 'north of the ocean and south of the Himālaya, where the descendants of Bharata live' (ViP 2.3.1), the only 'land of action' (karmabhūmi); the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas name it after Bharata son of Ṛṣabha, the Mahābhārata's genealogy after Bharata son of Śakuntalā.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Kiṃpuruṣavarṣa

nodes.details: The Nārada Purāṇa (1.83) describes Rādhā as dwelling eternally in Goloka; the Brahmāṇḍa (2.43.29, in its late Paraśurāma section) has Kṛṣṇa return to Goloka with Rādhā. The Brahmavaivarta's Goloka (Brahmakhaṇḍa) was not checked. Gauḍīya theology later systematises it.

nodes.details: Older scholarship speculated about foreign (even Christian) influence behind the Śvetadvīpa episode; that view is now generally rejected and the episode is read within Pāñcarātra theology.

nodes.name: Kalki Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A late Upapurāṇa narrating the future birth of Kalki in the village of Śambhala to Viṣṇuyaśas and Sumati, his education by Paraśurāma, his marriage and his destruction of the Kali age; probably composed in Bengal in the mid-second millennium CE.
nodes.details: Rocher (1986, p. 183) places it among the late Upapurāṇas, likely of Bengal origin. It expands the brief Kalki prophecies of the Viṣṇu (4.24) and Bhāgavata (12.2) into a full narrative.

nodes.name: Saura Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A Śaiva Upapurāṇa despite its name ('of the Sun'), spoken by Sūrya; it praises Vārāṇasī and its liṅgas and includes Purūravas and Urvaśī (ch. 31). Hazra dated it between c. 950 and 1050 CE in north-western India.

nodes.name: Ekāmra Purāṇa
nodes.summary: Odia-region Upapurāṇa (a sthala-purāṇa) glorifying Ekāmra-kṣetra — Bhubaneswar — and its Śiva as Kṛttivāsa (the Liṅgarāja), with the Bindusāgara tank and the surrounding shrines.

dates.label: c. 11th–13th c. CE (later than the Liṅgarāja temple's foundation)
dates.basis: dependence on the developed temple complex; not checked against a scholarly dating
dates.view: recall; to be checked against Hazra vol. II and Rocher

openQuestions: Hazra's and Rocher's datings of the Ekāmra Purāṇa were not consulted directly; the range given is a placeholder awaiting that check.

nodes.name: Kāśīkhaṇḍa (Skanda Purāṇa 4)
nodes.summary: The fourth khaṇḍa of the printed Skanda Purāṇa, a hundred-chapter māhātmya of Kāśī (Vārāṇasī) as Śiva's royal city where death brings liberation, cataloguing its liṅgas, tīrthas and guardian deities; it reached its present form around the mid-13th century.
nodes.details: Eck (1982) uses the Kāśīkhaṇḍa as the principal Sanskrit guide to Banaras' sacred geography. The Wikisource index lists 100 adhyāyas; the opening verses salute Gaṇeśa and Kāśī, 'the royal city of the enemy of Tripura' (4.1.2).

dates.label: c. mid-13th c. CE
dates.basis: references and dependence on the medieval sacred topography of Vārāṇasī

nodes.name: Revākhaṇḍa (printed as Skanda Purāṇa 5.3; assigned to the Vāyu Purāṇa)
nodes.summary: The 232-chapter Revākhaṇḍa, a māhātmya of the Narmadā (Revā) and its tīrthas from Amarakaṇṭaka and Oṃkāra to the sea, printed since 1910 as Skanda Purāṇa 5.3; its GRETIL editor, J. Neuss, argues from the manuscripts that it originally belonged to the Vāyu Purāṇa.
nodes.details: The GRETIL e-text (Neuss, proof-read by O. Hellwig) follows the Veṅkaṭeśvara edition (1910) but notes that 'all available manuscriptual evidence' assigns it to the Vāyupurāṇa. It describes the Narmadā pilgrimage (parikramā), e.g. Oṃkāra and Amareśvara at Amarakaṇṭaka (RKV 21.24–26; 230.15).

nodes.name: Matsya Purāṇa 103–112 (Prayāga-māhātmya)
nodes.summary: Ten chapters of the Matsya Purāṇa in which Mārkaṇḍeya tells Yudhiṣṭhira the glory of Prayāga, the confluence of Gaṅgā and Yamunā: bathing, dying and giving there bring liberation.

nodes.name: Gayā Māhātmya (Vāyu Purāṇa 105–112)
nodes.summary: Māhātmya of Gayā, the pilgrimage centre for śrāddha offerings to the ancestors: the asura Gaya, on whose body the gods' sacrifice is performed, and Viṣṇu's footprint (Viṣṇupada) that pins him down. Transmitted as the last chapters of the Vāyu Purāṇa; critically edited by Claude Jacques (1962).
openQuestions: Jacques' and Kane's datings of the Gayā-māhātmya were not consulted directly; no date is asserted here.

nodes.name: Saromāhātmya of the Vāmana Purāṇa (Kurukṣetra-māhātmya)
nodes.summary: A māhātmya of the lake (saras) and tīrthas of Kurukṣetra, inserted after chapter 23 of the Vāmana Purāṇa in A. S. Gupta's edition: Kuru's ploughing, the Sarasvatī, and Śiva as Sthāṇu at Sthāṇvīśvara (Thanesar).

nodes.name: Mahāpurāṇas
nodes.summary: The conventional set of eighteen 'great' Purāṇas. The tradition agrees on the number eighteen but not on the membership: lists such as Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.6 and Bhāgavata 12.7 name a Śaiva Purāṇa where the Matsya and Nārada lists name the Vāyu (the Kūrma names both).
nodes.details:
The constituted text of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa critical edition (Pathak) lists eighteen purāṇas at 3.6.21–23 (Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Bhāgavata, Nāradīya, Mārkaṇḍeya, Āgneya, Bhaviṣya, Brahmavaivarta, Laiṅga, Vārāha, Skānda, Vāmana, Kaurma, Mātsya, Gāruḍa, Brahmāṇḍa); the half-line naming them 'mahāpurāṇas' and adding 'upapurāṇas' is printed as an insertion (3.6.23*8). Rocher notes that the term mahāpurāṇa is rare and probably late.

Lists differ in the fourth place: Śaiva (ViP 3.6.21; BhP 12.7.23; Liṅga 1.39.61; Śiva P 7.1.1.43) versus Vāyavīya (Matsya 53.18; Nārada 1.92.26); the Kūrma (1.1.13–15) keeps Śaiva fourth and adds a Vāyavīya near the end. The Bhāgavata (12.13.4–9) assigns verse counts totalling 400,000. A later classification (Padma Purāṇa, recall) sorts the eighteen into sāttvika, rājasa and tāmasa groups; Matsya 53.68–69 already links sāttvika Purāṇas with Hari, rājasa with Brahmā and tāmasa with Agni and Śiva.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner
Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

nodes.limits: The eighteen-fold canon is a traditional classification; membership and the Mahā/Upa distinction are not stable across texts.
openQuestions: When did the term mahāpurāṇa enter the lists? (cf. its status as an insertion in the ViP critical edition)

nodes.name: Upapurāṇas
nodes.summary: 'Secondary' Purāṇas, also conventionally eighteen, whose lists disagree even more than those of the Mahāpurāṇas; several (Viṣṇudharmottara, Kālikā, Narasiṃha, Devī Bhāgavata in some lists) are as old or as influential as Mahāpurāṇas.
nodes.details: Matsya Purāṇa 53.60–63 already names 'subdivisions' (upabheda): a Nārasiṃha of 18,000 verses, a Nandī, a Sāmba and an Āditya Purāṇa. Hazra characterised the distinction as one of renown (a well-known Purāṇa is 'mahā', a lesser-known one 'upa'); Rocher regards the distinction as ahistorical.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

nodes.limits: Upapurāṇa status is a classification by later lists, not a property of the texts.

nodes.name: Dharmaśāstra
nodes.summary: The Sanskrit genre of normative treatises on dharma (Manu, Yājñavalkya, Nārada, Viṣṇu and others), together with their commentaries and digests; included here because Manusmṛti 1 supplies one of the earliest yuga reckonings.

nodes.name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A Vaiṣṇava Mahāpurāṇa of six books (aṃśas), narrated by Parāśara to Maitreya, often taken as the Purāṇa that best preserves the five 'marks' (pañcalakṣaṇa); book 5 is a sustained life of Kṛṣṇa.
nodes.details:
Book 1: creation, Varāha (1.4), time units and yugas (1.3), the churning of the ocean (1.9), Dhruva (1.11–12), Prahlāda (1.16–20). Book 2: cosmography. Book 3: manvantaras (3.1–2), Vyāsa and the Veda, the list of eighteen purāṇas and the five marks (3.6). Book 4: royal genealogies of the Solar and Lunar lines and the prophetic dynasties of the Kali age down to the Guptas (4.24). Book 5: Kṛṣṇa. Book 6: dissolution and liberation.

A critical edition (M. M. Pathak, Oriental Institute Vadodara 1997–99) exists; its apparatus relegates some well-known lines to insertions, including the half-verse that calls the eighteen 'mahāpurāṇas' (3.6.23*8).

Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

sources.locator: Dating section, reporting Doniger's approximate dates

dates.label: 11th c. CE (19th-c. view)
dates.basis: Wilson's estimate from manuscripts known in 1840/1864

attributes.panchalakshana: all five marks treated systematically (sarga 1.2–5; pratisarga 6; vaṃśa and vaṃśānucarita 4; manvantara 3.1–2)

nodes.limits: Dates below refer to scholarly estimates for layers or recensions, not to the text as printed today; the traditional attribution to Vyāsa is recorded as tradition, not as authorship history.
openQuestions: Relation of the Kali-age dynastic lists (ViP 4.24) to those of the Vāyu, Brahmāṇḍa and Matsya (Pargiter 1913).

nodes.name: Bhāgavata Purāṇa
nodes.summary: The most influential Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, in twelve books (skandhas), narrated by Śuka to King Parīkṣit; its tenth book on Kṛṣṇa's life became a foundation of later Kṛṣṇa devotion, and 1.3.28 declares Kṛṣṇa 'Bhagavān himself'.
nodes.details:
Key loci verified in the GRETIL e-text: the 22 avatāras (1.3.6–25) and the declaration 'ete cāṃśakalāḥ puṃsaḥ kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam' (1.3.28); a second, longer avatāra catalogue (2.7.1–38); time and yugas (3.11.18–24); Dhruva (4.8–12); Prahlāda and Narasiṃha (7.1–10, the pillar 7.8.17–19); Gajendra (8.2–4); the churning (8.5–12, Śiva drinks the hālāhala 8.7.43); the current manvantara (8.13.1–6); Vāmana and Bali (8.15–23); Matsya and Satyavrata (8.24); dynasties (9); Kṛṣṇa (10); ten lakṣaṇas of a Purāṇa (12.7.9–10, noting that some count five) and the list of eighteen (12.7.23–24); verse counts (12.13.4–9).

Dating is contested: many scholars, following Hardy's arguments for South Indian (Āḻvār-influenced) composition, place the final redaction in the 9th–early 10th century; others argue for a substantially earlier (Gupta-period) text. van Buitenen drew attention to its deliberately Vedic, archaising language. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Śiva Purāṇa
nodes.subtype: Mahāpurāṇa (contested; some lists give the Vāyu instead)
nodes.summary: A large Śaiva compilation organised in saṃhitās (seven in the common Bombay text: Vidyeśvara, Rudra, Śatarudra, Koṭirudra, Umā, Kailāsa, Vāyavīya) that narrates Śiva's manifestations, the Liṅgodbhava and Śaiva ritual.
nodes.details:
The text describes itself as an abridgement (24,000 verses, seven saṃhitās) of a 100,000-verse Śaiva Purāṇa of twelve saṃhitās (ŚivP 1.2.49–61, 7.1.1.49–60). Its Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā (1.5–9) tells the Liṅgodbhava with the distinctive episode of the ketakī flower as Brahmā's false witness (1.7.19–27).

Whether the 'Śaiva' of the eighteen-lists is this text or the Vāyu Purāṇa was debated in the 19th–20th centuries; modern scholarship treats them as different works. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Vāyu Purāṇa
nodes.summary: One of the oldest Purāṇas, Śaiva in orientation and closely parallel to the Brahmāṇḍa (the two are thought to derive from one original); the Mahābhārata (CE 3.189.14) already refers to a purāṇa 'proclaimed by Vāyu'.
nodes.details:
Matsya 53.18 describes the Vāyavīya as taught by Vāyu in connection with the Śveta-kalpa and 'joined with the greatness of Rudra', 24,000 verses — the same count the Bhāgavata gives for the 'Śaiva'. It occupies the fourth place in the Matsya and Nārada lists; the Kūrma names it after the Gāruḍa, possibly equating it with the Brahmāṇḍa.

With the Brahmāṇḍa and Matsya it is a principal witness for the Kali-age dynastic lists studied by Pargiter (1913). Its Gayā-māhātmya is a later addition (Hazra). Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Liṅga Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A Śaiva Mahāpurāṇa centred on the liṅga as Śiva's form; it narrates the Liṅgodbhava, in which Brahmā as a swan and Viṣṇu as a boar fail to find the ends of a fiery pillar (1.17), and prescribes how the scene is to be sculpted (1.76.60–61).
nodes.details: Its list of Purāṇas (1.39.61–63) gives Śaiva (not Vāyu) in fourth place. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Skanda Purāṇa
nodes.summary: The largest Purāṇa by reputation (81,100 verses per BhP 12.13.7), known in print as a vast compendium of khaṇḍas (Māheśvara, Vaiṣṇava, Brahma, Kāśī, Avantī, Nāgara, Prabhāsa) rich in tīrtha-māhātmyas; scholars distinguish it from the much earlier 'original' Skandapurāṇa preserved in Nepalese manuscripts.
nodes.details:
The printed khaṇḍas came into existence in many cases after the 12th century (the Kāśī-khaṇḍa reached its present form around the 13th–14th century); they serve as the principal sthala-purāṇic charters of north and west Indian pilgrimage. The edited early text (text:skandapurana-early) is a different, coherent work of the late 6th–early 7th century, sharing mainly the name.

Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Skandapurāṇa (early recension, Nepalese manuscripts)
nodes.summary: The 'original' Skandapurāṇa, a Pāśupata-milieu Śaiva Purāṇa composed probably in the late 6th or early 7th century (perhaps at Vārāṇasī) and transmitted in Nepalese palm-leaf manuscripts, one of which, dated 810 CE, is the oldest dated Purāṇa manuscript known; it is being critically edited by the Groningen–Leiden Skandapurāṇa project.
nodes.details:
The edition (vol. I 1998, Adriaensen–Bakker–Isaacson; later vols. by Bakker, Bisschop, Yokochi) shows a text centred on Śiva's family — the birth of Skanda, Pārvatī's asceticism, Andhaka — and on Śaiva holy places, with a strongly Pāśupata outlook. Bakker has proposed that it was conceived in Maukhari times and completed in the reign of Harṣa; the manuscripts S1 (dated 810 CE) and others are held in Kathmandu.

The ambiguity of the era used in the colophon leaves a small uncertainty (810/811 CE).

nodes.name: Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A comparatively non-sectarian and probably early Mahāpurāṇa narrated by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya to the wise birds; it contains the Devī Māhātmya (chapters 81–93 in the common text).
nodes.details:
Its frame (birds who heard the Mahābhārata) and its accounts of Hariścandra, Madālasā and the manvantaras make it one of the most varied Purāṇas. The Devī Māhātmya is set in the Sāvarṇika manvantara (colophons of MkP 81–93). A Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript dated 998 CE is reported in the secondary literature (not verified here).

Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Devī Māhātmya
nodes.summary: A 13-chapter, c. 700-verse glorification of the Goddess embedded in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, in which a supreme Goddess slays Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Mahiṣāsura and Śumbha–Niśumbha; Coburn calls it the 'crystallization' of the Goddess tradition.
nodes.details:
Structure (GRETIL MkP numbering): DM 1 = MkP 81 Madhu and Kaiṭabha; DM 2–4 = MkP 82–84 Mahiṣāsura (the Goddess formed from the gods' tejas 82.8–18, armed by them 82.19–30, riding a lion given by Himavat 82.29); DM 5–10 = MkP 85–90 Śumbha and Niśumbha (Ambikā/Kauśikī emerges from Pārvatī's body sheath 85.40–44; Kālī springs from her brow 87.5 and is named Cāmuṇḍā 87.26; Raktabīja 88); DM 11 = MkP 91 Nārāyaṇī-stuti; DM 12–13 = MkP 92–93 benefits and boons to Suratha and Samādhi.

A verse of DM 11 ('sarvamaṅgalamāṅgalye…', MkP 91.9 here) is quoted in the Dadhimatī-mātā inscription of 608 CE, a terminus ante quem for at least that hymn. In liturgical use it is the Durgāsaptaśatī / Caṇḍīpāṭha, whose 700-verse numbering differs from the Purāṇa's.

nodes.name: Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa

nodes.details: Rocher notes that the text is generally assumed to have reached its current structure by about 1000 CE, with later sections replacing older ones. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Matsya Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A Mahāpurāṇa presented as taught by Viṣṇu in fish form to Manu (1.10–2.19); it preserves a detailed list of the eighteen Purāṇas with verse counts and the five marks (53), the doctrine of ten manifestations caused by Bhṛgu's curse (47), and Satī's 108 tīrtha-names (13).
nodes.details:
Verified loci (Calcutta 1954 text on GRETIL): the fish identified as Janārdana/Vāsudeva (1.25–28; 2.17); the flood at the end of the Cākṣuṣa manvantara (2.14); twelve wars of gods and demons (47.41–45); ten manifestations of Viṣṇu due to Bhṛgu's curse — three divine and seven human (47.235–251); the eighteen Purāṇas with themes, verse counts and gifts (53.12–58), the upabhedas (53.60–63), the five marks (53.65) and the guṇa correlation (53.68–69); Satī's 108 names at tīrthas (13.26–53).

Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Kūrma Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A Mahāpurāṇa said to be taught by Viṣṇu as the tortoise; though framed as Vaiṣṇava it is strongly Śaiva in content (including the Īśvara Gītā) and its list of the Purāṇas names both a Śaiva (fourth) and a Vāyavīya (after the Gāruḍa).
nodes.details: Its opening states the pañcalakṣaṇa (1.1.12) and lists the Purāṇas with Śaiva fourth and, after the Gāruḍa, the Vāyavīya and 'the eighteenth, called Brahmāṇḍa' (1.1.13–15). Hazra argued for a Pāñcarātra original reworked in Pāśupata circles (recall). Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Varāha Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A Vaiṣṇava Mahāpurāṇa framed as Varāha's teaching to the Earth whom he has rescued; largely concerned with vows, ritual and tīrthas (notably Mathurā), and generally regarded as relatively late.
nodes.details: Matsya 53.39–40 describes it as Viṣṇu's account to the Earth (kṣoṇī) of the greatness of Mahāvarāha, of 24,000 verses. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Garuḍa Purāṇa
nodes.summary: An encyclopaedic Vaiṣṇava Mahāpurāṇa taught by Viṣṇu to Garuḍa, best known for its section on death and the afterlife (Pretakalpa); its opening avatāra list (1.1.14–33) reproduces Bhāgavata 1.3 almost verbatim, and 1.86.10–11 gives a ten-avatāra list.
nodes.details: Its Buddha verse reads 'buddho nāmnā jinasutaḥ kīkaṭeṣu bhaviṣyati' (1.1.32) where the Bhāgavata has 'añjanasutaḥ' (1.3.24) — one of several small divergences in an otherwise parallel list. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Padma Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A very large Vaiṣṇava Mahāpurāṇa (55,000 verses per BhP 12.13.4) extant in divergent Bengal and Devanāgarī recensions arranged in khaṇḍas; widely cited for its classification of the Purāṇas by the three guṇas.
nodes.details: Estimates for its layers range from the 4th to the 15th century or later; Wilson considered no part of the versions he knew older than the 12th century. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Agni Purāṇa
nodes.summary: An encyclopaedic Mahāpurāṇa taught by Agni to Vasiṣṭha; it opens with the avatāras of Viṣṇu (chapters 2–16, using the expression daśāvatāra) and gives iconographic rules for the ten (49), alongside chapters on ritual, polity, medicine, poetics and grammar.
nodes.details: Its iconographic list (49.1–9) runs Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma with the axe, Rāma with bow, Rāma with plough and pestle (Balarāma), Buddha and Kalki — i.e. it places Balarāma, not Kṛṣṇa, among the ten. Datable layers include metrics cited by Halāyudha (before c. 950) and much later grammatical chapters. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Brahma Purāṇa
nodes.summary: Counted 'first of all Purāṇas' (ViP 3.6.20), the extant Brahma Purāṇa is largely a compilation of tīrtha material for Orissa (Puruṣottama/Puri, Koṇārka) and the Godāvarī, much of it borrowed from other Purāṇas and generally dated late.
nodes.details: Hazra held the extant text to be compiled no earlier than the 10th century; its description of Koṇārka suggests the Orissa chapters postdate the 13th-century temple (Wilson, Winternitz). Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Nārada Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A Vaiṣṇava Mahāpurāṇa (also Nāradīya; distinct from the Bṛhannāradīya Upapurāṇa) whose Pūrvabhāga contains a detailed synopsis (anukramaṇī) of all eighteen Purāṇas.
nodes.details: Its synopsis lists Vāyavīya in fourth place (NārP 1.92.26) and then describes each Purāṇa in turn (from 1.92). Hazra dates the related Bṛhannāradīya to the 9th century and places the Nāradīya after it. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Bhaviṣya Purāṇa
nodes.summary: The 'Purāṇa of the future', a heterogeneous compilation with an early core on vows and Sun worship (shared with the Sāmba Purāṇa) and a Pratisargaparvan that 'prophesies' Mughal and even British-era history — accretions dated to the 18th–19th centuries.
nodes.details: Matsya 53.31–32 describes a Bhaviṣya taught by Brahmā to Manu concerning Āditya's greatness (14,500 verses). Hazra calls the extant work 'a loose collection of materials taken from various sources'; Hiltebeitel dates much of the Pratisargaparvan to the 19th century. Rocher (1986) stresses that no Purāṇa can be dated as a whole: each is a layered, 'fluid' text transmitted in divergent manuscript versions, so any date applies only to a layer, a recension or a datable reference.

nodes.name: Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A twelve-book Śākta Purāṇa that reworks the Bhāgavata model around the Goddess as supreme reality; Śāktas count it as the Mahāpurāṇa 'Bhāgavata', while most lists and scholars treat it as an Upapurāṇa.
nodes.details:
It retells the Devī Māhātmya battles (book 5), Satī's death and the seats of the Goddess (7.30), and contains the Devī Gītā (7.31–40, verified on GRETIL). Its partisans argue that the Matsya Purāṇa's description of 'the Bhāgavata' as beginning with the Gāyatrī and containing the slaying of Vṛtra (MatsP 53.20–21) fits the Devī Bhāgavata rather than the Śrīmad Bhāgavata.

Most scholars date it between the 9th and 14th centuries: Hazra to the 11th–12th, Pintchman 1000–1200, with parts of book 9 later (12th–15th).

attributes.statusDispute: Mahāpurāṇa for Śāktas; Upapurāṇa in Padma, Garuḍa, Kūrma-type lists (as reported)

nodes.limits: Its claim to be the Mahāpurāṇa 'Bhāgavata' is a sectarian position preserved as such.
openQuestions: Which 'Bhāgavata' did the author of Matsya 53.20–21 have in view?

nodes.name: Manusmṛti
nodes.summary: The most influential Dharmaśāstra, a verse treatise presented as Manu's (and Bhṛgu's) teaching; its first chapter gives a cosmogony and a yuga reckoning of 12,000 years for the four ages (1.68–73), the base of the Purāṇic scheme.
nodes.details: Manu 1.64–67 builds the time scale (nimeṣa → kāṣṭhā → kalā → muhūrta → day; a month is a day-night of the ancestors; a year a day-night of the gods); 1.68–71 gives Kṛta 4,000 years with sandhyā and sandhyāṃśa of 400 each, the others decreasing by a thousand and a hundred, totalling 12,000 — 'a yuga of the gods'; 1.72–73 a thousand such divine yugas make a day of Brahmā; 1.79 a manvantara is seventy-one of them. Manu does not itself multiply by 360; commentators and the Purāṇas read the 12,000 as divine years. The same verses occur in MBh (CE) 12.224.14–31.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text, text of Kullūka (Shastri 1983) with Medhātithi variants

nodes.limits: A normative text; its yuga reckoning is a traditional cosmology, not a historical chronology.

nodes.name: Kālikā Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A Śākta Upapurāṇa from the Kāmarūpa (Assam–north Bengal) region that glorifies the goddess Kāmākhyā, prescribes her worship including animal sacrifice, and tells how parts of Satī's corpse fell to earth, Kāmarūpa receiving her yoni.
nodes.details: Estimates for different sections range from the 7th to the 12th century (Rocher); several scholars favour the 10th–11th century. It is among the earliest texts devoted to Kāmākhyā.

dates.label: c. 10th–11th c. CE
dates.basis: references to Kāmarūpa rulers; regional geography

nodes.limits: Dates below refer to scholarly estimates for layers or recensions, not to the text as printed today; the traditional attribution to Vyāsa is recorded as tradition, not as authorship history.

nodes.name: Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa
nodes.summary: An encyclopaedic Vaiṣṇava Upapurāṇa, associated with Kashmir, whose third book contains the Citrasūtra, the most detailed early Sanskrit treatise on painting and image-making, with iconographic rules for many deities.
nodes.details: Pingree placed the completion of the compilation in the 5th–6th century; Kramrisch dated the painting chapters to the 7th century. Listed among the eighteen Upapurāṇas in the Bṛhaddharma Purāṇa (1.25.23–26, as reported).
nodes.limits: Dates below refer to scholarly estimates for layers or recensions, not to the text as printed today; the traditional attribution to Vyāsa is recorded as tradition, not as authorship history.

nodes.name: Narasiṃha Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A Vaiṣṇava Upapurāṇa (already named as an 'upabheda' of 18,000 verses in Matsya 53.60) devoted to Narasiṃha; its Prahlāda narrative occupies chapters 40–44 of the Jena edition.
nodes.details: Hazra (Studies in the Upapurāṇas) concluded that the original text was written in the later 5th century, with later additions; a Telugu rendering was made about 1300 CE.

sources.edition: S. Jena ed., The Narasiṃha Purāṇam (Delhi 1987); GRETIL e-text
Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

nodes.limits: Dates below refer to scholarly estimates for layers or recensions, not to the text as printed today; the traditional attribution to Vyāsa is recorded as tradition, not as authorship history.

nodes.name: Sāmba Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A Saura Upapurāṇa (named among the upabhedas in Matsya 53.62) narrating how Kṛṣṇa's son Sāmba, cured of leprosy by the Sun, installed Sun worship with Maga priests from Śākadvīpa; it shares material with the Bhaviṣya.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

nodes.name: Gaṇeśa Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A Gāṇapatya Upapurāṇa in two parts (Upāsanā- and Krīḍā-khaṇḍa) that presents Gaṇeśa as the supreme deity and includes the Gaṇeśa Gītā; usually dated to the first half of the 2nd millennium.
nodes.limits: Dates below refer to scholarly estimates for layers or recensions, not to the text as printed today; the traditional attribution to Vyāsa is recorded as tradition, not as authorship history.

nodes.name: Mudgala Purāṇa
nodes.summary: A Gāṇapatya Upapurāṇa organised around eight incarnations of Gaṇeśa (Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadanta, Mahodara, Gajānana, Lambodara, Vikaṭa, Vighnarāja, Dhūmravarṇa) who conquer personified vices.

dates.label: first half of 2nd millennium CE (estimates vary)

nodes.limits: Dates below refer to scholarly estimates for layers or recensions, not to the text as printed today; the traditional attribution to Vyāsa is recorded as tradition, not as authorship history.
nodes.details: Thapan (1997) holds that its kernel is old but that interpolation continued into the 17th–18th centuries.

nodes.name: Āryabhaṭīya
nodes.summary: Āryabhaṭa's astronomical treatise (499 CE), which states that he was 23 years old when 3,600 years of the Kali age had elapsed (3.10) — the basis of the later standard computation of the Kali epoch to 3102 BCE; it divides the mahāyuga into four equal quarters (3.10, cf. 1.5).
nodes.details: Verse 3.7 gives the scale: the solar (human) year ×30 = a year of the ancestors, ×12 = a divine year (i.e. 360 human years); 3.8 a mahāyuga is 12,000 divine years and a day of Brahmā 1,008 such yugas (not 1,000). The 'Thursday of the Bhārata' (1.5) marks the Kali epoch in his reckoning.

dates.label: 499 CE
dates.basis: author states his age (23) at Kali 3600 = 499 CE (3.10); the composition date is inferred from it

attributes.author: Āryabhaṭa (b. 476 CE)
attributes.yugaModel: four equal yugapādas of 1,080,000 years each

sources.quote: ṣaṣṭi-abdānām ṣaṣṭis yadā vyatītās trayas ca yuga-pādās / tri-adhikā viṃśatis abdās tadā iha mama janmanas atītās

nodes.limits: An astronomical computation backwards from planetary models; it is evidence for how the Kali epoch was fixed, not for the date of any narrated event.

nodes.name: Amarakośa
nodes.summary: Amarasiṃha's Sanskrit thesaurus (c. 5th–7th c. CE), which glosses purāṇa as 'pañcalakṣaṇam' (1.6.5) — an early datable witness to the five-mark definition.
nodes.limits: Shows the definition was current; does not show that existing Purāṇas conformed to it.

nodes.name: Devī Gītā
nodes.summary: The 'Song of the Goddess', chapters 7.31–40 of the Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa, in which the Goddess teaches Himālaya, modelled on the Bhagavad Gītā.
nodes.limits: Dated with its host text (see text:devi-bhagavata-purana).

nodes.name: Viṣṇu
nodes.summary: A Vedic god of the three strides who in the epics and Purāṇas becomes, for Vaiṣṇavas, the supreme being who preserves the world and descends in avatāras; the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas are his principal Purāṇic scriptures.
nodes.details: In the Ṛgveda Viṣṇu is a minor god celebrated for three strides (RV 1.154). By the late epic he is identified with Nārāyaṇa and Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa, and the Purāṇas make him the source of a series of descents whose number and membership vary by text (see the avatāra comparison). In the trimūrti scheme he preserves while Brahmā creates and Śiva destroys, though each sectarian Purāṇa subordinates the other two to its own god.

attributes.iconography: four-armed, dark-complexioned, crowned (kirīṭa), wearing the śrīvatsa mark and kaustubha gem, holding conch (śaṅkha), discus (cakra), mace (gadā) and lotus (padma)
attributes.abode: Vaikuṇṭha; reclines on Śeṣa on the cosmic ocean

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.limits: Describes how texts and traditions conceive the deity; it makes no claim about the deity's existence or about the historicity of narrated deeds.

nodes.name: Nārāyaṇa
nodes.summary: A cosmic deity whose name is interpreted as 'resting on the waters'; first prominent in late Vedic texts and the Mahābhārata's Nārāyaṇīya, he is identified with Viṣṇu and Vāsudeva and is the sleeping god from whose navel Brahmā is born.
nodes.details: The Nārāyaṇīya (MBh CE 12.321–339) presents Nārāyaṇa, revealed to Nārada at Śvetadvīpa, as the god of the Pāñcarātra; he expounds the four vyūhas (12.326.68–69) and foretells his manifestations (12.326.71–94). Nara and Nārāyaṇa are also a pair of ṛṣis at Badarī.

attributes.iconography: reclining on the serpent Śeṣa on the cosmic ocean (Anantaśayana), Brahmā on a lotus from his navel; also as the ṛṣi pair Nara–Nārāyaṇa

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.limits: Describes how texts and traditions conceive the deity; it makes no claim about the deity's existence or about the historicity of narrated deeds.

earliestText.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

nodes.name: Śiva
nodes.summary: The great god of Śaiva traditions, identified, from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad onward, with the Vedic Rudra; in the Purāṇas he is the ascetic and householder of Kailāsa, destroyer of Tripura and of Dakṣa's sacrifice, and, in the Liṅgodbhava, the infinite pillar of fire beyond Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
nodes.details: The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad already calls Rudra the one god who does not tolerate a second (3.2) and names him Śiva (3.11). The Purāṇas elaborate his family (Pārvatī, Skanda, Gaṇeśa), his forms (Naṭarāja, Bhairava, Ardhanārīśvara, Dakṣiṇāmūrti) and his worship in the liṅga.

attributes.iconography: matted locks (jaṭā) with crescent moon and Gaṅgā, third eye, blue throat (nīlakaṇṭha), serpents, ash-smeared body, tiger or elephant skin; often worshipped aniconically as liṅga

nodes.limits: Describes how texts and traditions conceive the deity; it makes no claim about the deity's existence or about the historicity of narrated deeds.

earliestText.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

nodes.name: Brahmā
nodes.summary: The four-faced creator god of the Purāṇas, born on the lotus from Viṣṇu's navel in Vaiṣṇava accounts; his cult declined, and Purāṇic myths such as the Liṅgodbhava often show him humbled.
nodes.details: ViP 1.3.5 gives Brahmā a life of a hundred of his years (para), half of which (parārdha) has elapsed (1.3.27–28). In the Mahābhārata's flood story the fish reveals itself as Prajāpati Brahmā (MBh CE 3.185.48).

attributes.iconography: four faces, four arms, bearded, holding Vedas (manuscript), water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), rosary (akṣamālā), ladle (sruc)

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.limits: Describes how texts and traditions conceive the deity; it makes no claim about the deity's existence or about the historicity of narrated deeds.

nodes.name: Devī (the Goddess)
nodes.summary: The Great Goddess (Mahādevī) of Śākta theology, conceived as the supreme power (śakti) of whom all goddesses are forms; the Devī Māhātmya (c. 5th–6th c.) is the first Sanskrit text to present her as supreme.
nodes.details: In DM 11 she is hymned as Nārāyaṇī; in the Devī Bhāgavata she is the ground of reality who teaches the Devī Gītā. Her forms include Durgā, Kālī, Cāmuṇḍā, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī.

attributes.iconography: variable by form; as Mahiṣāsuramardinī multi-armed, on a lion, bearing the gods' weapons (DM 2)

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition

nodes.limits: Describes how texts and traditions conceive the deity; it makes no claim about the deity's existence or about the historicity of narrated deeds.

nodes.name: Durgā
nodes.summary: The warrior form of the Goddess, above all as slayer of the buffalo-demon Mahiṣa (Mahiṣāsuramardinī); the Devī Māhātmya describes her formation from the gods' collected radiance and her arming with their weapons.
nodes.details: DM 2 (MkP 82.19–30): Śiva's trident, Kṛṣṇa's discus, Varuṇa's conch and noose, Agni's spear, Vāyu's bow and quivers, Indra's thunderbolt and bell, Yama's staff, Brahmā's water-pot, Kāla's sword and shield, Viśvakarman's axe, Himavat's lion and Kubera's cup.

attributes.iconography: eight-, ten- or eighteen-armed; standing on or striking the buffalo or the demon emerging from it (Mahiṣāsuramardinī)

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition

nodes.name: Pārvatī
nodes.summary: Daughter of the mountain Himavat and wife of Śiva, mother of Skanda and Gaṇeśa; Purāṇas present her as the rebirth of Dakṣa's daughter Satī who wins Śiva by asceticism.
nodes.details: In DM 5 (MkP 85.40–44) the goddess Ambikā/Kauśikī emerges from Pārvatī's body-sheath, after which Pārvatī turns dark and is called Kālikā.

attributes.iconography: two-armed beside Śiva or four-armed alone, holding lotus; as ascetic (Tapasvinī) with rosary amid fires
attributes.vahana: lion or tiger (in some traditions); the bull with Śiva

nodes.name: Lakṣmī
nodes.summary: Goddess of fortune, prosperity and royal glory (Śrī), consort of Viṣṇu; in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas she rises from the churned Ocean of Milk and chooses Viṣṇu.
nodes.details: ViP 1.9.98–103: Śrī rises seated on a lotus, is praised with the Śrīsūkta, bathed by the elephants of the quarters and goes to Hari's chest. In MBh (CE) 1.16.34 Śrī rises from the ghee in the ocean without a choosing scene.

attributes.iconography: seated or standing on a lotus, holding lotuses, often lustrated by two elephants (Gajalakṣmī)
attributes.vahana: owl (ulūka) in later and regional iconography; lotus seat

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Kālī
nodes.summary: The dark, terrifying form of the Goddess who in the Devī Māhātmya springs from Ambikā's brow to slay Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (and is then named Cāmuṇḍā) and drinks the blood of Raktabīja.

attributes.iconography: emaciated or black, gaping mouth, lolling tongue, garland of severed heads (naramālā), skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), sword and noose (MkP 87.5–6)
attributes.consort: Śiva (in later Śākta and Tantric iconography)

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition

nodes.name: Gaṇeśa
nodes.summary: Elephant-headed god of beginnings and remover of obstacles, son of Pārvatī (and Śiva); the Purāṇas give competing accounts of his birth and head, and Gāṇapatya Upapurāṇas make him supreme.
nodes.details: Widely told (e.g. Śiva Purāṇa, Rudra-saṃhitā) is the story of Pārvatī fashioning him to guard her door and Śiva beheading and restoring him with an elephant's head; other Purāṇas (e.g. Brahmavaivarta) attribute the loss of his head to Śani's gaze. These versions are kept separate (recall).

attributes.iconography: elephant head with one tusk, pot belly, four arms holding goad (aṅkuśa), noose (pāśa), broken tusk and sweet (modaka)

nodes.limits: Describes how texts and traditions conceive the deity; it makes no claim about the deity's existence or about the historicity of narrated deeds.

nodes.name: Skanda
nodes.summary: Warrior son of Śiva (born in the epics and Purāṇas with the help of Agni, Gaṅgā and the Kṛttikās), general of the gods and slayer of the demon Tāraka; the early Skandapurāṇa is named after him.
nodes.details: Mann (2012) traces his transformation from a Kuṣāṇa-period god of possession and disease to the Gupta-period Mahāsena. The Tamil god Murukaṉ is a distinct id joined to Skanda by an IDENTIFIED_WITH assertion qualified by tradition.

attributes.iconography: youthful, six-headed or one-headed, holding a spear (śakti/vel) and cock banner

nodes.name: Gaṅgā
nodes.summary: The goddess of the Ganges, brought down from heaven by Bhagīratha's austerities and caught in Śiva's hair; she also appears as mother of Bhīṣma and as one of Skanda's nurses.

attributes.iconography: woman standing on a makara, holding a water-pot; often paired with Yamunā on a tortoise at temple doorways (Gupta period onward)

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.name: Matsya
nodes.summary: The fish avatāra of Viṣṇu who saves Manu (and the seeds of creatures, or the Vedas) from the flood; in the earlier Śatapatha and Mahābhārata versions the fish is unnamed or identifies itself as Brahmā.

attributes.iconography: a fish, or a fish lower body with four-armed human upper body holding conch and discus (Agni P 49.1: 'matsyākāras tu matsyaḥ syāt')

nodes.name: Kūrma
nodes.summary: The tortoise avatāra who supports Mount Mandara during the churning of the ocean; in the Mahābhārata critical text the supporting tortoise is the 'king of tortoises' Akūpāra, not Viṣṇu.

nodes.name: Varāha
nodes.summary: The boar avatāra who dives into the cosmic waters to raise the Earth; the image of the boar-headed god lifting Bhūdevī (e.g. Udayagiri, early 5th c.) is among the earliest monumental avatāra sculptures.
nodes.details: In the Śatapatha (14.1.2.11) a boar Emūṣa raises the earth (Vedic antecedent, vedic domain). ViP 1.4.8 places Varāha in the current (Vārāha) kalpa. In the Liṅgodbhava Viṣṇu takes boar form to seek the base of the pillar.

attributes.iconography: boar-headed man (nṛvarāha) with mace and conch, Earth (or Lakṣmī) on his left elbow or tusk, Ananta and the Earth at his feet (Agni P 49.2–3); or wholly zoomorphic boar

nodes.name: Narasiṃha
nodes.summary: The man-lion avatāra who emerges from a pillar to kill the demon-king Hiraṇyakaśipu at twilight, on the threshold, with his claws, circumventing the demon's boon and protecting his devotee Prahlāda.

nodes.name: Vāmana

nodes.name: Hayagrīva (Hayaśiras)
nodes.summary: The horse-headed form of Viṣṇu who recovers the Vedas; the Nārāyaṇīya names the Haṃsa and Hayaśiras manifestations (MBh CE 12.326.94), and the Bhāgavata lists Hayaśīrṣa among the descents (2.7.11). Distinct from the demon Hayagrīva of BhP 8.24.

nodes.name: Dattātreya

nodes.name: Prahlāda
nodes.summary: Son of the demon-king Hiraṇyakaśipu who, despite persecution, remains devoted to Viṣṇu; his father's death at the hands of Narasiṃha and his teaching make him the model devotee of the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas.

In the Matsya (47.235) Prahlāda's authority over the asuras is invoked in Bhṛgu's curse narrative.

nodes.name: Manu (Vaivasvata)
nodes.summary: Son of Vivasvat (the Sun), the Manu of the present (seventh) manvantara and progenitor of humanity, saved from the flood by the fish; the Bhāgavata identifies him with the royal sage Satyavrata, lord of the Draviḍas.
nodes.details: His sons, the founders of the Solar line, are ten in BhP 8.13.2–3 (Ikṣvāku, Nabhaga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti, Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga, Diṣṇa/Diṣṭa, Tarūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, Vasumān) but described as nine in ViP 3.1.33–34 (with Nṛga in place of Nabhaga and Karūṣa). The Matsya places him as a king who retired to the Malaya (1.11–12); the Bhāgavata as Satyavrata worshipping at the Kṛtamālā (8.24.12–13). The author of the Manusmṛti is traditionally the earlier Svāyambhuva Manu, a different figure.

nodes.name: Avatāra
nodes.summary: The 'descent' of a deity, above all Viṣṇu, into a bodily form to restore dharma; the theory develops from the Bhagavad Gītā's 'yuge yuge' (4.7–8) and the Nārāyaṇīya's prādurbhāvas into the Purāṇic lists of ten, twenty-two or 'innumerable' avatāras.
nodes.details: The early epic term is prādurbhāva ('manifestation', MBh CE 12.326.94; HV CE 31); avatāra becomes the standard term in the Purāṇas. The Bhāgavata distinguishes partial descents (aṃśa, kalā) from Kṛṣṇa as Bhagavān himself (1.3.28). Lists differ in number and membership; the 'standard ten' (Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa or Balarāma, Buddha, Kalki) is a later convention, appearing e.g. in Garuḍa P 1.86.10–11 and Agni P 49.

nodes.name: Yuga

nodes.name: Pañcalakṣaṇa (five marks of a Purāṇa)
nodes.summary: The classical definition of a Purāṇa by five topics — sarga (creation), pratisarga (re-creation/dissolution), vaṃśa (genealogy), manvantara (ages of the Manus) and vaṃśānucarita (dynastic history) — stated in the Amarakośa and in several Purāṇas.
nodes.details: The Bhāgavata gives a ten-mark definition (12.7.9–10) while noting that some count five. Rocher and Dimmitt–van Buitenen stress that the extant Purāṇas devote only a small part of their bulk to these five topics.

nodes.name: The churning of the ocean
nodes.summary: Gods and asuras churn the ocean with Mount Mandara and the serpent Vāsuki to obtain amṛta; the versions differ on who supports the mountain, who takes the poison, what emerges and how the nectar is withheld from the asuras.
nodes.details: MBh (CE) 1.15–17: Ananta uproots Mandara; the 'king of tortoises' Akūpāra bears it; Soma, Śrī, Surā, a white horse, the Kaustubha and Dhanvantari with the nectar rise; Nārāyaṇa as Mohinī takes the nectar; Rāhu is beheaded; no poison episode in the constituted text. VR (CE) 1.44: set in the Kṛta age; Dhanvantari, the apsarases, Vāruṇī (whose acceptance makes the 'suras'), Uccaiḥśravas, Kaustubha and amṛta; no tortoise and no poison. ViP 1.9: caused by Durvāsas' curse; Viṣṇu as tortoise; the nāgas take the poison; Śrī chooses Hari. nodes.name: Satī's body and the origin of the Śakti Pīṭhas

nodes.name: Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa / Ikṣvāku)

nodes.name: Vaiṣṇava traditions
nodes.summary: Traditions that worship Viṣṇu (with Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa, Rāma and other forms) as supreme; their Purāṇic canon centres on the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas and the avatāra doctrine.
nodes.details: Earliest evidence: Vāsudeva and Saṅkarṣaṇa worship attested by the Heliodorus pillar (Besnagar, late 2nd c. BCE), the Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions and the coins of Agathocles (material domain). Textually the Bhagavad Gītā, the Nārāyaṇīya and the Harivaṃśa precede the Purāṇic synthesis; Pāñcarātra and later Śrīvaiṣṇava and Gauḍīya schools are sub-traditions.
nodes.limits: An umbrella category; Vaiṣṇava communities differ widely in doctrine and practice.

nodes.name: Śaiva traditions
nodes.summary: Traditions that worship Śiva as supreme, from the Pāśupatas and the 'Śaiva age' of early medieval India (Sanderson) to Śaiva Siddhānta, Kashmir Śaivism and Vīraśaivism; their Purāṇas include the Liṅga, Śiva, Vāyu, Kūrma and Skanda.
nodes.details: Material evidence for early Śiva worship includes the Gudimallam liṅga and Kuṣāṇa coins of Wima Kadphises (material domain); the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad gives the first theistic Rudra–Śiva theology.
nodes.limits: An umbrella category.

nodes.name: Śākta traditions
nodes.summary: Traditions that worship the Goddess (Devī, Śakti) as supreme; the Devī Māhātmya (c. 5th–6th c.) is their first great Sanskrit text, followed by the Kālikā and Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇas and Tantric literature.
nodes.details: Pre-Purāṇic signs include Mahiṣāsuramardinī images of the Kuṣāṇa period and the Harivaṃśa's Vindhya goddess; the Dadhimatī-mātā inscription (608 CE) quotes the Devī Māhātmya.
nodes.limits: An umbrella category.

nodes.name: Smārta tradition
nodes.summary: Brahmanical orthopraxy based on the smṛti (Dharmaśāstra, Purāṇa), associated with the worship of five deities (pañcāyatana: Viṣṇu, Śiva, Devī, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa) and, since the medieval period, with Advaita monasteries.
nodes.limits: Attribution of the pañcāyatana to Śaṅkara is traditional.

nodes.name: Early Bhāgavata (Vāsudeva) devotion
nodes.summary: The early devotional cult of Vāsudeva (and Saṅkarṣaṇa) whose adherents called themselves bhāgavata; the Heliodorus pillar's donor styles himself 'bhāgavata' (late 2nd c. BCE), and the tradition flows into later Vaiṣṇavism.
nodes.limits: The relation of this early cult to the later Bhāgavata Purāṇa is one of continuity of name and devotion, not of text.

nodes.name: Pāśupata Śaivism
nodes.summary: The earliest known Śaiva ascetic order, tracing itself to Lakulīśa (c. 2nd c. CE); its milieu shaped the Vāyu, Liṅga, Kūrma and the early Skandapurāṇa.
nodes.limits: Pāśupata self-descriptions and inscriptions (material domain) are the primary evidence.

nodes.name: Saura (Sun) worship
nodes.summary: Worship of Sūrya as supreme, prominent in western and northern India between the Gupta and early medieval periods, with Maga priests from 'Śākadvīpa'; textual charters are the Sāmba and parts of the Bhaviṣya and Brahma Purāṇas.
nodes.limits: An umbrella category.

nodes.name: Gāṇapatya
nodes.summary: Traditions that worship Gaṇeśa as supreme, crystallised in the Gaṇeśa and Mudgala Upapurāṇas (2nd millennium) and in Maharashtrian centres such as Morgaon and Chinchwad.
nodes.limits: An umbrella category.

nodes.name: The Kali age began in 3102 BCE
nodes.summary: The traditional Indian astronomical epoch of the Kali-yuga (midnight 17/18 February 3102 BCE, Ujjain, as computed in later siddhāntas), derived backwards from planetary models; Āryabhaṭa's 499 CE statement implies it, and the 634 CE Aihole inscription counts 3,735 years from the Bhārata war.
nodes.details: Āryabhaṭa (AB 3.10) was 23 when 3,600 years of Kali had passed, i.e. Kali 3600 = 499 CE, giving an epoch of 3102 BCE (astronomical year −3101). The Aihole inscription of Pulakeśin II (Śaka 556 = 634/635 CE) dates itself 3,735 years after the Bhārata war, consistent with equating the war with the Kali epoch. Fleet (1911) argued the era was an astronomers' construction of about the 5th–6th century; the Purāṇas place the onset of Kali at Kṛṣṇa's departure (ViP 4.24.27, 4.24.32; 5.38.8) without giving a CE equivalent.
nodes.limits: A traditional and astronomical epoch; it is not evidence for the date of the Bhārata war or of any narrated event.

nodes.name: The Devī Bhāgavata is the Mahāpurāṇa 'Bhāgavata'
nodes.summary: The Śākta position that the 'Bhāgavata' of the eighteen-lists is the Devī Bhāgavata, supported by the Matsya's description of the Bhāgavata as beginning with the Gāyatrī and containing the slaying of Vṛtra (MatsP 53.20–21); Vaiṣṇava tradition and most scholars hold it to be the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, with the Devī Bhāgavata an Upapurāṇa.

nodes.name: The term 'mahāpurāṇa' is late
nodes.summary: Rocher's observation that the term mahāpurāṇa occurs rarely in Purāṇic literature and is probably late; in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa critical edition the half-verse calling the eighteen 'mahāpurāṇas' is an insertion (3.6.23*8).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

nodes.limits: An argument from distribution of a term; it does not date individual texts.

nodes.name: Vāsudeva was worshipped by self-styled bhāgavatas by the 2nd century BCE
nodes.summary: The scholarly conclusion, from the Heliodorus pillar (Besnagar), the Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī and Mora well inscriptions and the coins of Agathocles, that a devotional cult of Vāsudeva (and Saṅkarṣaṇa) existed in the last centuries BCE, long before the Purāṇas.
nodes.limits: Establishes cult and devotion to Vāsudeva by the 2nd–1st c. BCE; not the historicity of Kṛṣṇa or the content of later Purāṇic theology.

nodes.name: Śiva was worshipped in iconic and liṅga form by the early centuries CE
nodes.summary: The conclusion, from the Gudimallam liṅga and Kuṣāṇa coinage (Wima Kadphises' deity with bull), that Śiva worship in liṅga and anthropomorphic form predates the Śaiva Purāṇas.
nodes.limits: Dates of the objects are debated (material domain); the evidence establishes worship, not Purāṇic narratives.

nodes.name: The Devī Māhātmya was in circulation by 608 CE
nodes.summary: A verse of the Devī Māhātmya's eleventh chapter is quoted in a dated inscription of 608 CE, giving a firm terminus ante quem for at least part of the text.
nodes.limits: Dates the hymn, not necessarily the whole of the Devī Māhātmya.

nodes.name: Āryabhaṭa
nodes.summary: Indian astronomer-mathematician (b. 476 CE) whose Āryabhaṭīya (499 CE) states his age in the Kali era and adopts a mahāyuga of four equal quarters.
nodes.limits: Historical person; his yuga model is an astronomical one, distinct from the Purāṇic 4:3:2:1 scheme.

nodes.name: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.3 (units of time, yugas, kalpa)
nodes.summary: Parāśara's account of time: nimeṣa to day, human and divine years (1.3.8–10), the caturyuga of 12,000 divine years (1.3.11–14), 1,000 caturyugas as Brahmā's day with fourteen Manus (1.3.15–16), a manvantara of a little over 71 caturyugas = 852,000 divine or 306,720,000 human years (1.3.18–21), and the present Vārāha kalpa (1.3.27–28).

nodes.name: Liṅga Purāṇa 1.17 (Liṅgodbhava)
nodes.summary: Brahmā's account of the quarrel with Viṣṇu, the fiery liṅga, his swan form and Viṣṇu's boar form (1.17.31–45).

sources.quote: vārāham aham apy āśu haṃsatvaṃ prāptavān surāḥ

nodes.name: Liṅga Purāṇa 1.76 (image of the Liṅgodbhava)
nodes.summary: Prescription for an image with Candraśekhara within the flaming liṅga, Brahmā as swan above and Viṣṇu as boar below (1.76.60–61).

sources.quote: vyomni kuryāt tathā liṅgaṃ brahmāṇaṃ haṃsarūpiṇam / viṣṇuṃ varāharūpeṇa liṅgasyādhas tv adhomukham

nodes.name: Śiva Purāṇa, Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā 5–9 (Liṅgodbhava and the ketakī)
nodes.summary: The pillar of fire between Brahmā and Viṣṇu; Brahmā's false witness, the ketakī flower (1.7.19–27).

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay c. 1920), books 1 and 7; GRETIL e-text
sources.quote: staṃbhāgram etat samudīkṣitaṃ hare tatraiva sākṣī nanu ketakaṃ tv idam

nodes.limits: A textual locus; numbering follows the edition named in the sources and may differ in other editions.

nodes.name: Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1 (five marks and list of eighteen)
nodes.summary: The pañcalakṣaṇa (1.1.12) and a list of the Purāṇas that keeps Śaiva fourth and ends with the Vāyavīya and 'the eighteenth, called Brahmāṇḍa' (1.1.13–15).

sources.quote: kaurmaṃ mātsyaṃ gāruḍaṃ ca vāyavīyam anantaram

nodes.limits: A textual locus; numbering follows the edition named in the sources and may differ in other editions.

nodes.name: Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.31–40 (Devī Gītā)
nodes.summary: The Goddess's teaching to Himālaya, transmitted separately as the Devī Gītā.
nodes.limits: A textual locus; numbering follows the edition named in the sources and may differ in other editions.

nodes.name: Caṅkam (Sangam) literature
nodes.summary: The earliest corpus of Tamil poetry — the Eight Anthologies (Eṭṭuttokai) and Ten Idylls (Pattuppāṭṭu) — together with the grammar Tolkāppiyam, composed roughly between the turn of the era and the 5th–6th century CE, with later layers such as the Paripāṭal and Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai.
nodes.limits: The corpus is largely secular (akam love and puṟam heroic poetry); religious references are scattered and later poems are more devotional.

nodes.name: Tirumurai
nodes.summary: The twelve-book canon of Tamil Śaiva devotional literature: Tēvāram (1–7), Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār (8), Tiruvicaippā and Tiruppallāṇṭu (9), Tirumūlar’s Tirumantiram (10), a miscellany including the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai (11) and Cēkkiḻār’s Periya Purāṇam (12).

dates.event: arrangement of books 1–11 (Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi) and addition of book 12
dates.label: c. late 10th – 12th c. CE
dates.basis: tradition of Nampi’s compilation; date of the Periya Purāṇam

nodes.name: Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās
nodes.summary: The scriptures of the Pāñcarātra tradition — traditionally 108, with over 200 known titles — including the Sāttvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya (“three gems”), the Ahirbudhnya, Pārameśvara, Īśvara and Lakṣmī Tantra.

dates.label: c. 7th–14th c. CE (disputed)
dates.basis: cross-citation and borrowing from Śaiva tantras

nodes.name: Śaiva Āgamas (Siddhānta tantras)
nodes.summary: The Sanskrit scriptures of the Śaiva Siddhānta, traditionally twenty-eight Āgamas with subsidiary Upāgamas, beginning with the Kāmika; the earliest surviving tantra of the wider Mantramārga is the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā.

dates.event: composition of the surviving Siddhānta scriptures
dates.label: c. 5th–12th c. CE

nodes.limits: The South Indian “28 Āgamas” in current temple use are in part later recastings; the early Siddhānta canon is reconstructed largely from Nepalese manuscripts.

nodes.name: Śākta Tantras
nodes.summary: Tantras centred on the Goddess and her retinue (yoginīs, Kālī, Tripurasundarī, Kubjikā), including the Brahmayāmala (Picumata) of the early Vidyāpīṭha, the Kaula texts and later Śrīvidyā literature.

dates.label: c. 7th–15th c. CE
dates.basis: manuscripts and citation by Kashmirian authors

nodes.name: Maṅgalkāvya
nodes.summary: Bengali narrative poems (c. 13th–18th c.) celebrating the power of local or Purāṇic deities — Manasā, Caṇḍī, Dharma Ṭhākur, Annadā — and the establishment of their worship among reluctant devotees.

nodes.name: Sthala-purāṇas (temple and place legends)
nodes.summary: Texts recounting the sacred history of a particular shrine or town — its deity’s manifestation, divine marriages, miracles and royal patrons — in Sanskrit (often as māhātmyas within Purāṇas) and in Tamil and other languages.
nodes.details: Shulman (1980) analyses the Tamil talapurāṇams as a genre with recurring motifs (the goddess’s marriage, the self-manifested liṅga, the local flood myth). Their claims are evidence of temple tradition (class 6), not of the dates of the temples’ structures.
nodes.limits: A sthala-purāṇa’s account of a temple’s foundation is not a date for the surviving building.

nodes.name: Tolkāppiyam
nodes.summary: The oldest extant Tamil grammar and poetics, in three books (phonology, morphology, “subject-matter” — poruḷ). Its Akattiṇaiyiyal assigns presiding deities to the landscapes: Māyōṉ to the forest-pasture (mullai), Cēyōṉ to the hills (kuṟiñci), Vēntaṉ to farmland (marutam) and Varuṇaṉ to the shore (neytal).
nodes.details: Sūtra 5 of the Akattiṇaiyiyal reads: “māyōṉ mēya kāṭuṟai ulakamum / cēyōṉ mēya maivarai ulakamum / vēntaṉ mēya tīmpuṉal ulakamum / varuṇaṉ mēya perumaṇal ulakamum / mullai kuṟiñci marutam neytal eṉac / colliya muṟaiyāṟ collavum paṭumē.” The commentator Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar glosses Māyōṉ as “the one of sea-dark colour” (kaṭalvaṇṇaṉ) and Cēyōṉ as “red Murukaṉ.”
nodes.limits: The sūtra names Māyōṉ and Cēyōṉ; their glosses as Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa and Murukaṉ come from medieval commentators and modern scholarship.
