nodes.name: Paripāṭal
nodes.summary: A late Caṅkam anthology (fifth of the Eight Anthologies) of musical poems: of the 24 that survive complete, 7 are addressed to Tirumāl (Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa), 8 to Murukaṉ (Cevvēḷ) and 9 to the river Vaikai at Madurai.
nodes.details: The poems to Murukaṉ celebrate the Tiruparaṅkuṉṟam hill near Madurai and know the Skanda birth story; the Tirumāl poems are among the earliest Tamil Vaiṣṇava devotional verse.

dates.label: c. 3rd–6th c. CE
dates.view: Vaiyapuri Pillai & Takahashi (3rd–4th c.); Ramanujan (c. 6th c.)

nodes.name: Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai
nodes.summary: Nakkīrar’s poem “guiding [the devotee] to Murukaṉ,” the first of the Ten Idylls and also included in Tirumurai 11. It describes six places where Murukaṉ is present and blends Tamil and northern (Skanda) imagery.
nodes.details: The poem (317 lines in the critical edition) uses the old guide-poem form, in which a bard directs another to a generous patron, now redirected to the god. Later tradition maps its six sites onto the six temples of the āṟupaṭai vīṭu.

dates.label: late Caṅkam (c. 3rd–6th c. CE); some scholars later

nodes.name: Tiruppāvai
nodes.summary: Āṇṭāḷ’s thirty Tamil verses in the voice of cowherd girls who rise before dawn in the month of Mārkaḻi to wake one another and Kṛṣṇa for a vow (nōṉpu). It is part of the Divya Prabandham and recited daily in Śrīvaiṣṇava worship.
nodes.details: The verses address Kṛṣṇa as born in “northern Mathurā” and living among the cowherds, and invoke Nappiṉṉai, his Tamil cowherd consort. Its title, with that of Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai, survives in the Thai royal Brahman ceremony Triyampawai–Trippawai (McGovern 2017).

nodes.name: Nācciyār Tirumoḻi
nodes.summary: Āṇṭāḷ’s 143 Tamil verses of longing for union with Viṣṇu–Kṛṣṇa, including the celebrated dream of her wedding to him (vāraṇam āyiram), part of the Divya Prabandham.

nodes.name: Tiruvāymoḻi
nodes.summary: Nammāḻvār’s 1,102-verse Tamil poem to Viṣṇu, in a hundred decads; Śrīvaiṣṇavas call it the Tamil (Drāviḍa) Veda and it was the subject of the first Śrīvaiṣṇava commentary, Piḷḷāṉ’s Āṟāyirappaṭi.

attributes.commentaries: Piḷḷāṉ’s Āṟāyirappaṭi (12th c.) and later maṇipravāḷa commentaries

nodes.name: Tiruvācakam
nodes.summary: Māṇikkavācakar’s Tamil hymns to Śiva, forming (with his Tirukkōvaiyār) Tirumurai book 8; intensely personal poems of grace, longing and Śiva as dancer at Tillai (Chidambaram).

nodes.name: Tiruvempāvai
nodes.summary: Māṇikkavācakar’s twenty-verse pāvai poem within the Tiruvācakam, in which young women wake each other at dawn in Mārkaḻi to bathe and praise Śiva — a Śaiva counterpart of Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai.

nodes.name: Tirumantiram
nodes.summary: Tirumūlar’s Tamil verse treatise on Śaiva doctrine, yoga and tantra (c. 3,000 verses), Tirumurai book 10, regarded as the earliest Tamil statement of Śaiva Siddhānta ideas; its date is much disputed.

nodes.name: Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam
nodes.summary: The Tamil sthala-purāṇa of Madurai narrating the sixty-four “sacred sports” (tiruviḷaiyāṭal) of Śiva as Cuntarēcuvarar, including his marriage to the warrior-princess Taṭātakai (Mīnākṣī). The best-known version is by Parañcōti Muṉivar.
nodes.details: Episodes include Mīnākṣī’s birth with three breasts and her conquest of the world until she meets Śiva at Kailāsa, Viṣṇu giving her in marriage, and stories involving Māṇikkavācakar (jackals turned into horses) and the Pāṇḍya kings. An earlier Tamil version is attributed to Perumpaṟṟappuliyūr Nampi, and the cycle has a Sanskrit counterpart in the Hālāsya Māhātmya.

dates.label: the reigns of the early (legendary) Pāṇḍya kings

nodes.limits: Temple-tradition narrative (class 6); it does not date the Mīnākṣī temple’s structures.

nodes.name: Kanta Purāṇam
nodes.summary: Kacciyappa Civācāriyar’s Tamil Skanda Purāṇa, recounting Murukaṉ’s birth and his war against the asura Cūrapatmaṉ (Śūrapadma), traditionally first recited at the Kumarakōṭṭam shrine in Kanchipuram.

attributes.author: Kacciyappa Civācāriyar
attributes.model text: Śaṅkara-saṃhitā of the Sanskrit Skanda Purāṇa (per tradition)

nodes.name: Āndhra Mahābhāratamu
nodes.summary: The Telugu Mahābhārata of the “poet trinity” (kavitrayam): Nannaya began it under the Eastern Cāḷukya king Rājarāja Narēndra (11th c.), Tikkana wrote fifteen books from the Virāṭa onward (13th c.), and Errana completed the Araṇya book (14th c.).

dates.event: Nannaya’s portion (Ādi, Sabhā, part of Araṇya)
dates.label: c. 1054–1061 CE

sources.locator: V. Narayana Rao, ch. on Telugu

nodes.name: Raṅganātha Rāmāyaṇamu
nodes.summary: Telugu Rāmāyaṇa in dvipada couplets by Gona Budda Reddy (pen-name Raṅganātha), 13th–14th c. Its singable metre suited folk and puppet performance; it contains popular episodes absent from Vālmīki, such as the squirrel who helps build the bridge and Lakṣmaṇa drawing a protective line.

nodes.name: Āndhra Mahābhāgavatamu (Pōtana)
nodes.summary: Bammera Pōtana’s 15th-century Telugu rendering of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, dedicated not to a king but to Rāma; much loved for its Gajendra-mokṣa and Kṛṣṇa narratives.

sources.locator: V. Narayana Rao, ch. on Telugu

nodes.name: Vikramārjuna Vijaya (Pampa Bhārata)
nodes.summary: The Kannada Mahābhārata in campū form by the Jain poet Pampa, completed c. 941 CE at the court of the Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya Arikēsari II; Pampa equates his patron with the hero Arjuna.
nodes.details: Pollock (2006) treats Pampa’s two works — the Jain Ādipurāṇa and this “worldly” (laukika) epic — as founding texts of cosmopolitan vernacular literature in Kannada. A Jain poet’s Mahābhārata, it is not a Jain purāṇa: it follows the Bhārata story while making Arjuna, rather than Yudhiṣṭhira, the crowned hero, an identification with the patron.

dates.label: c. 941 CE
dates.basis: internal dating of Pampa’s works (Ādipurāṇa 941; the epic shortly after, or c. 939–941)
dates.view: sources differ on the order of the two works

sources.locator: D. R. Nagaraj, ch. on Kannada

nodes.name: Karṇāṭa Bhārata Kathāmañjarī (Gadugina Bhārata)
nodes.summary: Kumāravyāsa’s Kannada Mahābhārata (first ten books) in bhāminī ṣaṭpadi six-line stanzas, completed c. 1430 under the Vijayanagara king Dēvarāya II; it remains a living recitation text (gamaka) in Karnataka.
nodes.details: Local legend says it was composed in the Vīranārāyaṇa temple at Gadag, where a pillar bears the poet’s name.

sources.locator: D. R. Nagaraj, ch. on Kannada

nodes.name: Vacanas of Basavaṇṇa
nodes.summary: The free-verse Kannada sayings (vacana) attributed to Basava, addressed to Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva, criticising temple ritual and caste and exalting the devotee’s body as Śiva’s temple.
nodes.limits: The vacanas were compiled long after Basava; individual attributions are uncertain.

nodes.name: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam Kiḷippāṭṭu
nodes.summary: Eḻuttacchaṉ’s 16th-century Malayalam rendering of the Sanskrit Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa in the “parrot-song” form, in which a parrot recites the story; it is read aloud in Kerala households during the month of Karkkaṭakam.

nodes.name: Saptakāṇḍa Rāmāyaṇa (Assamese)
nodes.summary: Mādhava Kandali’s 14th-century Assamese rendering of Vālmīki, made for the Barāhī (Kachari) king Mahāmāṇikya — among the earliest renderings of a Sanskrit epic into a modern Indo-Aryan language. Its first and last books were lost and replaced in the 16th century by Mādhavadeva (Ādi) and Śaṅkaradeva (Uttara).
nodes.details: Kandali’s Rāma and Sītā are portrayed in human rather than divine terms, which later Vaiṣṇava readers considered unsuitable for devotional use — part of why Śaṅkaradeva and Mādhavadeva supplied new frame books.

nodes.name: Kīrtana Ghoṣā
nodes.summary: Śaṅkaradeva’s Assamese collection of devotional narrative songs, largely drawn from the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the core scripture recited in the nāmghars and sattras of Ekaśaraṇa Vaiṣṇavism.

nodes.name: Śāraḷā Mahābhārata
nodes.summary: Śāraḷā Dāsa’s 15th-century Odia Mahābhārata, begun under the Gajapati Kapilendra Deva (r. 1435–1467). It follows the Bhārata outline but adds many episodes and Odia local colour, written in colloquial, unsanskritised Odia.

nodes.name: Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: Śāraḷā Dāsa’s Odia narrative of a war against a thousand-headed Rāvaṇa of the land of Vilaṅkā, after the defeat of the ten-headed one — a theme shared with the Sanskrit Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa’s Sahasra-Rāvaṇa.
openQuestions: Does Sītā (as goddess) or Rāma kill the thousand-headed Rāvaṇa in Śāraḷā’s text? Sources consulted say only “a battle between Rāma and the thousand-headed Rāvaṇa”.

nodes.name: Odia Bhāgabata
nodes.summary: Jagannātha Dāsa’s Odia rendering of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (late 15th – early 16th c.), in a simple nine-syllable metre; it became the most widely read devotional book of Odisha and the basis of village Bhāgabata-ghara reading houses.

dates.label: late 15th – early 16th c. CE
dates.basis: Jagannātha Dāsa’s association with Caitanya’s time at Puri

nodes.name: Manasāmaṅgal
nodes.summary: Bengali Maṅgalkāvya narratives of the snake goddess Manasā, centred on the merchant Cā̃d Sadāgar’s refusal to worship her and the devotion of his daughter-in-law Behulā, who wins back her dead husband Lakhindar.
nodes.details: Many poets composed Manasāmaṅgals; among the earliest named are Bijay Gupta and Bipradās Pipilāi (late 15th c.).

nodes.name: Caitanya Caritāmṛta
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja’s Bengali–Sanskrit biography and theology of Caitanya (early 17th c.), which the Gauḍīya tradition treats as definitive; it presents Caitanya as Kṛṣṇa who took on the emotion and complexion of Rādhā.

nodes.name: Eknāthī Bhāgavata
nodes.summary: Eknāth’s Marathi ovī commentary on the eleventh book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (the Uddhava-gītā), 16th c.

nodes.name: Tukārām Gāthā
nodes.summary: The collection of Marathi abhaṅgas attributed to Tukārām (traditionally c. 4,500), sung by Vārkarī pilgrims on the road to Pandharpur.
nodes.limits: Manuscripts are unsystematic collections; individual abhaṅgas cannot all be securely attributed.

nodes.name: Sūrsāgar
nodes.summary: The “Ocean of Sūr”: the corpus of Braj Bhāṣā songs attributed to Sūrdās, chiefly on Kṛṣṇa’s childhood and the love of Rādhā and the gopīs, arranged in later recensions in twelve books after the Bhāgavata. Most of the received corpus is later than Sūr; Hawley and Bryant reconstruct an early core from manuscripts.
nodes.details: The earliest dated manuscript containing poems in Sūr’s name is reported by Hawley as the Fatehpur manuscript of VS 1639 (1582 CE); it contains a few hundred poems, far fewer than the thousands of the later vulgate.

dates.label: 1582 CE (VS 1639)
dates.basis: manuscript colophon as reported by Hawley (not checked in this session)

nodes.limits: Attribution of individual songs to Sūrdās is mostly uncertain.

nodes.name: Hanumān Cālīsā
nodes.summary: Forty-verse Awadhi hymn to Hanumān, traditionally attributed to Tulsīdās and now the most widely recited Hindu devotional hymn in North India.
nodes.limits: The attribution to Tulsīdās is traditional; Lutgendorf (2007) notes it is not secure.

nodes.name: Vākhs of Lal Ded
nodes.summary: Kashmiri four-line mystical sayings (vākh) attributed to the 14th-century yoginī Lal Ded (Lallā), venerated by Hindus as Lalleśvarī and by Muslims as Lal ʿĀrifa; they survived orally and were first written down systematically in the 20th century.
nodes.limits: Recorded from oral tradition some six centuries after her lifetime; attributions are uncertain.

nodes.name: Gāhā Sattasaī
nodes.summary: An anthology of 700 Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit love verses attributed to the Sātavāhana king Hāla; dated between the 1st and 7th centuries (before Bāṇa, 7th c.). One verse mentions Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā, the earliest known literary mention of her.

dates.label: c. 3rd–4th c. CE
dates.basis: language; cited by Bāṇa before 640 CE

dates.label: by King Hāla (1st c. CE in tradition)

nodes.limits: The verses circulated in recensions; a given verse may be later than the anthology’s core.

nodes.name: Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: A Sanskrit Śākta-inflected Rāma narrative in 27 sargas framed as a secret telling by Vālmīki to Bharadvāja. Sītā is born to Mandodarī, and in the climax she takes the form of Mahākālī and destroys the thousand-headed Sahasra-Rāvaṇa after Rāma falls unconscious.
openQuestions: A secure date is lacking; scholarly study of the text has been minor.

nodes.name: Bhaṭṭikāvya (Rāvaṇavadha)
nodes.summary: Bhaṭṭi’s 6th–7th-century Sanskrit mahākāvya telling the Rāma story while illustrating the rules of Pāṇini’s grammar; it was the model for the first half of the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Uttarapurāṇa of Guṇabhadra
nodes.summary: The 9th-century Digambara Jain Sanskrit universal history completing Jinasena’s Ādipurāṇa; its Rāma section follows a different Jain line from Vimalasūri, making Sītā the daughter of Rāvaṇa and Mandodarī, abandoned at birth because of a prophecy.

nodes.name: Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra
nodes.summary: A Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra (c. 4th–5th c.) whose frame story has the Buddha visiting Laṅkā at the invitation of its king Rāvaṇa, who questions him on the dharma.
nodes.limits: Its Rāvaṇa is a devout questioner; the sūtra does not narrate the Rāmāyaṇa story.

nodes.name: Hikayat Seri Rama (Malay)
nodes.summary: The Malay prose Rāma narrative, put into its present form between the 13th and 17th centuries, with Islamic framing in some versions (Dasaratha as a descendant of the prophet Adam). Its oldest manuscript, in the Bodleian Library, was acquired by Archbishop Laud by 1633.
nodes.details: Characters: Seri Rama, Siti Dewi (Sītā), Laksamana, Maharaja Wana (Rāvaṇa), Hanuman Kera Putih. A related shadow-play repertoire (Hikayat Maharaja Wana) was among the most important wayang kulit tellings of the Malay peninsula.

nodes.name: Yama Zatdaw (Burmese)
nodes.summary: The Burmese Rāma tradition (Yamayana), known in Bagan-period terracottas as the Dasaratha Jātaka and in literature from a 1527 pyo poem; it was reshaped in the Konbaung period by Thai court drama brought back after the conquest of Ayutthaya.
nodes.details: Names: Yama (Rāma), Me Thida (Sītā), Lakkhana, Dasagiri (Rāvaṇa). Often called Myanmar’s unofficial national epic.

nodes.name: Phra Lak Phra Lam (Lao)
nodes.summary: The Lao Rāma epic, framed as a jātaka: Phra Lam is a previous birth of the Buddha, and Rāvaṇa (Hapmanasouane) is his cousin, compared with Devadatta or Māra. Versions were recorded on palm leaf from the 15th to the early 19th century.
nodes.details: Nang Sida is the daughter of Thôtsakane (Rāvaṇa) and Nang Chanta in the Lao character lists — another telling where Sītā is Rāvaṇa’s daughter.

nodes.name: Jayākhya Saṃhitā
nodes.summary: One of the “three gems” of the Pāñcarātra canon, a ritual and theological saṃhitā edited in 1931; its date is disputed, from an early proposal of c. 5th c. to later scholarship placing it around the 8th–9th c.

nodes.name: Sāttvata Saṃhitā
nodes.summary: Among the oldest and most authoritative Pāñcarātra saṃhitās (one of the “three gems”), with a commentary by Alaśiṅga Bhaṭṭa; date disputed.

nodes.name: Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā
nodes.summary: Pāñcarātra saṃhitā known for its doctrine of the Sudarśana (Viṣṇu’s discus) and its cosmology; the subject of Schrader’s pioneering 1916 study, which placed it early, a dating later scholars question.

nodes.name: Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā
nodes.summary: The earliest surviving tantra of the Śaiva Mantramārga, in five books; its editors date the oldest layer (Mūlasūtra) to c. 450–550 CE. It preserves an early stage of Śaiva Siddhānta ritual and the transition from the Atimārga.

dates.label: c. 450–550 CE
dates.basis: internal evidence; relationship to Pāśupata and Purāṇic material

nodes.name: Brahmayāmala (Picumata)
nodes.summary: An early Vidyāpīṭha tantra of the Bhairava stream, centred on Kapālīśabhairava and the goddess Caṇḍā Kāpālinī with their yoginīs; studied by Hatley as a key source for early Śākta-Śaiva yoginī cults.

dates.label: c. 7th–9th c. CE
dates.basis: Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript evidence and internal evidence

nodes.name: Civañāṉapōtam (Śivajñānabodham)
nodes.summary: Meykaṇṭār’s 13th-century twelve-sūtra Tamil treatise that founded the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta school; tradition calls it a rendering of twelve Sanskrit verses from the Raurava Āgama, a claim scholars treat cautiously.

nodes.name: Tantrāloka
nodes.summary: Abhinavagupta’s encyclopaedic Sanskrit exposition of Trika Śaiva ritual and doctrine (c. 1000 CE), in thirty-seven chapters, based above all on the Mālinīvijayottara Tantra.

nodes.name: Nāthamuni
nodes.summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya (9th–10th c.) of Vīranārāyaṇapuram (Kāṭṭumaṉṉārkōyil), credited with collecting and arranging the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham and setting it to music; grandfather of Yāmuna.

nodes.name: Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi
nodes.summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-compiler of Tirunāraiyūr (10th–11th c.) who arranged the Tēvāram and other hymns into the first eleven books of the Tirumurai; tradition links his work to Rājarāja I.

nodes.name: Māṇikkavācakar
nodes.summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint, author of the Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār (Tirumurai 8); hagiography makes him a minister of a Pāṇḍya king who renounced office after meeting Śiva at Tirupperuntuṟai. Most scholars place him in the 9th century, though earlier dates are proposed.

nodes.name: Cēkkiḻār
nodes.summary: Tamil poet and minister at the court of the Cōḻa king Kulōttuṅka II (12th c.), author of the Periya Purāṇam.

nodes.name: Nakkīrar
nodes.summary: Tamil poet to whom the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai is attributed; tradition (including the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam) makes him the president of the Madurai academy (caṅkam) who dared to challenge Śiva’s poem.

dates.label: late Caṅkam (c. 3rd–6th c. CE)
dates.basis: date of the poem; several poets of the name may be conflated

nodes.name: Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ
nodes.summary: The “venerable prince-ascetic,” brother of the Cēra king Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ according to the prologue of the Cilappatikāram, to whom the epic is attributed; the attribution rests on a later prologue and is doubted.
nodes.limits: Historicity and authorship uncertain.

nodes.name: Periyāḻvār
nodes.summary: Āḻvār of Śrīvilliputtūr (8th–9th c.), author of the Periyāḻvār Tirumoḻi with its celebrated poems of Kṛṣṇa’s infancy and of the Tiruppallāṇṭu; foster-father of Āṇṭāḷ.

nodes.name: Nannaya
nodes.summary: Telugu poet (11th c.), “first poet” (ādikavi) of Telugu, who began the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu at the request of the Eastern Cāḷukya king Rājarāja Narēndra.

nodes.name: Tikkana
nodes.summary: Telugu poet and minister (13th c.) who rendered fifteen books (Virāṭa to Svargārohaṇa) of the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu.

nodes.name: Errana
nodes.summary: Telugu poet (14th c.) at the court of Prolaya Vēma Reḍḍi who completed the Araṇya book of the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu.

nodes.name: Gona Budda Reddy (Raṅganātha)
nodes.summary: Telugu poet (13th–14th c.), author under the pen-name Raṅganātha of the dvipada Raṅganātha Rāmāyaṇamu.

nodes.name: Bammera Pōtana
nodes.summary: Telugu poet (15th c.) of Bammera near Warangal, author of the Āndhra Mahābhāgavatamu, who according to tradition refused to dedicate his work to the king of Rācakoṇḍa and offered it to Rāma.

nodes.name: Pampa (Ādikavi Pampa)
nodes.summary: Jain Kannada poet (902–c. 955) at the Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya court of Arikēsari II, author of the Ādipurāṇa (941) and the Vikramārjuna Vijaya.

nodes.name: Kumāravyāsa
nodes.summary: Kannada poet (Nāraṇappa, early 15th c.) of Gadag, author of the Karṇāṭa Bhārata Kathāmañjarī, active under Dēvarāya II of Vijayanagara.

nodes.name: Tuñcattu Rāmānujaṉ Eḻuttacchaṉ
nodes.summary: Malayalam poet (16th c.), called the father of modern Malayalam literature, author of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam Kiḷippāṭṭu and a Mahābhāratam Kiḷippāṭṭu.

dates.label: c. 1495–1575 CE (Ulloor); 16th–17th c. in other views

nodes.name: Mādhava Kandali
nodes.summary: Assamese poet (14th c.) who rendered Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa into Assamese for the Barāhī king Mahāmāṇikya.

nodes.name: Śrīmanta Śaṅkaradeva
nodes.summary: Assamese saint, poet, dramatist and founder of Ekaśaraṇa Vaiṣṇavism (traditionally 1449–1568, after the hagiographies), author of the Kīrtana Ghoṣā, the Aṅkīyā Nāṭ one-act plays and the Bargīt songs, and of the Uttara kāṇḍa of the Assamese Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Mādhavadeva
nodes.summary: Assamese poet and chief disciple of Śaṅkaradeva (16th c.), author of the Nām Ghoṣā and of the Ādi kāṇḍa of the Assamese Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Śāraḷā Dāsa
nodes.summary: Odia poet (15th c.) of the reign of the Gajapati Kapilendra Deva, author of the Odia Mahābhārata, the Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa and the Caṇḍī Purāṇa; his name, “by the grace of Sāraḷā,” refers to his goddess.

nodes.name: Jagannātha Dāsa
nodes.summary: Odia poet (late 15th – 16th c.) of Puri, one of the Pañcasakhā, author of the Odia Bhāgabata and founder of the Atibaḍī tradition.

nodes.name: Eknāth
nodes.summary: Marathi poet-saint of Paiṭhaṇ (c. 1533–1599), author of the Eknāthī Bhāgavata and the Bhāvārtha Rāmāyaṇa, who produced a corrected text of the Jñāneśvarī in 1584.

nodes.name: Tukārām
nodes.summary: Marathi poet-saint of Dehū (1608 or 1598 – 1649/1650), a grocer by caste whose abhaṅgas to Viṭṭhala are central to the Vārkarī pilgrimage.

dates.label: 1598/1608 – 1649/1650 CE
dates.basis: competing reconstructions; death in 1650 widely accepted

nodes.name: Nāmdev
nodes.summary: Marathi poet-saint (traditionally 1270–1350), a tailor of Pandharpur, devotee of Viṭṭhala and contemporary of Jñāneśvar; songs attributed to him are also in the Sikh Ādi Granth.

nodes.name: Sūrdās
nodes.summary: Braj Bhāṣā poet-singer of the 16th century to whom the Sūrsāgar is attributed; hagiography makes him blind and a disciple of Vallabha, claims modern scholarship treats as later constructions.

nodes.name: Lal Ded (Lalleśvarī)
nodes.summary: Kashmiri yoginī-poet of the 14th century, revered by Hindus as Lalleśvarī and by Muslims as Lal ʿĀrifa, to whom the vākhs are attributed.

nodes.name: Narsinh Mehtā
nodes.summary: Gujarati poet-saint of Junagadh (c. 1414 – 1480s), honoured as the Ādi Kavi of Gujarati, devotee of Kṛṣṇa and author of the bhajan “Vaiṣṇava jana to.”

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja
nodes.summary: Gauḍīya poet-theologian of Vṛndāvana (16th–17th c.), author of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta.

nodes.name: Meykaṇṭār
nodes.summary: Tamil Śaiva theologian (13th c.) of Tiruveṇṇainallūr, author of the Civañāṉapōtam and founder of the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta lineage.

nodes.name: Abhinavagupta
nodes.summary: Kashmirian Śaiva philosopher and aesthetician (fl. c. 975–1025), author of the Tantrāloka, of commentaries on Utpaladeva’s Pratyabhijñā and of the Abhinavabhāratī on the Nāṭyaśāstra.

nodes.name: Rama I (Phutthayotfa Chulalok)
nodes.summary: First king of the Chakri dynasty of Siam (r. 1782–1809), founder of Bangkok, under whom the canonical Ramakien was compiled (1797–1807), partly by the king himself.

nodes.name: Kulōttuṅka Cōḻa II
nodes.summary: Cōḻa king (r. 1133–1150) at whose court Cēkkiḻār composed the Periya Purāṇam; Śaiva tradition associates him with the expansion of the Chidambaram temple.

nodes.name: Lakṣmaṇasena
nodes.summary: King of the Sena dynasty of Bengal (r. c. 1178–1206), at whose court tradition places Jayadeva together with the poets Umāpatidhara, Śaraṇa, Govardhana and Dhoyī.

nodes.name: Arikēsari II
nodes.summary: Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya ruler (10th c.), a feudatory of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa Kṛṣṇa III, patron of Pampa, who equated him with Arjuna in the Vikramārjuna Vijaya.

nodes.name: Viṭṭhala (Viṭhobā) of Pandharpur
nodes.summary: The deity of Pandharpur in Maharashtra, standing with hands on hips upon a brick, worshipped by Vārkarīs as a form of Kṛṣṇa/Viṣṇu; scholars debate his origins (pastoral hero-stone, Jain, Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava elements).
nodes.details: The Puṇḍalīka legend explains the brick: Kṛṣṇa came to the devotee Puṇḍalīka, who, busy serving his parents, threw him a brick to stand on, and the god remains standing there. Dhere (2011) reads Viṭṭhala as an amalgam of pastoral hero-gods of the Dhangar herders absorbed into Kṛṣṇa devotion; Deleury suggested a hero-stone origin. A monument dated 1189 and a Hoysala inscription of 1237 are the earliest dated references noted in the literature.

dates.label: 1189 (monument) and 1237 CE (inscription)
dates.basis: inscriptions as reported in secondary literature

nodes.limits: Inscriptions attest worship at Pandharpur by the late 12th–13th c.; they do not settle the deity’s origins.

nodes.name: Māyōṉ (Tamil)
nodes.summary: The “dark one,” presiding deity of the mullai (forest-pasture) landscape in the Tolkāppiyam, and in Caṅkam poetry a dark cowherd god (also called Māl, Tirumāl) later identified with Viṣṇu and Kṛṣṇa. Kept distinct from deity:vishnu and joined by IDENTIFIED_WITH.
nodes.details: Hardy (1983) argues that the Tamil cowherd god of the mullai landscape, with his beloved Piññai and his dances with cowherd girls, contributed to the emotional (viraha) bhakti later expressed by the Āḻvārs and, through the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, to pan-Indian Kṛṣṇa devotion.
nodes.limits: The name Māyōṉ in the sūtra does not by itself establish a theology identical with Sanskrit Viṣṇu.

nodes.name: Nappiṉṉai (Piññai)
nodes.summary: The Tamil cowherd girl beloved of Kṛṣṇa (Māyavaṉ) in the Cilappatikāram’s round-dance of the cowherdesses and in the Āḻvārs’ hymns, where she is his consort; some scholars see her as a southern parallel or precursor of Rādhā, others identify her with Nīḷā Devī.
nodes.limits: Whether Piññai and Rādhā share an origin is a scholarly hypothesis; the texts keep them apart.

nodes.name: Vaḷḷi
nodes.summary: Murukaṉ’s Tamil consort, a hunter (kuṟava) girl of the hills whom the god woos in disguise; she stands beside Teyvāṉai (Devasenā), daughter of Indra, in Tamil tradition.

nodes.name: Suvannamaccha
nodes.summary: Mermaid princess, daughter of Thotsakan (Rāvaṇa), in Thai and other Southeast Asian Rāma tellings; sent to sabotage the causeway to Laṅkā, she falls in love with Hanumān and bears him a son, Macchanu.
nodes.limits: Absent from Vālmīki; a Southeast Asian figure.

nodes.name: Macchanu
nodes.summary: Son of Hanumān and the mermaid Suvannamaccha in the Ramakien, half monkey and half fish, who later meets and fights his father before they recognise each other.

nodes.name: Thotsakan
nodes.summary: The ten-faced king of Laṅkā in the Thai Ramakien — the counterpart of Rāvaṇa (the name renders Daśakaṇṭha) — who in this telling is the father of Sida, keeps his heart outside his body, and dies when Hanumān crushes it.
nodes.limits: Kept separate from char:ravana because the Ramakien gives him a different family and fate; identified with Rāvaṇa by an assertion.

nodes.name: Māyā-Sītā (the illusory Sītā)
nodes.summary: The illusory double or reflection of Sītā who, in the Kūrma Purāṇa, Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa and Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas, is the one Rāvaṇa abducts while the real Sītā is kept safe in Agni.
nodes.details: In the Mānas Rāma says: “tumha pāvaka mahuṃ karahu nivāsā, jau lagi karauṃ nisācara nāsā” (“dwell in the fire until I destroy the night-rovers”) and Sītā leaves “nija pratibimba,” her own reflection, “of the same character, form and modesty”; not even Lakṣmaṇa knows. At the fire-ordeal the reflection and the worldly stain burn in the fire and Agni returns the true Śrī to Rāma. Doniger (1999) traces the motif’s development and its theological work: protecting Sītā’s purity and recasting the ordeal.
nodes.limits: A theological and narrative motif of particular texts; not present in Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Bhāmaṇḍala
nodes.summary: In Jain Rāma tellings (Vimalasūri’s Paumacariya and successors), Sītā’s twin brother, carried off at birth and raised as a vidyādhara prince, who falls in love with Sītā from her portrait and seeks her hand before learning that she is his twin sister.

earliestText.label: c. 1st–5th c. CE (not later than the 3rd c. in the commonest view)

nodes.name: Sahasra-Rāvaṇa (the thousand-headed Rāvaṇa)
nodes.summary: A thousand-headed elder brother or double of Rāvaṇa who, in the Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa, is destroyed by Sītā in the form of Mahākālī after Rāma is struck down; a thousand-headed Rāvaṇa is also fought in Śāraḷā Dāsa’s Odia Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Kaṇṇaki
nodes.summary: Heroine of the Cilappatikāram, who proves her executed husband Kōvalaṉ innocent before the Pāṇḍya king, burns Madurai with her curse and is deified as the chaste goddess Pattiṉi, worshipped in Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Sri Lanka.

earliestMaterial.label: modern buildings (date not given in the reference)

nodes.name: Pandharpur
nodes.summary: Town on the Bhīmā (Candrabhāgā) river in Maharashtra, seat of the Viṭṭhala temple and goal of the Vārkarī pilgrimages (vārī) of Āṣāḍha and Kārttika.

nodes.name: Śrīvilliputtūr
nodes.summary: Temple town in Virudhunagar district, Tamil Nadu, home of Periyāḻvār and Āṇṭāḷ according to tradition, with twin shrines of Āṇṭāḷ and Vaṭapatrasāyī (Raṅganātha).

location.label: Srivilliputhur, Virudhunagar district, Tamil Nadu, India

nodes.name: Nevāsā
nodes.summary: Town on the Pravarā near its confluence with the Godāvarī (Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra), identified by tradition as the place where the Jñāneśvarī was composed, home of the Mohinīrāja (Mahālayā) temple named in the colophon.
nodes.limits: The colophon names the Godāvarī bank and Śrī Mahālayā; the identification with Nevāsā is traditional.

nodes.name: Vārkarī
nodes.summary: The Marathi devotional tradition of Viṭṭhala of Pandharpur, carried by pilgrims (vārkarī) who walk to Pandharpur twice a year singing the abhaṅgas of Jñāneśvar, Nāmdev, Eknāth, Tukārām and other saints.

nodes.name: Ekaśaraṇa Dharma
nodes.summary: The Assamese Vaiṣṇava movement founded by Śaṅkaradeva (15th–16th c.): exclusive refuge in Kṛṣṇa through congregational singing and hearing of his name and deeds, organised in sattras and village nāmghars; Rādhā is not worshipped alongside Kṛṣṇa.

nodes.name: Puṣṭimārga
nodes.summary: The Kṛṣṇa tradition founded by Vallabha (16th c.), centred on Śrīnāthjī and the “eight seals” (aṣṭachāp) of poets, among whom it counts Sūrdās.

nodes.name: Rāmānandī
nodes.summary: The North Indian Vaiṣṇava ascetic order tracing itself to Rāmānanda, centred on Rāma and Sītā; it claims Tulsīdās and is traditionally associated with the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Rāmlīlā
nodes.summary: North Indian staged performance of the Rāma story based on Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas, held around Dussehra over ten to twelve days or (at Ramnagar, Varanasi) a month; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2005).
nodes.details: UNESCO names the Rāmlīlās of Ayodhyā, Ramnagar, Banaras, Vṛndāvan, Almora, Sattna and Madhubani as the most representative. Lutgendorf (1991) describes the Ramnagar Rāmlīlā patronised by the Mahārājā of Banaras as an environmental performance in which the audience moves with the action across the town.

nodes.name: Kūṭiyāṭṭam
nodes.summary: Sanskrit theatre of Kerala performed by Cākyār and Nampyār families in temple theatres (kūttampalam), with long elaborations of single acts of Sanskrit plays (including Rāma plays); inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2001).

nodes.name: Yakṣagāna
nodes.summary: Dance-drama of coastal Karnataka, led by a singer-narrator (bhāgavata), performing episodes (prasaṅga) from the Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata; an inscription of 1556 at Kurugodu records land given to performers.

dates.label: 1556 CE
dates.basis: inscription as reported in secondary literature

nodes.name: Kathakaḷi
nodes.summary: Kerala dance-drama that crystallised in the 16th–17th centuries from Rāmanāṭṭam (attributed to the Kottarakkara Tampurāṉ) and Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam (of the Zamorin Mānavēdaṉ), performing Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata stories.

nodes.name: Wayang
nodes.summary: Indonesian puppet and shadow theatre (wayang kulit and related forms) led by a dalang with gamelan, performing stories from the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa among others; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2003).

nodes.name: Khon
nodes.summary: Thai masked dance-drama performing episodes of the Ramakien, historically a court art; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2018 as “Khon, masked dance drama in Thailand.”

nodes.name: Royal Ballet of Cambodia
nodes.summary: Khmer classical court dance, whose repertoire includes Reamker episodes; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2003).
nodes.limits: The UNESCO record itself does not name the Reamker; the repertoire link rests on secondary literature.

nodes.name: Triyampawai–Trippawai ceremony
nodes.summary: Thai royal Brahman new-year ceremony (December–January) whose name comes from two Tamil devotional poems — Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai and Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai — and during which hymns from these collections are chanted; it was historically linked to the Giant Swing in Bangkok.
nodes.details: McGovern (2017) writes that “Trīyampawāi is a corruption of Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai, and Trīppawāi is likewise a corruption of Āṇḍāḷ’s Tiruppāvai,” and reports Tamil texts in Thai and Grantha scripts in the National Library, Bangkok, together with recordings of the hymns sung in the ceremony. The present court Brahmans speak no Indian language.
nodes.limits: Shows the circulation of Tamil hymn names and texts into Thai court ritual; it does not show when or by whom they were brought.

nodes.name: Cāḷukyas of Vēmulavāḍa
nodes.summary: A 9th–10th-century dynasty in northern Telangana, feudatories of the Rāṣṭrakūṭas, patrons of the Kannada poet Pampa under Arikēsari II.

nodes.name: Rattanakosin Kingdom (Chakri dynasty)
nodes.summary: The Siamese kingdom ruled from Bangkok by the Chakri dynasty from 1782, under whose first kings the Ramakien was compiled and the Wat Phra Kaew murals painted.

nodes.name: Sena dynasty of Bengal
nodes.summary: Dynasty ruling Bengal in the 11th–13th centuries, whose king Lakṣmaṇasena is traditionally Jayadeva’s patron.

nodes.name: The Prambanan Rāmāyaṇa reliefs illustrate the Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: The claim that the 9th-century Rāmāyaṇa reliefs on the Śiva and Brahmā temples at Prambanan follow the Old Javanese Kakawin. Since Stutterheim (1925) scholars have noted episodes that diverge from the Kakawin and suggest another, possibly oral, telling.
nodes.limits: Both the reliefs and the poem belong to the Medang period; contemporaneity does not establish that one illustrates the other.

nodes.name: Sūrdās was a disciple of Vallabha
nodes.summary: The Puṣṭimārga hagiographic claim (Caurāsī Vaiṣṇavan kī Vārtā) that Sūrdās was initiated by Vallabha and became one of the aṣṭachāp poets; Hawley argues the connection is a later sectarian construction.

nodes.name: Basava founded the Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata tradition
nodes.summary: The traditional claim that Basava founded the Liṅgāyata community; modern scholars using Kalacuri-period inscriptions and the vacana corpus often see him as a reformer and organiser of an existing Śaiva milieu.

nodes.name: The Dasaratha Jātaka preserves an older form of the Rāma story than Vālmīki
nodes.summary: Argued in the 19th century (notably by Albrecht Weber) because of the jātaka’s simpler plot and sibling-marriage motif; most later scholars regard it as a Buddhist reworking of a story already known in Rāmāyaṇa form, though its verses may be old.

nodes.name: Dīpāvalī (Diwali)
nodes.summary: The autumn festival of lamps, spread over about five days around the new moon of Āśvina/Kārttika and observed across India and the diaspora. Different regions and communities give it different reasons — Kṛṣṇa’s killing of Narakāsura, Lakṣmī’s worship, Bali’s yearly reign, Rāma’s return to Ayodhyā, Kālī’s worship in Bengal, and Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa for Jains — which are recorded here as separate, unharmonised associations. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2025.
nodes.details:
Kane (1958) describes Dīpāvalī as not a festival of a single deity but a cluster of about five days with independent items: worship of wealth (13th of the dark half, Dhanteras), Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa’s victory over Narakāsura (14th), the worship of Lakṣmī (new moon), Viṣṇu’s victory over Bali and dice-play (Kārttika śukla 1, Balipratipadā), and the exchange of brotherly and sisterly affection (Bhrātṛdvitīyā). He notes older names: Yakṣarātri in Vātsyāyana’s Kāmasūtra, Sukhasuptikā in the Nīlamata Purāṇa (vv. 505–510) and in Hemādri, and Dīpālikā; the Bhaviṣyottara (ch. 140) gives the fullest description of the four days from the 14th. In Bengal the new-moon night is Kālī Pūjā.

UNESCO’s 2025 inscription describes Deepavali as marking the last harvest of the year and the start of a new year and season, and as symbolising the victory of light over darkness and good over evil; the element is tagged with the concepts “epic poetry” and “diaspora”.

dates.event: earliest textual names (Yakṣarātri in the Kāmasūtra; Sukhasuptikā in the Nīlamata)
dates.label: early centuries CE onward
dates.basis: literary references collected by Kane; the texts’ own dates are uncertain

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. X, pp. 194–209

nodes.limits: The festival’s several explanatory stories belong to different regions and periods; none of them is treated here as the original reason.

nodes.name: Naraka Caturdaśī
nodes.summary: The 14th of the dark half of Āśvina (Kārttika in the pūrṇimānta reckoning), the day before the Dīpāvalī new moon: a dawn oil-bath, a lamp lit for Naraka, and, in the south and west, the celebration of Kṛṣṇa’s killing of Narakāsura. Kane argues that the day was originally named for propitiating Yama against hell (naraka), and that the Narakāsura legend was attached later.
nodes.details: Kane: the Bhaviṣyottara prescribes an oil bath at daybreak, whirling apāmārga twigs over the head, tarpaṇa to Yama under seven names, a lamp for Naraka and illuminations in temples and public places; “It appears probable that originally the 14th was called Narakacaturdaśī because Yama was to be propitiated for fear of Hell. Later on the legend about the killing by Kṛṣṇa of Narakāsura, king of Prāgjyotiṣa (Kāmarūpa) … was pressed into service.” In the Deccan people crush a bitter fruit underfoot after the bath, which Kane takes to represent Narakāsura. The Kṛttyatattva calls the day Bhūtacaturdaśī.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. X, pp. 196–198

nodes.limits: Kane’s reconstruction of the day’s origin is a scholarly interpretation (class 5).

nodes.name: Lakṣmī Pūjā of Dīpāvalī
nodes.summary: The worship of Lakṣmī (with Kubera in some digests) on the new-moon night of Āśvina/Kārttika, the central night of Dīpāvalī in much of north and west India; merchants close their old account books and open new ones. The Bhaviṣyottara (ch. 140) and the Nīlamata Purāṇa (Sukhasuptikā) describe the night with lamps everywhere and the driving out of Alakṣmī (ill luck) at midnight.
nodes.details: Kane: “There is a popular legend that Brahmā gave to brāhmaṇas rakṣābandhana … as their festival, Dasara to kṣatriyas, Dīvālī to traders and Holikā to śūdras.” The Bhaviṣyottara has the king proclaim “today is the sovereignty of Bali; O people! enjoy yourselves”, and women beat winnowing baskets and drums at midnight to drive out Alakṣmī.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. X, pp. 199–201

nodes.name: Kālī Pūjā (Bengal)
nodes.summary: The worship of Kālī on the new-moon night of Kārttika in Bengal, Assam and Odisha — the same night on which much of India worships Lakṣmī for Dīpāvalī. Kane notes that in Bengal Kālī is worshipped on this day; McDermott traces its spread as a large public festival in Bengal from the eighteenth century.
nodes.limits: The eighteenth-century spread is a scholarly reconstruction (McDermott 2011), not checked here.

nodes.name: Balipratipadā
nodes.summary: The first day of the bright half of Kārttika, the day after the Dīpāvalī new moon, on which Bali, the asura king sent to the netherworld by Vāmana, is worshipped and said to reign for a day; it is also the day of dice-play (dyūta-pratipad) and, in the north, of Govardhana Pūjā. The Bhaviṣyottara (140.47–73) prescribes drawing Bali with his queen Vindhyāvalī and worshipping him with the mantra “salutation to you, O king Bali, son of Virocana … the future Indra”.
nodes.details: Kane connects the day with the Vāmana–Bali story (Brahma Purāṇa 73, Kūrma 1.17, Vāmana ch. 77 etc.) and cites the Mahābhāṣya on Pāṇini 3.1.26, where one who “recites the story of Bali’s imprisonment or represents it on the stage” is said to make Bali bound (Baliṃ bandhayati) — evidence that the story was dramatised long before the festival texts. The Vāmana Purāṇa calls the day Vīrapratipadā; the Purāṇas say Śiva lost to Pārvatī at dice on this day, hence the custom of gambling.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. X, pp. 199–204

nodes.name: Govardhana Pūjā and Annakūṭa
nodes.summary: Worship of Mount Govardhana and the offering of a “mountain of food” (annakūṭa) to Kṛṣṇa on Kārttika śukla 1, the day after the Dīpāvalī new moon, recalling Kṛṣṇa’s turning the cowherds from Indra’s worship to the hill and lifting it against Indra’s storm. Central in Braj and in the Puṣṭimārga temples.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, p. 205 (Padma Purāṇa calls it Annakūṭa, per the Smṛtikaustubha); list entry “Govardhanapūjā” citing Harivaṃśa 2.17

nodes.name: Bhrātṛdvitīyā (Bhai Dūj / Yamadvitīyā)
nodes.summary: The second day of the bright half of Kārttika, closing Dīpāvalī, on which sisters feed and bless their brothers; the Bhaviṣya tells that Yamunā fed her brother Yama on this day, hence the name Yamadvitīyā.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. X, pp. 207–209

nodes.name: Holī
nodes.summary: The spring festival of the Phālguna full moon: a bonfire (Holikā-dahana) on the full-moon night, followed by the throwing of coloured water and powder. Kane traces the name to Holākā, a usage known to Jaimini’s Mīmāṃsā sūtras (as explained by Śabara) and the Kāṭhaka Gṛhya, and regards it in origin as a spring festival; popular legend explains the bonfire by the burning of Holikā, who tried to kill Prahlāda, while Braj celebrates Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa’s play with colours.
nodes.details:
Kane: “Holī or Holikā is a festival of unmixed gaiety and frolics throughout India … One element, viz. bonfire, is present almost everywhere except in Bengal.” The Kāmasūtra (1.4.42) names Holākā, which the Jayamaṅgalā commentary explains as sprinkling with coloured water from horns on the Phālguna full moon. Hemādri quotes a long Bhaviṣyottara passage (ch. 132) in which Kṛṣṇa tells Yudhiṣṭhira of an ogress Ḍhauṇḍhā (Dhondhā) who troubled children in king Raghu’s realm and was destroyed by boys’ noise and a bonfire with rakṣoghna mantras; the next day the ashes are saluted and Kāma is worshipped. Bengal instead celebrates the Dolayātrā (swing festival of Kṛṣṇa). In the Deccan colour is thrown on the fifth day (Raṅgapañcamī). In South India the bonfire night is Kāma-dahanam, recalling Śiva’s burning of Kāma (reference sources).

Kane does not mention the Holikā–Prahlāda story, which is the explanation most widely told today (see char:holika).

dates.label: centuries around the turn of the era (Kane: “at least some centuries before Christ”)
dates.basis: mention of Holākā by Jaimini (as read by Śabara) and in the Kāṭhaka Gṛhya

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. XII, pp. 237–241

nodes.limits: The antiquity argued by Kane rests on the identification of Holākā with Holī and on disputed dates for the sūtras.

nodes.name: Holikā (sister of Hiraṇyakaśipu)
nodes.summary: In the legend most widely told for Holī, the sister of the asura king Hiraṇyakaśipu, immune to fire, who sat in a pyre with the child Prahlāda to burn him; she was consumed and Prahlāda survived. The bonfire on the eve of Holī is called Holikā-dahana after her.
nodes.details: The Sanskrit vrata literature summarised by Kane explains the Holikā bonfire with a different story — the ogress Ḍhauṇḍhā of the Bhaviṣyottara (char:dhaundha) — and treats Holikā as the name of the festival itself. The textual history of the Holikā–Prahlāda version was not traced in this round.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. XII, pp. 237–241

openQuestions: Which Purāṇic or vernacular text first tells the Holikā–Prahlāda episode?

nodes.name: Ḍhauṇḍhā (Dhondhā), the ogress of the Bhaviṣyottara
nodes.summary: An ogress, daughter of Mālin, who in the Bhaviṣyottara’s account of Holī troubled children in king Raghu’s realm; protected by Śiva’s boon from gods, men, weapons and weather, she could be overcome only by boisterous boys, and died when they lit a bonfire with rakṣoghna mantras on the Phālguna full moon.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. XII, pp. 238–239

nodes.name: Dolayātrā (Dol Pūrṇimā)
nodes.summary: The swing festival of Kṛṣṇa on the Phālguna full moon in Bengal and Odisha, Bengal’s form of Holī: an image of Govinda is installed on a swing in a sixteen-pillared pavilion, bathed and swung, with coloured powder (abir). Śūlapāṇi wrote a Dolayātrāviveka on it, recording the tradition that king Indradyumna began the swing festival in Vṛndāvana. Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas keep the day as Caitanya’s birthday (Gaura Pūrṇimā).

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. XII, pp. 239–240

nodes.name: Navarātri
nodes.summary: The nine nights of the Goddess from the first to the ninth of the bright half of Āśvina (with a spring Navarātri in Caitra), observed across India in regional forms — Durgā Pūjā in Bengal, Garbā and Dāṇḍiyā in Gujarat, Golu doll displays in Tamil Nadu, Dasarā in Mysore — and closing with Vijayadaśamī. The Devī Māhātmya is recited during the nine days.
nodes.details: Kane: “From the 1st of Āśvina bright half to the 9th is celebrated the Durgāpūjā festival, otherwise called Navarātra, observed all over India in some form or other.” Some works require both an autumn (Śarad) and a spring (Vasanta) Durgotsava. The Kālikā, Devī and Bṛhannandikeśvara Purāṇas and digests such as Śūlapāṇi’s Durgotsavaviveka, Raghunandana’s Durgārcanapaddhati and Vidyāpati’s Durgābhaktitaraṅgiṇī prescribe its rites; the Devī Māhātmya (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa chs. 78–90 or 81–93 by edition) narrates the Goddess’s victories.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. IX, pp. 154–187

nodes.name: Durgā Pūjā (Bengal)
nodes.summary: Bengal’s great autumn festival of the Goddess, worshipped with her children (Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṇeśa, Kārttikeya) in clay images made from Gaṅgā clay, from Mahālayā through the 6th–9th days to immersion on Vijayadaśamī; in Kolkata it has become a city-wide public art festival of community pavilions (pandals). “Durga Puja in Kolkata” was inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2021.
nodes.details:
UNESCO: in the months before the festival artisans sculpt the images “using unfired clay pulled from the Ganga River”; the eyes are painted on Mahālayā; on the tenth day the images are immersed in the river from which the clay came, so that the festival “has also come to signify ‘home-coming’ or a seasonal return to one’s roots”. Kane notes the congregational and social character of the pūjā and the śabarotsava of the tenth day after immersion.

Bengali tradition frames the autumn worship as Rāma’s untimely awakening (akāla-bodhana) of the Goddess before his battle with Rāvaṇa — an episode found in Kṛttivāsa’s Bengali Rāmāyaṇa and in late Purāṇic texts, but not in the Devī Māhātmya or in Vālmīki (see cmp:durga-puja-vs-devi-mahatmya).

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. IX, pp. 154–187

nodes.name: Vijayadaśamī (Dasarā / Dussehra)
nodes.summary: The tenth of the bright half of Āśvina, the day after Navarātri, one of the three most auspicious days of the year: worship of the goddess Aparājitā and of the śamī tree, crossing the village boundary (sīmollaṅghana), worship of weapons and tools, and — in north India — the burning of Rāvaṇa’s effigy at the end of the Rāmlīlā. In Bengal it is the day of Durgā’s immersion (Bijayā).
nodes.details: Kane: Hemādri and the Nirṇayasindhu quote Kaśyapa that “since Rāma started on his invasion (against Rāvaṇa) on Śravaṇa-nakṣatra, men should celebrate the crossing of the limits of their village on that day”. A late verse addressed to the śamī says it “held (concealed) the arrows of Arjuna and … appealed lovingly to Rāma”, alluding to the Pāṇḍavas’ hiding their weapons in a śamī tree before their year incognito (Virāṭaparvan). “In some parts of Northern India Rāmalīlā celebrations go on for ten days and culminate on the 10th of Āśvina in the burning of a tall hollow paper and wickerwork structure concealing crackers representing Rāvaṇa and his hosts.” Former princely states such as Mysore and Baroda held durbars and processions; Kane inclines to a military origin (the season for campaigns) and cites Raghuvaṃśa 4.24–25 for the autumn lustration of horses (nīrājana).

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. X, pp. 188–194

nodes.name: Mysore Dasarā
nodes.summary: The ten-day royal Dasarā of Mysore (Karnataka), centred on the goddess Cāmuṇḍeśvarī of Chamundi Hill, who in local tradition killed Mahiṣāsura there; the Wodeyar kings held a durbar and the procession of the goddess on an elephant (Jambū Savārī) closes the festival on Vijayadaśamī. It continues the royal Mahānavamī of the Vijayanagara court.
nodes.limits: The continuity with the Vijayanagara Mahānavamī is a commonly stated tradition, not checked here against the Portuguese accounts.

nodes.name: Mahāśivarātri
nodes.summary: The “great night of Śiva”, the 14th of the dark half of Māgha (Phālguna by the pūrṇimānta reckoning), kept with fasting, worship of the liṅga with bilva leaves and an all-night vigil (jāgaraṇa). The Garuḍa, Skanda, Padma and Agni Purāṇas contain its māhātmya, illustrated by the story of a hunter who, keeping awake in a bilva tree, unknowingly worshipped a liṅga below and won liberation.
nodes.details: Kane: “The Garuḍapurāṇa I.124, Skanda I.1.33, Padma VI.240, Agni 193 contain the Māhātmya of the Śivarātri on the 14th of the dark half of Māgha.” In the Garuḍa version (which Kane thinks the oldest) the hunter is Sundarasenaka, a niṣāda king on Mount Abu, who goes hunting with his dog; in the Skanda he is a cruel Kirāta named Caṇḍa. The vrata’s three elements are fast, worship and vigil. Major observances are held at Paśupatinātha (Kathmandu), Kāśī and the jyotirliṅga temples, and in Mauritius at Grand Bassin.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. XI, pp. 225–236

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa Janmāṣṭamī
nodes.summary: The celebration of Kṛṣṇa’s birth on the 8th of the dark half of Bhādrapada (Śrāvaṇa in the pūrṇimānta reckoning), with a fast and a vigil until midnight, the hour at which the Bhāgavata says Kṛṣṇa appeared to Devakī. In Maharashtra the next day’s Gopāḷkālā includes the breaking of pots of curd (Dahi Handi).
nodes.details: BhP 10.3.8: “niśīthe tama-udbhūte jāyamāne janārdane … āvirāsīd yathā prācyāṃ diśīndur iva puṣkalaḥ” — at midnight, when darkness had arisen, Viṣṇu appeared in Devakī like the full moon in the east. Kane discusses at length the digests’ debates over the tithi, Rohiṇī-nakṣatra and the midnight hour.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. VII, pp. 124–143 (Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī section)

nodes.name: Rāma Navamī
nodes.summary: The celebration of Rāma’s birth on the 9th of the bright half of Caitra, with a fast and midday worship. The Rāmcaritmānas dates the birth to “the holy navamī tithi of the month of Madhu (Caitra), bright fortnight, at abhijit (midday)”, and dates its own beginning to a Rāma Navamī; the constituted text of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa Critical Edition narrates the birth without naming a month or tithi.
nodes.details: RCM Bāla (after dohā 190): “naumī tithi madhu māsa punītā, sukala paccha abhijita haripriītā”. RCM Bāla (before dohā 34) dates the beginning of the poem to Saṃvat 1631, “naumī bhauma bāra madhu māsā” — a Tuesday Rāma Navamī in 1574 CE. In the GRETIL e-text of the Baroda Critical Edition, VR 1.17.6 says only that Kausalyā bore Rāma “endowed with divine marks, half of Viṣṇu”; the familiar statement of the date (Caitra, navamī, Punarvasu) belongs to the vulgate and is not in the constituted text checked. Kane (ch. IV) treats the Rāmanavamī-vrata as obligatory and open even to caṇḍālas.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. IV, pp. 81–94

nodes.name: Gaṇeśa Caturthī
nodes.summary: The festival of Gaṇeśa on the 4th of the bright half of Bhādrapada, when a clay image is installed, worshipped for one to ten days and immersed in water. Kane treats the domestic vrata in ch. VIII of his History; in Maharashtra Bal Gangadhar Tilak promoted a public (sārvajanik) form from 1893, which became a mass civic festival.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. VIII, pp. 144–153

nodes.limits: Kane’s chapter on the domestic vrata was located in the text but its details were not excerpted here.

nodes.name: Sārvajanik Gaṇeśotsav (public Gaṇeśa festival)
nodes.summary: The public, neighbourhood-organised form of Gaṇeśa Caturthī with large images in street pavilions and processions to immersion, promoted by Bal Gangadhar Tilak in Pune from 1893 as a vehicle of Hindu mobilisation and nationalist politics; it spread through Maharashtra and to Mumbai, Hyderabad and the diaspora.
nodes.limits: Public Gaṇeśa images in Pune predate 1893 in some accounts; Tilak’s role was promotion and politicisation rather than invention.

nodes.name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
nodes.summary: Marathi nationalist leader, journalist and scholar (1856–1920), editor of Kesari, who from 1893 promoted public Gaṇeśa festivals and from 1895 the Śivājī festival in Maharashtra; also author of The Orion (1893) and The Arctic Home in the Vedas (1903) on Vedic chronology.

nodes.name: Makara Saṅkrānti
nodes.summary: The day the sun is reckoned to enter Capricorn (Makara), about 14 January in traditional almanacs, kept with bathing, gifts of sesame and sugarcane and, in Gujarat, kite-flying (Uttarāyaṇ); it corresponds to Pongal in Tamil Nadu and Māgh Bihu in Assam. Kane notes that the traditional date lags the true winter solstice (21 December) by about twenty-three days because of the precession of the equinoxes.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, ch. XI, pp. 211–225

nodes.name: Gaṅgāsāgar Melā
nodes.summary: The pilgrimage and bathing fair at the mouth of the Hooghly on Sagar Island (West Bengal) at Makara Saṅkrānti, where tradition places the hermitage of Kapila and the descent of the Gaṅgā that freed the ashes of Sagara’s sons.

nodes.name: Pongal (Tai Pongal)
nodes.summary: The Tamil harvest festival at the beginning of the month of Tai (mid-January), named after the dish of new rice boiled over in milk and offered to the Sun; it runs over three or four days — Bhōgi, Pongal, Māṭṭu Pongal (for cattle) and Kāṇum Pongal. Kane notes that it corresponds to the Makara Saṅkrānti of northern and western India and lasts three days.

nodes.name: Onam
nodes.summary: The harvest festival of Kerala in the month of Ciṅṅam (August–September), culminating on Tiruvōṇam with floral carpets (pūkkaḷam), the feast (sadya), boat races and the Pulikaḷi; Malayali tradition holds that it welcomes the annual return of the just asura king Mahābali, sent to the netherworld by Vāmana. The earliest Tamil reference, in the Caṅkam poem Maduraikkāñci, instead calls Ōṇam the day of Māyōṉ (Viṣṇu) who overcame the asuras.
nodes.details: Maduraikkāñci 590–591 (Project Madurai e-text): “kaṇaṅkoḷ avuṇark kaṭanta polantār / māyōṉ mēya ōṇa naṉṉāḷ” — “the good day of Ōṇam that belongs to Māyōṉ of the golden garland, who overcame the crowding asuras”, describing a festival in Pāṇḍya Madurai, not Kerala. Tiruvōṇam (Śravaṇa) is also Viṣṇu’s (Vāmana’s) birth-asterism in Vaiṣṇava tradition. The Kerala story of Mahābali’s welcome is the dominant modern explanation; its literary history is compared with the Purāṇic Bali in cmp:onam-mahabali-vs-puranic-bali.
nodes.limits: The Maduraikkāñci line attests a festival named Ōṇam in early Tamil Madurai; it does not show that this is the same festival as modern Kerala Onam or date the Mahābali legend.

nodes.name: Maduraikkāñci
nodes.summary: A Caṅkam poem of 782 lines by Māṅkuṭi Marutaṉār, one of the Ten Idylls (Pattuppāṭṭu), addressed to the Pāṇḍya king Neṭuñceḻiyaṉ and describing a day and night in Madurai; it contains the earliest known mention of the Ōṇam festival (lines 590–591).

nodes.name: Chhaṭh Pūjā
nodes.summary: A festival of the Sun (Sūrya) and of the goddess Chhaṭhī Maiyā kept chiefly in Bihar, Jharkhand, eastern Uttar Pradesh and the Nepal Tarai on the 6th of the bright half of Kārttika, six days after Dīpāvalī: after days of fasting, worshippers stand in rivers and ponds to offer arghya to the setting and then the rising sun. It has travelled with Bhojpuri- and Maithili-speaking migrants to Indian cities and the diaspora.

nodes.name: Chhaṭhī Maiyā
nodes.summary: The mother goddess worshipped with the Sun at Chhaṭh in Bihar and neighbouring regions, regarded as a protector of children; often identified in modern accounts with Ṣaṣṭhī, the goddess of the sixth day after birth, and sometimes called the Sun’s sister or consort.
nodes.limits: Identifications vary between local tellings and are not settled by any text checked here.

nodes.name: Ratha Yātrā of Puri
nodes.summary: The chariot festival of Jagannātha at Puri on the second day of the bright half of Āṣāḍha: Jagannātha, Balabhadra and Subhadrā are drawn on three newly built wooden chariots along the Bada Danda to the Guṇḍicā temple and back after nine days. The Gajapati king sweeps the chariots (chera pahanra). Caitanya’s ecstatic dancing before the chariots is a central scene of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta.

nodes.name: Thaipusam
nodes.summary: The Tamil festival of Murukaṉ on the Pūcam asterism of the month of Tai (January–February), when devotees carry kāvaṭi burdens, milk pots and lances piercing the body in fulfilment of vows; tradition says it commemorates Pārvatī’s gift of the vēl (lance) to Murukaṉ for his war against the asura Cūrapatmaṉ. It is kept at Paḻaṉi and other Murukaṉ shrines and, on the largest scale, in Malaysia (Batu Caves, since the 1890s), Singapore and Mauritius.

dates.event: first Thaipusam at Batu Caves, Selangor

nodes.name: Kumbh Melā
nodes.summary: The “festival of the sacred pitcher”, a mass bathing pilgrimage held in rotation at Prayāga (Allahabad/Prayagraj), Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik, each roughly every twelve years by an astronomical reckoning, so that one of the four falls about every three years; UNESCO calls it “the largest peaceful congregation of pilgrims on earth”. Its primary bearers are the ascetic akhāṛās and āśramas. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2017.
nodes.details:
UNESCO: devotees believe that bathing in the Gaṅgā frees them from sins; the congregation includes ascetics, sādhus, kalpavāsīs and visitors; the knowledge is transmitted through “ancient religious manuscripts, oral traditions, historical travelogues” and above all the teacher–pupil relationship of the sādhus in the akhāṛās and āśramas.

Tradition, often described as Purāṇic, explains the four sites as the places where drops of amṛta fell from the pitcher (kumbha) carried away after the churning of the ocean; the textual basis of that explanation was not traced in this round. Maclean (2003, 2008) argues that the Allahabad gathering was long known as the annual Māgh Melā and acquired the name and twelve-year “Kumbh” status in the nineteenth century, through the Prayāgvāl priests’ adaptation of Haridwar’s Kumbh under colonial administration — “the modern beginnings of the ancient Kumbh Mela” (see claim:kumbh-mela-antiquity).
nodes.limits: The amṛta-drop explanation is recorded as tradition (class 6); its earliest textual source was not identified here.

nodes.name: The Kumbh Melā is an ancient institution with a continuous history at its four sites
nodes.summary: The popular and official view presents the Kumbh Melā as of great antiquity, sometimes citing Xuanzang’s seventh-century account of a great gathering at Prayāga; Maclean argues from colonial and pilgrim-priest records that the Allahabad Kumbh in its present form and name is a nineteenth-century development of the annual Māgh Melā.
nodes.details: Xuanzang describes Harṣa’s quinquennial distribution of wealth at the confluence of the rivers at Prayāga, which is not called a Kumbh and is not on a twelve-year cycle; Haridwar’s Kumbh is attested earlier than Allahabad’s. Maclean’s thesis concerns Allahabad specifically.
openQuestions: When is the word Kumbh first applied to the Prayāga gathering in a dated source?

nodes.name: Pandharpur Vārī (Āṣāḍhī pilgrimage)
nodes.summary: The annual foot-pilgrimage of the Vārkarīs to Viṭṭhala at Pandharpur for Āṣāḍhī Ekādaśī (June–July): hundreds of thousands walk for about three weeks in organised groups (diṇḍīs) singing abhaṅgas, escorting palanquins (pālkhīs) bearing the sandals (pādukās) of the saints — chiefly Jñāneśvar’s from Āḷandī and Tukārām’s from Dehū. A second, smaller vārī falls on Kārttikī Ekādaśī.
nodes.details: Irawati Karve’s essay “On the Road” (1962) and D. B. Mokashi’s Pālkhī (trans. 1987) are classic first-hand accounts. A vārkarī is “one who performs the vārī”; the pilgrimage is the defining practice of the tradition.

nodes.name: Ayyappa (Ayyappan, Śāstā)
nodes.summary: The celibate forest god of Śabarimala in Kerala, worshipped as Dharmaśāstā and as Hariharaputra, the son born of Śiva and Viṣṇu in his female form Mohinī; local tradition also tells of the foundling prince Maṇikaṇṭhan of Pandalam who killed the buffalo-demoness Mahiṣī. His cult draws millions of male pilgrims each season.
nodes.details: Sekar (1992) distinguishes the older Śāstā/Aiyaṉār cult from the Pandalam Ayyappa legend and the modern pilgrimage cultus; the identification of Ayyappa with the Tamil village guardian Aiyaṉār is a scholarly and devotional association, not an identity.
nodes.limits: The Mohinī–Śiva parentage is a tradition of the cult (later Sanskrit māhātmyas and Malayalam songs), not a Purāṇic narrative of the major Purāṇas checked here.

nodes.name: Śabarimala pilgrimage
nodes.summary: The season-long pilgrimage (mid-November to January) to the hill shrine of Ayyappa at Śabarimala in the Western Ghats of Kerala. Pilgrims keep a 41-day vow (vratam) of celibacy, vegetarian diet and black or blue dress, address one another as “Ayyappa”, and climb carrying the irumuḍi bundle of offerings; the season culminates at Makaravilakku (Makara Saṅkrānti). Many visit the shrine of Vāvar, a Muslim companion of Ayyappa, at Erumeli on the way.
nodes.details: Osella and Osella (2003) analyse the pilgrimage as a rite of masculinity in which men temporarily become renouncers. Customary exclusion of women aged about 10–50 from the shrine was set aside by India’s Supreme Court in 2018 (Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala), a ruling referred to a larger bench in 2019; the matter remained contested.
nodes.limits: Legal developments are summarised from reference sources only.

nodes.name: Kāṁvaṛ (Kāvaḍ) Yātrā
nodes.summary: The pilgrimage of the month of Śrāvaṇa in which devotees of Śiva (kāṁvaṛiyās), dressed in saffron, carry Gaṅgā water in pots slung from a shoulder pole (kāṁvaṛ) — from Haridwar, Gaumukh or Sultanganj — on foot to pour over the liṅgas of their home temples or of Baidyanāth at Deoghar. It has grown since the 1980s into one of the largest annual pilgrimages in north India.

nodes.name: Garbā of Gujarat
nodes.summary: The ritual and devotional circle dance of Gujarat performed during Navarātri around a perforated earthenware pot lit with an oil lamp (garbo) or an image of the mother goddess Ambā, moving counter-clockwise while singing and clapping, slow at first and building to whirling. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2023.

nodes.name: Yoga (UNESCO living-heritage element)
nodes.summary: The practice of yoga as a living tradition — postures, meditation, controlled breathing and chanting aimed at self-realisation and liberation — inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2016 on India’s nomination. UNESCO describes it as traditionally transmitted from guru to disciple and now also through āśramas, schools and media worldwide.
nodes.limits: This record is the heritage element as inscribed; the philosophical school of Yoga and its texts belong to the darśana records.

nodes.name: Muṭiyēṯṯu
nodes.summary: A ritual dance-drama of central Kerala enacting the battle between the goddess Kāḷī (Bhadrakāḷī) and the demon Dārika, performed by the whole village after the summer harvest in the goddess temples (Bhagavati kāvus) along the Chalakudy, Periyar and Moovattupuzha rivers; a great image of Kāḷī (kaḷam) is first drawn on the temple floor in coloured powders. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2010.
nodes.details: UNESCO: “the divine sage Nārada importunes Śiva to contain the demon Dārika, who is immune to defeat by mortals. Śiva instead commands that Dārika will die at the hand of the goddess Kāḷī.” Each caste has a role in the ritual.

nodes.name: Dārika
nodes.summary: An asura of Kerala tradition who, by a boon that no mortal could kill him, oppressed the worlds until Bhadrakāḷī, born from Śiva’s third eye, slew him; the story is enacted in Muṭiyēṯṯu and other Bhagavati rituals of Kerala.

nodes.name: Kāḷī slays Dārika
nodes.summary: The Kerala myth of the goddess Bhadrakāḷī’s war against the asura Dārika, whom no mortal could kill; Nārada informs Śiva, who decrees that Dārika shall die by the Goddess. It is the plot of Muṭiyēṯṯu and of songs and rites in the Bhagavati temples of central Kerala.

nodes.name: Rammāṇ
nodes.summary: A religious festival and masked ritual theatre held each year in late April in the twin villages of Saloor-Dungra (Chamoli, Uttarakhand) in honour of the village tutelary god Bhūmiyāl Devtā, combining recitation of a version of the Rāma story and other legends with songs and masked dances; only the Bhaṇḍārīs may wear the most sacred mask, that of Narasiṃha. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2009.

nodes.name: Bhūmiyāl Devtā (Saloor-Dungra)
nodes.summary: The tutelary village god of Saloor-Dungra in the Garhwal Himalaya, in whose honour and temple the Rammāṇ festival is held; the family that hosts the god during the year keeps a strict daily routine.

nodes.name: Chhau
nodes.summary: A masked and martial dance tradition of eastern India in three styles — Seraikella (Jharkhand), Purulia (West Bengal) and Mayurbhanj (Odisha), the first two masked — enacting episodes from the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa, local folklore and abstract themes, closely tied to the spring festival Caitra Parva. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2010.

nodes.name: Saṅkīrtana of Manipur
nodes.summary: The ritual singing, drumming and dancing of the Vaiṣṇavas of the Manipur plains, performed at temples, festivals and life-cycle rites: two drummers and about ten singer-dancers narrate the life and deeds of Kṛṣṇa in a hall or courtyard ringed by seated devotees, and the performance is regarded as a visible manifestation of God. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2013.

nodes.name: Tradition of Vedic chanting (UNESCO element)
nodes.summary: The oral transmission of the four Vedas by memorised recitation with exact accentuation and the mnemonic recitation patterns (pāṭhas), proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2003 and inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008.
nodes.limits: UNESCO’s summary dates the Vedas to “over 3,500 years ago”; that is the nominating text’s statement, not a dating adopted here.

nodes.name: Sbek Thom (Khmer shadow theatre)
nodes.summary: Cambodian shadow theatre with two-metre-high, non-articulated puppets cut from a single hide, held up before a fire-lit screen by dancers while two narrators and an orchestra perform scenes of the Reamker, the Khmer Rāmāyaṇa, over several nights with up to 160 puppets. Proclaimed a Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed in 2008.
nodes.details: UNESCO: dating from before the Angkorian period, it was considered sacred together with the Royal Ballet and mask theatre; many puppets were destroyed under the Khmer Rouge and the art has been revived since 1979.
nodes.limits: The pre-Angkorian origin is UNESCO’s (nominating state’s) statement.

nodes.name: Lkhon Khol Wat Svay Andet
nodes.summary: Khmer masked dance-drama performed by men in the community around the Buddhist monastery of Wat Svay Andet on the Mekong east of Phnom Penh, to propitiate the Neak Ta guardian spirits for the community and its harvest; spirit mediums attend the performance. Inscribed in 2018 on UNESCO’s List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding.
nodes.limits: UNESCO’s summary does not name the repertoire; the Reamker link rests on reference sources.

nodes.name: Three genres of traditional dance in Bali
nodes.summary: Balinese dance in its three genres — sacred (wali), semi-sacred (bebali) and for public enjoyment (balih-balihan) — performed to gamelan by male and female dancers in gold-painted costumes, and transmitted informally to children from an early age. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2015.
nodes.limits: The names of the three genres are from reference sources; UNESCO’s summary gives them as sacred, semi-sacred and for enjoyment.

nodes.name: Geet-Gawai (Bhojpuri folk songs in Mauritius)
nodes.summary: A pre-wedding ceremony of Bhojpuri-speaking Mauritians of Indian descent, held at the bride’s or groom’s home, combining rituals, prayers, songs honouring Hindu gods and goddesses, the drum (dholak) and dance; it begins with five married women sorting turmeric, rice, grass and money in a cloth. Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2016.

nodes.name: Sant tradition (nirguṇa bhakti)
nodes.summary: The loose lineage of north and west Indian poet-saints — Nāmdev, Kabīr, Raidās, Dādū and others — who addressed a formless (nirguṇa) Lord, usually named Rām or Hari, through the divine Name and the true guru, and criticised caste, image-worship and ritual. Scholars treat “sant” as a family resemblance rather than an organised sect; Kabīr Panth, Dādū Panth and the Sikh Gurus draw on it.
nodes.details: Schomer and McLeod (1987) frame the Sants as a tradition defined by shared teaching and mutual citation rather than by institutions. Songs of Kabīr, Nāmdev and Raidās were collected both in the Sikh Ādi Granth (compiled 1604) and in the Dādūpanthī Pañcvāṇī anthologies of Rajasthan; those collections are referenced here, not modelled.
nodes.limits: The sant/saguṇa–nirguṇa division is partly a modern scholarly classification (Hawley 2015).

nodes.name: Rāmānanda
nodes.summary: North Indian Vaiṣṇava teacher (14th–15th c.), traditionally of Vārāṇasī, revered as founder of the Rāmānandī order; hagiography from the Bhaktamāl onward makes Kabīr, Raidās and others his disciples, which historians treat as a later construction of lineage.

nodes.name: Kabīr
nodes.summary: Weaver-poet of Vārāṇasī (15th c.), raised in a Muslim julāhā family, the most quoted of the north Indian Sants: his sākhīs, padas and ramainīs address a formless Rām, mock both brāhmaṇ and mullā, and insist on the Name and the true guru. Verses in his name are preserved in three main collections — the eastern Bījak, the Rajasthani (Dādūpanthī) Kabīr Granthāvalī and the Sikh Ādi Granth.
nodes.details: Vaudeville (1974) doubted the traditional association with Rāmānanda and saw Kabīr as heir to the Nāth yogis as much as to Vaiṣṇava bhakti. Kabīr’s Rām is not Daśaratha’s son: in the Bījak he repeatedly says the true Rām is unborn and not the king of Ayodhyā (see cmp:kabir-rama-vs-tulsidas-rama). The Sikh scripture includes a large number of verses in his name (reference only).

dates.label: traditionally 1398–1518; scholars place his activity in the 15th c. (c. 1440–1518 on some views)
dates.basis: hagiography (120-year traditional life) vs. Vaudeville’s and others’ estimates

nodes.limits: Very little of the corpus can be shown to go back to Kabīr himself; the three recensions overlap only partly.

nodes.name: Kabīr Panth
nodes.summary: The religious community of Kabīr’s followers, organised in monastic and householder branches (notably the Kabīr Chaurā at Vārāṇasī and the Dharamdāsī branch of central India), which treats Kabīr as the true guru and the Bījak (or the Kabīr Sāgar) as scripture.

nodes.name: Bījak
nodes.summary: The “Seed” or “Account”: the collection of Kabīr’s ramainīs, śabdas and sākhīs canonical in the Kabīr Panth, representing the eastern (Bhojpuri-coloured) transmission of his poetry.
nodes.limits: Attribution of individual verses to Kabīr is uncertain.

nodes.name: Kabīr Granthāvalī (Rajasthani recension)
nodes.summary: The western collection of Kabīr’s verses transmitted in Dādūpanthī manuscripts of Rajasthan and edited in the twentieth century; with the Bījak and the Sikh Ādi Granth one of the three main recensions of Kabīr.

nodes.name: Raidās (Ravidās)
nodes.summary: Leatherworker (camār) poet-saint of Vārāṇasī (15th–16th c.) whose songs to a formless Lord reject caste hierarchy; preserved in the Sikh Ādi Granth and the Dādūpanthī Pañcvāṇī, he is revered as guru by the Ravidassia community and, in Rajasthani legend, as Mīrābāī’s guru.

nodes.name: Padas of Raidās
nodes.summary: The songs attributed to Raidās, transmitted in the Sikh Ādi Granth (about forty śabads), in the Dādūpanthī Pañcvāṇī of Rajasthan and in later collections; edited and translated by Callewaert and Friedlander (1992).

nodes.name: Ravidassia (Ravidās Panth)
nodes.summary: The community of followers of Guru Ravidās, largely of Dalit background (many identify as Ad-Dharmi or Ravidassia) in Punjab and its diaspora; historically close to Sikh practice, its leading centre, Dera Sachkhand Ballan, proclaimed it a distinct religion in 2010 with the Amritbāṇī of Ravidās as scripture.

dates.event: proclamation as a distinct religion (Dera Sachkhand Ballan)

nodes.limits: Members differ on the relation of the community to Sikhism and Hinduism; this record takes no position.

nodes.name: Mīrābāī
nodes.summary: Rajput princess-poet of Merta and Mewar (16th c.), devotee of Kṛṣṇa as Giridhar Gopāl, whose legend of defiance of her in-laws and of caste and gender norms is told across north India; the earliest datable reference to her is a stanza in Nābhādās’s Bhaktamāl (c. 1600). Hundreds of songs bear her name, nearly all of uncertain authorship.

dates.label: c. 1498–1547 (traditional; married 1516 into the Mewar house)

nodes.limits: Hawley (2005) shows that few if any of the poems in her name can be traced to early manuscripts.

nodes.name: Padāvalī of Mīrābāī
nodes.summary: The large and open corpus of songs (padas) in Rajasthani, Braj and Gujarati attributed to Mīrābāī, addressed to Kṛṣṇa as lover and husband; very few are found in early dated manuscripts.

nodes.name: Nābhādās
nodes.summary: Rāmānandī poet of Galtā near Jaipur (late 16th–early 17th c.), author of the Bhaktamāl, the “Garland of Devotees”, the first comprehensive hagiographical anthology of north Indian bhakti.

nodes.name: Bhaktamāl
nodes.summary: Nābhādās’s Braj Bhāṣā “Garland of Devotees” (c. 1600), some two hundred short chappay stanzas on devotees from the mythic past to his contemporaries — Kabīr, Raidās, Mīrā, Sūrdās, Tulsīdās and many others — and the earliest datable reference for several of them. Priyādās’s commentary (1712) expanded it into narrative hagiography.

nodes.name: Priyādās
nodes.summary: Gauḍīya-influenced poet of Vṛndāvan who completed in 1712 the Bhaktirasabodhinī, a verse commentary on the Bhaktamāl that turned its terse stanzas into the miracle-rich stories of the saints known today.

nodes.name: Bhaktirasabodhinī
nodes.summary: Priyādās’s Braj commentary (1712) on Nābhādās’s Bhaktamāl, the main source of the popular stories of Kabīr, Mīrā, Tulsīdās and others.

dates.basis: colophon date as reported in secondary literature

nodes.name: Dādū Dayāl
nodes.summary: Sant poet of Rajasthan (1544–1603), a cotton-carder by tradition, whose followers founded the Dādū Panth; the Dādūpanthīs compiled the Pañcvāṇī anthologies preserving the songs of Kabīr, Nāmdev, Raidās and Hardās with Dādū’s own.

nodes.name: Vinaya Patrikā
nodes.summary: Tulsīdās’s “Petition of Humility”, 279 Braj Bhāṣā hymns framed as a petition to Rāma’s court, addressed first to Gaṇeśa, Śiva, Hanumān and other deities and then to Rāma; valued for its personal devotion and its theology of the Name.

dates.label: late 16th–early 17th c.
dates.basis: life of Tulsīdās (1574 is the Mānas’s self-dated start)

nodes.name: Kavitāvalī
nodes.summary: Tulsīdās’s Braj collection of kavitt, savaiyā and other stanzas retelling the Rāma story in seven kāṇḍas, with a long Uttarakāṇḍa of personal and social verses on Kali-age Banaras and the power of Rāma’s name.

dates.label: late 16th–early 17th c.
dates.basis: life of Tulsīdās (1574 is the Mānas’s self-dated start)

nodes.name: Gītāvalī
nodes.summary: Tulsīdās’s Braj Rāmāyaṇa in songs: 328 padas in seven kāṇḍas set to rāgas, elaborating some episodes and abridging others.

dates.label: late 16th–early 17th c.
dates.basis: life of Tulsīdās (1574 is the Mānas’s self-dated start)

nodes.name: Hanumān Bāhuk
nodes.summary: A Braj prayer of 44 stanzas to Hanumān, traditionally composed by Tulsīdās in old age when he suffered acute pain in his arm (c. 1607).

dates.label: early 17th c. (traditionally c. 1607)
dates.basis: life of Tulsīdās (1574 is the Mānas’s self-dated start)

nodes.name: Viṭṭhalnāth (Gusāiṃjī)
nodes.summary: Younger son and successor of Vallabha (1515–1586) who organised the Puṣṭimārga’s temple liturgy of eight daily darśans and, by tradition in 1565, named eight poets — the Aṣṭachāp — whose songs were to be sung in it.

nodes.name: Aṣṭachāp (the “eight seals”)
nodes.summary: The eight poet-singers recognised by Viṭṭhalnāth as the authorised singers of the Puṣṭimārga liturgy at the Śrīnāthjī temple on Govardhana: Sūrdās, Kumbhandās, Paramānanddās and Kṛṣṇadās (counted as Vallabha’s disciples) and Nanddās, Chītasvāmī, Govindasvāmī and Caturbhujdās (Viṭṭhalnāth’s). Their padas form the core of havelī saṅgīt.
nodes.limits: The grouping and the poets’ biographies come from the sect’s Vārtā literature (17th c.); Hawley questions Sūrdās’s membership (claim:surdas-disciple-of-vallabha).

nodes.name: Kumbhandās
nodes.summary: Farmer-poet of Jamunavato near Govardhana, the earliest of Vallabha’s disciples among the Aṣṭachāp; Puṣṭimārga hagiography tells that he refused the emperor’s summons to Fatehpur Sikri.

nodes.name: Paramānanddās
nodes.summary: Aṣṭachāp poet from Kannauj, a disciple of Vallabha, whose Braj padas on Kṛṣṇa’s childhood are collected as the Paramānandsāgar.

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇadās (Aṣṭachāp)
nodes.summary: Aṣṭachāp poet of Gujarati origin and long-time manager (adhikārī) of the Śrīnāthjī temple under Vallabha and Viṭṭhalnāth.

nodes.name: Nanddās
nodes.summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, disciple of Viṭṭhalnāth, celebrated for the refined Braj of his Rāspañcādhyāyī and Bhramargīt, which recast Bhāgavata episodes.

nodes.name: Chītasvāmī
nodes.summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, a Mathurā Caube priest who became Viṭṭhalnāth’s disciple.

nodes.name: Govindasvāmī
nodes.summary: Aṣṭachāp poet and musician, a disciple of Viṭṭhalnāth, who lived near Govardhana.

nodes.name: Caturbhujdās
nodes.summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, son of Kumbhandās and a disciple of Viṭṭhalnāth.

nodes.name: Caurāsī Vaiṣṇavan kī Vārtā
