nodes.summary: The Braj prose “Accounts of Eighty-four Vaiṣṇavas”, Puṣṭimārga hagiographies of Vallabha’s disciples (including Sūrdās and the other early Aṣṭachāp poets), attributed to Gokulnāth and transmitted with Harirāy’s commentary (17th c.).

nodes.name: Rūpa Gosvāmī
nodes.summary: Senior of the Six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvan (1489–1564), a former minister of the Bengal sultanate who met Caitanya at Prayāga; in the Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu and Ujjvalanīlamaṇi he recast Sanskrit aesthetic theory (rasa) as a theology of devotion, and wrote the Kṛṣṇa dramas Vidagdhamādhava and Lalitamādhava.

nodes.name: Sanātana Gosvāmī
nodes.summary: Elder brother of Rūpa and one of the Six Gosvāmīs (1488–1558), instructed by Caitanya at Vārāṇasī according to the Caitanya Caritāmṛta; author of the Bṛhadbhāgavatāmṛta and a commentary on the Bhāgavata’s tenth book, and traditionally of the ritual code Haribhaktivilāsa.

nodes.name: Jīva Gosvāmī
nodes.summary: Nephew of Rūpa and Sanātana and the systematic theologian of the Gauḍīya school (c. 1513–c. 1598), author of the six Sandarbhas, which ground Caitanya’s teaching in the Bhāgavata, and founder of the Rādhā-Dāmodara temple in Vṛndāvan.

nodes.name: Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī
nodes.summary: One of the Six Gosvāmīs (1503–1578), from a Śrīvaiṣṇava family of Śrīraṅgam, traditionally co-author of the Haribhaktivilāsa and founder of the Rādhāramaṇa temple in Vṛndāvan.

nodes.name: Raghunātha Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī
nodes.summary: One of the Six Gosvāmīs (1505–1579), remembered as a reciter of the Bhāgavata in Vṛndāvan.

nodes.name: Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī
nodes.summary: One of the Six Gosvāmīs, a renunciant son of a wealthy Bengali family who lived for years at Rādhākuṇḍa; his memories of Caitanya’s last years at Puri are a main source for Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja’s Caitanya Caritāmṛta.

nodes.name: Works of the Six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvan
nodes.summary: The Sanskrit theological, ritual, aesthetic and dramatic works of Rūpa, Sanātana, Jīva and their colleagues (16th c.) that define Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava doctrine and practice.

nodes.name: Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu
nodes.summary: Rūpa Gosvāmī’s Sanskrit “Ocean of the Nectar of Devotional Rasa”, which classifies devotion (bhakti) and its emotions with the categories of Sanskrit poetics, making bhakti itself the supreme rasa. Its closing verse says it was completed while the author dwelt in Gokula, in a Śaka year given by a word-numeral.
nodes.details: GRETIL e-text (Gaudiya Grantha Mandir, based on the 1984 reprint of Haridās Dās’s edition), closing verse: “rāmāṅga-śatru-gaṇite śāke gokulam adhiṣṭhitenāyam / bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhur viṭaṅkitaḥ kṣudra-rūpeṇa”. The commonly cited date 1541 depends on reading the third word-numeral as śakra (= 14).

dates.label: 1541 CE (Śaka 1463)
dates.basis: colophon chronogram as read by Haberman (“rāmāṅga-śakra” = 1463); the GRETIL e-text reads “rāmāṅga-śatru”

openQuestions: Which manuscripts read śakra and which śatru in the colophon?

nodes.name: Ujjvalanīlamaṇi
nodes.summary: Rūpa Gosvāmī’s Sanskrit treatise on the erotic mode of devotion (madhura-rasa), a sequel to the Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, which classifies Kṛṣṇa’s beloveds and makes Rādhā, with Candrāvalī, the chief of his eternal beloveds in Vraja.
nodes.details: GRETIL e-text: “rādhā-candrāvalī-mukhyāḥ proktāḥ nitya-priyā vraje” and “rādhāyām eva kṛṣṇasya suprasiddhānukūlatā”.

nodes.name: Haribhaktivilāsa
nodes.summary: The Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava ritual digest (16th c.) on initiation, daily worship, festivals and conduct, attributed to Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī with a commentary ascribed to Sanātana.

nodes.name: Ṣaṭ Sandarbha
nodes.summary: Jīva Gosvāmī’s six “Treatises” (Tattva-, Bhagavat-, Paramātma-, Kṛṣṇa-, Bhakti- and Prīti-sandarbha), a systematic theology of the Gauḍīya school built on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.

nodes.name: Vṛndāvana Dāsa Ṭhākura
nodes.summary: Bengali poet (1507–1589), disciple of Nityānanda, whose Caitanya Bhāgavata is the first full-length Bengali biography of Caitanya.

nodes.name: Caitanya Bhāgavata
nodes.summary: Vṛndāvana Dāsa’s Bengali verse biography of Caitanya (16th c.), the earliest full-length life in Bengali, concentrating on his youth in Navadvīpa and his early ministry; it presents him as Kṛṣṇa (and Rādhā) descended.

nodes.name: Śikṣāṣṭaka
nodes.summary: Eight Sanskrit verses of instruction on the chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s names, humility and longing, attributed to Caitanya and quoted in the last chapter of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta; the only verses Gauḍīyas ascribe to him directly.

nodes.name: Śākta Padāvalī (Bengali songs to the Goddess)
nodes.summary: The Bengali song literature to Kālī and Umā from the eighteenth century onward — Śyāmā-saṅgīt to Kālī and the Āgamanī–Bijayā songs of Umā’s homecoming at Durgā Pūjā — initiated by Rāmprasād Sen and Kamalākānta Bhaṭṭācārya.

nodes.name: Rāmprasād Sen
nodes.summary: Bengali Śākta poet of Halisahar (c. 1718/1723–c. 1775) whose intimate, often reproachful songs to Kālī as mother (Rāmprasādī) created the genre of Śyāmā-saṅgīt; patronised by Rājā Kṛṣṇacandra of Nadia, who gave him the title Kavirañjana.

nodes.name: Kamalākānta Bhaṭṭācārya
nodes.summary: Bengali Śākta poet and tantric practitioner (1769–1821), court poet of the Mahārājā of Burdwan, who after Rāmprasād shaped the Śākta padāvalī, including the Āgamanī songs of Umā’s homecoming.

nodes.name: Baḍu Caṇḍīdās
nodes.summary: Bengali poet to whom the Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtan is ascribed (late 14th–15th c.?). Songs signed “Caṇḍīdās” — with the epithets Baḍu, Dvija and Dīna — appear to belong to more than one poet, a puzzle known as the Caṇḍīdās problem.

dates.label: 14th–15th c. (disputed)
dates.basis: language of the Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtan; disputed identity

nodes.name: Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtan
nodes.summary: A Bengali dramatic song-cycle of the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa ascribed to Baḍu Caṇḍīdās, known from a single incomplete manuscript found in the early twentieth century in a cowshed in Bankura district and published by the Bangiya Sahitya Parishad; among the earliest monuments of Middle Bengali.

dates.label: later 14th–15th c. (pre-Caitanya; disputed)
dates.basis: language; palaeography of the unique manuscript

nodes.limits: The date and the relationship of this Caṇḍīdās to the lyric Caṇḍīdās poems are unsettled.

nodes.name: Vidyāpati
nodes.summary: Maithili and Sanskrit poet, scholar and courtier of the Oinwāra kings of Mithilā (c. 1352–1448), whose Maithili songs of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa were taken up by Bengali Vaiṣṇavas (and imitated in Brajabuli), while his songs to Śiva (nacārī) and his Sanskrit works on Durgā worship show a Smārta devotion to several deities.

dates.label: c. 1352–1448
dates.basis: court records and colophons as reported

nodes.name: Padāvalī of Vidyāpati
nodes.summary: The Maithili love-songs (padas) of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa and songs to Śiva and the Goddess attributed to Vidyāpati, transmitted in Mithilā, Nepal and Bengal; Caitanya is said to have delighted in them.

nodes.name: Durgābhaktitaraṅgiṇī
nodes.summary: Vidyāpati’s Sanskrit manual of the autumn worship of Durgā, cited by Kane among the special treatises on the Durgotsava/Navarātra.

nodes.name: Nām Ghoṣā
nodes.summary: Mādhavadeva’s Assamese “Proclamation of the Name”, about a thousand verses in praise of the Name of Kṛṣṇa (Rāma/Hari), with Śaṅkaradeva’s Kīrtana Ghoṣā a principal scripture of the Ekaśaraṇa sattras and nāmghars.

nodes.name: Bargīt
nodes.summary: The “great songs” of Śaṅkaradeva and Mādhavadeva (15th–16th c.) in Brajāvalī, set to rāgas but not necessarily to tāla, sung to open services in the sattras and nāmghars of the Ekaśaraṇa Dharma.

nodes.name: Aṅkīyā Nāṭ and Bhāonā
nodes.summary: The one-act devotional plays in Brajāvalī created by Śaṅkaradeva in the early sixteenth century, mostly on Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, and their performance (bhāonā) in the nāmghars and sattras of Assam, directed and narrated by a sūtradhāra.

nodes.name: Sattriya
nodes.summary: The dance tradition of the Ekaśaraṇa sattras, created within the bhāonā performances of Śaṅkaradeva’s plays and maintained by celibate monks; recognised among India’s classical dances by the Sangeet Natak Akademi in 2000.

dates.event: recognition as a classical dance (Sangeet Natak Akademi)
dates.label: 15 November 2000

nodes.name: Sattra (Vaiṣṇava monasteries of Assam)
nodes.summary: The monastic and congregational institutions of the Ekaśaraṇa Dharma — chiefly on Majuli and in upper Assam — that preserve its scriptures, Bargīt, plays and dance under a sattrādhikār.

nodes.name: Pañcasakhā (the “five friends” of Odia literature)
nodes.summary: The five sixteenth-century Odia poet-saints — Balarāma Dāsa, Jagannātha Dāsa, Acyutānanda Dāsa, Yaśovanta Dāsa and Ananta Dāsa — who rendered Sanskrit scriptures into Odia and joined Jagannātha devotion with a meditative, nirguṇa-leaning Vaiṣṇavism, sometimes called Utkalīya Vaiṣṇavism.

nodes.name: Balarāma Dāsa
nodes.summary: Eldest of the Odia Pañcasakhā, author of the Jagamohana (Dāṇḍi) Rāmāyaṇa, the Lakṣmī Purāṇa and the Bhakti-tattva of the “Bata Abakasha”; tradition calls him Krupāsiddha.

nodes.name: Acyutānanda Dāsa
nodes.summary: Odia Pañcasakhā poet and saint, prolific author of Mālikās (prophetic verses), genealogical and devotional works, and a figure of popular prophecy in Odisha.

nodes.name: Yaśovanta Dāsa
nodes.summary: Odia Pañcasakhā poet, remembered for devotional and yogic songs (the Prema Bhakti Brahma Gītā and Mālikās are attributed to him).

nodes.name: Ananta Dāsa
nodes.summary: Odia Pañcasakhā poet, author by tradition of the Hetu-udaya Bhāgavata and devotional songs.

nodes.name: Jagamohana Rāmāyaṇa (Dāṇḍi Rāmāyaṇa)
nodes.summary: Balarāma Dāsa’s Odia Rāmāyaṇa (early 16th c.), in the popular dāṇḍi metre, a free retelling rather than a translation of Vālmīki, long recited in Odisha’s village prayer-houses.

nodes.name: Janābāī
nodes.summary: Marathi Vārkarī poet-saint (d. 1350 by tradition), a low-caste orphan who served as a maid in Nāmdev’s household at Pandharpur; her abhaṅgas address Viṭṭhal with startling intimacy as mother, friend and helper in her chores.

nodes.name: Muktābāī
nodes.summary: Younger sister of Jñāneśvar (13th c.) and Vārkarī poet of about forty abhaṅgas, remembered in tradition as the teacher of the yogī Cāṅgdev.

nodes.name: Cokhāmeḷā
nodes.summary: Vārkarī poet-saint of the Mahār (untouchable) caste (13th–14th c.), of Mangalvedhe, a companion of Nāmdev; barred from the Viṭṭhal temple, he sang of the god outside it, and his samādhi lies at the foot of the temple steps in Pandharpur. He is a key figure for modern Dalit memory.

nodes.name: Bahiṇābāī
nodes.summary: Marathi Vārkarī poet-saint (1628–1700), a brāhmaṇ woman who took Tukārām as her guru in a vision and whose autobiography in abhaṅgas (Ātmanivedana) records the conflict of devotion with her married life.

nodes.name: Samarth Rāmdās
nodes.summary: Marathi saint (c. 1608–1682), devotee of Rāma and Hanumān, founder of the Rāmdāsī order and of Hanumān shrines across Maharashtra, author of the Dāsbodh and the Manāce Ślok; later tradition makes him guru to the Maratha king Śivājī.

nodes.name: Dāsbodh
nodes.summary: Rāmdās’s Marathi “Advice to the Servant” (1654), 7,751 ovīs in twenty chapters of ten sub-chapters each, a dialogue of guru and disciple on devotion, knowledge and worldly conduct, dictated to his disciple Kalyāṇ Svāmī.

nodes.name: Manāce Ślok
nodes.summary: Rāmdās’s 205 Marathi verses “to the mind”, a widely memorised didactic poem urging the mind toward Rāma.

nodes.name: Vaiṣṇava jana to
nodes.summary: Narsinh Mehtā’s Gujarati pad defining the true devotee of Viṣṇu by ethical conduct — feeling others’ pain, humility, freedom from greed — rather than caste or ritual; it was sung daily in Gandhi’s āśrams.

nodes.name: Premānand Bhaṭṭ
nodes.summary: Gujarati poet and professional storyteller (māṇbhaṭ, 1636–1714) of Vadodara, master of the ākhyāna — sung narratives of Purāṇic and bhakti stories such as Okhāharaṇ, Nalākhyān and Sudāmā-caritra, and of Narsinh Mehtā’s life.

nodes.name: Swaminarayan (Sahajānand Svāmī)
nodes.summary: Ascetic and religious founder (1781–1830), born Ghanaśyām Pāṇḍe near Ayodhyā, who after years of wandering was initiated by Rāmānand Svāmī in Gujarat in 1800 and succeeded him in 1802; his followers worship him as the supreme manifestation of God (Puruṣottama), and the Swaminarayan Sampradāya grew from his reforms.

nodes.name: Swaminarayan Sampradāya
nodes.summary: A Vaiṣṇava tradition founded in Gujarat in the early nineteenth century around Sahajānand Svāmī (Swaminarayan), rooted in Rāmānuja’s Viśiṣṭādvaita, organised around the dioceses of Ahmedabad and Vadtal and temples built in his lifetime, and spread by Gujarati migrants to East Africa, Britain and North America.

dates.event: succession of Sahajānand Svāmī to Rāmānand Svāmī’s fellowship

nodes.name: Vacanāmṛt
nodes.summary: The 273 Gujarati discourses of Swaminarayan delivered between 1819 and 1829, compiled by five senior disciples and approved by him; the principal theological scripture of the Swaminarayan Sampradāya.

nodes.name: Śikṣāpatrī
nodes.summary: Swaminarayan’s code of conduct in 212 Sanskrit verses (1826) for his followers; on 26 February 1830 at Rajkot he presented a copy to Sir John Malcolm, Governor of Bombay, which is now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford.

dates.event: copy presented to Sir John Malcolm (now Bodleian Library)
dates.label: 26 February 1830

nodes.limits: The Bodleian copy was not checked in the library’s catalogue here.

nodes.name: BAPS (Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha)
nodes.summary: A Swaminarayan denomination formed in 1905 by Shastri Yagnapurushdas (Shastriji Maharaj), teaching that Swaminarayan (Puruṣottama) remains present through a succession of gurus who embody Akṣara, beginning with Guṇātītānand Svāmī; known worldwide for its large stone mandirs, including Neasden (London) and Robbinsville (New Jersey).

nodes.name: Shastriji Maharaj (Shastri Yagnapurushdas)
nodes.summary: Swaminarayan monk and scholar (1865–1951) who in 1905 left the Vadtal diocese to found BAPS around the Akṣara–Puruṣottama doctrine.

nodes.name: Haridāsa (Dāsa Kūṭa)
nodes.summary: The movement of Kannada devotional singers — “servants of Hari” — within the Mādhva (Dvaita) tradition, from Śrīpādarāja and Vyāsatīrtha to Purandaradāsa and Kanakadāsa and later Vijayadāsa, whose simple Kannada songs (kīrtanas, ugābhogas, suḷādis) carried Dvaita devotion to the people and shaped Carnatic music.

nodes.name: Purandaradāsa
nodes.summary: Kannada Haridāsa poet-composer (c. 1484–1564), a wealthy merchant who became a disciple of Vyāsatīrtha; his songs signed “Purandara Viṭhala” and his graded exercises made him the “grandfather” (pitāmaha) of Carnatic music.

nodes.name: Kanakadāsa
nodes.summary: Kannada Haridāsa poet (1509–1609 or 1606), of the Kuruba (shepherd) community, disciple of Vyāsatīrtha; Udupi tradition says Kṛṣṇa turned to face him through a window in the temple wall (Kanakana kiṇḍi) when he was barred from entering. Author of the Mohanataraṅgiṇi and the allegory Rāmadhānya Caritre.

nodes.name: Mohanataraṅgiṇi
nodes.summary: Kanakadāsa’s Kannada narrative poem (in sāṅgatya metre) on Kṛṣṇa’s life at Dvārakā, including the love of Uṣā and Aniruddha.

nodes.name: Rāmadhānya Caritre
nodes.summary: Kanakadāsa’s Kannada allegory in which ragi (finger millet), the grain of the poor, wins a debate with rice before Rāma and earns the name rāmadhānya — read as a protest against caste privilege.

nodes.name: Annamācārya (Annamayya)
nodes.summary: Telugu composer of Tāḷḷapāka (1408–1503) who sang to Veṅkaṭeśvara of Tirumala; family tradition credits him with some 32,000 saṅkīrtanas, of which about 14,900 survive engraved on copper plates kept at Tirumala, the earliest large body of songs in the kīrtana form.

dates.basis: family copper-plate tradition and biography by his grandson

nodes.name: Saṅkīrtanas of Annamācārya
nodes.summary: The Telugu (and some Sanskrit) songs of Annamācārya on Veṅkaṭeśvara, in devotional (adhyātma) and erotic (śṛṅgāra) modes, preserved on the Tāḷḷapāka copper plates at Tirumala; translated in part by Narayana Rao and Shulman (2005).

nodes.name: Carnatic music
nodes.summary: The classical music tradition of south India, built on rāga and tāla and on a repertoire of devotional song (kṛti, kīrtana, padam, varṇam) — from the Haridāsas and Annamācārya to the eighteenth–nineteenth-century “Trinity” of Tyāgarāja, Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri.

nodes.name: Tyāgarāja
nodes.summary: Telugu composer of Tiruvaiyaru in the Thanjavur country (1767–1847), the most celebrated of the Carnatic “Trinity”, whose hundreds of kṛtis — among them the five Pañcaratna kṛtis — are songs of devotion to Rāma; he is said to have refused royal patronage.

nodes.name: Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar
nodes.summary: Sanskrit-language composer of the Carnatic “Trinity” (1775/76–1835), signing as “Guruguha”; his some 500 kṛtis describe the deities, temples and tantric worship of dozens of shrines, including the Kamalāmbā Navāvaraṇa kṛtis of Tiruvārūr.

nodes.name: Śyāma Śāstri
nodes.summary: Eldest of the Carnatic “Trinity” (1762–1827), a priest of the goddess Kāmākṣī (Bangāru Kāmākṣī) at Thanjavur, whose compositions are almost all addressed to the Goddess.

nodes.name: Pañcaratna kṛtis
nodes.summary: Five Telugu kṛtis of Tyāgarāja in the rāgas Nāṭa, Gauḷa, Ārabhi, Varāḷi and Śrī, sung together by assembled musicians at his annual ārādhanā at Tiruvaiyaru.

nodes.name: Tyāgarāja Ārādhanā
nodes.summary: The annual music festival at Tyāgarāja’s samādhi on the Kāvēri at Tiruvaiyaru on the anniversary of his death (Puṣya bahuḷa pañcamī), culminating in the collective singing of the Pañcaratna kṛtis.

nodes.name: Bhadrācala Rāmadāsu (Kañcarla Gopanna)
nodes.summary: Telugu devotee-composer (c. 1620–1688), revenue official under the Qutb Shāhī sultans of Golconda, who by tradition spent government money rebuilding the Rāma temple at Bhadrācalam, was imprisoned for twelve years and released when Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa repaid the sum; author of kīrtanas and the Dāśarathi Śatakam.

nodes.name: Dāśarathi Śatakam
nodes.summary: A Telugu śatakam of about a hundred verses addressed to Rāma, son of Daśaratha, attributed to Kañcarla Gopanna (Bhadrācala Rāmadāsu).

nodes.name: Kṣetrayya
nodes.summary: Telugu composer of padams (c. 1600–1680) from Muvva in the Krishna delta, whose love songs to Muvva Gopāla (Kṛṣṇa), voiced mostly by courtesans and women, became central to the repertoire of dance (devadāsī and later Bharatanāṭyam).

nodes.name: Padams of Kṣetrayya
nodes.summary: Several hundred surviving Telugu padams (of thousands attributed) signed with the mudrā “Muvva Gopāla”, translated in part in When God Is a Customer (1994).

nodes.name: Akka Mahādēvi
nodes.summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva poet-saint of the twelfth century from Uḍutaḍi, who renounced marriage (and, in legend, clothing) for her divine husband Śiva as Cennamallikārjuna, “the lord white as jasmine”, and joined the gathering of Basava and Allama at Kalyāṇa before ending her life on Śrīśaila; some 430 vacanas are attributed to her.

nodes.name: Allama Prabhu
nodes.summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva mystic poet of the twelfth century, presiding figure of the Anubhava Maṇṭapa of Kalyāṇa in tradition, whose enigmatic vacanas to Guhēśvara (“lord of the caves”) criticise ritual and teach the unity of self and Śiva.

nodes.name: Vacanas of Akka Mahādēvi
nodes.summary: The Kannada free-verse sayings (vacanas) signed “Cennamallikārjuna”, about 430 attributed to Akka Mahādēvi.

nodes.name: Vacanas of Allama Prabhu
nodes.summary: The Kannada vacanas signed “Guhēśvara” attributed to Allama Prabhu, admired for paradox and riddling imagery.

nodes.name: Śūnya Sampādane
nodes.summary: A fifteenth-century Kannada anthology that arranges the vacanas of Allama, Basava, Akka Mahādēvi and others as dialogues in the Anubhava Maṇṭapa around Allama, the “attainment of the void”; compiled in several redactions in the Vijayanagara period.

nodes.name: Aruṇakirinātar
nodes.summary: Tamil Śaiva poet of Tiruvaṇṇāmalai (c. 1370–1450 on Zvelebil’s dating), author of the Tiruppukaḻ, rhythmically intricate songs to Murukaṉ at his shrines, and of the Kantar Anupūti and Kantar Alaṅkāram.

nodes.name: Tiruppukaḻ
nodes.summary: Aruṇakirinātar’s “Holy Praise”, some 1,300 surviving Tamil songs to Murukaṉ in elaborate rhythmic patterns (cantam), arranged by the shrines they praise; the Project Madurai edition numbers the songs 1–1326.
nodes.details: The Project Madurai part 1 (songs 1–330) opens with a song to Vināyaka (“kaittala niṟaikaṉi”) and contains songs headed for Tirupparaṅkuṉṟam, Tiruccentūr, Paḻani and Tiruttaṇikai among other shrines (checked 2026-11-08).

nodes.name: Mēlputtūr Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri
nodes.summary: Kerala Sanskrit poet and grammarian (1560–1646/1666), author of the Prakriyāsarvasva on Pāṇinian grammar and of the Nārāyaṇīyam, a condensation of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa in a thousand verses addressed to Kṛṣṇa of Guruvāyūr.

nodes.name: Nārāyaṇīyam
nodes.summary: A Sanskrit devotional poem of 100 cantos (daśakas), 1,034 verses, condensing the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and addressed throughout to Kṛṣṇa of Guruvāyūr (“pavanapurapate”). Its last verse ends with the phrase “āyurārogyasaukhyam”, which as a kali-day chronogram gives a date in 1586 CE.
nodes.details: GRETIL e-text, Nār. 100.10: “nityaṃ cittasthitaṃ me pavanapurapate kṛṣṇa kāruṇyasindho”; 100.11 ends “… idam iha kurutām āyurārogyasaukhyam”. The decoding of the chronogram is traditional; the arithmetic is shown in the date basis. Wikipedia notes that the earliest manuscripts are much later than the poem.

dates.label: 1586 CE (kali-day 1,712,210)
dates.basis: kaṭapayādi reading of “āyurārogyasaukhyam” (y=1, r=2, r=2, g(y)=1, s=7, kh(y)=1, read right to left) = 1,712,210 days of the Kali age

nodes.limits: The 1586 date depends on accepting the final phrase as an intended chronogram.

nodes.name: Pūntānam Nampūtiri
nodes.summary: Malayalam devotional poet (1547–1640) of Keezhattoor, devotee of Guruvāyūrappan, author of the Jñānappāna; Guruvāyūr legend contrasts his simple bhakti, which the god preferred, with Bhaṭṭatiri’s learned Sanskrit.

nodes.name: Jñānappāna
nodes.summary: Pūntānam’s Malayalam “Song of Divine Wisdom” (16th c.), a meditation in simple verse on the transience of life and devotion to Kṛṣṇa of Guruvāyūr.

nodes.name: Rāmaliṅga Swāmigaḷ (Vaḷḷalār)
nodes.summary: Tamil saint and poet (1823–1874) of Marutūr near Chidambaram, who preached compassion to all living beings (jīvakāruṇyam), founded the Samaraca Cutta Caṉmārka Caṅkam (1865), a free kitchen at Vadalur (1867) and the Sathya Gnana Sabai (1872) to a formless “Arutperuñjōti” (Grace-Light); his collected hymns, the Tiruvaruṭpā, provoked the “Aruṭpā–Maruṭpā” controversy with Śaiva Siddhāntins.

nodes.name: Samaraca Cutta Caṉmārkam (Vaḷḷalār’s path)
nodes.summary: The universalist movement founded by Rāmaliṅga Swāmigaḷ in 1865, centred on the worship of God as light and on feeding the hungry, with its Sathya Gnana Sabai at Vadalur (1872).

nodes.name: Tiruvaruṭpā
nodes.summary: The collected Tamil hymns of Rāmaliṅga Swāmigaḷ, arranged in six tirumuṟais, the first parts published in his lifetime (1867); their claim to scriptural status was attacked by Āṟumuka Nāvalar in the “Aruṭpā–Maruṭpā” dispute.

nodes.name: Bhānubhakta Ācārya
nodes.summary: Nepali poet (1814–1868) honoured as Ādikavi, the first poet of Nepali, for his Nepali Rāmāyaṇa; also known for verse letters and satire written while imprisoned. His birthday (Bhānu Jayantī) is a cultural holiday in Nepal and among Nepali speakers in India.

nodes.name: Bhānubhakta Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: Bhānubhakta’s Nepali Rāmāyaṇa in seven kāṇḍas, circulated orally and in manuscript and published complete in 1887 by Motirām Bhaṭṭa; regarded as the first Nepali epic and a foundation of the literary language. Hutt treats it as based on the Sanskrit Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa.
nodes.details: Wikipedia’s article calls it a translation of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa; Hutt (1988) and older Nepali scholarship identify the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa as its source. Both views are recorded.
openQuestions: A canto-by-canto comparison with the Adhyātma would settle the source question.

nodes.name: Śivastotrāvalī
nodes.summary: Utpaladeva’s “Garland of Hymns to Śiva”, twenty Sanskrit stotras of personal devotion grounded in Pratyabhijñā non-dualism, collected after him with a commentary by Kṣemarāja; still recited by Kashmiri Paṇḍits.

sources.locator: Śivastotrāvalī (GRETIL e-text based on Bailly’s edition)

nodes.name: Rūpa Bhavānī
nodes.summary: Kashmiri Paṇḍit woman mystic and poet (c. 1621–1721), whose Kashmiri vākhs in the line of Lal Ded express Śaiva yogic experience; she is commemorated by Kashmiri Paṇḍits on her birth anniversary (Sahib Saptami).

nodes.name: Old Javanese kakawin and parwa literature
nodes.summary: The court literature of Java and Bali in Old Javanese: prose renderings of Mahābhārata books (parwa, from the late 10th c.) and long poems in Sanskrit metres (kakawin) retelling epic and Purāṇic stories — Rāmāyaṇa, Arjunawiwāha, Kṛṣṇāyana, Bhāratayuddha, Hariwangsa and others — preserved mainly in Balinese palm-leaf manuscripts.

nodes.name: Airlangga
nodes.summary: King in East Java (r. 1019–1042), of Balinese birth, who restored the kingdom after the fall of Dharmawangsa Teguh’s court (c. 1016) and is named in the Arjunawiwāha as the poet Mpu Kanwa’s king; his Pucangan inscription of 1041 recounts his career.

nodes.name: Mpu Kanwa
nodes.summary: Old Javanese poet of King Airlangga’s court (early 11th c.), known only from his Arjunawiwāha, in whose last stanza (36.2) he names himself, the work and the king.

nodes.name: Arjunawiwāha (Kakawin)
nodes.summary: Mpu Kanwa’s Old Javanese kakawin “Arjuna’s Wedding” (11th c.), the oldest dated kakawin after the Rāmāyaṇa: Arjuna’s ascetic penance, his resistance to the nymphs sent to test him, the fight with Śiva as a hunter over the boar Muka, and his victory for Indra over the demon Niwātakawaca, rewarded with marriage to the nymphs. It retells the Mahābhārata’s Āraṇyakaparvan episodes and remained a favourite of Javanese and Balinese wayang.

nodes.name: Jayabhaya (king of Kaḍiri)
nodes.summary: King of Kaḍiri (Daha) in East Java (r. c. 1130/1135–1157), known from inscriptions of 1135, 1136 and 1144 under the consecration name Śrī Warmeśwara, patron of the Bhāratayuddha; later Javanese tradition made him a prophet-king (the Jangka Jayabaya prophecies).

dates.label: c. 1130/1135 – 1157
dates.basis: inscriptions of 1135, 1136, 1144 and the Bhāratayuddha chronogram

nodes.name: Mpu Sedah
nodes.summary: Old Javanese court poet of King Jayabhaya of Kaḍiri, who began the Bhāratayuddha in 1157; Javanese legend that he was put to death for modelling Śalya’s queen on the king’s consort is dismissed by Zoetmulder as having no basis in the text.

nodes.name: Mpu Panuluh
nodes.summary: Old Javanese court poet who completed the Bhāratayuddha begun by Mpu Sedah and wrote the kakawins Hariwangsa and Ghaṭotkacāśraya (12th c.).

sources.locator: pp. 339–341 and chapters on Hariwangsa and Ghaṭotkacāśraya

nodes.name: Bhāratayuddha (Kakawin)
nodes.summary: The Old Javanese kakawin of the Mahābhārata war, begun by Mpu Sedah and completed by Mpu Panuluh for King Jayabhaya of Kaḍiri; a chronogram in its prologue (“sang akuda suddha candrama”) gives Śaka 1079, 1157 CE — the paraphrase even yields the day, 6 September 1157. It became the basis of the Javanese and Balinese tradition of the great war.
nodes.details: Zoetmulder (Kalangwan, Indonesian ed. 1983, p. 340): Mpu Sedah composed a chronogram for the king “drawn by horses (the sun) and the pure moon” — sang akuda suddha candrama — yielding Śaka 1079 = 1157 CE; the epilogue tells that Mpu Panuluh was charged with writing the last part.

dates.label: 1157 CE (Śaka 1079), 6 September
dates.basis: chronogram in the prologue, read by Zoetmulder

nodes.name: Hariwangsa (Kakawin)
nodes.summary: Mpu Panuluh’s Old Javanese kakawin (12th c.) on Kṛṣṇa’s abduction of Rukmiṇī and the war with Jarāsandha, drawing on the Harivaṃśa tradition; edited by A. Teeuw (1950).

dates.label: 12th c.
dates.basis: court and poet as identified by Zoetmulder

sources.locator: chapter list and chapters on the work

nodes.name: Ghaṭotkacāśraya (Kakawin)
nodes.summary: Mpu Panuluh’s Old Javanese kakawin (12th c.) on Ghaṭotkaca’s help to Abhimanyu in winning his bride — an episode not found in the Sanskrit Mahābhārata.

dates.label: 12th c.
dates.basis: court and poet as identified by Zoetmulder

sources.locator: chapter list and chapters on the work

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇāyana (Kakawin)
nodes.summary: Mpu Triguṇa’s Old Javanese kakawin on Kṛṣṇa’s abduction of Rukmiṇī, written at the court of King Warsajaya (early 12th c.).

dates.label: 12th c.
dates.basis: court and poet as identified by Zoetmulder

sources.locator: chapter list and chapters on the work

nodes.name: Mpu Triguṇa
nodes.summary: Old Javanese poet of King Warsajaya’s court (early 12th c.), author of the Kṛṣṇāyana kakawin.

sources.locator: chapter “Mpu Dharmaja, Mpu Monaguna dan Mpu Triguna”

nodes.name: Wirāṭaparwa (Old Javanese prose)
nodes.summary: The Old Javanese prose rendering of the Mahābhārata’s Virāṭaparvan, made at the court of King Dharmawangsa Teguh; its epilogue records that it was recited before the king over a month, which Zoetmulder computes as 14 October–12 November 996 CE — one of the earliest dated works of Old Javanese literature.

dates.label: 14 October – 12 November 996
dates.basis: dates in the epilogue converted by Zoetmulder (who allows that the epilogue may have been added by another hand)

nodes.name: Agama Hindu Dharma (Balinese Hinduism)
nodes.summary: The Hindu religion of Bali (and of Hindu communities elsewhere in Indonesia), joining temple-centred Śaiva and Buddhist priestly ritual inherited from Java with local ancestor and village temple cults. Under Indonesia’s state requirement of monotheism, Balinese reformers recast it around Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa as one supreme God and secured its recognition by the Ministry of Religion around 1958–59; the Parisada Hindu Dharma was founded as its council in 1959, and “Agama Hindu Bali” became the national “Agama Hindu” in the 1960s.

dates.event: recognition by Indonesia’s Ministry of Religion
dates.label: c. 1958–1962
dates.basis: Picard’s history of the recognition campaign

nodes.limits: The dates of recognition and renaming are summarised from Picard’s title and reference works; the ministerial decrees were not consulted.

nodes.name: Parisada Hindu Dharma Indonesia
nodes.summary: The council of Indonesian Hindus, founded in Bali in 1959 as Parisada Dharma Hindu Bali and later renamed for the whole country, which standardises doctrine and represents Hinduism to the state.

nodes.name: Maharadia Lawana (Maranao)
nodes.summary: A Maranao epic song from the Lake Lanao region of Mindanao (Philippines) whose hero is Maharadia Lawana — Rāvaṇa — to whom the gods grant immortality; a local, Islamised telling of the Rāma story. Juan R. Francisco heard it sung by Maranao bards in 1968 and published an English rendering with the Maranao scholar Nagasura Madale (1969), arguing that the story reached the Philippines between the 17th and 19th centuries through Javanese and Malay contacts.

dates.event: recorded by Francisco from Maranao bards
dates.label: heard 1968; published 1969

nodes.limits: The plot and character correspondences were not checked against Francisco’s text in this round.
openQuestions: Reference summaries disagree on whether Maharadia Lawana is presented as a monkey-king or as the Rāvaṇa figure abducting the heroine; Francisco 1969 should be consulted.

nodes.name: Hinduism in Mauritius
nodes.summary: The Hindu traditions of Mauritius, brought by indentured labourers from Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Andhra and Maharashtra from the 1830s; Hindus are the largest religious group (about 48% in the 2022 census), the only Hindu plurality in Africa. Its signature observances are the Mahāśivarātri pilgrimage to Ganga Talao (Grand Bassin), Thaipusam and Tamil kāvaṭi, and the Bhojpuri Geet-Gawai.

nodes.name: Grand Bassin (Ganga Talao) pilgrimage
nodes.summary: The Mahāśivarātri pilgrimage of Mauritian Hindus, many walking from across the island carrying decorated kāṁvaṛ, to the crater lake Grand Bassin, renamed Ganga Talao and ritually linked with the Gaṅgā; the island’s largest Hindu festival and, for Eisenlohr, a “cultural touchstone” of Indo-Mauritian identity.

nodes.name: Indo-Caribbean Hinduism
nodes.summary: The Hinduism of the descendants of Indian indentured labourers in Trinidad and Tobago (from 1845), British Guiana/Guyana (from 1838) and Suriname (from 1873), largely of Bhojpuri-speaking north Indian origin: Sanātanī temple and pandit organisations, Rāmāyaṇ (Mānas) recitation and Rāmlīlā, Phagwah (Holī) and Divālī as public festivals. Guyana has the highest proportion of Hindus in the Western Hemisphere.

dates.event: arrival of the first indentured labourers in Trinidad (Fatel Razack, 30 May 1845)
dates.label: 30 May 1845

dates.event: indentured migration to the Caribbean (Guyana 1838 – c. 1917)

nodes.name: Sanatan Dharma Maha Sabha (Trinidad and Tobago)
nodes.summary: The largest Hindu organisation of Trinidad and Tobago, formed in 1952 when Bhadase Sagan Maraj merged two Sanātanī bodies; it runs some 150 mandirs, over fifty schools and broadcast media.

nodes.name: Rāmlīlā of Trinidad
nodes.summary: Open-air village performances of the Rāma story in Trinidad, based on Tulsīdās’s Mānas and staged by Indo-Trinidadian communities from the late nineteenth century, culminating in the burning of Rāvaṇa’s effigy around Dussehra.
nodes.limits: The date of the first Trinidad Rāmlīlā (often said to be the 1880s) was not verified.

nodes.name: Phagwah (Caribbean Holī)
nodes.summary: The Caribbean form of Holī among Indo-Guyanese, Indo-Trinidadians and Indo-Surinamese, named from the Bhojpuri month Phāgun, with chowtal singing and the throwing of coloured water (abeer); a public holiday in Guyana and Suriname.

nodes.name: Hinduism in Fiji
nodes.summary: The Hinduism of Indo-Fijians, descendants of indentured labourers brought to the sugar plantations between 1879 and 1916; about a quarter of Fiji’s population (24% in 2017). Rāmāyaṇ maṇḍalīs reciting the Mānas, Sanātanī and Ārya Samāj organisations and south Indian fire-walking are among its institutions; Kelly (1991) studies its colonial-era politics of virtue.

nodes.name: Hinduism in Malaysia
nodes.summary: The Hinduism of Malaysia’s Indian (mostly Tamil) community, about 6% of the population (2020), formed largely by nineteenth- and early twentieth-century labour migration to the plantations; its great public festival is Thaipusam at Batu Caves near Kuala Lumpur, with its 43-metre Murukaṉ statue.

nodes.name: Hinduism in South Africa
nodes.summary: The Hinduism of Indian South Africans, mainly in KwaZulu-Natal, descended chiefly from indentured labourers brought to Natal from 1860 to 1911 and from later “passenger” migrants; Tamil, Telugu, Hindi- and Gujarati-speaking traditions coexist, with fire-walking festivals for Draupadī and Kāvaṭi for Murukaṉ.

nodes.name: Hindu temple-building in Britain
nodes.summary: The growth of British Hindu congregations from converted houses and halls in the 1960s–70s, after migration from India and East Africa, to purpose-built temples such as the BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir at Neasden (1995) and many regional and sectarian mandirs; the temples belong to the temple records, this record to the community movement.

nodes.name: Hindu temple-building in the United States
nodes.summary: The establishment of temples by Indian professionals who arrived after the 1965 Immigration Act — among the first the Ganesha temple of the Hindu Temple Society of North America in Flushing, New York, and the Sri Venkateswara temple at Penn Hills, Pittsburgh (both consecrated 1977) — often built by south Indian craftsmen on Āgamic plans and serving pan-Hindu congregations.

dates.basis: temple histories as summarised by Eck and Waghorne

nodes.limits: Which temple was “first” depends on definition (consecration, construction, earlier Vedanta Society buildings).

nodes.name: ISKCON (International Society for Krishna Consciousness)
nodes.summary: A Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava movement founded in New York on 13 July 1966 by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda, which spread the chanting of the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra, Caitanya’s theology and his own translations of the Gītā and Bhāgavata among Western converts and later the Indian diaspora; its headquarters are at Māyāpur, West Bengal. It holds Ratha Yātrās in cities worldwide.

nodes.name: A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
nodes.summary: Bengali Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava teacher (1896–1977), initiated in the Gauḍīya Maṭh line of Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī, who sailed to New York in 1965 aged 69 and founded ISKCON in 1966; his English translations and commentaries on the Bhagavad Gītā, Bhāgavata Purāṇa and Caitanya Caritāmṛta became the movement’s scriptures.

nodes.name: Āgamas and Tantras
nodes.summary: The large body of post-Vedic scriptures (Āgama, Tantra, Saṃhitā) of the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra and Śākta traditions, which regulate initiation, mantra, temple building, image worship, festivals and yoga.
nodes.details:
The corpus is not one canon but several: the Śaiva Mantramārga (Siddhānta and the non-dualist Bhairava/Kaula streams), the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās (traditionally 108), the Vaikhānasa texts, and Śākta Tantras. Sanderson (2009) describes the early medieval period as a “Śaiva Age” in which these ritual systems, and the royal and temple institutions that used them, spread across South and Southeast Asia.

The earliest surviving Śaiva tantra is generally taken to be the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā, whose oldest layer its editors place c. 450–550 CE. Most Pāñcarātra saṃhitās are later and their dates are disputed. In South Indian temple practice the Śaiva Āgamas (traditionally 28) and selected Pāñcarātra saṃhitās remain the ritual authorities.

dates.label: c. 5th–14th c. CE
dates.basis: manuscript dating, cross-citation and internal evidence

nodes.limits: A collection label: dates and authority differ sharply between sub-corpora; traditional claims of eternal or divine origin are recorded as tradition, not as dates.

nodes.name: Devotional (bhakti) literature
nodes.summary: Devotional poetry, song and hagiography addressed to Śiva, Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa/Rāma, the Goddess and other deities in Tamil, Kannada, Telugu, Marathi, Hindi dialects, Bengali, Assamese, Odia, Gujarati, Kashmiri and other languages, from the Tamil saints of c. 6th–9th c. onward.
nodes.details: Treated here as an umbrella for regionally distinct corpora with their own canons (Nālāyira Divya Prabandham, Tirumurai, Vārkarī abhaṅgas, Vīraśaiva vacanas, Sūrsāgar, the Assamese Kīrtana Ghoṣā…). The common label is a modern scholarly one; each tradition defines its own corpus and authority.

dates.event: composition (Tamil beginnings to early-modern North India)
dates.label: c. 6th–17th c. CE

nodes.limits: “Bhakti movement” as a single pan-Indian wave is a scholarly construct that some historians question; the dates are ranges for disparate corpora.

nodes.name: Regional and vernacular retellings
nodes.summary: Tellings of the Rāma and Bhārata narratives (and of Purāṇic material) in Indian languages, in later Sanskrit, and in Jain and Buddhist traditions. Each telling is recorded as a work with its own date, author and theology, not as a deviation from an original.
nodes.details: Ramanujan’s essay “Three Hundred Rāmāyaṇas” proposed speaking of many “tellings” sharing a pool of signifiers rather than of versions of a single Ur-text, a framing taken up in Richman (ed.) 1991. This collection follows that approach: RETELLS / DERIVED_FROM edges record documented literary dependence only, and differences are recorded in Comparison tables rather than as errors.
nodes.limits: Membership in this collection says nothing about relative “authenticity”; Jain and Buddhist tellings are included as members of the Rāma narrative tradition, not as Hindu texts.

nodes.name: Southeast Asian adaptations
nodes.summary: Rāma and other Indic narratives as written, carved, recited and performed in Java, Bali, Cambodia, Thailand, Laos, Myanmar and the Malay world, from the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa (late 9th–early 10th c.) to the Thai Ramakien of Rama I (1797–1807).
nodes.details: These tellings are often Buddhist (Lao Phra Lak Phra Lam is framed as a jātaka), Islamic-framed (some Malay Hikayat Seri Rama versions) or court-ritual (Thai and Khmer royal drama). Characters are renamed and re-characterised: Rāvaṇa becomes Thotsakan (Thai) or Krong Reap (Khmer), Sītā is sometimes Rāvaṇa’s daughter, and Hanumān is an amorous hero who fathers a son with the mermaid Suvannamaccha.

dates.event: composition of the surviving literary tellings
dates.label: c. 856 – 1807 CE
dates.basis: Robson’s dating of the Kakawin; Rama I’s Ramakien

nodes.limits: Temple reliefs (Prambanan, Angkor Wat) attest the circulation of the story but do not by themselves show which telling the sculptors followed.

nodes.name: Kamba Rāmāyaṇam (Irāmāvatāram)
nodes.summary: The Tamil Rāma epic of the poet Kampaṉ, in six kāṇṭams of viruttam verse (c. 10,500 stanzas in the standard edition), dated variously between the 9th and 12th centuries. It is the most celebrated Tamil telling and is shaped by Tamil poetics and Śrīvaiṣṇava devotion.
nodes.details:
Kampaṉ names his patron, Caṭaiyappa Vaḷḷal of Tiruveṇṇainallūr, at intervals in the poem. The standard text is the edition prepared by a committee of the Kamban Kazhagam (1976) which set aside many interpolated verses; the seventh book (Uttara kāṇṭam) is attributed to Oṭṭakkūttar, not Kampaṉ.

Among the episodes that distinguish the telling: Rāma and Sītā glimpse each other in Mithilā before the breaking of the bow; in the Āraṇya kāṇṭam Rāvaṇa does not touch Sītā but lifts her away with the earth on which her hermitage stands; and Rāvaṇa is given tragic grandeur. Temple tradition holds that the poem was first publicly recited (araṅkēṟṟam) at the Raṅganātha temple, Srirangam.

dates.label: Śaka 807 (≈ 885 CE), per an anonymous traditional verse
dates.basis: traditional verse giving a Śaka year; widely doubted

dates.label: 12th c. CE
dates.basis: references to Rāmānuja’s era, patron identification, language

dates.label: 9th c. CE
dates.view: minority view of some Tamil scholars

openQuestions: Which external evidence (inscription, datable citation) gives the firmest terminus ante quem for Kampaṉ?

nodes.name: Rāmcaritmānas
nodes.summary: Tulsīdās’s Awadhi Rāma epic in seven kāṇḍs of caupāī–dohā verse, begun at Ayodhyā in Saṃvat 1631 (1574 CE) according to the poem itself. It is the dominant Rāma text of North India and the basis of the Rāmlīlā.
nodes.details:
The poem is framed as a set of nested dialogues: Śiva to Pārvatī, the crow-sage Kākabhuśuṇḍi to Garuḍa, and Yājñavalkya to Bharadvāja. Its theology presents Rāma as the supreme Brahman who takes on a human līlā; following the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, it has Sītā enter the fire before the abduction and leave her reflection (pratibimba) to be carried off, and the fire-ordeal burns the reflection (Laṅkākāṇḍa chand before dohā 109).

The text states its own starting date: “saṃbata soraha sai ekatīsā … naumī bhauma bāra madhu māsā, avadhapurīṃ yaha carita prakāsā” — the year 1631, on the ninth, a Tuesday, in the month Madhu (Caitra), at Ayodhyā. This is Rāmanavamī, Rāma’s birthday.

dates.label: 1574 CE (Saṃvat 1631, Caitra śukla 9)
dates.basis: date stated in the poem itself (Bālakāṇḍa)

sources.quote: संबत सोरह सै एकतीसा। करउँ कथा हरि पद धरि सीसा ॥ नौमी भौम बार मधु मासा। अवधपुरीं यह चरित प्रकासा ॥

dates.label: c. 1576–77 CE (traditional: 2 years 7 months after starting)

attributes.metre: caupāī with dohā, soraṭhā and chand
attributes.author: Tulsīdās

nodes.limits: The internal date fixes when composition began, not when the text reached its received form; the oldest manuscripts and their dates were not checked in this session.

nodes.name: Kṛttivāsī Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: The Bengali Rāma narrative (Śrīrām Pā̃cālī) attributed to Kṛttibās Ojhā, composed probably in the 15th century in the pā̃cālī form for recitation and singing, and the most widely read Rāmāyaṇa in Bengal.
nodes.details: The received text has been heavily reworked by singers and editors; it was first printed at the Serampore Mission Press (1803). It keeps Vālmīki’s overall plot while adding localised episodes — popularly, Rāma’s out-of-season worship of Durgā (akāla-bodhana) before the final battle, and the devotion of Rāvaṇa’s side characters such as Taraṇīsen — which are central to its Bengali reception.

dates.label: 15th c. CE (if the popular identification of the poet is correct)
dates.basis: autobiographical verses in some manuscripts; identification of the Gauḍa king named

nodes.limits: The printed vulgate reflects centuries of performance; episodes popularly ascribed to Kṛttibās may be later accretions.

nodes.name: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: A Sanskrit Rāma narrative in seven kāṇḍas presented as a Śiva–Pārvatī dialogue within the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, re-reading the story through Advaita Vedānta: Rāma is the supreme Brahman and events are his līlā. Dated to roughly the 13th–15th c.
nodes.details: The work is c. 65 chapters (about 4,500 verses). Its best-known innovation is the māyā-Sītā: Rāma, knowing what is to come, asks Sītā to enter the fire and leave an illusory double, who is the one Rāvaṇa carries off; at the fire-ordeal the double vanishes and Agni restores the real Sītā. The text deeply influenced Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas and was rendered into Malayalam by Eḻuttacchaṉ. Tradition also links it to Rāmānanda.

dates.label: c. 13th–15th c. CE
dates.basis: doctrinal content, citations, relation to Rāmānandī circles

dates.label: part of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, by Vyāsa (traditional)

openQuestions: Exact sarga locators for the māyā-Sītā episode in a named edition (recalled as Araṇyakāṇḍa 7).

nodes.name: Tēvāram
nodes.summary: The Tamil Śaiva hymns (patikams) of Campantar, Appar and Cuntarar (7th–8th c.), forming the first seven books of the Tirumurai; about 796 hymns survive. The hymns praise Śiva at named temples, which tradition counts as the 275 Pāṭal Peṟṟa Talams.
nodes.details: Books 1–3 are Campantar’s (c. 383–384 hymns), 4–6 Appar’s (c. 313), 7 Cuntarar’s (c. 100). According to the Tirumuṟai Kaṇṭa Purāṇam tradition, the Cōḻa king Rājarāja I sought the hymns and Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi found palm-leaf manuscripts, partly eaten by white ants, in a sealed chamber of the Chidambaram temple; Nampi then arranged them by musical mode (paṇ). The hymns are still sung by hereditary ōtuvār singers in Tamil Śaiva temples.

dates.label: c. 7th–8th c. CE
dates.basis: synchronisms with Pallava and Pāṇḍya kings named in hagiography; internal evidence

dates.label: late 10th–11th c. CE
dates.basis: tradition linking the recovery to Rājarāja I (r. 985–1014)

nodes.limits: The recovery story is a later traditional account; it does not by itself date the compilation.

nodes.name: Nālāyira Divya Prabandham
nodes.summary: The “Four Thousand Sacred Compositions”: Tamil hymns of the twelve Āḻvārs (c. 6th–9th c.) praising Viṣṇu at named shrines, compiled by Nāthamuni in the 9th–10th century. Śrīvaiṣṇavas regard it as a Tamil Veda and recite it in temple worship.
nodes.details: The collection includes Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai and Nācciyār Tirumoḻi and Nammāḻvār’s Tiruvāymoḻi (1,102 verses). The shrines praised in the hymns are counted by tradition as the 108 Divya Deśams. Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiography holds that Nāthamuni recovered the hymns after reciting Madhurakavi’s Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu at Kurukūr until Nammāḻvār appeared to him.

dates.label: c. 6th–9th c. CE
dates.basis: internal references, relation to Pallava-period Tamil

nodes.name: Periya Purāṇam
nodes.summary: Cēkkiḻār’s 12th-century Tamil hagiography of the sixty-three Śaiva saints (Nāyaṉmār), composed at the Cōḻa court of Kulōttuṅka II and placed as the twelfth and last book of the Tirumurai.
nodes.details: It expands the list of devotees in Cuntarar’s Tiruttoṇṭattokai and Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi’s Tiruttoṇṭar Tiruvantāti into full narratives. Tradition holds that Kulōttuṅka II asked his minister Cēkkiḻār to write it to wean him from the Jain epic Cīvaka Cintāmaṇi, and that it was first recited at Chidambaram.

dates.label: 12th c. CE (reign of Kulōttuṅka II, 1133–1150)
dates.basis: regnal synchronism from tradition and internal references

nodes.limits: A hagiography composed four to five centuries after most of its subjects; it is evidence for 12th-century Śaiva memory, not a contemporary record of the saints.

nodes.name: Gītagovinda
nodes.summary: Jayadeva’s 12th-century Sanskrit lyrical poem in twelve cantos (24 songs, aṣṭapadī) on the love, separation and reunion of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. It is the first major Sanskrit work centred on Rādhā and is sung nightly in the Jagannātha temple, Puri.
nodes.details: The opening hymn on the ten avatāras (daśāvatāra) includes Balarāma and the Buddha. The poem was taken up as ritual song (sevā) in the Puri temple and as a foundational text in Gauḍīya and other Kṛṣṇa traditions, and inspired a large painting tradition. Jayadeva’s birthplace “Kindubilva” is claimed for Kenduli (Birbhum, Bengal), Kenduli Sasan (Odisha) and a village in Mithilā.

dates.label: 12th c. CE (late)
dates.basis: tradition of Jayadeva at the court of Lakṣmaṇasena; manuscript and commentary history

nodes.name: Jñāneśvarī
nodes.summary: Jñānadeva’s Marathi ovī commentary (Bhāvārthadīpikā) on the Bhagavad Gītā in eighteen chapters, completed in Śaka 1212 (1290 CE) according to its colophon. It is the foundational scripture of the Vārkarī tradition and among the earliest major works of Marathi literature.
nodes.details: The colophon places the work “on the bank of the Godāvarī” in the ancient pañcakrośa kṣetra where Śrī Mahālayā dwells — traditionally identified with Nevāsā — during the reign of Śrī Rāmacandra “of the Yadu line” (the Yādava king Rāmacandra), written by Jñānadeva, disciple of Nivṛttinātha, with Saccidānanda Bābā as scribe. An appended verse records that Eknāth produced a corrected text in Śaka 1506 (1584 CE) because variant readings had crept in.

dates.label: Śaka 1212 (1290 CE)
dates.basis: colophon with regnal reference to the Yādava king Rāmacandra
