nodes.name: Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa (Old Javanese)
nodes.summary: The Old Javanese Rāmāyaṇa in kakawin (Indic-metre court poetry), the longest kakawin of the Hindu-Buddhist period, composed in Central Java c. 856–930 CE. Its first half closely follows the Sanskrit Bhaṭṭikāvya rather than Vālmīki.
nodes.details: The poem is anonymous in the manuscripts; Balinese tradition names a poet Yogīśvara. It belongs to the period of the Medang (Mataram) kingdom, which also built the Prambanan temple compound with its Rāmāyaṇa reliefs; whether the reliefs follow this poem or another telling has been debated since Stutterheim (1925). The text survives in Balinese manuscripts and is still recited in Bali.

dates.label: c. 856 – c. 930 CE
dates.basis: linguistic and historical evidence; links with Medang court culture

nodes.name: Ramakien (Thai)

scripts.text: รามเกียรติ์

nodes.summary: The Thai national Rāma epic. Earlier Ayutthaya-period versions were largely lost in 1767; the canonical recension was compiled under King Rama I (Phutthayotfa Chulalok) in 1797–1807, partly written by the king, and a shorter version for dance-drama was made under Rama II.
nodes.details: Phra Ram is an incarnation of Phra Narai (Nārāyaṇa) and Nang Sida of Lakshmi; Thotsakan (Rāvaṇa) is Sida’s father in this telling, who sets her adrift because of an ill omen, after which she is raised by King Chanok (Janaka). Hanuman is a brilliant, amorous white monkey who fathers Macchanu with the mermaid Suvannamaccha. The Ramakien is painted in the galleries of Wat Phra Kaew, Bangkok, and performed in khon masked drama.

dates.event: compilation of the Rama I recension
dates.label: 1797–1807 CE
dates.basis: court records of Rama I’s reign

dates.label: Ayutthaya period, before 1767
dates.basis: fragmentary survivals after the sack of Ayutthaya

nodes.name: Reamker (Khmer)

scripts.text: រាមកេរ្តិ៍

nodes.summary: The Khmer Rāma epic (Rāmakerti, “Glory of Rāma”), whose surviving text dates from the 16th–17th c. (first part) and later centuries. It recasts the story in Theravāda Buddhist terms and is a mainstay of Cambodian court dance and Lkhon Khol masked theatre.
nodes.details: Characters: Preah Ream (Rāma), Neang Seda (Sītā), Preah Leak (Lakṣmaṇa), Krong Reap (Rāvaṇa), Hanuman. The surviving first part does not narrate Rāvaṇa’s death; the second part includes Seda’s second exile and her descent into the earth. The encounter of Hanuman and the mermaid Sovann Maccha is a favourite episode. Rāma narratives were carved at Angkor (e.g. Angkor Wat, 12th c.) centuries before the surviving Reamker text.

dates.event: composition of the surviving first part
dates.label: 16th–17th c. CE

nodes.limits: Angkorian reliefs show the Rāma story was known in the Khmer world; they are not evidence for the Reamker text, which is later.

nodes.name: Paumacariya of Vimalasūri (Jain)
nodes.summary: The earliest Jain telling of the Rāma story, in Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit, by Vimalasūri. Its own colophon dates it 530 (variant 520) years after Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa; scholars disagree on how to convert this and many place the work between the 1st and 5th centuries CE.
nodes.details: Rāma is “Pauma” (Padma). The work rationalises the story for Jain readers: rākṣasas and vānaras are human vidyādhara clans (the monkey is a banner emblem), Rāvaṇa is a learned Jain devotee who is not literally ten-headed, and in keeping with the Jain pattern of Baladeva, Vāsudeva and Prativāsudeva it is Lakṣmaṇa, not Rāma, who kills Rāvaṇa. Rāma ends as a Jain monk and attains liberation; Rāvaṇa is to become a future tīrthaṅkara. The frame has King Śreṇika asking Gautama how the popular tellings — monkeys defeating rākṣasas, Kumbhakarṇa sleeping six months — can be true, so the work presents itself as a corrective telling.

dates.label: 530 (var. 520) years after Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa
dates.basis: praśasti at the end of the text

dates.event: composition (colophon read on the traditional Vīra era)
dates.label: c. 4 CE

dates.event: composition (colophon read on Jacobi’s nirvāṇa date)
dates.label: c. 53–63 CE
dates.basis: colophon converted with Jacobi’s later Vīra-nirvāṇa

dates.label: c. 1st–5th c. CE (not later than the 3rd c. in the commonest view)
dates.basis: language, metre, content; terminus ante quem the Kuvalayamālā of 778 CE

nodes.limits: A Jain work: it belongs to the Rāma narrative tradition but is not a Hindu scripture, and its corrective framing is a Jain literary strategy, not evidence about an “original” Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Dasaratha Jātaka (Buddhist)
nodes.summary: Jātaka no. 461 of the Pali canon’s Jātaka collection: a birth-story in which Rāma-paṇḍita, the Bodhisatta, his brother Lakkhaṇa and their sister Sītā, children of King Dasaratha of Bārāṇasī, live twelve years in the Himalaya. There is no abduction and no Rāvaṇa.
nodes.details:
Dasaratha sends his children away to protect them from a second queen who wants the throne for her son Bharata; he dies in the ninth year, but Rāma-paṇḍita keeps to his father’s twelve-year term and sends his sandals to rule in his place. On their return Sītā is made queen consort and Rāma reigns sixteen thousand years. In the closing identification the Buddha says that Suddhodana was Dasaratha, the mother of Rāhula was Sītā, Ānanda was Bharata, and “I myself was Rāmapaṇḍita.”

The verse (gāthā) portion is older than the prose commentary in which the narrative is told; whether the story preserves an older form of the Rāma legend than Vālmīki’s (Weber’s view) or is a Buddhist reworking (the more common view) is disputed.
nodes.limits: A Buddhist text; it is part of the Rāma narrative tradition but not a Hindu text. Its relative age vis-à-vis Vālmīki is unresolved.

nodes.name: Cilappatikāram
nodes.summary: The Tamil epic of Kaṇṇaki and Kōvalaṉ attributed to Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ, in three books set in the Cōḻa, Pāṇḍya and Cēra capitals, probably composed around the 5th–6th century. It contains early Tamil depictions of Kṛṣṇa, Murukaṉ and Koṟṟavai worship.
nodes.details: Kōvalaṉ is executed in Madurai on a false charge of stealing the queen’s anklet; Kaṇṇaki proves his innocence, curses and burns the city, and is deified as the goddess Pattiṉi. The epic’s set-piece songs include the hunters’ song to Koṟṟavai, the cowherdesses’ round-dance (āycciyar kuravai) in which girls enact Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and Piññai, and the hill-people’s dance for Murukaṉ (kuṉṟakkuravai). The attribution to the Cēra prince-ascetic Iḷaṅkō rests on a later prologue; the author is often thought to have been Jain, but the poem honours Vedic, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva and Jain religion alike.

nodes.name: Rādhā
nodes.summary: The cowherd beloved of Kṛṣṇa. She is not named in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa; the earliest datable literary mentions are scattered Prakrit and Sanskrit verses (Gāhā Sattasaī, 9th-c. poetics), she becomes the heroine of Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda (12th c.), and the supreme goddess of the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa and Gauḍīya theology.
nodes.details:
Her development is a clear case of a figure growing across texts. (1) A single Gāhā Sattasaī verse addresses Kṛṣṇa about Rādhā (date of the anthology disputed, before 640 CE); (2) 9th–10th-c. poetics (Ānandavardhana’s Dhvanyāloka, Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa’s Veṇīsaṃhāra) cite verses about her; (3) the Bhāgavata’s rāsa narrative has Kṛṣṇa vanish with one unnamed favoured gopī, whom later commentators identify as Rādhā; (4) the Gītagovinda makes her love the poem’s subject; (5) the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa (extant version c. 15th–16th c., Bengal) makes her Kṛṣṇa’s eternal śakti in Goloka; (6) Gauḍīya theologians call her Kṛṣṇa’s hlādinī-śakti and regard Caitanya as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one body.

The Tamil cowherd beloved Piññai (Nappiṉṉai) of the Cilappatikāram and the Āḻvārs is a separate figure; some scholars see her as a southern parallel or precursor (Hardy 1983).

dates.label: before 640 CE (anthology dated 1st–7th c.; disputed)
dates.basis: date of the anthology; Bāṇa cites it in the 7th c.

dates.event: supreme goddess in the extant Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa
dates.label: c. 15th–16th c. CE

openQuestions: Verse number of the Gāhā Sattasaī Rādhā verse in a named edition (often cited as 1.89 in Weber’s numbering — unverified).

nodes.name: Murukaṉ (Tamil)
nodes.summary: The Tamil god of the hills, Cēyōṉ (“the red one”) of the Tolkāppiyam, praised in the Paripāṭal and Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai. From the late Caṅkam period he converges with the northern Skanda-Kārttikeya; the two are kept as separate ids here, joined by an IDENTIFIED_WITH assertion.
nodes.details:
The Tolkāppiyam assigns Cēyōṉ to the kuṟiñci (hill) landscape alongside Māyōṉ (forest-pasture), Vēntaṉ (riverine farmland) and Varuṇaṉ (seashore) — the medieval commentator Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar glosses Cēyōṉ as “red Murukaṉ.” Early poetry knows him as Vēlaṉ, the spear-bearer, worshipped in possession dances (veṟiyāṭṭu). By the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai and the Paripāṭal (c. 3rd–6th c.) he has the six faces and twelve arms, the Kṛttikā birth and the war against Cūr (Śūrapadma) of northern Skanda mythology. His Tamil consort Vaḷḷi, a hunter girl, stands beside Teyvāṉai (Devasenā), Indra’s daughter.

The Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai names six places of the god; later tradition identifies these with six temples, the āṟupaṭai vīṭu (Tiruparaṅkuṉṟam, Tiruccentūr, Paḻaṉi, Cuvāmimalai, Tiruttaṇi, Paḻamutircōlai). The identification of the poem’s sites with these six shrines is itself a traditional reading.

dates.event: convergence with Skanda evident in Tamil poetry
dates.label: c. 3rd–6th c. CE
dates.basis: Skanda motifs in Paripāṭal and Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai

nodes.limits: Tamil Murukaṉ and Sanskrit Skanda are distinct in origin; their identification is historical convergence plus theological identification, not a single original deity.

nodes.name: Pāñcarātra
nodes.summary: The Vaiṣṇava ritual and theological tradition of the Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās, centred on Vāsudeva-Nārāyaṇa and the doctrine of four emanations (vyūha: Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha). It governs worship in many South Indian Vaiṣṇava temples, including Srirangam.
nodes.details: The name appears already in the Nārāyaṇīya section of the Mahābhārata’s Śāntiparvan. Tradition counts 108 saṃhitās, though more than 200 titles are known; the Sāttvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya are called the “three gems.” Rāmānuja and Yāmuna defended the Vedic validity of Pāñcarātra against critics. Temple practice: according to the tradition, Srirangam follows the Pārameśvara Saṃhitā, Melkote the Īśvara Saṃhitā and the Varadarāja temple at Kanchipuram the Jayākhya.

dates.label: c. 7th–10th c. CE (disputed)
dates.basis: textual borrowing from Śaiva tantras, citations

nodes.name: Śaiva Siddhānta
nodes.summary: The dualist, Veda-congruent school of the Śaiva Mantramārga, based on the Siddhānta Āgamas (traditionally 28), systematised by Kashmirian exegetes (Sadyojyoti, Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha) and later by Aghoraśiva at Chidambaram. In Tamil it fused with the Tirumurai hymns through Meykaṇṭār’s Civañāṉapōtam (13th c.).
nodes.details: Sanderson (2009) traces the rise of the Siddhānta and its ritual (initiation, daily worship, temple consecration) as the institutional backbone of early medieval Śaivism across India, Cambodia and Java. The Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta of the Meykaṇṭār lineage claims the Tirumurai poets as its saints; the relation between this Tamil school and the older pan-Indian Sanskrit Siddhānta is a subject of scholarship.

dates.label: c. 450–550 CE
dates.basis: editors’ dating of the Niśvāsa Mūlasūtra

nodes.name: Śrīvaiṣṇava
nodes.summary: The South Indian Vaiṣṇava tradition that joins the Tamil hymns of the Āḻvārs (as a “Tamil Veda”) with Sanskrit Vedānta (Viśiṣṭādvaita) and Pāñcarātra temple ritual, centred on Viṣṇu with Śrī (Lakṣmī). Its ācāryas include Nāthamuni, Yāmuna, Rāmānuja and Vedānta Deśika.
nodes.details: The tradition calls its dual heritage ubhaya-vedānta (Sanskrit and Tamil Vedas). Its great temples are Srirangam, Tirumala–Tirupati, Kanchipuram and Melkote; the Divya Prabandham is recited in their liturgy. From the 14th c. it divided into the Vaṭakalai and Teṉkalai schools.

nodes.name: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava
nodes.summary: The Bengal Vaiṣṇava tradition stemming from Caitanya (1486–1534), centred on the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, with a theology elaborated by the Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana and a hagiographic canon including Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja’s Caitanya Caritāmṛta.
nodes.details: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa is its principal scripture; Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda and Bengali songs of Caṇḍīdās and Vidyāpati were loved by Caitanya. The Gosvāmīs (Rūpa, Sanātana, Jīva and others) systematised a theology of devotional rasa and of Rādhā as Kṛṣṇa’s hlādinī-śakti. Caitanya is regarded by followers as Kṛṣṇa, and as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa combined.

dates.label: early 16th – early 17th c. CE
dates.basis: Caitanya’s life; dates of Gosvāmī works and the Caitanya Caritāmṛta

nodes.name: Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata
nodes.summary: The Kannada-speaking Śaiva tradition associated with Basava (12th c.) and the vacana poets (Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahādēvi and others), marked by wearing the personal iṣṭaliṅga, devotion to Śiva alone, and — in the vacanas — criticism of caste, temple ritual and Brahmanical sacrifice.
nodes.details: Whether Basava founded the tradition or reshaped an existing one is debated (Michael 1992). The relation between the names “Vīraśaiva” and “Liṅgāyata” is also contested in modern Karnataka; both are recorded as aliases without taking sides. The vacanas were written down long after Basava’s time.

dates.event: formative period (Basava and the vacanakāras at Kalyāṇa)
dates.label: 12th c. CE

nodes.name: Kashmir Śaivism (Trika)
nodes.summary: The non-dualist Śaiva traditions of Kashmir — Trika, Krama, Spanda and the Pratyabhijñā philosophy of Somānanda and Utpaladeva — culminating in Abhinavagupta (c. 975–1025) and Kṣemarāja.
nodes.details: Sanderson stresses that “Kashmir Śaivism” is a modern umbrella for several Kashmirian Śaiva systems, including Kashmirian Śaiva Siddhānta, which was dualist. The fourteenth-century Kashmiri poet Lal Ded (Lallā) is associated by later tradition with Trika thought.

dates.label: c. 9th–11th c. CE
dates.basis: dated works of Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta

nodes.name: Jain tradition
nodes.summary: The Jain religion, here recorded chiefly as the source of its own Rāma and Kṛṣṇa tellings (Vimalasūri’s Paumacariya, Raviṣeṇa’s Padmapurāṇa, Svayambhū’s Paumacariu, Guṇabhadra’s Uttarapurāṇa, Hemacandra) and of Jain poets in Kannada and Tamil such as Pampa.
nodes.details: In Jain universal history Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Rāvaṇa are the eighth Baladeva, Vāsudeva and Prativāsudeva among the sixty-three “illustrious persons” (śalākāpuruṣa); Kṛṣṇa is likewise a Vāsudeva. Jain tellings therefore differ systematically from Hindu ones (e.g. Lakṣmaṇa kills Rāvaṇa). Tagging a work trad:jain records its tradition; it does not make it a deviant Hindu text.

nodes.name: Buddhist tradition
nodes.summary: The Buddhist religion, here recorded as the source of the Dasaratha Jātaka, of the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra’s frame story with Rāvaṇa, and of the Theravāda-framed Rāma tellings of mainland Southeast Asia (Lao Phra Lak Phra Lam as a jātaka; Khmer Reamker; Thai Ramakien).
nodes.details: In these tellings Rāma is often a bodhisatta, a previous birth of the Buddha, and Rāvaṇa may be compared with Devadatta or Māra. They are part of the Rāma narrative tradition, not Hindu texts.

nodes.name: Kampaṉ (Kambar)
nodes.summary: Tamil poet, author of the Irāmāvatāram (Kamba Rāmāyaṇam), patronised by Caṭaiyappa Vaḷḷal of Tiruveṇṇainallūr. His date is disputed between the 9th and the 12th century, with most modern scholars favouring the 12th.
nodes.details: Tradition places his birth at Tiruvaḻuntūr in the Cōḻa country and has him honoured by a Cōḻa king with the title Kavicakravarti. Temple tradition holds that his epic was first recited at Srirangam. Other works attributed to him include poems in praise of Nammāḻvār (Caṭakōpar Antāti) and of the plough (Ēr Eḻupatu); these attributions are traditional.

nodes.name: Tulsīdās
nodes.summary: Awadhi and Braj poet (d. 1623), author of the Rāmcaritmānas (begun 1574), the Vinaya Patrikā, Kavitāvalī and other Rāma-devotional works; he lived in Ayodhyā and above all in Kāśī (Vārāṇasī).
nodes.details: Hagiography (e.g. Priyādās’s commentary on Nābhādās’s Bhaktamāl) tells of his marriage, renunciation and visions of Hanumān; the Hanumān Cālīsā is attributed to him by tradition, an attribution some scholars question. He is claimed by the Rāmānandī order.

dates.label: 1574 (Mānas begun) – 1623 CE (death)
dates.basis: internal date of the Mānas; death year in tradition widely accepted

dates.label: Saṃvat 1554 (1497 CE) per some hagiographies; c. 1532 in common scholarly estimates

nodes.name: Kṛttibās Ojhā
nodes.summary: Bengali poet to whom the Śrīrām Pā̃cālī (Kṛttivāsī Rāmāyaṇa) is attributed; tradition places him at Phuliyā on the Bhāgīrathī and in the 15th century, though the identification of the king he mentions is disputed.

nodes.name: Jayadeva
nodes.summary: Sanskrit poet of the late 12th century, author of the Gītagovinda; tradition makes him a poet at the court of Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal, and both Bengal and Odisha claim his birthplace “Kindubilva.” Two hymns attributed to him are in the Sikh Ādi Granth.
nodes.details: Odia tradition links him to Puri and to his wife Padmāvatī, a temple dancer; early commentators and modern scholars do not support the Padmāvatī story. Sixteenth-century texts call him a native of Utkala.

dates.label: late 12th c. CE
dates.basis: court of Lakṣmaṇasena (r. c. 1178–1206) per tradition

nodes.name: Jñāneśvar
nodes.summary: Marathi poet-saint (traditionally 1275–1296), disciple of his elder brother Nivṛttinātha, author of the Jñāneśvarī (1290) and the Amṛtānubhava, and revered as a founder of the Vārkarī tradition of Viṭṭhala devotion.
nodes.details: In the colophon he calls himself “Jñānadeva, son (disciple) of Śrī Nivṛttinātha, born of the line of Maheśa” (i.e. in Nivṛtti’s Nātha lineage). Tradition holds that he entered living samādhi at Āḷandī in 1296.

dates.label: 1275–1296 CE (traditional)
dates.basis: hagiography; colophon date 1290 falls within it

nodes.name: Āṇṭāḷ
nodes.summary: The only woman among the twelve Āḻvārs, foster-daughter of Periyāḻvār at Śrīvilliputtūr, author of the Tiruppāvai (30 verses) and Nācciyār Tirumoḻi (143 verses in the standard count); she is usually dated to the 8th–9th century.
nodes.details: Hagiography tells that Periyāḻvār found her as an infant under a tulasī plant in the temple garden, that she wore the garland meant for the god before it was offered (hence “she who gave the garland she had worn”), and that she was united with Raṅganātha at Srirangam. The Tiruppāvai is sung during the month of Mārkaḻi; its name survives, with that of Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai, in the Thai royal Brahman ceremony Triyampawai–Trippawai.

dates.label: c. 8th–9th c. CE
dates.basis: relation to Periyāḻvār and Pāṇḍya synchronisms

nodes.name: Nammāḻvār
nodes.summary: The foremost Āḻvār (Caṭakōpaṉ, Māṟaṉ) of Kurukūr (Āḻvārtirunagari) in the far south of Tamil Nadu, author of the Tiruvāymoḻi (1,102 verses) and three shorter works; scholars date him to the 8th–9th century.
nodes.details: His works: Tiruvāymoḻi (1,102 verses), Tiruviruttam (100), Tiruvāciriyam (7) and Periya Tiruvantāti (87). Śrīvaiṣṇavas regard the four as Tamil counterparts of the four Vedas. Hagiography says he sat in silent meditation in a tamarind tree until his disciple Madhurakavi came to him.

nodes.name: Appar (Tirunāvukkaracar)
nodes.summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint of the 7th century, author of Tirumurai books 4–6. The Periya Purāṇam tells that he was first a Jain monk named Dharmasena, returned to Śaivism, and brought the Pallava king Mahendravarman I back to Śiva.

dates.label: 7th c. CE
dates.basis: synchronism with Mahendravarman I in hagiography

nodes.name: Campantar (Tiruñāṉacampantar)
nodes.summary: Tamil Śaiva child-poet of Cīrkāḻi (7th c.), author of Tirumurai books 1–3 — the largest share of the Tēvāram. The Periya Purāṇam narrates his contest with Jain monks at Madurai and the return of the Pāṇḍya king to Śaivism.

dates.label: 7th c. CE
dates.basis: synchronism with Appar and Pāṇḍya Neṭumāṟaṉ in hagiography

nodes.limits: The Madurai contest is a hagiographic narrative (12th c.); it is evidence of later Śaiva–Jain polemic, not a contemporary record.

nodes.name: Cuntarar
nodes.summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint of the 8th century (Cuntaramūrtti), author of Tirumurai book 7; his Tiruttoṇṭattokai lists the devotees whom the Periya Purāṇam later expanded into the sixty-three Nāyaṉmār. Tradition calls him the “friend of Śiva” and links him to Tiruvārūr.

dates.label: 8th – early 9th c. CE
dates.basis: internal references to earlier saints and to Pallava-period kings

nodes.name: Rāmānuja
nodes.summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya and Vedāntin of Śrīperumbudūr, chief exponent of Viśiṣṭādvaita and author of the Śrībhāṣya; he reorganised worship at Srirangam and, during a sojourn in the Hoysala country, at Melkote. Traditional dates are 1017–1137; many scholars prefer 1077–1157.

nodes.name: Caitanya
nodes.summary: Bengali Vaiṣṇava saint (1486–1534), born at Navadvīpa, who spent his last two decades at Puri; the Gauḍīya tradition regards him as Kṛṣṇa, and as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one body. The eight-verse Śikṣāṣṭaka is the only work accepted as his.

dates.label: 1486–1534 CE
dates.basis: hagiographies and regnal synchronisms (Pratāparudra of Odisha)

nodes.name: Basava
nodes.summary: Kannada Śaiva poet and minister at the Kalacuri court of Bijjala II at Kalyāṇa (12th c.), whose vacanas, addressed to Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva, are central to the Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata tradition.
nodes.details: The vacanas attributed to him reject caste distinctions, temple worship and sacrifice in favour of devotion and the personal liṅga; tradition credits him with the Anubhava Maṇṭapa assembly of devotees. The vacana collections were compiled long after his death, so individual attributions are uncertain.

dates.label: mid-12th c. CE (minister of Bijjala II)

nodes.name: Vimalasūri
nodes.summary: Jain (Śvetāmbara) monk-poet, author of the Prakrit Paumacariya, the earliest surviving Jain Rāma narrative. His date depends on the disputed reading of his colophon (530 years after Mahāvīra) and is placed by scholars anywhere from the 1st to the 5th century CE.

nodes.name: Sapta Purī (the seven liberating cities)
nodes.summary: The seven cities — Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā (Haridvāra), Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantikā (Ujjayinī) and Dvārakā — named in a widely recited Sanskrit verse as the places that grant liberation (mokṣa); a pan-Indian pilgrimage set rather than a single route.
nodes.details:
The list is usually quoted from a verse that runs “ayodhyā mathurā māyā kāśī kāñcī avantikā / purī dvāravatī caiva saptaitā mokṣadāyikāḥ” (recited in later Purāṇic and stotra literature; the earliest textual locus is not verified here). Two of the seven (Kāñcī and Kāśī) are also the seats of major Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava temple clusters; Haridvāra and Ujjayinī are two of the four Kumbha Melā sites.

The network is recorded here as MEMBER_OF edges from place records. The cities themselves are ancient, but the grouping is a devotional and geographical construct; scholars of sacred geography treat it as one of several overlapping pan-Indian schemes (Char Dhām, the twelve jyotirliṅgas, the Śakti pīṭhas).
nodes.limits: The verse that defines the seven is widely recited but its earliest textual source is not verified here; membership in the set says nothing about the age of any particular monument in the cities.
openQuestions: Earliest dated text that gives the seven-city verse.

nodes.name: Pañca Kedāra (five Kedāras of Garhwal)
nodes.summary: Five Śiva shrines in the Garhwal Himalaya — Kedārnāth, Tuṅgnāth, Rudranāth, Madhyamaheśvar and Kalpeśvar — joined by a legend in which Śiva, fleeing the Pāṇḍavas in the form of a bull, reappears in five parts at the five sites.
nodes.details: In the regional legend the Pāṇḍavas seek Śiva to expiate the killing of kin at Kurukṣetra; Śiva hides as a bull and sinks into the ground at Kedārnāth, leaving the hump there, while the arms appear at Tuṅgnāth, the face at Rudranāth, the navel (or belly) at Madhyamaheśvar and the matted hair at Kalpeśvar. The Pāṇḍava legend is a Garhwali tradition and is not found in the Mahābhārata itself; the shrines are stone temples of the regional Nāgara type whose surviving fabric is generally not securely dated.
nodes.limits: The grouping and the bull legend are regional tradition (class 6); they do not date the shrines, which have no securely dated foundation inscriptions.

nodes.name: Aṣṭavināyaka (eight Gaṇeśa shrines of Maharashtra)
nodes.summary: A pilgrimage circuit of eight Gaṇeśa temples around Pune in Maharashtra — Morgaon, Siddhatek, Pali, Mahad, Theur, Lenyadri, Ozar and Ranjangaon — each holding a self-manifest (svayambhū) image with its own legend.
nodes.details: Tradition prescribes a fixed sequence beginning and ending at Morgaon (Mayureśvara), the principal seat of the Gāṇapatya tradition, whose mythology is set out in the Gaṇeśa and Mudgala Purāṇas. The temples in their present form are mostly 17th–18th-century Marāṭhā-period buildings or rebuildings, several of them patronised by the Peśvās and their officials.
nodes.limits: The circuit is a devotional grouping whose present form is early modern; the svayambhū images and their legends are temple tradition.

nodes.name: Navagraha temples of the Kaveri delta
nodes.summary: A set of nine temples near Kumbakonam and Mayiladuthurai in Tamil Nadu, each associated in tradition with one of the nine planetary deities (navagraha); eight are Śiva temples with a graha shrine, and only Sūryanār Kōvil is dedicated to the graha (Sūrya) as principal deity.
nodes.details: Members and their grahas: Sūryanār Kōvil (Sūrya), Tiṅkaḷūr (Candra), Vaitīsvaran Kōvil (Aṅgāraka/Mars), Tiruveṇkāṭu (Budha), Āluṅkuṭi (Guru/Bṛhaspati), Kañcaṉūr (Śukra), Tirunaḷḷāṟu (Śani), Tirunāgeśvaram (Rāhu) and Kīḻapperumpaḷḷam (Ketu). Most are Cōḻa-period Śiva temples that also appear among the Tēvāram shrines; the grouping of the nine as a planetary circuit is a later devotional and astrological practice whose origin is not securely dated.
nodes.limits: The planetary association is temple tradition; the date at which the nine were grouped as a circuit is not established in the sources consulted.

nodes.name: Ahom kingdom
nodes.summary: Kingdom of the Brahmaputra valley (Assam) founded by Tai-speaking Ahoms in the 13th century; its later kings, notably Gadādhar Siṃha and Śiva Siṃha, patronised Śaiva and Śākta temples around Guwahati.

nodes.name: Māṇikya dynasty of Tripura
nodes.summary: Ruling house of the kingdom of Tripura (Twipra) from the 15th century until 1949; Dhanya Māṇikya is credited with founding the Tripura Sundarī temple at Udaipur.

nodes.name: Kingdom of Manipur
nodes.summary: Meitei kingdom of the Manipur valley; from the 18th century its rulers adopted Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism and built the royal Govindajī temple at Imphal.

dates.label: c. 12th c.–1949 CE (standard chronology; earlier dates are traditional)

nodes.name: Utpala dynasty of Kashmir
nodes.summary: Kashmiri dynasty founded by Avantivarman (r. c. 855–883), builder of the Avantisvāmin and Avantīśvara temples at Avantipura; its history is told in Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī.

nodes.name: Gurjara-Pratīhāra dynasty
nodes.summary: North Indian imperial dynasty (c. 8th–11th c.) based at Kanauj, under whose rule many of the early Māru-Gurjara and central Indian Nāgara temples (Osian, Bateshwar) were built.

nodes.name: Kacchapaghāta dynasty
nodes.summary: Dynasty of the Gwalior region (c. 10th–12th c.); a later inscription at Mitaoli associates the circular Causaṭh Yoginī temple with the Kacchapaghāta king Devapāla.

nodes.name: Kalacuris of Tripurī
nodes.summary: Dynasty of the upper Narmadā valley (Ḍāhala), with its capital at Tripurī near Jabalpur, c. 7th–13th c.; the Bhedaghat Causaṭh Yoginī temple and the early temples at Amarkantak are attributed to their period.

nodes.name: Bundelā kingdom of Orchha
nodes.summary: Rajput state of Bundelkhand founded in 1531 with its capital at Orchha; its rulers built the Rām Rājā and Caturbhuj temples.

nodes.name: Marāṭhā state (Chhatrapatis and Peśvās)
nodes.summary: The Marāṭhā state founded by Śivājī (crowned 1674), later directed by the Peśvās from Pune until 1818; Marāṭhā rulers, ministers and generals rebuilt or endowed many temples across western and northern India.

nodes.name: Kingdom of Mysore (Woḍeyar dynasty)
nodes.summary: South Indian kingdom ruled by the Woḍeyars (with the interregnum of Haidar ʿAlī and Ṭīpū Sulṭān), patrons of the Cāmuṇḍeśvarī temple on Chamundi Hill.

nodes.name: Cāḷukyas of Kalyāṇī (Western Cāḷukyas)
nodes.summary: Deccan dynasty (973–1189) whose ornate temples at Lakkundi, Itagi and elsewhere define the “Kalyāṇī Cāḷukya” or later Cāḷukya style.

nodes.name: Cāḷukyas of Veṅgī (Eastern Cāḷukyas)
nodes.summary: Dynasty of coastal Andhra (c. 624–1070) to whom the Bhīmeśvara temple at Draksharama is attributed.

nodes.name: Malla kings of Mallabhūm (Bishnupur)
nodes.summary: Bengal dynasty of Mallabhūm whose 17th-century Vaiṣṇava rulers, converts under Śrīnivāsa Ācārya’s influence, built the brick and laterite temples of Bishnupur.

dates.label: c. 16th c.–1806 CE (earlier dates are traditional)

nodes.name: Mughal empire
nodes.summary: Empire of the Timurid Mughals (1526–1857); under Akbar Hindu nobles such as Mān Siṃh of Amber built major temples (Govindadeva at Vrindavan, 1590), while some later rulers ordered temples demolished.

nodes.name: Kachvāhā kingdom of Amber (Jaipur)
nodes.summary: Rajput kingdom of Amber, later Jaipur; its rulers served the Mughals and patronised Kṛṣṇa temples in Braj and, from 1714–35, rehoused the Govindadeva image at Jaipur.

dates.label: 16th c.–1949 CE (as a Mughal-allied state; earlier origins traditional)

nodes.name: Shah dynasty of Nepal
nodes.summary: The Gorkha (Shah) dynasty that unified Nepal from 1768 until the abolition of the monarchy in 2008; patrons of Kathmandu valley shrines such as Manakāmanā and Dakṣiṇkālī.

nodes.name: Jaffna kingdom (Āryacakravarti dynasty)
nodes.summary: Tamil kingdom of northern Sri Lanka (c. 13th c.–1619) under the Āryacakravartis; tradition and the Yālppāṇa Vaipava Mālai credit it with the first Nallur Kandaswamy temple.

nodes.name: Chenla
nodes.summary: Khmer polity (6th–8th c.) known from Chinese sources and Sanskrit and Khmer inscriptions; Īśānavarman I’s capital Īśānapura is identified with Sambor Prei Kuk.

nodes.name: Pagan kingdom
nodes.summary: Burmese kingdom centred on Bagan (c. 849–1297); among its thousands of Buddhist monuments the Nathlaung Kyaung is the one surviving Vaiṣṇava temple.

nodes.name: Majapahit
nodes.summary: East Javanese kingdom (1293–c. 1527) whose state temple Penataran carries Rāmāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇāyana reliefs.

nodes.name: Irukkuvēḷ chiefs of Kodumbalur
nodes.summary: Tamil chiefly family of Kodumbalur, allies and feudatories of the early Cōḻas, to whom the Mūvarkōvil temples are attributed by inscription.

nodes.name: Śailodbhava dynasty
nodes.summary: Dynasty of Koṅgoda in coastal Odisha (c. 6th–8th c.) under whom the earliest surviving Bhubaneswar temples, including Paraśurāmeśvara, were built.

nodes.name: Bhauma-Kara dynasty
nodes.summary: Dynasty of Odisha (c. 8th–10th c.) with Śākta and Buddhist patronage; the Vaitāl Deul at Bhubaneswar is generally placed in their period.

nodes.name: Guhilas of Mewar
nodes.summary: Rajput dynasty of Mewar (Guhilas, later Sisodiyās), whose rulers style themselves the dīvān (regent) of Ekaliṅgajī, the tutelary Śiva of the Eklingji temple.

nodes.name: Umānanda temple, Guwahati
nodes.summary: Śiva temple on Umananda (Peacock) Island in the Brahmaputra at Guwahati, first built in 1694 on the orders of the Ahom king Gadādhar Siṃha; badly damaged in the 1897 Assam earthquake and later rebuilt.
nodes.details: The island hill is called Bhasmācala in local tradition, which places here Śiva’s burning of Kāma to ashes (bhasma). Contemporary accounts summarised in the sources state that the brick temple was raised in 1694 by the Barphukan Garhganya Handique at the order of Gadādhar Siṃha (r. 1681–1696). The 1897 earthquake wrecked it; the present building is a later reconstruction by a local merchant, whose interior carries Vaiṣṇava inscriptions.

nodes.name: Hayagrīva Mādhava temple, Hajo
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu temple on Maṇikūṭa hill at Hajo near Guwahati whose present stone building is attributed to the Koch ruler Raghudeva Nārāyaṇa (late 16th c.); it is also revered by some Buddhists as the place of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
nodes.details: The temple stands on a high plinth with a frieze of elephants and wall reliefs of the ten avatāras and episodes from the epics. The image is worshipped as Mādhava with Hayagrīva associations. Bhutanese and Tibetan Buddhist pilgrims have long identified the site with Kuśinagara, a reattribution recorded in later Buddhist pilgrimage literature; Hajo is accordingly a shared Hindu–Buddhist (and, with the nearby Poa Mecca, Muslim) pilgrimage centre.

nodes.name: Ugratārā temple, Guwahati
nodes.summary: Śākta temple of the goddess Ugratārā at Latasil/Uzan Bazaar in Guwahati, built by the Ahom king Śiva Siṃha in 1725; local tradition links it to the navel of Satī.
nodes.details: The shrine stands west of the Jor Pukhuri tanks, which Śiva Siṃha had excavated a few years before. The goddess here has been compared with the Buddhist Tārā forms Ekajaṭā and Tīkṣṇakāntā, reflecting the Tantric milieu of Kāmarūpa. The temple was damaged in the 1897 earthquake and repaired.

nodes.name: Madan Kāmdev temple ruins
nodes.summary: Ruined complex of stone temples at Baihata Chariali near Guwahati, dated on stylistic grounds to about the 10th–12th centuries, with erotic and divine sculpture associated in local tradition with Kāmadeva.
nodes.details: The site was reported in the 19th century and taken over by the Directorate of Archaeology, Assam, in 1977, which cleared and partly reassembled the ruins. Archaeologists disagree on the date and on which dynasty built the temples; the sculpture (Umā-Maheśvara, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, vidyādharas) belongs to the early medieval art of Kāmarūpa. The name links the ruins to the Kālikā Purāṇa legend in which Kāma is restored to life in Kāmarūpa.

nodes.name: Tripura Sundarī temple, Udaipur (Tripura)
nodes.summary: Śākta temple on a tortoise-backed hillock at Udaipur, Tripura, founded according to tradition by Mahārāja Dhanya Māṇikya around 1501; counted among the 51 Śakti pīṭhas as the place where Satī’s right foot fell.
nodes.details: The temple is a single-cell building of the Bengali ek-ratna type with a curved roof. The state of Tripura is popularly said to take its name from the goddess. Animal sacrifice, part of the temple’s worship, was halted for some weeks in 2019 by a court order and then resumed. The adjoining Kalyāṇ Sāgar tank keeps tortoises sacred to the shrine.

nodes.name: Unakoti rock reliefs
nodes.summary: Śaiva rock-cut reliefs and loose images on a forested hill near Kailashahar, Tripura, ascribed on stylistic grounds to the 7th–9th centuries; the central Unakotīśvara Kāla Bhairava head is about 9 m high.
nodes.details: The name “one less than a crore” comes from a legend in which Śiva, travelling to Kāśī with 99,99,999 gods, cursed them to stone when they overslept. Besides the colossal Śiva head flanked by female figures (one identified as Durgā on a lion), the site has large Gaṇeśa reliefs. The only inscription, on a caturmukha liṅga, is in Bengali characters of the 11th–12th centuries and names one Śrī Jayadeva, probably a pilgrim. The site is protected by the ASI and was placed on India’s UNESCO Tentative List in 2022.

nodes.name: Śrī Govindajī temple, Imphal
nodes.summary: Royal Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava temple of Rādhā-Govinda beside the old palace of the Manipur kings at Imphal; first built in 1846, rebuilt after an 1868 earthquake and reconsecrated in 1876, with the images reinstalled in the present temple in 1908.
nodes.details: Manipuri tradition holds that King Bhāgyacandra (r. 1763–1798) had the image of Govindajī carved after a vision and consecrated it in 1779 in his palace. Mahārāja Nara Siṃh commissioned a temple on 16 January 1846; it was rebuilt to the same design under Candrakīrti and consecrated on 26 April 1876. After the Anglo-Manipur war of 1891 the images were moved and in 1908 were reconsecrated in the present temple by Mahārāja Churachand Siṃh. The temple is the centre of Manipuri Vaiṣṇava ritual, including the rāsa-līlā dance.

nodes.name: Vaidyanātha temple, Baijnath (Kangra)
nodes.summary: Nāgara Śiva temple at Baijnath in the Kangra valley, built in 1204 CE by two merchants, Ahuka and Manyuka, according to its own inscriptions; Śiva is worshipped as Vaidyanātha, “lord of physicians”.
nodes.details: Two long inscriptions on stone slabs in the hall, in Sanskrit (Śāradā script) and a local language (Ṭākarī), record the building of the temple by the merchants and praise the local ruler. The spire and outer roof were repaired in 1786 under Saṃsār Cand of Kangra, whose family priest supervised the work according to a further inscription. The temple survived the 1905 Kangra earthquake and is protected by the ASI (N-HP-17).

nodes.name: Hiḍimbā Devī temple, Manali
nodes.summary: Wooden pagoda-roofed temple at Manali built in 1553 over a rock worshipped as the goddess Hiḍimbā, whom local tradition identifies with the rākṣasī wife of Bhīma in the Mahābhārata.
nodes.details: The four-tiered roof and carved wooden doorway are typical of Kullu valley temple building. The doorway inscription, as generally reported, names the Kullu ruler Bahādur Siṃh. In Kullu tradition Hiḍimbā is the tutelary goddess of the valley’s former rulers, and the identification with the epic Hiḍimbā is a local devotional reading.

nodes.name: Bhīmakālī temple, Sarahan
nodes.summary: Tower-like wooden-and-stone temple of the goddess Bhīmakālī at Sarahan, the tutelary goddess of the former Bushahr rulers, built in the Himalayan kāṭh-kuṇi technique; it is regarded locally as being as holy as the Śakti pīṭhas.
nodes.details: Two towers with overhanging galleries rise from a courtyard of the old Bushahr palace complex. Silver-sheathed doors bear an inscription of Rājā Padam Siṃh dated 1927. The date of the original foundation is uncertain (a 13th-century founding is claimed in the reference work, unsupported there by a dated record), and timber temples of this type are repeatedly renewed.

nodes.name: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa temple group, Chamba
nodes.summary: Group of stone śikhara temples with wooden canopies in Chamba town, Himachal Pradesh, whose main Viṣṇu temple is attributed to Rājā Sāhila Varman, the 10th-century founder of Chamba; a gilded finial was added in 1678.
nodes.details: Chamba tradition holds that Sāhila Varman moved his capital from Brahmaur to the lower Ravi valley around 920 and named it after his daughter Campāvatī. The temples of the group range from the 10th to the 19th century; their Nāgara śikharas carry wooden umbrella roofs adapted to snowfall. A metal Garuḍa stands on the pillar before the main shrine, and Rājā Chatar Siṃh added gold-plated pinnacles in 1678.

nodes.name: Masrur rock-cut temples
nodes.summary: Monolithic complex of Nāgara temples carved from a sandstone ridge in the Kangra valley in the early 8th century, dedicated chiefly to Śiva with Viṣṇu, Devī and Sūrya imagery; unfinished and earthquake-damaged.
nodes.details: The fifteen or so shrines are cut from the living rock around a central shrine and face a tank, a rare northern counterpart to the monolithic temples of Ellora and Mamallapuram. Henry Shuttleworth reported the site in 1913 and Harold Hargreaves of the ASI surveyed it in 1915. Michael Meister has read it as a “temple-mountain” embodying the surrounding Dhauladhar range. Much sculpture is lost and the complex was left incomplete.

nodes.name: Amarnāth cave
nodes.summary: Glacial cave at about 3,888 m in the Lidder–Sind watershed of Kashmir where an ice stalagmite is worshipped as a self-formed liṅga of Śiva (Amareśvara); the summer yātrā is one of the largest Himalayan pilgrimages.
nodes.details: Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī (12th c.) and the Nīlamata Purāṇa refer to Amareśvara and its pilgrimage. The reference work reports a tradition that Queen Sūryamatī (11th c.) gave tridents and bāṇa-liṅgas to the shrine; Abu’l Faẓl’s Āʾīn-i Akbarī (16th c.) describes the waxing and waning ice formation, and François Bernier (1663) described the cave. The pilgrimage is administered by a shrine board and opens only in summer.

nodes.name: Vaiṣṇo Devī cave shrine
nodes.summary: Cave shrine on Trikūṭa mountain above Katra in Jammu, where the goddess Vaiṣṇo Devī is worshipped in three natural rock forms (piṇḍīs) identified with Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī; one of the most visited pilgrimage sites in India.
nodes.details: Nineteenth-century travellers still called the goddess “Trikūṭā Devī”, and scholars trace the present Vaiṣṇavī identity and the pan-Indian popularity of the pilgrimage to the 19th–20th centuries. Court chronicles of Jammu (Rājdarśanī, 1847) claim royal visits as early as 996 CE, which are traditional. Since 1986 the shrine has been run by the Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board.

nodes.name: Kṣīra Bhavānī temple, Tulmul
nodes.summary: Spring shrine of the goddess Rājñā (Kṣīra Bhavānī) at Tulmul near Srinagar, whose present marble temple in the spring-fed pool was built under Mahārāja Pratāp Siṃh in the 1910s; its annual Jyeṣṭha aṣṭamī fair is the main festival of Kashmiri Paṇḍits.
nodes.details: The name refers to the offering of milk-rice (kṣīra) to the goddess. Devotees observe the changing colour of the spring water as an omen; Walter Lawrence recorded a violet tinge in 1886. The fair continued through the disruption of 1990, when most Kashmiri Paṇḍits left the valley, and remains a focus of return pilgrimage.

nodes.name: Avantisvāmin temple, Avantipura
nodes.summary: Ruined Viṣṇu temple at Avantipura on the Jhelum, built by King Avantivarman (r. c. 855–883) of the Utpala dynasty, as recorded by Kalhaṇa; with the nearby Avantīśvara Śiva temple it is a key example of Kashmiri stone architecture.
nodes.details: Kalhaṇa states that Avantivarman built the Viṣṇu temple Avantisvāmin before his accession and the Śiva temple Avantīśvara afterwards. The colonnaded courtyard (peristyle) with trefoil arches, the gateway and the reliefs survive in ruin; the site was excavated in the early 20th century and is protected by the ASI. Locals call it “Pāṇḍav Lari”.

nodes.name: Pandrethan Śiva temple, Srinagar
nodes.summary: Small, well-preserved Kashmiri stone temple of the 8th–9th century standing in a spring-fed tank at Pandrethan, the site of the ancient capital (Purāṇādhiṣṭhāna) east of Srinagar.
nodes.details: The temple’s pyramidal stone roof and carved ceiling attracted 19th-century visitors and photographers. Its earlier identification with the 10th-century Meruvardhanasvāmin temple named in the Rājataraṅgiṇī has been rejected, as has an identification with an early 12th-century Śiva temple; the date rests on style.

nodes.name: Śaṅkarācārya (Jyeṣṭheśvara) temple, Srinagar
nodes.summary: Stone Śiva temple on the hill above Srinagar known to Kalhaṇa as Gopādri; its date is disputed between an early medieval core and a later superstructure, and its modern name links it to Ādi Śaṅkara.
nodes.details: Kalhaṇa says that King Gopāditya granted land at the foot of the hill to Brahmins and built a shrine of Jyeṣṭheśvara on its top. James Fergusson dated the standing building to the 17th–18th century; Aurel Stein accepted that the superstructure is recent but held the base and stairs to be much older. The Dogra ruler Gulāb Siṃh built the stairway from the Durgā Nāg side, and a statue of Śaṅkara was installed in 1961. The temple is an ASI-protected monument.

nodes.name: Jvālāmukhī temple
nodes.summary: Śākta temple at Jawalamukhi in the Kangra valley where natural gas flames issuing from the rock are worshipped as the goddess Jvālā; counted among the Śakti pīṭhas (the tongue of Satī in common lists).
nodes.details: There is no image: the flames themselves are the goddess. Popular tradition credits the Mughal emperor Akbar with testing and then honouring the flames, and the gilded roof to Mahārājā Raṇjīt Siṃh (early 19th c.); both are reported here from recall. The temple is a centre of the northwestern Goddess cult studied by Erndl.

nodes.name: Haridvāra (Haridwar)
nodes.summary: City where the Gaṅgā leaves the Śivālik hills for the plains, one of the Sapta Purī (as Māyā) and one of the four Kumbha Melā sites; its main bathing ghāṭ is Har kī Pauṛī.
nodes.details: Xuanzang (629–645) describes a city on the Gaṅgā, “Mo-yu-lo”, identified with Māyāpur at the south of the modern town. Kaṅkhal (place:kanakhala), the traditional site of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, lies within the city. Timur sacked the town in January 1399.

nodes.name: Har kī Pauṛī, Haridwar
nodes.summary: The principal bathing ghāṭ of Haridwar, held to bear the footprint of Viṣṇu (Hari) at the Brahmakuṇḍ, focus of the evening Gaṅgā āratī and the Kumbha Melā baths.
nodes.details: Tradition attributes the first ghāṭ to King Vikramāditya in memory of his brother Bhartṛhari. In 1819 the ghāṭ was still a narrow passage, and a crush at the Kumbha of that year killed some 430 people; the ghāṭs were enlarged in 1938 and again in 1986, when the clock tower area was also rebuilt.

nodes.name: Ṛṣikeśa (Rishikesh)
nodes.summary: Pilgrimage town on the Gaṅgā above Haridwar, traditionally where Viṣṇu appeared as Hṛṣīkeśa to the sage Raibhya; a centre of ascetic āśramas and, since the 20th century, of international yoga.
nodes.details: The Lakṣmaṇ Jhūlā suspension bridge (rebuilt 1927 after an 1889 bridge was washed away in 1924) and the Rām Jhūlā (1986) carry pilgrims across the river; the Bharat Mandir is the town’s principal old temple. Rishikesh is the traditional gateway to the Char Dhām pilgrimage of Garhwal.

nodes.name: Rani ki Vav (Queen’s Stepwell), Patan
nodes.summary: Monumental seven-storey stepwell at Patan, Gujarat, built for the Caulukya queen Udayamatī in the 11th century and conceived as an inverted temple; its walls carry hundreds of sculptures, overwhelmingly Vaiṣṇava, including the avatāras of Viṣṇu. UNESCO World Heritage Site (2014).
nodes.details:
Merutuṅga’s Prabandhacintāmaṇi (1304) records that Udayamatī, daughter of Naravarāha Khengāra, built a novel stepwell at Śrīpattana (Patan) surpassing the Sahasraliṅga tank. One account dates its commissioning to 1063 with completion some twenty years later; M. S. Commissariat instead placed it around 1032 by comparison with the Vimala Vasahī at Mount Abu. Silted up by the shifting Sarasvatī, it was cleared in the 1940s and excavated and restored by the ASI between 1981 and 1987.

The sculptural programme turns the descending galleries into a temple to water: Viṣṇu in many forms, the daśāvatāra, Śeṣaśāyī Viṣṇu at the well end, goddesses, apsarās and nāga-kanyās. The site is ASI monument N-GJ-160.

dates.label: c. 1063–1083 (commissioned 1063, per one account)
dates.basis: later chronicle tradition and architectural history; competing dates

nodes.name: Ambājī temple, Arasur

The nearby Gabbar hill is part of the pilgrimage. The large Bhādrapada pūrṇimā fair draws pilgrims on foot from across Gujarat.

nodes.name: Kālikā Mātā temple, Pavagadh
nodes.summary: Goddess temple on the summit of Pavagadh hill inside the Champaner-Pavagadh World Heritage property, with a core of the 10th–11th centuries and images of Mahākālī flanked by Kālī and Bahucarā Mātā; its spire was rebuilt and a flag raised in 2022.
nodes.details: The reference work reports that the Mahākālī image was once installed as the guardian goddess of the Śvetāmbara Jain Añcalagaccha established on the hill in the 12th century, and that the shrine is described in the 15th-century drama Gaṅgādāsa-pratāpa-vilāsa. For centuries a Muslim shrine (dargāh) stood on the temple roof; after an agreement it was moved and a new śikhara was built, completed in 2022 (recall). The temple is a Śakti pīṭha in some lists (the toe of Satī).

nodes.name: Śāmaḷājī temple
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu temple at Shamlaji in north Gujarat whose present building dates from the 15th–16th centuries on an earlier (perhaps 11th-century) foundation; the site was a major 6th-century sculpture centre, and the sanctum image of Viṣṇu as Gadādhara is probably of the 7th–8th century.
nodes.details: Sara Schastok’s study of the “Śāmalājī sculptures” shows a 6th-century workshop whose style reaches as far as the Parel relief in Mumbai. A Garuḍa image before the temple carries an inscription dated 1584. The Buddhist monastery and stūpa at Devnimori nearby (3rd–4th c.) are now under the Meshvo reservoir; the temple at Harishchandra ni Chori nearby is of the 10th century.

nodes.name: Ekaliṅgajī temple, Kailashpuri
nodes.summary: Śiva temple complex near Udaipur housing the tutelary deity of the rulers of Mewar, who govern as his dīvān; tradition credits Bappā Rāwal (8th c.), but the present main temple results from 15th-century rebuildings culminating under Rāṇā Rāimal (r. 1473–1509).
nodes.details: The 15th-century Ekaliṅga Māhātmya ascribes the first temple to Bappā Rāwal. Hammīr Siṃh (14th c.) installed the earliest extant image and renovated the temple; Rāṇā Kumbhā rebuilt it, and his inscription of 1460 calls him “the personal servant of Ekaliṅga”. After Ghiyāth Shāh of Malwa sacked the temple, Rāimal used the ransom paid for him to rebuild the complex and install the present four-faced image. The temple probably belonged first to the Pāśupatas (a Lakulīśa temple of 971 stands in the complex), then to the Nāthas, and from the 16th century to the Rāmānandīs.

nodes.name: Śrīnāthjī temple, Nathdwara
nodes.summary: Principal temple of the Puṣṭimārga, built at Nathdwara in Mewar in 1672 to house the image of Śrīnāthjī (Kṛṣṇa raising Govardhana) brought from Braj to protect it from Mughal iconoclasm; the temple is laid out as a residence (havelī) rather than a temple.
nodes.details: Puṣṭimārga tradition holds that the image emerged from Govardhana hill — an arm first appearing in 1410/1466 — and was revealed to Vallabhācārya, who instituted its worship. In 1669–72 the custodians carried the image out of Braj; under the protection of Mahārāṇā Rāj Siṃh of Mewar it was installed at Sinhad, renamed Nāthdvāra. The temple’s seva follows the daily round of the child Kṛṣṇa, and its painted cloth hangings (picchavāī) and Nathdwara painting form a distinct school. In 1802 the image was briefly taken to Udaipur during the Holkar raids.

nodes.name: Osian temple group (Harihara temples)
nodes.summary: Cluster of 8th–12th-century Hindu and Jain temples at the desert oasis of Osian near Jodhpur, among the earliest Māru-Gurjara monuments; it includes three Harihara temples, a Sūrya temple, the Sacciyā Mātā temple and the Mahāvīra temple of 783.
nodes.details: Osian (ancient Upakeśapura) flourished under the Gurjara-Pratīhāras. An inscription of 956 at the Mahāvīra temple states that it was built in the time of the Pratīhāra king Vatsarāja (Śaka 705 = 783 CE is his date in the Jain Harivaṃśa). The Harihara temples combine Viṣṇu and Śiva in a single image type; the hilltop Sacciyā Mātā temple is largely a 12th-century rebuilding. The town was attacked by Muḥammad of Ghūr’s armies in 1195.

nodes.name: Galtājī, Jaipur
nodes.summary: Temple and spring-tank complex in a ravine of the hills east of Jaipur, a seat (gaddī) of the Rāmānandī order since the early 15th century, when Payohārī Kṛṣṇadās displaced the yogīs who lived there.

The present pavilions and temples (including those of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa and a hilltop Sūrya temple) are generally ascribed to the 18th century, when Jaipur’s courtiers built here; that date is from recall.

nodes.name: Śrī Maṅgeśa temple, Priol (Goa)
nodes.summary: Śiva temple of the Gauḍa Sārasvata Brahmins at Mangueshi in Ponda, Goa, re-founded here in 1560 when the deity was carried out of Portuguese-ruled territory; the present building is of the later 18th–19th century, with a third building phase in 1890.
nodes.details: After the Portuguese took Goa (1510), temples in their territories were destroyed and deities moved inland. Temple records date the removal of Maṅgeśa from Kuśasthalī (Cortalim) to Priol to Śaka 1482 (1560), and Jesuit letters confirm a migration before 1 May 1560. In 1739 the Peśvās granted the village to the temple; the area came under Portuguese rule in 1763, after which the temple was protected under a later policy of tolerance. A further building was raised in 1890.

nodes.name: Viṭṭhala-Rukmiṇī temple, Pandharpur
nodes.summary: Main temple of Viṭhobā (Viṭṭhala) and Rakhumāī at Pandharpur on the Bhīmā, goal of the Vārkarī pilgrimages; inscriptions show a small shrine set up in 1189, a gateway in 1237 and a temple built in 1273–77, though the standing structure is mainly of the 17th century or later.
nodes.details: A popular account credits the Hoysaḷa Viṣṇuvardhana (1108–1152) with the temple at the request of Puṇḍalīka; the epigraphic record is later. An inscription of 1189 records the first setting-up of a small shrine to Viṭhobā on the site; one of 1237 records a gateway built by the reigning (Yādava) king and gives the earliest epigraphic link between Pandharpur and Puṇḍarīka; inscriptions of 1273–77 record the building of a temple on the site of the earlier shrine. R. C. Dhere’s study traces the god’s pastoral origins. The present fabric shows later Deccan forms (domes, lobed arches).

nodes.name: Khaṇḍobā temple, Jejuri
nodes.summary: Hill temple of Khaṇḍobā (Mallāri Mārtaṇḍa), the warrior and pastoral god of the Deccan worshipped by farmers, Dhangar herders and Brahmins alike; worship is attested from the 12th–13th century and the present complex was built and enlarged under Marāṭhā and Holkar patronage.
nodes.details: Khaṇḍobā is regarded as a form of Śiva; the sanctum holds a liṅga and paired images of Khaṇḍobā and his wife Mhāḷsā. The temple stands in the Hemāḍpantī manner with an outer hall, dīpamāḷās (lamp towers) and a brass-covered tortoise in the court. In 1737–39 Cimājī Āppā gave the temple church bells taken from the Portuguese at Vasai. The reference work consulted attributes building to Ahilyābāī Holkar while calling it 17th-century, which is inconsistent; the Holkar connection (the Holkars’ family deity) is secure, the dating is not.

nodes.name: Rām Rājā temple, Orchha
nodes.summary: Palace-temple at Orchha where Rāma is worshipped as a reigning king (rājā), with a daily armed guard of honour; tradition holds that Queen Gaṇeś Kuṃvarī brought the image from Ayodhyā in 1574–75 and that it refused to move from her palace into the Caturbhuj temple built for it.
nodes.details: In the local account King Madhukar Śāh (r. 1554–1592), a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, challenged his queen, a devotee of Rāma, to bring Rāma to Orchha; she travelled to Ayodhyā and returned on foot (1574–75) with an image of the child Rāma, which, once set down in her palace, could not be moved. The palace thus became the temple, and the towering Caturbhuj temple nearby was left without its intended image. Rāma is shown seated with sword and shield, flanked by Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva and Narasiṃha, with Hanumān and Jāmbavān below; the state police mount a daily salute.

nodes.name: Bateshwar temple group (Morena)
nodes.summary: Ravine site of nearly 200 small sandstone Śiva, Viṣṇu and Śakti temples north of Gwalior, built from about 750–800 to the 11th century in the early Pratīhāra Nāgara style; mostly collapsed, many were reassembled by the ASI from 2005.

The temples fell after the 13th century, perhaps by earthquake. A Navagraha lintel indicates a post-600 date (Mevissen). The ASI’s reconstruction campaign led by K. K. Muhammed began in 2005.

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa Janmasthān temple complex, Mathurā
nodes.summary: Temple complex in Mathurā built from 1953 (completed 1982) on the site revered as Kṛṣṇa’s birthplace, beside the Shahi Idgah mosque raised after Aurangzeb ordered the great Keśavadeva temple destroyed in 1670; the site has a long history of temple building and destruction and is the subject of ongoing litigation.
nodes.details:
Excavations have yielded pottery and terracottas from the 6th century BCE, and Vaiṣṇava worship nearby is attested from the early centuries CE. A Sanskrit inscription found on the site records that in VS 1207 (1150) one Jajja, probably a Gāhaḍavāla vassal, built a Viṣṇu temple there. In the early 17th century the Bundelā ruler Bīr Siṃh Deo built a great Keśavadeva temple (described by European travellers), which was demolished on Aurangzeb’s orders in 1670; the Shahi Idgah mosque stands on part of its site.

The present complex — the Keśavadeva temple, the Garbha Gṛha shrine (the “birth-chamber”) and the Bhāgavata Bhavan — was built from 1953 with funds from the Dalmia and Birla families and completed in 1982. Since 2020 suits concerning the mosque and the land have been before the courts; this record does not take a position on them.

nodes.name: Govindadeva temple, Vrindavan
nodes.summary: Monumental red-sandstone temple at Vrindavan built for the Gauḍīya image of Govindadeva by Rājā Mān Siṃh of Amber, dated by inscription to 1590; its upper storeys were lost after the image was taken away for safety in 1670, and the image now resides at Jaipur.
nodes.details: Gauḍīya tradition holds that Rūpa Gosvāmī rediscovered the self-manifested image at Gomā-ṭīlā in 1525 and built a first temple around 1535 at the Yogapīṭha. An Akbar farmān of 1568 recognised Jīva Gosvāmī as manager of the Govindadeva and Madana-mohana temples. Mān Siṃh I of Amber, Akbar’s general, built the great cruciform temple — an unusual fusion of Hindu plan and Mughal vaulting — whose inscription gives 1590. When Vrindavan was attacked on Aurangzeb’s orders in 1670 the image was removed; after decades in Kachvāhā territory it was installed at Jaipur (worship from 1719; final shrine by 1735). The temple is ASI-protected (N-UP-A195).

nodes.name: Hanumān Gaṛhī, Ayodhyā
nodes.summary: Fortress-like hill temple of Hanumān in Ayodhyā, held by the Nirvāṇī akhāṛā of Rāmānandī bairāgīs; the present temple grew under Awadh nawabi land grants in the 18th–19th centuries, and an 1855 dispute over it was a major Hindu–Muslim conflict in Ayodhyā.
nodes.details: Tradition holds that Hanumān lived here to guard Ayodhyā after Rāma’s return. Peter van der Veer’s ethnography describes the temple’s ownership by the Nirvāṇī akhāṛā and its central place in Ayodhyā’s monastic economy. The reference consulted reports that the Nawab of Awadh granted land revenue for the temple; the historian S. Gopal noted that the 1855 conflict concerned Hanumān Gaṛhī rather than the Bābrī site.

nodes.name: Rājarāṇī temple, Bhubaneswar

nodes.details: Style places it in the mid-11th century (a date also reached by an analysis published in 1953); Fergusson proposed a start in 1105. The eight guardians of the directions (dikpālas) stand at the corners, and the temple’s sensuous female figures have earned it the local name “love temple”. It collapsed into ruins and was repaired in 1903.

nodes.name: Mahāmaham tank, Kumbakonam
nodes.summary: Large temple tank in Kumbakonam where, once every twelve years (when Jupiter enters Leo in the month of Māsi), the Mahāmaham festival is held; tradition holds that the sacred rivers of India bathe here then, and the 1992 festival drew about a million pilgrims.
nodes.details: Sixteen small maṇḍapas with liṅgas line the banks; one on the north bank carries an inscription of a tulāpuruṣadāna (weighing a donor against gold). Appar’s Tēvāram mentions the presence of the Gaṅgā and other rivers in the tank. Inscriptions at other sites record Kṛṣṇadevarāya’s visit to the festival. A crush during the 1992 festival killed dozens of pilgrims (recall).

nodes.name: Tyāgarāja temple, Tiruvarur
nodes.summary: Vast Śiva temple of Tiruvārūr, seat of Tyāgarāja (Somāskanda) and of the goddess Kamalāmbikā, praised in the Tēvāram; Cōḻa masonry from the 9th century, with a long inscription of Rājendra I listing gold and copper gifts, and the largest temple chariot in Tamil Nadu.
nodes.details: Tiruvārūr (Ārūr) is the town of the Nāyaṉār Cuntarar and the setting of several Periya Purāṇam episodes; it is the chief of the seven Saptaviṭaṅka sites where Tyāgarāja images, said to have been brought from Indra’s heaven by the Cōḻa king Mucukunda, dance distinctive steps. The Kamalāmbikā shrine is a centre of Śrīvidyā worship. The inscription of Rājendra I’s 20th regnal year on the north and west walls of the Tyāgarāja shrine records gifts in detail; Kulottuṅga III was the last Cōḻa closely involved with the temple.

The temple is closely linked with the Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi maṭha and Śrīvidyā worship; Kāñcī is counted in some lists as the navel pīṭha of Satī.

nodes.name: Śabarimala Dharmaśāstā (Ayyappan) temple
nodes.summary: Hill shrine of Ayyappan (Dharmaśāstā) in the Periyar forests of Kerala, reached by pilgrims after a 41-day vow and the climb of the eighteen sacred steps; restored after a fire in 1902 and rebuilt after an arson attack in 1950, it receives millions of pilgrims in the Maṇḍala–Makaravilakku season.
nodes.details:
Ayyappan is held to be the son of Śiva and Mohinī (Viṣṇu’s female form); his cult combines forest, warrior and ascetic traits, and pilgrims of all castes and religions take the same vow, addressing each other as “Swami”. In 1902 the Travancore ruler ordered restoration after a fire; in 1950 the temple was rebuilt after an arson attack, the stone image being replaced by a pañcaloha image, and the flagstaff was installed in 1969. The sanctum roof is gold-plated.

The temple’s custom of excluding women aged about 10–50 was struck down by the Supreme Court of India on 28 September 2018 (Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala); review petitions were referred to a larger bench in 2019, and the matter remains contested. Radhika Sekar’s study describes the pilgrimage and cult.

nodes.name: Kataragama devālaya complex
nodes.summary: Shrine complex in the jungle of southern Sri Lanka of the god Kataragama — a Buddhist guardian deity and, for Hindus, Murukaṉ (Skanda) — venerated by Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims and Vedda; its annual Esala festival and fire-walking are major pilgrimages.
nodes.details: The village appears in the Mahāvaṃsa (5th c.); the first literary reference to Kataragama as a sacred place of Skanda-Murukaṉ is in Aruṇakirinātar’s 15th-century Tiruppukaḻ, and the Pali Jinakālamālī (16th c.) names the god as a guardian of the island. S. Pathmanathan places the Tamil identification between the 13th and 15th centuries. Gananath Obeyesekere has studied the rise of ecstatic bhakti and fire-walking here in the 20th century. The main shrine and the nearby Kiri Vehera stupa are under Buddhist management.

nodes.name: Śāradā Pīṭha (ruins), Neelum valley

nodes.details: The Nīlamata Purāṇa is the earliest text to mention it; by the 8th century pilgrims came from as far as Bengal, and in the 11th century Al-Bīrūnī described its venerated wooden image. Since 1947 the site has been across the Line of Control, and Kashmiri Hindu groups have campaigned for a pilgrim corridor.

nodes.name: Phnom Bakheng, Angkor

nodes.name: Prasat Phanom Rung
nodes.summary: Khmer sanctuary of Śiva on the rim of an extinct volcano in Buriram province, Thailand, built between the 10th and 13th centuries; its Nārāyaṇa lintel (Viṣṇu Anantaśāyin), stolen in the 1960s and held by the Art Institute of Chicago from 1967, was returned in 1988 after a public campaign.

The “Phra Narai” lintel, displayed in Chicago as “the Birth of Brahma with Reclining Vishnu on a Makara”, was returned that year and reinstalled over the eastern entrance.

nodes.name: Bujang Valley candi (Kedah)
nodes.summary: Remains of brick and laterite Hindu and Buddhist shrines (candi) in the Bujang Valley of Kedah, Malaysia, part of a trading complex of the 5th–14th centuries; the reconstructed Candi Bukit Batu Pahat is the best-known Śaiva shrine.

nodes.name: Ganga Talao (Grand Bassin), Mauritius
nodes.summary: Crater lake in southern Mauritius made a Hindu tīrtha after a priest of Triolet, Jhummun Giri, dreamed in 1887 (or the 1890s) that its waters flowed from the Gaṅgā; Gaṅgā water was poured into it in 1972, it was declared a sacred lake in 1998, and the Mahāśivarātri pilgrimage draws hundreds of thousands.

Shrines line the shore, and a 33 m statue of Śiva (Maṅgal Mahādev) stands at the entrance (2007, recall).

nodes.name: Yamunā river
nodes.summary: Sacred river of northern India rising at Yamunotri and joining the Gaṅgā at Prayāga; personified as the goddess Yamunā, sister of Yama, it is the river of Kṛṣṇa’s Braj (Mathurā and Vṛndāvana) and is named in the Ṛgveda’s river hymn.
nodes.details: Ṛgveda 10.75.5 (the Nadīstuti) invokes “Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī …”. In the Bhāgavata and Harivaṃśa the Yamunā is the river of Kṛṣṇa’s childhood (Kāliya, the rāsa). David Haberman’s study documents both the river’s theology in Braj and its severe modern pollution.

nodes.name: Bṛhadīśvara temple, Thanjavur
nodes.summary: Granite Śiva temple built by the Cōḻa king Rājarāja I at his capital Thanjavur and consecrated in 1010 CE; its c. 60 m vimāna was the tallest of its age and the walls carry a large corpus of Rājarāja’s own Tamil inscriptions.
nodes.details:
The temple, called Rājarājeśvaram in its inscriptions, was built between c. 1003 and 1010 CE. Its inscriptions record that on the 275th day of Rājarāja I’s 25th regnal year (1010 CE) the king presented the gold-plated finial (kalaśa) for the vimāna, and they list endowments, temple staff and the bronzes the king and his family gave.

The circumambulatory passage around the sanctum preserves Cōḻa-period wall paintings (partly over-painted in the Nāyaka period). Later Nāyaka and Marāṭhā rulers of Thanjavur added subsidiary shrines and halls within the enclosure. The temple remains in worship.

nodes.details: Rājendra I (r. 1014–1044) took the title Gaṅgaikoṇḍa (“who took the Gaṅgā”) after his army reached the Gaṅgā and established the city of Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram as Cōḻa capital around 1025; it remained the capital for about two and a half centuries. The temple is usually dated to c. 1035, i.e. within his reign. Famous sculptures include Śiva garlanding the devotee Caṇḍeśa.

nodes.name: Naṭarāja temple, Chidambaram
nodes.summary: Temple of Śiva as Naṭarāja, the cosmic dancer, worshipped in the gold-roofed Kaṉakasabhā; it is the “ether” (ākāśa) shrine among the five element liṅgas and one of the most celebrated temples sung in the Tēvāram.
nodes.details:
Copper-plate inscriptions credit the Cōḻa king Parāntaka I (10th c.) with gilding the roof of the hall in which Naṭarāja dances. Most of the surviving plan and the great gopuras date from the late 12th and 13th centuries, with later additions. The temple is administered by the hereditary Dīkṣitar priests, and its ritual combines Vedic and Āgamic elements.

The temple tradition identifies Chidambaram as the place where Śiva performed the ānanda-tāṇḍava before the sages Patañjali and Vyāghrapāda; the “Chidambara rahasya” is worshipped as the formless ākāśa.

dates.label: Śiva danced the ānanda-tāṇḍava here before Patañjali and Vyāghrapāda (sthala tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

nodes.name: Śrī Raṅganāthasvāmī temple, Srirangam
nodes.summary: Island temple of Viṣṇu as Raṅganātha reclining on the serpent, set within seven concentric enclosures on an island of the Kāvēri; first among the 108 Divya Deśams of the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition.
nodes.details:
The temple is praised in the hymns of the Āḻvārs collected in the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham. Its many inscriptions, from the Cōḻa period onwards, record gifts from Cōḻa, Pāṇḍya, Hoysaḷa and Vijayanagara rulers and show the temple’s role as a landholder and charitable institution. Rāmānuja is held by tradition to have spent his last decades here and organised its worship.

The outer Rājagopuram, about 73 m high, was completed only in 1987 with support from the Ahobila Maṭha.

dates.label: Image brought by Vibhīṣaṇa from Ayodhyā and left on the island (temple tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: c. 10th–17th c. CE (inscribed fabric)
dates.basis: inscriptions from the Cōḻa period onward and architectural style

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Inscriptions and fabric document a temple continuously endowed from the Cōḻa period to modern times; the tradition that Vibhīṣaṇa left the image here is a sthala narrative, not evidence for the date of the cult.

nodes.name: Mīnākṣī–Sundareśvara temple, Madurai
nodes.summary: Twin-shrine temple of the goddess Mīnākṣī and her consort Sundareśvara (Śiva) at the heart of Madurai; its fourteen painted gopuras, the tallest c. 52 m, largely date from Nāyaka rebuilding in the 16th–17th centuries.
nodes.details: Madurai (Ālavāy) is celebrated in the Tēvāram, and the temple’s sacred history is told in the Tiruviḷaiyāṭaṟpurāṇam (the “sacred games” of Śiva). After the raids of the Delhi Sultanate armies in the early 14th century the temple was restored, and it was massively expanded by the Madurai Nāyakas in the 16th–17th centuries. The annual Cittirai festival re-enacts the marriage of Mīnākṣī and Sundareśvara, with Viṣṇu (Aḻakar) arriving as the bride’s brother.

dates.label: Mīnākṣī, born as a Pāṇḍya princess, married Śiva as Sundareśvara at Madurai (Tiruviḷaiyāṭaṟpurāṇam tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 14th c. CE restoration after Sultanate-period destruction

nodes.limits: The surviving complex is predominantly Nāyaka-period; earlier phases are known from texts and inscriptions rather than standing fabric. The divine-marriage narrative is temple mythology and festival practice, not a historical event.

nodes.name: Rāmanāthasvāmī temple, Rameswaram
nodes.summary: Śiva temple on Pamban (Rameswaram) island where, according to tradition, Rāma worshipped a liṅga; it is counted among the twelve jyotirliṅgas and as the southern dhāma of the Char Dham, and is known for its very long pillared corridors.
nodes.details:
The temple tradition holds that Rāma, returning from (or according to other versions, before) the war with Rāvaṇa, worshipped Śiva here; the liṅga is said to have been made of sand by Sītā (Rāmaliṅgam), while a second liṅga (Viśvaliṅgam) was brought by Hanumān from Kailāsa. The story is told in later retellings and sthala texts, not in the critical text of Vālmīki.

The temple was expanded in the 12th century under the Pāṇḍyas, with sanctum renovations credited to the Āryacakravarti kings of Jaffna; the famous corridors were built mainly under the Sētupati rulers of Ramnad in the 17th–18th centuries.

dates.label: Liṅga worshipped by Rāma (Rāmaliṅga made by Sītā; Viśvaliṅga brought by Hanumān) — temple tradition
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.name: Aruṇācaleśvara temple, Tiruvannamalai
nodes.summary: Large temple at the foot of Aruṇācala hill, worshipped as the fire (agni) liṅga among the five element shrines; the hill itself is identified in tradition with the column of fire of the Liṅgodbhava story.
nodes.details: The temple tradition holds that Śiva appeared here as an infinite column of fire to settle the dispute between Brahmā and Viṣṇu; the annual Kārttikai Dīpam lights a beacon on the summit. The present masonry structure goes back to the Cōḻa period (9th c.), with major Vijayanagara and later additions including the thousand-pillared hall and the tall gopuras. Tiruvannamalai is sung in the Tēvāram.

dates.label: Śiva manifested as a column of fire (Liṅgodbhava) at Aruṇācala — sthala tradition
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

nodes.name: Jambukeśvara temple, Thiruvanaikaval
nodes.summary: Śiva temple on Srirangam island worshipped as the water (jala) liṅga among the five element shrines; a spring keeps the sanctum floor moist.
nodes.details: The temple tradition tells of a spider and an elephant (āṉai, hence the name) that worshipped the liṅga under a jambu tree; the spider was reborn as the early Cōḻa king Kōcceṅkaṇāṉ, credited with building many Śiva temples. The surviving structure is medieval Cōḻa and later. The temple is sung in the Tēvāram.

dates.label: Founded by the early Cōḻa king Kōccēṅkaṇāṉ, reborn from a spider devotee (sthala tradition)

nodes.name: Ekāmbareśvara temple, Kanchipuram
nodes.summary: Major Śiva temple of Kanchipuram worshipped as the earth (pṛthvī) liṅga among the five element shrines, centred on a sacred mango tree; its southern gopura is among the tallest in South India.
nodes.details: The temple tradition holds that Pārvatī made a liṅga of sand beneath a mango tree (ekāmra, “single mango”) and embraced it when Śiva tested her with a flood. The masonry temple goes back to the Cōḻa period, with very large Vijayanagara additions including the thousand-pillared hall and the gopura. It is sung in the Tēvāram.

dates.label: Pārvatī worshipped a sand liṅga under the mango tree (sthala tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

nodes.name: Kailāsanātha temple, Kanchipuram
nodes.summary: Sandstone Śiva temple built by the Pallava king Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha around 700 CE, with additions by his son Mahendravarman III; one of the earliest large structural temples of Tamil Nadu.
nodes.details: The temple is enclosed by a wall lined with small shrine-cells (58 in number) carrying sculpture of Śiva’s forms. Rājasiṃha’s inscriptions on the temple give it his name (Rājasiṃheśvara). The style develops the Drāviḍa vimāna first tried in the Mamallapuram monoliths.

nodes.name: Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ temple, Kanchipuram
nodes.summary: Eighth-century Pallava Viṣṇu temple built by Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, with three superimposed sanctums and a cloister of relief panels that narrate Pallava dynastic history; a Divya Deśam sung by Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār.
nodes.details: Originally called Parameśvara-viṇṇakaram (“Viṣṇu-house of Parameśvara”), the temple has sanctums on three levels showing Viṣṇu seated, standing and reclining. The cloister reliefs with labels are an important source for Pallava history, including the accession of Nandivarman II. Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār, a contemporary of the king, praised the temple in the Periya Tirumoḻi. Dating views range from c. 690 to c. 770–775 CE.

dates.label: late 8th c. CE (reign of Nandivarman II, c. 731–796; stylistically c. 770–775)

nodes.name: Varadarāja Perumāḷ temple, Kanchipuram
nodes.summary: Large Viṣṇu temple of Kanchipuram on the Hastigiri mound, a Divya Deśam closely associated with Rāmānuja; renovated under the Cōḻas from 1053 and expanded by later dynasties.
nodes.details: The temple was renovated by the Cōḻas in 1053 and expanded under Kulōttuṅga I and Vikrama Cōḻa; further walls and gopuras were added in the 14th century and later. It is famous for the wooden Atti Varadar image kept submerged in the temple tank and displayed only every 40 years (most recently in 2019).

nodes.name: Group of Monuments at Mamallapuram
nodes.summary: Seventh- and eighth-century Pallava port with rock-cut cave temples (maṇḍapas), monolithic rathas, open-air reliefs and the structural Shore Temple; a World Heritage property since 1984.
nodes.details: Most monuments are attributed to Narasiṃhavarman I Māmalla (c. 630–668), after whom the town is named, with earlier work under Mahendravarman I and later work under Rājasiṃha (Narasiṃhavarman II). The great open-air relief is identified by some scholars as the Descent of the Gaṅgā (Bhagīratha’s penance) and by others as Arjuna’s penance to obtain the Pāśupata weapon; the Mahiṣamardinī cave shows the Goddess battling the buffalo demon and the Kṛṣṇa maṇḍapa shows Kṛṣṇa lifting Govardhana.

dates.label: c. 630–728 CE (Narasiṃhavarman I to Rājasiṃha)
dates.basis: Pallava inscriptions, royal titles carved on monuments and style

nodes.name: Shore Temple, Mamallapuram
nodes.summary: Granite structural temple on the shore at Mamallapuram, built under Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha around 700–728 CE, combining two Śiva shrines with a shrine of the reclining Viṣṇu.
nodes.details: Inscriptions name the shrines Kṣatriyasiṃha-Pallaveśvara-gṛham and Rājasiṃha-Pallaveśvara-gṛham (both Śiva) and a Viṣṇu shrine of Narapatisiṃha, a title of Rājasiṃha. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami briefly exposed remains of other structures along the coast.

nodes.name: Pañca Rathas, Mamallapuram
nodes.summary: Five monolithic shrines carved from a single granite outcrop in the 7th century, popularly named after the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī; they model the main types of early Drāviḍa shrine and were never consecrated.
nodes.details: The popular names (Dharmarāja, Bhīma, Arjuna, Nakula–Sahadeva and Draupadī rathas) are later and have no connection with the original dedications. The monuments are usually attributed to Narasiṃhavarman I, although newer readings of inscriptions have suggested work continued into the reign of Rājasiṃha.

nodes.name: Subrahmaṇya temple, Tirupparankundram
nodes.summary: Rock-cut and structural temple of Murukaṉ on a hill outside Madurai, counted first of the six abodes; tradition places Murukaṉ’s marriage to Deivayāṉai (Devasenā) here.
nodes.details: The core is a rock-cut cave shrine converted into a Hindu temple under a minister of a later Pāṇḍya king in the late 8th century CE, with pillared halls added by the Madurai Nāyakas. A separate Pāṇḍya rock-cut Śiva cave lies at the foot of the hill.

nodes.details: The temple was occupied by the Dutch East India Company in 1646–1648 during its war with the Portuguese; the images were removed and later recovered (1653). Most of the fabric, including the nine-storey gopura, is early-modern.

nodes.name: Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi temple, Palani
nodes.summary: Hilltop temple of Murukaṉ as the renunciant Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi, counted third of the six abodes and one of the most visited temples in Tamil Nadu.
nodes.details: Temple tradition holds that the image was fashioned by the Siddha Bhōgar from nine medicinal minerals (navapāṣāṇam). The hill shrine is associated with the story of Murukaṉ leaving his family after the contest for the fruit of knowledge. The surviving structure has been rebuilt several times; Wikipedia’s claim of a 2nd–5th-century Cēra foundation is not supported by dated fabric checked here.

nodes.name: Guruvāyūr temple
nodes.summary: Kerala temple of Kṛṣṇa as Guruvāyūrappaṉ (a four-armed Viṣṇu image worshipped as the child Kṛṣṇa), one of the most visited temples of South India.

The sanctum murals were damaged in a fire in 1970 and restored in the 1980s. Entry is restricted to Hindus.
