nodes.name: Padmanābhasvāmī temple, Thiruvananthapuram
nodes.summary: Temple of Viṣṇu reclining on Ananta at the heart of Thiruvananthapuram, a Divya Deśam and the tutelary shrine of the Travancore royal house; the opening of its vaults in 2011 revealed a very large treasure.
nodes.details: The temple in its present form was rebuilt in the 18th century under Mārtāṇḍa Varma of Travancore, who in 1750 dedicated his kingdom to Padmanābha (the Thṛppaṭidānam). Records of the temple (the Mathilakam records) were kept in a record room built c. 1425. The vault inventory ordered by the Supreme Court of India from 2011 made it internationally known.

nodes.name: Veṅkaṭeśvara temple, Tirumala
nodes.summary: Hill temple of Veṅkaṭeśvara on the Tirumala range above Tirupati, among the most visited and richest religious institutions in the world; a Divya Deśam sung by the Āḻvārs.
nodes.details: The site (Vēṅkaṭam) is named in old Tamil literature and praised by the Āḻvārs. The temple’s epigraphic record, published by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams, includes a Pallava-period gift of a silver image by the queen Sāmavai (966 CE) and very many Vijayanagara grants; Kṛṣṇadevarāya visited repeatedly and on 2 January 1517 installed portrait statues of himself and his queens. The temple has been administered by the TTD under state legislation since the 20th century.

nodes.name: Mallikārjuna temple, Srisailam
nodes.summary: Fortified hilltop temple above the Krishna gorge that is counted both as a jyotirliṅga (Mallikārjuna) and as a Śakti Pīṭha (Bhramarāmbā); it is also sung in the Tēvāram.
nodes.details: Much of the present complex was added under the Vijayanagara kings from the 14th century, and the enclosure walls carry narrative reliefs; a gopura is associated by tradition with Śivājī’s visit in 1677. Wikipedia reports Sātavāhana-period epigraphic references to Śrīparvata; these refer to the hill, not to the standing temple.

nodes.name: Śrīkāḷahastīśvara temple, Srikalahasti
nodes.summary: Śiva temple on the Svarṇamukhī river worshipped as the air (vāyu) liṅga among the five element shrines and associated with the hunter-saint Kaṇṇappa; it is sung in the Tēvāram.
nodes.details: The name combines śrī (spider), kāḷa (serpent) and hasti (elephant), three animal devotees of the temple legend. The main structure is credited to Rājendra Cōḻa I (11th c.), with gopuras of Kulōttuṅga I and large Vijayanagara-period additions.

dates.label: Worshipped by a spider, a serpent and an elephant, and by the hunter Kaṇṇappa (sthala tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 11th c. CE Cōḻa main structure (Rājendra I; gopuras of Kulōttuṅga I)

location.label: Srikalahasti, Tirupati district, Andhra Pradesh, India

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Dates the Cōḻa and later fabric; the infobox’s 5th-century foundation and the animal-devotee legend are tradition.

nodes.name: Paraśurāmeśvara temple, Gudimallam
nodes.summary: Village temple near Renigunta whose apsidal sanctum enshrines the Gudimallam liṅga, a realistic liṅga carved with a standing two-armed figure that is among the earliest surviving images connected with Śiva; the liṅga is dated by most scholars between the 2nd/1st c. BCE and the early centuries CE.
nodes.details: The liṅga has remained in worship while the temple around it has been rebuilt; the present structure belongs to later centuries (Pallava/Bāṇa to Cōḻa-period inscriptions and later rebuilding), on an earlier apsidal plan. Excavation by I. K. Sarma (ASI) in 1973 investigated the original setting of the liṅga. The temple is ASI-protected.

dates.label: Liṅga worshipped by Paraśurāma (temple name and tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: liṅga: c. 2nd–1st c. BCE (majority) to 1st–3rd c. CE (some)
dates.basis: style and stratigraphy of the 1973 excavation

dates.label: temple fabric rebuilt c. 9th–13th c. CE on the earlier apsidal plan

location.label: Gudimallam, Tirupati district, Andhra Pradesh, India

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The liṅga establishes early worship of a phallic emblem with an anthropomorphic deity (generally read as Śiva/Rudra); its exact date and the identity of the figure remain debated, and the standing temple is much later.

nodes.name: Navabrahma temples, Alampur
nodes.summary: Group of nine Śiva temples of the Bādāmi Cālukya period (7th–8th c.) near the confluence of the Tuṅgabhadrā and Kṛṣṇā, unusual in the south for their Nāgara (curvilinear) towers; the nearby Jogulāmbā shrine is counted among the eighteen Mahāśakti Pīṭhas.
nodes.details: Early 8th-century inscriptions at the site indicate a Śaiva maṭha. Much of the area was re-sited when the Srisailam dam reservoir was created, and the Jogulāmbā temple was rebuilt in modern times.

location.label: Alampur, Jogulamba Gadwal district, Telangana, India

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Dates Cālukya patronage of northern-style towers in the Deccan; the Śakti-pīṭha identification of Jogulāmbā belongs to the later eighteen-pīṭha list.

nodes.name: Rāmappa (Rudreśvara) temple, Palampet
nodes.summary: Kākatīya Śiva temple at Palampet commissioned in 1213 by the general Recherla Rudra under king Gaṇapati; inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2021 and popularly named after its sculptor.
nodes.details: A pillar inscription in the courtyard records the commission in 1213; construction is said to have taken about four decades. The temple is known for its bracket figures of dancers and for very light porous bricks used in the superstructure.

attributes.unesco: Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple, Telangana — inscribed 2021; UNESCO list no. 1570
attributes.protection: ASI Monument of National Importance (N-TG-5, as listed on Wikipedia)
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Dates the temple securely; the naming after the sculptor Rāmappa is local tradition.

nodes.name: Bādāmi cave temples
nodes.summary: Four rock-cut cave temples (three Hindu, one Jain) in the sandstone cliff of Vātāpi, capital of the early Cālukyas; Cave 3, dedicated to Viṣṇu, carries an inscription of Śaka 500 (578 CE), making it one of the earliest precisely dated Brahmanical cave temples.
nodes.details: Cave 1 is Śaiva (with an eighteen-armed dancing Śiva), Caves 2 and 3 are Vaiṣṇava, with large panels of Trivikrama (Vāmana’s three strides), Varāha and Narasiṃha, and Cave 4 is Jain. The Cave 3 inscription records its dedication by Maṅgaleśa in the twelfth regnal year of his brother Kīrtivarman I.

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The Cave 3 inscription dates the excavation and royal Vaiṣṇava patronage; the reliefs show which avatāra narratives were current in 6th-c. Karnataka, not their origin.

nodes.name: Meguti Jain temple, Aihole
nodes.summary: Jain temple on a hill at Aihole whose east wall bears the Aihole praśasti of Pulakeśin II composed by Ravikīrti and dated Śaka 556 (634/635 CE); it is one of the earliest securely dated structural temples in the Deccan.
nodes.details: The inscription, in Sanskrit verse, praises Pulakeśin II’s victories (including over Harṣa) and records Ravikīrti’s building of this Jina temple. It is also an early external attestation of the poets Kālidāsa and Bhāravi, whom Ravikīrti names, and dates itself by the Kali era as well as the Śaka era.

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The inscription securely dates the temple and Ravikīrti’s patronage; its account of Pulakeśin II’s victories is royal panegyric.

nodes.name: Durgā temple, Aihole
nodes.summary: Apsidal-ended early Cālukya temple at Aihole (late 7th–early 8th c.) surrounded by a colonnaded ambulatory; its name derives from a later fort (durga) built on it, not from the goddess.
nodes.details: The original dedication is debated (Viṣṇu and Sūrya have both been proposed), and the temple has served as a test case for the historiography of early Indian architecture, as Tartakov has shown. Niche sculptures include Narasiṃha, Varāha, Mahiṣamardinī and Śiva.

attributes.architecture: early Cālukya, apsidal plan with Nāgara śikhara
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The name “Durgā” is a misnomer from a later fort; the original cult image and dedication are not certainly known.
openQuestions: Original dedication of the sanctum (Viṣṇu or Sūrya).

nodes.name: Lāḍ Khān temple, Aihole
nodes.summary: Flat-roofed early Cālukya Śiva temple at Aihole, named after a later occupant; its date is a classic problem of Indian architectural history, with proposals ranging from the 5th to the early 8th century.
nodes.details: Early surveys (Cousens and others) treated Lāḍ Khān as a 5th-century prototype of the Hindu temple; later scholarship generally moved it to the late 7th or early 8th century on stylistic grounds. The current Wikipedia article reverses this, saying it is “now dated” to the 5th century, with weak sourcing. This dataset records both views as competing.

dates.label: c. 5th c. CE
dates.basis: early typological dating; repeated on Wikipedia

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: No dedicatory inscription dates the building; any date rests on stylistic comparison.

nodes.name: Virūpākṣa temple, Pattadakal
nodes.summary: The largest temple at Pattadakal, built c. 740–745 CE by Queen Lokamahādevī to commemorate her husband Vikramāditya II’s victory over the Pallavas; its Drāviḍa design closely follows the Kailāsanātha temple of Kanchipuram.
nodes.details: Inscriptions call it the Lokeśvara (after its patron). It was built by a queen of Vikramāditya II after his capture of Kanchipuram, and its style reflects contact with Pallava architecture. The walls carry reliefs from the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata and Purāṇic themes; the temple remains in worship. The Group of Monuments at Pattadakal was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1987.

dates.label: c. 740–745 CE
dates.basis: inscriptions of Lokamahādevī and regnal synchronism with Vikramāditya II

attributes.unesco: Group of Monuments at Pattadakal — inscribed 1987; UNESCO list no. 239
attributes.protection: World Heritage property managed by the ASI
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikidata P625

nodes.limits: Royal inscriptions date the temple and its patron; the commemorated victory is presented from the Cālukya side.

nodes.name: Pāpanātha temple, Pattadakal
nodes.summary: Mid-8th-century Cālukya Śiva temple at Pattadakal that fuses Nāgara and Drāviḍa elements and is known for its narrative panels from the Rāmāyaṇa and the Kirātārjunīya.
nodes.details: The temple stands about half a kilometre south of the main group. The ASI and Michell date it towards the end of early Cālukya rule.

attributes.unesco: part of Group of Monuments at Pattadakal (1987; no. 239)
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikidata P625

nodes.limits: The reliefs show the circulation of Rāmāyaṇa and Kirātārjunīya narratives in 8th-c. Karnataka; they do not date the narratives themselves.

nodes.name: Kailāsa temple (Ellora Cave 16)
nodes.summary: A complete Drāviḍa temple carved downward and inward from the basalt hillside at Ellora in the 8th century, generally attributed to the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Kṛṣṇa I (r. c. 756–773); its form evokes Mount Kailāsa, Śiva’s abode.
nodes.details: The temple has no dedicatory inscription. Its attribution rests on later epigraphs: the Baroda (Vadodara) copper plates of Karkarāja II (812 CE) praise a marvellous temple built by Kṛṣṇarāja at Elāpura that astonished even its architect, and another grant similarly credits Kṛṣṇarāja. The best-known relief shows Rāvaṇa shaking Kailāsa while Śiva steadies it with his toe; the walls also carry long Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata friezes. Ellora was inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1983.

dates.label: c. 756–773 CE (main excavation, reign of Kṛṣṇa I), with later elements
dates.basis: later copper-plate inscriptions crediting Kṛṣṇarāja; no dedicatory inscription

location.label: Ellora (Verul), Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, Maharashtra, India

attributes.unesco: Ellora Caves — inscribed 1983; UNESCO list no. 243
attributes.protection: World Heritage property managed by the ASI
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Attribution to Kṛṣṇa I is inferred from inscriptions of his successors; the Rāvaṇa relief is evidence for the narrative’s popularity, not for its events.

nodes.name: Daśāvatāra cave (Ellora Cave 15)
nodes.summary: Two-storeyed rock-cut temple at Ellora whose plan follows the Buddhist vihāras nearby but whose sculpture is Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava; an inscription of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa founder Dantidurga on the back wall of the front maṇḍapa is key to its date.
nodes.details: The cave was probably begun as a Buddhist excavation and completed as a Hindu temple. The Dantidurga inscription places its completion in the mid-8th century, just before the Kailāsa.

attributes.unesco: part of Ellora Caves (1983; no. 243)
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

sources.locator: infobox coordinates of the Ellora group

nodes.limits: Coordinates are those of the Ellora group, not the individual cave.

nodes.name: Elephanta Caves (Cave 1)
nodes.summary: Great Śiva cave on Elephanta island in Mumbai harbour, completed in the mid-6th century, whose colossal three-headed Sadāśiva (Maheśamūrti) is among the masterpieces of Indian sculpture.
nodes.details: Cave 1 has a pillared hall with a free-standing liṅga shrine and large relief panels: Sadāśiva, Ardhanārīśvara, Gaṅgādhara, the marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī, Rāvaṇa shaking Kailāsa, Andhakāntaka and Naṭarāja. Most scholars date its completion to the second quarter of the 6th century; the patron is unknown, with the Kalacuri king Kṛṣṇarāja among the candidates. The Portuguese named the island after a stone elephant found there. Inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1987.

location.label: Elephanta Island, Raigad district (Mumbai harbour), Maharashtra, India

attributes.unesco: Elephanta Caves — inscribed 1987; UNESCO list no. 244
attributes.protection: World Heritage property managed by the ASI
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: There is no foundation inscription; patron and exact date are inferred. The panels document 6th-c. Śaiva iconography, not the antiquity of the myths.
openQuestions: Patron: Kalacuri, Maurya of Konkan, or other — unresolved.

nodes.name: Virūpākṣa temple, Hampi
nodes.summary: Living Śiva temple of Virūpākṣa–Pampāpati on the Tuṅgabhadrā at Hampi, whose small early shrine was enlarged into a vast complex under the Vijayanagara kings; it predates and outlived the imperial city.
nodes.details: The shrine core is early (7th c. per some accounts), and the tutelary god Virūpākṣa became the patron deity of the Vijayanagara rulers. The great complex was built by Lakkaṇa Daṇḍeśa, a chief under Devarāya II, and Kṛṣṇadevarāya commissioned the ranga-maṇḍapa in 1510 to mark his accession. Worship continued after the sack of the city in 1565.

dates.label: Pampā (Pārvatī) won Śiva by penance at Hampi (sthala tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: early shrine core (7th c. per secondary sources) with pre-Vijayanagara additions
major enlargement under Devarāya II (by Lakkaṇa Daṇḍeśa)

attributes.unesco: part of Group of Monuments at Hampi (1986; no. 241)
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Dates the stages of royal building; the tradition of Pampā’s penance is local mythology.

nodes.name: Hazāra Rāma temple, Hampi
nodes.summary: Royal chapel of the Vijayanagara palace zone dedicated to Rāma, whose outer and inner walls are covered with friezes of the Rāmāyaṇa and of royal processions; it is attributed to Devarāya I in the early 15th century.
nodes.details: The temple, known in inscriptions as the Rāmacandra temple, sits at the centre of the royal enclosure. Its narrative panels follow the story from Daśaratha’s sacrifice to the war with Rāvaṇa, and outer friezes show the Mahānavamī festival. Dallapiccola, Fritz, Michell and Rajasekhara published the full sculptural programme (1992).

dates.label: early 15th c. CE (attributed to Devarāya I)
dates.basis: inscription and style as discussed by Dallapiccola et al.

attributes.unesco: part of Group of Monuments at Hampi (1986; no. 241)
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikidata P625

nodes.limits: The friezes are evidence for the Rāmāyaṇa’s role in Vijayanagara royal ideology; they say nothing about the historicity of Rāma.

nodes.name: Vijaya Viṭṭhala temple, Hampi
nodes.summary: Vijayanagara temple of Viṭṭhala (a form of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa worshipped at Pandharpur) at Hampi, famous for its “musical” pillars and the stone chariot that serves as Garuḍa’s shrine; mostly built in the 15th–16th centuries, with major additions under Kṛṣṇadevarāya.
nodes.details: The temple complex sits within a bazaar street in the north-east of the city. Its halls were expanded in the early 16th century; the stone ratha in the courtyard is a Garuḍa shrine. It has not been in worship since the city’s fall in 1565.

dates.label: 15th–16th c. CE, with major expansion under Kṛṣṇadevarāya (1509–1529)

attributes.unesco: part of Group of Monuments at Hampi (1986; no. 241)
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikidata P625

nodes.limits: The monument dates Vijayanagara devotion to Viṭṭhala; it does not establish when the Pandharpur cult began.

nodes.name: Cennakeśava temple, Belur
nodes.summary: Hoysaḷa temple of Viṣṇu as Cennakeśava commissioned by King Viṣṇuvardhana in 1117 CE at his early capital Belur; its bracket figures and lathe-turned pillars are hallmarks of the Hoysaḷa style.
nodes.details: The temple is still in worship. The dedication date of 1117 is given in inscriptions at the site, and the work continued for decades under Viṣṇuvardhana’s successors. With Halebidu and Somanathapura it forms the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas World Heritage property (2023).

attributes.unesco: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas — inscribed 2023; UNESCO list no. 1670
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Securely dated royal Vaiṣṇava foundation; later traditions that link it to Rāmānuja’s influence on Viṣṇuvardhana are hagiographic.

earliestMaterial.label: first quarter of the 12th century CE

nodes.name: Hoysaḷeśvara temple, Halebidu
nodes.summary: Twin-shrined Śiva temple at the Hoysaḷa capital Dvārasamudra (Halebidu), begun c. 1121 under Viṣṇuvardhana by his officer Ketamalla; its friezes carry thousands of sculptures including Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata scenes.
nodes.details: An inscription found near the Kalleśvara ruins at Ghattadahalli records Ketamalla’s construction. The city was sacked by Delhi Sultanate armies in the early 14th century. Part of the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (2023).

attributes.unesco: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas — inscribed 2023; UNESCO list no. 1670
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Dates the temple; the narrative friezes attest which epic and Purāṇic stories were current in 12th-c. Karnataka.

nodes.name: Keśava temple, Somanathapura
nodes.summary: Triple-shrined (trikūṭa) Hoysaḷa Viṣṇu temple on a star-shaped plan, consecrated by Somanātha Daṇḍanāyaka, a general of Narasiṃha III; Wikipedia gives 1258 CE while many guides give 1268.
nodes.details: The town is named after the patron. The temple is not in worship. Part of the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (2023).

dates.label: 1268 CE
dates.basis: date widely repeated in guidebooks; an entrance inscription of c. 1268 is reported

attributes.unesco: Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas — inscribed 2023; UNESCO list no. 1670
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The patron is secure; the exact year (1258 or 1268) needs a check against the published inscription (Epigraphia Carnatica).
openQuestions: 1258 vs 1268: Narasiṃha III’s accession is usually placed in 1263, which sits awkwardly with 1258.

nodes.name: Śiva temple, Ambarnath
nodes.summary: Bhūmija-style Śiva temple near Mumbai bearing an inscription of 1060 CE from the Śilāhāra period, one of the best-preserved 11th-century temples of the northern Konkan.
nodes.details: Wikipedia states that it was probably built by the Śilāhāra king Chittarāja and possibly rebuilt by his son Mummuṇi (Māmvāṇi). The temple is ASI-protected.

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikidata P625

nodes.limits: The inscription dates the building; attribution to a particular Śilāhāra king is less certain.

nodes.name: Bhīmaśaṅkara temple
nodes.summary: Śiva temple in the Sahyādri forest at the source of the Bhīmā river, claimed as the Bhīmaśaṅkara jyotirliṅga (a claim also made for sites in Assam and elsewhere).
nodes.details: The black-stone temple goes back to around the 13th century; its hall and śikhara were improved in the 18th century under Nānā Phaḍṇavīs.

dates.label: 18th c. CE additions under Nānā Phaḍṇavīs

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The fabric dates the present temple; its jyotirliṅga status rests on traditional lists and does not date the cult.

nodes.name: Tryambakeśvara temple
nodes.summary: Jyotirliṅga temple near the source of the Godāvarī in the Brahmagiri hills, whose liṅga is a hollow with three small lingas (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva); the present temple was built by the Peshwa Bāḷājī Bājīrāv in the mid-18th century.
nodes.details: The Kuśāvarta tank in the precinct is regarded as the ritual source of the Godāvarī. Trimbak is one of the sites of the Kumbha Melā (with Nashik).

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The fabric dates the present temple; its jyotirliṅga status rests on traditional lists and does not date the cult.

nodes.name: Ghṛṣṇeśvara temple
nodes.summary: Jyotirliṅga temple near Ellora, restored by Mālojī Bhosale in the 16th century and rebuilt in its present red-stone form in the 18th century under Holkar patronage.
nodes.details: Sources differ on the 18th-century patron: Wikipedia names Gautamābāī Holkar (rebuilding of 1729), while many accounts credit Ahilyābāī Holkar. The Śiva Purāṇa names the twelfth jyotirliṅga Ghuśmeśa after the devotee Ghuśmā.

dates.label: Ghuśmā’s devotion restored her son, and Śiva remained as Ghuśmeśa (Śiva Purāṇa)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 16th c. CE restoration by Mālojī Bhosale
18th c. CE rebuilding under Holkar patronage
dates.basis: secondary accounts differ (1729 Gautamābāī Holkar vs Ahilyābāī Holkar)

location.label: Verul (Ellora), Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, Maharashtra, India

nodes.name: Vaijanātha temple, Parli
nodes.summary: Śiva temple at Parli in Marathwada, one of the candidates for the Vaidyanātha jyotirliṅga (the other main claimant being Deoghar in Jharkhand).
nodes.details: The present Hemāḍpanthī-style temple was renovated in 1706 according to Wikipedia; many accounts credit Ahilyābāī Holkar with later work.

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The fabric dates the present temple; its jyotirliṅga status rests on traditional lists and does not date the cult.

nodes.name: Nāganātha temple, Aundha
nodes.summary: Hemāḍpanthī-style Śiva temple in Marathwada claimed as the Nāgeśvara jyotirliṅga, one of three competing claimants (with Dwarka and Jageshwar).
nodes.details: Local tradition attributes the first temple to Yudhiṣṭhira during the Pāṇḍavas’ exile. The surviving fabric is medieval (often assigned to the Seuṇa/Yādava period, 13th c.), with 18th-century renovation by Ahilyābāī Holkar.

dates.label: Built by Yudhiṣṭhira during the exile (local tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: c. 13th c. CE (Seuṇa period, by style)
18th c. CE renovation by Ahilyābāī Holkar

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The fabric dates the present temple; its jyotirliṅga status rests on traditional lists and does not date the cult.

nodes.name: Udayagiri caves (Vidiśā)
nodes.summary: Group of about twenty rock-cut shrines near Vidiśā excavated under the Gupta king Candragupta II, the only cave site securely tied to a Gupta monarch by inscriptions; Cave 5 holds the monumental relief of Varāha raising the Earth.
nodes.details: An inscription in Cave 6 is dated Gupta year 82 (c. 401/402 CE) in the reign of Candragupta II, and a Jain cave (Cave 20) has an inscription of 425/426 CE. Besides the Varāha panel, the caves include an early Mahiṣāsuramardinī, a reclining Viṣṇu, river goddesses and ekamukha-liṅgas. Scholars have read the Varāha panel as a political allegory of the Gupta king rescuing the earth (Williams; Willis), a reading that remains interpretive. The site is ASI-protected, close to Besnagar, findspot of the Heliodorus pillar.

sources.locator: CII III, Udayagiri cave inscription of Candragupta II, year 82

dates.label: late 4th–early 5th c. CE (main Hindu caves); Jain cave 425/426 CE

location.label: Udayagiri, Vidisha district, Madhya Pradesh, India

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Establishes Gupta royal patronage of Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva and Śākta imagery around 400 CE; the political reading of the Varāha panel is scholarly interpretation, and the panel does not date the Varāha myth.

nodes.name: Daśāvatāra temple, Deogarh
nodes.summary: Late Gupta stone temple of Viṣṇu (c. 500–550 CE) on the Betwā, one of the earliest surviving North Indian temples with a tower; its wall panels show Viṣṇu reclining on Śeṣa, Gajendra-mokṣa and Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
nodes.details: The temple stands on a raised terrace and originally had four corner shrines (pañcāyatana plan). Its name is modern; the iconography is Vaiṣṇava throughout. Cunningham reported Gupta-script inscriptions in the area. The site is ASI-protected.

location.label: Deogarh, Lalitpur district, Uttar Pradesh, India

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Undated by inscription; the panels attest Vaiṣṇava narrative iconography around 500 CE.

nodes.name: Pārvatī temple, Nachna
nodes.summary: Early stone temple at Nachna with a sanctum surrounded by a covered ambulatory and an upper chamber, carved with rock-like rustication; dated by style to the 5th or 6th century.
nodes.details: The Pārvatī temple is one of the Nachna group in Panna district. After Cunningham’s visit its upper cella collapsed and was later reconstructed. The nearby Caturmukha Mahādeva temple is later (9th c.). Its exact date and dedication are debated.

location.label: Nachna, Panna district, Madhya Pradesh, India

attributes.architecture: early Gupta-period flat-roofed type with upper chamber
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Undated by inscription; current name may not reflect the original dedication.

nodes.name: Bhitargaon brick temple
nodes.summary: Late 5th-century Gupta-period brick temple near Kanpur, the oldest surviving roofed brick/terracotta Hindu shrine with a high śikhara; its terracotta panels include Viṣṇu and other Purāṇic subjects.
nodes.details: The temple is built on a square plan with double-recessed corners and faces east; its upper chamber was damaged in the 18th century. It is ASI-protected.

location.label: Bhitargaon, Kanpur Nagar district, Uttar Pradesh, India

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Undated by inscription; the original dedication is inferred from the terracotta programme.

nodes.name: Kaṅkālī Devī temple, Tigawa
nodes.summary: Small flat-roofed Gupta-period temple (c. 400–425 CE) with a pillared porch, one of the earliest structural Hindu temples to survive; the doorway shows the river goddesses Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
nodes.details: The site once had dozens of temples. The surviving shrine is now worshipped as Kaṅkālī Devī; its original dedication is thought to have been Vaiṣṇava (Narasiṃha imagery is reported), with Cāmuṇḍā images also present.

location.label: Tigawa, Katni district, Madhya Pradesh, India

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Undated by inscription; current name reflects later worship.

nodes.name: Muṇḍeśvarī temple
nodes.summary: Octagonal stone temple on a hill in Kaimur district, Bihar, worshipped for Muṇḍeśvarī and a four-faced liṅga; it is often promoted as the oldest functioning Hindu temple (108 CE), a date most historians of architecture reject.
nodes.details: An inscription found in the debris mentions year 30 of an unstated era and a Mahārāja Udayasena. Read in the Śaka era it would give 108 CE, the date displayed by the ASI and the Bihar State Religious Trust Board; read in the Harṣa era it gives 636 CE, and Neuss argues from palaeography for c. 570–590 CE. Architectural historians generally date the existing sculpture to the 6th–7th century, and Buckee has argued that the octagonal shrine itself may be a 16th–17th-century reconstruction reusing earlier doorways and mouldings.

dates.label: 108 CE (if the inscription’s year 30 is Śaka)
dates.view: ASI site plaque / Bihar State Religious Trust Board

dates.label: present octagonal shrine possibly 16th–17th c., reusing 7th-c. members

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The inscription’s era is not stated, so its year cannot by itself date the temple; the “oldest functioning temple” claim rests on one reading.

nodes.name: Lakṣmaṇa temple, Sirpur
nodes.summary: Brick temple at Sirpur (Śrīpura) in Chhattisgarh with a well-preserved śikhara and stone doorframe, the earliest dated monument of the Sirpur group (c. 595–605 CE per Wikipedia; other accounts c. 650).
nodes.details: The temple is associated with the Pāṇḍuvaṃśī rulers of Dakṣiṇa Kosala; tradition credits its construction to Queen Vāsaṭā, mother of Mahāśivagupta Bālārjuna, in memory of her husband. Its brick śikhara is among the best surviving examples of early brick temple architecture.

dates.label: c. 595–650 CE
dates.basis: inscription and style (sources differ within this range)

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Coordinates are those of the Sirpur group; the attribution to Queen Vāsaṭā rests on an inscription read in secondary literature not checked here.

nodes.name: Kandarīya Mahādeva temple, Khajuraho
nodes.summary: The largest and most elaborate of the Khajuraho temples, a Śiva temple of c. 1025–1050 CE built under the Candela king Vidyādhara, whose clustered śikhara rises like a mountain range.
nodes.details: The temple’s tower is built of 84 miniature spires, and its walls carry some 870 figures, including the celebrated mithuna (erotic) groups. Its construction is placed in the reign of Vidyādhara (r. c. 1003–1035) and slightly after.

location.label: Khajuraho, Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh, India

attributes.unesco: Khajuraho Group of Monuments — inscribed 1986; UNESCO list no. 240
attributes.protection: World Heritage property managed by the ASI
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Attribution to Vidyādhara is by regnal synchronism, not by a dedicatory inscription.

nodes.name: Lakṣmaṇa temple, Khajuraho
nodes.summary: Candela temple of Vaikuṇṭha Viṣṇu completed by Yaśovarman (Lakṣavarman) and dated by an inscription of Vikrama 1011 (953/954 CE), the earliest securely dated of the great Khajuraho temples.
nodes.details: The 49-verse Sanskrit inscription, issued in the reign of Dhaṅga, gives the Candela genealogy from Nannuka and records that Yaśovarman built a temple for an image of Vaikuṇṭha that had come from Kailāsa via the Śāhi king of Kabul and the Pratīhāra Herambapāla/Devapāla. The four-headed (three visible) Vaikuṇṭha image reflects Pāñcarātra theology.

location.label: Khajuraho, Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh, India

attributes.unesco: Khajuraho Group of Monuments — inscribed 1986; UNESCO list no. 240
attributes.protection: World Heritage property managed by the ASI
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The inscription dates the temple and recounts the image’s route as told by the Candela court; the route itself is not independently confirmed.

nodes.name: Sun Temple, Konark
nodes.summary: Colossal 13th-century temple of Sūrya conceived as the Sun god’s chariot with 24 carved wheels and seven horses, built c. 1250 under the Eastern Gaṅga king Narasiṃhadeva I; the tower collapsed, and the surviving jagamohana is the largest standing part.
nodes.details: European sailors called it the “Black Pagoda”. The main vimāna, estimated at about 70 m, had fallen by the 19th century (Wikipedia notes 1837); in 1903 the jagamohana was filled with sand and sealed to stabilise it. The cause of the destruction is disputed. The wheels are often described as sundials. Inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1984.

dates.label: c. 1250 CE (reign of Narasiṃhadeva I, 1238–1264)
dates.basis: Eastern Gaṅga copper plates and regnal synchronism

dates.label: 1903 CE: jagamohana filled with sand and sealed

attributes.architecture: Kaliṅga (Nāgara: rekhā deuḷa with pīḍhā jagamohana)
attributes.unesco: Sun Temple, Konârak — inscribed 1984; UNESCO list no. 246
attributes.protection: ASI Monument of National Importance N-OR-63 (per Wikipedia); World Heritage property

nodes.name: Jagannātha temple, Puri
nodes.summary: Temple of Jagannātha with Balabhadra and Subhadrā, worshipped in wooden images periodically renewed (Navakalevara), at Puri; the present temple was begun by the Eastern Gaṅga king Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga in the 12th century, and Puri is the eastern dhāma of the Char Dham.
nodes.details: The temple chronicle (Mādaḷā Pāñji) attributes the first temple to the legendary king Indradyumna. The present tower was begun under Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga (r. c. 1078–1147/50) and is usually said to have been completed under his successors; Wikipedia’s infobox gives 1161. The annual Rathayātrā carries the deities through the town. Caitanya lived in Puri for his last two decades (1510–1533), and singing of Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda became part of the temple’s ritual. Entry is restricted to Hindus.

dates.label: First temple built by King Indradyumna (Mādaḷā Pāñji / Puruṣottama-māhātmya tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

nodes.name: Liṅgarāja temple, Bhubaneswar
nodes.summary: The largest temple of Bhubaneswar (Ekāmra Kṣetra), an 11th-century Kaliṅga-style Śiva temple whose deity is worshipped as Harihara (Śiva–Viṣṇu); it is attributed to Somavaṃśī kings with later Gaṅga additions.
nodes.details: Some accounts credit Yayāti I (11th c.); others the Somavaṃśī line generally, with the bhoga-maṇḍapa and other halls added under the Eastern Gaṅgas, during whose rule the Jagannātha cult gained prominence. The Bindusāgara tank lies to the north. Entry is restricted to Hindus.

dates.label: 11th c. CE (main deuḷa)
dates.basis: style and regnal attribution to Somavaṃśī kings

dates.label: 12th–13th c. CE halls added under the Eastern Gaṅgas

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Royal attributions vary in the sources; the temple documents a Śaiva–Vaiṣṇava (Harihara) theology in 11th–13th-c. Odisha.

nodes.name: Mukteśvara temple, Bhubaneswar
nodes.summary: Small 10th-century Kaliṅga-style Śiva temple in Bhubaneswar (c. 950–975 CE), celebrated for its arched gateway (toraṇa) and refined carving, marking the transition to the mature Odishan style.
nodes.details: Most scholars place it after the Paraśurāmeśvara and before the Brahmeśvara (1060 CE); Panigrahi proposed c. 966 under the Somavaṃśī Yayāti I.

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Undated by inscription; the date is stylistic.

nodes.name: Causaṭh Yoginī temple, Hirapur
nodes.summary: Small circular, roofless (hypaethral) sandstone shrine near Bhubaneswar housing images of sixty-four yoginīs around a central Kālī/Mahāmāyā, dated to the 9th century and associated with the Bhauma-Kara queen Hīrādevī.
nodes.details: Circular yoginī temples are a distinctive tantric building type found in Odisha and central India. The attribution to Hīrādevī (c. 864 CE per Wikipedia) is traditional.

dates.label: 9th–10th c. CE (traditionally c. 864 under Queen Hīrādevī)

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Evidence of a tantric yoginī cult in early medieval Odisha; patronage by Hīrādevī is not inscriptionally confirmed here.

nodes.name: Kāmākhyā temple, Guwahati
nodes.summary: Principal temple of the goddess Kāmākhyā on Nīlācala hill, Guwahati, where an aniconic yoni-shaped stone in a cave is worshipped; one of the oldest centres of tantric Śākta practice and a Śakti Pīṭha in all major lists. The present temple was rebuilt in 1565 under the Koch king Naranārāyaṇa by his brother Chilarai.
nodes.details: The stone base of an earlier Kāmarūpa-period temple survives; a brick śikhara was added in the Koch reconstruction. An inscription in the temple records that Chilarai built it in 1565 in the reign of Naranārāyaṇa (Wikipedia, citing Sarkar 1992). The older story that the Bengal general Kālāpāhāḍ destroyed the temple is now doubted, since the reconstruction precedes his campaign; destruction during Husain Shah’s invasion of Kamata (1498) is suggested instead. The Ahom kings were later patrons. The annual Ambuvācī Melā marks the goddess’s menstruation.

dates.label: Place where Satī’s yoni fell (Kālikā Purāṇa and pīṭha traditions)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 1565 CE reconstruction by Chilarai under Naranārāyaṇa
dates.basis: dated temple inscription (as cited by Wikipedia from Sarkar 1992)

attributes.architecture: Nīlācala type (Kāmarūpa stone base with Koch brick superstructure)
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The 1565 inscription dates the rebuilding; the site’s older history is inferred from the earlier stone base and Kāmarūpa-period records. The pīṭha identity is mythic tradition.

nodes.name: Kālīghāṭ temple, Kolkata
nodes.summary: Temple of Kālī on the old course of the Hooghly (Ādi Gaṅgā) in Kolkata, counted as a Śakti Pīṭha where the toes of Satī’s right foot fell; the present building was completed in 1809 under the Sābarṇa Rāy Caudhurī family.
nodes.details: Construction of the present temple began in 1798 under Santosh Roy Chowdhury and was completed in 1809. Kālīghāṭ gave its name to a 19th-century school of popular painting.

dates.label: Toes of Satī’s right foot fell here (pīṭha tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The present building is early 19th century; earlier shrines are known only from tradition and texts.

nodes.name: Dakṣiṇeśvar Kālī temple
nodes.summary: Navaratna-style temple of Kālī as Bhavatāriṇī on the Hooghly north of Kolkata, founded by Rāṇī Rāsmaṇi and consecrated on 31 May 1855; Rāmakṛṣṇa served as its priest.
nodes.details: The complex also has twelve Śiva shrines and a Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa temple along the river.

location.label: Dakshineswar, North 24 Parganas, West Bengal, India

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: A documented 19th-century foundation; included as a modern reference point for Bengal Śākta temple building.

nodes.name: Viṣṇupada temple, Gaya
nodes.summary: Temple at Gaya enshrining a footprint of Viṣṇu in basalt, central to the śrāddha rites for ancestors performed at Gaya; the present temple was rebuilt in 1787 by Ahilyābāī Holkar.
nodes.details: Temple tradition links the site to Viṣṇu’s subduing of the demon Gayāsura. Gaya as a place of ancestral rites is described in the Gayā-māhātmya sections of the Vāyu Purāṇa.

dates.label: Viṣṇu pressed the demon Gayāsura underground, leaving his footprint (Gayā-māhātmya tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The present temple is 18th century; the footprint’s cult is older but undated here.

nodes.name: Baidyanātha temple, Deoghar
nodes.summary: Complex of 22 temples at Deoghar in Jharkhand, the most widely accepted claimant to the Vaidyanātha jyotirliṅga and also claimed as a Śakti Pīṭha; the month of Śrāvaṇa brings very large kāṃvaṛ pilgrimages carrying Gaṅgā water.
nodes.details: Local tradition links the liṅga to Rāvaṇa, who was carrying it to Laṅkā when he was obliged to set it down here. The dates of the present buildings were not verified in this pass.

dates.label: Liṅga set down by Rāvaṇa on his way to Laṅkā (local tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: present main temple probably 16th–18th c. (not verified)

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The jyotirliṅga identification is contested with Parli (Maharashtra) and Baijnath (Himachal); the building date is unverified.
openQuestions: Date and patron of the present main temple.

nodes.name: Kāśī Viśvanātha temple, Varanasi
nodes.summary: Temple of Śiva as Viśvanātha (Viśveśvara), “Lord of the Universe”, at Varanasi, one of the twelve jyotirliṅgas; the present temple was built in 1780 by Ahilyābāī Holkar on a site adjacent to the earlier temple.
nodes.details: The temple has been rebuilt several times. A reconstruction associated with Rāja Todar Mal in 1585 was demolished on the order of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb in 1669, and the Gyānvāpī mosque stands on that site. Ahilyābāī Holkar of Indore built the present temple nearby in 1780, and in 1835 Mahārājā Ranjit Singh donated gold to plate its tower. A large redevelopment, the Kashi Vishwanath Dham corridor linking the temple to the Gaṅgā, was inaugurated on 13 December 2021. The temple is administered by the Shri Kashi Vishwanath Temple Trust under the Government of Uttar Pradesh.

dates.label: Kāśī as Śiva’s eternal city, never abandoned by him (Kāśī-khaṇḍa tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The present fabric is 18th century; the antiquity of Viśveśvara worship is attested by texts and earlier rebuildings, not by the standing building.

nodes.name: Somanātha temple, Prabhas Patan
nodes.summary: Seashore Śiva temple at Prabhāsa Pāṭan, first of the twelve jyotirliṅgas in the Śiva Purāṇa list; repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt, the present temple in Māru-Gurjara (Cālukya) style was completed in 1951.
nodes.details: Mahmud of Ghazni raided the temple in January 1026 during the reign of the Caulukya king Bhīma I, an event remembered very differently in Persian, Sanskrit and Jain sources, as Romila Thapar has shown. The temple was rebuilt and damaged several more times; Ahilyābāī Holkar built a separate temple nearby in 1783. After Independence, reconstruction on the old site was initiated by Vallabhbhai Patel, and the new temple was inaugurated in May 1951 by President Rajendra Prasad. It is managed by the Shree Somnath Trust.

dates.label: Liṅga established by Soma (the Moon) to be freed from Dakṣa’s curse (Śiva Purāṇa / Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

nodes.name: Dvārakādhīśa temple, Dwarka
nodes.summary: Temple of Kṛṣṇa as “King of Dvārakā” at Dwarka on the Gujarat coast, the western dhāma of the Char Dham and a Divya Deśam; the present five-storeyed structure dates from the 15th–16th centuries.
nodes.details: Tradition holds that the first shrine was built by Vajranābha, Kṛṣṇa’s great-grandson, over Kṛṣṇa’s palace. Archaeological work near the temple has found earlier occupation, and offshore explorations have been interpreted by some as Kṛṣṇa’s submerged city, a claim not accepted by most archaeologists. The Dvārakā Śāradā Pīṭha maṭha is associated with Śaṅkara in tradition.

nodes.name: Nāgeśvara temple, Dwarka
nodes.summary: Śiva temple between Dwarka and Bet Dwarka promoted as the Nāgeśvara jyotirliṅga, one of three competing claimants (with Aundha in Maharashtra and Jageshwar in Uttarakhand).
nodes.details: The present temple with its large seated Śiva statue is largely a late-20th-century reconstruction (not precisely dated in this pass). The Śiva Purāṇa places Nāgeśa in the Dārukā forest, whose location is disputed.

dates.label: Śiva protected his devotee Supriya from the demon Dāruka in the Dārukā forest (Śiva Purāṇa)

nodes.name: Sun temple, Modhera
nodes.summary: Caulukya (Solaṅkī) temple of Sūrya at Modhera with a stepped tank (Sūrya Kuṇḍa) and a detached dance hall; its shrine was built in the reign of Bhīma I, shortly after 1026–27 CE.
nodes.details: An upside-down inscription “Vikrama Saṃvat 1083” (1026–27 CE), carelessly incised on a block of the cella’s western wall, is the only date found; because it is inverted it is taken as evidence that the cella was destroyed and reconstructed, and the date coincides with Mahmud of Ghazni’s campaign in Gujarat. The dance hall and tank were added later, perhaps under Karṇa I. The temple is ASI-protected and not in worship.

nodes.name: Mahākāleśvara temple, Ujjain
nodes.summary: Jyotirliṅga temple of Śiva as Mahākāla in Ujjain, whose south-facing (dakṣiṇāmūrti) liṅga is worshipped with the dawn bhasma-ārati; the present temple is an 18th-century Marāṭhā-period reconstruction.
nodes.details: Ujjain’s Mahākāla is celebrated in classical Sanskrit literature, including Kālidāsa’s Meghadūta. The earlier temple complex was destroyed by Iltutmish during his raid of 1234–35. It was rebuilt under Marāṭhā rule in the 18th century, credited by Wikipedia to the diwan Rāmacandra Sukthankar of the Śinde (Scindia) administration. A large precinct development (Mahakal Lok) was opened in 2022.

nodes.name: Oṃkāreśvara temple
nodes.summary: Jyotirliṅga temple on the island of Māndhātā in the Narmadā, whose island is said to resemble the syllable Om; the jyotirliṅga is shared in tradition with the Amaleśvara (Mamaleśvara) temple on the south bank.
nodes.details: Wikipedia states the temple was built by Paramāra kings in the 11th century and rebuilt by the Holkars in the 18th century. The Śiva Purāṇa’s list names “Oṃkāre Parameśvaram”, read by some as the Amaleśvara shrine.

nodes.name: Bhojeśvara temple, Bhojpur
nodes.summary: Unfinished 11th-century Śiva temple at Bhojpur near Bhopal attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja, housing one of the largest liṅgas in India; construction drawings engraved on the surrounding rock show how the temple was to be completed.
nodes.details: Because the temple was never completed it has no dedicatory inscription; the attribution to Bhoja (r. c. 1010–1055) rests on the town’s name and context. The engraved architectural drawings and the earthen ramp used to raise stones make it an important document of medieval building technique.

location.label: Bhojpur, Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh, India

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Attribution to Bhoja is circumstantial; the site documents construction technique.

nodes.name: Brahmā temple, Pushkar
nodes.summary: Temple of Brahmā beside the sacred lake of Puṣkara in Rajasthan, among the very few temples in India dedicated to Brahmā; the present structure dates from the 14th century with later rebuilding.
nodes.details: Puṣkara is praised as a tīrtha in the Mahābhārata, and the Padma Purāṇa tells of Brahmā’s sacrifice there. Temple tradition says that Sāvitrī cursed Brahmā to be worshipped only at Puṣkara after he took Gāyatrī as consort for the rite.

dates.label: Brahmā performed a sacrifice at Puṣkara; Sāvitrī’s curse restricts his worship (Padma Purāṇa and temple tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The building is late medieval; the lake’s sanctity is attested much earlier in texts.

nodes.name: Rām Mandir, Ayodhya
nodes.summary: Temple of Rāma in Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, built in the Nāgara (Māru-Gurjara) style after the Supreme Court of India’s judgment of 9 November 2019 and consecrated (prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā) on 22 January 2024; many Hindus regard the site as Rāma’s birthplace (Rāma Janmabhūmi).
nodes.details:
The site was previously occupied by the Babri Masjid, a mosque built around 1528–29 by a general of the Mughal emperor Babur and demolished on 6 December 1992. In its 2019 judgment the Supreme Court awarded the disputed land for the construction of a temple by a trust and directed that alternative land be allotted for a mosque (at Dhannipur). Construction under the Shri Ram Janmbhoomi Teerth Kshetra trust began after a bhūmi-pūjana in August 2020. The principal image consecrated in 2024 is the child Rāma (Bālak Rām); the earlier Rām Lallā Virājmān image is retained in the temple.

Images had been placed inside the mosque on the night of 22–23 December 1949. In its judgment of 9 November 2019 the Supreme Court held both that placement and the 1992 demolition to be illegal — describing the demolition as an egregious violation of the rule of law — decided the title dispute on the evidence of possession, and directed that five acres be allotted for a mosque.

dates.label: Site regarded by many Hindus as Rāma’s birthplace (tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: A 21st-century building; it documents contemporary religious practice. The identification of the site as Rāma’s birthplace is a matter of faith, which the Supreme Court judgment did not decide as historical fact.

nodes.name: Kedāranātha temple
nodes.summary: High-altitude stone temple of Śiva at about 3,580 m in the Garhwal Himalaya, a jyotirliṅga, one of the Chota Char Dham and the chief of the Pañca Kedāra; it survived the 2013 flash flood that devastated the town.
nodes.details: Legend credits the Pāṇḍavas with the first temple and associates Ādi Śaṅkara with its revival and with his death nearby; neither is documented. Who built the present temple, and when, is not certain. The liṅga is an irregular rock worshipped as the hump of Śiva in bull form. The temple is open only from about May to November.

dates.label: First temple built by the Pāṇḍavas seeking Śiva’s forgiveness after the war (tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

nodes.name: Badrīnātha temple
nodes.summary: Temple of Viṣṇu as Badrīnārāyaṇa at about 3,100 m on the Alaknandā, the northern dhāma of the Char Dham, one of the Chota Char Dham and a Divya Deśam; it was largely rebuilt after the 1803 Garhwal earthquake.
nodes.details: Tradition holds that Ādi Śaṅkara recovered the image from the Alaknandā and re-established worship; the chief priest (Rāval) is still a Nambūdiri brāhmaṇa from Kerala. After the earthquake of 1803 the temple was largely rebuilt with support from the King of Jaipur. It is administered with Kedarnath by the Shri Badarinath–Kedarnath Temple Committee.

dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

nodes.limits: The present fabric is 19th century; earlier phases are known from tradition and texts.

nodes.name: Gaṅgotrī temple
nodes.summary: Temple of the goddess Gaṅgā at about 3,100 m on the Bhāgīrathī, one of the Chota Char Dham; the original temple was built in the early 19th century by the Gorkha general Amar Singh Thapa.
nodes.details: Tradition places here the penance of King Bhagīratha that brought the Gaṅgā down from heaven. The glacier source at Gaumukh lies about 18 km upstream.

dates.label: Bhagīratha’s penance brought the Gaṅgā to earth here (tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: early 19th c. CE (Amar Singh Thapa), later restored

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The temple is 19th century; coordinates are those of Gangotri town.

nodes.name: Yamunotrī temple
nodes.summary: Temple of the river goddess Yamunā near the source of the Yamunā in the Garhwal Himalaya, the westernmost of the Chota Char Dham; built in the 19th century by a ruler of Tehri Garhwal and rebuilt after destruction by snow and floods.
nodes.details: Pilgrims cook rice in the hot spring Sūrya Kuṇḍa as an offering.

dates.label: 19th c. CE (Mahārāja Pratāp Śāh of Tehri Garhwal per Wikipedia), rebuilt since

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Coordinates are approximate.

nodes.name: Jageśvara temple group
nodes.summary: Group of more than 100 stone temples (7th–14th c.) in a deodar valley near Almora, claimed locally as the Nāgeśa jyotirliṅga “in the Dāruka forest”; ASI-protected.
nodes.details: Over 200 structural temples are spread over the valley clusters. Wikipedia notes that the tradition crediting Ādi Śaṅkara has no textual or epigraphic support, and that the temples were patronised and maintained by Pāśupata ascetics (including a Lakulīśa temple).

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The jyotirliṅga claim competes with Dwarka and Aundha.

nodes.name: Mārtaṇḍa Sun temple, Kashmir
nodes.summary: Ruined 8th-century temple of Sūrya (Mārtaṇḍa) on a plateau near Anantnag, built by the Kārkoṭa king Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa according to Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī and destroyed in the early 15th century.
nodes.details: The temple stood in a colonnaded courtyard with a trefoil-arched peristyle characteristic of Kashmiri architecture. Kalhaṇa (12th c.) credits Lalitāditya with the temple. Later chroniclers (Jonarāja) attribute its destruction to Sultan Sikandar (r. 1389–1413). The ruins are ASI-protected.

dates.event: recorded destruction (an event, not surviving fabric)
dates.label: destroyed under Sultan Sikandar (r. 1389–1413)

location.label: Mattan, Anantnag district, Jammu and Kashmir, India

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

image.credit: Varun Shiv Kapur from New Delhi, India (Wikimedia Commons)

nodes.limits: The patron is known from a 12th-century chronicle written four centuries later; the ruin shows Saura royal worship in 8th-c. Kashmir.

nodes.name: Paśupatinātha temple, Kathmandu
nodes.summary: Pagoda-roofed temple of Śiva as Paśupati (“Lord of creatures”) on the Bāgmatī at Deopatan, Kathmandu, Nepal’s principal Hindu shrine; worship here is attested from the Licchavi period, and the present building dates from a renovation of 1692.
nodes.details: Chronicles such as the Gopālarājavaṃśāvalī attribute an early temple to the Licchavi king Pracaṇḍadeva; Licchavi inscriptions from the 5th–8th centuries in the area attest the cult of Paśupati. The present two-tiered pagoda was renovated in 1692 after damage by termites and earthquakes (Wikipedia, citing Sharma). Cremation ghāṭs line the river, and the Guhyeśvarī temple nearby is counted as a Śakti Pīṭha. The temple’s priests (Bhaṭṭas) have long been brāhmaṇas from South India. Part of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property.

dates.label: Śiva as a deer in the Śleṣmāntaka forest; liṅga revealed by a cow (Nepāla-māhātmya tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

nodes.name: Changu Narayan temple
nodes.summary: Hilltop Viṣṇu temple east of Kathmandu that preserves the pillar inscription of the Licchavi king Mānadeva (Saṃvat 386, 464 CE), the earliest dated inscription of Nepal; the two-tiered pagoda itself is a later rebuilding, heavily damaged in 2015 and restored.
nodes.details: The site holds outstanding Licchavi sculptures of Viṣṇu (Viśvarūpa, Trivikrama, Garuḍa). The present pagoda was rebuilt after a fire around 1702 (recall; not verified online) and reconstructed with Chinese assistance after the 2015 earthquake. Part of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property.

nodes.limits: The inscription and Licchavi sculptures establish 5th-c. Vaiṣṇava royal worship at the site; the standing pagoda is early modern.

nodes.name: Jānakī Mandir, Janakpur
nodes.summary: White marble-and-stone temple of Sītā (Jānakī) at Janakpur, Nepal, built in 1910 by Queen Vṛṣabhānu of Tikamgarh (Orchha) in a Hindu–Rajput (Mughal-influenced) style; Janakpur is identified by tradition with Mithilā, Sītā’s city.
nodes.details: The temple is a focus of the Vivāha Pañcamī festival celebrating the marriage of Rāma and Sītā. The surrounding area is a protected monument zone under Nepal’s Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1956.

dates.label: Janakpur is Mithilā, where Sītā was found in a furrow and married Rāma (tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: A modern building; the identification of Janakpur with the epic Mithilā is tradition.

nodes.name: Muktinātha temple
nodes.summary: High-altitude pagoda shrine (c. 3,700 m) in Mustang, Nepal, sacred to Hindus as Viṣṇu Muktinārāyaṇa — a Divya Deśam (Sāḷagrāmam) — and to Tibetan Buddhists as Chumig Gyatsa, an abode of Avalokiteśvara.
nodes.details: The temple has 108 water spouts and a nearby spring where natural gas burns over water (Jvālā Māī). The present shrine was built c. 1814–1815, credited to Queen Subarna Prabha Devi of Nepal. The Gaṇḍakī valley below is the source of the śālagrāma fossil stones used in Viṣṇu worship.

location.label: Ranipauwa, Mustang District, Gandaki Province, Nepal

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Shared Hindu and Buddhist sanctity is documented in practice; the shrine’s fabric is early 19th century.

nodes.name: Kōṇēsvaram temple, Trincomalee
nodes.summary: Śiva temple on Swami Rock above Trincomalee bay, Sri Lanka, praised in the Tēvāram hymns of Campantar and Cuntarar; the medieval complex was destroyed by the Portuguese in 1622–1624 and a fort built from its stones, and the temple was rebuilt in 1952.
nodes.details: The temple is the foremost of the five ancient Īśvarams of Sri Lanka. The Kōṇēcar Kalveṭṭu and Tamil literature describe its patronage; the Polonnaruwa king Gajabāhu II (r. 1131–1153) is remembered as a benefactor. Some lists of the eighteen Mahāśakti Pīṭhas name “Laṅkā (Śāṅkarī)”, which tradition places at Trincomalee — an identification also contested.

dates.label: Ancient shrine linked by tradition to Rāvaṇa’s worship of Śiva (temple tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.event: recorded destruction (an event, not surviving fabric)
dates.label: 1622–1624 CE destruction by the Portuguese

nodes.limits: The present temple is a 20th-century rebuilding; early dates claimed in the infobox (6th c. BCE) rest on tradition. The Rāvaṇa association is tradition, and the epic Laṅkā is not assumed to be Sri Lanka.

nodes.name: Muṉṉēsvaram temple, Chilaw
nodes.summary: Śiva temple near Chilaw on Sri Lanka’s west coast, in existence since at least c. 1000 CE; tradition holds that Rāma worshipped Śiva here after the war with Rāvaṇa. It was destroyed twice by the Portuguese and rebuilt in 1753.
nodes.details: The complex includes a Kālī shrine popular with both Hindus and Buddhists. The Kandyan king Kīrti Śrī Rājasiṃha is credited with supporting the 1753 rebuilding (recall).

dates.label: Rāma worshipped Śiva here after killing Rāvaṇa (tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

nodes.name: Katās Rāj temples
nodes.summary: Group of Hindu temples (6th century onward) around a sacred pond in the Salt Range of Punjab, Pakistan; tradition holds that the pond formed from Śiva’s tears after Satī’s death and that the Pāṇḍavas met the Yakṣa here.
nodes.details: The name is derived from Sanskrit kaṭākṣa (“tearful eyes”). Indian pilgrims visited for Mahāśivarātri until 1965 and again from 1984. Pakistan began a restoration project in 2006.

dates.label: Pond formed from Śiva’s tears for Satī; Yakṣa-praśna of the Pāṇḍavas (tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

nodes.name: Hiṅglāj Mātā cave shrine
nodes.summary: Natural cave shrine of the goddess Hiṅgulā in the Hingol valley of Balochistan, Pakistan, counted as a Śakti Pīṭha where part of Satī’s head fell; the spring Hinglaj Yātrā draws very large numbers of pilgrims and is also revered by local Muslims as “Nani”.
nodes.details: The Hinglaj Sheva Mandali, founded in 1986, organises pilgrim services; a wall built by it in 1996 marks the entrance to the valley. The shrine is a natural cave with modern facilities rather than an architectural temple.

dates.label: Part of Satī’s head fell here (pīṭha tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

location.label: Hingol National Park, Lasbela District, Balochistan, Pakistan

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: No historic architecture is dated here; the pīṭha identity is tradition. Coordinates are approximate.

nodes.name: Prambanan (Candi Rara Jonggrang)
nodes.summary: Ninth-century Hindu temple compound in Central Java with towering shrines to Śiva, Brahmā and Viṣṇu; it is identified with the Śiva temple whose inauguration on 12 November 856 is recorded in the Śivagṛha inscription, and its balustrade reliefs tell the Rāmāyaṇa and the Kṛṣṇa story.
nodes.details: Construction was probably begun by Rakai Pikatan of Medang (a painted name “pikatan” was found on a finial of the Śiva temple) and inaugurated by his successor Lokapāla. The Śivagṛha inscription (856), edited by de Casparis, describes a Śiva temple compound and a river diversion that closely match Prambanan. The Rāmāyaṇa reliefs run on the Śiva and Brahmā temples, the Kṛṣṇāyana on the Viṣṇu temple. Prambanan Temple Compounds were inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1991.

dates.label: Legend of Rara Jonggrang, the princess turned to stone (Javanese folk tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 12 November 856 CE (Śivagṛha inscription)
dates.basis: dated Śivagṛha inscription, identified with the compound by argument

dates.label: c. 850 CE (begun under Rakai Pikatan)
dates.basis: painted name on finial and inscription

location.label: Prambanan, Sleman Regency, Yogyakarta / Central Java, Indonesia

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The identification of the Śivagṛha inscription with Prambanan is a strong scholarly argument (class 5), not an inscription found on the temple. The reliefs show a Javanese Rāmāyaṇa tradition, not the events themselves.

nodes.name: Arjuna temple group, Dieng Plateau
nodes.summary: Small Śaiva stone temples on the volcanic Dieng Plateau of Central Java (mid-7th to late 8th c.), among the oldest standing stone structures in Java; their Mahābhārata names (Arjuna, Semar, Srikandi, Puntadewa) were given much later by local people.
nodes.details: Dates for the Dieng temples range from the mid-7th to the end of the 8th century; an inscription of 809 CE is often cited for the site (not verified here).

location.label: Dieng Plateau, Banjarnegara Regency, Central Java, Indonesia

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikidata P625

nodes.limits: The Pāṇḍava names are modern and do not indicate original dedications or any link with the Mahābhārata.

nodes.name: Angkor Wat
nodes.summary: State temple of the Khmer king Sūryavarman II (r. 1113–c. 1150), built as a temple-mountain to Viṣṇu at Yaśodharapura (Angkor); its galleries carry vast bas-reliefs of the churning of the ocean, the Kurukṣetra battle and the war in Laṅkā. From the late 13th century it became a Theravāda Buddhist monastery.
nodes.details: The temple faces west, unusually, which has been linked to Viṣṇu and to a funerary function. The western gallery shows the Battle of Laṅkā (northern half) and the Kurukṣetra war (southern half); the eastern gallery shows the Churning of the Ocean of Milk (Samudra-manthana), with 92 asuras and 88 devas pulling the serpent Vāsuki; the northern gallery shows Kṛṣṇa’s victory over Bāṇa; another gallery shows Sūryavarman II himself in procession. Angkor was inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1992. Astronomical alignments proposed by Stencel et al. (1976) and Mannikka (1996) remain debated.

dates.label: c. 1113–1150 CE (reign of Sūryavarman II)
dates.basis: regnal synchronism; labelled relief of the king

dates.label: conversion to Theravāda Buddhist use from the late 13th c.

attributes.unesco: Angkor — inscribed 1992; UNESCO list no. 668
attributes.principalDeity: Viṣṇu (original); Buddhist worship since the late 13th c.
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The reliefs are a 12th-century Khmer reading of Sanskrit epic and Purāṇic narratives; they attest the reception of those texts, not the historicity of the events.

nodes.name: Banteay Srei
nodes.summary: Small, exquisitely carved red-sandstone Śiva temple near Angkor consecrated on 22 April 967 CE, unusual in having been built not by a king but by the court official Yajñavarāha; its pediments include Rāvaṇa shaking Mount Kailāsa.
nodes.details: Yajñavarāha (and Viṣṇukumāra) served as counsellors to Rājendravarman II and tutor to Jayavarman V. The temple’s Khmer name means “citadel of women”, a modern name; its original name was Tribhuvanamaheśvara. Part of the Angkor World Heritage property.

location.label: near Angkor, Siem Reap Province, Cambodia

attributes.unesco: part of Angkor (1992; no. 668)
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: Securely dated; the Rāvaṇa pediment attests the Rāvaṇānugraha narrative in 10th-c. Cambodia.

nodes.name: Preah Vihear temple
nodes.summary: Khmer Śiva temple stretched along a north–south axis on a cliff of the Dângrêk escarpment, built mainly in the 11th–12th centuries under Sūryavarman I and Sūryavarman II; the International Court of Justice ruled in 1962 that it lies in Cambodia, and it was inscribed as a World Heritage property in 2008.
nodes.details: The temple was dedicated to Śiva as Śikhareśvara (“Lord of the peak”). The 2008 inscription was followed by armed clashes on the border; the ICJ’s 2013 interpretation judgment concerned the surrounding promontory.

location.label: Choam Khsant District, Preah Vihear Province, Cambodia

attributes.unesco: Temple of Preah Vihear — inscribed 2008; UNESCO list no. 1224
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.name: Vat Phou
nodes.summary: Khmer-period Śiva sanctuary at the foot of Mount Phou Kao (Liṅgaparvata, named for its liṅga-shaped summit) in southern Laos, with structures from the 5th to the 13th century; now a Theravāda Buddhist site and a World Heritage property (2001).
nodes.details: The sanctuary was associated with the early city of Śreṣṭhapura on the Mekong. Most standing buildings date from the 11th–12th centuries. The World Heritage property is the Vat Phou and Associated Ancient Settlements within the Champasak Cultural Landscape.

attributes.unesco: Vat Phou and Associated Ancient Settlements within the Champasak Cultural Landscape — inscribed 2001; UNESCO list no. 481
attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: UNESCO number (481) from recall. The liṅga-mountain is a natural feature venerated as Śiva.

nodes.name: Mỹ Sơn sanctuary
nodes.summary: Valley of Cham brick temple-towers in central Vietnam, the principal religious centre of the kings of Champa from the 4th to the 13th century, dedicated chiefly to Śiva as Bhadreśvara; inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1999.
nodes.details: The first sanctuary is associated with the 4th-century king Bhadravarman. Many towers were destroyed by US bombing in a single week during the Vietnam War. The valley lies in former Quảng Nam province, which was merged into Đà Nẵng city in Vietnam’s 2025 administrative reorganisation.

dates.basis: architectural style and inscriptions of the standing buildings

nodes.name: Pura Besakih
nodes.summary: The “mother temple” of Balinese Hinduism, a complex of more than twenty temples terraced on the slopes of Mount Agung; in use as a Hindu sanctuary at least since the 14th century.
nodes.details: The principal Pura Penataran Agung is dedicated to Śiva, with associated temples for Brahmā and Viṣṇu. Wikipedia states it was used as a Hindu place of worship from 1284. The complex survived the 1963 eruption of Mount Agung.

dates.label: in Hindu use from the late 13th–14th c. CE

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikipedia article coordinates

nodes.limits: The terraced sanctuary may be older; the buildings themselves are frequently renewed.

nodes.name: Batu Caves temple
nodes.summary: Murukaṉ shrine in limestone caves north of Kuala Lumpur, completed in 1891 and the focus since 1892 of one of the largest Thaipūsam festivals outside India; a very tall gilded statue of Murukaṉ was unveiled beside the steps in January 2006.
nodes.details: The Tamil trader K. Thamboosamy Pillai promoted the caves as a place of Hindu worship, reportedly inspired by the resemblance of the cave mouth to Murukaṉ’s vel (spear). Its festival reflects the Tamil diaspora in Malaysia.

attributes.coordinateSource: Wikidata P625

nodes.limits: A diaspora foundation of the colonial period; it shows the reach of Murukaṉ worship, not an ancient sanctuary.

nodes.name: Naṭarāja (Śiva as lord of dance)
nodes.summary: Śiva as the king of dancers, above all in the South Indian ānanda-tāṇḍava form standardised in Cōḻa bronzes: four-armed, dancing within a ring of flames on the dwarf Apasmāra, worshipped above all at Chidambaram.
nodes.details:
Dancing forms of Śiva appear in Deccan cave sculpture from the 6th century (e.g. the many-armed dancer of Bādāmi Cave 1 and the Elephanta panel). The canonical Tamil ānanda-tāṇḍava type, with the drum (ḍamaru), fire, the abhaya gesture and the raised leg, was fixed in bronze under the Cōḻas by the 10th century. Śaiva Siddhānta theology reads the dance as Śiva’s five acts (pañcakṛtya): creation, preservation, destruction, concealment and grace.

In the Chidambaram tradition Naṭarāja dances in the golden hall before the sages Patañjali and Vyāghrapāda. The form is a Tamil and wider South Asian theological elaboration of Śiva; this dataset treats it as FORM_OF Śiva, qualified by tradition, not as a separate god.

dates.label: 6th c. CE (Deccan cave temples)
dates.basis: dated and stylistically dated cave reliefs (Bādāmi Cave 1, Elephanta)

dates.label: by the 10th c. CE (Cōḻa bronzes)
dates.basis: dated bronzes and inscriptions recording gifts of images

nodes.limits: Images and texts establish the history of the iconographic form and its theology; they say nothing about the antiquity of the idea of Śiva’s dance beyond the dated evidence.

nodes.name: Jagannātha
nodes.summary: “Lord of the world”, the deity of Puri worshipped in a stylised wooden image with large round eyes and stump arms, together with Balabhadra and Subhadrā; Vaiṣṇavas regard him as Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa, while scholars debate the cult’s tribal, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist and Jain antecedents.
nodes.details:
The images are renewed in the Navakalevara rite (most recently 1996 and 2015), when the “life substance” is transferred to new figures carved from specially chosen nīm trees, and the Daitā priests — said to descend from the Śabara chief Viśvāvasu of the temple legend — have a central role. The Indradyumna legend itself tells that the deity was first worshipped by a Śabara as Nīlamādhava.

Eschmann, Kulke and Tripathi (1978) argued that Jagannātha developed from a tribal wooden deity progressively “Hinduised” and made into an imperial Vaiṣṇava cult by the Eastern Gaṅga kings, who styled themselves the god’s deputies; nineteenth-century writers proposed Buddhist origins (relic, triratna), which most modern scholars reject. For the Gauḍīya tradition, Caitanya’s ecstatic devotion at Puri identified Jagannātha with Kṛṣṇa.
nodes.limits: The temple, rituals and inscriptions document the cult from the 12th century; its earlier origins are reconstructed and contested.
openQuestions: Which pre-12th-century references to Puruṣottama/Puri refer to the same cult?

earliestMaterial.label: begun under Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga, early–mid 12th c.; completion given as 1161 in Wikipedia’s infobox

nodes.name: The tribal (Śabara) origin hypothesis for Jagannātha
nodes.summary: The scholarly hypothesis that Jagannātha began as a wooden deity of tribal (Śabara) communities of Odisha and was progressively integrated into Brahmanical Vaiṣṇavism and royal cult, culminating under the Eastern Gaṅgas.
nodes.details: Argued in Eschmann, Kulke and Tripathi (eds.) 1978. Supporting points: the aniconic wooden images and their periodic renewal, the role of the Daitā (non-brāhmaṇa) servitors, and the temple’s own Śabara legend. Competing views: Buddhist-origin theories of the 19th century; a continuous Vaiṣṇava (Puruṣottama) cult; Jain readings. The claim concerns history, not the theology of the tradition, which regards Jagannātha as Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa.

nodes.name: The claim that the Muṇḍeśvarī temple dates to 108 CE
nodes.summary: The claim, displayed by the ASI and the Bihar State Religious Trust Board, that the Muṇḍeśvarī temple was built in 108 CE and is the oldest functioning Hindu temple in the world.
nodes.details: The claim reads the year 30 of an inscription of Mahārāja Udayasena as Śaka 30. Palaeography indicates a post-Gupta script (Neuss: c. 570–590 CE), and a Harṣa-era reading gives 636 CE; architectural historians date the surviving sculpture to the 6th–7th century and have suggested that the octagonal shrine itself is a later reconstruction.

nodes.name: Veṅkaṭeśvara
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu as Lord of the Vēṅkaṭa hill, worshipped at Tirumala in a standing four-armed image; one of the most widely worshipped forms of Viṣṇu in South India and the diaspora.
nodes.details: The hill is praised by the Āḻvārs, and the temple’s epigraphy runs from the 10th century. The Veṅkaṭācala-māhātmya tells how Viṣṇu came to the hill as Śrīnivāsa and married Padmāvatī, borrowing from Kubera for the wedding — a debt devotees help repay through offerings. Older sectarian polemics debated whether the image was originally Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Śākta or Murukaṉ; the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition credits Rāmānuja with settling its Vaiṣṇava identity.
nodes.limits: Hymns and inscriptions date the cult’s history; the descent narrative is the tradition’s own.

earliestMaterial.label: 966 CE gift of a silver image by the Pallava queen Sāmavai (earliest dated gift commonly cited)

nodes.name: Mīnākṣī
nodes.summary: The “fish-eyed” goddess of Madurai, who in the temple’s myth is born as a three-breasted Pāṇḍya princess, conquers the world and marries Śiva as Sundareśvara; she is identified with Pārvatī.
nodes.details: The myth is told in the Tiruviḷaiyāṭaṟpurāṇam and enacted at the Cittirai festival. Fuller (1984) documents the priests and ritual of her temple.
nodes.limits: A regional goddess integrated into Śaiva theology; the Pāṇḍya-princess story is temple mythology.

earliestMaterial.label: 14th c. CE restoration after Sultanate-period destruction

nodes.name: Raṅganātha
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu reclining on the serpent Ādiśeṣa, “lord of the stage (raṅga)”, worshipped above all at Srirangam on the Kāvēri.
nodes.limits: A temple-specific form; theological identity with Viṣṇu is recorded as FORM_OF.

nodes.name: Yamunā
nodes.summary: The river Yamunā personified as a goddess, daughter of Sūrya and sister of Yama, worshipped at her Himalayan source at Yamunotri and along the river, notably at Mathurā and Vṛndāvana.
nodes.limits: Thin record created to anchor the Yamunotri temple.

nodes.name: Hampi
nodes.summary: Ruined capital of the Vijayanagara empire on the Tuṅgabhadrā in Karnataka, a pilgrimage centre of Virūpākṣa–Pampā and, in local tradition, the Kiṣkindhā of the Rāmāyaṇa; the Group of Monuments at Hampi was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1986.
nodes.details: The city flourished from the mid-14th century until it was sacked in 1565 after the battle of Tāḷikōṭa. Local tradition identifies its rocky landscape with Kiṣkindhā, the monkey kingdom: Ṛṣyamūka, Mataṅga hill and the Añjanādri hill (claimed as Hanumān’s birthplace, a claim also made for Añjanerī near Nashik and Tirumala’s Añjanādri) lie around the river. The World Heritage property was on the List in Danger from 1999 to 2006.

attributes.unesco: Group of Monuments at Hampi — inscribed 1986; UNESCO list no. 241 (List in Danger 1999–2006)

nodes.limits: Archaeology documents the Vijayanagara city and its temples; the identification with Kiṣkindhā is tradition and does not locate the epic geography.

nodes.name: Adam’s Bridge (Rāma Setu)
nodes.summary: Chain of limestone shoals and sandbanks, about 48 km long, between Pamban (Rameswaram) Island in India and Mannar Island in Sri Lanka; Hindu tradition identifies it with the causeway built by Rāma’s army to reach Laṅkā.
nodes.details: Geologists regard the shoals as a natural formation of sand and coral-derived limestone shaped by sea-level change and longshore currents; claims that it is a man-made structure are treated separately (claim:rama-setu-built). The name “Adam’s Bridge” derives from Islamic tradition. The identification with Rāma’s setu is ancient in the pilgrimage tradition of Rameswaram–Dhanushkodi, but the critical text of the Rāmāyaṇa does not locate the setu by modern geography, and this dataset keeps the epic’s Laṅkā distinct from Sri Lanka.

location.label: Palk Strait between Pamban Island (India) and Mannar Island (Sri Lanka)

nodes.limits: The physical feature is natural by current geological consensus; its sanctity is a matter of tradition and says nothing about the historicity of the setu-bandha episode.

nodes.name: Rameswaram (Pamban island)
nodes.summary: Island in the Gulf of Mannar off Tamil Nadu, linked to the mainland by the Pamban bridges, home of the Rāmanāthasvāmī temple and of Dhanushkodi at its south-eastern tip, where pilgrimage tradition places the start of Rāma’s bridge.
nodes.details: Dhanushkodi was destroyed by the 1964 cyclone. The island’s pilgrimage circuit includes bathing at Agnitīrtham and the 22 wells in the temple.
nodes.limits: Island geography and pilgrimage practice; the Rāmāyaṇa associations are tradition.

nodes.name: Pāṇḍya dynasty
nodes.summary: Tamil dynasty centred on Madurai, attested from the early historic period and powerful again in the 7th–10th and 13th centuries; patrons of rock-cut and structural temples in southern Tamil Nadu.

dates.label: c. 3rd c. BCE – 14th c. CE (with interruptions)

nodes.name: Nāyakas of Madurai
nodes.summary: Telugu-speaking governors of Vijayanagara who became independent rulers of Madurai (c. 1529–1736) and rebuilt the Mīnākṣī temple on a monumental scale.

nodes.name: Hoysaḷa dynasty
