nodes.summary: Karnataka dynasty (c. 10th–14th c.) whose capitals Belur and Dvārasamudra (Halebidu) gave their name to the ornate Hoysaḷa temple style.

nodes.name: Kākatīya dynasty
nodes.summary: Telugu dynasty ruling from Warangal (c. 1163–1323), patrons of the Rāmappa and Thousand Pillar temples.

nodes.name: Caulukya (Solaṅkī) dynasty of Gujarat
nodes.summary: Dynasty ruling Gujarat from Aṇahilapāṭaka (c. 940–1244), patrons of the Māru-Gurjara temple style including Modhera and the medieval Somanātha.

nodes.name: Paramāra dynasty
nodes.summary: Dynasty of Mālava (c. 9th–14th c.) ruling from Dhārā, best known for King Bhoja.

nodes.name: Kārkoṭa dynasty
nodes.summary: Dynasty of Kashmir (c. 625–855) whose greatest king, Lalitāditya, is credited with the Mārtaṇḍa temple.

nodes.name: Koch kingdom
nodes.summary: Kingdom in western Assam and northern Bengal founded by Viśva Siṃha in the early 16th century; it rebuilt the Kāmākhyā temple in 1565.

nodes.name: Somavaṃśī dynasty of Odisha
nodes.summary: Dynasty of Dakṣiṇa Kosala and Odisha (c. 9th–12th c.) credited with early Bhubaneswar temples including the Mukteśvara and Liṅgarāja.

nodes.name: Holkar state of Indore
nodes.summary: Marāṭhā ruling house of Indore (18th c. – 1948), best known for Ahilyābāī Holkar’s temple patronage.

nodes.name: Malla dynasty of Nepal
nodes.summary: Rulers of the Kathmandu Valley (c. 1200–1769) under whom much of the valley’s surviving temple architecture was built or rebuilt.

nodes.name: Champa
nodes.summary: Cham kingdoms of central and southern Vietnam (c. 2nd–17th c.) whose royal sanctuary at Mỹ Sơn was dedicated to Śiva Bhadreśvara.

nodes.name: Kingdom of Travancore
nodes.summary: Kerala kingdom (1729–1949) whose rulers styled themselves servants of Padmanābha (Padmanābhadāsa).

nodes.name: Śilāhāra dynasty (northern Konkan)
nodes.summary: Dynasty of the northern Konkan (c. 800–1265) during whose rule the Ambarnath Śiva temple was built.

nodes.name: Pāṇḍuvaṃśīs of Dakṣiṇa Kosala
nodes.summary: Dynasty ruling from Śrīpura (Sirpur) in Chhattisgarh in the 6th–7th centuries, patrons of the brick Lakṣmaṇa temple.

nodes.name: Divya Deśams (the 108)
nodes.summary: The 108 abodes of Viṣṇu sung by the twelve Āḻvār poet-saints in the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham; 105 are in India, one in Nepal (Muktinath/Sāḷagrāmam), and two (Tiruppāṟkaṭal, the milk ocean, and Paramapadam) are beyond the earth.
nodes.details: The list is central to Śrīvaiṣṇava pilgrimage and theology. Srirangam is counted first. Most are in Tamil Nadu and Kerala; northern members include Badrinath, Ayodhyā, Naimiṣāraṇya, Mathurā and Dvārakā.
nodes.limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

nodes.name: Pāṭal Peṟṟa Talaṅkaḷ (the 276 Tēvāram shrines)
nodes.summary: The Śiva temples (275 or 276, depending on the list) praised in the Tēvāram hymns of the three Nāyaṉmār Appar, Campantar (Sambandar) and Cuntarar (Sundarar), 7th–9th c.; most are in the Kāvēri delta, with a few in Sri Lanka, northern India and the Himalaya.
nodes.details: Being “sung” in the Tēvāram is a defining mark of antiquity and sanctity in Tamil Śaiva tradition. The Sri Lankan members are Kōṇēsvaram (Trincomalee) and Kētīsvaram (Mannar); northern members include Kedarnath and Mount Kailāsa. Temples founded after the hymns (such as Thanjavur’s Bṛhadīśvara) are not on the list.
nodes.limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

nodes.name: Char Dham (the four dhāmas)
nodes.summary: Four pilgrimage “abodes” at the corners of India — Badrinath (north), Dwarka (west), Puri (east) and Rameswaram (south) — associated in tradition with Ādi Śaṅkara.
nodes.details: Three are Vaiṣṇava and Rameswaram Śaiva. The scheme is often aligned with the four maṭhas attributed to Śaṅkara (Jyotirmaṭh near Badrinath, Dvārakā, Govardhana at Puri and Śṛṅgeri — the last not at Rameswaram), a link that is traditional. Not to be confused with the Chota Char Dham of Uttarakhand.
nodes.limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

nodes.name: Chota Char Dham (Uttarakhand)
nodes.summary: Circuit of four Himalayan shrines in Garhwal — Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath — that became a mass pilgrimage after road access in the second half of the 20th century.
nodes.details: The circuit is traditionally made west to east, from Yamunotri to Badrinath. Seasonal opening runs roughly from April/May to October/November.
nodes.limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

nodes.name: Pañca Bhūta Sthalas (five element liṅgas)
nodes.summary: Five South Indian Śiva temples each identified with one of the five elements: earth (Kanchipuram Ekāmbareśvara), water (Tiruvanaikaval Jambukeśvara), fire (Tiruvannamalai Aruṇācaleśvara), air (Srikalahasti) and space/ether (Chidambaram).
nodes.details: Four are in Tamil Nadu and one (Srikalahasti) in Andhra Pradesh. Some versions give Tiruvarur rather than Kanchipuram as the earth shrine (recall; not verified).
nodes.limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

nodes.name: Āṟupaṭai Vīṭu (six abodes of Murukaṉ)
nodes.summary: Six Tamil Nadu shrines of Murukaṉ — Tirupparankundram, Tiruchendur, Palani, Swamimalai, Tiruttani and Pazhamudircholai — traditionally identified with the places named in Nakkīrar’s Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai, a guide-poem of the Pattuppāṭṭu.
nodes.details: The poem’s fifth “abode” is a general reference to Murukaṉ dancing on every hill (kuṉṟutōṟāṭal), conventionally assigned to Tiruttani, and the identification of the sixth with the modern Pazhamudircholai shrine is also traditional. Clothey (1978) analyses the network and its history.
nodes.limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

nodes.name: Rival identifications of jyotirliṅga sites
nodes.summary: The question of which modern temple corresponds to several of the twelve jyotirliṅgas named in the Śiva Purāṇa list, where the text gives only a region or an ambiguous name: Vaidyanātha, Nāgeśa, Bhīmaśaṅkara and Oṃkāra/Amaleśvara.
nodes.details: Vaidyanātha (“at the cremation ground”, citābhūmi): Deoghar (Jharkhand) is most widely accepted; Parli (Maharashtra) and Baijnath (Himachal Pradesh) are rival claimants. Nāgeśa (“in the Dārukā forest”): Nāgeśvara near Dwarka, Aundha Nāganātha (Maharashtra) and Jageshwar (Uttarakhand) all claim it. Bhīmaśaṅkara (“in Ḍākinī”): the Pune-district temple is most visited, but sites in Assam (near Guwahati) and Odisha are also claimed. Oṃkāra: the jyotirliṅga is shared in tradition between Oṃkāreśvara on Māndhātā island and Amaleśvara (Mamaleśvara) on the south bank. These are competing traditions; none can be settled by archaeology, since the list is a textual and devotional construct.

nodes.name: Sāṅkhya
nodes.subtype: darśana (one of the six orthodox schools)
nodes.summary: The dualist school that analyses reality into conscious, plural selves (puruṣa) and one unconscious, productive nature (prakṛti) made of three guṇas, which unfolds into twenty-three further principles (tattvas); liberation (kaivalya) comes from discriminating knowledge of the two.
nodes.details:
Sāṅkhya ideas appear in the Kaṭha and Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣads, in the Mokṣadharma of the Mahābhārata and in the Bhagavad Gītā before the school’s classical statement, the Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa (c. 4th–5th c. CE). The Kārikā (SK 69–71) itself names a lineage: a supreme sage (identified by commentators with Kapila) taught Āsuri, Āsuri taught Pañcaśikha, and the doctrine reached Īśvarakṛṣṇa “through a succession of pupils”; SK 72 says its seventy verses summarise the whole Ṣaṣṭitantra, a lost earlier treatise.

Kauṭilya’s Arthaśāstra (1.2.10) already lists sāṃkhya, yoga and lokāyata as the three kinds of ānvīkṣikī (investigative reasoning). Classical Sāṅkhya is non-theistic; Vijñānabhikṣu (16th c.) argued that Kapila admitted God. The Brahma Sūtra (2.1.1–3; 2.2.1–10) and Śaṅkara criticise it as the chief rival to Vedānta.

dates.label: c. 350–450 CE (Kārikā)
dates.basis: Chinese translation by Paramārtha (546–569) as terminus ante quem; doctrinal history

dates.event: first named as a branch of ānvīkṣikī
dates.label: Arthaśāstra 1.2.10 (text dated c. 1st–3rd c. CE)
dates.basis: date of the Arthaśāstra as compiled and redacted

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)

nodes.name: Yoga (Pātañjala darśana)
nodes.subtype: darśana (one of the six orthodox schools)
nodes.summary: The darśana founded on Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtra, which shares Sāṅkhya’s metaphysics of puruṣa and prakṛti but adds a special self called Īśvara and teaches the stilling of mental fluctuations through the eightfold discipline, culminating in samādhi and kaivalya.
nodes.details:
The colophons of the oldest commentary call the work “the Yoga treatise of Patañjali, an exposition of Sāṅkhya” (pātañjale sāṃkhyapravacane yogaśāstre), and the tradition counts Yoga as Sāṅkhya with God (seśvara-sāṅkhya). Philipp Maas argues that sūtras and Bhāṣya form a single work, the Pātañjalayogaśāstra, composed c. 325–425 CE; the traditional view separates the sūtra-author Patañjali from the commentator Vyāsa.

The name “yoga” is far older and broader: the Kaṭha (6.11) and Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣads and the Mahābhārata describe yoga practice, and haṭhayoga (from c. 11th c.) is a distinct later tradition.

dates.event: composition of the Pātañjalayogaśāstra (sūtra with Bhāṣya)
dates.label: c. 325–425 CE
dates.basis: quotations and doctrinal relation to Vasubandhu’s Abhidharmakośa

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Pātañjalayogaśāstra, input P. A. Maas, ed. Āgāśe 1904)

nodes.name: Nyāya
nodes.subtype: darśana (one of the six orthodox schools)
nodes.summary: The school of logic and epistemology based on the Nyāya Sūtra of Gautama (Akṣapāda), which recognises four means of valid knowledge (perception, inference, comparison and testimony), develops a theory of debate and of the five-membered inference, and holds that knowledge of the sixteen topics leads to liberation (apavarga).
nodes.details: Its classical line runs through Vātsyāyana’s Bhāṣya (c. 5th c.), Uddyotakara’s Vārttika (6th–7th c.), Vācaspati Miśra’s Tātparyaṭīkā (9th or 10th c.) and Udayana (10th–11th c.), whose Nyāyakusumāñjali is the classic argument for God (Īśvara). From Udayana on Nyāya merged with Vaiśeṣika ontology; Gaṅgeśa’s Tattvacintāmaṇi (14th c.) founded Navya-Nyāya, the “new” logic of Mithilā and Navadvīpa.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text (not proof-read); numbering of that file)

nodes.name: Navya-Nyāya
nodes.summary: The “new” Nyāya inaugurated by Gaṅgeśa’s Tattvacintāmaṇi (14th c.), organised around the four means of knowledge and developing a precise technical language of relations, limitors (avacchedaka) and absences, later centred at Mithilā and Navadvīpa (Raghunātha Śiromaṇi).

dates.label: c. 14th–16th c. CE
dates.basis: dates of Gaṅgeśa and Raghunātha Śiromaṇi

nodes.name: Vaiśeṣika
nodes.subtype: darśana (one of the six orthodox schools)
nodes.summary: The realist school of natural philosophy based on Kaṇāda’s Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, which classifies everything that exists into categories (padārthas) — substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity and inherence — and holds that eternal atoms combine to form the material world.
nodes.details: The Sūtra opens by promising to explain dharma (VS 1.1.1–2) and lists nine substances and seventeen qualities; Praśastapāda (6th c.) systematised the six categories, extended the qualities to twenty-four and opened with homage to Īśvara “the cause”. Later authors (Śrīdhara, Udayana) added absence (abhāva) as a seventh category, the form taught in Annaṃbhaṭṭa’s Tarkasaṃgraha. The Brahma Sūtra (2.2.11–17) rejects its atomism.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Nozawa Masanobu; numbering of that file)
GRETIL e-text (ed. V. P. Dvivedin, Benares 1895 (Vizianagram Sanskrit Series 6))

nodes.name: Pūrva Mīmāṃsā
nodes.subtype: darśana (one of the six orthodox schools)
nodes.summary: The school of Vedic exegesis founded on Jaimini’s Mīmāṃsā Sūtra, which defines dharma as what is known through Vedic injunction (codanā), treats the Veda as authorless and intrinsically valid, and develops rules for interpreting ritual texts that shaped Indian law and hermeneutics.
nodes.details: Śabara’s Bhāṣya (early centuries CE) is the base commentary; in the 7th c. the school split into the lines of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa (Bhāṭṭa) and Prabhākara (Prābhākara). Its interpretive maxims (nyāyas) were adopted by Dharmaśāstra commentators and by Vedānta, which calls itself the “later” (uttara) Mīmāṃsā. Classical Mīmāṃsā does not posit a creator god; Kumārila argues against an omniscient author of the Veda.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (based on B. D. Basu’s edition, Allahabad 1923–25)

nodes.name: Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā
nodes.summary: The line of Mīmāṃsā following Kumārila Bhaṭṭa (7th c.), which accepts six means of knowledge (adding postulation and non-apprehension) and teaches the intrinsic validity of cognition; continued by Maṇḍana Miśra, Pārthasārathi Miśra and Khaṇḍadeva.

nodes.name: Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā
nodes.summary: The line of Mīmāṃsā following Prabhākara (6th–7th c.), called the “teacher’s view” (gurumata), which accepts five means of knowledge (rejecting non-apprehension as separate) and explains error as non-apprehension (akhyāti); its main later author is Śālikanātha Miśra.

nodes.name: Vedānta
nodes.subtype: darśana (one of the six orthodox schools)
nodes.summary: The family of schools that interpret the Upaniṣads (the “end of the Veda”), the Brahma Sūtra and the Bhagavad Gītā — the prasthānatrayī — to explain brahman, the self and liberation; its sub-schools (Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, Bhedābheda, Dvaitādvaita, Śuddhādvaita, Acintya-bhedābheda) disagree chiefly on how brahman, selves and the world are related.
nodes.details: The Brahma Sūtra itself names earlier teachers — Āśmarathya, Auḍulomi, Kāśakṛtsna, Bādari and Jaimini — whose views it weighs (e.g. BS 1.4.20–22). Pre-Śaṅkara Vedānta, mostly lost, included Bhartṛprapañca’s bhedābheda. From the 8th c. each major school is defined by its commentary on the Brahma Sūtra.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtra text extracted from Śaṅkara’s commentary (555 sūtras); Śaṅkara’s numbering)

nodes.name: Bhedābheda Vedānta
nodes.summary: The Vedānta view that the self and the world are both different and not different from brahman, held before and after Śaṅkara by Bhartṛprapañca, Bhāskara (8th–9th c.) and Yādavaprakāśa; Nimbārka’s Dvaitādvaita and Caitanya’s Acintya-bhedābheda are later forms.
nodes.details: Bhāskara taught that brahman’s transformation into the world is real and that the difference of selves is due to limiting adjuncts (aupādhika bhedābheda). Rāmānuja’s Vedārthasaṃgraha (§59) calls the bhedābheda position “worse even than the view that brahman is ignorant” — that is, worse than Advaita.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Sadanori Ishitobi; section numbers RVas_n)

nodes.name: Viśiṣṭādvaita
nodes.summary: The Vedānta of Rāmānuja and the Śrīvaiṣṇava ācāryas, for which brahman is the personal Viṣṇu–Nārāyaṇa possessed of infinite auspicious qualities, and conscious selves and matter are real, eternally distinct modes that form his “body” (śarīra), inseparable from him as qualities from a substance.
nodes.details: Its key formula, “brahman has everything as its body” (sarvaśarīraṃ brahma), is stated in Rāmānuja’s Vedārthasaṃgraha. Yāmuna (10th–11th c.) prepared it in the Siddhitraya and Gītārthasaṃgraha; Vedānta Deśika (1268–1369) systematised it. The doctrinal school is the philosophy of the Śrīvaiṣṇava sampradāya (`trad:srivaishnava`).

dates.label: c. 11th–14th c. CE
dates.basis: dates of Yāmuna, Rāmānuja and Vedānta Deśika

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Sadanori Ishitobi; section numbers RVas_n)

nodes.name: Dvaita Vedānta
nodes.summary: The realist Vedānta of Madhva (Ānandatīrtha, 13th c.), called Tattvavāda by its followers, which teaches that Viṣṇu alone is independent (svatantra) and that five differences — God/self, God/matter, self/self, self/matter, matter/matter — are real and eternal; liberation is by Viṣṇu’s grace and selves retain graded differences even in release.
nodes.details: Madhva’s Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya (1.69–70) states the five differences (pañcabheda) and declares the world-stream real. Jayatīrtha’s Nyāyasudhā (14th c.) and Vyāsatīrtha’s Nyāyāmṛta and Tarkatāṇḍava (16th c.) made Dvaita a leading dialectical school; Madhusūdana Sarasvatī’s Advaitasiddhi answered the Nyāyāmṛta.

nodes.name: Dvaitādvaita (Nimbārka sampradāya)
nodes.summary: The Vedānta of Nimbārka and his commentator Śrīnivāsa, a form of bhedābheda in which selves and world are naturally (svābhāvika) both different from and identical with brahman, worshipped as Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā.

nodes.name: Śuddhādvaita
nodes.summary: The Vedānta of Vallabha (1479–1531), the doctrinal basis of the Puṣṭimārga: brahman, identified with Kṛṣṇa, becomes the world without undergoing change (avikṛta-pariṇāma), so the world is real and “pure” of māyā; grace (puṣṭi) and devotion are the means.

nodes.name: Acintya-bhedābheda
nodes.summary: The Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava Vedānta systematised by Jīva Gosvāmī, holding that Kṛṣṇa’s energies (śakti) — internal, external and marginal (the selves) — are simultaneously one with and different from him in a way that is “inconceivable”, i.e. beyond ordinary reasoning yet established by scripture.
nodes.details: In the Bhagavat-sandarbha Jīva writes that inconceivability means making possible what seems impossible (durghaṭa-ghaṭatvaṃ hy acintyatvam) and divides the Lord’s śakti into antaraṅgā, bahiraṅgā and taṭasthā. In the 18th c. Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa supplied the school with its own Brahma Sūtra commentary (Govinda-bhāṣya) and linked it to Madhva’s lineage, a link discussed critically by Okita.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (GRETIL e-text interleaving Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa’s ṭīkā (marked “bd:”))

nodes.name: Lokāyata (Cārvāka)
nodes.summary: The materialist school, known chiefly through its opponents, that accepts perception as the only reliable means of knowledge, denies a self surviving the body, rebirth and the authority of the Veda; its own Bṛhaspati-sūtra survives only in fragments.
nodes.details: The Arthaśāstra (1.2.10) names lokāyata with sāṅkhya and yoga as forms of ānvīkṣikī; Mādhava’s Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha (14th c.) opens with it. Ramkrishna Bhattacharya has collected and studied the fragments.

nodes.name: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
nodes.summary: Author of the Sāṃkhyakārikā, the classical summary of Sāṅkhya in about seventy āryā verses; he names himself in SK 71 as receiving the doctrine through a succession of pupils from Kapila, Āsuri and Pañcaśikha.

dates.label: c. 350–450 CE
dates.basis: Chinese translation of the Kārikā with a commentary by Paramārtha (546–569) as terminus ante quem

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)

nodes.name: Āsuri
nodes.summary: The pupil to whom “the sage” (identified by commentators with Kapila) first taught Sāṅkhya, and who passed it to Pañcaśikha, according to Sāṃkhyakārikā 70 and a quotation in the Yoga Bhāṣya (on YS 1.25).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)
GRETIL e-text (Pātañjalayogaśāstra, input P. A. Maas, ed. Āgāśe 1904)

nodes.limits: Known only as a link in the traditional lineage; no dates or works.

nodes.name: Pañcaśikha
nodes.summary: An early Sāṅkhya teacher, pupil of Āsuri in the lineage given by Sāṃkhyakārikā 70, said there to have expanded the doctrine; later tradition ascribes to him quotations found in the Yoga Bhāṣya, and he appears as a teacher in the Mahābhārata’s Mokṣadharma.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)

nodes.limits: Known only from later citations and narrative; dates unknown.

nodes.name: Vijñānabhikṣu
nodes.summary: Sixteenth-century scholar who commented on the Sāṃkhyasūtra (Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya), the Yoga Bhāṣya (Yogavārttika) and the Brahma Sūtra (Vijñānāmṛtabhāṣya), arguing that Sāṅkhya, Yoga and a bhedābheda Vedānta agree and that Kapila admitted God.

nodes.name: Patañjali (author of the Yoga Sūtra)
nodes.summary: The author named in the colophons of the Pātañjalayogaśāstra; tradition often identifies him with the grammarian Patañjali, but most scholars keep the two apart. Maas argues he composed both sūtras and Bhāṣya c. 325–425 CE.

dates.label: c. 325–425 CE (if author of sūtra and Bhāṣya)

nodes.limits: Nothing biographical is securely known; the identification with the grammarian is a separate, disputed claim (`claim:patanjali-identity`).

nodes.name: Vyāsa (author of the Yoga Bhāṣya)
nodes.summary: The name under which tradition transmits the oldest commentary on the Yoga Sūtra (“vyāsabhāṣya” in the colophons); later authors identify him with the epic Vyāsa, while Maas argues the Bhāṣya is Patañjali’s own.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Pātañjalayogaśāstra, input P. A. Maas, ed. Āgāśe 1904)

nodes.limits: A traditional attribution; not a datable historical person. Kept apart from `char:vyasa`.

nodes.name: Svātmārāma
nodes.summary: Compiler of the Haṭhayogapradīpikā (c. 15th c.), the best-known manual of haṭhayoga, which presents haṭha practices as a ladder to rājayoga.

dates.label: c. 15th c. CE
dates.basis: sources quoted in the text and its earliest citations

nodes.name: Akṣapāda Gautama
nodes.summary: The figure to whom the Nyāya Sūtra is ascribed; nothing is known of his life, and the text he is credited with is composite, reaching its final form around the early centuries CE.
nodes.limits: A traditional author; kept apart from other Gautamas (`char:gautama-ahalya`, the Dharmasūtra author).

nodes.name: Vātsyāyana Pakṣilasvāmin
nodes.summary: Author of the Nyāyabhāṣya, the earliest surviving commentary on the Nyāya Sūtra; distinct from Vātsyāyana Mallanāga of the Kāmasūtra.

dates.label: c. 5th c. CE
dates.basis: relation to Dignāga (who criticises him) and Vasubandhu

nodes.name: Uddyotakara
nodes.summary: Author of the Nyāyavārttika, a sub-commentary defending Vātsyāyana’s Nyāya against the Buddhist logician Dignāga.

dates.label: c. 6th–7th c. CE
dates.basis: responds to Dignāga; criticised by Dharmakīrti

nodes.name: Vācaspati Miśra
nodes.summary: Scholar of Mithilā who wrote standard commentaries on almost every school: the Bhāmatī on Śaṅkara’s Brahma Sūtra commentary, the Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, the Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī, the Tattvavaiśāradī on the Yoga Bhāṣya and works on Mīmāṃsā.
nodes.details: His Nyāyasūcīnibandha is dated in the year 898 of an unnamed era (“vasvaṅkavasu-vatsare”): read as the Vikrama era it gives 841 CE, the usual view; read as Śaka, 976 CE.

dates.label: fl. c. 841 CE (Nyāyasūcīnibandha dated year 898, read as Vikrama)
fl. c. 976 CE (the same year 898 read as Śaka)

nodes.name: Udayana
nodes.summary: Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika philosopher of Mithilā, author of the Nyāyakusumāñjali (the classic Nyāya proof of Īśvara), the Ātmatattvaviveka against Buddhism, and the Kiraṇāvalī on Praśastapāda; Gaṅgeśa calls him simply “the Teacher”.

dates.label: c. 975–1050 CE
dates.basis: his Lakṣaṇāvalī is dated Śaka 906 (984 CE)

nodes.name: Gaṅgeśa
nodes.summary: Logician of Mithilā whose Tattvacintāmaṇi, arranged under the four means of knowledge, founded Navya-Nyāya.

nodes.name: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi
nodes.summary: Navadvīpa logician whose Dīdhiti on the Tattvacintāmaṇi and Padārthatattvanirūpaṇa (revising the Vaiśeṣika categories) made Bengal the centre of Navya-Nyāya.

nodes.name: Annaṃbhaṭṭa
nodes.summary: Author of the Tarkasaṃgraha with his own Dīpikā, the standard primer of the combined Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, which opens by listing seven categories including absence.

nodes.name: Kaṇāda
nodes.summary: The sage to whom the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra is ascribed; Praśastapāda praises “the sage Kaṇāda” in his opening verse. His dates are unknown.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (ed. V. P. Dvivedin, Benares 1895 (Vizianagram Sanskrit Series 6))

nodes.limits: A traditional author; no biography is known.

earliestText.label: c. second half of the 6th c. CE

nodes.name: Praśastapāda
nodes.summary: Author of the Padārthadharmasaṃgraha, the systematic restatement of Vaiśeṣika that fixed its six categories and twenty-four qualities and opened with homage to Īśvara as cause.

dates.label: c. second half of the 6th c. CE

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (ed. V. P. Dvivedin, Benares 1895 (Vizianagram Sanskrit Series 6))

nodes.name: Jaimini
nodes.summary: The teacher to whom the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra is ascribed; the Brahma Sūtra cites “Jaimini” for views on ritual and on the gods (e.g. BS 1.2.28, 1.3.31, 3.4.2), while the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra cites Bādarāyaṇa (MS 1.1.5).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtra text extracted from Śaṅkara’s commentary (555 sūtras); Śaṅkara’s numbering)

nodes.limits: Kept apart from the Jaimini of epic and Purāṇic narrative (pupil of Vyāsa); identity not assumed.

nodes.name: Śabarasvāmin
nodes.summary: Author of the Śābarabhāṣya, the oldest surviving commentary on the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra, which embeds an older commentator’s (the Vṛttikāra’s) views and became the base for Kumārila and Prabhākara.

dates.label: early centuries CE (c. 3rd–5th c.)
dates.basis: after Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya, before Kumārila; relation to Buddhist idealism

nodes.name: Kumārila Bhaṭṭa
nodes.summary: Mīmāṃsā philosopher whose Ślokavārttika, Tantravārttika and Ṭupṭīkā on Śabara founded the Bhāṭṭa school; he defended the authorless Veda and the intrinsic validity of cognition against Buddhist and other critics.

nodes.name: Prabhākara
nodes.summary: Mīmāṃsā commentator, author of the Bṛhatī and Laghvī on Śabara, founder of the Prābhākara (“Guru”) school; tradition makes him Kumārila’s pupil, which modern scholars doubt.

dates.label: c. 6th–7th c. CE
dates.basis: Harisvāmin’s commentary on the Śatapatha (638 CE) discusses Prābhākara views

nodes.name: Śālikanātha Miśra
nodes.summary: The principal later Prābhākara author, whose Prakaraṇapañcikā sets out the school’s doctrines and whose Ṛjuvimalā comments on Prabhākara’s Bṛhatī.

nodes.name: Pārthasārathi Miśra
nodes.summary: Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsaka, author of the Śāstradīpikā on the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra and the Nyāyaratnākara on Kumārila’s Ślokavārttika.

nodes.name: Maṇḍana Miśra
nodes.summary: Mīmāṃsā and Advaita author of the Vidhiviveka, Bhāvanāviveka, Vibhramaviveka and the Brahmasiddhi; until the 10th c. his Brahmasiddhi was the most authoritative Advaita treatise besides Śaṅkara’s works, and Vācaspati’s Bhāmatī follows him.

dates.label: c. late 7th–8th c. CE
dates.basis: cites Kumārila; is cited by Vācaspati Miśra

nodes.name: Bādarāyaṇa
nodes.summary: The teacher to whom the Brahma Sūtra is ascribed; the Sūtra names him in the third person (e.g. BS 1.3.26; 3.4.1; 4.4.7) and the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra cites him (MS 1.1.5). Later tradition identifies him with Vyāsa.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtra text extracted from Śaṅkara’s commentary (555 sūtras); Śaṅkara’s numbering)
GRETIL e-text (based on B. D. Basu’s edition, Allahabad 1923–25)

nodes.limits: The identification with Vyāsa (`char:vyasa`) is a traditional claim recorded as an IDENTIFIED_WITH edge, not a merge.

nodes.name: Gauḍapāda
nodes.summary: Author of the Āgamaśāstra (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā), the earliest surviving systematic Advaita work, which teaches non-origination (ajātivāda) — “no self is born” — and calls duality mere māyā; tradition makes him the teacher of Śaṅkara’s teacher Govinda.

dates.label: c. 6th–7th c. CE
dates.basis: engagement with Mahāyāna (Madhyamaka and Yogācāra) thought; relation to Śaṅkara

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input P. Schreiner, based on V. G. Apte’s edition)

nodes.name: Govinda Bhagavatpāda
nodes.summary: The teacher of Śaṅkara according to Advaita tradition and the colophons of Śaṅkara’s works (“pupil of the revered Govinda”), himself a pupil of Gauḍapāda; no works of his survive.
nodes.limits: Known only from colophons and hagiography.

nodes.name: Sureśvara
nodes.summary: Direct pupil of Śaṅkara, author of the Naiṣkarmyasiddhi and of vast verse sub-commentaries (vārttikas) on Śaṅkara’s Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Taittirīya commentaries; hagiography identifies him with Maṇḍana Miśra.

nodes.name: Padmapāda
nodes.summary: Direct pupil of Śaṅkara whose Pañcapādikā (on the opening of Śaṅkara’s Brahma Sūtra commentary) became, through Prakāśātman’s Vivaraṇa, the basis of the Vivaraṇa school of Advaita.

nodes.name: Vidyāraṇya
nodes.summary: Advaita author of the Pañcadaśī and Jīvanmuktiviveka, head of the Śṛṅgeri maṭha in the later 14th c. and associated with the founding of Vijayanagara; his identity with Mādhava, brother of Sāyaṇa and author of the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha, is traditional and debated.

nodes.name: Sadānanda Yogīndra
nodes.summary: Author of the Vedāntasāra, a short manual of Advaita (late 15th c.) that became the standard introduction, teaching superimposition (adhyāropa) and its retraction (apavāda) and the fourfold qualification of the student.

dates.label: c. late 15th c. CE
dates.basis: citations of earlier Advaita works; commentaries of the 16th c.

nodes.name: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī
nodes.summary: Bengali Advaitin of Vārāṇasī, author of the Advaitasiddhi (a reply to Vyāsatīrtha’s Nyāyāmṛta), the Siddhāntabindu, the Gūḍhārthadīpikā on the Gītā and the Bhaktirasāyana, which combines Advaita with Kṛṣṇa devotion.

dates.label: c. 1540–1640 CE
dates.basis: relation to Vyāsatīrtha’s Nyāyāmṛta and Mughal-period Vārāṇasī

nodes.name: Bhāskara (Vedāntin)
nodes.summary: Bhedābheda Vedāntin whose Brahma Sūtra commentary criticises Śaṅkara and argues that brahman really transforms into the world; distinct from the astronomers Bhāskara I and II.

nodes.name: Yāmuna
nodes.summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher at Srirangam, grandson of Nāthamuni, whose Siddhitraya, Āgamaprāmāṇya and Gītārthasaṃgraha prepared Rāmānuja’s Viśiṣṭādvaita; Rāmānuja salutes him at the opening of the Vedārthasaṃgraha and the Gītābhāṣya.

nodes.name: Vedānta Deśika
nodes.summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava polymath of Kāñcī (1268–1369) who systematised Viśiṣṭādvaita (Tattvamuktākalāpa, Nyāyapariśuddhi, Śatadūṣaṇī, Rahasyatrayasāra) and is revered as the founding authority of the Vaṭakalai branch.

nodes.name: Madhva (Ānandatīrtha)
nodes.summary: Founder of Dvaita (Tattvavāda) Vedānta, from the Tuḷu country near Udupi, who commented on the Brahma Sūtra (Bhāṣya and Anuvyākhyāna), the Upaniṣads and the Gītā and wrote the Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya, teaching the reality of five differences and Viṣṇu’s supremacy.

dates.label: 1238–1317 CE
dates.basis: Mādhva tradition and inscriptions as assessed by B. N. K. Sharma

nodes.name: Jayatīrtha
nodes.summary: The “commentator” (ṭīkācārya) of Dvaita, whose Nyāyasudhā on Madhva’s Anuvyākhyāna and Pramāṇapaddhati gave the school its dialectical foundations.

dates.label: c. 1345–1388 CE
dates.basis: Mādhva tradition as assessed by Sharma

nodes.name: Vyāsatīrtha
nodes.summary: Dvaita dialectician and rājaguru at the Vijayanagara court under Kṛṣṇadevarāya, author of the Nyāyāmṛta (against Advaita), Tarkatāṇḍava (against Nyāya) and Tātparyacandrikā; patron and teacher of the Haridāsa poets Purandaradāsa and Kanakadāsa.

nodes.name: Nimbārka
nodes.summary: Founder of Dvaitādvaita Vedānta, author of the Vedāntapārijātasaurabha (a brief Brahma Sūtra commentary) and the Daśaślokī; his date is among the most disputed in Vedānta, from the 7th to the 13th c. CE.

dates.label: c. 7th c. CE
dates.basis: style of the Brahma Sūtra commentary; rejection of the Madhvamukhamardana attribution

dates.label: c. 12th–13th c. CE
dates.basis: assumed authorship of the Madhvamukhamardana; doxographic silence

nodes.name: Śrīnivāsa (Nimbārka school)
nodes.summary: Pupil of Nimbārka according to the sampradāya, author of the Vedāntakaustubha, the fuller commentary on the Brahma Sūtra that expounds Nimbārka’s Vedāntapārijātasaurabha.

nodes.name: Vallabha (Vallabhācārya)
nodes.summary: Telugu brahmin teacher who founded the Puṣṭimārga (“path of grace”) devoted to the child Kṛṣṇa as Śrīnāthjī of Govardhana and its Śuddhādvaita Vedānta; author of the Aṇubhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtra, the Subodhinī on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and the Ṣoḍaśagrantha.

dates.label: 1478–1530 CE
dates.basis: sampradāya records as converted on Wikipedia

nodes.name: Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
nodes.summary: Eighteenth-century Gauḍīya scholar at Jaipur who wrote the Govinda-bhāṣya, the school’s Brahma Sūtra commentary, and commentaries on Jīva’s Sandarbhas, and presented the Gauḍīyas as heirs of Madhva’s lineage.

dates.label: fl. 18th c.; died by 1793 CE
dates.basis: Jaipur archive document of 1793 recording his condolence ceremony

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (GRETIL e-text interleaving Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa’s ṭīkā (marked “bd:”))

nodes.name: Bhartṛhari
nodes.summary: Grammarian-philosopher (5th c.) whose Vākyapadīya teaches that the meaning-bearing word (sphoṭa) is an indivisible whole and that brahman is of the nature of the Word (śabdabrahman).

dates.label: c. 5th c. CE
dates.basis: cited by Dignāga; relation to Vasubandhu

nodes.limits: Probably distinct from the poet of the Śatakatraya; identity disputed.

nodes.name: Kauṭilya
nodes.summary: The author named in the Arthaśāstra; tradition identifies him with Cāṇakya, minister of Candragupta Maurya (4th c. BCE), while Olivelle and McClish date the surviving text to the 1st–3rd c. CE.
nodes.limits: The Maurya-minister identification is traditional; not assumed here.

nodes.name: Vijñāneśvara
nodes.summary: Jurist at the court of the Cālukya king Vikramāditya VI of Kalyāṇi, author of the Mitākṣarā on the Yājñavalkya Smṛti, whose doctrine of ownership by birth governed Hindu inheritance in most of India under colonial courts.

dates.label: late 11th – early 12th c. CE
dates.basis: reign of Vikramāditya VI (1076–1126) named in the work; Kane and Derrett differ on the exact span

nodes.name: Jīmūtavāhana
nodes.summary: Bengali jurist, author of the Dāyabhāga (part of his Dharmaratna), whose rule that heirs acquire ownership only on the death of the owner governed inheritance in Bengal.

dates.label: c. 12th c. CE (not earlier than c. 1125)

nodes.name: Medhātithi
nodes.summary: The oldest surviving commentator on the Manusmṛti (Manubhāṣya), probably Kashmirian, cited as an authority by the Mitākṣarā.

dates.label: between c. 820 and 1050 CE (c. 10th c.)
dates.basis: cites earlier commentators; cited by Vijñāneśvara

nodes.name: Piṅgala
nodes.summary: Author of the Chandaḥśāstra (Chandaḥsūtra), the Vedāṅga text on metre, whose procedures for enumerating metres (prastāra) use a binary representation of light and heavy syllables.

dates.label: c. 3rd–2nd c. BCE (approximate)
dates.basis: relation to Pāṇini and the Vedic metrical tradition

nodes.name: Lagadha
nodes.summary: The authority whose “knowledge of time” the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa says it sets out (verse 2: kālajñānaṃ pravakṣyāmi lagadhasya mahātmanaḥ).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Ṛk recension; source given as K. V. Sarma (INSA))

nodes.limits: Known only from this attribution; dates are those of the text, which are disputed.

nodes.name: Āpastamba
nodes.summary: Eponymous teacher of a Taittirīya (Black Yajurveda) school whose complete Kalpa Sūtra survives — Śrauta, Gṛhya, Dharma and Śulba Sūtras; Olivelle notes the works may have been composed within the school rather than by one person.
nodes.limits: A school-founder name; authorship by one historical person is not established.

nodes.name: Baudhāyana
nodes.summary: Eponymous teacher of the oldest Taittirīya ritual school, to whom Śrauta, Gṛhya, Dharma and Śulba Sūtras are ascribed; the Baudhāyana Śulba Sūtra states the relation of the sides and diagonal of a rectangle.
nodes.limits: A school-founder name; authorship by one historical person is not established.

nodes.name: Āśvalāyana
nodes.summary: Ṛgvedic ritual authority to whom the Āśvalāyana Śrauta and Gṛhya Sūtras are ascribed; the Kaivalya Upaniṣad opens with an Āśvalāyana asking Brahmā for the highest knowledge.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (ed. Rāmamaya Tarkaratna, The Atharvana Upanishads, Calcutta 1872)

nodes.limits: Identity of the sūtrakāra with the Āśvalāyana of the Kaivalya Upaniṣad (or of Praśna Up. 1.1, Kausalya Āśvalāyana) is not assumed.

nodes.name: Kātyāyana
nodes.summary: Name of the author of the Vārttikas on Pāṇini (3rd c. BCE) and of the Śukla Yajurveda’s Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra and Vājasaneyi Prātiśākhya; whether these are one person is uncertain.
openQuestions: Are the vārttikakāra and the sūtrakāra of the Śukla Yajurveda the same Kātyāyana?

nodes.name: Sāṃkhyakārikā
nodes.summary: Īśvarakṛṣṇa’s summary of Sāṅkhya in about seventy āryā verses — the oldest surviving systematic Sāṅkhya text — covering suffering and its removal, the three means of knowledge, the twenty-five principles, the guṇas, the plurality of selves and liberation by discrimination.
nodes.details: SK 2 judges Vedic ritual means (ānuśravika) “like the visible means”, impure and marked by decay and excess; SK 4 accepts three means of knowledge (perception, inference, reliable testimony); SK 9 argues that the effect pre-exists in its cause (satkārya); SK 18 proves the plurality of selves; SK 62 says that no self is ever bound or released — only prakṛti; SK 67 compares the liberated person who lives on to a potter’s wheel still spinning. A Chinese translation with commentary was made by Paramārtha in the 6th c.

dates.label: c. 350–450 CE
dates.basis: terminus ante quem from Paramārtha’s Chinese translation; doctrinal history

dates.event: Chinese translation with commentary by Paramārtha
dates.label: 546–569 CE

attributes.verses: 72 in the e-text used (SK_1–SK_73 numbering with variants)

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)

nodes.name: Yuktidīpikā
nodes.summary: An anonymous, detailed commentary on the Sāṃkhyakārikā, rediscovered in the 20th c., that preserves otherwise lost views of early Sāṅkhya teachers.

dates.label: c. 6th–7th c. CE
dates.basis: citations of Dignāga; relation to other Kārikā commentaries

nodes.name: Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī
nodes.summary: Vācaspati Miśra’s concise commentary on the Sāṃkhyakārikā, the most widely studied Sāṅkhya commentary in traditional teaching.

nodes.name: Sāṃkhyasūtra
nodes.summary: A collection of Sāṅkhya aphorisms ascribed by tradition to Kapila but generally dated to the late medieval period (c. 14th–15th c.), known chiefly through Vijñānabhikṣu’s Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya.

dates.label: c. 14th–15th c. CE
dates.basis: absence from earlier doxographies; first commentary by Aniruddha (15th c.)

nodes.name: Tattvasamāsa
nodes.summary: A very short list of Sāṅkhya topics (“eight prakṛtis, sixteen modifications, the puruṣa, the three guṇas …”) ascribed to Kapila, of uncertain but probably late date.

nodes.name: Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya
nodes.summary: Vijñānabhikṣu’s commentary on the Sāṃkhyasūtra (16th c.), which reads Sāṅkhya as compatible with theism and with Vedānta.

nodes.name: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali
nodes.summary: The root text of the Yoga darśana: 195 aphorisms in four chapters (samādhi, sādhana, vibhūti, kaivalya) defining yoga as the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind (YS 1.2), teaching the eight limbs (2.29) and ending with kaivalya, the isolation of pure consciousness (4.34).
nodes.details:
Counted from the GRETIL e-text (Āgāśe 1904): 51 + 55 + 55 + 34 = 195 sūtras. YS 1.7 names three means of knowledge (perception, inference, testimony); YS 1.23–27 define Īśvara as a special self untouched by afflictions, karma and its fruits, whose expression is the syllable Om; YS 2.3–5 list five afflictions headed by ignorance (avidyā), defined as taking the impermanent, impure, painful and not-self for their opposites.

Dating depends on whether the sūtras are read apart from the Bhāṣya: Maas argues both are one work of c. 325–425 CE; others place the sūtra collection somewhere in the last centuries BCE to early centuries CE. David Gordon White describes a long eclipse of the text between the 12th and 19th c. and its modern revival.

dates.label: c. 325–425 CE (with the Bhāṣya, as one work)
c. 2nd c. BCE – 4th c. CE (sūtra layer; range of estimates)
dates.basis: doctrinal parallels with Sāṅkhya and Buddhism

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtras extracted by P. A. Maas from Āgāśe’s edition (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47, 1904))

nodes.name: Yoga Bhāṣya (Vyāsabhāṣya)
nodes.summary: The oldest commentary on the Yoga Sūtra, transmitted under the name of Vyāsa; it glosses YS 1.1 by stating that “yoga is samādhi” and supplies much of classical Yoga’s doctrine.

dates.label: c. 325–425 CE
dates.basis: see Yoga Sūtra; Maas treats sūtra and Bhāṣya as one work

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Pātañjalayogaśāstra, input P. A. Maas, ed. Āgāśe 1904)

nodes.name: Tattvavaiśāradī
nodes.summary: Vācaspati Miśra’s sub-commentary on the Yoga Bhāṣya, printed with it in Āgāśe’s edition and translated by Woods (1914).

nodes.name: Rājamārtaṇḍa
nodes.summary: King Bhoja of Dhārā’s brief commentary on the Yoga Sūtra (11th c.), also included in Āgāśe’s 1904 edition.

nodes.name: Yogavārttika
nodes.summary: Vijñānabhikṣu’s sub-commentary on the Yoga Bhāṣya (16th c.).

nodes.name: Haṭhayogapradīpikā
nodes.summary: Svātmārāma’s 15th-century compilation of haṭhayoga teachings — postures, breath control, seals (mudrā) and inner sound — which presents haṭha as a means to rājayoga.

nodes.name: Nyāya Sūtra
nodes.summary: The root text of Nyāya, in five books, which opens by promising liberation from knowledge of sixteen topics — means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, doubt, debate and its faults — and defines the four means of knowledge (NS 1.1.3).
nodes.details: NS 1.1.2 traces suffering back through birth, activity and faults to false knowledge, whose removal brings release (apavarga), defined at 1.1.22 as absolute freedom from suffering. NS 1.1.10 lists desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition as marks of the self. NS 2.1.69 (2.1.68 in other numberings) grounds the Veda’s validity in that of its reliable author, “like the validity of spells and medicine”. NS 4.1.19–21 discuss God as cause. The text is composite.

dates.label: c. 2nd c. BCE – 3rd c. CE (final redaction in the early centuries CE)
dates.basis: composite text; references to Buddhist positions in books 3–4

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text (not proof-read); numbering of that file)

nodes.name: Nyāyabhāṣya
nodes.summary: Vātsyāyana’s commentary on the Nyāya Sūtra (c. 5th c.), the earliest surviving and the base of all later Nyāya exegesis.

nodes.name: Nyāyavārttika
nodes.summary: Uddyotakara’s sub-commentary on the Nyāyabhāṣya (6th–7th c.), written to defend Nyāya against Dignāga’s Buddhist logic.

nodes.name: Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā
nodes.summary: Vācaspati Miśra’s commentary on Uddyotakara’s Nyāyavārttika.

nodes.name: Nyāyakusumāñjali
nodes.summary: Udayana’s “handful of flowers of reasoning”, the classical Nyāya argument for the existence of Īśvara as creator and author of the Veda, against Mīmāṃsā, Buddhist and Cārvāka objections.

nodes.name: Tattvacintāmaṇi
nodes.summary: Gaṅgeśa’s “Jewel of Reflection on Reality” (14th c.), in four books on perception, inference, comparison and verbal testimony, the founding text of Navya-Nyāya and the object of a vast commentarial literature.

nodes.name: Tarkasaṃgraha
nodes.summary: Annaṃbhaṭṭa’s primer of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika (17th c.), written “for the easy understanding of beginners”, which lists seven categories including absence (abhāva).

nodes.name: Vaiśeṣika Sūtra
nodes.summary: The root text of Vaiśeṣika, ascribed to Kaṇāda, which opens “Now we shall explain dharma”, defines dharma as that from which prosperity and the highest good arise, and enumerates nine substances, seventeen qualities and five kinds of motion.
nodes.details: In the GRETIL e-text (316 sūtras) VS 1.1.3 grounds the authority of the Veda (āmnāya) in its being “his” word; VS 3.2.4 lists breath, blinking, life, mental motion, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion and effort as marks of the self; VS 3.2.16 argues for many selves from their distinct situations; VS 5.2.19 calls mokṣa the absence of contact and non-arising once adṛṣṭa ceases; VS 6.1.1 says the composition of sentences in the Veda presupposes intelligence. The six-category formula familiar from later Vaiśeṣika is not a sūtra in this recension; it is explicit in Praśastapāda.

dates.label: c. 2nd c. BCE – turn of the era (final form)
dates.basis: critical-edition studies; no reference to Buddhism

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Nozawa Masanobu; numbering of that file)

nodes.name: Padārthadharmasaṃgraha
nodes.summary: Praśastapāda’s systematic exposition of Vaiśeṣika (6th c.), which opens by saluting Īśvara the cause and the sage Kaṇāda, lists six categories (substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence) and counts twenty-four qualities.

dates.label: c. second half of the 6th c. CE

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (ed. V. P. Dvivedin, Benares 1895 (Vizianagram Sanskrit Series 6))

nodes.name: Mīmāṃsā Sūtra
nodes.summary: Jaimini’s sūtras in twelve books, the longest of the darśana root texts, which open “Now, therefore, the inquiry into dharma” and define dharma as a purpose known by Vedic injunction (MS 1.1.2); the bulk sets out rules for interpreting and applying ritual texts.
nodes.details: MS 1.1.5 argues that the relation of word and meaning is original (autpattika), so that the Veda is an independent means of knowledge — “according to Bādarāyaṇa”. MS 1.1.27–32 meet the objection that the Vedas bear human names by explaining such names as those of expounders (ākhyā pravacanāt, 1.1.30). MS 1.2.1 raises the purposiveness of non-injunctive passages (arthavāda). The GRETIL e-text (Basu’s edition) has 2,727 sūtra numbers.

dates.label: c. 3rd–2nd c. BCE (common estimate)
dates.basis: relation to Kalpa Sūtras and Pāṇinian grammar

attributes.sutras: 2,727 numbered sūtras in the GRETIL e-text

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (based on B. D. Basu’s edition, Allahabad 1923–25)

nodes.name: Śābarabhāṣya
nodes.summary: Śabarasvāmin’s commentary on the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra, the oldest surviving and the common base of the Bhāṭṭa and Prābhākara schools; it argues that dharma, lying in the future, cannot be known by perception or inference but only through the Veda.

nodes.name: Ślokavārttika
nodes.summary: Kumārila Bhaṭṭa’s verse exposition of Śabara’s commentary on MS 1.1, a major work of Indian epistemology covering perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison, postulation, absence, the self and the authorless Veda, with refutations of Buddhist idealism.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (partial (5.4–5.9), with Sucaritamiśra’s Kāśikā; not proof-read)

nodes.name: Tantravārttika
nodes.summary: Kumārila’s prose sub-commentary on Śabara for MS 1.2–3.8, important for its treatment of the authority of smṛti and custom.

nodes.name: Bṛhatī
nodes.summary: Prabhākara’s large commentary on the Śābarabhāṣya, the root text of the Prābhākara school.

nodes.name: Prakaraṇapañcikā
nodes.summary: Śālikanātha Miśra’s independent exposition of Prābhākara doctrine in topical chapters (prakaraṇas).

nodes.name: Śāstradīpikā
nodes.summary: Pārthasārathi Miśra’s Bhāṭṭa commentary on the whole Mīmāṃsā Sūtra, a standard reference for the school.

nodes.name: Brahmasiddhi
nodes.summary: Maṇḍana Miśra’s Advaita treatise in four chapters (brahman, reasoning, injunction, success), which locates ignorance in individual selves and admits a role for meditation and action; edited by Kuppuswami Sastri in 1937.

nodes.name: Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Āgamaśāstra)
nodes.summary: Gauḍapāda’s verses in four chapters (āgama, vaitathya, advaita, alātaśānti) on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, the earliest surviving Advaita treatise, teaching that duality is mere māyā (1.17) and that “no self is ever born” (3.48).
nodes.details: GK 2.32 states the highest truth: “there is no dissolution, no origination, no one bound, no seeker, no one desirous of release and no one released.” The fourth chapter uses Mahāyāna Buddhist vocabulary and images (the fire-brand circle); Richard King studies this Mahāyāna context.

attributes.verses: 211 in the GRETIL e-text (29 + 38 + 48 + 96); usually counted as 215

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input P. Schreiner, based on V. G. Apte’s edition)
sources.quote: na nirodho na cotpattir na baddho na ca sādhakaḥ

nodes.name: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtra
nodes.summary: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, the foundational work of Advaita Vedānta, which reads the sūtras as teaching one brahman known only from the Upaniṣads and treats the world of plurality as the product of ignorance (avidyā).
nodes.details: On BS 1.1.1 Śaṅkara argues that “then” (atha) means after acquiring the fourfold qualification — discrimination of the eternal and non-eternal, detachment from enjoyment here and hereafter, the six virtues beginning with calm, and desire for release — not after study of ritual (Mīmāṃsā): the inquiry into brahman is possible “even before inquiry into dharma”. On 1.1.3 he reads śāstrayonitvāt both ways: brahman is the source of the Ṛgveda and the other scriptures, and brahman is known through scripture. Sub-commentaries include Padmapāda’s Pañcapādikā, Vācaspati’s Bhāmatī and Govindānanda’s Ratnaprabhā.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text of the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (begins at sūtra 1.1.1; the adhyāsa preamble is not in this file))

nodes.name: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā
nodes.summary: The oldest surviving commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā, generally accepted as Śaṅkara’s, which reads the Gītā as teaching liberation by knowledge, with action as preparatory purification.

nodes.name: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka commentary the most securely authentic of his Upaniṣad commentaries; Sureśvara wrote a verse vārttika on it.

nodes.name: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, accepted as authentic by Hacker and Mayeda; it reads “tat tvam asi” (CU 6.8.7) as identity of self and brahman.

nodes.name: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Kaṭha Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: Commentary on the Kaṭha Upaniṣad ascribed to Śaṅkara and accepted as authentic by Hacker and Mayeda.

nodes.name: Commentary on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad and Kārikā ascribed to Śaṅkara
nodes.summary: The commentary on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad together with Gauḍapāda’s Kārikā transmitted under Śaṅkara’s name; its authenticity is questioned more than that of his other Upaniṣad commentaries.

sources.locator: GRETIL file header: Āgamaśāstra with commentary attributed to Śaṅkara
sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input P. Schreiner, based on V. G. Apte’s edition)

nodes.name: Upadeśasāhasrī
nodes.summary: The only independent (non-commentarial) work almost universally accepted as Śaṅkara’s, in a prose part on how to teach and a verse part of nineteen chapters; critically edited and translated by Sengaku Mayeda.

nodes.name: Vivekacūḍāmaṇi
nodes.summary: A popular Advaita verse manual on discrimination (viveka) and liberation, traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara; most scholars regard it as a later work (see `claim:vivekachudamani-authorship`).

nodes.name: Naiṣkarmyasiddhi
nodes.summary: Sureśvara’s treatise arguing that liberation is attained by knowledge alone, not by action combined with knowledge.

nodes.name: Pañcapādikā
nodes.summary: Padmapāda’s sub-commentary on the opening of Śaṅkara’s Brahma Sūtra commentary (the superimposition preamble and the first four sūtras), the root of the Vivaraṇa school.

nodes.name: Bhāmatī
nodes.summary: Vācaspati Miśra’s sub-commentary on Śaṅkara’s Brahma Sūtra commentary, which follows Maṇḍana Miśra and gave its name to the Bhāmatī school of Advaita (ignorance located in individual selves).

nodes.name: Pañcadaśī
nodes.summary: A popular Advaita manual in fifteen chapters on discrimination, illumination and bliss, ascribed to Vidyāraṇya (14th c.), with some chapters attributed by tradition to Bhāratītīrtha.

nodes.name: Jīvanmuktiviveka
nodes.summary: Vidyāraṇya’s treatise on liberation while living (jīvanmukti), which joins Advaita with yogic practice and renunciation; studied by Andrew Fort.

nodes.name: Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha
nodes.summary: A 14th-century survey of sixteen systems, from Cārvāka through Buddhism, Jainism, the Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva schools, grammar and the darśanas, ascribed to Mādhava of Vijayanagara and ordered to lead toward Advaita (which it does not itself expound).

nodes.name: Vedāntasāra
nodes.summary: Sadānanda’s short manual of Advaita (c. late 15th c.), long the usual introduction to the system, covering the qualified student, superimposition and its retraction, and the mahāvākyas.

nodes.name: Siddhāntabindu
nodes.summary: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī’s commentary on the Daśaślokī ascribed to Śaṅkara, edited by P. C. Divanji (1933).

nodes.name: Advaitasiddhi
nodes.summary: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī’s point-by-point defence of Advaita against Vyāsatīrtha’s Nyāyāmṛta, which provoked further Mādhva replies (Taraṅgiṇī) and Advaita counter-replies.

nodes.name: Aṣṭāvakra Gītā
nodes.summary: An anonymous Advaita dialogue between the sage Aṣṭāvakra and king Janaka on the self as pure witness; its date is unknown and probably late (scholarly guesses run from the 8th to the 14th c.).

nodes.name: Bhāskara’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtra
nodes.summary: Bhāskara’s bhedābheda commentary on the Brahma Sūtra (8th–9th c.), which attacks Śaṅkara’s doctrine of illusion and holds brahman’s transformation into the world to be real.

nodes.name: Śrībhāṣya
nodes.summary: Rāmānuja’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, the authoritative statement of Viśiṣṭādvaita, whose long treatment of BS 1.1.1 (the mahāsiddhānta) refutes Advaita’s doctrines of attributeless brahman and of ignorance in seven “untenabilities”.
nodes.details: Rāmānuja reads atha in BS 1.1.1 as “after the knowledge of works” (the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā), so that Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta form one continuous śāstra; brahman is the highest Person, free of all imperfection and possessed of infinite auspicious qualities (Thibaut, SBE 48). The GRETIL link to the Śrībhāṣya e-text returned “not found” on 2026-11-08; the reading here relies on Thibaut’s translation and Carman.

nodes.name: Vedārthasaṃgraha
nodes.summary: Rāmānuja’s “Summary of the meaning of the Veda”, an independent treatise that states Viśiṣṭādvaita against Advaita and Bhedābheda, opening with a salute to Yāmuna and teaching that brahman has the whole conscious and unconscious world as its body.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Sadanori Ishitobi; section numbers RVas_n)

nodes.name: Rāmānuja’s commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā
nodes.summary: Rāmānuja’s Gītā commentary, which opens with homage to Yāmuna and a long description of Viṣṇu as “husband of Śrī”, and reads the Gītā as teaching devotion (bhakti) as the means to the Lord.

nodes.name: Gītārthasaṃgraha
nodes.summary: Yāmuna’s summary of the Bhagavad Gītā in 32 verses, which Rāmānuja follows in his Gītā commentary.

nodes.name: Siddhitraya
nodes.summary: Yāmuna’s three “proofs” — Ātmasiddhi, Īśvarasiddhi and Saṃvitsiddhi — on the self, God and consciousness, foundational for Viśiṣṭādvaita.

nodes.name: Tattvamuktākalāpa
nodes.summary: Vedānta Deśika’s verse treatise on Viśiṣṭādvaita ontology (substance, non-substance) with his own commentary Sarvārthasiddhi.

nodes.name: Nyāyapariśuddhi
nodes.summary: Vedānta Deśika’s treatise on epistemology and logic from the Viśiṣṭādvaita standpoint, recasting Nyāya for Śrīvaiṣṇava use.

nodes.name: Madhva’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtra
nodes.summary: Madhva’s short commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, which reads brahman as Viṣṇu, the independent reality, and the sūtras as establishing real difference between God, selves and matter.

nodes.name: Anuvyākhyāna
nodes.summary: Madhva’s verse commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, supplementing his Bhāṣya; it opens by saluting Nārāyaṇa “whose sole body is the fullness of all qualities” and lists the five differences.

nodes.name: Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya
nodes.summary: Madhva’s verse work “Determining the purport of the Mahābhārata”, which retells the epic and the Rāmāyaṇa as teaching Viṣṇu’s supremacy and states the five real differences in its first chapter.

nodes.name: Nyāyasudhā
nodes.summary: Jayatīrtha’s massive commentary on Madhva’s Anuvyākhyāna, the dialectical centre of Dvaita scholarship.

nodes.name: Nyāyāmṛta
nodes.summary: Vyāsatīrtha’s systematic refutation of Advaita (early 16th c.), answered by Madhusūdana Sarasvatī’s Advaitasiddhi.

nodes.name: Tarkatāṇḍava
nodes.summary: Vyāsatīrtha’s “Dance of Logic”, a critique of Nyāya and Navya-Nyāya positions from the Dvaita standpoint.

nodes.name: Vedāntapārijātasaurabha
nodes.summary: Nimbārka’s brief commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, the root text of Dvaitādvaita; Ramnarace notes that its style resembles pre-Śaṅkara commentaries.

nodes.name: Vedāntakaustubha
nodes.summary: Śrīnivāsa’s fuller Brahma Sūtra commentary expounding Nimbārka’s Vedāntapārijātasaurabha; translated with it by Roma Bose.

nodes.name: Daśaślokī (Nimbārka)
nodes.summary: Nimbārka’s ten verses summarising Dvaitādvaita doctrine; not to be confused with the Daśaślokī ascribed to Śaṅkara.

nodes.name: Aṇubhāṣya
nodes.summary: Vallabha’s commentary on the Brahma Sūtra, the root text of Śuddhādvaita, completed by his son Viṭṭhalanātha.

nodes.name: Subodhinī
nodes.summary: Vallabha’s commentary on parts of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, central to Puṣṭimārga theology.

nodes.name: Govinda-bhāṣya
nodes.summary: Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa’s Brahma Sūtra commentary (18th c.), written at Jaipur to give the Gauḍīyas a commentary on the third foundation text of Vedānta.

nodes.name: Vākyapadīya
nodes.summary: Bhartṛhari’s treatise in three books on sentence and word, which opens by identifying brahman with the Word (śabdatattva) and teaches the indivisible sphoṭa.

nodes.name: Arthaśāstra
nodes.summary: The treatise on government ascribed to Kauṭilya; its account of the sciences (1.2.10) is the earliest dated list naming sāṃkhya, yoga and lokāyata as forms of ānvīkṣikī, “the lamp of all sciences”.

dates.label: 4th c. BCE (by Kauṭilya, minister of Candragupta Maurya)

nodes.name: Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya
nodes.summary: The Jain author Haribhadra’s “Compendium of the six views” (8th c.), one of the earliest doxographies; its six are the Buddhist, Naiyāyika, Sāṅkhya, Jaina, Vaiśeṣika and Jaiminīya (Mīmāṃsā) systems — not the later “six orthodox schools”.

nodes.name: Śikṣā and Prātiśākhyas
nodes.summary: The phonetic limb of the Veda: the Prātiśākhyas, each tied to the text of one Vedic school, which describe sounds, accents and the sandhi rules that convert the word-by-word recitation (padapāṭha) into the continuous text, and later manuals titled Śikṣā (e.g. the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā).
nodes.details: The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (1.2) opens its Śikṣāvallī with the topics of phonetics (sound, accent, quantity, articulation, euphony). Allen’s Phonetics in Ancient India remains the standard study of their articulatory analysis.

nodes.name: Vyākaraṇa (grammar)
nodes.summary: The grammatical limb of the Veda, whose central tradition is the Pāṇinian: Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī, Kātyāyana’s Vārttikas and Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya (the “three sages”), continued by Bhartṛhari’s philosophy of language.

nodes.name: Chandas (metrics)
nodes.summary: The metrical limb of the Veda, represented by Piṅgala’s Chandaḥśāstra, which covers Vedic and classical metres and devises combinatorial procedures for listing them.

nodes.name: Jyotiṣa (calendar and astronomy)
nodes.summary: The limb of the Veda that fixes the times of sacrifice, represented in its Vedāṅga form by the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa (Ṛk and Yajus recensions); later Jyotiḥśāstra grew into mathematical astronomy and astrology.

nodes.name: Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya
nodes.summary: The phonetic manual of the Śākala school of the Ṛgveda, ascribed to Śaunaka, which describes how Śākalya’s word-by-word text (padapāṭha) is turned into the continuous recited text.

dates.label: c. 5th–2nd c. BCE (approximate)
dates.basis: relation to Pāṇini and to Śākalya’s padapāṭha

nodes.name: Taittirīya Prātiśākhya
nodes.summary: The phonetic manual of the Taittirīya school (Black Yajurveda), notable for its detailed articulatory phonetics.

nodes.name: Vājasaneyi Prātiśākhya
nodes.summary: The phonetic manual of the Vājasaneyi (White Yajurveda) school, ascribed to Kātyāyana.

nodes.name: Śaunakīyā Caturādhyāyikā (Atharvaveda Prātiśākhya)
nodes.summary: The Prātiśākhya of the Śaunakīya Atharvaveda in four chapters, edited and translated by Madhav Deshpande (HOS 52, 1997).

nodes.name: Pāṇinīya Śikṣā
nodes.summary: A short verse manual of phonetics ascribed by tradition to Pāṇini but later than him, describing places and manners of articulation.

nodes.name: Chandaḥśāstra of Piṅgala
nodes.summary: Piṅgala’s sūtras on metre, the Vedāṅga text on chandas, whose procedures for enumerating metres of light and heavy syllables (prastāra and related operations) have been analysed as a binary system; Halāyudha’s 10th-c. commentary develops them further.

nodes.name: Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa
nodes.summary: The Vedāṅga text on time-reckoning, in Ṛk (35 numbered verses in the GRETIL e-text) and longer Yajus recensions, presenting the “knowledge of time of the great-souled Lagadha”: a five-year yuga of lunar and solar months with the winter solstice at the beginning of the asterism Śraviṣṭhā.
nodes.details: Verse 1 salutes Prajāpati “consisting of the five-year yuga”; verse 6 places the northward turn of sun and moon at the beginning of Śraviṣṭhā and the southward turn at the middle of Āśleṣā. Taken as an observation, these positions correspond to the late second millennium BCE, the basis of early datings; Pingree regarded the text as later and its scheme as related to Mesopotamian models. The extant text is generally placed in the last centuries BCE.

dates.label: final centuries BCE (extant text)
dates.basis: language and metre; relation to other calendrical texts

dates.event: epoch implied by the stated solstice positions
dates.label: c. 1400–1200 BCE (astronomical computation from verse 6)
dates.basis: back-calculation of the solstice at the start of Śraviṣṭhā

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Ṛk recension; source given as K. V. Sarma (INSA))

nodes.name: Śrauta Sūtras
nodes.summary: Manuals of the solemn (śrauta) sacrifices performed with the three fires — new- and full-moon offerings, agnihotra, soma sacrifices, the agnicayana — each belonging to a Vedic school.

nodes.name: Gṛhya Sūtras
nodes.summary: Manuals of the domestic rites performed in the household fire, including the life-cycle rites (saṃskāras) from conception to marriage and death.

nodes.name: Dharma Sūtras
nodes.summary: Prose manuals of dharma attached to Vedic schools; four survive — Āpastamba, Gautama, Baudhāyana and Vasiṣṭha — which Olivelle dates from about the 3rd c. BCE to around the turn of the era, Āpastamba being the oldest.

nodes.name: Śulba Sūtras
nodes.summary: Manuals for constructing fire altars with the cord (śulba), the earliest Indian geometry, including constructions of squares and rectangles and the relation of a rectangle’s sides to its diagonal; those of Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, Mānava and Kātyāyana survive.

nodes.name: Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra
nodes.summary: The śrauta manual of the Āpastamba school of the Taittirīya (Black Yajurveda), part of the only Kalpa Sūtra that survives complete in all four divisions.

nodes.name: Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra
nodes.summary: The oldest śrauta manual of the Taittirīya tradition, in a discursive, Brāhmaṇa-like prose.

nodes.name: Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra
nodes.summary: The śrauta manual of the White Yajurveda (Vājasaneyin) school, following the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.

nodes.name: Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra
nodes.summary: The śrauta manual for the Ṛgvedic hotṛ priest of the Āśvalāyana school, in twelve books.

nodes.name: Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra
nodes.summary: The śrauta manual of the Śāṅkhāyana (Kauṣītaki) school of the Ṛgveda, edited by Hillebrandt.

nodes.name: Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra
nodes.summary: The domestic-ritual manual of the Āśvalāyana school of the Ṛgveda, in four books, covering marriage, the rites of childhood, Vedic study and funerals.

nodes.name: Pāraskara Gṛhya Sūtra
nodes.summary: The domestic-ritual manual of the White Yajurveda school, widely followed in north India for life-cycle rites.

nodes.name: Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra
nodes.summary: The domestic-ritual manual of the Āpastamba school (Taittirīya), used with its own mantra collection (Mantrapāṭha).

nodes.name: Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra
nodes.summary: The dharma manual of the Āpastamba school, in two praśnas; it names the agreement of those who know dharma and the Vedas as authorities (1.1.1.2–3) and lists four āśramas — householder, studentship at the teacher’s house, silence (the wandering ascetic) and forest life — as equally valid paths (2.9.21.1).
nodes.details: Olivelle regards it as the oldest surviving Dharma Sūtra and notes it may have been composed within the school rather than by Āpastamba himself; it possibly comes from the region between the Godāvarī and Kṛṣṇā.

dates.label: c. 3rd c. BCE (Olivelle, approximate)
dates.basis: relative chronology of the four Dharmasūtras (Āpastamba oldest) and internal evidence

sources.locator: Dharmaśāstra — Dharmasūtras (Kane’s dates as reported by Olivelle 1999, p. xxxi)

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (based on Bühler’s edition (3rd ed. 1932); praśna.paṭala.khaṇḍa.sūtra numbering)
sources.quote: catvāra āśramā gārhasthyam ācārya.kulaṃ maunaṃ vānaprasthyam iti

nodes.name: Gautama Dharma Sūtra
nodes.summary: An independent Dharma Sūtra associated with the Sāmaveda, which opens “The Veda is the root of dharma” (1.1) and reports that some allow a choice among āśramas while the teachers recognise only the householder’s (3.1, 3.36).

dates.label: c. 2nd c. BCE (Olivelle, approximate)
dates.basis: relative chronology of the four Dharmasūtras (Āpastamba oldest) and internal evidence

sources.locator: Dharmaśāstra — Dharmasūtras (Kane’s dates as reported by Olivelle 1999, p. xxxi)

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (based on Gokhale’s edition, Pune 1910 (Stenzler numbering))

nodes.name: Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra
nodes.summary: The dharma manual of the Baudhāyana school (Taittirīya), in four praśnas of which Olivelle takes book 1 and most of book 2 as the older core; like Gautama it reports the teachers’ view that there is only one āśrama (2.6.11.27).

dates.label: c. 2nd–1st c. BCE (Olivelle, approximate; core earlier than later books)
dates.basis: relative chronology of the four Dharmasūtras (Āpastamba oldest) and internal evidence

sources.locator: Dharmaśāstra — Dharmasūtras (Kane’s dates as reported by Olivelle 1999, p. xxxi)

nodes.name: Vasiṣṭha Dharma Sūtra
nodes.summary: The latest of the four surviving Dharma Sūtras, named after the Ṛgvedic sage Vasiṣṭha but composed by unknown authors; it opens with the inquiry into dharma “for the sake of the highest good of man” (1.1).

dates.label: c. 1st c. BCE – 1st c. CE (Olivelle, approximate)
dates.basis: relative chronology of the four Dharmasūtras (Āpastamba oldest) and internal evidence

sources.locator: Dharmaśāstra — Dharmasūtras (Kane’s dates as reported by Olivelle 1999, p. xxxi)

nodes.name: Baudhāyana Śulba Sūtra
nodes.summary: The oldest surviving Śulba Sūtra, with constructions for altar bricks and the statement that the diagonal of a rectangle produces both areas produced separately by its two sides.

nodes.name: Āpastamba Śulba Sūtra
nodes.summary: The altar-geometry manual of the Āpastamba school.

nodes.name: Yājñavalkya Smṛti
nodes.summary: A concise verse Dharmaśāstra in three books — conduct (ācāra), legal procedure (vyavahāra) and expiation (prāyaścitta) — presented as the teaching of Yājñavalkya to sages; later than Manu and more systematic, it became through the Mitākṣarā the basis of Hindu law in most of India.
nodes.details: In the Mitākṣarā recension on GRETIL the three books have 369, 307 and 335 verses (1,011 in all). YSm 1.7 names five sources of dharma: śruti, smṛti, the conduct of good people, what is pleasing to oneself, and desire born of right intention. YSm 2.121 states that in land acquired by the grandfather, a corporate holding or movables, “the ownership of father and son is equal” — the verse on which Vijñāneśvara builds ownership by birth.

dates.label: c. 3rd–5th c. CE
dates.basis: relation to Manu and Nārada; legal content
dates.view: Olivelle (later part of the range); Kane (earlier)

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Mitākṣarā text, ed. N. R. Acharya, Bombay 1949)
sources.quote: bhūr yā pitāmahopāttā nibandho dravyam eva vā

nodes.name: Mitākṣarā
nodes.summary: Vijñāneśvara’s commentary on the Yājñavalkya Smṛti (late 11th – early 12th c.), best known for holding that sons acquire ownership of ancestral property by birth; colonial courts applied it as the law of inheritance outside Bengal.
nodes.details: Arguing against the view that ownership arises from partition, the Mitākṣarā (on YSm 2.114 ff.) states that “in the world, the ownership of sons and others by birth itself is well established and cannot be denied” (loke ca putrādīnāṃ janmanaiva svatvaṃ prasiddhataraṃ nāpahnavam arhati).

dates.label: late 11th – early 12th c. CE
dates.basis: names Vikramāditya VI of Kalyāṇi; cites Medhātithi and Viśvarūpa

sources.quote: loke ca putrādīnāṃ janmanaiva svatvaṃ prasiddhataraṃ nāpahnavam arhati

nodes.name: Dāyabhāga
nodes.summary: Jīmūtavāhana’s treatise on inheritance (12th c.), part of his Dharmaratna, which holds that heirs acquire ownership only when the owner dies (or renounces), so a father may dispose of ancestral property; it governed Hindu inheritance in Bengal.

nodes.name: Nārada Smṛti
nodes.summary: The only Dharmaśāstra devoted wholly to law and legal procedure (vyavahāra); it opens by explaining that litigation arose when people ceased to be wholly devoted to dharma, and organises law under eighteen titles (mātṛkā 1.19).

dates.label: c. 5th–6th c. CE
dates.basis: legal content and relation to Yājñavalkya

nodes.name: Parāśara Smṛti
nodes.summary: A Dharmaśāstra on conduct and expiation that presents itself as the law for the Kali age: “in the Kṛta age the dharmas of Manu, in the Tretā those of Gautama, in the Dvāpara those of Śaṅkha and Likhita, in the Kali those of Parāśara” (1.24); Mādhava (14th c.) wrote a major commentary on it.

nodes.name: Viṣṇu Smṛti
nodes.summary: A Dharmaśāstra framed as Viṣṇu’s teaching to the Earth, incorporating an older Dharma Sūtra of the Kaṭha school and reworked with Vaiṣṇava material; Olivelle dates the redaction to about the 7th c. CE.

nodes.name: Kātyāyana Smṛti
nodes.summary: A lost legal smṛti on procedure and evidence, reconstructed from quotations in later digests (Kane’s reconstruction is the basis of the GRETIL e-text).

nodes.name: Manubhāṣya of Medhātithi
nodes.summary: Medhātithi’s commentary on the Manusmṛti, the oldest surviving, frequently cited by later jurists; translated by Ganganatha Jha.

nodes.name: Muktikā canon of 108 Upaniṣads
nodes.summary: The list of 108 Upaniṣads given in the Muktikā Upaniṣad, where Rāma teaches Hanumān, grouped by Veda and, in modern presentations, into ten principal (mukhya), Sāmānya-Vedānta, Yoga, Saṃnyāsa, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva and Śākta Upaniṣads; it became the standard canon in South India and in modern printed collections.
nodes.details: The list is late: the Muktikā itself is a minor Upaniṣad of uncertain but probably second-millennium date, and Dārā Shikoh’s mid-17th-century Persian translation (Sirr-i Akbar) has a different selection of about fifty. Most of the 108 are much later than the principal Upaniṣads; dates range from the 1st millennium BCE (principal) to the early modern period (some sectarian ones). Upaniṣad Brahmayogin (18th c.) commented on all 108.

sources.locator: pp. 556–558 (Muktikā list, as cited on Wikipedia)

nodes.name: Yoga Upaniṣads
nodes.summary: The twenty Upaniṣads of the Muktikā list that teach yoga — breath, sound (nāda), the syllable Om, postures and, in many, kuṇḍalinī; dates are widely disputed, from Flood’s 100 BCE–300 CE for some to Bouy’s argument that the collection as transmitted in the South was redacted in the 18th c. under the influence of Nātha haṭhayoga.

nodes.name: Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads
nodes.summary: About twenty Upaniṣads on renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and the life of the wandering ascetic; Sprockhoff dates a core group (Āruṇi, Kuṇḍikā, Kaṭhaśruti, Paramahaṃsa, Jābāla, Brahma) before the 3rd c. CE, while others are medieval; nearly all have an Advaita orientation, which Olivelle links to Advaita monastic control of their transmission.

nodes.name: Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣads
nodes.summary: Minor Upaniṣads of the Muktikā list that identify brahman with Viṣṇu or his forms — Narasiṃha, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa (Gopāla), Nārāyaṇa — among them the Tāpanīya Upaniṣads; most are medieval.

nodes.name: Śaiva Upaniṣads
nodes.summary: Minor Upaniṣads of the Muktikā list that identify brahman with Śiva–Rudra, such as the Atharvaśiras and Kaivalya; most are of the first or early second millennium CE.

nodes.name: Muktikā Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A dialogue in which Rāma teaches Hanumān the kinds of liberation and lists 108 Upaniṣads, the basis of the Muktikā canon; its date is late and uncertain.

dates.label: late (second millennium CE; uncertain)
dates.basis: presupposes sectarian Upaniṣads and Rāma devotion

nodes.name: Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A late prose Upaniṣad of the Maitrāyaṇī school (Black Yajurveda) in which king Bṛhadratha is taught by Śākāyanya; it presupposes Sāṅkhya and Yoga ideas (guṇas, a sixfold yoga) and is a key witness for their early history.

dates.label: late 1st millennium BCE or slightly later

nodes.name: Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: The tenth book of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, a collection of mantras and prayers (including Nārāyaṇa and Rudra material) used in later worship; edited and translated by Jean Varenne. Its date is uncertain, usually placed after the early prose Upaniṣads.

dates.label: later Vedic, roughly the last centuries BCE (uncertain)
dates.basis: mixed mantra content; relation to the Taittirīya corpus

nodes.name: Jābāla Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: One of the oldest Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads, attached to the White Yajurveda, which allows renunciation directly from studentship, householdership or forest life and describes the paramahaṃsa ascetic.

nodes.name: Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A short Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣad describing the highest class of renouncer, the paramahaṃsa; Sprockhoff places it in the last centuries BCE or early CE.

nodes.name: Āruṇeya (Āruṇi) Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A Sāmavedic Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣad in which Prajāpati teaches Āruṇi the renouncer’s life; part of Sprockhoff’s early group.

nodes.name: Kaivalya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: An Atharvan Upaniṣad in which Āśvalāyana asks Brahmā (Parameṣṭhin) for the highest knowledge and is taught faith, devotion and meditation on the self identified with Śiva; Deussen praised its description of the realised person.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (ed. Rāmamaya Tarkaratna, The Atharvana Upanishads, Calcutta 1872)

nodes.name: Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A Śaiva Upaniṣad in which Rudra declares to the gods “I alone was first, I am and shall be”, and which identifies Rudra with all gods and beings; its “vow of the head” is associated with Pāśupata practice.

sources.quote: aham ekaḥ prathamam āsodvartāmi ca bhaviṣyāmi ca

nodes.name: Garbha Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A short Upaniṣad describing the body as made of five elements and the development of the embryo, closer to a medical text than to speculative Upaniṣads.

nodes.name: Brahmabindu Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A short verse Upaniṣad which teaches that “mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings” (verse 2).

nodes.name: Nādabindu Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A Yoga Upaniṣad describing the syllable Om as a bird whose wings, tail and head are its parts, and meditation on inner sound (nāda).

dates.label: c. 100 BCE–300 CE (Flood, for the Yoga Upaniṣads)
dates.basis: general dating of the Yoga Upaniṣads

sources.quote: akāro dakṣiṇaḥ pakṣa ukāras tūttaraḥ smṛtaḥ

nodes.name: Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A Yoga Upaniṣad that teaches a six-limbed yoga, placing concentration (dhāraṇā) after meditation (dhyāna) as the Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad does; Deussen thought it older than the Yoga Sūtra.
nodes.details: The content described here is that of the text usually called the Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad (Deussen’s “Amṛtabindu”); it is distinct from the Brahmabindu, which some lists, including the Muktikā, call Amṛtabindu.

nodes.name: Haṃsa Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A Yoga Upaniṣad on meditation on the self as the “swan” (haṃsa) and on inner sounds; a late text, known before the 17th c. since Dārā Shikoh included it.

nodes.name: Paiṅgala Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A Sāmānya Upaniṣad in which Yājñavalkya teaches Paiṅgala the Sāṅkhya-coloured stages of creation and the Advaita doctrine of liberation.

nodes.name: Subāla Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A Sāmānya Upaniṣad attached to the White Yajurveda that interprets the Puruṣasūkta and identifies Nārāyaṇa as the supreme being.

nodes.name: Vajrasūcī Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A short Upaniṣad that asks who is truly a brahmin and answers that it is not birth, body or learning but realisation of the self; a Buddhist work of the same name is ascribed to Aśvaghoṣa.

nodes.name: Nṛsiṃha-tāpanīya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad in two parts (pūrva and uttara) centred on the Narasiṃha mantra; Farquhar dated it before the 7th c. on the grounds that Gauḍapāda knew it, a dating others find early.

dates.label: before c. 7th c. CE (Farquhar); others later

nodes.name: Rāma-tāpanīya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad in two parts identifying Rāma with brahman and expounding the Rāma mantra; a late text important for Rāma-devotional (Rāmānandī) theology.

nodes.name: Gopāla-tāpanī Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad identifying Kṛṣṇa as cowherd (Gopāla) with brahman, valued by the Gauḍīya tradition (Jīva Gosvāmī commented on it); placed after the Nṛsiṃha-tāpanīya and before the 16th c.

nodes.name: Gaṇapati Atharvaśīrṣa
nodes.summary: A short Upaniṣad identifying Gaṇeśa with brahman, ātman and Om, widely recited in Maharashtra; Courtright and others date it to the 16th–17th c.

nodes.name: Śivasaṃkalpa Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A set of verses with the refrain “may my mind be of auspicious resolve” (tan me manaḥ śivasaṃkalpam astu), drawn from the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (VS 34.1–6) and circulated as an Upaniṣad.

nodes.name: Ṣaḍdarśana (the six orthodox darśanas)
