nodes.summary: The modern standard grouping of six Veda-accepting (āstika) schools in three pairs — Sāṅkhya–Yoga, Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā–Vedānta. The grouping is late: Haribhadra’s 8th-c. “six views” include Buddhists and Jains, and Nicholson traces the āstika six-fold scheme to doxographers of the 15th–16th c. such as Vijñānabhikṣu and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī.

nodes.name: Āstika and nāstika
nodes.summary: The traditional division of views into those that accept (āstika) and reject (nāstika) the authority of the Veda — or, in older usage (e.g. Pāṇini 4.4.60), those who affirm or deny the other world; Buddhists, Jains and Cārvākas are the nāstikas of later doxography.

nodes.name: Pramāṇa
nodes.summary: A means of valid knowledge. The schools disagree on their number: Cārvāka one (perception), Vaiśeṣika two, Sāṅkhya and Yoga three (SK 4; YS 1.7), Nyāya four (NS 1.1.3), Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā five, Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā and Advaita six (adding postulation and non-apprehension).

nodes.name: Prakṛti
nodes.summary: In Sāṅkhya, the single, unconscious, uncreated source of everything except consciousness — the “root nature” (mūlaprakṛti) composed of the three guṇas, which evolves into intellect, ego, mind, senses, subtle and gross elements (SK 3; 22).

nodes.name: Puruṣa (Sāṅkhya)
nodes.summary: In Sāṅkhya and Yoga, pure consciousness, the witnessing, inactive self — neither produced nor productive (SK 3) — of which there are many (SK 18); distinct from the cosmic Puruṣa of RV 10.90.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)

nodes.name: Guṇa
nodes.summary: The three constituents of prakṛti in Sāṅkhya — sattva (light, illuminating), rajas (active, stimulating) and tamas (heavy, obstructing) — which interact like the parts of a lamp (SK 12–13); in Vaiśeṣika “guṇa” means quality, a different category.

nodes.name: Twenty-five tattvas (Sāṅkhya)
nodes.summary: Sāṅkhya’s inventory of reality: puruṣa; prakṛti; and its twenty-three products — intellect (buddhi/mahat), ego (ahaṃkāra), mind, five sense and five action capacities, five subtle and five gross elements (SK 3; 22–25).

nodes.name: Satkāryavāda
nodes.summary: The doctrine that the effect pre-exists in its material cause, argued in SK 9 and shared in different forms by Yoga and Vedānta; opposed by Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika’s asatkāryavāda (the effect is a new beginning, ārambha).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)

nodes.name: Kaivalya
nodes.summary: The Sāṅkhya–Yoga name for liberation: the isolation of pure consciousness from prakṛti once the guṇas have fulfilled their purpose and resolved back into their source (YS 4.34; SK 68).

nodes.name: Samādhi
nodes.summary: Meditative absorption, the eighth limb of yoga in which the object alone shines forth “as if empty of its own form” (YS 3.3); the Yoga Bhāṣya glosses yoga itself as samādhi.

nodes.name: Aṣṭāṅga yoga (eight limbs)
nodes.summary: The eight limbs of Patañjali’s yoga (YS 2.29): restraints (yama), observances (niyama), posture, breath control, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation and absorption; the restraints begin with non-violence (2.30).

nodes.name: Kleśa
nodes.summary: The five afflictions of Yoga — ignorance, I-am-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging to life (YS 2.3) — of which ignorance is the field of the others (2.4).

nodes.name: Īśvara
nodes.summary: The Lord. The darśanas disagree sharply: Yoga defines Īśvara as a special self untouched by affliction and karma (YS 1.24); classical Sāṅkhya and Mīmāṃsā have no creator; Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika from Praśastapāda and Udayana argue for God as cause; for Advaita, Īśvara is brahman as associated with māyā; for the theistic Vedāntas, Viṣṇu or Kṛṣṇa is the supreme reality.

nodes.name: Padārtha (Vaiśeṣika categories)
nodes.summary: The Vaiśeṣika categories of what exists and can be named: six in Praśastapāda — substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence — and seven, adding absence, in later Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika (Tarkasaṃgraha).

earliestText.label: c. second half of the 6th c. CE

nodes.name: Paramāṇu (atomism)
nodes.summary: The Vaiśeṣika doctrine that earth, water, fire and air consist of eternal, partless atoms that combine (as dyads and triads) into perceptible things; criticised by the Brahma Sūtra (2.2.11–17) and by Śaṅkara.

nodes.name: Apūrva
nodes.summary: In Mīmāṃsā, the “unprecedented” potency produced by a sacrificial act that links it to a result (such as heaven) arriving later; developed by Śabara and Kumārila to explain how a completed act bears fruit.

nodes.name: Apauruṣeyatva
nodes.summary: The Mīmāṃsā doctrine that the Veda has no author, human or divine, and is therefore free of the faults that make testimony unreliable; it rests on the claim that the word–meaning relation is original (MS 1.1.5) and that Vedic names refer to expounders, not composers (MS 1.1.30).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (based on B. D. Basu’s edition, Allahabad 1923–25)

nodes.name: Māyā
nodes.summary: Power of appearance or illusion. In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (4.10) māyā is prakṛti and the great Lord its wielder (māyin); for Gauḍapāda duality is “mere māyā” (GK 1.17); in Advaita it is the inexplicable power by which brahman appears as the world; Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita reject an illusory world and read māyā as the Lord’s wondrous power.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input P. Schreiner, based on V. G. Apte’s edition)

earliestText.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

nodes.name: Avidyā
nodes.summary: Ignorance. For Yoga it is the first affliction, mistaking the impermanent, impure, painful and not-self for their opposites (YS 2.5); for Advaita it is the beginningless ignorance (identified by Śaṅkara with superimposition) through which the one brahman appears as many; Rāmānuja’s critique of its “seven untenabilities” is central to Viśiṣṭādvaita.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtras extracted by P. A. Maas from Āgāśe’s edition (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47, 1904))

earliestText.label: c. 325–425 CE (with the Bhāṣya, as one work)

nodes.name: Adhyāsa
nodes.summary: Superimposition: the appearance of one thing in another, as silver in mother-of-pearl; Śaṅkara’s preamble to his Brahma Sūtra commentary treats the mutual superimposition of self and not-self as the root of worldly experience and calls it avidyā.

nodes.name: Vivarta
nodes.summary: The Advaita account of the world as an apparent, not real, transformation of brahman (like the snake seen in a rope), contrasted with pariṇāma, real transformation, as held by Sāṅkhya and the bhedābheda Vedāntins; the term is systematised by post-Śaṅkara Advaitins.

nodes.name: Līlā
nodes.summary: Play: the Brahma Sūtra (2.1.33) answers the objection that a self-sufficient brahman could have no motive to create by saying creation is “mere sport, as in the world” (lokavat tu līlākaivalyam); Gauḍapāda (GK 1.9) mentions and rejects the view that creation is for sport, while the devotional Vedāntas make līlā central.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtra text extracted from Śaṅkara’s commentary (555 sūtras); Śaṅkara’s numbering)

nodes.name: Jīva
nodes.summary: The individual living self. For Advaita the jīva is brahman as limited by ignorance; for Viśiṣṭādvaita it is an eternal, atomic mode of brahman’s body; for Dvaita it is eternally distinct from God and from other jīvas (MBTN 1.69–70); for Acintya-bhedābheda it belongs to the Lord’s marginal (taṭasthā) energy.

nodes.name: Saccidānanda
nodes.summary: The characterisation of brahman as being (sat), consciousness (cit) and bliss (ānanda), drawing on Upaniṣadic phrases such as “brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite” (TU 2.1) and “consciousness, bliss is brahman” (BU 3.9.28); the compound itself is post-Upaniṣadic and common in later Vedānta.

nodes.name: Mahāvākyas (the great sayings)
nodes.summary: Four Upaniṣadic sentences taken by Advaita as directly teaching the identity of self and brahman — prajñānaṃ brahma (Aitareya 3.3), ahaṃ brahmāsmi (BU 1.4.10), tat tvam asi (CU 6.8.7) and ayam ātmā brahma (Māṇḍūkya 2), one from each Veda; the fourfold scheme is later than Śaṅkara, and Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita read the same sentences differently.

nodes.name: Jīvanmukti
nodes.summary: Liberation while still embodied. Sāṅkhya compares the liberated person who lives on to a potter’s wheel still turning from past impetus (SK 67); Advaita accepts it (Vidyāraṇya’s Jīvanmuktiviveka); Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita generally hold that full liberation comes only after death.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)

nodes.name: Viveka
nodes.summary: Discrimination: in Yoga, unwavering discriminating insight (vivekakhyāti) between puruṣa and prakṛti is the means of release (YS 2.26); in Advaita, discrimination of the eternal from the non-eternal is the first of the four qualifications for inquiry into brahman.

nodes.name: Sādhana-catuṣṭaya (fourfold qualification)
nodes.summary: The four prerequisites Śaṅkara names on BS 1.1.1 for inquiry into brahman: discrimination of eternal and non-eternal, detachment from enjoyment here and hereafter, the six virtues beginning with calm and self-control, and the desire for liberation.

nodes.name: Śarīra–śarīrin relation
nodes.summary: Rāmānuja’s model of the God–world relation: conscious selves and matter are the “body” of brahman, inseparable from and wholly dependent on him as a body on its soul, so that brahman “has everything as its body” (Vedārthasaṃgraha 65).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Sadanori Ishitobi; section numbers RVas_n)

nodes.name: Pañcabheda (five differences)
nodes.summary: The five real and eternal differences of Madhva’s Dvaita — between God and selves, God and matter, self and self, self and matter, and matter and matter — stated in the Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya (1.69–70) and the Anuvyākhyāna.

nodes.name: Sphoṭa
nodes.summary: The indivisible meaning-bearing unit of language, manifested by sequential sounds, central to Bhartṛhari’s Vākyapadīya and rejected by Mīmāṃsā (Kumārila) and Nyāya.

nodes.name: Bhakti
nodes.summary: Devotion or loving participation directed to a deity or teacher; Pāṇini (4.3.95–98) already forms names for devotees of Vāsudeva and Arjuna, the Śvetāśvatara (6.23) speaks of highest bhakti to god and teacher, and the Gītā, the Bhāgavata and the theistic Vedāntas make it the chief means to the Lord.

earliestText.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

nodes.name: Turīya
nodes.summary: The “fourth” state beyond waking, dream and deep sleep, identified with the self in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad (7) and elaborated by Gauḍapāda.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input P. Schreiner, based on V. G. Apte’s edition)

earliestText.label: around the beginning of the common era

nodes.name: Ahiṃsā
nodes.summary: Non-injury, listed in Chāndogya 3.17.4 among the gifts of the inner sacrifice and as the first restraint (yama) of yoga (YS 2.30); Mīmāṃsā debated whether Vedic animal sacrifice violates it.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtras extracted by P. A. Maas from Āgāśe’s edition (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47, 1904))

nodes.name: Āśrama (orders of life)
nodes.summary: The orders of life — student, householder, forest-dweller, renouncer. Olivelle shows that in the oldest Dharma Sūtras they were alternative lifelong choices (ĀpDh 2.9.21.1; GDh 3.1) and that some teachers recognised only the householder (GDh 3.36; BDh 2.6.11.27); the sequential “four stages” is a later classical scheme.

nodes.name: Saṃskāra (life-cycle rites)
nodes.summary: The rites of passage prescribed in the Gṛhya Sūtras and Dharmaśāstra — from conception and birth through initiation (upanayana) and marriage to death — whose number varies by text.

nodes.name: Vyavahāra (legal procedure)
nodes.summary: Litigation and legal procedure, the subject of the second book of the Yājñavalkya Smṛti and the whole of the Nārada Smṛti, which classifies disputes under eighteen titles (Nārada mātṛkā 1.19).

nodes.name: Dāya (inheritance)
nodes.summary: Inheritance and partition of property, on which the two classical schools of Hindu law divide: the Mitākṣarā (ownership by birth) and the Dāyabhāga (ownership on the owner’s death).

nodes.name: Brahma Sūtra 1.1.1–4 (catuḥsūtrī)
nodes.summary: The four opening sūtras of the Brahma Sūtra — “Then, therefore, the desire to know brahman”; “from which the origin etc. of this”; “because scripture is its source”; “but that, because of harmony” — on whose reading the Vedānta schools define themselves.

nodes.name: Brahma Sūtra 2.2 (refutation of other systems)
nodes.summary: The second pāda of book 2, which rejects in turn Sāṅkhya (2.2.1–10), Vaiśeṣika atomism (2.2.11–17), Buddhist schools (2.2.18–32), the Jains (2.2.33–36), the Pāśupatas (2.2.37–41) and — on Śaṅkara’s reading — the Pāñcarātra doctrine of the origin of the soul (2.2.42–45).

nodes.name: Yoga Sūtra 1.2 (definition of yoga)
nodes.summary: “Yoga is the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind” (yogaś cittavṛttinirodhaḥ); with 1.3, when it is achieved the seer abides in its own nature.

nodes.name: Yoga Sūtra 2.29–3.3 (the eight limbs)
nodes.summary: The list and definitions of the eight limbs of yoga, from the restraints (2.30) to absorption (3.3).

nodes.name: Sāṃkhyakārikā 69–72 (lineage and Ṣaṣṭitantra)
nodes.summary: The closing verses: the doctrine was taught by the supreme sage, given to Āsuri, by Āsuri to Pañcaśikha, and reached Īśvarakṛṣṇa through a succession of pupils; the seventy verses summarise the Ṣaṣṭitantra without its stories and polemics.

nodes.summary: The sixteen topics whose true knowledge leads to the highest good, the causal chain from false knowledge to suffering whose removal is release, and the four means of knowledge.

nodes.name: Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.1.1–5
nodes.summary: The opening of Mīmāṃsā: the inquiry into dharma; dharma as a purpose known by injunction; perception cannot know it; the word–meaning relation is original, so the Veda is an independent authority “according to Bādarāyaṇa”.

nodes.name: Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.1–6
nodes.summary: The opening of Vaiśeṣika: the explanation of dharma, its definition by prosperity and the highest good, the Veda’s authority as “his” word, and the lists of nine substances, seventeen qualities and five motions.

nodes.name: Gauḍapāda Kārikā 2.32 (the highest truth)
nodes.summary: “There is no dissolution, no origination, no one bound, no seeker, no one desirous of liberation and no one liberated — this is the highest truth.”

sources.quote: na mumukṣur na vai mukta ity eṣā paramārthatā

nodes.name: Arthaśāstra 1.2.10 (ānvīkṣikī)
nodes.summary: “Sāṅkhya, Yoga and Lokāyata — this is ānvīkṣikī”: the earliest dated grouping of philosophical traditions under investigative reasoning, which the Arthaśāstra calls “the lamp of all sciences”.

nodes.name: Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya 1.68–70 (the five differences)
nodes.summary: Madhva’s statement that Viṣṇu’s qualities, the difference of selves and God, of selves from each other and the world are all real, that the world-stream “endowed with five differences” is real, and that “these five differences are eternal”.

nodes.name: Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.121 (equal ownership of father and son)
nodes.summary: “In land acquired by the grandfather, in a corporate holding or in movables, the ownership of father and son is equal” — the verse at the centre of the Mitākṣarā–Dāyabhāga divide.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Mitākṣarā text, ed. N. R. Acharya, Bombay 1949)
sources.quote: tatra syāt sadṛśaṃ svāmyaṃ pituḥ putrasya caiva hi

nodes.name: The author of the Yoga Sūtra is the grammarian Patañjali
nodes.summary: A traditional identification, stated in a verse ascribed to Bhoja and in later hagiography, of the Yoga Sūtra’s author with Patañjali the author of the Mahābhāṣya (2nd c. BCE); most modern scholars treat them as different persons on grounds of date and doctrine.
nodes.details: If Maas is right that the Yoga Sūtra and its Bhāṣya form one work of c. 325–425 CE, the grammarian (c. 150 BCE) cannot be its author; supporters of the identity point to the common name and to the tradition’s threefold praise of Patañjali for grammar, yoga and medicine.

nodes.name: The Yoga Sūtra and its Bhāṣya were composed together as one work
nodes.summary: Philipp Maas’s thesis that the sūtras and the commentary ascribed to Vyāsa form a single composition, the Pātañjalayogaśāstra, by one author (Patañjali) c. 325–425 CE, rather than a root text with a later commentary.
nodes.details: Evidence cited: manuscript colophons name the whole “Pātañjala Yogaśāstra”; early authors quote sūtra and bhāṣya alike as Patañjali’s; the commentary supplies doctrine the sūtras presuppose. Bronkhorst (1981) earlier argued a similar unity. Others retain the traditional distinction of sūtrakāra and bhāṣyakāra.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Pātañjalayogaśāstra, input P. A. Maas, ed. Āgāśe 1904)

nodes.name: Maṇḍana Miśra became Śaṅkara’s pupil Sureśvara
nodes.summary: The hagiographic tradition (the Śaṅkaradigvijaya literature) holds that the Mīmāṃsaka Maṇḍana Miśra, defeated in debate by Śaṅkara, became his disciple under the monastic name Sureśvara; modern scholars generally regard the two as different authors with different doctrines.
nodes.details: Kuppuswami Sastri’s introduction to his edition of the Brahmasiddhi (1937) and Hiriyanna showed doctrinal differences between Maṇḍana’s Brahmasiddhi and Sureśvara’s works (e.g. on the locus of ignorance and on the role of action); Bader surveys the traditional accounts.

nodes.name: The Vivekacūḍāmaṇi is a work of Śaṅkara
nodes.summary: The popular attribution of the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi to Ādi Śaṅkara; most scholars of Śaṅkara (Hacker, Mayeda) regard it as a later Advaita work, because its terminology and its stress on yoga and samādhi differ from the commentaries securely by Śaṅkara.

sources.locator: Introduction (authenticity of works ascribed to Śaṅkara)

nodes.name: Nimbārka lived before Śaṅkara (7th c. CE)
nodes.summary: A contested dating of Nimbārka: the Nimbārka sampradāya places him in remote antiquity; Roma Bose and others put him in the 12th–13th c., partly on the assumption that he wrote the anti-Mādhva Madhvamukhamardana; Vijay Ramnarace (2014) rejects that attribution and argues for the 7th c. CE.

nodes.name: Utpaladeva
nodes.summary: Kashmirian Śaiva philosopher and poet, pupil of Somānanda and teacher of Lakṣmaṇagupta (Abhinavagupta’s teacher), who founded the Pratyabhijñā (“Recognition”) philosophy in the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā with his own Vṛtti and Vivṛti, and wrote the devotional Śivastotrāvalī.
nodes.details: The Kārikā opens: “Having somehow attained servitude to Maheśvara and wishing to help people as well, I shall establish the recognition of him, the cause of attaining all fulfilment” (ĪPK 1.1.1). Pratyabhijñā argues, against Buddhist epistemology, that the self is the one Lord whose freedom (svātantrya) appears as the world, so that liberation is a recognition of one’s identity with Śiva. Abhinavagupta commented on the Kārikā (Vimarśinī) and on the Vivṛti (Vivṛtivimarśinī).

dates.label: c. 925–975 CE
dates.basis: teacher–pupil chronology from Somānanda to Abhinavagupta (whose works are dated 990/91 and 1014/15)

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (ed. M. K. Shastri, Srinagar 1921 (KSTS 34), revised after R. Torella, Rome 1994)

nodes.name: Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā
nodes.summary: Utpaladeva’s verses on the “recognition of the Lord”, with his own brief Vṛtti, in four sections (knowledge, action, scripture, summary): the root text of the Pratyabhijñā philosophy of Kashmir Śaivism, critically studied and translated by Raffaele Torella.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (ed. M. K. Shastri, Srinagar 1921 (KSTS 34), revised after R. Torella, Rome 1994)

nodes.name: Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī
nodes.summary: Abhinavagupta’s commentary on Utpaladeva’s Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, completed 1014/15 CE according to its colophon as reported by Sanderson; with the longer Vivṛtivimarśinī it is the main exposition of Pratyabhijñā.

nodes.name: Nāṭyaśāstra
aliases: Nāṭyaveda (as the text calls its subject)
nodes.summary: The treatise on drama, dance and music ascribed to the sage Bharata, which presents theatre as a “fifth Veda” created by Brahmā for all social classes from elements of the four Vedas, and which first formulates the theory of rasa and the 108 karaṇas of dance later carved on South Indian temples.
nodes.details:
In chapter 1 the gods, led by Indra, ask Brahmā for a pastime to be both seen and heard; since the Vedas may not be recited to śūdras, he is to create “another Veda, a fifth, for all the classes” (NŚ 1.11–12). Brahmā makes the nāṭyaveda “from the limbs of the four Vedas”, taking recitation from the Ṛgveda, song from the Sāmans, gesture and acting from the Yajurveda and rasa from the Atharvaveda (1.16–17). The first performance is followed by the building of a protected playhouse (nāṭyamaṇḍapa, 1.82–83), described in chapter 2.

Chapter 4 tells how Śiva had his attendant Taṇḍu teach Bharata the dance, hence called tāṇḍava, and defines “these hundred and eight karaṇas” (4.55); the karaṇa reliefs of the Bṛhadīśvara temple at Thanjavur and the gopuras of Chidambaram depict them (`concept:karanas`). Chapter 6 lists eight rasas (6.15) and gives in prose the rasa-sūtra — “rasa arises from the conjunction of determinants, consequents and transitory states” — which Abhinavagupta’s Abhinavabhāratī (c. 1000) made the basis of Indian aesthetics and which Rūpa Gosvāmī transposed to devotion. Pāṇini (4.3.110) already knows “actors’ sūtras” (naṭasūtra) of Śilālin, an earlier dramaturgical tradition.

nodes.name: Bharata (author of the Nāṭyaśāstra)
nodes.summary: The sage to whom the Nāṭyaśāstra is ascribed and who, in its frame story, receives the nāṭyaveda from Brahmā and stages the first performance with his hundred sons; whether one historical author lies behind the name is unknown.

nodes.name: Abhinavabhāratī
nodes.summary: Abhinavagupta’s commentary on the Nāṭyaśāstra (c. 1000 CE), the only surviving early commentary, whose reading of the rasa-sūtra — rasa as a universalised tasting of emotion by the sensitive spectator — became the classical theory of Indian aesthetics.

nodes.name: Nāṭyaśāstra 1.11–18 (the fifth Veda)
nodes.summary: The origin story of drama: the gods ask Brahmā for a pastime to be seen and heard and open to all classes; he composes the nāṭyaveda, “a fifth Veda with the itihāsa”, from recitation, song, acting and rasa taken from the four Vedas.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input P. Dadegaonkar, S. Krishnapur, H. Bakshi; source edition not stated; bhn_chapter.verse numbering)

nodes.name: Rasa (aesthetic relish)
nodes.summary: The “taste” or relish of an emotion evoked in a cultivated spectator. The Nāṭyaśāstra lists eight rasas — erotic, comic, compassionate, furious, heroic, fearful, odious and marvellous (6.15) — and states that rasa arises from the conjunction of determinants, consequents and transitory states; later theory added a ninth, the tranquil (śānta), and Gauḍīya theology made devotion (bhakti) itself a rasa.

nodes.name: Vedic Saṃhitās
nodes.summary: The four mantra collections — Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, Yajurveda (Śukla and Kṛṣṇa) and Atharvaveda — that form the base of the Vedic canon and were transmitted orally by recitation schools (śākhās).
nodes.details:
Each Saṃhitā belongs to one or more schools (śākhās) that also transmitted a Brāhmaṇa, and often an Āraṇyaka and Upaniṣad; in the traditional wide sense “Veda” covers this whole sequence Saṃhitā → Brāhmaṇa → Āraṇyaka → Upaniṣad. Scholars (e.g. Witzel) distinguish a Ṛgvedic period, a Mantra period (Atharvaveda, Sāmaveda, Yajurveda mantras), a period of Yajurveda Saṃhitā prose, the Brāhmaṇa period, and the late Vedic Upaniṣads and Sūtras.

Transmission was oral and remains so in living recitation lineages. UNESCO recognised the “Tradition of Vedic chanting” (India): proclaimed in 2003 and inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008; UNESCO notes that only thirteen of over a thousand recitation branches survive. Written manuscripts are late (second millennium CE).

nodes.name: Brāhmaṇas
nodes.summary: Prose texts attached to each Vedic school that explain the meaning, origin and correct performance of the śrauta rites, often through myths (ākhyāna) and identifications (bandhu).
nodes.details: Examples: Aitareya and Kauṣītaki (Ṛgveda); Pañcaviṃśa/Tāṇḍya and Jaiminīya (Sāmaveda); Taittirīya and Śatapatha (Yajurveda); Gopatha (Atharvaveda). Several first narrate stories later retold in the epics and Purāṇas: the flood of Manu (ŚB 1.8.1), the dwarf Viṣṇu winning the earth (ŚB 1.2.5), Purūravas and Urvaśī (ŚB 11.5.1), Śunaḥśepa (AB 7.13–18). Witzel places the main Brāhmaṇa period roughly in the early first millennium BCE, before the Upaniṣads.

nodes.name: Āraṇyakas
nodes.summary: Late Vedic texts, studied apart from the village, that treat esoteric or dangerous rites (e.g. the Pravargya) and contain or shade into the oldest Upaniṣads.
nodes.details: The Aitareya Āraṇyaka contains the Aitareya Upaniṣad (AĀ 2.4–6); the Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) Āraṇyaka contains the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad; the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka contains the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (TĀ 7–9) and the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad (TĀ 10); the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (“great Āraṇyaka”) forms the last part of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. These embeddings are the textual basis for the layered sequence Saṃhitā → Brāhmaṇa → Āraṇyaka → Upaniṣad.

sources.locator: Introduction (the Upaniṣads within the Vedic corpus)

nodes.name: Upaniṣads
nodes.summary: Texts at the end of the Vedic corpus (hence “Vedānta”) that discuss the self (ātman), brahman, death and rebirth, and liberation; the principal (“early”) Upaniṣads number about thirteen.
nodes.details:
Olivelle’s relative chronology: the prose Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya are the oldest and pre-Buddhist (c. 7th–6th c. BCE, give or take a century); Taittirīya, Aitareya and Kauṣītaki follow (c. 6th–5th c. BCE); the verse Upaniṣads — Kena (the earliest of them), Kaṭha, Īśā, Śvetāśvatara, Muṇḍaka — belong to the last few centuries BCE; Praśna and Māṇḍūkya cannot be much older than the beginning of the common era. Olivelle warns that dating closer than a few centuries is unstable. Hundreds of later works also call themselves Upaniṣads.

The Upaniṣads, the Bhagavad Gītā and the Brahma Sūtra form the “triple foundation” (prasthānatrayī) on which Vedānta schools, including Advaita, write commentaries.

dates.label: c. 7th c. BCE – turn of the common era (principal Upaniṣads, as a group)
dates.basis: linguistic, stylistic and internal evidence; relative chronology of the Upaniṣads

nodes.name: Vedāṅgas
nodes.summary: The six “limbs of the Veda” — phonetics (śikṣā), ritual (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), metre (chandas) and astronomy/calendar (jyotiṣa) — developed to preserve, understand and apply the Vedic texts.
nodes.details: The six are listed together in Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.5, which classes the four Vedas and these six disciplines as the “lower knowledge” (aparā vidyā). Representative works: the Prātiśākhyas and Śikṣās (phonetics), the Kalpa Sūtras (ritual), Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī (grammar), Yāska’s Nirukta (etymology), Piṅgala’s Chandaḥsūtra (metre) and the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa.

sources.quote: tatrāparā ṛgvedo yajurvedaḥ sāmavedo ’tharvavedaḥ śikṣā kalpo vyākaraṇaṃ niruktaṃ chando jyotiṣam iti

nodes.name: Kalpa Sūtras
nodes.summary: Aphoristic manuals of each Vedic school that codify the solemn (śrauta) rites, domestic (gṛhya) rites, rules of conduct (dharma) and altar geometry (śulba).
nodes.details: Well-known sets belong to Āpastamba, Baudhāyana and Hiraṇyakeśin (Taittirīya school), Āśvalāyana and Śāṅkhāyana (Ṛgveda), Kātyāyana (Śukla Yajurveda) and others. The Śrauta Sūtras are the operative manuals of living śrauta performances; the Dharma Sūtras precede the metrical Dharmaśāstras such as the Manusmṛti (`text:manusmriti`). Dating is debated; the older Sūtras are usually placed in the last centuries BCE.

sources.locator: vol. I (Dharmasūtras) and vol. II (śrauta and gṛhya rites)

nodes.name: Rigveda
nodes.summary: The oldest Vedic collection: 1,028 hymns in ten books (maṇḍalas) addressed chiefly to Indra, Agni and Soma, composed by hereditary poet families and transmitted orally with exceptional fidelity.
nodes.details:
Structure (checked against Aufrecht’s text on GRETIL): ten maṇḍalas of 191, 43, 62, 58, 87, 75, 104, 103 (incl. the eleven Vālakhilya hymns 8.49–59), 114 and 191 hymns — 1,028 in all, 10,552 verses. The “family books” 2–7 are each attributed to one poet clan (Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha) and form the oldest layer; maṇḍala 9 gathers all hymns to Soma Pavamāna; maṇḍalas 1 and 10 (191 hymns each) are later collections, maṇḍala 10 containing the late cosmogonic hymns (10.90, 10.121, 10.129) and dialogue hymns (10.10, 10.95, 10.108).

Only the Śākala recension survives complete; Śākalya’s word-by-word padapāṭha and the more complex recitation patterns (krama, jaṭā, ghana) protected the text in oral transmission, which UNESCO recognised (2003/2008). The oldest surviving manuscripts are of the 11th century CE (Nepal, per Witzel); the BORI collection in Pune (`ms:rigveda-bori`, owned by the material agent) was placed on UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register in 2007. Sāyaṇa’s 14th-century commentary is the standard traditional exegesis.

nodes.name: Samaveda
nodes.summary: The Veda of chants (sāman): verses, almost all drawn from the Ṛgveda, arranged for singing by the udgātṛ priests in the soma rites, with separate song-books (gāna) recording the melodies.
nodes.details: Three recensions are known: Kauthuma, Rāṇāyanīya and Jaiminīya. Its Brāhmaṇas include the Pañcaviṃśa (Tāṇḍya) and Jaiminīya; the Chāndogya Upaniṣad belongs to the Kauthuma school and the Kena Upaniṣad to the Jaiminīya (Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa). It is commonly stated that all but about 75 of its verses occur in the Ṛgveda (recall; check against an edition).

dates.label: c. 1200–1000 BCE (Mantra period)
dates.basis: relative stratigraphy of Vedic language and texts (Mantra period after the Ṛgveda)

nodes.name: Yajurveda
nodes.summary: The Veda of sacrificial formulas (yajus) recited by the adhvaryu priest who performs the manual acts of the rite; it exists in a “Black” (Kṛṣṇa) branch mixing mantra and explanatory prose and a “White” (Śukla) branch with mantras alone.
nodes.details: Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Saṃhitās: Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇī, Kāṭhaka and Kapiṣṭhala-Kaṭha. Śukla Yajurveda: the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā in Mādhyandina and Kāṇva recensions, with the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. Upaniṣads of the branch include the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Īśā (Śukla) and the Taittirīya, Kaṭha and Śvetāśvatara (Kṛṣṇa).

dates.label: c. 1200–800 BCE (Mantra and Saṃhitā-prose periods; approximate)

nodes.name: Śukla Yajurveda (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā)
nodes.summary: The “White” Yajurveda, the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā in forty chapters (Mādhyandina and Kāṇva recensions), whose mantras are separated from the explanatory prose collected in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.
nodes.details: Tradition, already in Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.5.3, attributes these “white formulas” to Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya. Notable chapters: VS 16 (the Śatarudriya, parallel to TS 4.5), VS 31 (a version of the Puruṣa hymn) and VS 40 (= the Īśā Upaniṣad). Witzel associates the school with the eastern, Videha region in the late Vedic period.

dates.label: c. 1000–700 BCE (approximate; later than the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Saṃhitās)

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

nodes.name: Taittirīya Saṃhitā (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda)
nodes.summary: The principal Saṃhitā of the Black Yajurveda, in seven books (kāṇḍas) mixing ritual formulas with Brāhmaṇa-style prose explanation; it contains the Śatarudrīya litany to Rudra (TS 4.5).
nodes.details: The Taittirīya school, with its Brāhmaṇa, Āraṇyaka (incl. the Taittirīya Upaniṣad) and the Āpastamba, Baudhāyana and Hiraṇyakeśin Sūtras, is the most widely transmitted Yajurveda school in South India. TS 4.5 (eleven anuvākas, “namas te rudra manyave …”) and 4.7 (Camaka) are recited as the Śrī Rudram–Camakam in Śaiva worship.

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Weber 1871–72
sources.quote: námas te rudra manyáva utó ta íṣave námaḥ

nodes.name: Atharvaveda
nodes.summary: The fourth Veda, a collection of hymns and spells for healing, protection, prosperity, love, kingship and domestic life, alongside speculative cosmological hymns; preserved in the Śaunaka and Paippalāda recensions.
nodes.details: The Śaunaka Saṃhitā has twenty books (about 730 hymns); books 19–20 are later supplements, book 20 consisting largely of Ṛgvedic hymns to Indra plus the Kuntāpa hymns (which praise a king Parikṣit). The Paippalāda recension survives in Kashmiri and Orissan manuscript traditions. Upaniṣads of this Veda include the Muṇḍaka, Praśna and Māṇḍūkya; its Brāhmaṇa is the Gopatha.

dates.label: c. 1200–1000 BCE (Mantra period; books 19–20 later)
dates.basis: relative stratigraphy of Vedic language and texts (Mantra period after the Ṛgveda)

nodes.name: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa
nodes.summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda, the largest and most systematic Brāhmaṇa (“of a hundred paths”), and a source of many narratives later retold in the epics and Purāṇas.
nodes.details: Mādhyandina recension: 14 kāṇḍas (100 adhyāyas); a Kāṇva recension also exists. Books 1–5 often cite Yājñavalkya, books 6–10 (the fire-altar) Śāṇḍilya; book 14 ends with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. Passages checked on GRETIL for this dataset include: the flood of Manu (1.8.1), the dwarf Viṣṇu who wins the earth for the gods (1.2.5), “yajño vai viṣṇuḥ” (1.1.2.13), Videgha Māthava and the eastward course of Agni Vaiśvānara (1.4.1.10–17), Rudra left behind by the gods (1.7.3.1), the eight names of the new-born Kumāra/Rudra (6.1.3.7–18), Purūravas and Urvaśī (11.5.1), Janaka’s sacrifice (11.6.3), the aśvamedha kings Janamejaya Pārikṣita and Bharata Dauḥṣanti, son of Śakuntalā (13.5.4), Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa’s five-night sacrifice (13.6.1.1) and the beheading of Viṣṇu (14.1.1).

dates.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)
dates.basis: relative stratigraphy; geography of the eastern (Kosala–Videha) Vedic schools

nodes.name: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa
nodes.summary: A Ṛgvedic Brāhmaṇa for the hotṛ priest in forty adhyāyas (eight pañcikās), best known for the royal consecration (rājasūya) material and the story of Śunaḥśepa (AB 7.13–18).
nodes.details: The Śunaḥśepa narrative (pañcikā 7, khaṇḍas 13–18 = adhyāya 33) is recited to the consecrated king in the rājasūya. Keith regarded books 1–5 as older than books 6–8. Sāyaṇa commented on it; Keith translated it (HOS 25, 1920).

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Aufrecht 1879

nodes.name: Taittirīya Āraṇyaka
nodes.summary: The Āraṇyaka of the Taittirīya school in ten prapāṭhakas; books 7–9 are the Taittirīya Upaniṣad and book 10 the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad.
nodes.details: Includes material on the Pravargya and on the creation and cosmology; its embedded Upaniṣads show the gradual transition from Āraṇyaka to Upaniṣad.

nodes.name: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: The largest and, with the Chāndogya, the oldest Upaniṣad, forming the end of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; it presents Yājñavalkya’s teachings at Janaka’s court, his dialogues with Maitreyī and Gārgī, and the earliest explicit doctrine of karma and rebirth.
nodes.details: Six adhyāyas in Kāṇva and Mādhyandina recensions: the Madhu-kāṇḍa (1–2), the Yājñavalkya-kāṇḍa (3–4) and supplements (5–6), each section closing with teacher lineages (vaṃśa). Key passages verified on GRETIL: 1.4 (the self alone in the beginning; “ahaṃ brahmāsmi” 1.4.10), 2.3.6 (“neti neti”), 2.4 and 4.5 (Maitreyī), 3.1–9 (the contest at Janaka’s sacrifice, incl. Gārgī 3.6 and 3.8), 3.2.13 and 4.4.5–6 (karma), 6.2 (Pravāhaṇa Jaivali’s doctrine of the two paths), 6.3.7 (Uddālaka Āruṇi teaches Yājñavalkya) and 6.5.3 (the “white” formulas of Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya). Śaṅkara’s commentary on it is accepted as authentic.

dates.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)
dates.basis: linguistic, stylistic and internal evidence; relative chronology of the Upaniṣads

dates.label: parts possibly still being composed c. 4th–2nd c. BCE
dates.basis: relative chronology with grammarians and early Buddhist sources

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

nodes.name: Chāndogya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: An early prose Upaniṣad of the Kauthuma Sāmaveda school, in eight prapāṭhakas, containing Uddālaka Āruṇi’s instruction of Śvetaketu (“tat tvam asi”), the “five fires” doctrine of rebirth, and the only Vedic mention of a Kṛṣṇa son of Devakī (3.17.6).
nodes.details: Verified passages: 1.1.1 (meditation on Om as the udgītha), 3.14.1 (“sarvaṃ khalv idaṃ brahma”, Śāṇḍilya), 3.17.6 (Ghora Āṅgirasa teaches Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra), 4.4 (Satyakāma Jābāla), 5.3–10 (Pravāhaṇa Jaivali and the five fires; rebirth according to conduct 5.10.7), 6.1–16 (Uddālaka and Śvetaketu; “tat tvam asi” nine times from 6.8.7), 7.1.1 (Nārada approaches Sanatkumāra), 8.7–12 (Indra and Virocana as pupils of Prajāpati).

dates.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)
dates.basis: linguistic, stylistic and internal evidence; relative chronology of the Upaniṣads

nodes.name: Taittirīya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: Books 7–9 of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, in three vallīs (Śikṣā, Brahmānanda, Bhṛgu), known for the five sheaths of the self and Varuṇa’s instruction of his son Bhṛgu on brahman.
nodes.details: TU 3.1.1 (verified): Bhṛgu Vāruṇi approaches his father Varuṇa asking to be taught brahman and is told “that from which these beings are born, by which they live, into which they pass — seek to know that; that is brahman.” Śaṅkara’s commentary on TU is accepted as authentic.

dates.label: c. 6th–5th c. BCE (probably pre-Buddhist)
dates.basis: linguistic, stylistic and internal evidence; relative chronology of the Upaniṣads

sources.quote: bhṛgurvai vāruṇiḥ / varuṇaṃ pitaramupasasāra / adhīhi bhagavo brahmeti

nodes.name: Aitareya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A short Ṛgvedic Upaniṣad (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.4–6) describing creation by the self (“ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt”) and ending with the equation “prajñānaṃ brahma” (3.3).

dates.label: c. 6th–5th c. BCE (probably pre-Buddhist)
dates.basis: linguistic, stylistic and internal evidence; relative chronology of the Upaniṣads

nodes.name: Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A Ṛgvedic Upaniṣad in four chapters, part of the Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) Āraṇyaka, in which kṣatriya teachers instruct brahmins: Citra Gāṅgyāyani teaches Āruṇi, Indra teaches Pratardana, and Ajātaśatru teaches Bālāki.
nodes.details: Its fourth chapter parallels Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.1 (the dialogue of Ajātaśatru of Kāśī and Bālāki Gārgya). Locators here are from recall (Olivelle 1998) and should be checked against an edition.

dates.label: c. 6th–5th c. BCE (probably pre-Buddhist)
dates.basis: linguistic, stylistic and internal evidence; relative chronology of the Upaniṣads

sources.locator: text and translation of the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad

nodes.name: Kena Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A short Upaniṣad of the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda school: two verse sections on the unknowable brahman, followed by the prose parable in which Agni, Vāyu and Indra fail to recognise a mysterious being until Umā Haimavatī reveals that it is brahman.
nodes.details: Four khaṇḍas (checked in the Sanskrit Documents e-text): 1–2 in verse, 3–4 in prose. It forms part of the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (traditionally JUB 4.18–21; recall). Olivelle regards it as the oldest of the verse Upaniṣads.

nodes.name: Kaṭha Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A verse Upaniṣad in six vallīs framed by the story of the boy Naciketas, who receives three boons from Yama, the third being the teaching about what happens after death and the imperishable self.
nodes.details: The frame narrative develops a story told in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (3.11.8; recall). Verses verified on GRETIL (Olivelle numbering): 1.1 (Vājaśravasa’s gift and his son Naciketas), 1.11 (the father called “Auddālaki Āruṇi”), 2.15 (Om), 2.18–19 (the self is not born and does not die; “if the killer thinks he kills …” — closely paralleled in Bhagavad Gītā 2.19–20), 3.7 (the word saṃsāra), 3.9 (“that highest step of Viṣṇu”) and 6.14 (the mortal becomes immortal).

nodes.name: Īśā Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A brief verse Upaniṣad forming the final chapter (40) of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, opening “īśā vāsyam idaṃ sarvaṃ” — all this is to be dwelt in by the Lord.

nodes.name: Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A verse Upaniṣad of the Atharvaveda in three muṇḍakas that distinguishes the “lower” knowledge (the four Vedas and six Vedāṅgas) from the “higher” knowledge of the imperishable, taught by Aṅgiras to Śaunaka.
nodes.details: Opens with a transmission line: Brahmā → Atharvan → Aṅgir → Satyavāha Bhāradvāja → Aṅgiras, whom the householder Śaunaka approaches (1.1.1–3). 3.1.1 reuses RV 1.164.20 (“two birds, companions …”), and 3.1.6 contains “satyam eva jayate”, the motto of the Republic of India.

nodes.name: Praśna Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A prose Upaniṣad of the Atharvaveda in which six students — among them Sukeśā Bhāradvāja, Satyakāma Śaibya and Kausalya Āśvalāyana — put six questions to the sage Pippalāda.
nodes.details: Note: its Satyakāma Śaibya (1.1) is a different figure from Satyakāma Jābāla of the Chāndogya.

dates.label: around the beginning of the common era

nodes.name: Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: The shortest principal Upaniṣad (twelve verses), which identifies the syllable Om with all that is, past, present and future, and the self (ātman) with brahman, analysed into four states (waking, dream, deep sleep and the “fourth”).
nodes.details: Verse 2: “sarvaṃ hy etad brahmāyam ātmā brahma” (verified). Gauḍapāda’s Māṇḍūkya Kārikā is the earliest surviving systematic Advaita treatise; the authenticity of the commentary on it ascribed to Śaṅkara is questioned.

dates.label: around the beginning of the common era

nodes.name: Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A theistic verse Upaniṣad in six chapters that proclaims one Rudra, called Śiva and Maheśvara, as creator and lord, using Sāṃkhya and Yoga vocabulary; it is the earliest text to make Rudra–Śiva the supreme god and closes with the word bhakti.
nodes.details: Verified verses: 3.2 (“eko hi rudro na dvitīyāya tasthe”), 3.4, 3.5–6 (reusing Śatarudriya mantras), 3.11 (“sarvagataḥ śivaḥ”), 3.15 (= RV 10.90.2), 3.16 (paralleled in Bhagavad Gītā 13.13), 4.10 (māyā and the māyin Maheśvara), 4.21–22 (4.22 = RV 1.114.8), 5.2 (the seer Kapila), 6.16 (saṃsāra and mokṣa), 6.21 (the sage Śvetāśvatara) and 6.23 (supreme bhakti to god and teacher).

nodes.name: Aṣṭādhyāyī of Pāṇini
nodes.summary: Pāṇini’s grammar of Sanskrit in nearly 4,000 sūtras arranged in eight chapters, describing both the spoken language of his time and Vedic usage; it is an external, datable witness to names and cults of its period, including Vāsudeva and Arjuna (4.3.98).
nodes.details: Sūtra 4.3.98 “vāsudeva-arjunābhyāṃ vun” (verified) forms derivatives meaning “one whose bhakti is Vāsudeva / Arjuna” under the heading 4.3.95 “bhaktiḥ”; it is widely cited as the earliest reference to devotion to Vāsudeva. Pāṇini also cites earlier grammarians (e.g. Śākalya, 1.1.16).

dates.label: c. 5th – mid-4th c. BCE (not later than the early-to-mid 4th c. BCE)
c. mid-4th c. BCE or later (terminus post quem c. 350 BCE)
dates.basis: history of writing and numismatic arguments (von Hinüber, Falk), accepted by Bronkhorst

nodes.name: Mahābhāṣya of Patañjali
nodes.summary: Patañjali’s “Great Commentary” on Pāṇini and Kātyāyana’s vārttikas (c. mid-2nd c. BCE), whose example sentences incidentally attest the Kṛṣṇa–Kaṃsa story, its performance by actors (śobhikas), devotees of Vāsudeva, and contemporary events.
nodes.details: Verified in Kielhorn’s text (GRETIL): on P. 3.1.26 — “kaṃsavadham ācaṣṭe kaṃsaṃ ghātayati, balibandham ācaṣṭe baliṃ bandhayati”; śobhikas “before one’s eyes have Kaṃsa killed and Bali bound”; paintings show the blows; those who present the story (granthikas) are seen divided into “kaṃsabhaktāḥ” and “vāsudevabhaktāḥ” (Kielhorn II 34.14–36.21). On 3.2.111 — “jaghāna kaṃsaṃ kila vāsudevaḥ” and “aruṇad yavanaḥ sāketam / madhyamikām”. On 3.2.123 — “iha puṣyamitraṃ yājayāmaḥ”. On 2.2.24 — “saṅkarṣaṇadvitīyasya balaṃ kṛṣṇasya vardhatām”. On 2.2.34 — music “prāsāde dhanapati-rāma-keśavānām”. On 5.3.99 — images (arcā) set up by the Mauryas for gain. The GRETIL file lacks the commentary on adhyāya 4, so Patañjali’s remark on 4.3.98 was not checked.

dates.label: c. mid-2nd c. BCE
dates.basis: internal references to Puṣyamitra’s sacrifice and Yavana sieges of Sāketa and Madhyamikā

dates.label: late Maurya period (321–185 BCE)
dates.basis: alternative reading of the internal evidence

nodes.limits: Grammatical examples show that the Kṛṣṇa–Kaṃsa and Bali stories were known and performed in the 2nd c. BCE; they do not date the events narrated.

nodes.name: Nirukta of Yāska
nodes.summary: Yāska’s explanatory commentary on the Nighaṇṭu word-lists, the oldest surviving work of Vedic exegesis, which records rival schools of interpretation — the etymologists (nairuktas) and the “historians” (aitihāsikas).
nodes.details: Verified examples: 2.16 — “What is Vṛtra? A cloud, say the nairuktas; an asura, son of Tvaṣṭṛ, say the aitihāsikas”; 7.5 — the nairuktas hold there are only three deities: Agni (earth), Vāyu or Indra (mid-region) and Sūrya (sky); 12.1 — competing identifications of the Aśvins; 12.10 — the itihāsa of Saraṇyū, Yama and Yamī and the birth of the Aśvins and Manu.

dates.label: c. 6th–5th c. BCE (generally placed before Pāṇini)

nodes.name: Indra
nodes.summary: The most frequently praised god of the Ṛgveda (about 250 hymns, roughly a quarter), the soma-drinking warrior who wields the vajra and slays Vṛtra to release the waters; in the Upaniṣads, epics and Purāṇas he remains king of the gods but loses supremacy and is often humbled.
nodes.details:
Ṛgvedic profile: slayer of Vṛtra (RV 1.32), breaker of the Vala cave with the Aṅgirases, patron of the Bharata king Sudās in the Battle of the Ten Kings (RV 7.18, 7.33), sender of Saramā (RV 10.108). RV 10.86 refrains “viśvasmād indra uttaraḥ” (Indra above all). Yāska (Nirukta 7.5) records the view that Vāyu or Indra is the single god of the middle region.

Shift of prominence: in the Kena Upaniṣad (3–4) Indra cannot grasp the mysterious being and learns from Umā Haimavatī that it is brahman, though he is then called foremost of the gods for coming nearest; in the Chāndogya (8.7–12) he is a patient pupil of Prajāpati for 101 years. In epic and Purāṇic narrative he is the ruler of svarga and the guardian of the east, repeatedly threatened, cursed or displaced (e.g. the guilt of killing Vṛtra; the Govardhana episode of the Bhāgavata, where Kṛṣṇa turns the cowherds from Indra’s worship). Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

nodes.name: Agni
nodes.summary: The sacrificial fire as god — messenger between gods and humans, divine hotṛ and purohita — praised in about 200 Ṛgvedic hymns, including the first (RV 1.1); central to all Vedic ritual and still present in every Hindu rite.
nodes.details: The family books 2–7 open with Agni hymns, as does the whole Ṛgveda (“agnim īḻe purohitaṃ”, RV 1.1.1). The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.4.1.10–17) narrates Agni Vaiśvānara burning eastward from the Sarasvatī to the Sadānīrā with Videgha Māthava. In the Kena (3.3–6) Agni Jātavedas cannot burn a straw before brahman. Later he becomes guardian of the south-east and a secondary figure in sectarian theology while remaining indispensable in ritual. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

sources.quote: agnim īḻe purohitaṁ yajñasya devam ṛtvijam

nodes.name: Soma
nodes.summary: The pressed ritual drink and its god, praised in about 120 Ṛgvedic hymns, including all 114 hymns of maṇḍala 9 to Soma Pavamāna (“self-purifying”); in later tradition Soma is identified with the Moon and becomes ancestor of the Lunar dynasty.
nodes.details: The identity of the original soma plant is unknown and debated. The identification of Soma with the Moon is already Vedic (late Saṃhitā and Brāhmaṇa texts) and becomes standard; Purāṇic genealogies trace the Candravaṃśa (`lin:chandravamsha`) from Soma through Budha and Purūravas. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

attributes.approx. RV hymns: ≈120 (all 114 of maṇḍala 9 plus a few elsewhere)

sources.locator: RV 9.1–9.114 (114 hymns counted in the e-text)

openQuestions: Botanical identity of soma (ephedra, a mushroom and other candidates are argued).

nodes.name: Varuṇa
nodes.summary: The sovereign Āditya of the Ṛgveda who guards cosmic and moral order (ṛta), sees all and binds wrongdoers with his fetters; praised alone in about a dozen hymns and often with Mitra. Later he declines to lord of the waters and guardian of the west.
nodes.details: Varuṇa is the deity of the Vasiṣṭha hymns of contrition (RV 7.86–89) and the god who releases the bound Śunaḥśepa (RV 1.24.12–13); in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa he grants Hariścandra a son and then claims him. RV 7.33.11 makes Vasiṣṭha a son of Mitra and Varuṇa (maitrāvaruṇa). In Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1 he teaches his son Bhṛgu about brahman. With RV 2.27.1 he is one of the Ādityas, sons of Aditi. In the epics and Purāṇas his ethical sovereignty fades and he becomes ruler of the ocean and the waters. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

nodes.name: Mitra
nodes.summary: An Āditya personifying alliance and contract, almost always paired with Varuṇa; only one Ṛgvedic hymn (RV 3.59) is addressed to him alone. He is cognate with Iranian Mithra.
nodes.details: With Varuṇa he is named father of Vasiṣṭha and (by tradition) Agastya (RV 7.33.10–13). Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra and the Nāsatyas (Aśvins) are invoked as divine witnesses in a Mitanni treaty of the 14th c. BCE — an important external attestation that belongs to the material agent’s domain (no entity yet). Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

nodes.name: Sūrya
nodes.summary: The Sun as god, praised in about ten Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.50, 1.115); closely related solar deities include Savitṛ, addressed in the Gāyatrī (RV 3.62.10). Sūrya later becomes the focus of Saura worship and of great temples such as Konark.
nodes.details: Note on identity: in the Ṛgveda Savitṛ (“impeller”) and Sūrya are distinct names with overlapping functions; the registry lists Savitṛ under Sūrya as “related”, and the Gāyatrī (to Savitṛ) is linked here with that caution. RV 5.40.6–9 tells how Atri found the Sun hidden by the darkness of Svarbhānu. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

nodes.name: Uṣas
nodes.summary: The goddess Dawn, daughter of heaven, celebrated in about twenty of the most admired Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.113); she has little independent cult in later Hinduism.
nodes.details: In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (7.16) the bound Śunaḥśepa is finally released while praising Uṣas. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Aufrecht 1879

nodes.name: Rudra
nodes.summary: A fierce Ṛgvedic archer-god of storms, disease and healing, addressed in only about three hymns (RV 1.114, 2.33, 7.46), who through the Yajurvedic Śatarudrīya and the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad becomes the supreme god Śiva.
nodes.details: Ṛgveda: RV 2.33 asks him to spare and heal; he is “lord of this world” (īśāna, 2.33.9) and father of the Maruts. Brāhmaṇas: the gods leave him behind when they go to heaven by sacrifice (ŚB 1.7.3.1, “Vāstavya”); the new-born Kumāra receives eight names — Rudra, Sarva (Śarva), Paśupati, Ugra, Aśani, Bhava, Mahān Deva, Īśāna — as forms of Agni (ŚB 6.1.3.7–18). Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5 (Śatarudrīya) pays homage to him in hundreds of forms and includes “namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca” (4.5.8.1). The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (3–4) proclaims the one Rudra, called śiva and maheśvara, as creator and lord of all. Śaiva traditions identify Rudra with Śiva; historians describe a gradual convergence of Rudra with other, non-Vedic elements (Kramrisch; Chakravarti). Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

sources.quote: īśānād asya bhuvanasya bhūrer na vā u yoṣad rudrād asuryam

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Weber 1871–72
