nodes.name: Prajāpati
nodes.summary: “Lord of creatures”, named as creator in the last verse of RV 10.121 and the central creator-god of the Brāhmaṇas, whose dismembered body is restored in the fire-altar ritual; his role passes to Brahmā in the epics and Purāṇas.
nodes.details: RV 10.121 repeatedly asks “to which god (kasmai devāya) shall we offer?”; its final verse answers “Prajāpati”, and the Brāhmaṇas make “Ka” (“Who?”) a name of Prajāpati. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (8.7–12) Prajāpati teaches Indra and Virocana about the self. The epics often call Brahmā “Prajāpati”, and Purāṇic cosmogony assigns him Prajāpati’s functions.

sources.quote: prajāpate na tvad etāny anyo viśvā jātāni pari tā babhūva

nodes.name: Yama
nodes.summary: Son of Vivasvat and, in the Ṛgveda, the first mortal who found the path to the world of the fathers and rules there (RV 10.14); he is the teacher of Naciketas in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad and later the god of death and judge of the dead (Dharmarāja).
nodes.details: Ṛgveda: three or so hymns (e.g. RV 10.14, 10.135) and the dialogue with his twin sister Yamī (RV 10.10); his two four-eyed dogs are “Sārameya”, sons of Saramā (RV 10.14.10). Yāska (Nirukta 12.10) records the itihāsa of Saraṇyū bearing the twins Yama and Yamī to Vivasvat. In the Mahābhārata Yama appears in the Sāvitrī story, and Dharma, the divine father of Yudhiṣṭhira, is often identified with him (the epic agent’s domain).

sources.quote: vaivasvataṁ saṁgamanaṁ janānāṁ yamaṁ rājānaṁ haviṣā duvasya

nodes.name: Vāyu
nodes.summary: The Wind, first to drink the soma, often paired with Indra (Indra–Vāyu); praised in a few Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.134–135, 7.90) and, as Vāta, in RV 10.168. Later he is the father of Hanumān and Bhīma.
nodes.details: In the Kena (3.7–10) Vāyu Mātariśvan cannot lift a straw before brahman. Yāska (Nirukta 7.5) gives “Vāyu or Indra” as the god of the middle region. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

attributes.approx. RV hymns: a few (alone and with Indra); Vāta in RV 10.168, 10.186

nodes.name: Aśvins
nodes.summary: Twin horsemen gods of the dawn, healers and rescuers who appear in more than fifty Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.116–120); in the Mahābhārata they are the fathers of Nakula and Sahadeva.
nodes.details: Yāska (Nirukta 12.1) lists competing identifications — heaven and earth, day and night, sun and moon, or (according to the aitihāsikas) two virtuous kings — and (12.10) the story of their birth from Saraṇyū in horse form. As Nāsatyas they are also named in the 14th-c. BCE Mitanni treaty. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

nodes.name: Aditi
nodes.summary: “Boundlessness”, mother of the Ādityas (Mitra, Varuṇa and others), who has no Ṛgvedic hymn of her own but is praised as all things (RV 1.89.10); later the wife of Kaśyapa, mother of the gods and of Vāmana.
nodes.details: RV 10.72 (verses 4–5, 8–9) has Dakṣa born from Aditi and Aditi from Dakṣa, and Aditi’s eight sons of whom she cast away Mārtāṇḍa; RV 2.27.1 names Mitra, Aryaman, Bhaga, Varuṇa, Dakṣa and Aṃśa as Ādityas. In Purāṇic narrative (e.g. the Bhāgavata) she bears Vāmana, who recovers the worlds from Bali.

sources.quote: aditir dyaur aditir antarikṣam aditir mātā sa pitā sa putraḥ

nodes.name: Sarasvatī
nodes.summary: In the Ṛgveda both a mighty river and its goddess, praised in three hymns (RV 6.61, 7.95, 7.96); identified with Vāc (speech) in the Brāhmaṇas, she becomes the goddess of learning, music and speech and consort of Brahmā.
nodes.details: The river (`place:sarasvati-river`, owned by the purana agent) is named with the Gaṅgā and Yamunā in the river hymn RV 10.75.5; ŚB 1.4.1.14 places Videgha Māthava on the Sarasvatī before the eastward migration. The goddess and the river are kept as separate ids here and joined by an IDENTIFIED_WITH assertion qualified by the Ṛgveda.

earliestMaterial.label: ruined Kashmiri stone temple (8th–10th c., recall)

nodes.name: Vasiṣṭha
nodes.summary: Ṛgvedic poet-priest to whose family maṇḍala 7 is attributed; priest of the Bharata king Sudās in the Battle of the Ten Kings, and in the Rāmāyaṇa the family priest of Daśaratha and rival of Viśvāmitra.
nodes.details: RV 7.33 (verified) makes him son of Mitra and Varuṇa, born “from the mind of Urvaśī” (7.33.11), and tells of his and Māna’s (Agastya’s) birth from a jar (7.33.13); RV 7.18 and 7.33.3–5 describe the Vasiṣṭhas’ prayers bringing Indra’s help to Sudās. In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa he is the brahman priest at Hariścandra’s rite (AB 7.16). In the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (Bālakāṇḍa) his wish-granting cow is coveted by king Viśvāmitra, the root of their famous enmity; the Mahābhārata also tells Vasiṣṭha–Viśvāmitra episodes (Ādiparvan).

nodes.name: Viśvāmitra
nodes.summary: Ṛgvedic poet of the Kuśika clan to whom maṇḍala 3 — including the Gāyatrī (RV 3.62.10) — is attributed; he adopts Śunaḥśepa in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa and, in the Rāmāyaṇa, takes the young Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to protect his sacrifice.
nodes.details: RV 3.33 (dialogue with the rivers Vipāś and Śutudrī) and RV 3.53 (verified: “viśvāmitrasya rakṣati brahmedam bhārataṁ janam”, 3.53.12; Viśvāmitra conveyed Sudās, 3.53.9). AB 7.17–18: he renames the freed Śunaḥśepa Devarāta and adopts him; those of his hundred sons who refuse are cursed. Epic tradition makes him a kṣatriya king who attains brahminhood through austerity and the father of Śakuntalā (Mahābhārata).

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Aufrecht 1879

nodes.name: Agastya
nodes.summary: Ṛgvedic poet to whom RV 1.165–191 are attributed, husband of Lopāmudrā (RV 1.179), who becomes in the Rāmāyaṇa the forest sage who arms Rāma, and in Tamil tradition (as Akattiyar) the founder of Tamil grammar and a culture-hero of the south.
nodes.details: RV 7.33.10–13 links his birth with Vasiṣṭha’s (Māna “rose from the jar”), whence the epithets Maitrāvaruṇi and Kumbhayoni; RV 1.165.15 calls the poet “Mānya”. The Mahābhārata (Āraṇyakaparvan) tells of Agastya and Lopāmudrā, the digestion of the demon Vātāpi and the drinking of the ocean; in the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (Araṇyakāṇḍa) Rāma visits his hermitage and receives weapons. Tamil tradition (attested in medieval commentarial literature) makes Akattiyar the first grammarian of Tamil and links him with the Potiyil hill; this is a separate, regional tradition and its relation to the Vedic poet is a matter of identification, not of evidence for a historical migration (Zvelebil).
openQuestions: Earliest Tamil source naming Akattiyar as grammarian (the regional agent may hold this).

nodes.name: Aṅgiras
nodes.summary: Primeval seer and eponym of the Āṅgirasa priestly clan; in the Ṛgveda the Aṅgirases are ancestral “fathers” who with Indra or Bṛhaspati opened the Vala cave and found the cows, and in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad Aṅgiras teaches the higher knowledge to Śaunaka.
nodes.details: RV 1.62.2 (“arcanto aṅgiraso gā avindan”), 10.14.6 (Aṅgirases, Atharvans and Bhṛgus as fathers), 10.108.10 (Saramā names the “terrible Aṅgirases”). The Atharvaveda is called Atharvāṅgirasaḥ. Patronymics such as Āṅgirasa (Ghora Āṅgirasa) mark clan membership, not necessarily direct descent.

nodes.name: Bhṛgu
nodes.summary: Ancestor of the Bhārgava priestly clan; in the Ṛgveda the Bhṛgus establish Agni among men, and in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and Taittirīya Upaniṣad Bhṛgu Vāruṇi is the son and pupil of Varuṇa.
nodes.details: RV 1.58.6 (“dadhuṣ ṭvā bhṛgavo mānuṣeṣv ā”), 10.14.6. ŚB 11.6.1.1: Bhṛgu Vāruṇi thought himself superior to his father Varuṇa in knowledge and is shown the other world; TU 3.1–6: Varuṇa teaches him brahman. In the Mahābhārata the Bhārgavas are prominent from the Paulomaparvan onward; V. S. Sukthankar argued (1936) that Bhārgava redactors shaped the epic — an influential but debated hypothesis.

sources.quote: bhṛgurha vai vāruṇiḥ  varuṇam pitaraṃ vidyayātimene

nodes.name: Atri
nodes.summary: Ṛgvedic seer whose family (the Ātreyas) is credited with maṇḍala 5; RV 5.40 tells how Atri found the Sun hidden by Svarbhānu’s darkness. In the Rāmāyaṇa Rāma visits Atri and his wife Anasūyā.

sources.quote: gūḻhaṁ sūryaṁ tamasāpavratena turīyeṇa brahmaṇāvindad atriḥ

nodes.name: Yājñavalkya
nodes.summary: The pre-eminent teacher of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad and an authority of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, who wins the debate at Janaka’s sacrifice, teaches Janaka and his wife Maitreyī, and to whom the “white” formulas of the Śukla Yajurveda are attributed.
nodes.details: BU 3 (verified) shows him claiming Janaka’s thousand cows and answering eight challengers including Gārgī Vācaknavī (3.6, 3.8) and Uddālaka Āruṇi (3.7); BU 4.1–4 his teaching of Janaka; BU 2.4 and 4.5 his parting instruction to Maitreyī; BU 6.3.7 names him the pupil of Uddālaka Āruṇi; BU 6.5.3 attributes the white yajus to him. The later Yājñavalkya Smṛti carries his name (attribution, not authorship).

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

nodes.name: Gārgī Vācaknavī
nodes.summary: A woman philosopher who twice questions Yājñavalkya at Janaka’s court (BU 3.6, 3.8), pressing him on what the worlds are “woven upon” until he warns her not to ask too much; her second questioning elicits the teaching of the imperishable (akṣara).
nodes.details: BU 3.6.1: “atha hainaṃ gārgī vācaknavī papraccha”; 3.8.8: “etad vai tad akṣaraṃ gārgi brāhmaṇā abhivadanti …”. After 3.8 she tells the assembled brahmins none of them will defeat Yājñavalkya.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: parts possibly still being composed c. 4th–2nd c. BCE

nodes.name: Maitreyī
nodes.summary: One of Yājñavalkya’s two wives, described as a discourser on brahman (brahmavādinī), who on his departure asks for the teaching of immortality instead of wealth (BU 2.4; 4.5).
nodes.details: BU 2.4.5: “ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyo maitreyi”; BU 4.5.1: “tayor ha maitreyī brahmavādinī babhūva; strīprajñaiva tarhi kātyāyanī”.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: parts possibly still being composed c. 4th–2nd c. BCE

nodes.name: Uddālaka Āruṇi
nodes.summary: A leading Kuru-Pañcāla teacher of the early Upaniṣads who instructs his son Śvetaketu with the refrain “tat tvam asi” (CU 6), questions Yājñavalkya at Janaka’s court (BU 3.7) and, by the lineage in BU 6.3.7, was Yājñavalkya’s own teacher.
nodes.details: He also appears as a learner from kṣatriyas: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali teaches him the five fires (CU 5.3–10; BU 6.2), and the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad (1.1) has Citra Gāṅgyāyani teach Āruṇi. Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.11 calls Naciketas’s father “Auddālaki Āruṇi” — a patronymic (“son/descendant of Uddālaka”) whose relation to this figure is unresolved.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Śvetaketu
nodes.summary: Son and pupil of Uddālaka Āruṇi who returns proud from twelve years of Vedic study and is taught by his father that the self is the subtle essence of all (“tat tvam asi, śvetaketo”, CU 6); in CU 5.3 and BU 6.2 he cannot answer Pravāhaṇa Jaivali’s questions on the afterlife.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Satyakāma Jābāla
nodes.summary: The boy of the Chāndogya (4.4) who, not knowing his father, truthfully reports his mother Jabālā’s words and is accepted as a pupil by Hāridrumata Gautama for that truthfulness; he later teaches Upakosala (CU 4.10–15).
nodes.details: Not to be confused with Satyakāma Śaibya, a pupil of Pippalāda in the Praśna Upaniṣad (1.1).

sources.quote: satyakāmo ha jābālo jabālāṃ mātaram āmantrayāṃ cakre

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Janaka of Videha (Upaniṣadic king)
nodes.summary: The king of Videha in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad who holds a sacrifice with lavish gifts, sets a prize of a thousand cows for the most learned brahmin, and becomes Yājñavalkya’s student.
nodes.details: BU 3.1.1 (verified): “janako ha vaideho bahudakṣiṇena yajñeneje”; ŚB 11.6.3.1 has a parallel. BU 2.1.1 records that people ran about crying “Janaka, Janaka” — his patronage was proverbial. Identity caution: the Rāmāyaṇa’s Janaka of Mithilā, father of Sītā (`char:janaka`, epic agent), shares the name and kingdom, and later tradition treats “Janaka” as a dynastic title; the Vedic texts say nothing of Sītā, and this dataset does not assert identity (see `claim:janaka-videha-sita-father`).

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

nodes.name: Naciketas
nodes.summary: The boy of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad whose father, angered by his questioning, gives him to Death; waiting three nights at Yama’s house, he receives three boons and refuses all worldly gifts in favour of the knowledge of what lies beyond death.
nodes.details: The frame story is older than the Upaniṣad (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.11.8; recall). A later retelling is the Nāciketa episode of the Mahābhārata (Anuśāsanaparvan; recall).

sources.quote: tasya ha naciketā nāma putra āsa

earliestText.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

nodes.name: Ghora Āṅgirasa
nodes.summary: A teacher of the Āṅgirasa clan who, according to Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.17.6, taught Kṛṣṇa son of Devakī a doctrine likening a man’s life to a soma sacrifice, after which Kṛṣṇa “became free from thirst”.

sources.quote: tad dhaitad ghora āṅgirasaḥ kṛṣṇāya devakīputrāyoktvovāca

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra (Chāndogya)
nodes.summary: The pupil of Ghora Āṅgirasa named in a single sentence of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (3.17.6) — “Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī” — the only Vedic occurrence of that name-pair; whether he is the epic and Purāṇic Kṛṣṇa is disputed.
nodes.details: Proponents of identity (Bhandarkar 1913; Raychaudhuri 1920) point to the same name and mother and to ethical themes (austerity, generosity, non-injury, truthfulness — CU 3.17.4) resembling the Gītā. Sceptics note that nothing else in the passage connects him with the Yādavas, Mathurā or Vāsudeva, that “Kṛṣṇa” and “Devakī” were not unique names, and that the Chāndogya’s student has no divine status. Kept as a separate id; see `claim:krishna-devakiputra-identity` (material agent).
openQuestions: Can any independent evidence connect the Chāndogya’s pupil with the Vṛṣṇi hero Vāsudeva?

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Purūravas
nodes.summary: A mortal king, called “son of Iḍā” (aiḍa), who loses his apsaras wife Urvaśī; their dialogue is RV 10.95 and the full story ŚB 11.5.1. In Purāṇic genealogy he is the first king of the Lunar dynasty.

sources.quote: iti tvā devā ima āhur aiḻa

nodes.name: Urvaśī
nodes.summary: An apsaras who lives with the mortal Purūravas on conditions he breaks, then leaves him (RV 10.95; ŚB 11.5.1); RV 7.33.11 also links her with Vasiṣṭha’s birth. She is a celebrated heroine of later literature, notably Kālidāsa’s Vikramorvaśīya.

nodes.name: Vṛtra
nodes.summary: The serpent (ahi) or “obstruction” who encloses the waters and is slain by Indra (RV 1.32). Yāska records two readings — a cloud (nairuktas) or an asura son of Tvaṣṭṛ (aitihāsikas); later texts make Vṛtra a brahmin-born asura whose killing brings Indra guilt, and the Bhāgavata a devotee of Viṣṇu.

nodes.name: Śunaḥśepa
nodes.summary: Son of the brahmin Ajīgarta, sold to prince Rohita as a substitute victim for Varuṇa; bound to the stake at Hariścandra’s rājasūya, he is freed by praising the gods and adopted by Viśvāmitra as Devarāta (AB 7.13–18).
nodes.details: RV 1.24.12–13 already mentions Śunaḥśepa, bound and calling on Varuṇa; the Anukramaṇī attributes RV 1.24–30 to him (recall). The Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (Bālakāṇḍa) retells the story with king Ambarīṣa and the sage Ṛcīka in place of Hariścandra and Ajīgarta, making Viśvāmitra Śunaḥśepa’s maternal uncle.

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Aufrecht 1879

sources.quote: śunaḥśepo yam ahvad gṛbhītaḥ so asmān rājā varuṇo mumoktu

nodes.name: Saramā
nodes.summary: Indra’s messenger who tracks the cows stolen by the Paṇis and demands them back in the dialogue hymn RV 10.108; later tradition makes her the bitch of the gods, mother of Yama’s two dogs (Sārameya, RV 10.14.10).
nodes.details: RV 10.108.2: “indrasya dūtīr iṣitā carāmi”. In the Mahābhārata (Ādiparvan, Pauṣyaparvan) Saramā curses Janamejaya after his brothers beat her son (recall).

nodes.name: Brahman
nodes.summary: In the Ṛgveda (neuter bráhman) the potent sacred formulation of the poet-priest; in the Upaniṣads the ultimate reality, the ground from which beings arise and into which they return, often identified with the self (ātman).
nodes.details: Key Upaniṣadic loci (verified): BU 1.4.10 (“ahaṃ brahmāsmi”), BU 2.3.6 (“neti neti” as the description of brahman), CU 3.14.1 (“sarvaṃ khalv idaṃ brahma”), TU 3.1.1 (the definition by origin, sustenance and dissolution), Kena 1–4, Māṇḍūkya 2 (“ayam ātmā brahma”), Aitareya 3.3 (“prajñānaṃ brahma”). These sentences become the “great sayings” (mahāvākyas) of Advaita Vedānta. The concept is central in the Bhagavad Gītā (e.g. brahma-nirvāṇa) and the Brahma Sūtra.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Ātman
nodes.summary: The self — originally the body or breath, then the inner essence of a person — which the early Upaniṣads make the object of liberating knowledge and identify with brahman.
nodes.details: BU 1.4.1 (“ātmaivedam agra āsīt puruṣavidhaḥ” — in the beginning this was the self alone, in the form of a person), BU 2.4.5 (“ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ …”), BU 4.4.5 (“sa vā ayam ātmā brahma”), CU 6.8.7 (“tat tvam asi”), Kaṭha 2.18–19 (the self is unborn and undying), Māṇḍūkya 2. The Bhagavad Gītā (2.19–20) reuses the Kaṭha verses on the unkillable self.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Ṛta
nodes.summary: The Ṛgvedic principle of cosmic, ritual and moral order and truth, guarded above all by Varuṇa and Mitra; in later thought its role is largely taken over by dharma.
nodes.details: RV 10.190.1 (“ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ cābhīddhāt tapaso ’dhy ajāyata” — order and truth were born from kindled heat), RV 10.85.1 (“ṛtenādityās tiṣṭhanti”). Cognate with Avestan aša. The word dhárman also occurs in the Ṛgveda (e.g. RV 10.90.16 “dharmāṇi prathamāni”), and post-Vedic dharma absorbs much of ṛta’s scope.

sources.quote: ṛtaṁ ca satyaṁ cābhīddhāt tapaso ’dhy ajāyata

nodes.name: Yajña
nodes.summary: Vedic sacrifice — offerings into the fire with recitation, chant and formula — the central religious act of the Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas, which the Brāhmaṇas identify with Prajāpati and with Viṣṇu (“yajño vai viṣṇuḥ”).
nodes.details: RV 10.90.16: “yajñena yajñam ayajanta devāḥ” (with the sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice). ŚB 1.1.2.13 and 14.1.1.6 identify Viṣṇu with the sacrifice. The Upaniṣads reinterpret the rite inwardly (e.g. CU 3.17, life as a soma sacrifice); the Bhagavad Gītā (3–4) generalises yajña to all action offered without attachment. Living śrauta performance continues in a few lineages (e.g. the 1975 Agnicayana in Kerala).

nodes.name: Om
nodes.summary: The sacred syllable recited at the beginning and end of Vedic recitation; the Upaniṣads make it an object of meditation and a symbol of brahman (CU 1.1.1; Kaṭha 2.15–17; the whole Māṇḍūkya).
nodes.details: CU 1.1.1: “om ity etad akṣaram udgītham upāsīta”. Kaṭha 2.15: “om ity etat”. Māṇḍūkya 1: Om is all this, past, present and future, and what is beyond the three times. In BU 3.9.1 Yājñavalkya’s “om” is an affirmation (“yes”). The Bhagavad Gītā (8.13; 17.23–24) continues the Upaniṣadic use.

sources.quote: om ity etad akṣaram udgītham upāsīta

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Karma
nodes.summary: Action — first, in the Brāhmaṇas, ritual action — which the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad makes the determinant of one’s future: “as one acts, so one becomes” (BU 4.4.5); the earliest explicit statements of the doctrine of moral retribution in Indian texts.
nodes.details: BU 3.2.13 (verified): Yājñavalkya and Ārtabhāga, speaking privately, discuss karma — “one becomes good by good action, bad by bad”. BU 4.4.5: “yathākārī yathācārī tathā bhavati …”, linking desire, resolve, action and outcome. CU 5.10.7: those of pleasant conduct (ramaṇīyacaraṇa) quickly reach a pleasant birth, those of foul conduct a foul one. The Bhagavad Gītā’s karma-yoga (BG 3–4) reworks the notion as action without attachment to fruits.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Saṃsāra
nodes.summary: The cycle of death and rebirth. The early prose Upaniṣads describe the cycle (the “five fires” and the two paths, BU 6.2; CU 5.3–10) before the word saṃsāra itself appears in the verse Upaniṣads (Kaṭha 3.7; Śvetāśvatara 6.16).
nodes.details: BU 6.2.15–16: those who know go by the path of the gods and do not return; those who sacrifice go by the path of the fathers to the moon and return via space, wind, rain and food; those who know neither path become worms, insects and snakes. Kaṭha 3.7: the one without understanding “does not reach that place and goes on to saṃsāra” (saṃsāraṃ cādhigacchati). The doctrine is shared, in different forms, with Buddhist and Jain traditions.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Mokṣa
nodes.summary: Liberation from the cycle of rebirth. The early Upaniṣads speak of immortality and of the desireless knower who, being brahman, goes to brahman (BU 4.4.6); the noun mokṣa itself appears in the Śvetāśvatara (6.16).
nodes.details: BU 4.4.6: “athākāmayamāno … na tasya prāṇā utkrāmanti; brahmaiva san brahmāpyeti”; Kaṭha 6.14: “atha martyo ’mṛto bhavaty atra brahma samaśnute”; ŚvU 6.16 names the lord as cause of “saṃsāra, mokṣa, continuance and bondage”. Mokṣa becomes the highest human aim (puruṣārtha) of the epics, the Gītā (18.66) and the Vedānta schools.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

nodes.name: Indra slays Vṛtra
nodes.summary: The central Ṛgvedic combat myth: fortified with soma and armed with the vajra fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, Indra kills the serpent Vṛtra who lies on the mountain enclosing the waters, and the waters flow to the sea (RV 1.32).
nodes.details: Later versions: the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.6.3) makes Vṛtra a creation of Tvaṣṭṛ after Indra kills Tvaṣṭṛ’s son Viśvarūpa; Yāska (Nirukta 2.16) records the naturalistic (cloud and rain) and “historical” (asura) readings; the Mahābhārata (Udyogaparvan) and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (book 6) retell it with the theme of Indra’s guilt and, in the Bhāgavata, Vṛtra’s devotion.

sources.quote: indrasya nu vīryāṇi pra vocaṁ yāni cakāra prathamāni vajrī

nodes.name: The three strides of Vishnu
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu measures out the earthly realms in three wide strides, his highest step holding a spring of honey (RV 1.154; 1.22.16–21); the Brāhmaṇas re-enact the strides in ritual and identify Viṣṇu with the sacrifice. The motif is the Vedic root of the later Vāmana–Bali story.
nodes.details: RV 1.154.1–5 (verified) and RV 1.22.20 (“tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padaṃ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ”). ŚB 1.1.2.13 and 1.9.3.9: the sacrificer takes the “Viṣṇu strides” because “Viṣṇu is the sacrifice” who strode through earth, air and sky. Kaṭha Up. 3.9 names the goal of the journey “that highest step of Viṣṇu”.

nodes.name: The sacrifice of Puruṣa
nodes.summary: RV 10.90: the gods sacrifice the thousand-headed cosmic Man (Puruṣa), and from his dismembered body come the verses, the animals, the four social classes, the moon, sun, Indra and Agni, and the worlds.
nodes.details: RV 10.90.12 (verified) derives the brāhmaṇa, rājanya, vaiśya and śūdra from Puruṣa’s mouth, arms, thighs and feet — the earliest statement of the four varṇas. Versions occur in VS 31 and AV 19.6; ŚvU 3.14–15 reuses its opening verses; ŚB 13.6.1.1 names a Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa who performs a five-night (pañcarātra) human-sacrifice rite.

nodes.name: The Nāsadīya creation hymn
nodes.summary: RV 10.129, a speculative cosmogony: in the beginning there was neither non-being nor being; the One breathed windlessly; desire (kāma) arose as the first seed of mind — and perhaps even the overseer in the highest heaven does not know how creation came about.

sources.quote: nāsad āsīn no sad āsīt tadānīṁ

nodes.name: Manu and the fish (the flood)
nodes.summary: The earliest Indian flood story (ŚB 1.8.1.1–11): a small fish caught in Manu’s washing water asks for protection, grows, warns of a flood, and tows Manu’s ship by a rope tied to its horn to the northern mountain; alone surviving, Manu sacrifices and obtains a daughter, Iḍā, through whom he generates humankind.
nodes.details: In the Śatapatha the fish is unnamed and not identified with any god. The Mahābhārata (Āraṇyakaparvan, Matsyopākhyāna) makes the fish Brahmā Prajāpati (recall); the Matsya and Bhāgavata Purāṇas make it Viṣṇu’s Matsya avatāra (`narr:matsya-flood`).

earliestText.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

nodes.name: Purūravas and Urvaśī
nodes.summary: The apsaras Urvaśī lives with king Purūravas on condition she never sees him naked; tricked by the gandharvas, she vanishes, and the grieving king finds her among the apsarases, who appear as birds; she foretells their son and the gandharvas’ gift of a fire by which he becomes one of them (RV 10.95; ŚB 11.5.1).
nodes.details: RV 10.95 is a cryptic dialogue; the Śatapatha (11.5.1, verified) gives the narrative frame and places the king’s wandering around Kurukṣetra (11.5.1.4). Later retellings: Viṣṇu Purāṇa (book 4), Bhāgavata Purāṇa (book 9), and Kālidāsa’s drama Vikramorvaśīya.

nodes.name: Saramā and the Paṇis
nodes.summary: Indra’s messenger Saramā crosses the Rasā river to the Paṇis, who have hidden cows in a cave; she refuses their bribe and warns that Indra, Bṛhaspati, Soma and the Aṅgirases will recover the cows (RV 10.108) — a form of the Vala myth.

nodes.name: The story of Śunaḥśepa
nodes.summary: King Hariścandra, sonless, is advised by Nārada to vow a son to Varuṇa; when Rohita is born the king delays the sacrifice, Varuṇa afflicts him, and Rohita buys Śunaḥśepa from his father Ajīgarta as a substitute; bound to the stake, Śunaḥśepa praises a sequence of gods until his bonds fall away at the verses to Uṣas, and Viśvāmitra adopts him as Devarāta (AB 7.13–18).
nodes.details: The story is recited to the king during the rājasūya consecration. Priests at the rite: Viśvāmitra (hotṛ), Jamadagni (adhvaryu), Vasiṣṭha (brahman) and Ayāsya (udgātṛ) (TITUS AB 7.16). The Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa’s Bālakāṇḍa version differs (king Ambarīṣa; father Ṛcīka; Viśvāmitra as maternal uncle).

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Aufrecht 1879
sources.quote: Hariścandro ha Vaidʰasa Aikṣvāko rājāputra āsa

nodes.name: Naciketas and Yama
nodes.summary: Vājaśravasa gives away his worthless cows; his son Naciketas asks repeatedly “to whom will you give me?” and is told “to Death”; after three nights unfed at Yama’s house he receives three boons — his father’s calm, the fire-altar that leads to heaven (named after him), and the truth about what happens after death.

sources.quote: uśan ha vai vājaśravasaḥ sarvavedasaṃ dadau

earliestText.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

nodes.name: Uddālaka teaches Śvetaketu: “tat tvam asi”
nodes.summary: Uddālaka Āruṇi teaches his son Śvetaketu through examples — clay, the banyan seed, salt dissolved in water — that the subtle essence of everything is the self, ending each lesson “tat tvam asi, Śvetaketu” (CU 6.8.7–6.16.3).
nodes.details: Advaita Vedānta takes the sentence as a mahāvākya affirming the identity of the individual self and brahman (“you are that”). Brereton (1986) and Olivelle argue that in context it means “that is how you are” — the essence (tat) is the self of the world — a reading that does not by itself decide the metaphysical question.

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Umā Haimavatī reveals Brahman to the gods
nodes.summary: After a victory the gods take pride; a mysterious being (yakṣa) appears; Agni cannot burn and Vāyu cannot lift a straw before it; when Indra approaches it vanishes, and in its place he meets a radiant woman, Umā Haimavatī, who tells him it was brahman (Kena 3–4).
nodes.details: Kena 3.12 (“umāṃ haimavatīm”) and 4.1 (“sā brahmeti hovāca”). Later Śaiva and Śākta readers identify Umā Haimavatī (“daughter of Himavat”) with Pārvatī; in the Kena she is a revealer of brahman whose relation to Rudra is not stated.

earliestText.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

nodes.name: The debates at Janaka’s court
nodes.summary: At a sacrifice of king Janaka of Videha attended by brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas, a thousand cows with gold on their horns are offered to the most learned; Yājñavalkya drives them off and defeats in turn Aśvala, Ārtabhāga, Bhujyu, Uṣasta, Kahoḍa, Gārgī, Uddālaka Āruṇi and Vidagdha Śākalya (BU 3.1–9).

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

nodes.name: Vedic Śrauta ritual tradition
nodes.summary: The tradition of the solemn public Vedic rites performed with three fires by specialist priests (hotṛ, adhvaryu, udgātṛ, brahman) according to the Brāhmaṇas and Śrauta Sūtras; it survives in a few lineages, e.g. among Nambudiri brahmins of Kerala.
nodes.details: A twelve-day Agnicayana (building of the bird-shaped fire altar) was performed and documented at Panjal, Kerala, in 1975 (Staal 1983). Domestic (gṛhya) rites and Vedic recitation are far more widely preserved than the śrauta rites.

dates.event: documented performance of the Agnicayana (Panjal, Kerala)
dates.label: 1975 (Agnicayana at Panjal, documented by F. Staal)

nodes.name: Advaita Vedānta
nodes.summary: The non-dualist school of Vedānta, systematised by Gauḍapāda and Śaṅkara, which reads the Upaniṣads, the Bhagavad Gītā and the Brahma Sūtra as teaching that the self (ātman) is identical with brahman and that the world of plurality is not ultimately real.
nodes.details:
Its “great sayings” (mahāvākyas) are drawn from Upaniṣadic passages in this dataset: “prajñānaṃ brahma” (Aitareya 3.3), “ahaṃ brahmāsmi” (BU 1.4.10), “tat tvam asi” (CU 6.8.7) and “ayam ātmā brahma” (Māṇḍūkya 2). The fourfold mahāvākya scheme is a later Advaita systematisation.

Round 2 links: a school of `trad:vedanta`; its lineage runs Gauḍapāda → Govinda → Śaṅkara → Sureśvara and Padmapāda (traditional), with Maṇḍana Miśra and Vācaspati Miśra (Bhāmatī school), Vidyāraṇya and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī as later authorities. Key concepts: māyā, avidyā, adhyāsa, vivarta, jīvanmukti, the fourfold qualification and the mahāvākyas.

nodes.name: Pāṇini
nodes.summary: The grammarian of Gandhāra (traditionally of Śalātura) who composed the Aṣṭādhyāyī, the foundational grammar of Sanskrit, probably in the 5th–4th c. BCE (disputed).

dates.label: c. mid-4th c. BCE or later

nodes.name: Patañjali (grammarian)
nodes.summary: Author of the Mahābhāṣya on Pāṇini and Kātyāyana, generally placed in the mid-2nd c. BCE from his references to Puṣyamitra’s sacrifice and Yavana attacks. Whether he is the same person as the author of the Yoga Sūtra is disputed and not assumed here.

dates.label: c. mid-2nd c. BCE
dates.basis: internal references (Puṣyamitra; Yavana sieges of Sāketa and Madhyamikā)

nodes.name: Yāska
nodes.summary: Author of the Nirukta, the earliest surviving Vedic exegesis and etymology, usually placed before Pāṇini (c. 6th–5th c. BCE; disputed).

nodes.name: Sāyaṇa
nodes.summary: Fourteenth-century scholar and minister at the Vijayanagara court under Bukka I and Harihara II whose commentaries (Vedārthaprakāśa) on the Ṛgveda and much of the Vedic corpus are the fullest traditional exegesis; he died in 1387.
nodes.details: Brother of Mādhava (sometimes identified with Vidyāraṇya); several works ascribed to him were produced with collaborators. Thirteen of the thirty BORI Ṛgveda manuscripts inscribed on UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register contain his commentary.

dates.label: c. 1340–1387 CE
dates.basis: court records and colophons as summarised by Modak (1995)

nodes.name: Ādi Śaṅkara
nodes.summary: The Advaita Vedānta philosopher whose commentaries on the Brahma Sūtra, the principal Upaniṣads and the Bhagavad Gītā define the school; modern scholarship dates him c. 700–750 CE, though older scholarship gave 788–820 and maṭha traditions much earlier dates.
nodes.details: Authenticity: the commentaries on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Taittirīya are generally accepted; Hacker and Mayeda also accept those on the Chāndogya, Aitareya, Kena, Īśā, Kaṭha, Muṇḍaka and Praśna; the commentary on the Māṇḍūkya with Gauḍapāda’s Kārikā is questioned.

dates.label: c. 700–750 CE
dates.basis: probable earliest and latest limits from citations and doxographies

dates.label: 788–820 CE (older scholarly view)
dates.basis: traditional verse dates accepted by 19th–20th c. scholars (Tiele, Müller, Deussen)

dates.label: 5th c. BCE (birth dates of 509 or 483 BCE in Kāñcī and Śṛṅgeri maṭha traditions)

nodes.name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 1
nodes.summary: A later composite book of 191 hymns by many poets (including Agastya’s group 1.165–191 and the riddle hymn 1.164); it and maṇḍala 10 frame the older family books.

dates.label: c. 1200–1000 BCE (late Ṛgvedic layer; approximate)
dates.basis: language, metre and content later than the family books

nodes.name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 2 (Gṛtsamada family book)
nodes.summary: Family book of 43 hymns attributed to the Gṛtsamadas; includes the Rudra hymn 2.33.

dates.label: c. 1500–1200 BCE (older Ṛgvedic layer; approximate)
dates.basis: relative stratigraphy: family books older than maṇḍalas 1 and 10

nodes.name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 3 (Viśvāmitra family book)
nodes.summary: Family book of 62 hymns attributed to Viśvāmitra and the Kuśikas; includes the river dialogue 3.33, the Bharata hymn 3.53 and the Gāyatrī 3.62.10.

dates.label: c. 1500–1200 BCE (older Ṛgvedic layer; approximate)
dates.basis: relative stratigraphy: family books older than maṇḍalas 1 and 10

nodes.name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 4 (Vāmadeva family book)
nodes.summary: Family book of 58 hymns attributed to Vāmadeva Gautama; RV 4.26.1 (“aham manur abhavaṃ sūryaś ca”) is quoted in BU 1.4.10.

dates.label: c. 1500–1200 BCE (older Ṛgvedic layer; approximate)
dates.basis: relative stratigraphy: family books older than maṇḍalas 1 and 10

nodes.name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 5 (Atri family book)
nodes.summary: Family book of 87 hymns attributed to the Ātreyas; RV 5.40 tells how Atri recovered the hidden Sun.

dates.label: c. 1500–1200 BCE (older Ṛgvedic layer; approximate)
dates.basis: relative stratigraphy: family books older than maṇḍalas 1 and 10

nodes.name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 6 (Bharadvāja family book)
nodes.summary: Family book of 75 hymns attributed to the Bhāradvājas; includes the Sarasvatī hymn 6.61 and the Indra–Viṣṇu hymn 6.69.

dates.label: c. 1500–1200 BCE (older Ṛgvedic layer; approximate)
dates.basis: relative stratigraphy: family books older than maṇḍalas 1 and 10

nodes.name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 7 (Vasiṣṭha family book)
nodes.summary: Family book of 104 hymns attributed to Vasiṣṭha and his descendants; includes the Ten Kings hymns 7.18 and 7.33, the Varuṇa hymns 7.86–89 and the Sarasvatī hymns 7.95–96.

dates.label: c. 1500–1200 BCE (older Ṛgvedic layer; approximate)
dates.basis: relative stratigraphy: family books older than maṇḍalas 1 and 10

nodes.name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 9 (Soma Pavamāna)
nodes.summary: All 114 hymns to Soma Pavamāna, gathered from the poet families into one book arranged by metre.

nodes.name: Ṛgveda maṇḍala 10
nodes.summary: The youngest book (191 hymns), with the cosmogonies (10.90, 10.121, 10.129), funeral and Yama hymns (10.14–18), the river hymn (10.75), Vāc (10.125) and dialogue hymns (10.10, 10.95, 10.108).

dates.label: c. 1200–1000 BCE (late Ṛgvedic layer; approximate)
dates.basis: language, metre and content later than the family books

nodes.name: RV 1.24 (Śunaḥśepa’s plea to Varuṇa)
nodes.summary: A hymn attributed to Śunaḥśepa Ājīgarti in which the bound Śunaḥśepa calls on King Varuṇa to release him (1.24.12–13).

sources.quote: śunaḥśepo hy ahvad gṛbhītas triṣv ādityaṁ drupadeṣu baddhaḥ

nodes.name: RV 1.32 (Indra slays Vṛtra)
nodes.summary: The classic hymn of Indra’s victory over Vṛtra: “I shall now proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra …” (1.32.1); the waters released run to the sea.

sources.quote: indrasya nu vīryāṇi pra vocaṁ yāni cakāra prathamāni vajrī

nodes.name: RV 1.154 (Viṣṇu’s three strides)
nodes.summary: Hymn to Viṣṇu who measured the earthly realms in three strides; in his highest step is a spring of honey (1.154.5).

sources.quote: viṣṇor nu kaṁ vīryāṇi pra vocaṁ yaḥ pārthivāni vimame rajāṁsi

nodes.name: RV 1.164.46 (“ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti”)
nodes.summary: Verse of the riddle hymn 1.164: “They call it Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni … the inspired speak of the one that is in many ways”.

sources.quote: ekaṁ sad viprā bahudhā vadanty agniṁ yamam mātariśvānam āhuḥ

nodes.name: RV 1.165–191 (hymns of Agastya)
nodes.summary: The group of hymns closing maṇḍala 1 that the Anukramaṇī attributes to Agastya Maitrāvaruṇi, including the Indra–Maruts–Agastya dialogue (1.165, 1.170) and the dialogue of Agastya and Lopāmudrā (1.179).

nodes.name: RV 2.33 (hymn to Rudra)
nodes.summary: The longest Ṛgvedic hymn to Rudra, father of the Maruts, asking the fearsome, tawny, many-formed lord to spare and heal; “from Rudra, lord of this world, lordship does not depart” (2.33.9).

sources.quote: īśānād asya bhuvanasya bhūrer na vā u yoṣad rudrād asuryam

nodes.name: RV 3.53 (Viśvāmitra and the Bharatas)
nodes.summary: Hymn of Viśvāmitra in which the great seer conveys king Sudās (3.53.9) and declares that his formulation protects the Bharata people (3.53.12); tradition reads verses 21–24 as imprecations against Vasiṣṭha.

nodes.name: RV 3.62.10 (the Gāyatrī / Sāvitrī)
nodes.summary: The verse to Savitṛ in gāyatrī metre — “tat savitur vareṇyam …” — recited daily by twice-born Hindus and taught at initiation.

sources.quote: tat savitur vareṇyam bhargo devasya dhīmahi | dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt

nodes.name: RV 7.18 (the Battle of the Ten Kings)
nodes.summary: Vasiṣṭha’s hymn celebrating Indra’s help to king Sudās of the Tṛtsus/Bharatas against a coalition of ten kings on the Paruṣṇī river.

sources.quote: arṇāṁsi cit paprathānā sudāsa indro gādhāny akṛṇot supārā

nodes.name: RV 7.33 (Vasiṣṭha’s birth and the Ten Kings)
nodes.summary: Hymn of the Vasiṣṭhas recalling how their prayer won Indra’s aid for Sudās (7.33.3–5) and telling of Vasiṣṭha’s birth from Mitra and Varuṇa, “from the mind of Urvaśī”, and Māna’s (Agastya’s) birth from a jar (7.33.10–13).

sources.quote: utāsi maitrāvaruṇo vasiṣṭhorvaśyā brahman manaso ’dhi jātaḥ

nodes.name: RV 7.59.12 (the Tryambaka verse)
nodes.summary: The verse “tryambakaṃ yajāmahe …” (we worship the three-mothered/three-eyed one … may I be released from death like a cucumber from its stalk), appended to a Marut hymn; recited later as the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya mantra to Śiva.

nodes.name: RV 10.14 (Yama, king of the dead)
nodes.summary: Funeral hymn honouring Yama Vaivasvata, who first found the path for many, and sending the dead past Yama’s two four-eyed dogs, the Sārameyas.

sources.quote: vaivasvataṁ saṁgamanaṁ janānāṁ yamaṁ rājānaṁ haviṣā duvasya

nodes.name: RV 10.75 (Nadīstuti, praise of rivers)
nodes.summary: Hymn praising the Sindhu (Indus) and naming the rivers from the Gaṅgā and Yamunā in the east to the Kubhā and Gomatī in the west (10.75.5–6); besides this verse the Ṛgveda has only the adjective gāṅgya (RV 6.45.31), so the Gaṅgā is marginal in the oldest text.

sources.quote: imam me gaṅge yamune sarasvati śutudri

nodes.name: RV 10.90 (Puruṣasūkta)
nodes.summary: The hymn of the cosmic Man sacrificed by the gods, from whose body the world and the four varṇas arise.

sources.quote: brāhmaṇo ’sya mukham āsīd bāhū rājanyaḥ kṛtaḥ

nodes.name: RV 10.95 (Purūravas and Urvaśī)
nodes.summary: Dialogue hymn in which Purūravas begs the departing Urvaśī to return; she refuses: “Go home again, Purūravas; I am hard to catch, like the wind” (10.95.2).

sources.quote: purūravaḥ punar astam parehi durāpanā vāta ivāham asmi

nodes.name: RV 10.108 (Saramā and the Paṇis)
nodes.summary: Dialogue between Indra’s messenger Saramā and the Paṇis who hold the stolen cows.

sources.quote: indrasya dūtīr iṣitā carāmi maha icchantī paṇayo nidhīn vaḥ

nodes.name: RV 10.121 (Hiraṇyagarbha)
nodes.summary: Hymn to the Golden Embryo who arose in the beginning as lord of all, with the refrain “to which god shall we offer?”; the last verse names Prajāpati.

sources.quote: hiraṇyagarbhaḥ sam avartatāgre bhūtasya jātaḥ patir eka āsīt

nodes.name: RV 10.125 (Vāc hymn; Devīsūkta)
nodes.summary: Speech (Vāc) speaks in the first person as the power moving with the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas and all gods and supporting Mitra–Varuṇa, Indra–Agni and the Aśvins; later recited as the Devīsūkta in goddess worship.

sources.quote: ahaṁ rudrebhir vasubhiś carāmy aham ādityair uta viśvadevaiḥ

nodes.name: RV 10.129 (Nāsadīyasūkta)
nodes.summary: The hymn of creation “Then there was neither non-being nor being …”, ending in doubt whether even the overseer knows.

sources.quote: so aṅga veda yadi vā na veda

nodes.name: ŚB 1.2.5 (the dwarf Viṣṇu wins the earth)
nodes.summary: The asuras divide the earth; the gods, putting Viṣṇu — the sacrifice — at their head, ask for a share “as much as this Viṣṇu lies upon”; Viṣṇu was a dwarf (vāmano ha viṣṇur āsa), but enclosed by the metres he gains the whole earth for the gods.

nodes.name: ŚB 1.4.1.10–17 (Videgha Māthava and Agni Vaiśvānara)
nodes.summary: King Videgha Māthava, then on the Sarasvatī, follows Agni Vaiśvānara burning eastward across the rivers to the Sadānīrā, which Agni did not burn; east of it the land of Videha is settled.

nodes.name: ŚB 1.7.3.1–8 (Rudra left behind; Vāstavya)
nodes.summary: When the gods went to heaven by sacrifice, the god who rules over cattle (Rudra) was left behind, hence called Vāstavya; he claims a share of the offering, and the rite of the Sviṣṭakṛt is explained.

sources.quote: atha yo ’yaṃ devaḥ paśūnāmīṣṭe sa ihāhīyata

nodes.name: ŚB 1.8.1.1–11 (Manu and the fish)
nodes.summary: The flood story of the Śatapatha: the fish, the ship tied to its horn, the northern mountain (“Manu’s descent”), and Manu’s daughter Iḍā born of his offerings.

nodes.name: ŚB 6.1.3.7–18 (Kumāra receives eight names)
nodes.summary: A boy (kumāra) born of Uṣas from the seed of the Year cries and asks Prajāpati for names; he receives eight — Rudra, Sarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Aśani, Bhava, Mahān Deva, Īśāna — each a form of Agni.

nodes.name: ŚB 11.5.1 (Purūravas and Urvaśī)
nodes.summary: The prose narrative of the apsaras Urvaśī and Purūravas Aiḍa, framing the verses of RV 10.95 and explaining the origin of a fire rite; the king wanders around Kurukṣetra searching for her (11.5.1.4).

nodes.name: ŚB 13.5.4 (kings who performed the horse sacrifice)
nodes.summary: A list of aśvamedha performers with commemorative verses (gāthās), beginning with Janamejaya Pārikṣita and his brothers Bhīmasena, Ugrasena and Śrutasena, and including Bharata Dauḥṣanti, whom “the apsaras Śakuntalā Nāḍapitī bore” (13.5.4.13).

nodes.name: ŚB 14.1.1 (Viṣṇu best of the gods; his head severed)
nodes.summary: The gods hold a session at Kurukṣetra; Viṣṇu reaches the goal first and becomes the best of the gods (14.1.1.5); being the sacrifice and the sun, he cannot contain his glory, and ants gnaw his bowstring so that the bow-end cuts off his head — the origin of the Pravargya.

nodes.name: AB 7.13–18 (the Śunaḥśepa story)
nodes.summary: The Śunaḥśepa narrative recited at the royal consecration (pañcikā 7, khaṇḍas 13–18; adhyāya 33 in continuous numbering).

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Aufrecht 1879
sources.quote: Hariścandro ha Vaidʰasa Aikṣvāko rājāputra āsa

nodes.name: TS 4.5 (Śatarudrīya / Śrī Rudram)
nodes.summary: Eleven anuvākas of homage to Rudra in his hundred forms — benign and terrible, lord of cattle, of thieves, of mountains — beginning “namas te rudra manyave” and including “namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca” (4.5.8.1); used in the agnicayana to pacify Rudra (cf. ŚB 9.1.1) and recited in Śaiva worship as the Śrī Rudram.

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Weber 1871–72
sources.quote: námas te rudra manyáva utó ta íṣave námaḥ

nodes.name: BU 1.4 (the self in the beginning; “ahaṃ brahmāsmi”)
nodes.summary: Creation from the self alone in the form of a person, who says “I am”, fears, desires a second, splits into husband and wife and produces all pairs (1.4.1–5); whoever knows “I am brahman” (ahaṃ brahmāsmi, 1.4.10) becomes the whole world — as the seer Vāmadeva realised, “I was Manu and the Sun”.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)
sources.quote: tad idam apy etarhi ya evaṃ vedāhaṃ brahmāsmīti sa idaṃ sarvaṃ bhavati

nodes.name: BU 2.4 (Yājñavalkya and Maitreyī, first version)
nodes.summary: About to leave home, Yājñavalkya offers to divide his property between Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī; Maitreyī asks for what makes one immortal and is taught that all is dear for the sake of the self.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)
sources.quote: ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyo maitreyi

nodes.name: BU 3.6 (Gārgī’s first questions)
nodes.summary: Gārgī Vācaknavī asks Yājñavalkya on what each world is woven, back to the worlds of brahman, until he warns: “Gārgī, do not ask too much, or your head will shatter.”

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

nodes.name: BU 3.8 (Gārgī’s second questions; the imperishable)
nodes.summary: Gārgī returns with two questions “like arrows”; Yājñavalkya answers that all is woven on space, and space on the imperishable (akṣara), at whose command sun and moon stand apart.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)
sources.quote: etad vai tad akṣaraṃ gārgi brāhmaṇā abhivadanti

nodes.name: BU 4.4.5–6 (karma and rebirth)
nodes.summary: Yājñavalkya to Janaka: “as one acts, as one behaves, so one becomes”; the desiring man returns to this world for further action, while the desireless, being brahman, goes to brahman.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

nodes.name: BU 4.5 (Yājñavalkya and Maitreyī, second version)
nodes.summary: The longer version of the Maitreyī dialogue, introducing Maitreyī as a brahmavādinī and Kātyāyanī as knowing only what women know.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

nodes.name: BU 6.2 (Pravāhaṇa Jaivali: the five fires and two paths)
nodes.summary: Śvetaketu Āruṇeya cannot answer the Pañcāla king Pravāhaṇa Jaivali’s five questions about the dead; the king teaches his father Gautama the five fires and the paths of the gods and of the fathers (6.2.1–16).

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)
sources.quote: śvetaketur vā āruṇeyaḥ pancālānāṃ pariṣadam ājagāma

nodes.name: CU 3.17.6 (Ghora Āṅgirasa and Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra)
nodes.summary: Having explained man’s life as a soma sacrifice (3.17.1–5), “Ghora Āṅgirasa told this to Kṛṣṇa son of Devakī, and he became free from thirst”, with three formulas for the time of death.

sources.quote: tad dhaitad ghora āṅgirasaḥ kṛṣṇāya devakīputrāyoktvovāca

nodes.name: CU 4.4 (Satyakāma Jābāla)
nodes.summary: Satyakāma asks his mother Jabālā his lineage; she does not know; he repeats her words truthfully to Hāridrumata Gautama, who accepts him as a true brahmin for his truthfulness.

nodes.name: CU 5.3–10 (the five fires)
nodes.summary: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali’s questions to Śvetaketu and teaching to Gautama: the dead pass through five sacrificial fires (heaven, rain-cloud, earth, man, woman) to rebirth; the knowers go by the path of the gods, others by the path of the fathers, and rebirth follows conduct (5.10.7).

nodes.name: CU 6.8.7 and CU 6 (“tat tvam asi”)
nodes.summary: Uddālaka’s teaching of his son (CU 6.1–16), from the sat that alone existed in the beginning (6.2.1) to the refrain first given at 6.8.7: “that is the self; tat tvam asi, Śvetaketu”.

nodes.name: CU 8.7–12 (Indra and Virocana with Prajāpati)
nodes.summary: Indra for the gods and Virocana for the asuras live as students with Prajāpati; Virocana leaves content with the body as self, while Indra returns again and again over 101 years until taught the bodiless self.

nodes.name: Kaṭha Up. vallī 1 (Naciketas and the three boons)
nodes.summary: The frame story: Vājaśravasa’s gift, Naciketas sent to Death, three nights’ wait and Yama’s three boons (KaU 1.1–29).

sources.quote: tasya ha naciketā nāma putra āsa

nodes.name: Kaṭha Up. 2.18–19 (the self neither born nor slain)
nodes.summary: “The wise one is not born and does not die … unborn, eternal … it is not killed when the body is killed” (2.18); “If the killer thinks he kills … neither understands” (2.19) — verses reused in Bhagavad Gītā 2.19–20.

nodes.name: Kaṭha Up. 3.9 (“that highest step of Viṣṇu”)
nodes.summary: The man whose charioteer is understanding and whose reins are the mind “reaches the end of the road — that highest step of Viṣṇu” (tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam), echoing RV 1.22.20.

nodes.name: Kena Up. 3–4 (the yakṣa and Umā Haimavatī)
nodes.summary: The prose parable of the gods’ pride, the yakṣa, the failure of Agni, Vāyu and Indra, and Umā Haimavatī’s revelation that it was brahman.

nodes.name: Śvetāśvatara Up. 3–4 (the one Rudra)
nodes.summary: Chapters proclaiming the one Rudra who rules the worlds (3.2), source and origin of the gods (3.4), whose “auspicious form” (śivā tanūḥ) is invoked with Śatarudriya mantras (3.5–6), the all-pervading Śiva (3.11) and the māyin Maheśvara (4.10).

nodes.name: Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.23 (bhakti to god and teacher)
nodes.summary: The closing verse: these teachings shine forth for the great-souled one “who has the highest devotion (bhakti) to god, and as to god, so to the teacher”.

sources.quote: yasya deve parā bhaktir yathā deve tathā gurau

nodes.name: Taittirīya Up. 3.1–6 (Bhṛgu and Varuṇa)
nodes.summary: Bhṛgu Vāruṇi asks his father Varuṇa to teach him brahman; through repeated austerity he comes to know brahman as food, breath, mind, understanding and finally bliss (ānanda).

nodes.name: Muṇḍaka Up. 1.1 (lineage; lower and higher knowledge)
nodes.summary: Brahmā teaches brahman-knowledge to Atharvan, who passes it via Aṅgir and Satyavāha Bhāradvāja to Aṅgiras; Śaunaka asks Aṅgiras, who distinguishes the lower knowledge (four Vedas, six Vedāṅgas) from the higher.

nodes.name: Māṇḍūkya Up. 1–12 (Om and the four states)
nodes.summary: Om is all this; this self is brahman (verse 2) and has four quarters — waking, dream, deep sleep and the fourth — mapped onto a, u, m and the soundless syllable.

nodes.name: Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.3.98 (vāsudevārjunābhyāṃ vun)
nodes.summary: Sūtra prescribing the suffix -aka after Vāsudeva and Arjuna in the sense “one whose object of bhakti is …” (heading 4.3.95 bhaktiḥ), giving vāsudevaka, “devotee of Vāsudeva”.

nodes.name: Mahābhāṣya on Pāṇini 3.1.26 (Kaṃsa-vadha and Bali-bandha)
nodes.summary: Patañjali’s discussion of causatives used of narration: “kaṃsavadham ācaṣṭe kaṃsaṃ ghātayati, balibandham ācaṣṭe baliṃ bandhayati”; śobhikas (performers) enact these before one’s eyes, paintings show the blows, and the reciters (granthikas) are seen divided into partisans of Kaṃsa and of Vāsudeva, some with red faces and some with black.

nodes.name: Nirukta 2.16 (who is Vṛtra?)
nodes.summary: Yāska’s gloss on RV 1.32.10: “Who then is Vṛtra? A cloud, say the etymologists; an asura son of Tvaṣṭṛ, say the historians.” Battle imagery, he explains, is metaphor for the mingling of waters and light that produces rain.

nodes.name: Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: The commentary on the Kāṇva Bṛhadāraṇyaka ascribed to Śaṅkara, one of the two Upaniṣad commentaries (with the Taittirīya) whose authenticity is most widely accepted; a principal source for Advaita readings of “ahaṃ brahmāsmi” and “neti neti”.

nodes.name: Brahma Sūtra
nodes.summary: Aphorisms attributed to Bādarāyaṇa that systematise the teaching of the Upaniṣads in four chapters (adhyāyas) of four quarters (pādas) each; with the Upaniṣads and the Bhagavad Gītā it is one of the three foundations (prasthānatrayī) on whose interpretation every Vedānta school, from Śaṅkara and Bhāskara to Rāmānuja, Madhva, Nimbārka, Vallabha and Baladeva, defines itself.
nodes.details:
The sūtras open “Then, therefore, the desire to know brahman” (athāto brahmajijñāsā, 1.1.1). Book 1 harmonises Upaniṣadic statements about brahman (1.1.4 tat tu samanvayāt); book 2 answers objections and refutes rival systems — Sāṅkhya (2.1.1–3; 2.2.1–10), Vaiśeṣika atomism (2.2.11–17), Buddhist (2.2.18–32) and Jain (2.2.33–36) doctrines, the Pāśupatas and, on Śaṅkara’s reading, the Pāñcarātra (2.2.37–45) — and says creation is “mere play, as in the world” (2.1.33); book 3 treats rebirth and the meditations (vidyās); book 4 the fruits of knowledge and the path of the released. The text names earlier teachers — Jaimini, Āśmarathya, Auḍulomi, Kāśakṛtsna, Bādari, Ātreya — and itself in the third person as Bādarāyaṇa, while the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra (1.1.5) cites Bādarāyaṇa.

The number of sūtras depends on the commentator: the text extracted from Śaṅkara’s commentary on GRETIL has 555 sūtras (134/157/186/78 by book), the Sansknet sūtra text 545 (the count usually given for Rāmānuja); Madhva’s division differs again. How BS 1.1.1–4 is read by Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja and Madhva is compared in `cmp:brahma-sutra-1-1-1-4`.

nodes.name: Sāyaṇa’s commentary on the Ṛgveda (Vedārthaprakāśa)
nodes.summary: The comprehensive 14th-century commentary on the whole Ṛgveda produced at Vijayanagara under Sāyaṇa’s direction at the request of Bukka I; it was the basis of Max Müller’s edition and remains the standard traditional interpretation.

nodes.name: Vikramorvaśīya of Kālidāsa
nodes.summary: Kālidāsa’s five-act Sanskrit play on the love of king Purūravas and the apsaras Urvaśī, the best-known classical retelling of the Vedic story with a happy ending in place of the Vedic separation.

dates.label: c. 4th–5th c. CE (with Kālidāsa’s generally accepted Gupta-period date)

nodes.name: Lopāmudrā
nodes.summary: Wife of Agastya who, in the dialogue hymn RV 1.179, urges her ascetic husband to love; the Anukramaṇī counts her among the women seers, and the Mahābhārata tells her story at length.

nodes.name: Sudās
nodes.summary: Ṛgvedic king of the Tṛtsu–Bharatas, patron of Vasiṣṭha (RV 7.18, 7.33) and of Viśvāmitra (RV 3.53), victor with Indra’s help in the Battle of the Ten Kings.

nodes.name: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali
nodes.summary: A Pañcāla king who teaches the brahmin Gautama (Uddālaka Āruṇi) the doctrine of the five fires and the two paths of the dead, remarking that this knowledge had never before gone to brahmins (CU 5.3–10; BU 6.2).

nodes.name: Vāmadeva
nodes.summary: Ṛgvedic poet of maṇḍala 4 whose first-person verse “I was Manu and the Sun” (RV 4.26.1) the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.4.10) cites as the realisation of one who knows “I am brahman”.

nodes.name: Iḍā
nodes.summary: The woman born from Manu’s post-flood offering of ghee, curds, whey and curd (ŚB 1.8.1.7–11), through whom Manu generates his progeny; Purūravas is called her son (aiḍa). Purāṇic genealogies make Iḷā/Ila the parent of Purūravas with Budha, son of Soma.

earliestText.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

nodes.name: The dwarf Viṣṇu wins the earth for the gods
nodes.summary: In ŚB 1.2.5 the asuras agree to give the gods as much of the earth as the dwarf Viṣṇu lies upon; Viṣṇu, who is the sacrifice, is enclosed by the metres and so obtains the whole earth — an early prose form of the later Vāmana–Bali story, without Bali.

earliestText.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

nodes.name: The Battle of the Ten Kings
nodes.summary: The Ṛgvedic battle on the Paruṣṇī (Ravi) in which king Sudās of the Tṛtsu–Bharatas, aided by Indra through Vasiṣṭha’s prayers, defeats a coalition of ten kings (RV 7.18; 7.33.3–5; 7.83).
nodes.details: Witzel treats the battle as part of the background to the later formation of the Kuru polity; it is the only extended Ṛgvedic battle narrative and has no direct sequel in the epics.

nodes.name: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali teaches the five fires
nodes.summary: The episode in which Śvetaketu fails the Pañcāla king’s questions about the fate of the dead and the king teaches Śvetaketu’s father the five fires and two paths — the earliest systematic account of rebirth, told in two versions (CU 5.3–10; BU 6.2).

nodes.name: Videgha Māthava and the eastward course of Agni
nodes.summary: King Videgha Māthava and his priest Gotama Rāhūgaṇa follow Agni Vaiśvānara as it burns eastward from the Sarasvatī across the rivers to the Sadānīrā; the land beyond, once marshy, becomes Videha (ŚB 1.4.1.10–17).
nodes.details: Historians (e.g. Witzel) read the story as a memory of the eastward spread of Vedic ritual culture from the Sarasvatī region to north Bihar; the text itself presents it as an aetiology of Videha and of a ritual verse.

nodes.name: Videha
nodes.summary: The late Vedic land east of the Sadānīrā (usually identified with the Gaṇḍak) in present north Bihar and the Nepal Tarai, ruled in the Brāhmaṇas and Upaniṣads by kings called Janaka; the Rāmāyaṇa’s Mithilā is its capital.

location.label: Mithilā region, north Bihar (India) and eastern Tarai (Nepal)

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

nodes.limits: The location is a regional approximation; the identification of the Sadānīrā with the Gaṇḍak is conventional.

nodes.name: The Upaniṣadic Janaka of Videha is Sītā’s father
nodes.summary: A popular conflation of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka/Śatapatha king Janaka Vaideha, patron of Yājñavalkya, with Janaka of Mithilā, Sītā’s father in the Rāmāyaṇa; the Vedic texts never mention Sītā, and later tradition treats “Janaka” as a title borne by many Videha kings.
nodes.details: Recorded as a claim so that the two characters (`char:janaka-videha`, `char:janaka`) stay distinct. Evidence for the conflation: same name and kingdom. Evidence against: no shared narrative; the Rāmāyaṇa’s Janaka is Sīradhvaja in its genealogy (epic agent to verify); Purāṇic king lists give many Janakas.

comparisons.title: Sītā’s fate after the banishment: Vālmīki, Kālidāsa, Bhavabhūti
comparisons.subject: narr:sita-banishment
comparisons.question: What finally becomes of Sītā after Rāma banishes her?

rows.statement: At Rāma’s horse sacrifice Sītā swears that she has never thought of anyone but Rāma and asks the goddess Earth (Mādhavī) to open for her; the Earth rises on a throne, takes her in her arms and she enters the netherworld. There is no reunion.

sources.quote: tathā me mādhavī devī vivaraṃ dātum arhati

rows.statement: Kālidāsa follows Vālmīki: Sītā calls on the Earth, the Earth appears seated on a throne raised by serpents’ hoods and carries her down; Vasiṣṭha calms Rāma’s anger.

sources.quote: sā sītām aṅkam āropya bhartari prahitekṣaṇām

rows.statement: Bhavabhūti reverses the ending: in act 7 a play staged by Vālmīki shows Sītā rescued by Gaṅgā and the Earth; the real Sītā is then restored to Rāma before the people, who accept her, and the family is reunited with Lava and Kuśa.
The Kundamālā also ends with Sītā’s vindication and reunion with Rāma rather than her disappearance into the earth.

comparisons.note: Kālidāsa keeps Vālmīki’s tragic close; the dramatists, bound by the convention that a nāṭaka should end happily, substitute reunion. VR (CE) 7.89.4 adds that Rāma took no other wife and used a golden image of Sītā at his sacrifices.

comparisons.title: Why Duḥṣanta rejects Śakuntalā: Mahābhārata vs Kālidāsa
comparisons.subject: narr:shakuntala-dushyanta
comparisons.question: Why does the king reject Śakuntalā at court, and how is she finally recognised?

rows.statement: The king remembers her but denies it (“I do not remember any bond with you”); after a long exchange a bodiless voice from the sky declares the boy his son, and Duḥṣanta explains that he had feigned ignorance so that the people would not doubt the child’s legitimacy. There is no curse and no ring.

sources.quote: bhaved dhi śaṅkā lokasya naivaṃ śuddho bhaved ayam

rows.statement: The sage Durvāsas, slighted by the distracted Śakuntalā, curses her to be forgotten until the king sees a token; the signet ring slips from her finger, so the cursed king genuinely does not know her. A fisherman finds the ring, memory returns, and Mārīca explains the curse at the reunion.

comparisons.note: Kālidāsa’s two additions — the curse and the recognition-token that gives the play its title — exonerate the king, whom the epic shows knowingly denying his wife for reasons of state.

comparisons.title: The death of Duryodhana: Mahābhārata, Bhāsa, Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa
comparisons.subject: narr:duryodhana-thighs
comparisons.question: How and in what spirit does Duryodhana die after Bhīma breaks his thighs?

rows.statement: Bhīma, prompted by Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, strikes Duryodhana’s thighs against the rules of mace fighting; Balarāma protests. Duryodhana lies dying through the night; when Aśvatthāman reports the slaughter of the sleeping Pāṇḍava camp he exults that this was more than Bhīṣma or Karṇa did for him, feels equal to Indra, and dies.

sources.quote: ūrubhyāṃ prāhiṇod rājan gadāṃ vegena pāṇḍavaḥ
manye maghavatā samam ātmānam adya vai

rows.statement: Duryodhana dies on stage before the night raid: he restrains the furious Baladeva, tells his son Durjaya to serve the Pāṇḍavas, obey Kuntī and honour Draupadī and Subhadrā as mothers, sees Śantanu, Karṇa, his brothers, Abhimanyu and the apsarases, and departs in a celestial chariot; Aśvatthāman then leaves to attack the camp.

sources.quote: eṣa sahasra-haṃsa-prayukto māṃ netuṃ vīra-vāhī vimānaḥ

rows.statement: Duryodhana is killed off stage; Bhīma enters with hands smeared with his blood and binds Draupadī’s braid, fulfilling his vow, and Yudhiṣṭhira is consecrated.

comparisons.note: The Ūrubhaṅga is the classic exception to the rule that a hero may not die on the Sanskrit stage; its repentant, reconciling Duryodhana inverts the epic’s exultant one. The order of events also changes: in the epic he outlives the night raid, in the play he dies before it.

comparisons.title: Arjuna and Śiva the hunter: Mahābhārata 3.38–41 vs Bhāravi’s Kirātārjunīya
comparisons.subject: narr:kirata-arjuna
comparisons.question: How does Arjuna come to fight Śiva and obtain the Pāśupata weapon?

rows.statement: Sent by Yudhiṣṭhira, Arjuna reaches Indrakīla, where Indra, disguised as an ascetic, tests him and promises weapons once he has seen Śiva. Śiva comes as a kirāta with Umā, his goblins and women; Arjuna and the hunter shoot the boar-demon Mūka together, quarrel and fight until Śiva crushes Arjuna senseless, then reveals himself and gives the Pāśupata (brahmaśiras) weapon; the world-guardians add theirs.

sources.quote: tataḥ papāta saṃmūḍhas tataḥ prīto 'bhavad bhavaḥ
dadāni te 'straṃ dayitam ahaṃ pāśupataṃ mahat

rows.statement: Bhāravi adds the political frame — the spy’s report and the speeches of Draupadī and Bhīma urging war, and Vyāsa’s counsel (cantos 1–3) — and long descriptive cantos. Celestial nymphs try to seduce the ascetic (7–10); Indra’s visit comes after this, not on arrival (11). Śiva leads a whole kirāta army of his gaṇas (12), the boar is an unnamed demon (12.37), and the fight becomes a battle of armies and magical weapons (14–17) ending in wrestling (18) before Śiva grants the weapon (18.44).

comparisons.note: The epic’s two chapters become eighteen cantos; the expansion is mainly rhetorical and descriptive, but the sequence (Indra’s test) and the scale of Śiva’s following also change.

comparisons.title: The family of Viśravas: Vālmīki vs the Mahābhārata
comparisons.subject: lin:paulastya
comparisons.question: Who is Kubera’s father, and who are the mothers of Rāvaṇa and his siblings?

rows.statement: Viśravas is Pulastya’s son; Kubera (Vaiśravaṇa) is Viśravas’s son by Bharadvāja’s daughter. Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā and Vibhīṣaṇa are all children of Viśravas by Kaikasī, daughter of the rākṣasa Sumālin.

Kubera (Vaiśravaṇa) is Pulastya’s own son; Viśravas is produced from half of Pulastya’s body out of anger at Kubera. Kubera gives his father three rākṣasīs: Puṣpotkaṭā bears Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa, Mālinī bears Vibhīṣaṇa, Rākā bears the twins Khara and Śūrpaṇakhā.

sources.quote: tasya vaiśravaṇo nāma gavi putro 'bhavat prabhuḥ
mālinī janayām āsa putram ekaṃ vibhīṣaṇam

comparisons.note: Both texts make all of them Paulastyas (see the restored MEMBER_OF assertions epic:342–348), but they disagree on Kubera’s generation and on the mothers.

comparisons.title: Karṇa’s gift of his armour: Mahābhārata vs Bhāsa’s Karṇabhāra
comparisons.subject: narr:karna-armour-gift
comparisons.question: When and on what terms does Karṇa give his armour and earrings to Indra?

rows.statement: During the Pāṇḍavas’ exile, warned in a dream by the Sun, Karṇa nonetheless gives Indra (disguised as a brahmin) his armour and earrings, but first bargains for Indra’s unfailing spear, usable once; he flays them from his body.

On the battlefield, about to fight with Śalya as his charioteer, Karṇa gives the brahmin-disguised Indra his armour and earrings unasked for anything; afterwards a divine messenger brings the spear Vimalā from the remorseful Indra, which Karṇa at first refuses.

comparisons.note: Bhāsa moves the episode from the exile to the eve of Karṇa’s last battle and removes the bargain, turning it into pure generosity.

comparisons.title: How Bharata learns of Daśaratha’s death: Vālmīki vs Bhāsa
comparisons.subject: char:bharata-ramayana
comparisons.question: How does Bharata learn that his father has died?

rows.statement: Summoned home from his uncle’s, Bharata finds the palace empty; Kaikeyī tells him that his father “has gone the way of all beings”, and that Rāma is exiled.

sources.quote: yā gatiḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ tāṃ gatiṃ te pitā gataḥ

rows.statement: Returning, Bharata stops at the statue-house of the dead Ikṣvāku kings outside Ayodhyā and, seeing a new statue of Daśaratha among them, realises that his father is dead.

comparisons.note: The statue-house scene is the invention that gives the Pratimānāṭaka its name.

comparisons.title: Kṛṣṇa across the Mahābhārata, Gītā, Harivaṃśa, Viṣṇu Purāṇa and Bhāgavata Purāṇa
comparisons.subject: char:krishna
comparisons.question: How is Kṛṣṇa presented — hero, partial descent, or the supreme Lord himself — and how much of his cowherd childhood is told?

rows.statement: A Vṛṣṇi prince, ally and charioteer of the Pāṇḍavas, called a portion (aṃśa) of Nārāyaṇa (1.61.90) and born from Nārāyaṇa’s black hair (1.189.31). He reveals a cosmic form at the Kaurava court (5.129) and dies from a hunter’s arrow (16.5). His childhood exploits (Pūtanā, Govardhana) are only alluded to, in Śiśupāla’s mocking speech (2.38.4–9).
Kṛṣṇa speaks as the Lord who “whenever dharma declines” takes birth age after age to protect the good (6.26.7–8) and shows Arjuna his universal form (6.33). No childhood narrative.

sources.quote: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata

rows.statement: Viṣṇu resolves to descend; Kṛṣṇa is born to Devakī as Yaśodā bears a daughter (48.11), grows up in Vraja, subdues Kāliya (55–56), lifts Govardhana (61–62), sports at night with the cowherd women (63.24–35), kills Kaṃsa (76) and founds Dvārakā (85–86): the first connected childhood narrative.

Viṣṇu plucks a white and a black hair, which become Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa (5.1.60–64: “this eighth embryo will be my hair”); the life of Kṛṣṇa follows the Harivaṃśa closely — birth (5.3), Govardhana (5.11), the night with the gopīs (5.13.15–48), Kaṃsa’s death (5.20).

After listing the descents, it declares “these are portions and parts of the Puruṣa, but Kṛṣṇa is the Lord himself” (1.3.28), though 2.7.26 still speaks of him appearing with a portion as “white-and-black-haired”. Book 10 greatly expands the childhood, culminating in the rāsa with the gopīs (10.29–33).

sources.quote: ete cāṃśakalāḥ puṃsaḥ kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam

comparisons.note: The “hair” motif (MBh 1.189.31; ViP 5.1.60; BhP 2.7.26) and the Bhāgavata’s “bhagavān svayam” (1.3.28) are the textual poles of the later debate on whether Kṛṣṇa is an avatāra of Viṣṇu or their source (Gauḍīya view). See Matchett 2001.

comparisons.title: The Rāma story in Vālmīki and in the Mahābhārata’s Rāmopākhyāna
comparisons.subject: char:rama
comparisons.question: Which parts of the Rāma story does each version tell, and how do they differ?

rows.statement: Seven books: frame with Vālmīki, Nārada and the krauñca (1.1–4); births as portions of Viṣṇu (1.17); Viśvāmitra, Tāṭakā, Ahalyā, the bow and the four weddings (1.24–72); Paraśurāma (1.73–75); exile (Book 2); abduction (3.40–49); vānara alliance and Vālin (Book 4); Hanumān in Laṅkā (Book 5); war, fire ordeal and Brahmā’s hymn (6.103–106); consecration (6.116); Rāvaṇa’s back-story, Hanumān’s childhood, banishment, Śambūka, the twins and Sītā’s return to the earth (Book 7).

Told by Mārkaṇḍeya to console Yudhiṣṭhira. Opens with Rāvaṇa’s Paulastya genealogy and boon (3.258–259); Brahmā says Viṣṇu has descended and has the gods beget monkey allies, and sends the gandharvī Dundubhī as Mantharā (3.260). Omits the Viśvāmitra episodes, Ahalyā, the bow contest and the marriages (Sītā is simply Janaka’s daughter made by Tvaṣṭṛ, 3.258.9); compresses the exile; Lakṣmaṇa kills Kumbhakarṇa (3.271.16) and Indrajit (3.273); after Rāvaṇa’s death Sītā is vindicated by divine testimony without a fire-entry (3.275.10–36). No Uttarakāṇḍa material: no banishment, no twins.

comparisons.note: Whether the Rāmopākhyāna abridges Vālmīki (majority view) or preserves an older/independent telling is unresolved; see assertion text:ramopakhyana DERIVED_FROM text:valmiki-ramayana.

comparisons.title: Sītā’s birth
comparisons.subject: char:sita
comparisons.question: How was Sītā born and whose daughter is she?

rows.statement: Janaka found her rising from the furrow as he ploughed a field and named her Sītā; she is “not born of a womb” (ayonijā).
The Uttarakāṇḍa adds that she is the ascetic Vedavatī, reborn in the Tretā age to destroy Rāvaṇa.
“Janaka was king of Videha; Sītā was his daughter (ātmajā), whom Tvaṣṭṛ himself fashioned to be Rāma’s beloved queen.” No furrow-birth.
In the Jain telling Sītā is born to Janaka and his queen as twin of Bhāmaṇḍala (recall; not checked against the text).

comparisons.title: Sītā’s ordeal and banishment
comparisons.subject: char:sita
comparisons.question: After Rāvaṇa’s death, how is Sītā’s fidelity tested, and is she later banished?

rows.statement: Rāma publicly repudiates her; she has Lakṣmaṇa build a pyre and enters the fire calling Agni to witness (6.104.18–26); Brahmā hymns Rāma as Nārāyaṇa and Sītā as Lakṣmī (6.105); Agni returns her unharmed (6.106.1–3) and Rāma accepts her.

Uttarakāṇḍa: because of citizens’ gossip (7.44), Rāma has Lakṣmaṇa leave the pregnant Sītā near Vālmīki’s hermitage (7.46–47); she bears Lava and Kuśa (7.58); asked for a fresh oath at the horse sacrifice, she calls on the earth goddess Mādhavī, who takes her down on a throne (7.88.10–14).

Rāma tells Sītā to go, unwilling to take back a woman who lived in another’s house; she swears by the elements; Vāyu, Agni and Varuṇa declare her innocent, Brahmā reveals that Nalakūbara’s curse had protected her, and Daśaratha appears. No fire-entry; no banishment.
The real Sītā is placed in Agni’s keeping before the abduction and a “shadow” (māyā) Sītā is carried off; the fire ordeal restores the real Sītā (recall; a motif taken up by Tulsīdās).
Kampaṉ’s poem ends with the coronation; the Uttarakāṇḍa banishment is not part of his work (later supplements exist) (recall).

comparisons.note: Unreconciled: the fire-entry is Vālmīki-specific among the Sanskrit epic tellings; the banishment is confined to the Uttarakāṇḍa.

comparisons.title: Who kills Kumbhakarṇa?
comparisons.subject: char:kumbhakarna
comparisons.question: Who kills Rāvaṇa’s brother Kumbhakarṇa?

rows.statement: Rāma kills him (“having killed Kumbhakarṇa … Bharata’s elder brother rejoiced”).
Lakṣmaṇa burns him with the Brahmā weapon (“taṃ brahmāstreṇa saumitrir dadāha”).

comparisons.title: Karṇa’s parentage and status across the parvans
comparisons.subject: char:karna
comparisons.question: How do different parts of the Mahābhārata tell of Karṇa’s birth and social status?

rows.statement: The aṃśāvataraṇa makes him “a portion of Divākara” (1.61.89). The maiden Kuntī invokes the Sun with Durvāsas’s mantra, bears a son with armour and earrings, abandons him, and “the husband of Rādhā” takes him up (1.104.8–14).

At the tournament Kṛpa asks his mother, father and lineage; Duryodhana makes him king of Aṅga; when Adhiratha arrives Bhīma calls him a sūta’s son unfit for Aṅga; Kuntī secretly recognises him (1.127.22).

A long retelling: Sūrya warns him in a dream; Kuntī’s boon from Durvāsas; the basket set adrift on the Aśvanadī that drifts to the Carmaṇvatī, Yamunā and Gaṅgā (3.292.6–26); the childless Rādhā and Adhiratha adopt him (3.293); he gives Indra his armour and earrings for the spear (3.294).

Kṛṣṇa tells him that a kānīna son belongs to the mother’s husband, so “by dharma you are Pāṇḍu’s son” and the eldest Pāṇḍava, and offers him the throne (5.138.8–9, 11–27); Kuntī asks him to join his brothers and he promises to spare all but Arjuna (5.142–144).
After the war Kuntī reveals that Karṇa was her son; the Pāṇḍavas mourn him.

Yudhiṣṭhira grieves for his “elder brother Karṇa” (12.1.37); Nārada tells how Karṇa, posing as a Bhārgava brahmin, studied under Rāma Jāmadagnya and was cursed by him and by a brahmin (12.2–3); Yudhiṣṭhira curses all women never to keep a secret (12.6.10).
Kuntī confesses to Vyāsa that she cast the secretly born child into the water.

comparisons.note: Unreconciled: “sūtaputra” status (Ādi) versus legal Pāṇḍava status argued by Kṛṣṇa (Udyoga); McGrath (2004) discusses Karṇa as the epic’s alternative hero.

comparisons.title: Draupadī’s five husbands: the justifications in the Ādiparvan
comparisons.subject: char:draupadi
comparisons.question: What reasons does the Mahābhārata itself give for Draupadī’s marriage to all five Pāṇḍavas?

rows.statement: Kuntī, not seeing what her sons have brought, tells them to “enjoy it together”, and her word must be kept.
Objection within the text: Drupada calls it adharma, contrary to world and Veda; Dhṛṣṭadyumna cannot decide because of the subtlety of dharma.

Yudhiṣṭhira cites the Purāṇic precedent of Jaṭilā Gautamī, wife of seven sages, and the authority of the mother’s (guru’s) word. (A second precedent, Vārkṣī wife of the ten Pracetas, appears only in star passage *1910 after 1.188.14, not in the constituted text.)

Vyāsa privately tells Drupada that the Pāṇḍavas are five former Indras condemned by Śiva to human birth, and Draupadī is Śrī destined to be their common wife; he grants Drupada divine sight to see them.
A sage’s daughter, unable to find a husband, asked Śiva five times for a husband and was granted five in her next birth — told again by Vyāsa to the Pāṇḍavas at Ekacakrā (1.157.6–16).
The catalogue of incarnations says a part of Śrī was born in Drupada’s line from the altar, to captivate five men.

comparisons.note: Five distinct justifications (maternal command, precedent, divine plan, karmic boon, incarnation) stand side by side without harmonisation; Hiltebeitel (2001) reads them as a deliberate layering.

comparisons.title: Vidura’s origin: internal variation
comparisons.subject: char:vidura
comparisons.question: Whose incarnation or son is Vidura?

rows.statement: Son of Vyāsa by a servant woman, “Dharma in the form of Vidura, through the curse of that great-souled one”.
Explains the curse: Aṇī-Māṇḍavya, impaled though innocent, curses Dharma to be born of a śūdra woman.
The aṃśāvataraṇa says: “know Vidura, best of the wise, born in this world as … the son of Atri”, without mention of Dharma.

comparisons.title: Who restores Draupadī’s garment?
comparisons.subject: narr:draupadi-humiliation
comparisons.question: When Duḥśāsana pulls at Draupadī’s garment in the assembly hall, what makes it endless?

rows.statement: No agent is named: as he pulled, “another garment of the same kind appeared, many times over” (tadrūpam aparaṃ vastraṃ prādurāsīd anekaśaḥ).
Many manuscripts insert Draupadī’s prayer to Kṛṣṇa — “govinda dvārakāvāsin kṛṣṇa gopījanapriya …” — so that Kṛṣṇa (or Dharma) supplies the garments; the vulgate (Ganguli’s Sabhā Parva) follows this.

sources.locator: Sabhā Parva, Dyūta sub-parvan (vulgate; section number not checked)

comparisons.note: A clear case where the Critical Edition’s constituted text and the popular/vulgate tradition differ on a famous detail.

comparisons.title: Gaṇeśa in Gupta, Pāla and Cōḻa art (with the textual prescriptions)
comparisons.subject: deity:ganesha
comparisons.question: How is Gaṇeśa represented — arms, attributes, mount, posture and setting — in the Gupta, Pāla and Cōḻa traditions, and what do the texts prescribe?

rows.statement: Earliest securely datable images (4th–6th c.): two-armed, pot-bellied, without a mount; often holding his broken tusk and a bowl of sweets that the trunk reaches into; appears as an attendant figure (e.g. beside the Mothers) rather than as a main temple icon.

Eastern Indian steles (8th–12th c.): usually four-armed or more, often dancing (Nṛtta-Gaṇapati) on a lotus base with the rat below, framed by a carved back-slab with flying attendants; attributes include tusk, rosary, axe and sweets.

Tamil images (10th–13th c.) in bronze and stone: four-armed, seated or standing, goad and noose in the rear hands, tusk and modaka in the front; placed in the south niche of the main vimāna beside Dakṣiṇāmūrti in the Cōḻa programme.

Prescribes a human-bodied, big-bellied, elephant-faced Vināyaka with a sacred thread and a long trunk, holding his own tusk and an axe on one side and a laḍḍuka and a lotus on the other; gives the trunk 36 aṅgulas.
