Only Kern’s text has a verse on Gaṇeśa (58.58): lord of the pramathas, elephant-faced, pendulous belly, holding an axe, single-tusked, carrying a radish; Tripathi’s text and Utpala lack it.

comparisons.note: Rows are period styles, not single objects; each statement summarises typical features. The Pāla and Cōḻa rows are from recall and should be checked against specific museum objects.

comparisons.title: Dancing Śiva at Bādāmi Cave 1 and in Cōḻa bronzes
comparisons.subject: deity:nataraja
comparisons.question: How does the earliest dated dancing Śiva of the Deccan differ from the classic Cōḻa Naṭarāja?

rows.statement: Late 6th-century rock-cut relief on the façade of Cave 1: Śiva dances with eighteen arms fanned out like a wheel, several holding a drum, trident, serpent and other attributes, many simply in dance gestures; Nandin and Gaṇeśa accompany him. There is no ring of fire and no dwarf under his foot.
Mid-6th-century Naṭarāja panel in Cave 1: an eight-armed dancing Śiva surrounded by gods, part of a programme of Śaiva panels.

11th-century bronze: four arms — upper right drum, upper left fire, lower right abhaya, lower left across the body in the elephant-trunk gesture pointing to the raised left foot; right foot on the dwarf Apasmāra; flying locks with the tiny Gaṅgā; encircled by a flaming arch (prabhāmaṇḍala/tiruvāci). This ānanda-tāṇḍava type is associated with Chidambaram.
c. 1010: Śiva is carved dancing the karaṇas of the Nāṭyaśāstra in the upper passage of the vimāna, a different, textual approach to the dancing god from the single cult bronze.

comparisons.note: The Bādāmi relief is a many-armed tāṇḍava; the Cōḻa four-armed form is not derived from it in a straight line.

comparisons.title: Mahiṣāsuramardinī: Kuṣāṇa, Gupta, Pallava, Pāla and the Agni Purāṇa
comparisons.subject: deity:mahishasuramardini
comparisons.question: How are the Goddess and the buffalo demon shown at different periods, and how does that compare with the textual prescription?

rows.statement: Kuṣāṇa Mathurā (1st–2nd c.): a small four- or six-armed goddess, standing, pressing down or lifting an entirely animal buffalo with her hands; no lion and no battle.
Early 5th c.: the Goddess, with more arms and weapons, stands over the animal buffalo, piercing it with a trident; still a static cult image.
Mid–late 7th c.: a narrative battle relief: the eight-armed Goddess rides her lion with an army of gaṇas against a buffalo-headed warrior who retreats with his troops.
Eastern India (9th–12th c.): ten- or more-armed Goddess on the lion; the demon in human form emerges from the neck of the decapitated buffalo and is held by his hair or the noose.
Caṇḍī has twenty arms (or ten); a man springs, weapon raised, from the buffalo’s neck, bound by the noose and attacked by the lion — the composition of the later images.
The narrative: Mahiṣa changes form — buffalo, lion, man, elephant — and is killed as he half-emerges from the buffalo’s mouth, pinned under the Goddess’s foot and beheaded.

comparisons.note: The “emerging man” motif appears in images only after the narrative of the Devī Māhātmya was in circulation; the Kuṣāṇa images predate the surviving text.

comparisons.title: The image of Viṣṇu in the Bṛhat Saṃhitā, the Agni Purāṇa, the Viṣṇudharmottara and the Mayamata
comparisons.subject: deity:vishnu
comparisons.question: What arms, attributes and proportions do the treatises prescribe for an image of Viṣṇu?

rows.statement: Viṣṇu may have eight, four or two arms; dark as the flax flower, in yellow garments, with Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, crown and earrings. Eight-armed: right hands sword, mace, arrow and a peace-giving hand; left hands bow, shield, discus and conch. Four-armed: right peace-giving and mace; left conch and discus. Two-armed: right peace-giving, left conch. The image is twice the height of its pedestal, which is a third of the door height less an eighth.

The eight-armed Viṣṇu sits on Tārkṣya (Garuḍa): right hands sword, mace, arrow and varada; left hands bow, shield, discus and conch — the Bṛhat Saṃhitā’s list, but with a boon-giving instead of a peace-giving hand and with Garuḍa as mount.
The four-armed standing Viṣṇu takes twenty-four names according to the order of lotus, conch, discus and mace in the four hands (Keśava: lotus, conch, discus, mace).
The Viṣṇudharmottara gives Viṣṇu (as Vāsudeva) four arms with personified mace and discus beneath the lower hands and treats the four faces of the Vaikuṇṭha form theologically.

Southern practice: standing Viṣṇu with discus and conch in the rear hands, the front hands in abhaya/varada or resting on hip or thigh; the principal image measured on the large ten-tāla canon (uttama daśatāla).

comparisons.note: The two verified Sanskrit prescriptions (BS and AP) agree almost word for word on the eight-armed Viṣṇu; the Mayamata and Viṣṇudharmottara rows are from recall and need chapter-level checking.

comparisons.title: The mount of Varuṇa: goose or makara?
comparisons.subject: deity:varuna
comparisons.question: On what animal does Varuṇa ride?

rows.statement: Varuṇa rides a goose (haṃsa) and holds a noose.
Varuṇa rides a makara and holds a noose.

comparisons.note: Medieval temple images generally follow the makara tradition.

comparisons.title: The image of Sūrya: texts and early images
comparisons.subject: deity:surya
comparisons.question: How is the Sun god to be dressed and equipped?

rows.statement: Northern dress, covered from the feet to the chest; crown, earrings, long necklace, girdle, coat (kañcuka), jewelled halo; a lotus in each hand; nose, forehead, shanks, thighs, cheeks and chest prominent.
On a one-wheeled chariot with seven horses, holding two lotuses; Daṇḍin and Piṅgala at the door; alternatively a single Sūrya on horseback.
Kuṣāṇa Mathurā Sūryas (2nd c.): seated in a chariot drawn by two or four horses, wearing a tunic and boots, holding a lotus bud and a short sword.
13th c.: the whole temple is Sūrya’s chariot with 24 wheels and seven horses; standing booted Sūrya images in the niches.

comparisons.title: The divisions of the liṅga
comparisons.subject: deity:linga
comparisons.question: How is the liṅga divided and proportioned?

rows.statement: Divide the length in three: square at the base, octagonal in the middle, round above; the square part is set in the ground, the middle in the pedestal; a thin, over-long liṅga ruins the land.
The three parts are assigned to Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva; the octagonal part is Viṣṇu’s. Liṅgas are ranked by material, from salt, ghee and cloth through clay, wood and stone to pearl, metals and gems.

comparisons.title: Who are the Mothers? Bṛhat Saṃhitā, Devī Māhātmya and Agni Purāṇa
comparisons.subject: deity:matrikas
comparisons.question: Which Mothers are named, and how are they distinguished?

rows.statement: Gives no list: the band of Mothers is to be made with the marks of the gods whose names they bear.

Seven śaktis come out of the gods with their forms, ornaments and mounts: Brahmāṇī (swan-car, rosary, water-pot), Māheśvarī (bull, trident), Kaumārī (peacock, spear), Vaiṣṇavī (Garuḍa, conch, discus, mace, bow, sword), Vārāhī (boar form), Nārasiṃhī (lion form) and Aindrī (elephant, thunderbolt); Śivadūtī and Cāmuṇḍā fight beside them.

Seven Mothers: four-faced Brāhmī on a swan with rosary; white Śāṅkarī on a bull; red, two-armed Kaumārī on a peacock with a spear; Vaiṣṇavī (called Lakṣmī) with discus, conch, mace and lotus; Vārāhī on a buffalo; thousand-eyed Aindrī with thunderbolt; and emaciated Cāmuṇḍā on a corpse. Nārasiṃhī is absent.

comparisons.note: The Agni Purāṇa list matches the usual sculptural Saptamātṛkā row (ending with Cāmuṇḍā); the Devī Māhātmya’s seven include Nārasiṃhī instead.

comparisons.title: The rāsa-līlā in the Harivaṃśa, Viṣṇu Purāṇa and Bhāgavata
comparisons.subject: narr:rasa-lila
comparisons.question: How does each text tell Kṛṣṇa's nocturnal dance with the gopīs?

rows.statement: Short erotic description: on autumn nights Kṛṣṇa delights the young cowherd women, who sing his deeds in rows and pairs, imitate him and cling to him; no flute, no disappearance, no search, and the constituted text does not use the word rāsa (63.25, 63.35 'adorned with circles of gopīs').

Kṛṣṇa's song draws the gopīs; he vanishes; they act out his deeds and follow his footprints and those of a favoured gopī; he reappears and forms the rāsa-maṇḍala, holding each gopī by the hand; the chapter closes by declaring him the all-pervading Self.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Five chapters: the flute call, Kṛṣṇa's test of the gopīs, his disappearance at their pride, the search and footprints of one favoured gopī, the Gopī-gīta, the reunion, and the rāsa with Kṛṣṇa multiplied between each pair of women (10.33.3); Parīkṣit asks how the upholder of dharma could do this (10.33.26–37).
Reproduces the Viṣṇu Purāṇa account almost verbatim (rāsa-goṣṭhī, rāsa-maṇḍala).

sources.edition: Brahmapurāṇa 1–246, Tübingen Purāṇa Project (P. Schreiner, R. Söhnen-Thieme); GRETIL e-text

comparisons.note: The sequence HV → ViP → BhP is generally read as successive elaboration (Hardy 1983; Schweig 2005); the Brahma Purāṇa copies the ViP. The named favourite, Rādhā, is absent from all four.

comparisons.title: Where the Syamantaka jewel came from and how long Kṛṣṇa fought Jāmbavān
comparisons.subject: narr:syamantaka
comparisons.question: Who first obtained the jewel, from where, and how long did the fight with Jāmbavān last?

rows.statement: Prasena obtained the jewel 'from the ocean' as Dvāravatī was being founded; the story of the Sun giving it to Satrājit is a star (inserted) passage after 28.12. Kṛṣṇa fought Jāmbavān in the cave 'with his arms alone' for twenty-one days.
The Sun (Vivasvat) takes the jewel from his own neck and gives it to his friend Satrājit; the fight lasts twenty-one days.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Prasena(jit) obtained it 'from the Sun' (sūryād), with the Sun episode in the constituted text.

sources.edition: Brahmapurāṇa 1–246, Tübingen Purāṇa Project (P. Schreiner, R. Söhnen-Thieme); GRETIL e-text
sources.quote: divyaṃ syamantakaṃ nāma sa sūryād upalabdhavān

rows.statement: The Sun, pleased with Satrājit, gives him the jewel; Kṛṣṇa and Jāmbavān fight for twenty-eight days (aṣṭā-viṃśa-aham), and Jāmbavān recognises his lord Rāma; in 10.83.10 Jāmbavatī says twenty-seven days.

comparisons.note: The critical Harivaṃśa's 'from the ocean' reading versus the Sun-gift in the Viṣṇu, Brahma and Bhāgavata Purāṇas suggests the solar origin entered the story in later redaction; part of the Harivaṃśa manuscript tradition carries the Sun episode as an inserted passage.

comparisons.title: Order and form of Kṛṣṇa's infant exploits
comparisons.subject: char:krishna
comparisons.question: Which infancy episodes does each text tell, and in what form?

rows.statement: Cart overturned (50.4–19), then Pūtanā as a night-bird (50.20–24); then the binding to the mortar and the twin trees (51). No Tṛṇāvarta, Agha or Brahmā episode.
Pūtanā (5.5), then the cart (5.6.1–8), the binding and the trees (5.6.9–20). No Tṛṇāvarta.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Pūtanā (10.6), the cart and Tṛṇāvarta (10.7), butter-stealing and the universe in Kṛṣṇa's mouth (10.8), the binding (10.9) and the cursed yakṣas (10.10), then Vatsa, Baka (10.11), Agha (10.12) and Brahmā's theft (10.13–14).
Lists Pūtanā, the twin arjunas and the cart, then Kāliya, in a brief digest.

sources.edition: Rajendralal Mitra ed. (Bibliotheca Indica 1870–79); GRETIL e-text

comparisons.title: The burning of Tripura in the Mahābhārata, Matsya, Liṅga, Śiva and Bhāgavata
comparisons.subject: narr:tripura-dahana
comparisons.question: Who builds and defends the three cities, and what part does Viṣṇu play in their destruction?

rows.statement: The three sons of Tāraka receive from Brahmā cities of gold, silver and iron, built by Maya; Hari, son of Tārakākṣa, makes a pool that revives the dead. The gods build a chariot of the cosmos with Brahmā as charioteer; Viṣṇu, Soma and Agni form the arrow, and Śiva burns the cities with one shot. Told by Duryodhana as a model for Śalya's charioteership.

Maya is the protagonist, builder and war-leader; Keśava in bull form drinks the nectar pond (136.63–65); Nandin kills Vidyunmālin (140.38); Śiva's arrow burns the cities; Maya's house survives in the ocean (140.75–78).

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176
sources.quote: nandinā sādite daitye vidyunmālau hate mayaḥ

rows.statement: The asuras are pious Śiva-worshippers; Viṣṇu by his māyā creates an obstacle to their dharma (1.71.71–74) so that Śiva may destroy them.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay 1906), rev. O. Hellwig after Calcutta 1960; GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: Viṣṇu creates a shaven-headed teacher who converts the Tripura asuras to a 'Jina'/Arhat doctrine (2.5.4–5); Śiva first worships Gaṇeśa (2.5.10.7–14), then burns the cities; Maya, a devotee, is spared and given Vitala (2.5.12).

sources.edition: Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

rows.statement: Told within the Prahlāda book: Maya's reviving well; Viṣṇu as a cow, with Brahmā as the calf, drinks it dry; Śiva burns the cities.

comparisons.note: The motif of Viṣṇu destroying the demons' religion appears in several Purāṇas in Buddhist or Jain dress (cf. the 'Māyāmoha' whom Viṣṇu sends to the daityas in ViP 3.17.41–3.18.32, who preaches an 'Arhat' doctrine and appears red-robed); it reflects sectarian polemic, not a historical event.

comparisons.title: Who kills Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and how?
comparisons.subject: narr:madhu-kaitabha
comparisons.question: Which deity kills the two demons born during Viṣṇu's cosmic sleep, and what is the decisive device?

rows.statement: Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa) alone; the demons grant him a boon and ask to die where there is no covering; he beheads them with the discus on his bare thighs.
The demons steal the Vedas from Brahmā; Viṣṇu as Hayaśiras (horse-head) recovers them; the demons then fight Nārāyaṇa, who kills them.
Viṣṇu kills them on the single ocean; their fat (medas) forms the earth, hence 'Medinī'.
Brahmā praises the Goddess as Yoganidrā; she leaves Viṣṇu's eyes, he wakes and kills the demons — the Goddess is the enabling power and the first carita's true subject.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition

rows.statement: Prahlāda's hymn: in the form of Hayaśiras Viṣṇu killed the Veda-stealing Madhu and Kaiṭabha.

comparisons.title: How the androgynous Śiva (Ardhanārīśvara) originates
comparisons.subject: narr:ardhanarishvara-origin
comparisons.question: Why and how does Śiva appear as half-man, half-woman?

rows.statement: Rudra springs from Brahmā's angry brow with a body half woman, half man; told to divide himself, he separates the female and male and multiplies each.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Same account of Rudra born half-woman from Brahmā.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition

rows.statement: Same pattern: Rudra appears as ardhanārīnaravapu at creation.
Mahādeva, born as Brahmā's son, becomes Ardhanārīśvara, bright as the rising sun, and the female half is given to creation.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay 1906), rev. O. Hellwig after Calcutta 1960; GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: Brahmā cannot make creation increase because no women exist; he worships Śiva, who appears as Ardhanārīśvara and separates the Goddess from his body; Brahmā asks her to be born as Dakṣa's daughter.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay), books 1 and 7; GRETIL e-text

comparisons.note: The androgyne appears in sculpture from the Kuṣāṇa period at Mathurā; the textual aetiologies are later and differ on whether the androgyne is a birth-form of Rudra or a theophany of the supreme Śiva.

comparisons.title: Who takes the poison of the churning?
comparisons.subject: narr:nilakantha
comparisons.question: What happens to the poison that rises from the churned ocean?

rows.statement: Constituted text: no poison episode. Passages in the critical apparatus (App. I after 1.16.15 and 1.16.27; *268, *274) have Rudra drink the hālāhala and become Nīlakaṇṭha.
No poison episode in the constituted text.
The nāgas take the poison.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: The hālāhala rises first; at the Prajāpatis' plea Śiva, with Pārvatī's assent, drinks it from his palm and it turns his throat blue, 'an ornament of the good'.
Śiva tells Pārvatī how he drank the kālakūṭa at Brahmā's request and holds it in his throat.

comparisons.title: Gaṇeśa's birth and elephant head across the Purāṇas
comparisons.subject: deity:ganesha
comparisons.question: Who produces Gaṇeśa, and how does he come to have an elephant's head?

rows.statement: Pārvatī shapes an elephant-headed figure from her bath-unguent and throws it into the Gaṅgā; it comes alive as the Gaṅgā's son Gāṅgeya; Brahmā makes him lord of the Vināyakas. No beheading.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

rows.statement: At the gods' request Śiva himself takes the form of an elephant-faced Gaṇeśvara, born of Ambikā, to obstruct the asuras' rites. No beheading.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay 1906), rev. O. Hellwig after Calcutta 1960; GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: A radiant youth springs from Śiva's laughter; jealous when Umā admires him, Śiva curses him to be elephant-faced and pot-bellied; Vināyakas arise from Śiva's sweat.

Pārvatī makes a door-keeper son from her body's dirt; Śiva beheads him with the trident after a battle; an elephant head (the first one found facing north) is fitted and he is revived and made first-worshipped lord of the gaṇas. The text cites the Śani version as belonging to another kalpa.

sources.edition: Śiva Purāṇa (vulgate), Rudrasaṃhitā; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

rows.statement: The infant's head falls when Śani looks at him; Viṣṇu cuts the head from a sleeping elephant with his discus and fits it.

sources.edition: Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa (vulgate), Gaṇapatikhaṇḍa; Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

comparisons.note: Courtright (1985) reads the beheading-and-restoration plot as the dominant later form; the Matsya and Liṅga versions without a beheading are generally considered earlier, but none of these chapters is securely dated.

comparisons.title: What provokes the Narasiṃha manifestation?
comparisons.subject: narr:narasimha-prahlada
comparisons.question: Why does Viṣṇu appear as the man-lion, and what is Prahlāda's role?

rows.statement: Hiraṇyakaśipu, made invulnerable by Brahmā's boon, oppresses the gods; at their plea Viṣṇu enters his hall as Narasiṃha and tears him apart. Prahlāda plays no part.

Brahmā's boon and the gods' appeal again provide the cause; when the man-lion enters the court, Prahlāda alone sees with divine sight that it is the god and warns his father; Narasiṃha kills Hiraṇyakaśipu with his claws.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

rows.statement: The cause is the persecution of Prahlāda for his devotion (poison, serpents, elephants, fire, the sea); the killing by Narasiṃha is only alluded to afterwards (1.20.32).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Framed by the curse of Jaya and Vijaya; Hiraṇyakaśipu seeks revenge for Hiraṇyākṣa, wins Brahmā's boon (7.3.35–38), persecutes Prahlāda, and Narasiṃha emerges from a pillar to prove Prahlāda's word that the Lord is everywhere (7.8.17–29).
Narasiṃha appears in Hiraṇyakaśipu's city; the king sends his son Prahlāda to kill him; Prahlāda fights, is defeated, then recognises Vāsudeva and urges his father and Hiraṇyākṣa to submit.
Narasiṃha kills Hiraṇyakaśipu but his fury threatens the worlds; Śiva assumes the Śarabha form and subdues him.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay 1906), rev. O. Hellwig after Calcutta 1960; GRETIL e-text

comparisons.note: Prahlāda's persecution as the trigger is a Vaiṣṇava devotional development (ViP, BhP); the Harivaṃśa and Matsya keep the older deva–asura frame of a boon-proud tyrant.

comparisons.title: How Viṣṇu acquires the horse's head
comparisons.subject: deity:hayagriva
comparisons.question: Why does Viṣṇu take the horse-headed form?

rows.statement: To recover the Vedas stolen by Madhu and Kaiṭabha he assumes the horse-headed form, retrieves them from the underworld, and then kills the demons.
Hayaśiras kills Madhu and Kaiṭabha (7.9.37); separately, a demon named Hayagrīva steals the Vedas and is killed by the Fish (8.24).

A termite created by Brahmā gnaws the bowstring on which the sleeping Viṣṇu rests his chin; the string snaps and cuts off his head; the Goddess has a horse's head fitted so that he can kill the demon Hayagrīva, who could die only at a horse-headed being's hands.

sources.edition: Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa (vulgate); Sanskrit Wikisource e-text

comparisons.title: The seven continents and seven oceans in the Viṣṇu, Bhāgavata and Matsya Purāṇas
comparisons.subject: place:bhumandala
comparisons.question: In what order do the continents (dvīpas) and their encircling oceans run outward from Jambudvīpa?

rows.statement: Jambu (salt) — Plakṣa (sugarcane juice) — Śālmala (wine) — Kuśa (ghee) — Krauñca (curds) — Śāka (milk) — Puṣkara (fresh water); then the golden land and Lokāloka.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Jambu (salt) — Plakṣa (sugarcane juice) — Śālmali (wine) — Kuśa (ghee) — Krauñca (milk) — Śāka (curds) — Puṣkara (fresh water); Mānasottara divides Puṣkara; then Lokāloka. The milk and curd oceans are reversed relative to the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Jambu (salt) — Śāka (milk) — Kuśa (ghee) — Krauñca (curds) — Śālmala (wine) — Gomedaka (sugarcane juice) — Puṣkara (fresh water). No Plakṣa: a Gomedaka continent appears sixth.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

comparisons.note: Kirfel (1920) groups such variants into recensional families of the Purāṇic 'bhuvanakośa'; all agree on Jambudvīpa at the centre, Puṣkara outermost and seven oceans of different liquids.

comparisons.title: The names of the seven netherworlds (pātālas/talas)
comparisons.subject: place:patala
comparisons.question: What are the seven worlds below the earth called?

rows.statement: Atala, Vitala, Nitala, Gabhastimat, Mahākhya (Mahātala), Sutala, Pātāla.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner
sources.quote: atalaṃ vitalaṃ caiva nitalaṃ ca gabhastimat / mahākhyaṃ sutalaṃ cāgryaṃ pātālaṃ cāpi saptamam

rows.statement: Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Talātala, Mahātala, Rasātala, Pātāla; each is described with its inhabitants (Bali in Sutala, Maya in Talātala, the nāgas in Pātāla).

sources.quote: atalaṃ vitalaṃ sutalaṃ talātalaṃ mahātalaṃ rasātalaṃ pātālam

rows.statement: In the cosmic body of the Lord (virāṭ), the netherworlds are his feet, ankles and shanks: Pātāla, Rasātala, Mahātala, Talātala…

comparisons.title: Pūru to Duṣyanta in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas
comparisons.subject: lin:paurava
comparisons.question: How does each text give the Paurava line from Pūru to Duṣyanta, father of Bharata?

rows.statement: Pūru → Janamejaya → Pracinvān → Pravīra → Manasyu → Abhayada → Sudyu → Bahugava → Saṃyāti → Ahaṃyāti → Raudrāśva (ten sons, Ṛteyu and others) → Ṛteyu → Rantināra → Sumati, Apratiratha, Dhruva; Apratiratha → Kaṇva → Medhātithi (ancestor of the Kaṇvāyana brāhmaṇas); Apratiratha's other son Ailīna → Duṣyanta and three brothers; Duṣyanta → Bharata.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Pūru → Janamejaya → Pracinvān → Pravīra → Manusyu → Cārupada → Sudyu → Bahugava → Saṃyāti → Ahaṃyāti → Raudrāśva (ten sons by the apsaras Ghṛtācī) → Ṛteyu → Rantināva → Sumati, Dhruva, Apratiratha; Apratiratha → Kaṇva → Medhātithi; Sumati → Rebhi → Duṣmanta.

sources.quote: putro 'bhūt sumate rebhir duṣmantas tatsuto mataḥ

comparisons.note: The texts diverge on Manasyu's son (Abhayada / Cārupada) and on Duṣyanta's father (Ailīna son of Apratiratha / Rebhi son of Sumati). The Mahābhārata's Ādiparvan genealogies (1.89–90) differ again; individual Paurava kings between Pūru and Duṣyanta are not yet separate records in the graph.

comparisons.title: Ikṣvāku to Sagara in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas
comparisons.subject: lin:suryavamsha
comparisons.question: How does each text give the Solar line between Ikṣvāku and Sagara?

rows.statement: Ikṣvāku → Vikukṣi (Śaśāda) → Purañjaya (Kakutstha) → Anenas → Pṛthu → Viśvagaśva → Cāndra → Yuvanāśva → Śrāvasta → Bṛhadaśva → Kuvalayāśva (Dhundhumāra) → Dṛḍhāśva → Haryaśva → Nikumbha → Saṃhitāśva → Kṛśāśva → Prasenajit → Yuvanāśva → Māndhātṛ → Purukutsa → Trasadasyu → Anaraṇya → Pṛṣadaśva → Haryaśva → Vasumanas → Tridhanvan → Trayyāruṇa → Satyavrata (Triśaṅku) → Hariścandra → Rohitāśva → Harita → Cañcu → Vijaya (and brother Sudeva) → Ruruka → Vṛka → Bāhu → Sagara.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Ikṣvāku → Vikukṣi (Śaśāda) → Purañjaya (Indravāha, Kakutstha) → Anenas → Pṛthu → Viśvagandhi → Candra → Yuvanāśva → Śrāvasta → Bṛhadaśva → Kuvalayāśva (Dhundhumāra) → Dṛḍhāśva → Haryaśva → Nikumbha → Bahulāśva → Kṛśāśva → Senajit → Yuvanāśva → Māndhātṛ (also named Trasaddasyu by Indra) → Purukutsa → Trasaddasyu → Anaraṇya → Haryaśva → Aruṇa → Tribandhana → Satyavrata (Triśaṅku) → Hariścandra → Rohita → Harita → Campa → Sudeva → Vijaya → Bharuka → Vṛka → Bāhuka → Sagara.

comparisons.note: The two lists agree for some twenty generations and then diverge in names (Saṃhitāśva/Bahulāśva, Cañcu/Campa, Ruruka/Bharuka) and in length (ViP has Pṛṣadaśva and Vasumanas, BhP does not). Pargiter (1922) and Thapar (1978) read such lists as reconstructed tradition rather than chronicles.

comparisons.title: Bhagīratha to Khaṭvāṅga in the Viṣṇu and Bhāgavata Purāṇas
comparisons.subject: lin:suryavamsha
comparisons.question: How does each text give the line between Bhagīratha and Khaṭvāṅga (Dilīpa)?

rows.statement: Bhagīratha → Śruta → Nābhāga → Ambarīṣa → Sindhudvīpa → Ayutāyus → Ṛtuparṇa (Nala's friend) → Sarvakāma → Sudāsa → Saudāsa Mitrasaha (Kalmāṣapāda; queen Madayantī) → Aśmaka (by Vasiṣṭha) → Mūlaka (Nārīkavaca) → Daśaratha → Ilivila → Viśvasaha → Khaṭvāṅga (Dilīpa).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Bhagīratha → Śruta → 'another Nābha' → Sindhudvīpa → Ayutāyu → Ṛtuparṇa (Nala's friend) → Sarvakāma → Sudāsa → his son Mitrasaha (Kalmāṣāṅghri; queen named Damayantī) … Aśmaka → Mūlaka (Bālika, Nārīkavaca) → Daśaratha → Aiḍaviḍi → Viśvasaha → Khaṭvāṅga.

comparisons.title: Lists of Viṣṇu's manifestations, text by text
comparisons.subject: concept:avatara
comparisons.question: Which manifestations of Viṣṇu does each text list, in what number and order?

rows.statement: Foretells Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma Bhārgava (Tretā), Rāma Dāśarathi (Tretā–Dvāpara junction) and Kṛṣṇa at Mathurā (Dvāpara–Kali junction), and names Haṃsa and Hayaśiras as past manifestations. The constituted text has no Matsya, Kūrma or Kalki; the familiar ten-list beginning with Haṃsa is a vulgate reading.

Pauṣkara (lotus), Vārāha, Nārasiṃha, Vāmana, Dattātreya, Jāmadagnya, Rāma Dāśarathi, Kṛṣṇa (Māthura) and the future Kalki Viṣṇuyaśas (31.148); Vedavyāsa and the phrase 'ten manifestations of Vāsudeva' occur only in starred passages.

Gives no numbered list: Varāha raises the Earth 'as he took fish, tortoise and other forms in earlier kalpas' (1.4.8); Viṣṇu as tortoise (1.9.86) and in woman's form (1.9.107); the man-lion (1.20.32); Viṣṇu born fourfold as Rāma and his brothers (4.4.49); Kṛṣṇa as an aṃśa (4.24.27).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Twenty-two: the Kumāras, Varāha, Nārada, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Kapila, Dattātreya, Yajña, Ṛṣabha, Pṛthu, Matsya, Kūrma, Dhanvantari, Mohinī, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Vyāsa, Rāma, Balarāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki; avatāras are innumerable (1.3.26); these are portions, 'but Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān himself' (1.3.28).
A second catalogue (Brahmā to Nārada) of about twenty-four, adding Suyajña, Hayaśīrṣa, Hari who saves Gajendra, Haṃsa and Manu, and treating Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa together.

1.1 reproduces the Bhāgavata's twenty-two almost verbatim (Buddha 'jinasuta' for BhP's 'añjanasuta'); 1.86.10–11 gives ten: Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nṛhari, Vāmana, Rāma (Bhārgava), Rāma Dāśarathi, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki.

Because of Bhṛgu's curse Viṣṇu has three divine manifestations (a portion of Nārāyaṇa born of Dharma, Narasiṃha, Vāmana) and seven human ones: Dattātreya, Māndhātṛ, Jāmadagnya, Rāma Dāśarathi, Vedavyāsa, Buddha and Kalki — no Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha or Kṛṣṇa in this count (the fish is Janārdana at 1.28).

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

rows.statement: Narrates the avatāras in order (Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa via the Harivaṃśa, Buddha, Kalki) and calls them the 'ten' (16.12); its iconographic list (49) has Balarāma with plough and pestle in place of Kṛṣṇa.

sources.edition: Rajendralal Mitra ed. (Bibliotheca Indica 1870–79); GRETIL e-text

comparisons.note: The 'standard ten' (with Kṛṣṇa or Balarāma eighth and Buddha ninth) is a later convention; earlier and contemporaneous texts count three, six, nine, ten, twenty-two or 'innumerable'. Rows are not reconciled.

comparisons.title: Manu and the fish: the flood story from the Śatapatha to the Bhāgavata
comparisons.subject: narr:matsya-flood
comparisons.question: Who is the fish, who is saved, why, and where does the boat come to rest?

rows.statement: A small fish found in Manu's washing water asks protection and warns of a flood; Manu ties his boat to its horn and is carried to the 'northern mountain'; alone, he sacrifices and from the offering a woman (Iḍā) is born. The fish is not identified with a god.

Told by Mārkaṇḍeya: Manu Vaivasvata, performing austerities at Viśālā Badarī, saves a little fish which outgrows jar, pond, Gaṅgā and ocean; with the seven sages and all seeds he is towed to the Himālayan peak Naubandhana; the fish declares 'I am Prajāpati Brahmā' (3.185.48). The tale is called 'the purāṇa named Mātsyaka' (3.185.53).

King Manu, son of Ravi, practises yoga on the Malaya; the fish is recognised as Vāsudeva/Keśava/Janārdana (1.25–28); the flood comes at the end of the Cākṣuṣa manvantara (2.14); a serpent serves as the rope (2.18); the whole Purāṇa is the fish's teaching to Manu.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

rows.statement: The demon Hayagrīva steals the Vedas from sleeping Brahmā's mouths (8.24.8); Satyavrata, a royal sage devoted to Nārāyaṇa and lord of the Draviḍas, catches the fish in the Kṛtamālā (8.24.12–13); Viṣṇu as the fish teaches him, slays Hayagrīva and recovers the Vedas (8.24.57); Satyavrata becomes Vaivasvata Manu in this kalpa (8.24.58).
Manu Vaivasvata at the Kṛtamālā; the fish is addressed as Viṣṇu–Nārāyaṇa–Janārdana; a flood after seven days; the boat tied to the golden one-horned fish with a great serpent.

sources.edition: Rajendralal Mitra ed. (Bibliotheca Indica 1870–79); GRETIL e-text

comparisons.note: The Purāṇic identification of the fish with Viṣṇu is absent from the Śatapatha and contradicted by the Mahābhārata's Brahmā. The Śatapatha row is from Eggeling's translation (not re-checked online in this session).

comparisons.title: From Rudra to the Liṅgodbhava: portrayals of Śiva
comparisons.subject: deity:shiva
comparisons.question: How is the god Rudra–Śiva characterised and ranked in successive texts?

rows.statement: Rudra is a fierce archer-god, 'the strongest of the strong', implored to spare offspring and cattle and praised as the best of physicians; a god among many, not supreme.

Rudra is the one god who does not tolerate a second (3.2), creator and protector, who generated Hiraṇyagarbha (3.4), whose benign form is 'śivā' (3.5); he is called Śiva, all-pervading (3.11; 4.14). A theistic supreme god.

rows.locator: MBh (CE), various (e.g. Sauptika and Anuśāsana parvans)
rows.statement: Śiva is a mighty, ambivalent god: destroyer of Dakṣa's sacrifice, giver of weapons to Arjuna, praised with a thousand names; Vaiṣṇava passages subordinate him to Nārāyaṇa.

In the Liṅgodbhava Brahmā (swan) and Viṣṇu (boar) fail to find the ends of the fiery liṅga; Śiva is supreme over both. The text prescribes the image: Candraśekhara within the liṅga, swan above, boar below.
The same pillar myth with an added episode: Brahmā claims to have seen the top, citing a falling ketakī flower as witness, and is punished for the lie.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay c. 1920), books 1 and 7; GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: Śiva as the lord of a Pāśupata-coloured universe, his marriage to Pārvatī, the birth of Skanda and the subjugation of Andhaka; the text maps Śaiva holy places such as Vārāṇasī.

comparisons.note: The rows show a trajectory from a feared Vedic god to a supreme deity; no single line of development is implied.

comparisons.title: The Goddess from Umā Haimavatī to the Devī Bhāgavata
comparisons.subject: deity:devi
comparisons.question: How does each text present the Goddess?

rows.statement: A beautiful woman, Umā Haimavatī, appears to Indra and reveals that the mysterious being (yakṣa) was Brahman. She is a revealer of knowledge; her relation to Śiva is not stated.

Viṣṇu sends Nidrā to be born of Yaśodā; she will be Kauśikī, dwell eternally on the Vindhya, slay Śumbha and Niśumbha, love meat-offerings and be worshipped on the ninth day; the Āryā hymn proper stands outside the constituted text (starred/appendix).

A supreme Goddess, formed from all the gods' radiance (DM 2), slays Madhu–Kaiṭabha (through Viṣṇu), Mahiṣa and Śumbha–Niśumbha, emits Kālī/Cāmuṇḍā and the Mothers, is hymned as Nārāyaṇī and promises to return whenever demons arise.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition

rows.statement: The Goddess is the ground of all being who creates Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva; the DM battles are retold (book 5); the Devī Gītā (7.31–40) gives her Vedāntic teaching to Himālaya.

comparisons.note: Coburn's phrase 'crystallization' marks the DM as the point where earlier goddesses are understood as one Goddess.

comparisons.title: How long are the yugas? Manu, the Mahābhārata, the Purāṇas and Āryabhaṭa
comparisons.subject: concept:yuga
comparisons.question: What durations does each source give for the four yugas, and in what kind of years?

rows.statement: Kṛta 4,000 years + dawn 400 + dusk 400; Tretā 3,000 + 300 + 300; Dvāpara 2,000 + 200 + 200; Kali 1,000 + 100 + 100; the 12,000 together are 'a yuga of the gods'; a year is a day-night of the gods (1.67); a thousand such yugas are Brahmā's day; a manvantara is 71. Manu does not convert into human years.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text, text of Kullūka (Shastri 1983) with Medhātithi variants

rows.statement: Verses nearly identical to Manu 1.64–78 give the same 4,000/3,000/2,000/1,000 scheme with dawn and dusk and call the whole 'the twelve thousand known as a yuga' (12.224.28), without stating divine years.

The caturyuga is 12,000 divine years (1.3.11); 4, 3, 2, 1 thousand with sandhyās of as many hundreds (1.3.12–13). A manvantara is 852,000 divine years = 306,720,000 human years (1.3.19–21), i.e. 360 human years per divine year (equivalently 4,320,000 human years per caturyuga). ViP 4.24.33 states that Kali lasts 360,000 human years, and 4.24.34 '1,200 divine years'.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Four yugas of 12,000 divine years; 4, 3, 2, 1 thousand with twice as many hundreds for the junctions; a thousand caturyugas are Brahmā's day; a Manu rules a little over 71.

A divine year is 360 solar years (3.7); a yuga of 12,000 divine years is divided into four equal quarters (yugapāda), not 4:3:2:1; Brahmā's day is 1,008 yugas (3.8); 3,600 years of the Kali had elapsed in Āryabhaṭa's 23rd year (3.10).

comparisons.note: Traditional chronology. González-Reimann argues that the divine-year multiplier arose to reconcile the epic 12,000-year cycle with astronomical periods. The arithmetic equivalences (×360) are the editor's, stated as implied by ViP 1.3.19–21.

comparisons.title: The churning of the ocean in four tellings
comparisons.subject: narr:samudra-manthana
comparisons.question: Who supports Mount Mandara, what happens to the poison, what emerges, and how is the nectar kept from the asuras?

rows.statement: Ananta uproots Mandara; the king of tortoises Akūpāra bears it; Vāsuki is the rope; Soma, Śrī, Surā, a white horse, the Kaustubha and Dhanvantari with the nectar emerge; Nārāyaṇa as Mohinī takes the nectar; Rāhu is beheaded; Nara and Nārāyaṇa win the battle. No poison episode in the constituted text.

Set in the Kṛta age; Mandara and Vāsuki; Dhanvantari, sixty crores of apsarases, Vāruṇī (taken by Aditi's sons, hence 'suras'), Uccaiḥśravas, the Kaustubha and the nectar; a war in which the sons of Aditi destroy the sons of Diti. No tortoise and no poison in the constituted text.

Caused by Durvāsas' curse on Indra; Viṣṇu himself as tortoise bears Mandara and in other forms pulls the serpent and presses the summit; Surabhi, Vāruṇī, the Pārijāta, apsarases, the moon (taken by Maheśvara), Dhanvantari and Śrī emerge; the nāgas take the poison; Viṣṇu in a woman's form gives the nectar to the gods.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Viṣṇu as tortoise; Śiva drinks the hālāhala out of compassion (8.7.43); Lakṣmī chooses Mukunda (8.8.24); Mohinī distributes the nectar (8.9); Śiva later sees Mohinī and is infatuated (8.12).

comparisons.note: Critical-edition texts of the two epics lack episodes (Kūrma as Viṣṇu; Śiva and the poison) that the vulgate texts and the Purāṇas contain.

comparisons.title: Who are the eighteen? Purāṇa lists and verse counts
comparisons.subject: col:mahapuranas
comparisons.question: Which Purāṇa stands in the fourth (Śaiva/Vāyu) place, and what extents are given?

rows.statement: Brāhma (first), Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Bhāgavata, Nāradīya, Mārkaṇḍeya, Āgneya, Bhaviṣya, Brahmavaivarta, Laiṅga, Vārāha, Skānda, Vāmana, Kaurma, Mātsya, Gāruḍa, Brahmāṇḍa; 'mahāpurāṇa' only in starred insertion 3.6.23*8.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Same membership with Śaiva in fourth place; counts: Brāhma 10,000, Pādma 55,000, Vaiṣṇava 23,000, Śaiva 24,000, Bhāgavata 18,000, Nārada 25,000, Mārkaṇḍeya 9,000, Āgneya 15,400, Bhaviṣya 14,500, Brahmavaivarta 18,000, Laiṅga 11,000, Vārāha 24,000, Skānda 81,100, Vāmana 10,000, Kaurma 17,000, Mātsya 14,000, Sauparṇa 19,000, Brahmāṇḍa 12,000 = 400,000.

Fourth is the Vāyavīya, 'joined with Rudra's greatness', 24,000 verses; Brāhma 13,000, Āgneya 16,000, Brahmāṇḍa 12,200; describes the Bhāgavata as beginning with the Gāyatrī and including Vṛtra's slaying (53.20–21).

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

rows.statement: Keeps Śaiva fourth, then after Gāruḍa names the Vāyavīya and 'the eighteenth, called Brahmāṇḍa' (aṣṭādaśaṃ samuddiṣṭaṃ brahmāṇḍam iti saṃjñitam) — either a nineteenth title or an identification of the Vāyavīya with the Brahmāṇḍa.
Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Vāyavīya, Bhāgavata, Nāradīya, Mārkaṇḍeya, Āgneya, Bhaviṣya, Brahmavaivarta, Laiṅga …
Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Bhāgavata …; the Śaiva is fourth and 'accomplishes all aims'.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay c. 1920), books 1 and 7; GRETIL e-text

comparisons.note: The disagreement on the fourth place (Śaiva vs Vāyu) is preserved; Matsya's 24,000 for the Vāyavīya equals BhP's figure for the Śaiva.

comparisons.title: Rāma's ancestors: Raghu, Aja and the Vālmīki genealogy
comparisons.subject: lin:suryavamsha
comparisons.question: Who are the father and grandfather of Daśaratha, and where do Raghu, Nahuṣa and Yayāti stand?

rows.statement: … Dilīpa Khaṭvāṅga → Dīrghabāhu → Raghu → Aja → Daśaratha → Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, Śatrughna (Viṣṇu born fourfold). Nahuṣa and Yayāti belong to the Lunar line (4.8–10).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Khaṭvāṅga → Dīrghabāhu → Raghu ('pṛthuśravāḥ') → Aja → Daśaratha.

Ikṣvāku → Vikukṣi → Bāṇa → Anaraṇya → Pṛthu → Triśaṅku → Dhundhumāra → Yuvanāśva → Māndhātṛ → Susaṃdhi → Dhruvasaṃdhi → Bharata → Asita → Sagara → Asamañja → Aṃśumat → Dilīpa → Bhagīratha → Kakutstha → Raghu → Kalmāṣapāda → Śaṅkhaṇa → Sudarśana → Agnivarṇa → Śīghraga → Maru → Praśuśruka → Ambarīṣa → Nahuṣa → Yayāti → Nābhāga → Aja → Daśaratha.
Vaivasvata Manu has nine sons (Ikṣvāku, Nṛga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti, Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga-Diṣṭa, Karūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, Vasumān).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Vaivasvata Manu has ten sons (Ikṣvāku, Nabhaga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti, Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga, Diṣṭa, Tarūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, Vasumān).

comparisons.note: Homonymous kings (Nahuṣa, Yayāti, Nābhāga) in Vālmīki's list are kept as separate ids (char:nahusha-vr, char:yayati-vr, char:nabhaga-vr). Pargiter (1922) attempted to harmonise the lists; this table does not.

comparisons.title: How did the seats of the Goddess arise?
comparisons.subject: narr:shakti-pitha-origin
comparisons.question: Is Satī's body divided, and how many seats are there?

rows.statement: No dismemberment: at Dakṣa's sacrifice Satī names 108 tīrthas and the names she bears there (e.g. Viśālākṣī at Vārāṇasī), then burns herself and is reborn as Pārvatī.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

rows.statement: Śiva wanders with Satī's corpse; gods enter it and it falls in pieces; the yoni falls at Kāmarūpa, which becomes the pre-eminent pīṭha (Kāmākhyā).
Viṣṇu cuts the corpse and its parts fall at sacred sites; a list of 108 seats of the Goddess similar to the Matsya's follows.

comparisons.note: Sircar (1973) traces the growth of pīṭha lists from four to fifty-one and 108; the corpse-dismemberment motif appears to be later than the Matsya's naming of tīrthas.

comparisons.title: Why lamps at Dīpāvalī?
comparisons.subject: trad:dipavali
comparisons.question: What reason, if any, does each source give for the lamps and rites of Dīpāvalī?

rows.statement: The Bhaviṣyottara’s Dīpāvalī chapter prescribes a lamp “for Naraka” and tarpaṇa to Yama on the 14th, Lakṣmī’s worship and the driving out of Alakṣmī on the new moon, and on the next day the king’s proclamation “today is the sovereignty of Bali” and the worship of Bali as the future Indra. Several reasons are thus combined in one text.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, pp. 196–204 (Bhaviṣyottara ch. 140, vv. 14–29, 47–73)

rows.statement: Kṛṣṇa kills Naraka (Bhauma), king of Prāgjyotiṣa, cutting off his head with the discus, and frees the women he held captive; the Purāṇa connects the deed with no festival or lamps.
The story of Bali’s binding by Viṣṇu was recited and staged — one who does so is said to “make Bali bound” (Baliṃ bandhayati) — but no seasonal festival is named.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, p. 203 (Mahābhāṣya on Pāṇini 3.1.26)

rows.statement: A verse of the Anuśāsanaparvan says the giver of lamps “shines in heaven like a row of lamps” (dīpamāleva rājate); some writers took this as a reference to Dīvālī, which Kane thinks unclear.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, p. 207 (Anuśāsana 98.51, vulgate numbering)

rows.statement: The Critical Edition narrates Rāma’s return to Ayodhyā and his consecration; oil lamps are mentioned only among the furnishings brought in the preparations (6.116.43). No festival of lamps for the return appears in the constituted text.

rows.locator: RCM Uttarakāṇḍa, before dohā 3; after dohā 26
rows.statement: Ayodhyā adorns itself on learning of Rāma’s coming; in the description of his reign “jewel-lamps shine in every house” (gṛha gṛha prati mani dīpa birājahiṃ) — a picture of the city’s splendour, not a festival or its reason.

sources.locator: RCM Uttarakāṇḍa, caupāīs before dohā 3 and after dohā 26

comparisons.note: Kane (1958, p. 207) also records B. A. Gupte’s list of legends attached to the days of Dīvālī — the killing of Narakāsura, Bali’s loss of his empire, and the crowning of Rāma and of Vikrama — and the Jain observance of Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa is kept on the same night (Jinasena’s Harivaṃśapurāṇa of 783 CE is usually cited; not checked here). The Nīlamata Purāṇa (vv. 505–510) calls the new-moon night Sukhasuptikā. The rows show that the north Indian “return of Rāma” explanation is not found in the Rāma texts checked, while the Naraka, Lakṣmī and Bali reasons are found together in the Sanskrit festival literature. In Bengal the same new-moon night is Kālī Pūjā (Kane, p. 200).

comparisons.title: Mahābali of Onam and the Purāṇic Bali
comparisons.subject: char:bali
comparisons.question: Who is Bali (or the hero of the festival), how does he lose the earth, and what does he receive?

rows.statement: No Bali: the asuras divide the earth and agree to give the gods as much as the dwarf Viṣṇu (the sacrifice) lies upon — “vāmano ha viṣṇur āsa”; the gods thereby win the whole earth.

Bali, grandson of Prahlāda, gives Vāmana three steps; bound and humbled, he is sent to Sutala, a realm “desired even by the gods”, where Viṣṇu promises to guard him and remain always present, and he will be Indra in the Sāvarṇi manvantara.

On Balipratipadā (Kārttika śukla 1) the king and householders worship an image of Bali with his queen Vindhyāvalī as “son of Virocana … the future Indra”; the day is “the dominion of Bali”, when lamps make Lakṣmī stable.

The Ōṇam festival of Pāṇḍya Madurai is “the good day of Ōṇam that belongs to Māyōṉ of the golden garland, who overcame the crowding asuras” — the festival is Viṣṇu’s, and no returning asura king is mentioned.
Kabīr denies the story as a deed of the true Lord: “In the form of a dwarf he did not tempt Bali: that which tempts is Maya.”

sources.quote: In the form of a dwarf he did not tempt Bali: that which tempts is Maya.

comparisons.note: The Kerala Onam legend — Mahābali (Māvēli) as a just asura king of a golden age of equality, pressed down by Vāmana and allowed to visit his people once a year — is the living tradition of the festival (trad:onam; Thrikkakara Vāmanamūrti temple). None of the texts above tells of an annual homecoming; the Bhāgavata’s Sutala, where Viṣṇu guards Bali, and the Bhaviṣyottara’s one-day “dominion of Bali” at Dīpāvalī are the nearest Sanskrit parallels. Kerala tradition is not ranked against them.

comparisons.title: Kabīr’s Rām and Tulsīdās’s Rām
comparisons.subject: char:rama
comparisons.question: Is Rām the son of Daśaratha, and how is the formless (nirguṇa) related to the embodied (saguṇa)?

rows.statement: The true Rām is not the son of Daśaratha: “The three worlds know the son of Dasaratha. The secret of Rama’s name is other than this.” The Maker did not take avatāras: he “did not wed Sita: nor build a bridge of stone across the sea. This Raghunath they serve; but he who serves him is but blind.”

sources.quote: The three worlds know the son of Dasaratha. The secret of Rama’s name is other than this.

rows.statement: The avatāras themselves are Māyā and mortal: “In Mathura died Krishna the cowherd: one by one died the ten avatars.”

Śiva rebukes Pārvatī for suggesting that the Rāma of the Vedas is someone other than the prince: those who say so are deluded. “There is no difference between saguṇa and aguṇa … the formless, invisible, unborn becomes saguṇa through the love of devotees”; and “he whom the Vedas sing and sages meditate on — that same is Daśaratha’s son, lord of Kosala, for the devotees’ sake.”

sources.locator: RCM Bālakāṇḍa, dohā 114 and caupāīs after dohās 115 and 118

rows.statement: Rāma is born to Kausalyā as “half of Viṣṇu” (viṣṇor ardham), with Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna as further portions — an incarnational account in narrative form, without a doctrine of the nirguṇa.

comparisons.note: Read together, the Bījak denies precisely what the Mānas affirms. Tulsīdās’s insistence (Bāla 114–118) that the Vedic Brahman and Daśaratha’s son are one is often read by scholars as answering the nirguṇa Sants, though the Mānas names no opponent. The Bījak quotations are from Ahmad Shah’s 1917 translation; numbering differs in other editions.

comparisons.title: The Durgā Pūjā story and the Devī Māhātmya
comparisons.subject: trad:durga-puja
comparisons.question: Who first worshipped the Goddess in autumn, in what form, and why?

rows.statement: The frame story: king Suratha and the merchant Samādhi, taught by the sage Medhas, make an earthen image of the Goddess on a river sandbank and worship her with flowers, incense, fire and their own blood for three years until she appears. The Goddess herself promises that whoever hears this māhātmya at “the great annual worship performed in autumn” (śaratkāle mahāpūjā … vārṣikī) will be freed from all troubles.

Rāma, unable to defeat Rāvaṇa, invokes the Goddess out of season (akāla-bodhana) in autumn and offers 108 blue lotuses; when one is missing he prepares to offer his own lotus-like eye, and the pleased Goddess grants him victory. Bengali tradition presents this as the origin of the autumn Durgā Pūjā.

The Kālikā prescribes the great autumn festival of Durgā — whoever neglects it out of laziness or hatred has all his desires frustrated by the angry Goddess (63.18) — and lists the animals fit for sacrifice to Durgā; it is a principal Purāṇic authority for the Bengal rite. Whether it ties the autumn worship to Rāma was not checked.

sources.locator: vol. V pt. 1, pp. 156, 164 (Kālikā 63.18 and the list of sacrificial animals)

rows.statement: Before the final duel Rāma receives Brahmā’s weapon and is reminded by Mātali to use it; the Critical Edition’s constituted text contains no worship of Durgā and no Ādityahṛdaya hymn (the latter is in the vulgate).
Vidyāpati’s manual and other Bengal–Mithilā digests (Śūlapāṇi, Raghunandana) codify the domestic and congregational rite that UNESCO describes in its modern Kolkata form.

comparisons.note: The Devī Māhātmya gives the clay image and the autumn worship but not Rāma; the Bengali Rāma story gives Rāma but not Suratha. UNESCO’s description of the Kolkata festival (clay images from Gaṅgā clay, eyes painted on Mahālayā, immersion on the tenth day) matches both, without adjudicating origins.

comparisons.title: How Sītā is abducted
comparisons.subject: narr:abduction-of-sita
comparisons.question: What exactly does Rāvaṇa take, and does he touch Sītā?

rows.statement: Rāvaṇa approaches in the guise of a mendicant, reveals himself and seizes Sītā bodily — the description has him grasp her by the hair and the thighs — and carries her off through the sky in his chariot.

rows.locator: Kamba Rāmāyaṇam 3.8.74 (verse 3490), Caṭāyu uyir nītta paṭalam
rows.statement: Rāvaṇa does not touch Sītā: “the wicked one did not touch the jewelled lady, mindful of Brahmā’s word” (ayaṉ mēl urai, i.e. a curse), and with his pillar-like arms “dug up the ground a yojana below and above” and carried her off with it — the editor’s heading says, together with the leaf hut.

rows.locator: Araṇyakāṇḍa (commonly cited as sarga 7; not checked in an edition)
rows.statement: Before the golden-deer episode Rāma, knowing Rāvaṇa’s intention, tells Sītā to leave her shadow (chāyā) in the hut and to live hidden in the fire for a year; the illusory Sītā (māyā-Sītā) is the one Rāvaṇa carries off. Unlike the Kūrma Purāṇa, where Agni is the saviour, here Rāma himself devises the plan.

rows.locator: RCM Araṇyakāṇḍa, caupāīs before dohā 24 (common numbering)
rows.statement: While Lakṣmaṇa is away, Rāma tells Sītā to dwell in the fire until he has destroyed the rākṣasas; she enters the fire, leaving her own reflection (nija pratibimba), “of the same character, form and modesty.” Not even Lakṣmaṇa knows. Rāvaṇa abducts the reflection.
Rāvaṇa, a vidyādhara king, carries Sītā off to Laṅkā but does not force her; Jain tellings attribute his restraint to a vow taken before a Jain monk not to take a woman against her will.

comparisons.note: Ramanujan (1991) and the essays in Richman (1991) use divergences like these to argue for many “tellings” rather than one original with deviations. The rows are not ranked; they show how each telling protects (or does not protect) Sītā’s inviolability by different means.

comparisons.title: Who are Sītā’s parents?
comparisons.subject: char:sita
comparisons.question: How is Sītā born, and whose daughter (or sister) is she?

rows.statement: Janaka of Mithilā finds her in a furrow while ploughing the sacrificial ground; she is not born of a womb (ayonijā) and he raises her as his daughter.

She is the daughter of King Dasaratha of Bārāṇasī and his chief queen, sister of Rāma-paṇḍita and Lakkhaṇa; on their return from the Himalaya she is made queen consort. In the closing identification she is the mother of Rāhula in the Buddha’s last life.
She is the daughter of Janaka and Videhā, born as a twin with Bhāmaṇḍala, who is carried off at birth and raised among the vidyādharas.
She is born to Rāvaṇa’s queen Mandodarī; because she is foretold to cause Rāvaṇa’s ruin she is abandoned in a casket and found in Janaka’s realm, where she is raised.

rows.locator: sarga 8 (as summarised from Grierson’s and later accounts)
rows.statement: Rāvaṇa’s boon includes the condition that he will perish if he approaches his own daughter; his misdeeds lead to Sītā’s birth from his wife Mandodarī, and the sarga ends with Janaka finding her in a field being prepared for a sacrifice.
Nang Sida is born as Thotsakan’s daughter; because of an ill omen she is set adrift and is found and raised by King Chanok (Janaka). She is an incarnation of Laksami.
Nang Sida is the daughter of Thôtsakane (Rāvaṇa) and Nang Chanta, an incarnation of Nang Souxada — Indra’s wife, defiled by Hapmanasouane (Rāvaṇa), who vowed to take revenge in her next life as Sida.
Siti Dewi is presented in the summaries consulted as the adoptive daughter of Maharisi Kali; the details of her birth in the Laud-based text were not checked.

comparisons.note: Two clusters stand out: tellings in which Sītā is found in the earth (Vālmīki and many Hindu tellings) and tellings in which she is Rāvaṇa’s own daughter (Guṇabhadra’s Jain line, the Adbhuta, Thai and Lao tellings), with the Buddhist jātaka making her Rāma’s sister. The table does not decide which is earlier.

comparisons.title: Hanumān’s character
comparisons.subject: char:hanuman
comparisons.question: Who is Hanumān — what kind of being, what kind of devotee, and does he marry?

rows.locator: VR (CE) 4.65.8–28 (Jāmbavān’s account of his birth); Kiṣkindhā- and Sundarakāṇḍas
rows.statement: A vānara: Jāmbavān tells how the Wind god (Māruta) embraced Añjanā, wife of the monkey Kesarin, so that Hanumān is “Kesarin’s son by the field, Māruta’s own son” (kṣetraja / aurasa) and his equal in leaping; minister of Sugrīva, eloquent and learned, he leaps the ocean to find Sītā. No wife is mentioned.

rows.locator: RCM Sundarakāṇḍa passim; Uttarakāṇḍa before dohā 120(ka) for “rāma te adhika rāma kara dāsā”
rows.statement: The paradigmatic servant-devotee (dāsa) of Rāma. The Mānas also states in Kākabhuśuṇḍi’s discourse that “Rāma’s servant is greater than Rāma” — a general claim about devotees that later Hanumān devotion applied to him.

A vidyādhara prince — son of Pavanañjaya and Añjanā — not an animal; the monkey is his clan’s banner emblem. He marries (several wives in the Jain tradition) and at the end renounces the world as a Jain monk.

A brilliant white monkey warrior with a frankly amorous nature: he falls in love with the mermaid Suvannamaccha (Thotsakan’s daughter), fathering Macchanu, and in one episode takes Thotsakan’s form to sleep with his queen.

The Hanuman–Sovann Maccha romance during the building of the causeway, in which the mermaid princess steals the stones, falls in love with Hanuman and bears his son Macchanu, is one of the most loved episodes of Khmer performance; the standard written Reamker instead has Rāma compel the ocean god to cooperate.

comparisons.note: Lutgendorf (2007) traces how a vānara minister became, in North India, a celibate god and the archetypal devotee, while Jain and Southeast Asian tellings made him a married or amorous hero. None of these is treated here as the “real” Hanumān.

comparisons.title: Rāvaṇa’s portrayal
comparisons.subject: char:ravana
comparisons.question: What kind of being is Rāvaṇa, how is he judged, and who kills him?

rows.statement: A ten-headed rākṣasa king of Laṅkā, son of the sage Viśravas, mighty through ascetic boons, learned yet given to lust and arrogance; he abducts Sītā and is killed by Rāma.

rows.locator: Rāvaṇa episodes and final battle (uddesas not checked)
rows.statement: Rāvaṇa is a vidyādhara king of the rākṣasa lineage and the eighth Prativāsudeva of Jain universal history; he is killed by Lakṣmaṇa (the Vāsudeva), not by Rāma, goes to hell for his violence, and will become a Tīrthaṅkara in the next ascending half-cycle. (Jain tradition also explains “ten-faced” by the reflection of his face in a necklace of nine gems — not checked here.)

A figure of tragic grandeur who, mindful of Brahmā’s word, does not touch Sītā (3.8.74); Rāma kills him with Brahmā’s weapon (6.36.191–196), and his queen Maṇṭōtari, lamenting that she had known Rāma to be Nārāyaṇa, dies embracing his body (6.36.243–244). Readers have long seen Kampaṉ’s Rāvaṇa as a tragic hero rather than a mere villain.

Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas of Laṅkā, ascends his Puṣpaka chariot, approaches the Buddha, circumambulates him, plays the vīṇā and sings verses (“I am Rāvaṇa, the ten-necked lord of the rākṣasas, come here”), and invites him to Laṅkā to teach; no abduction is narrated.
Thotsakan, the ten-faced king of Laṅkā, is Sida’s father; he keeps his heart outside his body, and dies when Hanuman crushes it as Phra Ram’s arrows strike.

Hapmanasouane (Thôtsakane) is Phra Lam’s cousin; as Phra Lam is linked with a previous life of the Buddha, Hapmanasouane is compared with the Buddha’s cousin Devadatta (Phra Thevathat) or with Māra (Phra Man) — learned and powerful, but ruined by greed and desire.

comparisons.title: Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā
comparisons.subject: char:radha
comparisons.question: Is Rādhā named, and what is her relation to Kṛṣṇa?

rows.statement: No gopī is named Rādhā. When Kṛṣṇa vanishes with one favoured gopī, the others say “surely the Lord Hari was worshipped (ārādhitaḥ) by her” (anayārādhito nūnam); later commentators read the verb as a veiled reference to Rādhā.

rows.locator: one verse (often cited as 1.89, Weber — unverified)
rows.statement: A single Prakrit verse speaks of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā (Rāhiā) as lovers — the earliest known literary mention, in an anthology whose date is disputed (before 640 CE).

The cowherd women dance the kuravai that Māyavaṉ danced with his elder brother and with Piññai (piññaiyōṭu āṭiya kuravai) in the cowherds’ settlement — a Tamil beloved of Kṛṣṇa who is not named Rādhā.
Āṇṭāḷ’s girls wake Nappiṉṉai, “daughter-in-law of Nandagopa”, on whose breast Kṛṣṇa lies, and call her “Nappiṉṉai, lady, Tiru (Śrī)!” to intercede for them; Rādhā does not appear.
Rādhā is the heroine: the poem follows her longing, jealousy, the messages of her friend and her reunion with Kṛṣṇa, who is her lover, not her husband.

rows.locator: Brahma-khaṇḍa, Prakṛti-khaṇḍa and Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa (chapters not checked)
rows.statement: Rādhā is the main goddess, inseparable from Kṛṣṇa and dwelling with him in Goloka, the personification of mūlaprakṛti; in the Prakṛti-khaṇḍa she heads the five forms of Prakṛti (Rādhā, Durgā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī), and “every insult to a woman is an offence against Rādhā”. (Popular summaries add that Brahmā performs her marriage to Kṛṣṇa — not checked here.)

Rādhā is Kṛṣṇa’s hlādinī-śakti (power of bliss); Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, one in identity, separated eternally and are reunited in Caitanya, who is Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā’s sentiment and complexion, come to taste her love.
Śaṅkaradeva’s Ekaśaraṇa devotion centres on Kṛṣṇa alone; Rādhā is not worshipped alongside him in this tradition.

comparisons.note: The table shows Rādhā absent (Bhāgavata), marginal (Gāhā Sattasaī), central as beloved (Gītagovinda), supreme goddess (Brahmavaivarta) and theological principle (Caitanya Caritāmṛta), alongside Tamil tellings with a different beloved (Piññai / Nappiṉṉai) and an Assamese tradition that deliberately leaves her out.

comparisons.title: Who kills Rāvaṇa?
comparisons.subject: narr:lanka-war
comparisons.question: Who defeats the king of Laṅkā (or his double), and how?

rows.statement: Reminded by Mātali to use Brahmā’s weapon, Rāma fires the Brahmā-made arrow first given him by Agastya; it pierces Rāvaṇa’s heart and he falls from his chariot “like Vṛtra struck by the thunderbolt”.
Rāma kills Rāvaṇa; the poem makes the battle a display of Rāma’s divine līlā.
Rāma fits Brahmā’s weapon to his bow and releases it; it enters Rāvaṇa’s breast and drinks his life. Maṇṭōtari then dies embracing the body (6.36.244).
Lakṣmaṇa kills Rāvaṇa, as in all Jain universal history the Vāsudeva kills the Prativāsudeva; Rāma, a non-violent Baladeva, later becomes a monk and attains liberation.

After the ten-headed Rāvaṇa is dead, his elder brother, the thousand-headed Sahasra-Rāvaṇa of Puṣkara, scatters Rāma’s army and strikes Rāma unconscious; Sītā takes the form of Mahākālī and severs his thousand heads.
Śāraḷā Dāsa narrates a further war against a thousand-headed Rāvaṇa of Vilaṅkā; who strikes the final blow was not checked.
Phra Ram’s arrows cannot kill Thotsakan until Hanuman obtains and crushes the heart that Thotsakan has kept outside his body.
There is no Rāvaṇa and no war: the story ends with the return from exile and Rāma-paṇḍita’s long reign.

comparisons.title: Murukaṉ and Skanda across texts
comparisons.subject: deity:murugan
comparisons.question: How is the Tamil god Murukaṉ presented, and when does he carry Skanda’s attributes?

rows.statement: Cēyōṉ, “the red one,” presides over the hill (kuṟiñci) landscape, one of four deities assigned to landscapes; no mythology is given. The commentator Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar glosses him as “red Murukaṉ.”

Eight of the surviving poems are to Cevvēḷ (Murukaṉ) — beside six to Tirumāl and others to the river Vaiyai — praising him at Tirupparaṅkuṉṟam (“cool Paraṅkuṉṟu”, likened to the Himalaya) near Madurai; poem 5 narrates his birth from Śiva’s seed, the northern myth.

rows.locator: Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai, c. ll. 91–102 (the six faces) and the description of the twelve hands
rows.statement: A guide-poem leading the devotee to Murukaṉ’s shrines: each of his six faces has its own function (one radiates light, one grants boons, one guards the brāhmaṇs’ sacrifices …), he has twelve hands, and he is the “lord of six (faces) borne by six (mothers)” — Skanda’s Kṛttikā iconography in a Tamil poem.

The hill women dance the kuravai praising the vēl of the god who never leaves Centil, Ceṅkōṭu, Veṇkuṉṟu and Ērakam, the white-bladed spear that once slew Cūr in the sea; he has six faces and twelve hands and was nursed by six mothers in the Saravaṇa pool; the Vēlaṉ priest is called for the possession-dance (veṟiyāṭal).
A full Tamil Skanda Purāṇa: birth from Śiva’s fiery seed, the war against Cūrapatmaṉ, and marriages to Teyvāṉai (Indra’s daughter) and the Tamil hunter girl Vaḷḷi.

Skanda is born of Agni’s seed, gathered by Svāhā in the forms of the ṛṣis’ wives (a star passage adds birth from Rudra in the Gaṅgā and among the Kṛttikās); the spilled (skanna) seed gives his name, the Mothers attend him, Indra consecrates him general (senāpati) of the gods, and the Kṛttikās go to heaven — there is no Tamil Vaḷḷi.

comparisons.note: Read in sequence these rows support the scholarly account of convergence (Zvelebil 1973; Clothey 1978): a Tamil hill god acquires Skanda’s myth and iconography by the late Caṅkam period. The identification is recorded as IDENTIFIED_WITH, not as a merger.

comparisons.title: What is the self? Six darśanas and three Vedāntas
comparisons.subject: concept:atman
comparisons.question: What is the self (ātman / puruṣa / jīva), how many selves are there, and is consciousness its essence?

rows.statement: The self (puruṣa) exists because aggregates serve another, someone must experience and oversee, and activity aims at isolation; selves are many, since birth, death and faculties are allotted to each separately; the self is a witness, isolated, indifferent, a seer and not an agent.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)

rows.statement: The self is the seer, pure seeing only; though pure it beholds the mind’s contents; in the stilled mind the seer abides in its own nature.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtras extracted by P. A. Maas from Āgāśe’s edition (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47, 1904))

rows.statement: The self is known by its marks — desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition — so cognition is a quality the self has, not its nature.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text (not proof-read); numbering of that file)

rows.statement: Breath, blinking, life, mental motion, sense-modification, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion and effort are marks of the self; selves are many because their situations differ.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Nozawa Masanobu; numbering of that file)

rows.statement: Against those who deny a self, Śabara argues that “we apprehend the self through desire”, since one desires only what one has experienced before — the self is a lasting experiencer who reaps the fruits of ritual acts.
The individual self is in reality identical with brahman, pure consciousness; its apparent individuality and agency arise from superimposition and ignorance.
Selves are real, eternal and many; together with matter they are the body of brahman, which “has everything as its body” — distinct as a body from its soul, yet inseparable.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Sadanori Ishitobi; section numbers RVas_n)

rows.statement: The difference of selves from God and from one another is real and eternal; selves are dependent on Viṣṇu, who alone is independent.
Selves belong to the Lord’s marginal (taṭasthā) energy, one with and different from him in an inconceivable way.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (GRETIL e-text interleaving Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa’s ṭīkā (marked “bd:”))

comparisons.note: Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā all hold that selves are many and eternal but disagree on whether consciousness is the self’s essence (Sāṅkhya–Yoga) or a quality it acquires (Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika). The three Vedāntas then disagree on the self’s relation to brahman: identity, body–soul inseparability, or eternal difference. The rows are not harmonised.

comparisons.title: How is brahman related to the world?
comparisons.subject: concept:brahman
comparisons.question: Is the world real, and how does it relate to brahman?

rows.statement: Brahman is that from which the origin, maintenance and dissolution of this world proceed; the effect is non-different from the cause, “as shown by the word ārambhaṇa and others”; creation is mere play, as in the world.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtra text extracted from Śaṅkara’s commentary (555 sūtras); Śaṅkara’s numbering)

rows.statement: Duality is mere māyā; non-duality is the highest truth; nothing is ever originated — “no self is born”.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input P. Schreiner, based on V. G. Apte’s edition)
sources.quote: na kaścij jāyate jīvaḥ saṃbhavo 'sya na vidyate

rows.statement: Śaṅkara reads “non-different” as: the effect has no reality apart from the cause; the manifold world is a product of name and form projected by ignorance, real only from the empirical standpoint.
Brahman really transforms into the world (pariṇāma); difference and non-difference are both real, the difference of selves being due to limiting adjuncts.
The world is real and is brahman’s body; Rāmānuja rejects the Advaita view that brahman itself is ignorant and wanders in saṃsāra, and judges bhedābheda even worse.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Sadanori Ishitobi; section numbers RVas_n)

rows.statement: The world is real (“satyaṃ ca jagad īdṛśam”); the stream of the world, endowed with five differences, is real, and the five differences are eternal.
The world and selves are naturally (svābhāvika) both different and non-different from brahman, as effects from a cause and parts from a whole.
Brahman becomes the world without itself changing (avikṛta-pariṇāma); the world is real and “pure”, untouched by māyā.

The world is the real product of the Lord’s external (bahiraṅgā) energy; energies are one with and different from their possessor in a way that is inconceivable — “inconceivability is the making-possible of the impossible”.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (GRETIL e-text interleaving Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa’s ṭīkā (marked “bd:”))

comparisons.note: All schools comment on the same sūtras (BS 1.1.2; 2.1.14) yet disagree on whether the world is an appearance (Gauḍapāda, Śaṅkara), a real transformation (Bhāskara, Vallabha), the body of brahman (Rāmānuja), or a real, dependent and different reality (Madhva).

comparisons.title: Why is the Veda authoritative — or is it?
comparisons.subject: col:vedic-samhitas
comparisons.question: On what ground, if any, is the Veda a valid means of knowledge?

rows.statement: Dharma is known by Vedic injunction; the word–meaning relation is original, so the Veda is an independent authority needing nothing else; names like Kāṭhaka mark expounders, not authors.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (based on B. D. Basu’s edition, Allahabad 1923–25)
GRETIL e-text (based on B. D. Basu’s edition, Allahabad 1923–25)

rows.statement: Perception grasps only what is present; inference, comparison and postulation are based on perception and so cannot reveal dharma either — only the Veda can.
The Veda is valid like spells and medicine, “because of the validity of the reliable speaker” (āpta) — authority derives from a trustworthy author.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text (not proof-read); numbering of that file)

rows.statement: The authority of the Veda follows from its being “his” word; the composition of sentences in the Veda presupposes intelligence.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Nozawa Masanobu; numbering of that file)

rows.statement: Vedic ritual means are “like the visible means” — impure, marked by decay and excess; reliable testimony is a means of knowledge for what is beyond perception and inference.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)
sources.quote: dṛṣṭavad ānuśravikaḥ sa hy a-viśuddhi kṣayā'tiśaya-yuktaḥ

rows.statement: Testimony (āgama) is one of three means of valid knowledge, with perception and inference.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtras extracted by P. A. Maas from Āgāśe’s edition (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47, 1904))

rows.statement: Brahman is the source of the Ṛgveda and other scriptures, which only an omniscient being could produce; and brahman is known only through scripture.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text of the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (begins at sūtra 1.1.1; the adhyāsa preamble is not in this file))

rows.statement: Lokāyata is counted with Sāṅkhya and Yoga as a form of investigative reasoning; later doxographies present the Cārvākas as rejecting Vedic authority altogether.

comparisons.note: Mīmāṃsā makes the Veda authoritative because it has no author; Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika because it has a reliable (for later Nyāya, divine) author; Advaita because brahman is both its source and its sole object. Sāṅkhya accepts testimony but devalues Vedic ritual. Not harmonised.

comparisons.title: What is liberation, and how is it reached?
comparisons.subject: concept:moksha
comparisons.question: What is the highest goal according to each school, and what brings it about?

rows.statement: No self is bound or released; prakṛti is. From practice of the principles arises the complete knowledge “I am not, nothing is mine, there is no I”; the knower lives on like a spinning potter’s wheel, and at death attains final, absolute isolation (kaivalya).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)
sources.quote: nā 'smi na me nā 'ham ity a-pariśeṣam

rows.statement: Unwavering discriminative insight is the means of release; kaivalya is the return of the guṇas, their purpose fulfilled, or the power of consciousness established in its own nature.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtras extracted by P. A. Maas from Āgāśe’s edition (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47, 1904))

rows.statement: Release (apavarga) follows the successive removal of false knowledge, faults, activity, birth and suffering; it is absolute freedom from suffering.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text (not proof-read); numbering of that file)

rows.statement: Dharma brings prosperity and the highest good; mokṣa is the absence of conjunction (of self and body) and of further birth once the unseen force is spent.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input Nozawa Masanobu; numbering of that file)

rows.statement: The inquiry concerns dharma, the purpose known by injunction; the Sūtra’s concern is the fruit of rites (e.g. heaven), and liberation became a Mīmāṃsā theme only with later authors such as Kumārila.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (based on B. D. Basu’s edition, Allahabad 1923–25)

rows.statement: Knowledge of brahman, whose fruit is the highest good, depends on no further act; ritual results are impermanent (CU 8.1.6 quoted); the qualified seeker needs discrimination, detachment, calm and desire for release.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text of the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (begins at sūtra 1.1.1; the adhyāsa preamble is not in this file))

rows.statement: Liberation is attained by meditative devotion (bhakti) grounded in knowledge and by the Lord’s grace; the released self enjoys brahman’s bliss in its own distinct form.
Viṣṇu is the object of the inquiry; one is released only through his grace (prasāda), which follows the knowledge arising from inquiry.
Liberation comes from knowing the five differences, Viṣṇu’s faultlessness and the excellence of his qualities — “and not otherwise”.

sources.quote: pañcabhedāṃ śca vijñāya viṣṇoḥ svābhedameva ca

rows.statement: The highest goal is loving devotion (prema) to Kṛṣṇa, savoured as a rasa, which the Gauḍīyas place above liberation itself.

comparisons.note: The schools differ on whether liberation is isolation of consciousness (Sāṅkhya–Yoga), cessation of suffering (Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika), realised identity (Advaita), or loving communion by grace (theistic Vedānta). Not harmonised.

comparisons.title: How Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja and Madhva read Brahma Sūtra 1.1.1–4
comparisons.subject: psg:bs-1-1-1-4
comparisons.question: What do “then, therefore” (1.1.1) and “because scripture is its source” (1.1.3) mean, and what is the brahman being inquired into?

rows.statement: athāto brahmajijñāsā — janmādyasya yataḥ — śāstrayonitvāt — tat tu samanvayāt (the bare sūtras, open to all readings).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtra text extracted from Śaṅkara’s commentary (555 sūtras); Śaṅkara’s numbering)

rows.statement: “Then” means after the fourfold qualification, not after the study of ritual: inquiry into brahman is possible even before inquiry into dharma. 1.1.3 has two senses: brahman is the source of the Veda, and brahman is known only through the Veda.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text of the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (begins at sūtra 1.1.1; the adhyāsa preamble is not in this file))
GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text of the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (begins at sūtra 1.1.1; the adhyāsa preamble is not in this file))

rows.statement: “Then” means after acquiring knowledge of works (the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā): the two Mīmāṃsās form one śāstra. Brahman is the highest Person, free from all imperfection, with infinite auspicious qualities; the long “great discussion” on this sūtra refutes Advaita’s attributeless brahman and its doctrine of ignorance.

The Sūtra was composed by Hari as Vyāsa at the request of Brahmā, Śiva and others; brahman is Nārāyaṇa, “whose sole body is the fullness of qualities”, the meaning of Om and of all the Veda; the inquiry leads to release through his grace.

comparisons.note: Śaṅkara detaches Vedānta from prior ritual study; Rāmānuja binds Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā into one discipline; Madhva makes the Sūtra Viṣṇu’s own revelation. The Śrībhāṣya row relies on Thibaut’s translation because the GRETIL Śrībhāṣya file could not be retrieved.

comparisons.title: How many means of valid knowledge?
comparisons.subject: concept:pramana
comparisons.question: Which pramāṇas does each school accept?

rows.statement: Three: perception, inference and reliable testimony, since all other means are included in these.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (input F. Ruzsa 1998, collating Solomon, Takakusu, Wilson and others)

rows.statement: Three: perception, inference and testimony (āgama).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (sūtras extracted by P. A. Maas from Āgāśe’s edition (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47, 1904))

rows.statement: Four: perception, inference, comparison (upamāna) and verbal testimony.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (Sansknet e-text (not proof-read); numbering of that file)

rows.statement: Vaiśeṣika recognises two, perception and inference, treating testimony and comparison as forms of inference.
Śabara names perception, inference, comparison, postulation (arthāpatti) and verbal testimony, and treats absence (abhāva) as well.
Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā accepts five, rejecting non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) as a separate means.
Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā accepts six: perception, inference, testimony, comparison, postulation and non-apprehension; Advaita later adopts the same six.
The Lokāyata, here a branch of ānvīkṣikī, is known from later sources as accepting perception alone.

comparisons.title: When does a son acquire ownership of family property?
comparisons.subject: concept:daya
comparisons.question: Do heirs own ancestral property from birth, or only on the owner’s death?

rows.statement: After the death of father and mother the brothers, coming together, should divide the paternal estate equally, “for they have no power over it while the two are alive”.

sources.quote: bhajeran paitṛkaṃ riktham anīśās te hi jīvatoḥ

rows.statement: In land acquired by the grandfather, a corporate holding or movables, the ownership of father and son is equal.
